text:
INDIA: LOCATION, SIZE, AND NEIGHBOURS

  • LOCATION & EXTENT

    • HEMISPHERIC POSITION
      • Lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere.
      • Longitudinally, it lies in the Eastern Hemisphere.
    • LATITUDINAL EXTENT (MAINLAND)
      • 8°4' N to 37°6' N.
      • This large extent leads to large variations in climate and vegetation.
    • LONGITUDINAL EXTENT
      • 68°7' E to 97°25' E.
      • Causes a time difference of nearly 2 hours between the easternmost and westernmost points.
    • SOUTHERNMOST POINTS
      • Indira Point (in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands) is the southernmost point of the Indian Union (6°45' N).
      • Kanyakumari is the southernmost point of the Indian mainland.
    • TROPIC OF CANCER (23°30' N)
      • Divides India into almost two equal halves.
      • Passes through 8 states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, and Mizoram.

  • SIZE & BOUNDARIES

    • AREA & WORLD RANK
      • Total Area: 3.28 million sq. km.
      • Accounts for about 2.4% of the total geographical area of the world.
      • India is the 7th largest country in the world.
    • LAND & COASTAL BOUNDARIES
      • Land Boundary: Approx. 15,200 km.
      • Total Coastline: Approx. 7,516.6 km (including Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep Islands).
      • Mainland Coastline: 6,100 km.
    • MARITIME ZONES (UNCLOS)
      • Territorial Sea: Up to 12 nautical miles (nm) from the baseline. Full sovereignty like land territory.
      • Contiguous Zone: Up to 24 nm from the baseline. Rights related to customs, fiscal, immigration, and sanitation laws.
      • Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ): Up to 200 nm from the baseline. Sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving living/non-living resources.
    • NORTH-SOUTH & EAST-WEST EXTENT
      • North-south distance: 3,214 km.
      • East-West distance: 2,933 km.

  • NEIGHBOURS & STRATEGIC LOCATION

    • LAND NEIGHBOURS & BORDERING STATES
      • Pakistan: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh.
      • Afghanistan: Ladakh.
      • China: Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh.
      • Nepal: Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Sikkim.
      • Bhutan: Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh.
      • Bangladesh: West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.
      • Myanmar: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram.
    • SEA NEIGHBOURS
      • Sri Lanka: Separated from India by the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar.
      • Maldives: Situated to the south of the Lakshadweep Islands.
    • STRATEGIC LOCATION
      • India is located in the south-central part of Asia, at the head of the Indian Ocean.
      • The trans-Indian Ocean routes provide strategic control connecting Europe with East Asian countries.
      • Its long coastline has helped establish close contact with West Asia, Africa, and Europe.

  • STANDARD MERIDIAN & TIME

    • STANDARD MERIDIAN OF INDIA
      • The longitude 82°30' E is taken as the Standard Meridian.
      • It passes through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.
      • States it passes through: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh.
    • INDIAN STANDARD TIME (IST)
      • The local time at this meridian is taken as the standard time for the whole country.
      • This avoids confusion due to the 2-hour time lag between Gujarat and Arunachal Pradesh.
      • IST is 5 hours and 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

details.summary: Comprehensive notes on India's geographical location, extent, size, boundaries, neighboring countries (land and sea), strategic importance, and the concept of Indian Standard Time (IST) including the Standard Meridian of India.

subject: General Science
text:
Endoplasmic reticulum:

  • It forms most of the volume of the protoplasm.
  • It was discovered independently by Porter (1945) and Thompson (1945).
  • It is 3-dimensional interconnected system membranes that run along the cytoplasm from the plasma membrane to outer nuclear membrane.
  • They can be classified as,
    • Rough or granular endoplasmic reticulum – They are rough due to the presence of Ribosomes. Their main function is protein synthesis.
    • Smooth or a granular endoplasmic reticulum – They are smooth due to the absence of Ribosomes. They are involved in synthesis of lipids and steroid hormones.

subject: General Science
text:
Golgi apparatus:

  • Also known as the Golgi complex or Golgi bodies.
  • It is a sac-like flattened structure.
  • It is a packing organelle like the endoplasmic reticulum. It absorbs simple molecules and combines them into complex molecules.

subject: General Science
text:
Ribosomes:

  • Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis present inside the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The synthesized protein is transported by endoplasmic reticulum. They also occur in chloroplasts and mitochondria.
  • These are non-membranous and are formed of RNA molecules.
  • Based on molecular weight they are classified into,
    • 80 S – found in prokaryotes
    • 70 S – found in Eukaryotes

subject: General Science
text:
Lysosomes:

  • These are vacuole like bodies that secrete enzymes to digest food substances.
  • They are centers for cellular digestion.
  • Sometimes, they can even digest cellular organelles, resulting in the death of the cell.

subject: General Science
text:
Centrioles:

  • It is a microtubular structure; centrioles are concerned with cell division.
  • It initiates cell division.
  • A pair of centrioles forms centrosomes.

subject: General Science
text:
Mitochondria:

  • Also known as the powerhouse of the cells.
  • Mitochondria are a double membranous structure varies in diameter between 0.5 and 1.0 µm and 7 µm long.
  • Mitochondria are the sites of cellular respiration. They release energy in the form of ATP (Adenosine triphosphate); in mitochondria.

subject: General Science
text:
Plastids:

  • These are distinguishing features of plant cells and are present only in them.
  • They are of three types-
    • Chloroplasts – They contain chlorophyll. They synthesize sugar from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight.

Exam Trend Analysis: Around 12-15 questions are asked from the History section. Key high-yield topics include:

  • Ancient India: Harappan civilization, Rig Vedic age, Mauryan age, Six Indian philosophies, Gupta age, and Ancient literature.
  • Medieval India: Delhi Sultanate, Mughal empire, Foreign travellers, Maratha empire, Vijayanagar empire, Art, Architecture, and Literature.
  • Modern India: Indian National Movement.
  • World History: American War of Independence, Russian Revolution, French Revolution, World War I and II.

The Pre-History or Stone Age

The age when pre-historic man began to use stones for utilitarian purposes is termed the Stone Age. It is divided into four categories:

  1. The Paleolithic Age (Old Stone Age)
  2. The Mesolithic Age (Middle Stone Age)
  3. The Neolithic Age (New Stone Age)
  4. The Chalcolithic Age

1. The Paleolithic Age

  • Geological Period & Human Race: Developed in the Pleistocene period (Ice Age). Paleolithic men belonged to the Negrito race. Homo Sapiens first appeared in the last phase of this age.
  • Lifestyle & Tools: They were hunters and food gatherers. They had no knowledge of agriculture, fire, or pottery. They used tools of unpolished, undressed rough stones and lived in cave rock shelters.
  • Quartzite Men: Due to their reliance on quartzite stone for making tools, they are also referred to as Quartzite men.
  • Important Archaeological Site: Uttar Bahini in the Jammu area has revealed early paleolithic artifacts in the upper Shiwaliks.
  • Phases: Based on the nature of stone tools and climatic changes, this age is divided into three phases: Early or Lower Paleolithic, Middle Paleolithic, and Upper Paleolithic.

details.summary: Introduction to the Stone Age classification and detailed characteristics of the Paleolithic Age, including geological era, human race, lifestyle, tools, and key Indian sites.

mcq.question:
Which of the following statements regarding the Paleolithic Age in India is/are correct?
1. The Paleolithic culture developed during the Pleistocene period.
2. Paleolithic humans belonged to the Negrito race.
3. They possessed advanced knowledge of agriculture and pottery.
mcq.explanation: Paleolithic humans were hunters and food gatherers who had no knowledge of agriculture, fire, or pottery. They belonged to the Negrito race and lived during the Pleistocene period (Ice Age).

6. Coprime numbers Two natural numbers x and y are said to be coprime, if they do not have any common divisor other than 1.

  • e.g., (9, 2), (5, 6), (11, 15) are the pairs of coprime numbers.
  • If x and y are any two coprimes, a number p is divisible by x as well as by y, then the number is also divisible by xy.
  • Coprime are also called as relatively prime numbers.
  • Twin primes Twin primes are pair of primes which differ by 2. e.g., (3, 5), (7, 9), (11, 13) etc.

text:
INTEGERS

The collection of positive numbers, negative numbers and zero are called integers. The set of integers is denoted by Z or I.

Thus, Z or I = {..., –4, –3, –2, –1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...} is the set of integers. Every natural number and whole number is a part of integer. So, N ⊂ W ⊂ I.

details.summary: Definition of integers, their notation, and relationship with natural and whole numbers.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Types of Integers

Integers are of three types

(i) Positive Integers It is a set of all positive numbers. It is denoted by I+, I+ = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...}

(ii) Negative Integers It is a set of all negative numbers. It is denoted by I–, I– = {..., –3, –2 –1}

(iii) Non-negative Integers An integer that is either 0 or positive is called non-negative integer. {0, 1, 2, 3, ...}

Note '0' is neither positive nor negative.

details.summary: Classification of integers into positive, negative, and non-negative, with definitions and examples.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The set of rational numbers is represented by 'Q'.

  • e.g., 3/5, -3/7, -6 are rational numbers.
  • The decimal expansion of every rational number is either terminating or non-terminating repeating.
  • e.g., 1/5 = 0.2, 1/3 = 0.333..., 8/44 = 0.181818... etc.
  • The recurring decimal have been given a short notation as 0.3333 = 0.3̅, 0.181818 = 0.1̅8̅

Note

  • Zero is a rational number, since we can write 0 = 0/1.
  • Every natural number, whole number and integer is a rational number.

details.summary: Definition and properties of rational numbers, including decimal expansions and special notes.

subject: Mathematics
text:
IRRATIONAL NUMBERS

The number which cannot be expressed in the form p/q, where p and q both are integers and q ≠ 0 are known as irrational numbers. The irrational numbers when expressed in decimal form are in non-terminating and non-repeating form. e.g., √2, √5, √7, 0.101005001, etc.

  • Here, it is notable that exact value of π is not 22/7 or 3.14, as 22/7 is a rational number while π is irrational.

details.summary: Definition and examples of irrational numbers, including their decimal form and a note on pi.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Properties of Rational and Irrational Numbers
text:
IMPORTANT FACTS

  1. If a + √b = x + √y, where a and x are rational and √b and √y are irrational, then a = x and b = y.
  2. The sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is irrational number.
  3. The product of rational and irrational number is also an irrational number.
  4. If we add, subtract, multiply or divide two irrational numbers, we may get an irrational number or rational number.

details.summary: Key properties and rules regarding operations with rational and irrational numbers.

subject: English
text:
Understanding the difference between Weave, Wave, and Waive:

  • Weave: To interlace threads to make fabric, or metaphorically, to compose/connect elements (e.g., "to weave stories").
  • Wave: A disturbance traveling through a medium (like ocean waves) or a hand gesture.
  • Waive: To voluntarily surrender, relinquish, or refrain from insisting on a right or claim (e.g., "to waive his rights").

details.summary: Distinction between Weave (interlace/compose), Wave (water ridge/gesture), and Waive (relinquish rights).

mcq.question: Choose the correct word: The company decided to ______ the late fee for the customer.
mcq.explanation: 'Waive' means to refrain from insisting on or enforcing a rule or fee.

subject: English
text:
Understanding the difference between Peak, Peek, and Pique:

  • Peak: The pointed top of a mountain, or the point of highest activity/value (e.g., "peak traffic hours").
  • Peek: To look quickly or furtively, especially through a narrow opening (e.g., "peeked behind the curtain").
  • Pique: A feeling of irritation or resentment resulting from a slight, especially to one's pride (e.g., "in a fit of pique"). It can also mean to stimulate interest.

details.summary: Distinction between Peak (summit/maximum), Peek (quick look), and Pique (resentment/stimulate).

mcq.question: He left the meeting in a fit of ______ after his proposal was rejected.
mcq.explanation: 'Pique' refers to a feeling of irritation or resentment arising from wounded pride.

subject: English
text:
Understanding the difference between Sent, Scent, and Cent:

  • Sent: The past tense and past participle of the verb 'send'.
  • Scent: A distinctive, typically pleasant smell (e.g., "scent of wild flowers") or a trail left by an animal.
  • Cent: A monetary unit in various countries, equal to one-hundredth of a dollar, euro, or other basic unit.

details.summary: Distinction between Sent (past of send), Scent (aroma/trail), and Cent (monetary unit).

mcq.question: The bloodhound followed the ______ of the missing person.
mcq.explanation: 'Scent' refers to the distinctive smell or trail left by someone.

subject: English
text:
Understanding the difference between Aisle, Ale, and Isle:

  • Aisle: A passage between rows of seats in a plane, church, theater, or supermarket (e.g., "aisle seat").
  • Ale: A type of beer with a bitter flavor and relatively high alcohol content (e.g., "ginger ale").
  • Isle: An island, especially a small one (e.g., "isle in the middle of a lake").

details.summary: Distinction between Aisle (passage), Ale (beverage), and Isle (island).

mcq.question: Would you prefer a window seat or an ______ seat?
mcq.explanation: 'Aisle' refers to the passage between rows of seats.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
The Right to Equality is one of the core pillars of the Indian Constitution. This section details Articles 16, 17, and 18:

  • Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Matters of Public Employment
    • No citizen shall be denied employment on the basis of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence.
  • Article 17: Abolition of Untouchability
    • Abolition of untouchability and prohibition of its practice in any form.
  • Article 18: Abolition of Titles
    • Abolition of titles except military and academic.
    • It prohibits the State from conferring any title (except military and academic) on anybody, whether citizen or foreigner, without the consent of the President.

details.summary: Covers Article 16 (Equality of opportunity in public employment), Article 17 (Abolition of untouchability), and Article 18 (Abolition of titles except military and academic).

mcq.question: Which of the following grounds is NOT explicitly mentioned in Article 16 of the Indian Constitution for non-discrimination in public employment?
mcq.explanation: Article 16 prohibits discrimination in public employment on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence. Language is not explicitly mentioned as a ground under Article 16.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
The Right to Freedom guarantees individual rights that are vital for the functioning of a democracy:

  • Article 19: Guarantees six democratic freedoms to all citizens:
    • Freedom of speech and expression.
    • Right to assemble peacefully and without arms.
    • Right to form associations, unions, or co-operative societies.
    • Right to move freely throughout the territory of India.
    • Right to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India.
    • Right to practice any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade, or business.
  • Article 20: Protection against arbitrary and excessive punishment to an accused person (citizen or foreigner):
    • No ex-post-facto law: No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act.
    • No double jeopardy: No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.
    • No self-incrimination: No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.
  • Article 21: Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
    • No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
  • Article 21 A: Right to Education
    • Declares that the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years. Added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act (CAA).
  • Article 22: Protection against Detention or Arrest
    • The arrested person has the right to know the grounds of detention, to be defended by a legal practitioner, and must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding journey time). They cannot be detained beyond 24 hours without magistrate authorization.

details.summary: Covers Article 19 (Six democratic freedoms), Article 20 (Protection against conviction), Article 21 (Protection of life & personal liberty), Article 21A (Right to education), and Article 22 (Protection against arrest & detention).

mcq.question: The Right to Education under Article 21A was added to the Constitution of India by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
mcq.explanation: Article 21A, which provides free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14, was inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002.

subject: Physics
topic: Refraction of Light and Optical Density
text:
Refraction of light is the bending of light rays as they pass from one medium to another, thereby changing the path of the rays. Refraction occurs due to a change in the speed of the light ray or wave.

The ability of a medium to refract light is also expressed in terms of its optical density. Optical density has a definite connotation and is not the same as mass density.

  • Optically Denser Medium: In comparing two media, the one with the larger refractive index is the optically denser medium. When a ray of light travels from a rarer medium to a denser medium, it slows down and bends towards the normal.
  • Optically Rarer Medium: The medium with the lower refractive index is optically rarer. The speed of light is higher in a rarer medium than a denser medium. When light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

details.summary: Refraction is the bending of light due to speed changes across media. Optical density, determined by refractive index, dictates whether light bends towards or away from the normal.

mcq.question: When a ray of light travels from an optically denser medium to an optically rarer medium, what happens to its speed and direction?
options: It slows down and bends towards the normal
It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
It speeds up and bends towards the normal
mcq.explanation: The speed of light is higher in an optically rarer medium. Therefore, when travelling from a denser to a rarer medium, the light ray speeds up and bends away from the normal.

Snell's Law: This law states the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction and the refractive indices of the two media:

n1 sin(θ1) = n2 sin(θ2)

subject: Physics
text:
Equations of Motion

For a moving object, the relations among its velocity, displacement, time and acceleration can be represented by equations. These equations are called equations of motion.

  • For motion in a straight line with constant acceleration a:
  • (i) v = u + at
  • (ii) s = ut + 1/2 at²
  • (iii) v² = u² + 2as
  • Equation of motion under gravity (downward direction):
  • (i) v = u + gt
  • (ii) h = ut + 1/2 gt²
  • (iii) v² = u² + 2gh

Where, u = initial velocity
v = final velocity
g = gravitational acceleration

If an object is thrown vertically upward away from the earth, then we shall substitute -g in place of g in the above equations. The value of g is 9.8 m/s².

Note: If a body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration, then distance covered by the body in t sec is proportional to t² (i.e. s ∝ t²).

details.summary: Defines the standard kinematic equations for constant acceleration and gravity, including variable definitions and the specific value of g.

mcq.explanation: The text explicitly states: 'The value of g is 9.8 m/s².'

subject: Physics
text:
Projectile Motion

When a body moves under an acceleration whose direction is different from the direction of the initial velocity, then both the magnitude and direction of its velocity changes with time. Hence, the body moves on a curved path in a plane. This type of motion is called projectile motion.

  • A bullet fired from a rifle and a body dropped from the window of a moving train shows the projectile motion.

Key Formulas:

  • Flight time of projectile, T = 2u sinθ / g
  • Height of projectile, h = u² sin²θ / 2g
  • Range of projectile, R = u² sin 2θ / g

Important Facts:

  • The horizontal range is the same when the body is projected at θ and (90° - θ).
  • The horizontal range of a projectile is maximum when angle of projection is 45°.
  • When two balls of different masses are projected horizontally they will reach ground at same time.
  • We drop down a ball from a roof and at the same time throw another ball in a horizontal direction, then both the balls would strike the earth simultaneously at different places.

details.summary: Explains projectile motion, provides formulas for time, height, and range, and lists key properties regarding angles and mass independence.

mcq.question: At what angle of projection is the horizontal range of a projectile maximum?
mcq.explanation: The text states: 'The horizontal range of a projectile is maximum when angle of projection is 45°.'

subject: Physics
text:
Force

Force is a push or pull which produces or tends to produce a change in uniform motion of body; stops or tends to stop a body which is in motion. Its unit is Newton.

  • It is a vector quantity and the straight line along which a force is directed is called the line of action of the force.
  • The rotational effect of a force on a body about an axis of rotation is described in terms of moment of force.
  • CGS unit of force is dyne i.e. 1 dyne = 10⁻⁵ N.

Types of Force:

  • (i) Component of Force: Forces acting at same angle from the coordinate axes can be resolved into mutually perpendicular forces called components. The component of a force parallel to the X-axis is called x-component, parallel to the y-component and so on.
    Here,
    x-component of force F is F cosθ.
    y-component of force F is F sinθ.
  • (ii) Contact and Non-contact Force: The forces which act on bodies when they are in physical contact are called contact forces. e.g. muscular force, frictional force, etc.
    A force which can be exerted by an object on another object even from a distance (without physical contact with each other) is called a non-contact force. e.g. magnetic force, electrostatic force and gravitational force.

details.summary: Defines force, its units (SI and CGS), vector nature, and classifies them into components, contact, and non-contact forces.

mcq.explanation: The text states: 'CGS unit of force is dyne i.e. 1 dyne = 10⁻⁵ N.'

NEWTON'S LAWS OF MOTION

Newton has given three laws of motion as below:

First Law

It states that every body continues in its state of rest or in uniform motion in a straight line, unless it is compelled by an external force to change that state.

First law is also called law of Galileo or law of inertia.

  • The property of bodies by virtue of which they oppose only change in their present state is called inertia.
  • Mass is a measure of the inertia of a body.

  • The Punjab Plains: The western part, formed by the Indus and its tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj). This section is dominated by ‘doabs’ (land between two rivers).
  • The Ganga Plain: Extends between the Ghaggar and Teesta rivers. Spread over the states of North India, Haryana, Delhi, U.P., Bihar, and West Bengal.
  • The Brahmaputra Plain: The easternmost part of the plains, located mainly in Assam.

subject: Geography
text:
Divisions Based on Relief Features

  • The Bhabar: A narrow belt (8-16 km wide) lying parallel to the Shivalik foothills. Composed of pebbles and boulders deposited by rivers descending from the mountains. All streams disappear in this porous belt.
  • The Terai: A wet, swampy, and marshy region south of the Bhabar belt. The streams and rivers that disappeared in the Bhabar re-emerge here. Once thickly forested, much of it has been cleared for agriculture.
  • The Bhangar: The largest part of the Northern Plain, formed of older alluvium. Lies above the floodplains and presents a terrace-like feature. The soil contains calcareous deposits locally known as ‘Kankar’.
  • The Khadar: The newer, younger deposits of the floodplains. The soil is renewed almost every year, making this belt very fertile. Ideal for intensive agriculture.

details.summary: Based on relief, the plains are divided into Bhabar (porous pebble belt), Terai (marshy region), Bhangar (older alluvium/terrace), and Khadar (newer alluvium/floodplain).

mcq.question: Which part of the Northern Plains is known for 'Kankar' deposits?
mcq.explanation: The Bhangar region contains calcareous deposits locally known as 'Kankar'.

Formation

  • Created by the deposition of alluvium in a vast basin at the foothills of the Himalayas over millions of years.

General Features

  • A vast expanse of flat land, covering an area of about 7 lakh sq. km.
  • Densely populated due to fertile soil, adequate water, and a favorable climate.
  • Agriculturally a very productive part of India, known as the ‘granary of India’.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Article 25

  • All persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice and propagate religion.

Article 26

  • Every religious institution has the right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes.
  • Right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion.
  • Right to own and acquire movable and immovable property.
  • Right to administer such property in accordance with law.

Article 27

  • No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion.
  • The state should not spend the public money collected by way of tax for the promotion of any particular religion.

Article 28

  • No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institutions maintained wholly out of state funds.

Article 29

  • Any citizen residing anywhere have the right to conserve its language, script or culture of its own.

Article 30

  • All minorities have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

Article 32

  • If any citizen feels its fundamental rights have been breached they have the right to move to supreme court for the enforcement of the same.

Important Note: Article 15, 16, 19, 29, 30 are only available to citizens of India.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of Fundamental Rights Articles 25-32 covering religious freedom, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.

text:
Image Formation by Convex Lens

  • At infinity: Image is at focus F2. Highly diminished, point-sized. Real and inverted.
  • Beyond 2F1: Image is between F2 and 2F2. Diminished. Real and inverted.
  • At 2F1: Image is at 2F2. Same size. Real and inverted.
  • Between F1 and 2F1: Image is beyond 2F2. Enlarged. Real and inverted.
  • At focus F1: Image is at infinity. Infinitely large or highly enlarged. Real and inverted.
  • Between focus F1 and optical centre O: Image is on the same side of the lens as the object. Enlarged. Virtual and erect.

Law of Conservation of Energy

  • Energy can only be converted from one form to another.
  • It can neither be created nor destroyed.

Energy Conversion during Free Fall:

  • At the top: K.E = 0 (zero because velocity is zero), P.E = mgh.
  • Fall of the object continues: The P.E would decrease while K.E would increase.
  • When the object is about to reach the ground: h = 0, v will be highest.

Mechanical Energy: P.E + K.E = constant

text:
Indian Ocean Currents: Seasonal Variations

  • Summer (Monsoon Season):
    • South West Monsoon drives currents.
    • Somalia Current: Flows towards the northeast (towards India).
    • Mozambique Current: Flows south along the coast of Africa.
    • Agulhas Current: Flows south along the southern tip of Africa.
    • South Equatorial Current (S. eq. C): Flows westward.
    • West Aus. C (West Australian Current): Flows northward.
    • S. Indian oc. C (South Indian Ocean Current): Flows eastward.
  • Winter (Non-Monsoon Season):
    • N.E. Monsoon Current is active near India.
    • Somalia Current: Flows southwest (reverses direction).
    • Mozambique Current: Flows south.
    • Agulhas Current: Flows south.
    • S. eq. C: Flows westward.
    • West Aus. C: Flows northward.
    • S. Indian oc. C: Flows eastward.

Key Locations: Africa, Madagascar, Australia (Aus.), India.

details.summary: Handwritten notes detailing the direction of ocean currents in the Indian Ocean during Summer (South West Monsoon) and Winter (N.E. Monsoon) seasons, highlighting the reversal of the Somali Current.

  • Cold currents form coastal deserts.
  • Examples:
    • Atacama Desert (Chile)
    • Coobi Desert (m+c - likely referring to a specific region or typo for a coastal desert)
    • Ladakh

topic: Newton's First Law of Motion: Practical Examples
text:
Here some practical examples are as follows in which first law is used:

  • Athlete runs some distance, before taking a long jump.
  • A ball thrown upward in a train moving with uniform velocity returns to the hand of thrower.
  • The mud from the wheels of a moving vehicle flies-off tangentially.
  • When we shake the branch of a mango tree, the mangoes fall down.
  • A man jumping from a moving train may fall down.
  • If a cloth placed under a book is given a sudden pull, it comes out without disturbing the book.
  • When a horse suddenly starts moving, the rider falls backward.
  • When a running horse suddenly stops, the rider falls forwards.
  • We hit a carpet with a stick to remove the dust.

It is difficult to drive a nail into a wooden block without holding the block.

A jet plane moves on the principle of Newton's third law of motion. As exhaust gases come out from the nozzle at a greater speed, the reaction of the same moves the plane forwards.

details.summary: Practical examples illustrating Newton's First Law of Motion, including inertia of rest and motion, and a mention of Newton's Third Law for jet planes.

subject: Physics
topic: Validity of Newton's Laws of Motion
text:
Validity of Newton's Laws of Motion

Newton's laws are valid in classical physics only under certain conditions

  • In general, the distances which one work must be much greater than the size of atoms and molecules. Else, quantum mechanics must be used in place of classical mechanics.
  • In general, the speeds which one work must be much less than the speed of light. Else, relativistic mechanics must be used in place of classical mechanics.
  • Also, this is valid with respect to inertial frame of reference only.

details.summary: Conditions under which Newton's Laws of Motion are valid, specifying limitations related to scale (quantum mechanics) and speed (relativistic mechanics), and the requirement of an inertial frame of reference.

subject: Physics
text:
Second Law

The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts. According to second law

F ∝ dp/dt or F = k dp/dt

where, k is constant of proportionality

F = k d/dt (mv) = kma

for simplicity let k=1.

⇒ F = ma

1 newton = 105 dyne

  • Newton's second law gives the magnitude of force.
  • Newton's first law is contained in the second law.

Here some practical examples are as follows in which second law is used.

  • China wires are wrapped in straw or paper before packing.
  • A person falling on pucca floor (or frozen ice) is likely to receive more injuries than one falling on kuccha floor (loose earth).
  • While catching a ball, a cricket player lowers his hands to save himself from getting hurt.
  • Bogies of the trains are provided with buffers to avoid severe jerks during shunting of trains.

details.summary: Definition, mathematical formulation (F=ma), unit conversion (Newton to dyne), and practical examples of Newton's Second Law of Motion.

subject: Physics
text:
Linear Momentum

  • The linear momentum of a body is defined as, the product of its mass and its velocity i.e.
    Momentum = Mass × Velocity, p = m × v
  • It's direction is the same as the direction of velocity of the body. It is a vector quantity. It's SI unit is kg-m/s.
  • Concept of momentum was introduced by Newton.
  • A heavier body has a larger linear momentum than a lighter body moving with the same velocity. i.e. In the absence of external forces, the total momentum of the system is conserved.
  • i.e. m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ [For single body]
  • and m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ [For two bodies]

details.summary: Definition, formula, direction, SI unit, and the principle of conservation of linear momentum with associated formulae for single and two-body systems.

text:
Third Law

According to this law, to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. 'Action and reaction always act on the different bodies.' Here some practical examples are as follows in which third law is used

  • In order to walk, we press the ground in backward direction with our feet. As a result, the ground pushes us in forward direction.

text:
Applications of Conservation of Momentum

When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun recoils or gives a sharp pull in backward direction. While firing a bullet, the gun must be held tight to the shoulder.

  • When a man jump from a boat to the shore, the boat slightly moves away from the shore.
  • Rocket works on the principle of conservation of momentum.
  • If someone left on a frictionless floor desires to get out of it, he can do so by blowing air out of his mouth.

subject: Geography
text:
The Western Coastal Plains (Coast of Submergence- Narrow & Indented)

General Features

  • Geomorphology: Formed by submergence land, creating a narrow, indented coastline.
  • Width: Relatively narrow (avg. 65 km), ranging from 10-25 km in places.
  • Continental Shelf: Broad, especially off Mumbai (Bombay High-rich in oil & gas), excellent for fishing.
  • Rainfall: Receives heavy rainfall from South-West Monsoons (June-September).

Sections (North to South)

  1. Kachchh & Kathiawar Coast (Gujarat): Tidal flats, salt pans. Kathiawar is a peninsula.
  2. Konkan Coast (Maharashtra & Goa): Rocky, dissected terrain. Runs from Daman to Goa.
  3. Kannad Plain (Karnataka): Narrowest section, features cliffs, estuaries, and scenic waterfalls (e.g. Jog Falls nearby).
  4. Malabar Coast (Kerala): Famous for unique 'Kayals' (backwaters/lagoons) used for inland navigation & tourism.

Rivers & Landforms

  • Rivers: Short, swift rivers (Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati) that originate in Western Ghats.
  • River Mouths: Form estuaries (funnel-shaped river mouths), not deltas, due to hard rock and steep gradient.
  • Landforms: Dominated by cliffs, rocky shores, and the famous Kayals. Vembanad Lake is the largest Kayal, host to Nehru Trophy Boat Race.

Ports & Economy

  • Harbours: The indented nature provides excellent natural harbours.
  • Major Ports: Kandla (Tidal Port), Mumbai (India's Largest Natural Port), JNPT (Navasheva), Marmagao (Goa, in an estuary), New Mangalore, Kochi ("Queen of Arabian Sea").
  • Economy: Fishing, salt production, oil & natural gas, trade, cultivation of spices, coconut, rice, cashew.

Image Description: A map showing the coastal plains of India, highlighting the Western Coast. An image of a cargo ship at a port, illustrating ports and economy.

subject: Geography
text:
The Eastern Coastal Plains (Coast of Emergence - Wide & Smooth)

General Features

  • Geomorphology: Formed by emergence of land, resulting in a wide, smooth, and continuous coastline.
  • Width: Broader (avg. 120 km), especially in deltaic regions.
  • Continental Shelf: Narrow, with a sharp drop-off.
  • Rainfall: Receives rainfall from both SW Monsoons and significantly from NE Monsoons (retreating monsoon) during winter.

Sections (North to South)

  1. Utkal Coast (Odisha): Site of Mahanadi Delta & Chilika Lake.
  2. Northern Circars (Andhra Pradesh): Between Mahanadi & Krishna rivers. Very fertile.
  3. Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu): Extends from Krishna river to Kanyakumari. Receives most rainfall in winter from NE Monsoons.

Rivers & Landforms

  • Rivers: Large, perennial rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) with long courses.
  • River Mouths: Deposit huge amounts of sediment, forming very large and fertile deltas. These are known as the 'Granaries of South India'.
  • Landforms: Dominated by extensive deltas, sand dunes, and large lagoons.

Major Lakes (Lagoons)

  • Chilika Lake (Odisha): Largest brackish water lagoon/lake in India.
  • Kolleru Lake (Andhra): Freshwater lake, located between Godavari & Krishna deltas.
  • Pulicat Lake (Andhra/TN): Second largest brackish lagoon, separated by Sriharikota island (ISRO's Satish Dhawan Space Centre).

Ports & Economy

  • Harbours: Smooth coastline makes natural harbours difficult; most are artificial.
  • Major Ports: Tuticorin, Chennai (Oldest Artificial Port), Ennore, Visakhapatnam (Deepest, Land-locked Port), Paradip, Haldia.
  • Economy: Dominated by intensive agriculture (especially rice in deltas), fishing, and trade.

subject: General Science
text:
Nucleic acids:

  • The genes are made up of nucleic acids, which form the basis of heredity.
  • These are long polymers made of repeating units called nucleotides.
  • Each nucleotide consists of a nucleoside and a phosphate base, joined together by phosphate diester bond.
  • The nucleic acids are of two types-

DNA:

  • Acronym – Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid.
  • It has 4 bases – Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, and Thymine.
  • Adenine and Guanine are purine bases and Cytosine and Thymine are pyrimidine bases.
  • DNA generally has a double stranded structure.
  • They are the basic genetic materials, except in some viruses.
  • DNA can replicate to form two DNA molecules.
  • DNA controls heredity, evolution, metabolism, structure and differentiation.

RNA:

  • Acronym – Ribose Nucleic Acid.
  • RNA is the genetic material of only certain viruses.
  • RNA generally has a single-stranded structure.
  • It is made up of 4 bases – Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Uracil.
  • RNA cannot replicate itself to form two RNAs.
  • RNA cannot control heredity, it controls only protein synthesis.
  • There are 3 types of RNA-
    • mRNA – messenger RNA
    • tRNA – transfer RNA
    • rRNA – ribosomal RNA

Classification of cells:

  • Based on the number of cells.
ProkaryotesEukaryotes
These are unicellular organisms without a well-defined nucleus. Some prokaryotes are multi cellular. Eg- bacterial cellThese cells have a well-defined nucleus and internal cell organelles. Eg – plant and animal cell
They are primitive and simple cells.They are developed and complex cells.

subject: History
text: The neolithic settlers were the earliest farming communities. They produced ragi and horse-gram (kulathi). They domesticated cattle, sheep and goats. They wove cotton and wool to make clothes. Hand made pottery and use of potter wheel first appears during the Neolithic age.

subject: History
text: Neolithic men lived in caves and decorated their walls with hunting and dancing scenes. They knew the art of making boats. In the later phase, people lived a more settled life and lived in circular and rectangular houses made of mud and reed. It is interesting that in Burzahom domestic dogs were buried with their masters in their graves.

subject: History
text: Koldihwa in Uttar Pradesh revealed a three fold cultural sequence i.e. Neolithic, Chalcolithic and Iron age. Mehrgarh in Balochistan is the oldest Neolithic site in Pakistan (7000 BC).

subject: History

subject: History
text: The end of the Neolithic period saw the use of metals. Copper was the first metal to be used. Chalcolithic culture refers to the stone-copper phase. People also used hand-axes and other objects made up of copperware.

subject: History
text: Chalcolithic people were primarily rural communities. They domesticated animals and practised agriculture. They were not acquainted with burnt bricks and lived in thatched houses. They venerated the mother Goddess and worshipped the bull.

subject: History
text: The people of Chalcolithic culture were the first to use painted pottery. Black and red pottery painted with white line design was most popular. The ceramics obtained from malwa is considered the richest among the Chalcolithic ceramics.

subject: History

subject: Mathematics
text:
The collection of all rational and all irrational numbers together forms the set of real numbers and is denoted by 'R'. Thus, all natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational and irrational numbers are real numbers.

Properties of Real Numbers

Properties of real numbers are as follows

General Properties of R

  1. If x and y are two real numbers, then either x > y, y > x or x = y.
  2. If x and y are two real numbers, then
    • (i) x > y ⇒ 1/x < 1/y
    • (ii) x > y ⇒ -x < -y
    • (iii) x > y ⇒ x + a > y + a
    • (iv) x > y ⇒ xa > ya, when a > 0
  3. If xy = 0 ⇒ x = 0 or y = 0

details.summary: Definition of Real Numbers and their general properties including order, inequalities, and zero product property.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Properties of Operations on Real Numbers
text:
Properties of operations on R

Let '*' be any operation defined on R.

  1. Closure Property If a ∈ R and b ∈ R, then a * b ∈ R.
  2. Associative Property If a, b, c ∈ R, then a * (b * c) = (a * b) * c.
  3. Commutative Property If a, b ∈ R, then a * b = b * a.
  4. Identity Let 'I' be the identity, then I * a = a * I = a ∀ a ∈ R.
  5. Inverse Let a' be the inverse of a, then a' * a = a * a' = I ∀ a ∈ R.
  • The above properties hold for addition and multiplication on R.
  • The additive identity of R is O and additive inverse of a ∈ R is -a.
  • The multiplicative identity of R is 1 and multiplicative inverse of a ∈ R is 1/a.
  • R is closed for subtraction, if a, b ∈ R, then a - b ∈ R.
  • If a, b, c ∈ R, then a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c) is the distributive property on R.

details.summary: Detailed explanation of fundamental properties of operations on real numbers: Closure, Associativity, Commutativity, Identity, and Inverse, along with specific examples for addition, multiplication, and subtraction.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Absolute Value of a Real Number
text:
Absolute Value of a Real Number

The absolute value of a real number x is denoted by |x|. Thus,

|3| = 3 and |-4| = 4.

If x is any real number, then |x| = { x, when x > 0; 0, when x = 0; -x, when x < 0 }

e.g.

  1. If x = 5, |5| = 5, if x = 0, |0| = 0
  2. If x = -5, |-5| = -(-5) = 5

Also, |x-2| = x-2, if x > 2; |x-2| = 0, if x = 2; |x-2| = 2-x, if x < 2

details.summary: Definition and piecewise function for the absolute value of a real number, with examples.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Some Properties of Absolute Values

  1. |x| ≥ 0 for all real x.
  2. |x| = a means x = a or x = -a
  3. |x| > a means x > a or x < -a
  4. If n=x2; √n = √x2 = |x| = x, if x ≥ 0 = -x, if x < 0

details.summary: Four key properties of absolute values, including their definitions in terms of inequalities and square roots.

subject: Mathematics
text:
FACTORS IN SET OF INTEGERS

Let a, b ∈ I, we say that a is a factor of b, if there exists an integer p such that b = ap; in short we write a | b read it 'a' divides 'b'.

If a is factor of b, then b is called a multiple of a.

Properties of factor and multiples

For real numbers a and b, if b = ac then 'a' is a factor 'b' and we write a | b.

  1. a | b, b | c ⇒ a | c (This law is known as transitivity)
  2. a | a, ∀ a ∈ R (This law is known as reflexivity)
  3. a | b and a | c ⇒ a | b + c and a | b - c
  4. If p is prime number and p divides ab where a, b are integers, then p divides 'a' or p divides 'b'. Thus p | ab ⇒ p | a or p | b.

details.summary: Definitions of factors and multiples in the set of integers, along with four fundamental properties of factors and multiples, including transitivity, reflexivity, and properties related to prime numbers.

text:
Given a quadratic equation x² + x + 1 = 0. This equation has complex roots, which are the cube roots of unity (ω and ω²). A key property is that 1 + x + x² = 0 for these roots.

To find the value of x¹⁹⁹ + x²⁰⁰ + x²⁰¹, we can factor out x¹⁹⁹:

x¹⁹⁹ + x²⁰⁰ + x²⁰¹ = x¹⁹⁹(1 + x + x²)

Since 1 + x + x² = 0 (from the given equation), the expression simplifies to:

= x¹⁹⁹ × 0

= 0

This demonstrates how to use the given quadratic relation to simplify higher powers of x.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If x, y, z are in Geometric Progression (GP), then the middle term squared is equal to the product of the other two terms: y² = xz.

Statement 1: ln(3x), ln(3y), ln(3z) are in AP.

For terms to be in Arithmetic Progression (AP), the middle term is the average of the other two, or twice the middle term equals the sum of the other two:

2 ln(3y) = ln(3x) + ln(3z)

Using logarithm properties (n log a = log aⁿ and log a + log b = log ab):

ln((3y)²) = ln(3x ⋅ 3z)

ln(9y²) = ln(9xz)

9y² = 9xz

Since this matches the condition for x, y, z being in GP, Statement (1) is correct. Also, if x, y, z are in GP, then log x, log y, log z are in AP.

Statement 2: xyz + ln(x), xyz + ln(y), xyz + ln(z) are in HP.

If a, b, c are in AP, then 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in HP. Conversely, if a, b, c are in HP, then 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in AP.

The statement implies that if log x, log y, log z are in AP, then xyz + log x, xyz + log y, xyz + log z are in AP. This is incorrect. Adding a constant (xyz) to terms in AP keeps them in AP, but the statement claims they are in HP, which is generally not true unless xyz=0 or other specific conditions. Therefore, Statement (2) is wrong.

details.summary: Properties of Geometric Progression (GP), Arithmetic Progression (AP), Harmonic Progression (HP) and their relation with logarithms.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Given that log₁₀ 2, log₁₀ (2ˣ - 1), log₁₀ (2ˣ + 3) are in AP.

For terms a, b, c to be in AP, 2b = a + c.

So, 2 log₁₀ (2ˣ - 1) = log₁₀ 2 + log₁₀ (2ˣ + 3)

Using logarithm properties (n log a = log aⁿ and log a + log b = log ab):

log₁₀ (2ˣ - 1)² = log₁₀ [2(2ˣ + 3)]

Equating the arguments of the logarithms:

(2ˣ - 1)² = 2(2ˣ + 3)

Expand and simplify:

(2ˣ)² - 2 ⋅ 2ˣ + 1 = 2 ⋅ 2ˣ + 6

(2ˣ)² - 4(2ˣ) - 5 = 0

Let y = 2ˣ. Substitute y into the quadratic equation:

y² - 4y - 5 = 0

Factor the quadratic equation:

(y - 5)(y + 1) = 0

This gives two possible values for y:

y = 5 or y = -1

Since y = 2ˣ, and an exponential function 2ˣ is always positive, we must ignore y = -1.

Therefore, y = 5

Substitute back 2ˣ = y:

2ˣ = 5

To solve for x, take log base 2 on both sides:

x = log₂ 5

details.summary: Solving exponential equations involving logarithms and arithmetic progression properties.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Given set S = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9}. The number of elements in S is n(S) = 7.

We need to form different 3-digit numbers (with all digits different) that are less than 500.

For a 3-digit number to be less than 500, the hundreds digit must be less than 5. From the set S, the possible digits for the hundreds place are 2, 3, 4. So, there are 3 choices for the hundreds digit.

Since all digits must be different, after choosing the hundreds digit, we have 6 remaining digits in S.

For the tens digit, we can choose any of the remaining 6 digits. So, there are 6 choices for the tens digit.

After choosing the hundreds and tens digits, we have 5 remaining digits in S.

For the unit digit, we can choose any of the remaining 5 digits. So, there are 5 choices for the unit digit.

Using the multiplication principle (Fundamental Principle of Counting), the total number of such 3-digit numbers is:

Number of ways = (Choices for Hundreds) × (Choices for Tens) × (Choices for Units)

= 3 × 6 × 5 = 90

details.summary: Counting the number of permutations of digits from a given set to form numbers with specific conditions.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Given p = (1111 ... up to n digits). This can be written as a sum of a geometric progression:

p = 1 + 10 + 10² + ... + 10ⁿ⁻¹

This is a Geometric Progression with first term a = 1, common ratio r = 10, and n terms.

The sum of a GP is given by the formula: Sₙ = a(rⁿ - 1) / (r - 1)

Applying the formula:

p = 1(10ⁿ - 1) / (10 - 1)

p = (10ⁿ - 1) / 9

Now, we need to find the value of 9p² + p.

From the expression for p, we can write:

9p = 10ⁿ - 1

Rearranging this, we get:

9p + 1 = 10ⁿ

Now substitute 10ⁿ into the expression 9p² + p:

9p² + p = p(9p + 1)

= p(10ⁿ)

= 10ⁿ p

details.summary: Evaluating expressions involving numbers represented as repeating digits using Geometric Progression sum formula.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Given the quadratic equation: 3x² - (k² + 5k)x + 3k² - 5k = 0

For a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, if it has real roots of equal magnitude and opposite sign, two conditions must be met:

1. The sum of the roots must be zero (equal magnitude, opposite sign means α + (-α) = 0). Sum of roots = -b/a.

So, -(-(k² + 5k)) / 3 = 0

(k² + 5k) / 3 = 0

k² + 5k = 0

k(k + 5) = 0

This gives k = 0 or k = -5.

2. The product of the roots must be negative (one positive, one negative root). Product of roots = c/a.

So, (3k² - 5k) / 3 < 0

3k² - 5k < 0

k(3k - 5) < 0

To solve this inequality, consider the critical points k=0 and k=5/3. The parabola y = k(3k-5) opens upwards, so it is negative between its roots.

This gives 0 < k < 5/3.

Now, we need to find the values of k that satisfy BOTH conditions simultaneously.

From condition 1, k can be 0 or -5.

From condition 2, k must be strictly between 0 and 5/3 (i.e., 0 < k < 1.66...).

There is no common value of k that satisfies both k = 0 or k = -5 AND 0 < k < 5/3.

Therefore, no such value of k exists.

details.summary: Conditions for a quadratic equation to have real roots of equal magnitude and opposite sign.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
LIST OF FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES

  • To abide by the constitution and respect its ideal and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
  • To cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom.
  • To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
  • To defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so.
  • To promote harmony and the spirit of brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities and to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
  • To value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture.
  • To protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife and to have compassion for living creatures.
  • To develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
  • To safeguard public property and to abjure violence.
  • To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement.
  • To provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of six and fourteen years.

details.summary: This section outlines the eleven Fundamental Duties enshrined in the Indian Constitution, emphasizing civic responsibilities such as respecting the constitution, upholding national ideals, promoting unity, defending the country, fostering harmony, preserving heritage, protecting the environment, developing scientific temper, safeguarding public property, striving for excellence, and providing education for children.

subject: Physics
text:
Many optical instruments consist of a number of lenses combined to increase the magnification and sharpness of the image.

Net Power of Lenses in Contact

The net power (P) of lenses placed in contact is given by the algebraic sum of the individual powers P1, P2, P3, ... as:

P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ...

Practical Applications

  • Optician Testing: During eye-testing, an optician puts several different combinations of corrective lenses of known power, in contact, inside the testing spectacles' frame. The optician calculates the power of the lens required by simple algebraic addition.
    Example: A combination of two lenses of power +2.0 D and +0.25 D is equivalent to a single lens of power +2.25 D.
  • Minimizing Defects: The simple additive property of the powers of lenses can be used to design lens systems to minimise certain defects in images produced by a single lens. Such lens systems are commonly used in designing camera lenses and objectives of microscopes and telescopes.

details.summary: Explains the algebraic addition of lens powers when placed in contact and its practical utility in optometry and optical instrument design.

mcq.question: If two thin lenses of power +3.5 D and -1.5 D are placed in contact, what is the net power of the combination?
mcq.explanation: Using the formula P = P1 + P2, we get P = +3.5 D + (-1.5 D) = +2.0 D.

subject: Biology
topic: Structure and Optics of the Human Eye
text:
The human eye is a vital sensory organ that acts like a camera, focusing light to form images.

Anatomical Parts of the Eye

The eye consists of several key structures: Sclera, Choroid, Retina, Fovea, Artery and Vein, Optic Nerve, Central Retinal, Optic Disc (Blind Spot), Suspensory Ligament, Aqueous Humor, Cornea, Pupil, Iris, Lens, and Ciliary Body.

Key Optical Facts of the Eye

  • Its lens system forms an image on a light-sensitive screen called the retina.
  • Light enters the eye through a thin membrane called the cornea.
  • The eyeball is approximately spherical in shape with a diameter of about 2.3 cm.
  • Most of the refraction for the light rays entering the eye occurs at the outer surface of the cornea.

options: At the outer surface of the cornea

subject: English
topic: Ordering of Words in a Sentence
text:
Ordering of Words in a Sentence (PQRS) is a crucial topic in defence exams like CDS and NDA. To solve these questions efficiently, follow these core grammatical rules:

  • Identify the Subject: Look for the noun or pronoun that initiates the action. This usually forms the opening part of the sentence.
  • Correlative Conjunctions: Watch out for pairs like not only... but also, either... or, and neither... nor. For example, if segment Q contains 'not only' and segment S contains 'but also', Q will precede S.
  • Prepositional Links: Prepositions like 'of', 'at', 'by', and 'to' must connect logically to their respective objects (e.g., 'lives of' followed by 'generations of Indian women').
  • Relative Pronouns: Pronouns like 'that', 'which', and 'who' connect clauses to the nouns they modify (e.g., 'policies and behaviours' followed by 'that shaped...').

details.summary: A guide to solving PQRS sentence rearrangement questions using grammatical clues like correlative conjunctions, subject identification, and relative pronouns.

mcq.question: Identify the correct order of the segments: P: 'not only in India' / Q: 'but also globally' / R: 'climate change is a threat' / S: 'to biodiversity'
mcq.explanation: The correct sequence is RSPQ: 'climate change is a threat (R) to biodiversity (S) not only in India (P) but also globally (Q)'.

subject: Physics
text:
To calculate the electrical energy consumed by household appliances, follow these steps:

  • Convert power from Watts (W) to Kilowatts (kW): P (kW) = P (W) / 1000
  • Calculate daily energy consumption for each appliance: E (kWh) = Power (kW) × Time (hours)
  • Multiply by the number of appliances if there are multiple identical units.
  • Sum the daily energy consumption of all appliances to find the total daily energy: E_total = E_1 + E_2 + ...
  • Multiply the total daily energy by the number of days in the specified month (e.g., January has 31 days) to find the monthly consumption.

details.summary: Step-by-step methodology to calculate monthly electrical energy consumption in kilowatt-hours (kWh) for multiple appliances.

mcq.question: A 100W bulb is used for 5 hours daily and four 50W bulbs are used for 5 hours daily. What is the total energy consumed in the month of January?
mcq.explanation: Daily energy for 100W bulb = (100/1000) * 5 = 0.5 kWh. Daily energy for four 50W bulbs = 4 * (50/1000) * 5 = 1.0 kWh. Total daily energy = 1.5 kWh. Total energy for January (31 days) = 1.5 * 31 = 46.5 kWh.

subject: Biology
topic: Classification of Tissues and Meristematic Tissues
text:
Tissue Classification and Meristematic Tissues

Tissues are broadly classified into two main categories: Plant Tissue and Animal Tissue.

1. Plant Tissue Classification

  • Meristematic Tissue: Highly active dividing tissues responsible for plant growth. Divided into:
    • Apical Meristem: Present at growing tips of stems and roots; increases the length of the stem and root.
    • Lateral Meristem: Responsible for increasing the girth of the stem or root (cambium).
    • Intercalary Meristem: Located near the nodes and internodes.
  • Permanent Tissue: Divided into Simple and Complex:
    • Simple Permanent Tissue: Consists of Parenchyma, Chlorenchyma, Aerenchyma, Collenchyma, and Sclerenchyma.
    • Complex Permanent Tissue: Consists of Xylem and Phloem.

2. Animal Tissue Classification

  • Epithelial Tissue: Includes Simple Squamous, Columnar Epithelium, and Cuboidal Epithelium.
  • Muscular Tissue: Includes Voluntary Muscles, Involuntary Muscles, and Cardiac Muscles.
  • Connective Tissue: Includes Ligaments, Bones, Cartilage, Tendons, Blood, Areolar, and Adipose tissues.
  • Nervous Tissue: Specialized tissue for transmitting nerve impulses.

3. Characteristics of Meristematic Tissues

  • They are very active.
  • They have thin cellulose walls.
  • They possess dense cytoplasm.
  • They have prominent nuclei.
  • They lack vacuoles.

details.summary: This document provides a comprehensive classification of plant and animal tissues, with a detailed focus on the characteristics and types of plant meristematic tissues (Apical, Lateral, and Intercalary meristems).

mcq.question: Which of the following characteristics is NOT true for meristematic tissues?
options: They possess large and abundant vacuoles
They are highly active with dense cytoplasm
mcq.explanation: Meristematic tissues lack vacuoles because they are actively dividing cells and do not need to store food or waste materials.

text:
Cell Division:

  • The growth and development of all organisms depend upon the growth and division of cells.
  • Cell division occurs in two stages
    • Karyokinesis – Division of nucleus
    • Cytokinesis – Division of cytoplasm
  • There are two types of cell division – Mitosis and Meiosis.
    • Mitosis: It is the only form of cellular reproduction in single-cell organisms. Mitosis yields two genetically identical cells. This type of cell division occurs in asexual reproduction.
    • Meiosis: It occurs in reproductive cells. It results in the formation of four haploid cells from a single diploid cell. Hence, it is known as reduction division.

subject: Science & Technology
text:
Eye Structure and Function

  • A structure called iris behind the cornea. Iris is a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil.
  • The pupil regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
  • The eye lens forms an inverted real image of the object on the retina.
  • The retina is a delicate membrane having an enormous number of light-sensitive cells. These generate electrical signals. These signals are sent to the brain via the optic nerves.
  • The brain interprets these signals.

Visual Impairment

Damage to or malfunction of any part of the visual system can lead to significant loss of visual functioning. For example, if any of the structures involved in the transmission of light, like the cornea, pupil, eye lens, aqueous humour and vitreous humour or those responsible for conversion of light to electrical impulse, like the retina or even the optic nerve that transmits these impulses to the brain, is damaged, it will result in visual impairment.

details.summary: Overview of eye anatomy including iris, pupil, lens, and retina, and the consequences of visual system damage.

subject: Science & Technology
text:
Why do we have two eyes for vision and not just one?

There are several advantages of our having two eyes instead of one. It gives a wider field of view. A human being has a horizontal field of view of about 150° with one eye and of about 180° with two eyes. The ability to detect faint objects is, of course, enhanced with two detectors instead of one.

Some animals, usually prey animals, have their heads to give the widest possible field of view. But our two eyes are positioned on the front of our heads, and it thus reduces our field of view in favour of what is called stereopsis. Shut one eye and the world looks flat – two-dimensional. Keep both eyes open and the world takes on the third dimension of depth. Because our eyes are separated by a few centimetres, each eye sees a slightly different image. Our brain combines the two images into one, using the extra information to tell us how close or far away things are.

details.summary: Explanation of the benefits of binocular vision, including wider field of view and stereopsis (depth perception).

subject: Science & Technology
text:
Power of Accommodation

  • The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is called accommodation.
  • The change in the curvature of the eye lens can thus change its focal length. When the muscles are relaxed, the lens becomes thin. Thus, its focal length increases. This enables us to see distant objects clearly.
  • When looking at objects closer to the eye, the ciliary muscles contract. This increases the curvature of the eye lens. The eye lens then becomes thicker. The focal length of the eye lens decreases. This enables us to see nearby objects clearly.
  • The crystalline lens of people at old age becomes milky and cloudy. This condition is called cataract.

details.summary: Definition of accommodation, how the eye lens changes shape to focus on near and far objects, and the condition of cataracts.

These tissues take up a specific role and lose their ability to divide. The process of taking up permanent shape, size and a function is called differentiation.

subject: Biology
text:
SIMPLE PERMANENT TISSUE

1. PARENCHYMA

  • It consists of relatively unspecialized cells with thin cell walls.
  • They are living cells.
  • They are loosely arranged thus have large intercellular spaces in between them.
  • This tissue usually stores food.

2. CHLORENCHYMA

  • If parenchyma contains chlorophyll and performs photosynthesis it is called chlorenchyma.

3. AERENCHYMA

  • In aquatic plants large air cavities are present in parenchyma to help them float.

details.summary: Characteristics of Parenchyma, Chlorenchyma, and Aerenchyma.

mcq.question: Which tissue helps aquatic plants to float?
mcq.explanation: Aerenchyma contains large air cavities to help aquatic plants float.

subject: Biology
text:
4. COLLENCHYMA

  • The flexibility in plants is due to another permanent tissue.
  • It allows bending of various parts of plant like tendrils and stems of climbers without breaking.
  • It provides mechanical support.
  • The cells of this tissue are living, elongated and irregularly thickened at the corners with very little intracellular spaces.

5. SCLERENCHYMA

  • It is tissue which makes plant hard and stiff. E.g. husk of coconut.
  • Cells of this tissue are dead. They are long and narrow as the walls are thickened due to lignin.
  • This tissue is present in stems around vascular bundles, in the veins of leaves and in the hard covering of seeds and nuts.
  • It provides strength to the plant part.

details.summary: Characteristics of Collenchyma (flexibility) and Sclerenchyma (strength/hardness).

mcq.question: Which tissue provides flexibility to plants?
mcq.explanation: Collenchyma allows bending of plant parts without breaking.

subject: Biology
text:
COMPLEX PERMANENT TISSUE

In this all cells coordinate to perform a common function. Xylem and phloem are examples of such tissues.

XYLEM

  • It consists of Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibers.
  • Xylem performs the function of transportation of water and minerals vertically.
  • Tracheids and vessels have thick walls made up of dead cells which helps in transportation.
  • Parenchyma stores food.
  • Xylem fibers are mainly supportive in function.
  • It transports in one direction.

details.summary: Components and functions of Xylem tissue.

mcq.explanation: Sieve tubes are a component of Phloem, not Xylem.

subject: Biology
text:
PHLOEM

  • It consists of sieve cells, sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibers and phloem parenchyma.
  • Phloem transports food from leaves to other part of plant.
  • Except phloem fibers, other phloem cells are living cells.
  • It transports in two way.

Classification:

  • Anemone belongs to Cnidaria.
  • Coral also belongs to Cnidaria (Living).

Formation:

  • Coral reefs are made up of thousands of tiny animals called polyps.

Location & Depth:

Biological Relationship:

Ideal Conditions for Coral Growth:

  • Semi-hard or hard surface
  • Saline water
  • Clear water
  • Warm water
  • Rich supply of nutrients
  • Abundant plankton
  • NOT fresh water

subject: Physics
text:
Definition: The opposing force which comes into play when a body moves or tries to move the surface of another body is known as friction.

  • The maximum value of the force of friction which comes into play before a body just begins to slide over the surface of another body is called limiting friction.
  • The force of friction that comes into play between the surfaces of two bodies before the body actually starts moving is called static friction.
  • The force of friction that opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact is called kinetic or sliding friction.
  • The frictional force developed, when a body rolls over a surface, is known as the rolling friction.
  • Static friction is a self adjusting force and it adjusts itself, so that it becomes equal to the applied force.

subject: Physics
text:
Advantages of Friction

  • Due to friction, we are able to move on the surface of the earth.
  • The fibres of thread are held together due to force of friction.
  • The brakes applied in automobiles work only due to friction.
  • Sledges are used in Arctic region as friction is very low on the surface of ice.

Disadvantages of Friction

  • A lot of energy is wasted in the form of heat due to friction that causes wear and tear of the moving parts.
  • Due to friction, speed of automobiles cannot be increased beyond a certain limit.

subject: Physics
text:
Laws of Friction

  • Friction acts in a direction opposite to the direction of motion of the objects. It depends upon the nature of the two surfaces in contact.
  • Friction is independent of the area of contact of the two surfaces. Rolling friction is less than sliding friction.
  • Force of friction (F) is directly proportional to the normal reaction (R).
    i.e., F ∝ R
    F = μR
    where, μ = coefficient of friction.
  • Also, μ = tan α, where α is the angle of friction.
  • Angle of repose = Angle of friction i.e. θ = α

subject: Physics
text:
Methods for Reducing Friction

  • By using lubricants e.g. grease, oil, etc.
  • By using ball or roller bearings, which changes sliding into rolling.
  • By using soap solution.
  • By using powder.
  • Friction due to air is considerably reduced by streamlining the shape of the body moving at high speed in air. e.g. aircraft, jet-planes, fast cars are streamlined.
  • The tyres are provided with treads which increases the friction between the tyres and the road.
  • Note: Pulling is easier than pushing. While pushing, there is one component of force that acting downward on the object adds to the weight of the body hence there are more friction opposing the effort. Whereas on pulling, the vertical component of force is against the weight of the body and friction is less overall friction. So, it is easy to pull than push.

subject: Physics

Circular Motion

When an object moves along a circular path, then its motion is called circular motion as motion of top, etc. In circular motion force is always at right angles to the displacement therefore no work is done by the force on the particle.

  • When an object moves along a circular path with uniform speed, its motion is called uniform circular motion.
  • Circular motion is accelerated even, if the speed of the body is constant. The motion of a satellite is accelerated motion.

Cell enlargement: The size of individual cell increases after cell division due to increase in the volume of its protoplasm.

Cell differentiation: In this stage, the structure of the cell changes to perform specific functions. And a similar type of cells having the same functions forms a group, which is known as tissue.

  • In lower level organisms like bacteria and fungi, the cells along the entire body length grow.
  • But in higher organisms, growth is restricted to the cells present only in the growing regions, like stem apex and root tip or along the lateral sides of the stem and root.
  • Growth at the tips leads to elongation of body parts and grow at the lateral sides leads to increase in the thickness of the stem and root.

The naturally produced growth hormones are broadly grouped into five major classes. They are:

subject: Biology
text:
(i) Auxin:

  • Auxin is a growth promoter, generally produced by the growing apex of the stem and root of the plants. It helps in the elongation of the shoot and root tips behind apical meristem.
  • The naturally produced auxins are Indole-3-Acetic Acid (IAA).

Functions of Auxin:

  • It promotes cell elongation.
  • It suppresses the growth of lateral bud. If the tip of a plant is removed, the lateral branches begin to grow. In most of the plants, apical bud suppresses the development of lateral buds. This is called apical dominance.

text:

Functions of Gibberellins:

  • It helps in elongation of stems of genetically dwarf plants. By using gibberellin the height of the dwarf plants can be increased.
  • It induces parthenocarpy. (Formation of seedless fruits without fertilization).

details.summary: Details on Gibberellin (GA), its origin (Gibberella fujikuroi), production sites, and functions like stem elongation and parthenocarpy.

Functions of Cytokinins:

(iv) Ethylene:

  • Ethylene is a gaseous hormone. It is found in ripening fruits, young flowers, and young leaves.

Functions of Ethylene:

  • It induces ripening of fruits.
  • It promotes senescence and abscission of leaf and flowers.
  • In cells, it only increases the width not the length.

  • Abcissic acid also known as Dormin is a naturally occurring growth inhibitor found in a wide variety of plants. It is synthesized in leaves.

subject: Biology
text:
Germination of seeds:

  • Seed germination is the return of metabolic activities and growth of the seed tissue to give rise to a new plant by the development of the embryo.
  • There are two types of seed germination
  • Epigeal germination - In epigeal germination hypocotyl (the region below cotyledons) elongates and cotyledons come out above the soil surface. Examples: seeds of pumpkin, mustard, tamarind, and french bean.
  • Hypogeal Germination - In hypogeal germination the epicotyl (the region above cotyledons) elongates and cotyledons remain below the soil surface. Examples: Most monocots seed like rice, wheat, maize, and coconut.

Five factors affect the seed germination - water, temperature, oxygen, light and growth hormones.

details.summary: Definition of seed germination, classification into Epigeal and Hypogeal types with examples, and factors affecting germination.

text:

  • The effect of duration of light on the growth of plants is known as photoperiodism.
  • On the basis of light required by the plants for flowering, the plants are classified into the following three categories:
  • Short-day Plants - Some plants produce flowers when exposed to a light for a shorter period than usual. These are called Short-day Plants. Cosmos, Dahlia, Soyabean, are short-day plants.
  • Long-day Plants – Some plants, flowers when exposed to a light for a period longer than usual. Gulmohar, radish, spinach, are long-day plants.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the Pitts India Act 1784:

details.summary: The Pitts India Act of 1784 introduced a dual system of control by the British government and the East India Company, subordinated the presidencies of Bombay and Madras, and asserted the supremacy of the British Parliament over Indian affairs.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the Charter Act of 1813:

  • The Company's monopoly was deprived, except in trade with tea and trade with China.
  • One lakh rupees were earmarked for education in India.

details.summary: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company's trade monopoly in India, except for tea and trade with China, and allocated funds for the promotion of education.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the Charter Act of 1833:

  • The Governor-General of Bengal was now designated as the Governor-General of India (the first being William Bentinck).
  • It marked the end of the Company's commercial monopoly, and the Company was asked to wind up its business.
  • A Law member was added to the council of the Governor-General.
  • Acts passed from this point onwards were called Acts, not Regulations.
  • Provinces were deprived of legislative powers.
  • No Indian was to be discriminated against on the basis of religion, race, colour, or place of birth.

details.summary: The Charter Act of 1833 centralized administration by making the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India, ended the Company's commercial activities, introduced a law member to the council, and laid down principles against discrimination.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the Charter Act of 1853:

  • It separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council for the first time.
  • A legislative council of 6 members was created.
  • Four legislative members were to be appointed from provinces to the Central Legislature.

details.summary: The Charter Act of 1853 introduced a separate legislative council for India, marking the first step towards a parliamentary system by separating legislative and executive functions.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the Government of India Act 1858:

  • The Governor-General of India was also called the Viceroy (Lord Canning was the first Viceroy).
  • A Secretary of State for India was created, with a 15-member advisory body called the Council of India.
  • This Act did not alter the Indian administrative machinery substantially.

details.summary: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the powers of governance from the East India Company to the British Crown, establishing the office of Viceroy and Secretary of State for India.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the India Council Act 1861:

  • The Portfolio system was created.
  • It granted ordnance-making power to the Viceroy during emergencies.
  • The legislative council was expanded from 6 to 12 members, with non-official representation.
  • Decentralization of powers began, and legislative powers were devolved.

details.summary: The India Council Act of 1861 introduced the portfolio system, empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances, expanded the legislative council with non-official members, and initiated the process of decentralization of legislative powers.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the India Councils Act 1892:

  • The Governor-General of Bengal + 4 Council members (Warren Hastings) - Note: The mention of Warren Hastings here is historically inaccurate for 1892, likely a misplaced detail in the source.
  • The number of non-official members was increased, but the official majority was maintained.
  • Nomination of some non-official members of the Central Legislative Council (CLC) (Total: 16) was done on the recommendation of Provincial Legislative Councils (PLC) and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce.
  • PLC non-officials were to be recommended by local bodies, corporations, trade associations, zamindars, etc.
  • This Act marked the beginning of the representative system in India.

details.summary: The India Councils Act of 1892 increased the number of non-official members in legislative councils, introduced indirect elections for some seats, and marked the initial steps towards a representative system in India.

subject: Indian Polity
text:
Key provisions of the India Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Act):

  • The Governor-General (GG) + 2 council (from 1793) could override the council - Note: The 1793 reference here is likely a misplaced detail or a general statement of a continuing power from an earlier act.
  • The strength of the Central Legislative Council (CLC) was increased to 60.
  • Non-official members numbered 27 (non-official members of PLC, landholders, Muslims, etc., were allowed to vote).
  • A non-official majority was allowed in Provincial Legislative Councils (PLC).
  • It introduced a separate electorate for Muslims.

details.summary: The India Councils Act of 1909, also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, significantly increased the size of legislative councils, allowed for a non-official majority in provincial councils, and controversially introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
