subject: History
text:
Brahmo Samaj was founded by Raja Rammohan Roy in 1828 at Calcutta.

Roy believed in the modern scientific approach and principles of human dignity and social equality. He put his faith in monotheism.

He wrote the Gift to Monotheists (1809) and translated it into Bengali the Vedas and five Upanishads to prove his conviction to that ancient Hindu text.

In 1814, he set-up Atmiya Sabha in Calcutta to campaign against idolatry, caste rigidities, meaningless rituals and other social evils.

In 1825, he established a Vedanta college where courses in both Indian learning and Western social and physical science were offered.

Roy was a gifted linguist. He knew more than a dozen language including Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, English, French, Latin, Greek and Hebrew. He proposed English system of education.

details.summary: Founding and activities of Brahmo Samaj by Raja Rammohan Roy, emphasizing monotheism, social reform, and education.

subject: History
text:
Mahadev Gobind Ranade along with Dr Atmaram Pandurang reorganised Paramhansa Sabha under the guidance of Keshab Chandra Sen and founded Prarthana Samaj in 1867. It was primarily a Social Reform and Social Work Movement.

Beyond the religious concerns, the primary focus of the Prarthana Samaj was to improve the condition of women and depressed classes. The samajist demanded to end the caste system, abolish the child marriages and infanticide, educate the women and remarriage of windows.

A paper named Subodh Patrika was started in order to spread the teaching of the society. Some prominent Prarthana Samajist like Ramkrishna Gopal Bhandarkar, Narayan Ganesh Chandarvarkar, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, KT Telang etc contributed for overall development of the society.

details.summary: Overview of Prarthana Samaj’s formation, objectives, and key contributors.

subject: History
text:
Arya Samaj founded by Dayanand Saraswati or Mulshankar (1824-83).

The first Arya Samaj unit was formally set up by him at Bombay in 1975 and later the headquarter of the Samaj was established at Lahore.

Dayanand’s views were published in the famous work of Satyarth Prakash (The True Exposition). He gave slogan “Go Back to the Vedas”. He disregarded Puranas, idol worship, casteism and untouchability. He advocated widow remarriage.

Arya Samaj has established a large number of educational institutions in India particularly in the North, like Kanya Gurukuls and DAV (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) Schools and College.

Dayanand was the first man to use the term Swaraj and recognise Hindi as the National Language of India.

The Arya Samaj opposed all social evils of the Hindu society like sati, polygamy, child marriage, purdah, casteism etc and started the Shudhi movement.

details.summary: History and social reform activities of Arya Samaj founded by Dayanand Saraswati.

subject: History
text:
The first Rama Krishna Math was established by the disciple of Rama Krishna, Swami Vivekananda at Baranagar in 1897.

Vivekananda went to America in 1893 and attended the World Parliament of Religious Conference at Chicago.

Vivekananda revived Hindu Spiritualism and thus, established its superiority over Islam and Christianity.

Irish woman Margaret Nobel (known as sister Nivedita) popularised the mission.

details.summary: Founding and key figures of the Rama Krishna Mission and its spiritual outreach.

subject: History
text:
During the late 1820 and early 1830 there emerged a radical intellectual trend among the youth in Bengal, which came to be known as the ‘Young Bengal Movement’.

Founded by Henry Vivian Derozio, who taught in Hindu College Calcutta from 1826 to 1831. Derozio is considered as the first nationalist poet of Modern India.

He also edited Hosperus and Calcutta Literary Gazette.

He urged the students to live and die for truth. Derozio also supported women rights and education.

The movement was too radical, therefore it could not survive for long.

details.summary: Origins, key figures, and objectives of the Young Bengal Movement.

subject: History
text:
At Jhansi, Rani Laxmibai, the widow queen of Raja Gangadhar Rao, the last Maratha ruler of Jhansi, led the rebellion.

In Bihar, Kunwar Singh of Arrah, raised the banner of rebellion, which soon spread to many parts of Bihar, including Danapur, Chhotanagpur, Ranchi, Palamau etc. The tribals of the region also joined the rebellion. Kunwar Singh overthrew the British authority in Shahabad and established his own government. He marched to Kalpi to help Nana Sahib for a joint attack on Kanpur.

Prince Firoz Shah raised the banner of revolt at Mandsor (Madhya Pradesh) and kept the British forces engaged in Central India. Driven out of central provinces, he campaigned in Ruhelkhand and Awadh. He also joined the forces of Tantia Tope in Rajputana.

Khan Bahadur Khan raised the banner of revolt in Ruhelkhand with epicenter at Bareilly. He proclaimed himself the Nawab Nazim.

details.summary: Key leaders and their actions during the 1857 rebellion.

subject: History
topic: Various Movements (Satya Shodhak Samaj, Jajmani System, Theosophical Movement, etc.)
text:
Satya Shodhak Samaj (Truth Seeker’s Society) was founded by Jyotiba Phule in 1873. He belonged to the Mali (gardener) community and organised a powerful movement against upper caste domination and Brahminical supremacy.

  • Phule’s works ‘Sarvajanik Satyadharma’ and ‘Gulam Giri’ became sources of inspiration for the common masses.
  • Phule opened, with the help of his wife, a girls school at Poona and was a pioneer of widow remarriage movement in Maharashtra.

Jajmani System – an Indian social caste system involving interaction between upper and lower castes. It was an economic system where lower castes performed various functions for upper castes.

  • The terminology was introduced by William Wiser, who studied a village in Uttar Pradesh.
  • Based on agricultural production and distribution of goods and services.

Theosophical Movement

  • The Theosophical Society was founded by Madame Blavatsky and Col. Olcott in New York in 1875.
  • The founders arrived in India in January 1882 and established headquarters at Adyar near Madras.
  • Society believes in universal brotherhood of humanity without discrimination, study of comparative religion, philosophy and science, unexplained laws of nature and latent human powers.
  • In 1888, Mrs Annie Besant joined the society in England; she became President after Olcott’s death in 1907.
  • Annie Besant laid the foundation of Central Hindu College in Banaras in 1898, which became BHU in 1916.

Other Movements

  • Ved Samaj – Founder: Keshab Chandra Sen and K. Sridharula in 1864; renamed Brahmo Samaj of South India in 1871; translated into Tamil and Telugu.
  • Deva Samaj – Founder: Shiv Narain Agnihotri in 1887 at Lahore; teachings compiled in Deva Shastra; belief in Supreme Being, eternity of soul, supremacy of Guru.
  • Ahmadiya Movement – Founder: Mirza Ghulam in Punjab in 1889; belief that Islam is the final dispensation for humanity.
  • Dravida Kazhagam – Founders: John Rathinam and E.V. Ramaswamy; goals to eradicate caste ills including untouchability; renamed Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.
  • Dravida Mahajana Sabha – Founder: C. Iyothee Thass in 1891; emphasized Scheduled Caste people register as “casteless Dravidians”.
  • Self-Respect Movement – Founder: E.V. Ramaswamy in 1925; aim of achieving a society where backward castes have equal human rights and self‑respect.
  • Deoband Movement (Deobandis) – Founders: Rashid Ahmad Gangohi, Muhammad Yaqub Nanautawi in 1867; inspired by Shah Waliullah Dehlawi; founded Darul Uloom Deoband; advocated composite nationalism.
  • Radha Swami Movement – Founder: Tulsi Ram (Dayal Sahib) in 1861; belief in one Supreme Being, supremacy of Guru and simple social life.

National Movements – Indigo Revolt (1859‑60)

  • European planters forced peasants to grow unremunerative indigo crop in Eastern India.
  • In 1860, oppressed indigo peasants launched ‘non‑cultivation of indigo’ movements, starting with Ryots of Govindpur village in Nadia district (Bengal) and spreading rapidly.
  • Harish Chandra Mukherji, editor of Hindu Patriot, played an important role; ‘Deen Bandhu Mitra’s’ play Neel Darpan was based on this.
  • Michel Madhusudan Dutta translated Neel Darpan into English.
  • The government appointed an Indigo Commission in 1860; Indigo riots occurred in 1867‑68 in Champaran (Bihar).

details.summary: Summary of various social reform movements and the Indigo Revolt during the 19th‑20th centuries in India.

subject: History
text:
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by Allan Octavian Hume (AO Hume), a retired British member of the Indian Civil Service. His main purpose was to encourage the foundation of Congress to provide a ‘safety valve’ or ‘safety outlet’ to growing discontent among the educated Indians.

  • The first session of the Indian National Congress was held on 28th December 1885.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji changed the name of the organisation to Indian National Congress (INC).
  • Wyomesh Chandra Banerjee, a leading lawyer of Calcutta, was elected its President.
  • The session was held in Bombay under WC Banerjee in 1885 (72 delegates attended).
  • In 1890, Kadambini Ganguly, the first woman graduate of Calcutta University, addressed the Congress session.
  • Bal Gangadhar Tilak, later popularly known as Lokamanya Tilak, was born in 1856.
  • Extremist leaders: Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh, Lala Lajpat Rai.

details.summary: Founding of the Indian National Congress and key early leaders.

subject: History
text:
On 20th July 1905, Lord Curzon issued an order to divide the province of Bengal into two parts, partly to set up a communal gulf between Hindus and Muslims.

  • The Anti-Partition Movement was started by prominent leaders like Surendranath Banerjee and Krishna Kumar Mitra.
  • Cries of ‘Bande Mataram’ became a national song of Bengal.
  • Rabindranath Tagore composed the national song ‘Amar Sonar Bangla’ for the occasion, sung by a huge crowd parading the streets.
  • The song was adopted as the national anthem by Bangladesh in 1971 after liberation.
  • The ceremony of Raksha Bandhan was observed on 16th October 1905; Hindus and Muslims tied ‘rakhi’ in each other’s wrists as a symbol of unbreakable unity.

details.summary: Events and movements surrounding the Partition of Bengal and its cultural impact.

subject: History
text:
The leader of Bengal felt that mere demonstrations, public meetings and resolutions were not enough; something more concrete was needed, and the answer was Swadeshi and Boycott. People burnt foreign clothes and foreign goods.

  • The leaders of Bengal took up the work of national education in earnest; national educational institutions were opened, providing literary, technical and physical education.
  • On 15th August 1906, a national council of education was set up and Aurobindo Ghosh was appointed as the first Principal of the National College.
  • At the Calcutta session, the Congress decided to boycott British goods on 7th August 1905.
  • Lala Lajpat Rai, BG Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Aurobindo Ghosh played important roles in the Swadeshi Movement.

details.summary: The Swadeshi Movement’s strategies, educational initiatives and key leaders.

subject: History
text: In 1906, the All India Muslim League was founded under the leadership of Agha Khan, Nawab Salim-ul-lah of Dacca and Nawab Mohsin-ul-Mulk. The League supported separate electorate for the Muslim community and opposed the Nationalist moves of the Congress. In return, the British declared that they would protect the ‘special interest of the Muslims’.

details.summary: Formation and objectives of the All India Muslim League.

subject: History
text:
The Indian National Congress (INC) split into two groups, the moderate and extremist groups at the Surat session in 1907.

  • Extremists were led by Lal Lajpat Rai, BG Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
  • Moderates were led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
  • The government launched a massive attack on the extremists (1907-1911) by suppressing their newspaper (Incitement to offences) and their leaders.

details.summary: The Surat Split and its aftermath.

subject: History
text:
Taraknath Das, Sohan Singh Bhakana and Lala Hardayal founded the Ghadar Party Movement.

  • In November 1913, the Hind Association of America was founded by Sohan Singh Bhakana. It decided to publish a weekly paper Ghadar or Hindustan Ghadar in commemoration with the Revolt of 1857.
  • The organisation headquarters was at San Francisco.
  • Lal Hardayal, Bhai Parmanand and Ram Chandar were leading figures of the Ghadar Party Movement.
  • Ghadar party planned to initiate an armed revolt in India in 1915, starting in Punjab, then Bengal and rest of India. India units as far as Singapore were planned to participate in the revolt.
  • British intelligence infiltrated the Ghadarite movement and crushed the plan before it started.

details.summary: The Ghadar Party’s formation, objectives and suppression.

subject: History
text: The major problem at Champaran in Bihar was of the Indigo planters. The European planters forced the peasant to grow indigo on 3/20th of the total land area (tin katie system). Peasants were also forced to sell their produce at the prices fixed by the Europeans. When the German syntactic dyes replaced indigo, the planters demanded high rents and illegal dues from the peasants in order to maximise their profit.

details.summary: Champaran Satyagraha and the plight of indigo farmers.

subject: History
text:
Through tours in rural areas, he established direct contact with ordinary people and talked about their concerns in the language which they understood. This was a novel political technique; it had never been practiced by the educated leaders of the congress.

  • For the first time, the peasants were drawn into political agitation under a new type of leadership.
  • For the first time in India, Gandhi was displaying that magnetic personality, which was to draw multitudes to him and to earn him the title of Mahatma and the nickname of Bapu.
  • Under pressure from the Government of India, the Government of Bihar appointed a committee of enquiry (June, 1917). The recommendations of the committee were implemented, by the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1917. He was also member of this committee.
  • Some of leaders associated with Gandhiji in this Satyagraha were JB Kripalani, Rajendra Prasad, Mahadev Desai, Narhari Parikh etc.
  • Based on this movement, a book Neel Darpan was written by Dinbandhu Mitra.

details.summary: Champaran Satyagraha marked Gandhi's first major civil disobedience movement in India, focusing on peasant grievances against indigo planters and leading to the Champaran Agrarian Act.

subject: History
text:
While Gandhiji was still engaged in his task in Bihar, he received a letter from Shrimati Anasuyabai. She informed him about the condition of workers in Ahmedabad mills and requested him to take up their cause with the mill owners.

  • The terrible plague of 1917-18, led to a heavy decline in the number of workers in the major industrial city of Ahmedabad. In order to attract the workers, the mill owners started paying them 75% of their wages as plague bonus.
  • The mill-owners declaration of locking out the mills on 22nd February, 1918 made the situation even more serious. At last, the issue was resolved with the intervention of Mahatma Gandhi. The mill owners agreed to give 35% of wages as bonus. This offer was accepted by the workers.
  • Gandhiji intervened in a dispute between the workers and mill owners and he took a fast unto death to force a compromise.

details.summary: Ahmedabad Satyagraha was Gandhi's first industrial labor dispute, where he used fasting as a tool to achieve a wage increase for mill workers.

subject: History
text:
It was first Non-Cooperation Movement in India. In 1917 most of the kharif crops of the farmers of Kheda district in Gujarat were destroyed due to heavy rains thus, incapacitating them to pay the land revenue to the government. When the government refused to comply with the peasant’s demand to remit the land revenues, Gandhiji advised them to withhold the payment and launch a struggle against the government on 22nd March, 1918.

  • Gandhiji with his lieutenants like Vallabhbhai Patel, the young lawyer of Kheda (who had become Gandhiji’s follower during this Satyagraha), Indulal Yagnik and many other youth, toured villages to encourage the peasants.

details.summary: Kheda Satyagraha was Gandhi's first non-cooperation movement, where peasants refused to pay land revenue due to crop failure, establishing a pattern of mass civil disobedience.

subject: History
text:
Home Rule Leagues having been inspired by the Irish rebellion, Mrs Annie Besant (September, 1916) and BG Tilak (April, 1916) set-up the Home Rule League.

  • BG Tilak linked up Swaraj with the demand for the formation of linguistic states and education in Vernacular language. Tilak gave the popular slogan, “Freedom is my birth right and I shall have it.”

details.summary: The Home Rule Leagues, inspired by the Irish model, aimed for self-governance within the British Empire and were led by Annie Besant and Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

subject: History
text: The Lucknow session of the INC in 1916 was memorable event on account of two important development. First was re-admission of the extremists who had been expelled from the INC 9 years earlier. The second development was the alliance between the Congress and Muslim League.

details.summary: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 marked the reunion of Congress extremists and moderates and established a historic Hindu-Muslim alliance for joint political demands.

subject: History
text: The government passed the Rowlatt Act in March 1919, which empowered the British Government to detain any person without trial. The act was a serious betrayal of the promises made by the government during the world war period.

details.summary: The Rowlatt Act allowed detention without trial, sparking nationwide protests and leading to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

subject: History
text:
People were agitating against arrest of their popular leaders Dr Saif-ud-din Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal.

  • On 13th April, 1919, Baisakhi Day, hundreds of people were massacred and several thousand wounded in Jallianwala Bagh where they had assembled to held a protest meeting against the repressive policies of the government.
  • The troops led by General Dyer opened fire on the unarmed men and women, young and old, Hindu and Muslim. It was regarded as the worst massacre during the entire freedom struggle. Hunter Commission was appointed to enquire into it.
  • Sardar Udham Singh killed General Dyer on 13th March, 1940, when the latter was addressing a meeting in Caxton hall in London.

details.summary: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre, where General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd, became a turning point in the Indian freedom struggle, fueling widespread anger against British rule.

subject: History
text: The All India Khilafat Conference held at Delhi in November, 1919. Gandhiji was the head of Khilafat Committee. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad also led the movement. Later a Khilafat Manifesto was published which called upon the British to protect the Khalifa (Caliphate).

details.summary: The Khilafat Movement sought to protect the Ottoman Caliphate and was jointly led by Gandhi and Muslim leaders, laying groundwork for the Non-Cooperation Movement.

subject: History
text:
The Non-Cooperation Movement under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, was launched to press three main demands

  • i. The Khilafat issue.
  • ii. The redressal of the Punjab wrongs.
  • iii. The attainment of Swaraj.

details.summary: The Non-Cooperation Movement was Gandhi's first nationwide mass movement, aiming to address Khilafat concerns, Punjab injustices, and achieve self-rule through peaceful non-cooperation.

subject: History
text:
The programme of the movement had two main aspects

  • Destructive
  • Constructive

Under the first category came

  • Surrender of titles and honorary offices and resignation from nominated seats in local bodies.
  • Refusal to attend official functions.
  • Gradual withdrawal of children from officially controlled schools and colleges.
  • Boycott of British Courts by lawyers and litigants.
  • Refusal on the part of the military, clerical and labour classes to offer themselves as recruits for service in Mesopotamia.
  • Boycott the elections to the Legislative Council.
  • Boycott of the foreign goods.

Under the second category came

  • Use of Swadeshi goods.
  • Hand spinning and weaving.
  • Removal of social evils like casteism and untouchability.
  • Hindu-Muslim unity.
  • Collection of money for Tilak Swaraj fund.
  • Setting up national educational institutions.

The Prince of Wales visited India during this period.

Chauri Chaura Incident (1922)

  • In Chauri Chaura (Near Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh), a police station including 22 policemen was burnt on 5th February, 1922.
  • On 12th February, 1922, Gandhiji decided to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement.
  • Most of the nationalist leaders including CR Das, Motilal Nehru, Subhash Chandra Bose, Jawaharlal Nehru, however, expressed their bewilderment at Gandhi’s decision to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement on 12th February, 1922.
  • In March 1922, Gandhiji was arrested and sentenced for 6 years in jail.

The Swarajya Party (1923)

  • CR Das, Motilal Nehru and NC Kelkar suggested that instead of boycotting the councils, they should enter and expose them.
  • In December 1922, Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Congress Khilafat Swarajya Party with CR Das as the President and Motilal Nehru as one of the secretaries.
  • The Swarajists contested elections to the Legislative Assembly and Provincial Councils.
  • In 1923, elections they got 42 seats out of 101 elected seats in Bengal and Central Province.
  • The party broke in 1926 after the death of CR Das.

Simon Commission (1927)

  • In November 1927, the British Government appointed the Indian Statutory Commission known as the Simon Commission (after the name of Chairman).
  • John Simon, a British politician, was appointed as Chairman of the commission to review the situation in India with a view to introduce further reforms and extension of parliamentary democracy.
  • At Madras Session in 1927 presided over by Dr Ansari, the Indian National Congress decided to boycott the commission.
  • The police came down heavily on demonstrators. The lathi-charge at Lahore, led to the death of Lala Lajpat Rai because of injuries (30th October, 1928).
  • The agenda for the second round table conference held in London was to discuss the report of Simon Commission.

Bardoli Movement (1928)

  • Bardoli Movement against the payment of land tax led by Vallabhbhai Patel in a village called Bardoli in Gujarat.
  • Vallabhbhai Patel got the title Sardar from the women of this movement.

The Nehru Report (1928)

  • Having boycotted the Simon Commission, the Indian political parties tried to hammer out a common political programme.
  • All parties conference met in February, 1928 and appointed a sub-committee under the chairmanship of Motilal Nehru to draft a Constitution. This was the first major attempt by the Indians to draft a constitutional framework for the country.
  • The committee also included Tej Bahadur Sapru. The report was finalised on August, 1928.

Other Political Parties and Movements (1922-27)

  • The moderates who had walked out of the INC in 1918, formed National Liberal League, later known as the All India Liberal Federation and cooperated with the government.
  • The All India Khilafat Committee also ceased to function after the abolition of Khilafat in Turkey by Mustafa Kamal Pasha in 1924.
  • The Hindu Mahasabha, a communal organisation of the Hindus, founded in December 1915, also gained strength and Madan Mohan Malaviya was elected as its President at Belgaum Session.

details.summary: Overview of key political movements and events in India during 1922-1928, including the programme of the movement, Chauri Chaura Incident, Swarajya Party, Simon Commission, Bardoli Movement, Nehru Report, and other parties.

subject: History
text:
In October 1924, a meeting of revolutionaries from all parts of India was called at Kanpur. The meeting was attended by old revolutionary leaders such as Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee, and Ram Prasad Bismil, as well as newer revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh, Shiv Verma, Sukhdev, Bhagwati Charan Vohra, and Chandra Shekhar Azad.

At this meeting, it was decided to set up the Hindustan Republican Association, which was later recognised as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA). The HSRA was founded at Kanpur in October 1924 by Sachindra Nath Sanyal, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee, Ramprasad Bismil, and Chandra Shekhar Azad, and declared its objectives.

details.summary: Formation of HSRA in Kanpur, 1924, with key leaders and objectives.

subject: History
text:
Revolutionaries decided to commit a dacoity in a running train on 9th August 1925 at Kakori on the Lucknow-Saharanpur section of the Northern railway. Twenty-nine were arrested and tried in the Kakori Conspiracy Case.

Four revolutionaries—Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Roshan Lal, and Rajendra Lahiri—were sentenced to death.

details.summary: Kakori train robbery, 1925, and subsequent trial and death sentences.

subject: History
text:
The first revolutionary act of the HSRA was the murder of Mr. Saundars, the Assistant Superintendent of Police in Lahore, who had ordered a lathi-charge and brutally wounded Lala Lajpat Rai during the Anti-Simon Commission protest march at Lahore on 17th December 1928.

Saundars was killed at Lahore railway station on 30th October 1928 by Bhagat Singh, Chandra Shekhar Azad, and Rajguru.

details.summary: Murder of Mr. Saundars by HSRA members in Lahore, 1928.

subject: History
text:
Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw two crude bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly on 8th April 1929, when the assembly was discussing the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill.

Bhagat Singh and Dutt were arrested and tried in the Central Assembly Bomb Case. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, and Rajguru were hanged to death on 23rd March 1931 at Lahore jail for their role in Saundars murder case.

details.summary: Bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly, 1929, and subsequent executions.

subject: History
text: Surya Sen (1930), a revolutionary of Bengal, masterminded the raid on the Chittagong armoury. He was hanged in 1933. On 27th February 1931, Chandra Shekhar Azad was surrounded by the police at Alfred Park, Allahabad, where he shot himself dead.

details.summary: Chittagong armoury raid by Surya Sen and death of Chandra Shekhar Azad.

subject: History
text: Simon Commission was a British commission set up to report on the political situation in India. The Lahore Session or Poorna Swaraj (1929) was held under the presidency of Pandit JL Nehru, giving voice to a new militant spirit.

details.summary: Simon Commission and its impact on Indian nationalism.

subject: History
text:
On 19th December 1929, under the presidency of Pandit JL Nehru, the Lahore Session of the Congress passed a resolution declaring Poorna Swaraj (complete independence) to be the Congress objective.

On 31st December 1929 the newly adopted tri-colour flag of freedom was hoisted. On 26th January 1930, it was fixed as the first Independence Day, to be celebrated every year.

details.summary: Lahore Session outcomes: declaration of Poorna Swaraj and hoisting of the flag.

subject: History
text: The Civil Disobedience Movement was started by Gandhiji on 12th March 1930 with his famous Dandi March.

details.summary: Initiation of the Civil Disobedience Movement by Gandhi.

subject: History
text:
Mahatma Gandhi launched the Salt Satyagraha on 12th March 1930. Gandhiji marched from his Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad) with 78 followers. After a 24-day long march, he symbolically broke the Salt Law at Dandi on 6th April 1930. The breaking of the Salt Laws formally inaugurated the Civil Disobedience Movement.

This movement sparked patriotism among Indian soldiers in the British Army. The Garhwali soldiers refused to open fire on the people of Peshawar.

details.summary: Details of the Dandi March and its impact on Indian soldiers.

subject: History
text: The First Round Table Conference was held in London. Fifty-seven political leaders from India participated in the conference. Congress did not participate.

details.summary: First Round Table Conference in London, 1930-31.

subject: History
text: In March 1931, the famous Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed. Gandhi was appointed as the representative of the Congress of the Second Round Table Conference.

details.summary: Signing of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Gandhi's role.

subject: History
topic: Second Round Table Conference (1st September - 1st December 1931)
text: The Second Round Table Conference opened in September 1931 in London. Gandhiji represented the INC and met British PM Ramsay MacDonald. In 1932, the Indian National Congress was declared an illegal organisation. The British Government refused to concede the basic nationalist demand for freedom on the basis of immediate grant of dominion status.

details.summary: Second Round Table Conference outcomes and British stance.

subject: History
text: Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced his ‘Communal Award’ on 16th August, 1932. According to this award, the Muslim, European and Sikh voters would elect their candidates by voting in separate communal electorates. The award declared the depressed class (Scheduled caste of today) also to be Minority Community entitled to separate electorate and thus, separated them from the rest of the Hindus.

details.summary: Communal Award announced by Ramsay MacDonald on 16 August 1932, providing separate electorates for Muslims, Europeans, Sikhs and depressed classes.

subject: History
text:
• Gandhiji started his fast unto death in Yeravada jail near Poona on 25th September, 1932. He wanted the Communal Award to be withdrawn. The Poona Pact according to which the idea of separate electorates for the depressed classes was abandoned, but the seats reserved for them in the provincial legislatures were increased from 71 in the Award to 147 and in the Central Legislature to 18% of the total.
  • Poona Pact agreed upon to appoint electorate for upper and lower classes. Upliftment of harijan now became Gandhi’s main concern. He started an All India Anti-Untouchability League in September, 1932 and the weekly Harijan in January, 1933 even before his release. 8th January, 1933 was observed a ‘Temple Entry Day’.
  • After the Poona Pact, Mahatma Gandhi lost interest in the Civil Disobedience Movement and fully engrossed in the Anti-Untouchability Movement, which led to the foundation of the Harijan Sevak Sangh.

details.summary: Poona Pact of 25 September 1932 ended separate electorates for depressed classes, increased reserved seats, and shifted Gandhi's focus to anti-untouchability work.

subject: History
text: Held from 24th November to December, 1932. The Congress boycotted it and only 46 delegates attended the session.

details.summary: Third Round Table Conference (Nov-Dec 1932) was boycotted by Congress, attended by only 46 delegates.

subject: History
text:
• In 1940 at the Lahore, a resolution called for independent state for Muslims i.e. Pakistan, which was totally based on the Two-Nation Theory of Muslim League.
  • The term Pakistan had been coined by Choudhary Rahmat Ali in his Pakistan Declaration in 1933. He referred to the names of the five northern regions of the British India namely; Punjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan.

details.summary: Lahore Resolution (1940) demanded a separate Muslim state (Pakistan) based on Two-Nation Theory; term Pakistan coined by Rahmat Ali in 1933.

subject: History
text:
• In March, 1940 at the Lahore, demand for Pakistan was called. The session was chaired by Muhammad Ali Jinnah.
  • The Muslim League demanded that the areas in which the Muslims are numerically in a majority as in the North-Western and Eastern Zones of India should be grouped to constitute Independent states.
  • The Muslim League was encouraged by the British Government to press its demand for a separate state.
  • The demand for a separate state was opposed by Congress and large sections of Muslims such as, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan and others.

details.summary: March 1940 Lahore session under Jinnah demanded grouping of Muslim-majority NW and Eastern zones into independent states; British encouraged League; opposed by Congress and some Muslim leaders.

subject: History
text:
• There were two opinions in Congress about the launching of civil disobedience. Gandhi felt that the atmosphere was not in favour of civil disobedience as there were differences and indiscipline within the Congress. While some leaders of Congress, socialists and the All India Kisan Sabha were in favour of immediate struggle.
  • The August Offer had disillusioned the Congress. Finally, Gandhiji had a long meeting with the Viceroy at Simla in September, 1940, after which he was convinced that the British would not modify their policy in India.
  • He therefore, decided to launch Individual Satyagraha. The aim of the satyagraha was to disprove the British claim of India supporting the war effort wholeheartedly.
  • On 17th October, 1940, Acharya Vinoba Bhave (the first Satyagrahi) inaugurated the satyagraha by delivering an anti-war speech at Paunar; Bhave had been personally selected by Gandhiji for this.
  • Mahatma Gandhi suspended it on 17th December, 1940 due to little enthusiasm it created. Jawaharlal Nehru was the second to offer Satyagraha after Vinoba Bhave. It was during Individual Satyagraha that Gandhi declared Nehru as his chosen successor. Individual Satyagraha was also known as Delhi Chalo Satyagraha.

details.summary: Individual Satyagraha (Oct 1940-Dec 1940) launched by Gandhi to disprove British claim of wholehearted Indian war support; inaugurated by Vinoba Bhave, Nehru declared successor; suspended Dec 1940.

subject: History
text:
• To get Indian cooperation in the war effort the viceroy announced the August Offer (August 1940), which proposed dominion status as the objective for India, expansion of viceroy’s Executive Council, setting up of a Constituent Assembly would frame the Constitution after war according to their social, economic and political conceptions.
  • Subject to fulfillment of obligation of the government regarding defence, minority rights treaties with states. All India Services and no future Constitution to be adopted without the consent of minorities. The Congress rejected the August Offer, but it was accepted by the Muslim League.

details.summary: August Offer (Aug 1940) proposed dominion status, expanded Executive Council, Constituent Assembly after war; required defence obligations, minority rights; rejected by Congress, accepted by Muslim League.

subject: History
text:
• In March 1942, when Japan occupied Rangoon, after having overrun almost the whole of South-East Asia.
  • The British Government, with a view to get support from India, sent Sir Stafford Cripps, leader of the House of Commons to settle terms with the Indian leaders.

details.summary: Cripps Mission (Mar 1942) sent by British to secure Indian support amid Japanese advances in SE Asia; led by Sir Stafford Cripps.

subject: History
text:
The Quit India Movement (1942)

  • Also known as proposal and leaderless revolt.
  • Congress met at Bombay on 8th August 1942 and passed the Quit India Resolution.
  • Gandhiji gave the slogan ‘Do or Die.’
  • On 9th August 1942, Gandhiji and other Congress leaders were arrested; the Congress party was declared illegal.
  • Violence broke out across the country: government offices destroyed, telegraph wires cut, communication paralysed.
  • Gandhiji disclaimed responsibility for the violence, attributing it to repressive British measures.
  • A parallel government was set up in Ballia, Eastern Uttar Pradesh, by Chittu Pandey.
  • The movement was short‑lived but demonstrated intense nationalist feeling and willingness to sacrifice.
  • The Muslim League did not support the movement.
  • Key leaders: Achyut Patwardhan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali.

details.summary: The Quit India Movement of 1942 was a mass civil disobedience campaign launched by the Indian National Congress demanding an end to British rule, marked by widespread arrests, violent outbreaks, and a brief parallel government in Ballia.

subject: History
text:
Indian National Army (INA)

  • Led by Subhash Chandra Bose in cooperation with the Japanese.
  • Bose escaped from India in January 1941, traveling via Moscow to Berlin.
  • In 1943, Bose formed the INA in Singapore with Rashbehari Bose.
  • The INA aimed at a military campaign for India's liberation.
  • Comprised mainly of Indian soldiers captured by the Japanese after the fall of British colonies in Southeast Asia.
  • Three fighting brigades: Gandhi, Azad, and Nehru; also a women’s regiment called the Rani Jhansi Regiment.
  • July 1944: Bose sought Gandhi’s blessings; adopted the battle cry ‘Jai Hind’ and the slogan ‘Dilli Chalo.’li>
  • INA prisoners were tried at the Red Fort; defended by Tej Bahadur Sapru, Bhulabhai Desai, and Jawaharlal Nehru.
  • Headquarters: Rangoon and Singapore.
  • 12 November 1945 celebrated as INA Day.

details.summary: The INA, formed under Subhash Chandra Bose in 1943, fought alongside Japan during WWII, organized into three brigades and a women’s regiment, and became a symbol of armed resistance against British rule.

subject: History
text:
Rajagopalachari Formula (CR Plan)

  • C. Rajagopalachari, veteran Congress leader, proposed a Congress‑League cooperation formula accepting the League’s demand for Pakistan.
  • Main points:
    • Muslim League to endorse Congress demand for independence.
    • League to cooperate with Congress in forming a provisional central government.
    • After the war, a plebiscite in Muslim‑majority areas of North‑West and North‑East India to decide their future.
    • If partition accepted, joint agreement on defence, commerce, communication, etc.
    • Terms operative only if England transferred full powers to India.
  • Jinnah wanted Congress to accept the Two‑Nation Theory and limited the plebiscite to Muslims of the North‑West and North‑East.
  • Hindu leaders led by V.D. Savarkar condemned the CR Plan.

details.summary: The CR Plan proposed by C. Rajagopalachari sought a cooperative approach between Congress and the Muslim League, including a post‑war plebiscite in Muslim‑majority regions, but faced opposition from both Jinnah and Hindu nationalist leaders.

subject: History
text:
Wavell Plan and Shimla Conference (1945)

  • May 1945: Lord Wavell, Viceroy of India, visited London and discussed India’s future with the British administration.
  • The discussions led to the formulation of the Wavell Plan, made public in June 1945.
  • Key proposal: Reconstitution of the Viceroy’s Executive Council with members nominated by political parties.
  • Communities to receive proportional representation; parity reserved for caste‑Hindus and Muslims.

details.summary: The Wavell Plan of 1945 proposed a restructured Executive Council with balanced communal representation, aiming to facilitate a political settlement ahead of the Shimla Conference.

subject: History
text: Wavell called for a conference at Shimla on 25th June 1945 to discuss proposals. Leaders of both the Congress and the Muslim League attended the conference, which is known as the Simla Conference. Differences arose between the leadership of the two parties on the issue of representation of the Muslim community, leading to a deadlock. Finally, Wavell announced the failure of his efforts on 14th July 1945.

details.summary: The Simla Conference of 1945 was an attempt to resolve differences between Congress and Muslim League but ended in deadlock and failure.

subject: History
text: The Attlee Government announced in February 1946 the decision to send a high‑powered mission of three British Cabinet members: Pethick Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and AV Alexander to India to find out ways and means for a negotiated peaceful transfer of power. The mission rejected the Muslim League’s demand for Pakistan and proposed a Two‑Tier Federal Plan, which was initially accepted by both the Congress and the Muslim League. The Muslim League eventually decided to keep away.

details.summary: The 1946 Cabinet Mission proposed a federal plan and rejected the demand for Pakistan, leading to initial acceptance and later withdrawal by the Muslim League.

subject: History
text: The Muslim League joined the cabinet but decided to boycott the Constituent Assembly which started its work of framing the Constitution on December 1946. The Muslim League on 6th June and the Congress on 24th June 1946 accepted the long‑term plan, but forward by the Cabinet Mission. July 1946, elections were held in provincial assemblies for the Constituent Assembly. The Congress got 209 of the total 273 seats. 29th July 1946, the league withdrew its acceptance of the long‑term plan in a reaction against Nehru’s statement and gave a call for ‘direct action’ from 16th August 1946 to achieve Pakistan.

details.summary: Both parties initially accepted the Cabinet Mission plan, but the Muslim League later withdrew and called for direct action.

subject: History
text: Lord Wavell invited Jawaharlal Nehru, the leader of the largest party in India, to form an Interim Government which was sworn‑in on 2nd September 1946. It was composed of 12 members (including 3 Muslims) nominated by the Congress; Nehru was its Vice‑President. For the first time since the coming of the British, the Government of India was in Indian hands. The Muslim League at first refused to join the Interim Government but later changed its stand and joined not sincerely.

details.summary: The Interim Government of 1946 marked the first Indian‑led administration before independence.

subject: History
text: The setback in the election to the Constituent Assembly forced the League to reject the Cabinet Mission Plan. Jinnah gave the call for ‘Direct Action’, which postulated a campaign for the creation of Pakistan. The League withdrew its acceptance of the Cabinet Plan on 29th July 1946. From 16th August 1946 the country witnessed communal riots on an unprecedented scale. The League passed a Direct Action Resolution condemning both the British Government and Congress (16th August 1946). 27th March 1947 was celebrated as Pakistan Day by Jinnah.

details.summary: Jinnah’s Direct Action Resolution intensified the push for Pakistan and led to widespread communal violence.

subject: History
text: The Constituent Assembly met in New Delhi on 9th December 1946 without the participation of the League. Rajendra Prasad was elected as its President.

details.summary: The Constituent Assembly convened in December 1946, with Rajendra Prasad as President.

subject: History
text: The freedom with partition formula was coming to be widely accepted well before Mountbatten came. The important points of the plan were as follows: Punjab and Bengal Legislative Assemblies would meet in two groups – Hindus and Muslims – to vote for partition. In case of partition, two dominions and two Constituent Assemblies would be created. Sindh would take its own decision. The provision of referendum was provided in case of NWFP and Sylhet. Referendum in NWFP and Sylhet, district of Bengal would decide the fate of these areas. Freedom would come on 15th August 1947.

details.summary: Mountbatten’s 1947 plan outlined the partition of India and the creation of two dominions.

subject: History
text: A Boundary Commission would be set‑up if partition was to be effected. On July 1947 the British Parliament ratified the Mountbatten Plan as the ‘Independence of India’ Act, 1947. The act was implemented on 15th August 1947. Pakistan became independent on 14th August 1947. Jinnah became the first Governor‑General of Pakistan. At midnight of 15th August 1947 as the clock struck 12, India became free. Nehru proclaimed it to be the nation with his famous ‘tryst with destiny’ speech. On the morning of 15th August 1947, Lord Mountbatten was sworn‑in as Governor‑General and Jawaharlal Nehru as the first Prime Minister of free India. At the time of freedom, there were 562 small and big princely states. Sardar Patel, the first Home Minister, used iron hand in this regard.

details.summary: The Partition of India in 1947 led to the creation of India and Pakistan, with significant political changes.

subject: History
topic: List of Revolts and Peasant Movements
text:
Revolts

  • Kol Uprising: 1824-1828, 1839, 1899 – Gujarat
  • Bhils Uprising: 1818-1831 – Western Ghat
  • Khasi Rising: 1846-48, 1855, 1914 – Orissa
  • Kuki Rising under Gaidinliu: 1917-1819 – Manipur
  • Singpo Rising: 1830-1839 – Assam
  • Kol Rising under Buddha Bhagat: 1831-1832 – Chhotanagpur
  • Khond Rising under Chakrabisai: 1846-48, 1855, 1941 – Khandmal area in Orissa
  • Tharo Kuti Rising under Jadonand and Rani Gaidinliu: 1917-1919 – Manipur
  • Ramsoi Revolt under Vasudeo Balwant Fadke (Robin-hood of Maharashtra): 1822-1829 – Western Ghats
  • Munda Revolt under Birsa Munda: 1899-1900 – Chhotanagpur area

Famous Peasant Movements

  • Pagal Panthi Movement (1825-1835) – Bengal; Leaders: Karam Shah, Tipu Shah (Hajong and Garo tribes); Cause: Against hike in rents in Bengal.
  • Moplah Rebellion (1921) – Malabar region, Kerala; Leaders: Sayyid Ali, Sayyid Fazl; Cause: Against oppression and exploitation of Muslim Moplah peasants by Hindu Zamindars and British Government.
  • Indigo Revolt (1860) – Nadia district of Bengal; Leaders: Digambar Biswas, Bishnu Bishwas, Harish Chandra Mukherjee (editor of newspaper Hindu Patriot); Cause: Peasants forced to grow indigo by European factory owners; Dinbandhu Mitra wrote about it in the play Neel Darpan (translated by Madhusudan Datta).
  • Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) – Pune; Founder: MG Ranade; Aim: To popularise the peasant’s ‘legal rights’.
  • Eka Movement (1921) – Awadh; Leader: Madari Pasi; Cause: Higher extraction of rent.
  • Champaran Satyagraha (1917) – Bihar; Leaders: Gandhiji, Dr. Rajendra Prasad; Cause: Against the Tin Kathia System imposed by European Indigo planters.
  • Kheda Satyagraha (1918) – Gujarat; Leader: Gandhiji; Cause: Against ignored appeal for remission of band revenue in case of crop failure.
  • UP Kisan Sabha (1918) – Uttar Pradesh; Leaders: Indira Narain Dwivedi, Madan Mohan Malviya.
  • Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920) – Oudh; Leaders: JL Nehru, Baba Rama Chandra; Aim: To organise peasants.
  • Andhra Ryots Association (1928) – Andhra Pradesh; Leader: NG Ranga; Aim: Abolition of Zamindari.
  • All India Kisan Sabha (1936) – Lucknow; Leader: Swami Sahajananda; Aim: Protection of peasants from economic exploitation.
  • Bijolia Movement (1905, 1913, 1916, 1927) – Rajasthan; Leaders: Sitaram Das, Vijay Pathhik Singh; Cause: Imposition of 86 different types of cesses on peasants.
  • Tibhaga Movement (1946) – Bengal; Leaders: Communists; Cause: Against Zamindars and moneylenders.
  • Telangana Movement (1945-1951) – Hyderabad; Cause: Against moneylenders and officials of Nizam of Hyderabad.
  • All India Trade Union, 1920 – Bombay; Leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai, Joseph Baptista, NM Joshi; Aim: To establish a social state in India and safeguard workers' rights.

Important National Leaders

  • Annie Besant (1847-1933): Founded Theosophical Society in India, started Home Rule League, established Central Hindu School and College at Banaras (later BHU), President of Calcutta Session of INC (1917), edited New India and Commonwealth, translated Gita into English as The Lotus Song.
  • Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1857-1920): Title ‘Lokmanya’, established English school at Poona, joined INC (1891), started Arms Act Resolution, initiated Ganapati pooja (1893) and Shivaji festival (1896), part of the ‘Lal‑Bal‑Pal’ extremist trio, founded Home Rule League (1916), contributed to Lucknow Pact and Reforms Act (1919).

subject: History
text:
Bhagat Singh (1907-1931)

  • Started Punjab Naujawan Bharat Sabha in 1926 to carry out political work among youth, peasants and workers on Marxist ideologies.
  • Organised Lahore students union with Sukhdev for open legal work among students.
  • In 1928, collaborated with revolutionaries Chandrashekhar Azad, Bejoy Kumar Sinha, Shiv Verma, Jaidev Kapur and Bhagwati Charan Vohra to consolidate Kriti Kisan Party and Hindustan Republican Association into Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA).
  • Killed British official Saunders in 1928; involved in Lahore conspiracy and bombed Central Legislative Assembly.
  • Executed on 23 March 1931.

details.summary: Revolutionary leader involved in anti‑British activities and executed in 1931.

subject: History
text:
Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (1833-1894)

  • Great scholar best known for composition of hymn Bande Mataram.
  • Novel Durgesnandini published in 1864.
  • Published journal Bangadarsan.

details.summary: Author of national hymn and notable novelist.

subject: History
text:
Bipin Chandra Pal (1858-1932)

  • Title: Mightiest Prophet of Nationalism by Aurobindo Ghosh.
  • Supported Age of Consent Bill, 1891; Swadeshi Movement; fought for Assam tea‑gardeners.
  • Founded newspapers: Paridaashak (weekly); Public Opinion and Tribune (editor); Swaraj (English weekly in London); Hindu Review (English monthly); Independent (daily); Democrate (weekly).
  • Authored book New India.

details.summary: Nationalist leader and prolific journalist.

subject: History
text:
Chakravarthi Rajagopalachari (1879-1972)

  • Politician and lawyer from Tamil Nadu; gave up practice during NCM.
  • Started CDM in Tamil Nadu; arrested for leading Salt March from Trichinopoly to Vedaranniyam on Tanjore coast.
  • Governor of Bengal (Aug‑Nov 1947); first and last Indian Governor‑General of India (1948‑50).
  • Minister of Home Affairs in first cabinet; founded Swatantra Party in 1959.
  • Collected works titled Satyameva Jayate; awarded Bharat Ratna in 1954.

details.summary: First Indian Governor‑General and political leader.

subject: History
text:
Dadabhai Naoroji (1825-1917)

  • First Indian to demand Swaraj in Calcutta Session of INC, 1906.
  • Known as Indian Gladstone, Grand Old Man of India.
  • First Indian elected to House of Commons on Liberal Party ticket.
  • Authored Poverty and Un‑British Rule in India (1901) highlighting draining of wealth by British.

details.summary: Pioneer of Indian nationalism and economic critique.

subject: History
text:
Dr Bhimrao Ambedkar (1891-1956)

  • Leader of depressed classes; eminent jurist.
  • Founded Peoples Education Society; Depressed Classes Institute (1924); Samaj Samata Sangh (1927).
  • Participated in Three Round Table Conferences; signed Poona Pact with Gandhiji in 1932.
  • Embraced Buddhism towards end of life.

details.summary: Architect of Indian Constitution and social reformer.

subject: History
text:
Dr Rajendra Prasad (1884-1963)

  • Founded National College at Patna.
  • Minister in charge of Food and Agriculture in Interim Government (1946).
  • President of Constituent Assembly; first President of Indian Republic.
  • Honoured with Bharat Ratna in 1962.
  • Edited newspaper Desh (Hindi weekly).

details.summary: First President of India and key constitutional figure.

subject: History
text:
Gopal Krishna Gokhale (1886-1915)

  • Political guru of Gandhi.
  • President of Banaras Session of INC, 1905; supported Swadeshi Movement.
  • Founded Servants of Indian Society in 1905 to train national missionaries.
  • Edited newspaper sudharak.

details.summary: Reformist leader and mentor to Gandhi.

subject: History
text:
Jawaharlal Nehru (1889-1964)

  • General‑Secretary of INC in 1928; President in 1929.
  • Independence resolution passed under his presidency at Lahore Session.
  • First Prime Minister of Republic India (1947‑1964); architect of modern India.
  • Authored Doctrine of Panchseel; advocated non‑alignment.
  • Authored books: The Discovery of India, Glimpses of World History, A Bunch of Old Letters, The Unity of India, Independence and After, India and the World.

details.summary: First Prime Minister and visionary leader.

subject: History
text:
Lala Lajpat Rai (1865-1928)

  • Called The Lion of Punjab (Sher‑a‑Punjab).
  • Inspired by Mahatma Hans Raj; Arya Samajist; helped establish DAV College at Lahore.
  • President of special session of Congress at Calcutta, 1920.
  • Opposed withdrawal of NCM in 1922.

details.summary: Prominent nationalist leader from Punjab.

subject: History
text: Lala Lajpat Rai founded the Swaraj Party with Motilal Nehru and CR Das. He was injured during a demonstration against the Simon Commission in 1928. He served as the editor of the newspapers ‘Bande Matram’, ‘the Punjab’ and ‘the People’.

details.summary: Notes on Lala Lajpat Rai's role in the Swaraj Party, Simon Commission protest, and editorial work.

subject: History
text: Mahatma Gandhi came to India in 1915, having already started Satyagraha in South Africa. In 1907 he started Satyagraha against compulsory registration and passes for Indians. In 1910 he initiated Satyagraha against immigration restrictions and the derecognition of Non‑Christian Indian marriages. He led the Champaran Satyagraha in 1917 against the tinakathia system. In 1918 he led the Ahmedabad mill strike demanding plague bonus for workers. The Kheda Satyagraha was also led by him in 1918 for the demand of non‑payment of tax due to famine. During the Ahmedabad Satyagraha, Gandhi advised workers to strike and undertook a hunger strike, after which mill owners accepted a tribunal award of a 35% wage increase. In Kheda, peasants were in extreme distress due to crop failure; Gandhi advised them to withhold revenue and fight to death.

details.summary: Chronology of Gandhi's early Satyagraha movements and key actions in Champaran, Ahmedabad, and Kheda.

subject: History
text: Rabindranath Tagore (1861‑1941) was a poet, philosopher, educationist, internationalist and patriot. His elder brother, Satyendranath Tagore, was the first Indian to join the ICS. He founded Shantiniketan near Bolpore on 22 December 1901. He wrote Gitanjali, which earned him the Nobel Prize in 1913. On nationalism he remarked, “Nationalism is a great menace. It is the particular thing which for years has been at the bottom of India’s troubles. And in as such as we have been ruled and dominated by a nation that is strictly political in its attitude, we have tried to develop within ourselves despite our inheritance from the past, a belief in our eventual political destiny”. His compositions were adopted as national anthems by two nations: (i) India – Jana Gana Mana; (ii) Bangladesh – Amar Sonar Bangla.

details.summary: Overview of Tagore’s literary, educational contributions and his views on nationalism.

subject: History
text: Subhash Chandra Bose (1897‑1945) passed the Indian Civil Services Examination in 1920 in England but left it on Gandhiji’s call of the Non‑Cooperation Movement. He founded the Independence for India League with Jawaharlal Nehru. He was elected President of the Indian National Congress at its Haripura Session (1938) and Tripuri Session (1939), but resigned from the Tripuri presidency due to differences with Gandhiji. He founded the Forward Bloc in 1939. He escaped to Berlin in 1941 and met Hitler. He took charge of the Indian Army (Azad Hind Fauz) in 1943 in Singapore and set up the Indian Provisional Government there. He addressed Mahatma Gandhi as the Father of the Nation in a radio broadcast. He reportedly died in a plane crash in 1945. His famous slogans were “Dilli Chalo” and “Jai Hind”. His autobiography is titled The India Struggle.

details.summary: Key events in Bose’s life: ICS resignation, Congress presidency, Forward Bloc, Azad Hind Fauz, and his slogans.

subject: History
text: Sarojini Naidu (1879‑1949), popularly known as the Nightingale of India, became the first woman to participate in India’s struggle for independence. She joined the Dandi March with Gandhiji and presided over the Kanpur Session of Congress in 1925. She was the first woman to become the Governor of Uttar Pradesh State. Her notable books include: The Golden Threshold (1905), The Feather of the Dawn, The Bird of Time (1912) and The Broken Wing (1917).

details.summary: Highlights of Sarojini Naidu’s political role, governorship, and literary works.
