| Near | Close | Although he was near the truck, he nearly escaped. |
| Nearly | Almost | |

details.summary: Grammar rules regarding the correct usage of adjectives, including degree consistency, correct noun qualifiers, ordinal placement, and specific word usage.

subject: English
text:
Articles are members of the determiners family. 'A', 'An' and 'The' are articles. Articles are used before nouns.

  • e.g., My brother is a businessman.
  • e.g., An apple a day keeps the doctor away.

Here, 'a' is an article used before the noun 'businessman' and 'an' is an article used before the noun 'apple'.

details.summary: Definition and basic usage of articles A, An, and The.

subject: English
text:
Indefinite Articles

  • Indefinite article 'A' is used before words starting with consonants.
  • Indefinite article 'An' is used with words starting with vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u).

Examples:

  • An umbrella is kept there.
  • A European lives in our colony.
  • Meerut has a university.
  • An honest and hardworking person always succeeds in life.
  • An hour is left.
  • An MA, An SP, An LLB

Use of Indefinite Articles

  1. Before a common noun in singular to suggest the sense of one: e.g., Twelve inches make a foot; There is a fan in the room; A man is standing on the road.
  2. Before a common noun in singular to suggest the vague sense of a certain or any: e.g., A book is kept there.
  3. To make a common noun of a proper noun: e.g., Ajay is a Sherlok Holmes of our class; Samudragupta was the Napoleon of India.
  4. In the sense of each, every or per: e.g., The doctor advised the patient to take the medicine twice a day; He studies for two hours a day.
  5. In exclamations before singular countable nouns: e.g., What a shot!; What a beautiful girl!

details.summary: Detailed rules for the usage of indefinite articles 'A' and 'An'.

subject: English
text:
Definite Article

Use of Definite Article 'The'

  1. When we speak of a particular person or thing or one already referred to: e.g., The book is kept there; The CD of that movie is available in the market; The book you mentioned is available in the store; The pleasant weather is inviting us outside.
  2. Before the names of physical features in Geography: e.g., The Himalayas, The Gangas, The Indian Ocean, etc. Note: If the reference is to a Single Island or a Single Mountain, 'the' is not used (e.g., Kanchenjunga is the highest peak of the Himalayas in India; North Andaman is a part of the Andaman group of islands).
  3. Before common nouns which are names of things unique or of their kind: e.g., The Sun, The Moon, The Earth, The Sky.
  4. Before the names of countries which show federation: e.g., The United States of America, The United Kingdom, The Republic of Korea, The Republic of South Africa, etc. (Exception: The Netherlands, The Hague).
  5. Before the names of religious and mythological books, newspapers, magazines, journals, etc.: e.g., The Bible, The India Today, The Times of India, etc.
  6. Before Superlatives: e.g., I am the best; He is the cleverest.
  7. As an adverb with a comparative: e.g., The more, the merrier; The sooner, the better; The higher you go, the colder it is.
  8. Before terms denoting Nationality, Community and Castes: e.g., The Australians, The Indians, The Hindus, etc.
  9. Before historic events: e.g., The Ist Battle of Panipat, The Revolt of 1857, The Quit India Movement, The Gulf War, etc.
  10. Before musical instruments: e.g., I can play the flute very well; Ustad Amjad Ali Khan plays the sarod.

details.summary: Comprehensive rules for the usage of the definite article 'The'.

subject: English
text:
Usage of Articles:

  • (k) Before an adjective when it represents a class of people. e.g., The rich should help the poor., The old should be respected by the young.
  • (l) Before a unit of measurement. e.g., Cloth is sold by the metre., Bananas are sold by the dozen.
  • (m) Before a common noun to give the force of superlative. e.g., He is the man., This is the thing to do.
  • (n) Before the adjectives 'same' and 'whole' and after the adjectives 'all' and 'both'. e.g., He is the same person that I saw yesterday., The whole class performed splendidly., All the boys passed with flying colours., Both the friends were present there.
  • (o) Before a common noun to give it the meaning of an abstract noun. e.g., The moralist in Gandhi revolted against injustice., The judge in him prevailed upon the father and he sentenced his son to death.
  • (p) Before various Cups and Trophies. e.g., Sri Lanka has won the Asia Cup., Almost all countries participate in the Olympics.
  • (q) Before comparative degree in case of a choice. e.g., He is the stronger of the two friends.

Omission of Articles:

  • (a) Before proper nouns. e.g., The New Delhi is the capital of India. (X)
  • (b) Before material noun and abstract noun used in general sense. e.g., The building is made up of the brick and the stone. (X), The building is made up of brick and stone. (✓), I have the love for you. (X), I have love for you. (✓), The care of the old is necessary. (X), Care of the old is necessary. (✓). Note: If material/abstract noun shows specific cases, article should be used. e.g., The stone of Kota is of good quality., The love I have for you is unconditional and infinite.
  • (c) Before a noun used in its widest sense. e.g., The science is a subject based on facts. (X), Science is a subject based on facts. (✓), The man is immortal. (X), Man is immortal. (✓), The tiger is the national animal of India. (X), Tiger is the national animal of India. (✓)
  • (d) Before the noun following 'kind of'. e.g., What kind of a person you are? (X), What kind of person you are? (✓), What kind of a book is it? (X), What kind of book is it? (✓)
  • (e) Before uncountable nouns. e.g., He gave me advice., He passed on information to me.
  • (f) Before school, college, home, church, temple, sea, work, bed, table, hospital, market, prison, court. However, when their purpose is thought of rather than the actual building, 'the' is used. e.g., I go to church every Sunday., I go to bed early these days.
  • (g) Before names of diseases. e.g., AIDS can be prevented using safety measures., Cancer can be treated if detected early.
  • (h) Before regular meals except when preceded by an Adjective. e.g., I usually take breakfast at 9 o'clock., We should take dinner atleast two hours before the sleeping time to avoid indigestion., They gave us a sumptuous lunch.
  • (i) Before modes of travel. e.g., He will go by air., Journey by road takes time.
  • (j) Before names of relations like uncle, mother, father, etc. e.g., Uncle will come tomorrow., Father is working on a project.
  • (k) Before adjectives used as nouns signifying a language or colours. e.g., He doesn't know Hindi, but he knows English., I like red and blue.
  • (l) When two or more descriptive adjectives qualifying the same noun are connected by 'and', the Article is used before the first adjective only. e.g., It is a Hindi and English Dictionary. (Here, the dictionary is one).
  • (m) When two or more adjectives qualify different nouns, expressed or understood, the Article is used before each adjective. e.g., The inner and the outer wall were both strongly defended., He possesses a black dog and a white bitch.

details.summary: Detailed rules regarding the usage and omission of articles in English grammar, specifically focusing on common errors in sentence construction.

subject: English
text:
An adverb tells more about a verb, an adjective or another adverb.

Example: He is running fast. (Here 'fast' is the adverb which tells how he is running.)

Kinds of Adverb

  • Adverb of Time: Answers the question when, for how long or how often a certain thing happens. (e.g., I shall meet you tomorrow; We were late by two hours; The newspaper arrives daily.)
  • Adverb of Place: Answers the question where. (e.g., I shall meet you in the market; I shall meet you there; We were studying in the institute.)
  • Adverb of Manner: Answers the question how. (e.g., He is sitting quietly; He is dancing like Hritik Roshan.)
  • Adverb of Frequency: It tells us how often an action takes place. (e.g., Delhi Police is with you, always.)
  • Adverb of Degree or Quantity: These tell us how much or in what degree or to what extent. (e.g., We have studied enough; There is something fishy out here; There is little doubt of his success.)

details.summary: Definition and classification of adverbs into Time, Place, Manner, Frequency, and Degree/Quantity.

subject: English
text:
Rules of Adverbs

  • So and Too: They should not be used without their co-relatives 'that' and 'to'. (e.g., He is so rich (X); He is so rich that he can buy anything (✓); He is too intelligent (X); He is too intelligent to pass any exam (✓).)
  • Difference between very and much: (a) 'Very' is used in positive degree and 'much' is used in comparative degree. (b) 'Very' is used with V1 + ing. 'Much' is used with V3.
  • Form retention: Some words retain their form when they become adverbs: Fast, first, next, back, ill, better, best, etc.
  • Comparative/Superlative: Adverbs ending in -ly form the comparative by adding 'more' and superlative by adding 'most'.
  • MPT RULE: If adverbs of manner, place and time are used in a single sentence, then the sequence followed is that of MPT.
  • Placement: Adverbs of manner, place and time are generally placed after the verb or after the object of the verb.
  • Adjective modification: When an adverb modifies an adjective or another adverb, the adverb comes before it.
  • Frequency placement: Adverbs of frequency such as always, ever, never, seldom, frequently, etc., are always placed before the verb they modify.
  • 'Enough': Is both an Adjective and an Adverb. As an adverb, it is always placed after the adjective it modifies. As an adjective it is placed before the noun.
  • 'Only' and 'even': Should be placed immediately before the word intended to modify.
  • Sentence beginning: An adverb can be placed at the beginning of a sentence, when it is intended to qualify, not any word in particular, but sentence as a whole.
  • 'Ever' vs 'Never': 'Ever' is sometimes misused for 'never'. 'Seldom or never' and 'seldom if ever' are both correct, but 'seldom or ever' is incorrect.

details.summary: Comprehensive rules governing the usage, placement, and comparative forms of adverbs.

subject: English
text:
13. 'Else' should be followed by 'but', and not by 'than'.
e.g. - It is nothing else than / but his carelessness which has led to his failure.
- Aishwarya Rai is nothing else but a statue of beauty.

14. 'Rather' and 'Fairly' can mean moderately. But 'fairly' is used with favourable adjectives and adverbs while 'rather' is used with unfavourable adjectives and adverbs.
e.g. - She is fairly intelligent but my sister is rather stupid.
- He did fairly well in her exams but his sister did rather badly.
- He grew up in rather unusual circumstances.

15. 'Rather' can also be used when we are correcting something that we have just said.
e.g. - The process is not a circle but rather a spiral.

16. 'Rather' is also used in case of preference—would rather, had rather, rather than are used to express preference.
e.g. - I would rather study than sleep.
- I prefer getting up early rather than sleeping late.

17. We use 'rather' before verbs that introduce our thoughts and feelings, in order to express our opinion politely, especially when a different opinion has been expressed.
e.g. - I rather think that he was telling the truth.
- I rather like the decorative effect.

18. Adverb 'as' should be used to introduce predicative of the verbs such as regard, describe, define, treat, view, know.
e.g. - I regard him as my elder brother.
- The newspapers described the situation as horrible.
- Biology is defined as the study of nature.

19. Adverb 'as' should not be used to introduce predicative of the verbs such as name, elect, think, consider, call, appoint, make, choose.
e.g. - He was considered the best dancer of his time.
- He was appointed Governor by the President.
- Saurav Ganguly was chosen the captain.
- He was called dynamic by his mates.

20. Negative Adverbs should not be used with the words that are already negative in sense. So two negatives in the same sentence should be avoided. Seldom, nowhere, never, nothing, hardly, scarcely, neither, barely, rarely are some of the Adverbs. The verbs in such category are 'deny', 'forbid', while the conjunctions are 'unless', 'until', 'lest' and 'both'.
e.g. - No one scarcely practises all the exercises. (X)
- Scarcely anyone practises all the exercises. (✓)
- I rarely went to meet nobody/anybody in my childhood.
- She hardly knows anything/nothing about me.
- He does nothing without ever/never consulting me.
- He has denied that he was not going there.
- Walk steadily, lest you should not fall.
- Both of them are not coming. (X)
- Neither of them is coming. (✓)

21. Consider the following cases
(a) 'Coward', 'miser', 'niggard', 'rogue' are Nouns. 'Cowardly', 'miserly', 'niggardly', 'roguish' are Adjectives.
e.g. - An officer is trained never to fight cowardly/in a cowardly manner.
- Although he seems brave, he is actually a coward.
- It was a sheer cowardly act of violence.
(b) 'Fast' retains its form in both Adjective and Adverb.
e.g. - He is fast (Adjective).
- He is running fast (Adverb).
(c) 'Direct' and 'Directly' are adverbs. Direct means straight and Directly means at once.
e.g. - Don't stop anywhere, return home direct.
- Don't stop now, return home directly.
(d) 'Manly', 'masterly', 'slovenly', 'monthly', 'weekly', 'sickly', 'friendly' are Adjectives and should not be confused with Adverbs.
e.g. - He is earning fifty thousand rupees monthly / a month.
- He is a friendly old man.

22. The use of 'never' for 'not' is incorrect, because 'never' means not ever.
e.g. - I never remember having met him. (X)
- I do not remember ever having met him. (✓)
- We met the other day, but he never referred to the matter. (X)
- We met the other day, but he did not refer to the matter. (✓)

23. No sentence should begin with 'Due to'. It must be used after some form of the verb 'to be'.
e.g. - Due to bad weather, the match was abandoned. (X)
- It was due to bad weather, the match was abandoned. (✓)

24. Cent-per cent It should be hundred per cent.

25. Do the needful It should be do what is necessary.

details.summary: Grammar rules regarding the usage of adverbs, adjectives, and specific phrases for error spotting.

subject: English
text:
A conjunction is a part of speech that connects words, phrases, clauses or sentences. e.g. - and, but, while, though, although, lest etc.

Rules of Conjunctions

  • 1. 'Scarcely' and 'Hardly' should be followed by when and not by than. e.g. - Scarcely had I started for the institute, when the rain started. Hardly had he arrived, when he had to leave again.
  • 2. 'No sooner' is followed by than and not by when. e.g. - No sooner had I left, than the rain started. No sooner did he arrive, than he had to leave.
  • 3. 'Seldom or never' and 'seldom if ever' are both correct, but 'seldom or ever' is incorrect. e.g. - He seldom or never goes to see movies in a theatre.
  • 4. 'Either-or', 'Neither-nor', 'not only-but also', 'both-and', 'whether-or' etc., should be followed by the same parts of speech or of the same function.
  • 5. The conjunctions 'though' (or although) and 'but' do the work of setting one statement against another by way of oppositions or contrast and therefore, the correlative of 'though' is 'yet' or a comma (,). e.g. - Though he worked hard yet he could not top the class.
  • 6. After the adjective 'other' (which is regarded as a kind of comparative), the only word that can be correctly used for contrasting one thing with another is 'than'. The prepositions from, but, except in such a connection are wrong. e.g. - He had no other option than to fight. He had another reason from what he professed. She had no other claim to the post except her good looks.
  • 7. Conjunction 'that' is not used in the following cases: (a) Direct narration. e.g. - He said, "I am smart". (b) Indirect speech, if the sentence is interrogative. e.g. - He asked who he was.
  • 8. In a 'not only......but also' sentence, the verb should agree with the noun or pronoun mentioned second, because this is the part emphasised. e.g. - Not only the teacher but also the students are enjoying themselves.
  • 9. 'Such as' is used to denote a category, whereas 'such that' emphasises the degree of something by mentioning its consequences. e.g. - Yuvraj played such an innings as played by the best batsman. Yuvraj played such an innings that it took the match away from the opposition.
  • 10. 'Both' is followed by and not by as well as. Besides, both has positive sense and cannot be used in negative sentences.
  • 11. 'Unless' means if not and therefore, it should not be used in a sentence or clause which is already negative. e.g. - Unless you do not work hard, you will fail. (X) Unless you work hard, you will fail. (✓)
  • 12. 'Lest' expresses a negative sense and therefore cannot be used with not. 'Should' is always used with 'lest'. e.g. - Walk steadily, lest you should not fall. (X) Walk steadily, lest you should fall. (✓)
  • 13. When 'suppose' is used in the beginning of a sentence to denote a command or a request, it is not followed by if. e.g. - Suppose if you are caught, what will happen (X) Suppose you are caught, what will happen (✓)
  • 14. Avoid the error of using 'than' for 'from' after the adjective different. e.g. - He took a different role from the ones he has been doing for long.
  • 15. 'Nothing else' should be followed by but, not by than. e.g. - It is nothing else but your carelessness, that you have failed in the exam.
  • 16. The use of Present tense after as if and as though should be avoided. [Subjunctive Mood]. e.g. - He looks as if he suspects something. (X) He looks as if he suspected something. (✓)

details.summary: Grammatical rules governing the usage of various conjunctions in English language for competitive examinations.

subject: English
text:
Errors of Conjunction

  • 'Although' takes 'yet' as a correlative, not 'but'.
  • 'Such...that' is used for mentioning consequences.
  • 'Such' is often redundant in certain contexts.
  • 'Hardly' is followed by 'when', not 'where'.
  • 'No sooner' is followed by 'than'.
  • 'Not only' is followed by 'but also'.
  • 'Whether' is used for choices/alternatives.
  • 'Both' is followed by 'and'.
  • 'Seldom' is followed by 'if ever' or 'if never'.

details.summary: This section covers common grammatical errors related to conjunctions in English, focusing on correlative conjunctions and proper sentence structure.

subject: English
text:
Preposition is a word that connects a noun, pronoun to another word, especially to a verb, another noun or an adjective.

  • In: Used for bigger places (towns, cities, countries) while 'at' is used for smaller places. e.g., I live at Shastri Nagar in Meerut.
  • In / Into: 'In' is used in speaking of things at rest. 'Into' is used in speaking of things in motion. e.g., He is shopping in the market; He jumped into the well; He is falling in love; He is in the office; The snake crawled into the hole; The cup broke-off into a hundred pieces.
  • On / Upon: 'On' denotes position, 'upon' denotes movement. e.g., The cat is on the table; The cat pounced upon the mouse.
  • With / By: 'With' denotes the 'instrument' and 'by' denotes the 'agent'. e.g., The letter was written by him with his pen; The music was generated by/with a guitar; The murder was committed by him with a pistol; The ball was hit by the batsman with his bat.
  • Ago / Before: 'Ago' refers to past time while 'before' denotes precedence between two events. e.g., Long ago, there was a king named Rama; Ram existed before Mahabharata was fought; He came before me; The train arrived before the scheduled time; India achieved independence 69 years ago.
  • Above / Below / Over / Under: 'Above' and 'below' merely denote position while 'over' and 'under' also carry a sense of covering or movement. e.g., We live below the roof; Sky is above us; Train is running under the bridge; The train is standing below the bridge; The bird is flying over the pond; A wire is passing above the building; I was wearing two sweaters under the jacket.
  • Under: Used before a noun to indicate that a person or thing is being affected by something or is going through a particular process. e.g., I'm rarely under pressure and my co-workers are always nice to me. 'Under' can mean junior in ranks. e.g., He is under me. If something happens 'under' a particular person or government, it happens when that person or government is in power. e.g., There will be no new taxes under his leadership.

details.summary: Definitions and usage rules for common English prepositions including In, Into, On, Upon, With, By, Ago, Before, Above, Below, Over, and Under.

subject: English
text:
Usage of 'under' and 'beneath':

  • 'Under' is used for a particular name, e.g., The patient was registered under a false name.
  • 'Beneath' is used for abstract meanings, e.g., Beneath the festive mood, there is an underlying apprehension; Everybody thought that she was marrying beneath her; Many find themselves having to take jobs far beneath them.

7. Difference between 'on time', 'in time' and 'in good time':

  • 'On time' signifies absolutely right time, neither before nor after (e.g., The flight is on time).
  • 'In time' means you are not late for the event (e.g., I arrived just in time for my flight).
  • 'In good time' means with comfortable margin (e.g., I arrived at the airport in good time).

8. Difference between at the beginning/at the end and in the beginning/in the end:

  • 'At the beginning' means literally at the beginning (e.g., India scored fast at the beginning of the match).
  • 'At the end' means literally at the end (e.g., At the end of the book, you'll find the bibliography).
  • 'In the beginning' (or at first) implies the early stage (e.g., Sachin was nervous in the beginning, later he settled down).
  • 'In the end' (or at last) means eventually/after sometime (e.g., At first he was scared, but in the end he started enjoying).

9. Verbs requiring no preposition in active voice:

No preposition is placed after: Order, request, reach, attack, resemble, emphasise, accompany, discuss, investigate, comprise, enter (come into), flee (a place), join, affect, board, etc.

10. Omit 'to' after verbs of communication:

Omit 'to' after advise, tell, ask, beg, command, encourage, request, inform, order.

11. 'Till' vs 'Until':

  • 'Till' is used for particular time, 'until' for indefinite time.
  • Only 'until' is used at the starting of a sentence.

12. 'Till' for time and 'upto' for place:

e.g., We shall work till 5 pm; We walked upto the station.

13. Preposition usage with multiple words:

The same preposition should not be used with two words unless it is appropriate to each of them (e.g., It is different from and inferior to the other).

14. 'Since' and 'from':

'Since' is used in perfect tense for a point of time. 'From' is used with other tenses for a period of time.

15. Prepositions with time phrases:

  • Use 'in' for morning, afternoon, evening.
  • Use 'at' for dawn, daybreak, noon, midday, midnight.
  • No preposition if qualified by 'last' or 'next'.

16. Across / Through:

e.g., Walk across a road and pass through a tunnel.

details.summary: Detailed grammatical rules regarding the correct usage of prepositions and specific verb-preposition constraints in English grammar.

subject: English
text:
• Between/Among: 'Between' is used while referring to two persons/things whereas 'Among' is used for more than two. e.g., Between the two of you, who is stronger? The sweets are to be distributed among ten friends.
  • Beside/Besides: 'Beside' means by the side of, whereas 'Besides' means in addition to. e.g., Besides eating, he is also watching T.V. You were sitting beside him.
  • From/Between: 'From' is normally used with to/till, whereas 'Between' is used with and. e.g., He works from nine to six (or nine till six). The meeting was scheduled to be held between 2 pm and 3 pm.
  • Within/In: 'Within' means before the end of time, whereas 'In' means at the end of time. e.g., He will return in five minutes. He will return within five minutes.

subject: English
text:
This page provides detailed grammatical explanations for error spotting questions.

  • 2. Replace 'with' by 'by'.

subject: English
topic: Rules of Nouns and Correct Usage
text:
Key grammatical rules and error detection principles regarding nouns:

  • Rule of 'One of the': The phrase 'one of the' is always followed by a plural noun. For example, 'bad habit' must be replaced by 'bad habits'.
  • Uncountable Nouns Always Used in Singular Form:
    • The noun 'scenery' is uncountable and always used in the singular form (never 'sceneries').
    • The noun 'furniture' is singular and uncountable. Hence, correct phrasing is: 'All the furniture has been...'
    • The noun 'luggage' is always used in a singular form (e.g., 'They left their luggage...').
    • The word 'gear' is used in singular form rather than 'gears' when referring to equipment/apparatus in general.
  • Usage of 'Mob' vs. 'Crowd': A 'mob' specifically refers to a 'group of people with one common thought of criminal consequence' or an unruly gathering, whereas a general collection of people is a 'crowd'.
  • Force vs. Forces: When conveying military or armed personnel, the word 'forces' must be used instead of 'force' (e.g., Indian Military forces).
  • Collective Nouns / Collocations: A collection of flowers is a 'bouquet', whereas for grapes, the collective noun used is 'bunch'.
  • Compound Nouns Pluralization: The plural form of compound nouns formed with prepositions is made by adding '-s' to the root word. Thus, the plural of 'brother-in-law' is 'brothers-in-law'.
  • Agreement with Demonstratives/Quantifiers ('Kind' and 'Sort'): When referring to plural entities:
    • When referring to a plural number of items (e.g., shirts), use 'kinds' instead of 'kind'.
    • When referring to plural persons (e.g., 'people'), use 'sorts' instead of 'sort'.

details.summary: Covers essential rules on noun forms (uncountable singulars like scenery, luggage, furniture), proper collective nouns, pluralization of compound nouns, and distinction between terms like mob vs. crowd and force vs. forces.

mcq.question: Which of the following is the correct plural form of the compound noun 'brother-in-law'?
mcq.explanation: The plural of compound nouns joined by prepositions is formed by adding 's' to the principal word. Hence, 'brothers-in-law' is correct.

subject: English
text:
Essential rules concerning pronoun-antecedent agreement, placement, and redundancy in sentence correction:

  • Position of Impersonal Pronoun 'It': The pronoun 'It' must be placed before the phrase or clause to which it refers, usually coming at the beginning of the sentence.
  • Pronoun Agreement with 'One of them': As the subject refers to a singular individual ('One of them'), it must take a singular pronoun (e.g., replacing plural 'their' with singular masculine/generic 'his').
  • Singular Reference to Nouns: When referring to a singular individual (e.g., a single teacher), singular pronouns must be used (e.g., replacing 'them' with 'him').
  • Redundant Pronouns: Unnecessary pronouns should be removed if the noun subject has already been established and no relative or coordinating clause requires a separate subject pronoun (e.g., redundant use of 'he' or 'it').
  • Pronoun Usage with 'Each': In contextual pronoun references where a group represented distributively is referred to subsequently in plural context, proper case and number alignment must be maintained.

details.summary: Examines pronoun agreement rules, placement of introductory 'It', singular pronoun agreement with 'one of', and avoidance of superfluous/redundant pronouns.

mcq.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: One of them has submitted their project.
One of them has submitted his project.
One of them have submitted his project.
One of them have submitted their project.
mcq.explanation: 'One of them' takes a singular verb ('has') and a singular pronoun ('his').

subject: English
topic: Rules of Conjunctions, Negation, and Inversion
text:
Key grammatical rules governing conjunctions, double negatives, and inversion:

  • Correlative Conjunctions and Negatives: Use 'nor' instead of phrases like 'not to ignore' in negative correlative contexts (Item 68).
  • Double Negatives with 'Until' and 'Lest': 'Until' and 'lest' are inherently negative words. Do not use negative words like 'do not' or 'not' in clauses introduced by 'until' (Item 74) or 'lest' (Item 104).
  • Inversion with Negative Adverbs: Negative adverbs/words such as 'Hardly' and 'No sooner' require inverted sentence structure when placed at the beginning:
    • Use 'Hardly had I' instead of 'Hardly I had' (Item 79).
    • Use 'No sooner had he appeared' instead of direct word order (Item 137).
    • Avoid double negatives: remove 'not' when used in proximity to 'hardly' (Item 89).
  • Superfluous Conjunctions: 'Whether' and 'that' are both connectives and cannot be used simultaneously; remove 'that' (Item 105). Do not use 'because' when the sentence begins with 'The reason why...' or 'The reason is...' as 'because' becomes superfluous (Item 118).

details.summary: Rules concerning inverted sentence structure with negative adverbs (hardly, no sooner), eliminating double negatives with until/lest, and avoiding redundant conjunctions.

mcq.question: Which of the following sentences correctly applies inversion?
options: Hardly I had reached the station when the train departed.
Hardly had I reached the station when the train departed.
Hardly I reached the station when the train departed.
Hardly did I reached the station when the train departed.
mcq.explanation: When 'hardly' begins a sentence, auxiliary inversion is required: 'Hardly had I...'

subject: English
topic: Rules of Nouns, Pronouns, and Comparisons
text:
Essential rules on noun forms, pronoun reference, and degrees of comparison:

  • Uncountable and Singular Nouns: Nouns like 'equipment' are uncountable and are not used in a plural form (Item 139). Nouns like 'news', although ending in '-s', are treated as singular and take a singular verb (Item 109).
  • Plural-Only Nouns: The word 'manners' is always used in the plural form when referring to social conduct (Item 108).
  • Compound Noun Modifiers: When a numeral and noun function as an adjective modifying another noun, the modifying noun remains singular (e.g., 'hundred rupee notes' rather than 'hundred rupees notes') (Item 92).
  • Indefinite Pronouns and Quantifiers: 'Some' takes a plural countable noun after it (use 'men' instead of 'man') (Item 131). The structure 'one of the' must be followed by a plural noun and a singular verb (e.g., 'one of the poets') (Item 125).
  • Pronoun Redundancy: The noun 'coward' inherently refers to a person; therefore, using 'person' after coward (e.g., 'coward person') is redundant and 'person' must be omitted (Item 87).
  • Rules of Comparison: When comparing one thing with others of the same class using comparative degree, use 'other' (e.g., 'any other democracy', 'other poet') to exclude the subject from the group (Items 112, 120). In parallel comparisons, use the demonstrative pronoun 'that of' before the second term to maintain logical comparison (Items 76, 80).

details.summary: Rules governing noun numbers, uncountable nouns (equipment, news), plural usage (manners), compound adjectives, and logical parallel comparisons using 'that of' and 'any other'.

mcq.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: He bought five hundred rupees notes.
He bought five hundred rupee notes.
He bought five hundred rupees note.
He bought five hundreds rupee notes.
mcq.explanation: When functioning as a compound adjective before a noun, hyphenated/modifying currency units remain singular: 'hundred rupee notes'.

subject: English
topic: Rules of Verb Tenses, Indirect Speech, and Gerunds
text:
Important principles of verb forms, tenses, and indirect speech:

  • Past Perfect for Prior Actions: When two past events are described, the earlier/prior action must take the past perfect tense:
    • Use 'he had claimed' instead of 'he claimed' (Item 100).
    • Use 'had come' instead of 'came' for the former event (Item 107).
    • Use 'had seen' instead of 'has seen' where context requires past perfect (Item 94).
  • Present Perfect Continuous: For an action that started in the past and is continuing into the present, use the present perfect continuous tense ('have been waiting', 'has been' instead of 'am waiting' or 'is') (Items 134, 135).
  • Habitual and Stative Verbs: Verbs expressing habit or routine are not used in continuous/progressive forms (use 'goes' instead of 'is going') (Item 102). Stative verbs of cognition like 'know' do not take progressive aspect (use 'I knew' instead of 'I was knowing') (Item 90).
  • Indirect Speech and Reporting: In indirect narration, past reporting verbs require subordinate verbs to shift into the corresponding past form (use 'had' in place of 'has') (Item 116). The conjunction 'that' is omitted after the reporting verb 'asked' (Item 73). Indirect interrogative clauses follow assertive word order (e.g., 'why they had' instead of inverted 'why had they') (Item 75).
  • Gerunds and Non-finite Forms: The verb 'prefer' agrees with a gerund (use 'going' rather than 'to go') (Item 113). Ensure the infinitive marker is preserved where required (use 'to refund') (Item 97).
  • Proverbs: Universal truths and proverbs are always expressed in the simple present tense (use 'is' instead of 'was') (Item 82).

details.summary: Verb tense consistency, past perfect for antecedent past events, present perfect continuous for ongoing actions, non-progressive stative verbs, and indirect speech rules.

mcq.question: Which sentence follows the correct sequence of tenses for two completed past actions?
options: The patient died before the doctor arrived.
The patient had died before the doctor arrived.
The patient has died before the doctor arrived.
The patient died before the doctor had arrived.
mcq.explanation: The prior past action takes the Past Perfect tense ('had died') while the subsequent action takes Simple Past ('arrived').

subject: English
text:
Rules regarding prepositions, definite/indefinite articles, and redundant or improper word usage:

  • Fixed Prepositions:
    • 'Sympathise' is followed by 'with' (not 'for') (Item 132).
    • 'Victim' takes the preposition 'of' (not 'from') (Item 114).
    • 'Adhere' is followed by 'to' (Item 128).
    • Travel on foot is phrased as 'on foot', not 'by foot' (Item 91).
    • 'Cope' takes the preposition 'with' only when an object follows it (Item 110).
    • 'Consider' takes no preposition after it (remove 'as') (Item 106).
    • Use 'since' for point of time in perfect tenses instead of 'from' (Item 122).
  • Article Usage: When the preposition 'of' follows a superlative degree adjective (e.g., most, best, greatest), the definite article 'the' must precede it (Item 69). Remove indefinite article 'an' where inappropriate or unneeded (Item 99). Use definite article 'The' instead of 'Such' when referring to a definite antecedent noun (Item 124).
  • Superfluous and Redundant Words:
    • Do not use 'back' redundantly with verbs like return, revert, or recall (Items 77, 93).
    • Remove redundant phrases such as 'as to' (Item 70), 'did' (Item 81), and 'even' (Item 117).
  • Appropriate Word Choice:
    • Use 'room' (unoccupied space) instead of 'place' (Item 111).
    • Use 'complete' (thorough) instead of 'total' (sum of individuals) (Item 123).
    • Use 'watch' instead of 'see' when viewing a dynamic spectacle or event (Item 130).
    • Use 'respectfully' (with deference) instead of 'respectively' (in specified order) (Item 133).
    • Use adverb 'outdoors' in place of adjective 'outdoor' when modifying action (Item 95).
  • Subject-Verb Agreement: Singular verbs are used with the titles or names of books (e.g., 'is' instead of 'are') (Item 83). When the subject is plural, the verb must be plural ('have' instead of 'has') (Items 78, 140).

details.summary: Fixed preposition collocations (sympathise with, victim of, adhere to), proper idiom (on foot), article conventions with superlatives, and distinction between commonly confused words (room vs place, total vs complete, respectively vs respectfully).

mcq.question: Fill in the blank with the appropriate preposition: 'He always prefers to go to school _____ foot.'
mcq.explanation: The correct standard idiomatic expression is 'on foot', not 'by foot'.

subject: English
text:
This section provides grammatical corrections for common errors:

  • Sceneries: Incorrect; use 'scenery' as it is always singular.
  • Primary vs. Breathing: Use 'primary' to denote importance.
  • Conjunctions: Use 'but' for contradictory statements; use 'and' for combined actions.
  • Time Periods: Use 'for' instead of 'since' for durations like 'two days'.
  • Prepositions: Use 'besides' (meaning 'in addition to') instead of 'beside' (meaning 'next to').
  • Comparatives: Use 'the better' when comparing two objects.
  • Subject-Verb Agreement: Use 'is' instead of 'are' when 'either...or' connects subjects, depending on the nearer subject.
  • Pronouns: Use 'who' (nominative) instead of 'whom' (objective) where appropriate.
  • Tense Consistency: Ensure reporting verbs match the tense of the sentence.
  • Articles: Do not use articles before abstract nouns like 'temper'.
  • Gerunds vs. Infinitives: Use gerunds where appropriate for specific verb structures.

details.summary: A list of grammatical error corrections and usage rules for English language proficiency.

subject: English
text:
Vocabulary is a broad concept in itself. One can enhance one's language skills by acquiring a good hold over vocabulary. To score high in the CDS exam (English Paper), a candidate should improve his/her vocabulary skills. It helps one in solving questions of Comprehension, Cloze Test, Antonyms and Synonyms etc.

Here, we illustrate some steps to enrich vocabulary:

  • Step I: Identify the Word - Whenever we come across a new word in a sentence while reading a textbook, newspaper or a magazine, we should look up its meaning. This is the best way to enhance one's vocabulary. Suppose you come across a word 'Antique' and you don't know its meaning, you consult a dictionary and find its meaning which is 'old and often valuable'.
  • Step II: Identify the Antonyms of that Word - Along with the meaning of a word, its antonyms (words with opposite meaning) should also be taken into consideration. A good knowledge of words and their antonyms is very beneficial from the examination point of view. e.g. Opposite of Antique is modern.
  • Step III: Identify the Synonyms of that Word - The knowledge of words that are similar or closer in meaning to a word is very useful. It makes a student efficient enough to have a strong sense of the language. Example: 'Antique' can be replaced by Traditional or Ancient.
  • Step IV: Form a Proper Sentence - This is one of the most important parts in vocabulary building. It serves to stimulate memory by recalling the words as and when needed, apart from making the proper sense and the use of words clear. e.g. To be more familiar with a word, we should use it in sentence form. For 'Antique' a proper sentence is 'People love to purchase antique items.'

details.summary: This chapter outlines the fundamental methodology for building vocabulary for the CDS examination, emphasizing identifying new words, finding antonyms and synonyms, and practicing sentence construction.

subject: English
text:
• Aback: Taken by surprise. Synonyms: Surprised, thrown off guard. Antonyms: Relax, Contended. Example: Everyone was taken aback by Sachin's decision to quit.
  • Abandon: To leave something and never return to it. Synonyms: Desert, Leave. Antonyms: Continue, Carry on. Example: Railways has abandoned their outer signal.
  • Abase: To humiliate. Synonyms: Degrade, Disregard, Dishonour. Antonyms: Regard, Honour, Respect. Example: Abasing someone is immoral.
  • Abashed: Make someone feel embarrassed or ashamed. Synonyms: Embarrass, Humiliate. Antonyms: Unabashed, Undaunted. Example: He is abashed of his own mistakes.
  • Abate: To make or become less strong. Synonyms: Weaken, Lessen. Antonyms: Strengthen, Intensify. Example: We waited for the wind to abate.
  • Abbreviate: To shorten. Synonyms: To abridge, To curtail. Antonyms: Lengthen, Enhance. Example: The voluminous book was abbreviated for the convenience of the students.
  • Abdicate: To give up power. Synonyms: Relinquish, Renounce. Antonyms: Accept. Example: The old king abdicated the throne.
  • Aberrant: straying from the right or normal way. Synonyms: Deviant, atypical. Antonyms: Normal, Usual. Example: Aberrant behaviour can be a sign of rabies in an animal.
  • Abet: To encourage someone to do wrong. Synonyms: Assist, Incite, Encourage. Antonyms: Demotivate, Prevent. Example: She abetted the thief in the robbery.
  • Abeyance: A state of not happening or being used at present. Synonyms: Abandon, Suspension, Discontinuation. Antonyms: Continuation, Resumption. Example: The old generator has been in abeyance for six months.
  • Abhor: To feel hatred or dislike. Synonyms: Detest, Loathe. Antonyms: Like, Admire. Example: The world would be like heaven if all the people abhor none.
  • Abide: To accept something in accordance with. Synonyms: Obey, follow. Antonyms: Flout, Reject. Example: Citizens have to abide by the rules.
  • Abnegate: To give-up; renunciation. Synonyms: Discard, Reject. Antonym: Accept. Example: Abnegating superstitions is advantageous.
  • Abound: To exist in large numbers or amounts. Synonyms: Plenty, Suffice. Antonyms: Scarce, Scanty. Example: Kiwis abound in New Zealand.
  • Abrasive: Showing little concern for feeling of others. Synonyms: Rude, Annoying, Unfriendly. Antonyms: Pleasant, Friendly. Example: Abrasive behaviour of employees may prove harmful to a firm.
  • Abrogate: To end a law, agreement or custom formally. Synonyms: Abandon, Abort. Antonyms: Institute, Introduce. Example: Our country should abrogate outdated laws.
  • Abstain: Withhold or Refrain. Synonyms: Avoid, Cease. Antonyms: Do, Continue. Example: It is worth while to abstain from intoxicants.
  • Abstruse: Difficult to understand, obscure. Synonyms: Esoteric, Perplexing. Antonyms: Clear, Obvious. Example: You are not the only one who finds Enstein's theory abstruse.
  • Absurd: Ridiculous, Unreasonable. Synonyms: Foolish, Ridiculous. Antonyms: Reasonable, Genuine. Example: Political parties indulge in absurd arguments before the election.
  • Abut: To border upon. Synonyms: Adjoin, Lie next to, Adjacent. Antonyms: Far, Opposite. Example: Our land abuts a nature preserve.
  • Abysmal: extremely poor or bad. Synonyms: Awful, Terrible. Antonyms: Good, Pleasant. Example: The quality of her work is abysmal.
  • Accede: To agree. Synonyms: Consent, Acceptance. Antonyms: Disagree, Refusal, Denial. Example: The business contract between the two parties was acceded successfully.
  • Accentuate: To emphasise or to make noticeable. Synonyms: Highlight, Hype. Antonyms: Shadowed, Downtrodden. Example: People often shout to accentuate their opinion.
  • Accessible: Easy to obtain, approachable. Synonyms: Achievable, Acquiresome. Antonyms: Remote, Distant. Example: Everything is accessible with the Internet.
  • Accessory: A thing which can be added to something else in order to make it more useful, versatile or attractive. Synonyms: Adornment, Retrofit. Antonym: Subsidiary. Example: Cellular phones are incomplete without the accessories.
  • Acclaim: Public approval and praise. Synonyms: Praise, Applaud, Cheer. Antonyms: Criticise. Example: Sardar Patel was an acclaimed leader.
  • Accolade: An award or an expression of praise. Synonyms: Appreciation, Honour, Award. Antonym: Criticism. Example: Getting success is a great accolade.

details.summary: Alphabetical vocabulary list starting with 'A' from the CDS Pathfinder book.

subject: English
text:
• Accord: Be harmonious or consistent. Synonyms: Concord, Agreement. Antonyms: Disagree, Contrast. Example: The board of directors could not reach an accord in the annual meeting.
  • Accost: Approach and address angrily or aggressively. Synonyms: Annoy, Confront. Antonyms: Aid, Help. Example: On the mistake of the son, father accosted him.
  • Accrue: To increase in number or amount. Synonyms: To collect, To accumulate. Antonyms: Disperse, Dwindle. Example: Crossing for a single run accrued the score of the team.
  • Adept: Skilful. Synonyms: Expert, Efficient. Antonyms: Unskilled, Inapt. Example: It seems that he is adept in computers.
  • Adjourn: Temporary breaking-off. Synonyms: Suspend, Interrupt. Antonyms: Carry out, Advance. Example: He has adjourned his journey. The court is adjourned for the day.
  • Adjunct: Something joined or added to another thing but is not an essential part of it. Synonyms: Supplement, Addition. Antonyms: Subtraction, Lessening. Example: The witness of the case has adjuncted a new twist in it.
  • Adjure: To urge solemnly. Synonym: Request. Antonym: Answer. Example: On the continuous adjuring of students, a picnic was arranged.
  • Admonish: To warn. Synonyms: Scold, Reprove. Antonyms: Allow, Compliment. Example: The teacher admonished the student for his insolent behaviour.
  • Adorn: Make more beautiful or attractive. Synonyms: To embellish, To decorate. Antonyms: Malign, Deface. Example: The temple is adorned with flowers.
  • Adroit: Very skilful. Synonyms: Expert, Proficient. Antonyms: Unskilled, Incompetent. Example: The showroom needs an adroit mechanic.
  • Afflict: Affect adversely. Synonyms: Suffer, Bother. Antonyms: Comfort, Aid. Example: The flood has greatly afflicted the crops in this village.
  • Affluence: Having a lot of money. Synonyms: Wealth, Prosperity. Antonyms: Scarcity, Poverty. Example: Generally, affluent fathers have spoilt kids.
  • Affront: An action or remark that causes outrage or offence. Synonyms: Insult, Offence. Antonyms: Honour, Compliment. Example: Poor dressing sense often causes affront.
  • Aggrandize: Increase power, status or wealth of. Synonyms: Exalt, Boost. Antonyms: Abase, Degrade. Example: Its a movie that aggrandizes the bad guys.
  • Aggravate: To make a problem worse. Synonyms: Worsen, Compound. Antonyms: Soothe, Calm. Example: The symptoms were aggravated by drinking alcohol.
  • Agog: very eager or curious to hear or see something. Synonyms: Eager, Impatient. Antonyms: Reluctant, Uninterested. Example: He was all agog on hearing the news of his promotion.
  • Altercation: A noisy argument or disagreement, especially in public. Synonyms: Quarrel, Bickering. Antonyms: Agreement, Harmony. Example: A general political talk should not lead to an altercation.
  • Altruism: Disinterested and selfless concern for the well-being of others. Synonyms: Benevolence, Humanitarianism. Antonyms: Greediness, Meanness. Example: Mother Teresa is known for her altruism.
  • Amalgamate: To combine to form a larger group. Synonyms: To merge, Combine. Antonyms: Separate, Disjoin. Example: Hutchison and Essar group amalgamated to form Hutchison-Essar.
  • Ambiguous: Open to more than one interpretation, not having one obvious meaning. Synonyms: Unclear, Confusing. Antonyms: Clear, Obvious. Example: Ambiguous answers must be removed.
  • Ameliorate: Making a situation better, less painful. Synonyms: Mitigate, Improve. Antonyms: Worsen, Aggravate. Example: Government grant is ameliorating the situation in the territory.
  • Amenable: Open and responsive to suggestions. Synonyms: Compliant, Manageable, Persuadable. Antonyms: Stubborn, Rigid, Non-compliant. Example: A better way to resolve the problems is being amenable.
  • Amicable: Friendly behaviour of a person. Synonyms: Friendly, Good-natured. Antonyms: Unfriendly, Hostile. Example: Noble people are always amicable.
  • Annul: To make something legally void. Synonyms: Cancel, Abolish, Invalidate. Antonyms: Accept, Validate. Example: The contract was annulled by the second party.
  • Anomaly: Deviation from the standard. Synonyms: Oddity, Peculiarity. Antonyms: Conformity, Normality. Example: We do not publish cheap quality books as it is an anomaly to our policy.

details.summary: A comprehensive list of vocabulary words starting with 'A', including their definitions, synonyms, antonyms, and usage examples.

subject: English
text:
• Antagonism: A strong feeling of dislike or hatred. Synonyms: Hate, Prejudice. Antonyms: Love, Affection. Example: Man cannot be an antagonist as he has to live in the society.
  • Antipathy: A strong feeling of dislike. Synonyms: Aversion, Dislike. Antonyms: Affinity, Cordiality. Example: Pakistan's antipathy is open to India.
  • Antithesis: The direct or exact opposite. Synonyms: Counterpart, Converse. Antonym: Same. Example: It seems that he has decided to be in antithesis of my opinion.
  • Aphorism: A short, wise and true statement. Synonyms: Adage, Maxim. Antonyms: Nonsense, Absurdity. Example: 'Honesty is the best policy' is a very practical aphorism.
  • Aplomb: Confidence and style. Synonyms: Assurance, Poise. Antonyms: Gaucheness, Discomposure. Example: Continuous failure had a great effect on his aplomb.
  • Apocryphal: Well-known but probably not true. Synonyms: Fictitious, Made-up. Antonyms: Authentic, Real. Example: Existence of God is an apocryphal fact to the people world wide.
  • Apogee: Most successful part of something. Synonyms: The top, Apex. Antonyms: Bottom, Base. Example: Romance is the apogee of a relationship.
  • Appease: to make someone pleased or less angry by giving or saying something they desire. Synonyms: To pacify, Placate. Antonyms: Annoy, Irritate. Example: His appeasing behaviour is always appreciated.
  • Append: To add something to the end of a writing. Synonyms: Add, Attach. Antonyms: Disjoin, Detach. Example: It is always advisable to append the hints to a mathematical problem.
  • Apportion: To divide something among people. Synonyms: Distribute, Allocate. Antonyms: Keep, Withhold. Example: The property of the deceased man was apportioned between his two sons.
  • Babble: To talk or say something in a quick, confused, excited or silly way. Synonyms: Chatter, Bumble. Antonyms: Quiet, Sense. Example: He seems to be babbling.
  • Badger: To try to make someone do something by asking them many times. Synonyms: Pester, Bother, Torment. Antonyms: Aid, Delight. Example: The peon had to be badgered to get the form signed by the principal.
  • Baleful: Full of evil intentions, menacing. Synonyms: Destructive, Malignant. Antonyms: Good, Helping, Promising. Example: His baleful behaviour was strange.
  • Banal: Trite; something boring; ordinary and not original. Synonyms: Common place, Trite, Boring, Dull. Antonyms: Entertaining, Original. Example: I hate the places that seem banal.
  • Bane: A cause of great distress or annoyance. Synonyms: Ruin, Destruction. Antonyms: Blessing, Boon, Advantage. Example: Traffic congestion and air pollution are major banes for Delhi and Delhiites.
  • Bashful: Tending to feel uncomfortable with other people and be embarrassed easily; shy. Synonyms: Diffident, Modest, Meek, Coy, Nervous. Antonyms: Open, Confident. Example: She feels bashful in my company.
  • Berate: To criticize or scold severely. Synonyms: Lash out, Tear into, Abuse. Antonyms: Praise, Compliment. Example: Father berated his son for his mistakes.
  • Bereavement: The situation you are in when a close friend or a family member has just died. Synonyms: Death, Loss. Antonym: Happiness. Example: Bereavement caused by my father's death is immeasurable.
  • Bestow: To give or confer honour to someone. Synonyms: Award, Give, Grant, Present. Antonyms: Deprive, Refuse, Take. Example: A lot of awards are bestowed upon him.
  • Bigotry: Intolerance towards those who hold different opinion from oneself. Synonyms: Fanaticism, Prejudice. Antonyms: Tolerance, Impartiality. Example: A deeply ingrained bigotry prevented her from even considering the arguments.
  • Bizarre: Strange and difficult to explain. Synonyms: Strange, Weird. Antonyms: Explainable, Normal. Example: The bizarre events taking place in the deserted house led the people to assume that it was haunted.
  • Blabber: Talk foolishly. Synonyms: Chatter, Babble. Antonym: Sense. Example: Blabbering is what one can expect from fools.
  • Bohemian: A socially unconventional person, especially an artist or a writer. Synonym: Non-conformist. Antonym: Conformist. Example: The Bohemian attitude is considered rebellious.
  • Bolster: To support or strengthen. Synonyms: Strengthen, Reinforce. Antonyms: Discourage, Undermine. Example: More money is needed to bolster the industry.
  • Boor: A person who is rude and does not consider other people's feelings. Synonyms: Lout, Rogue. Antonyms: Civilised, Decent, Modest. Example: Terrorists are nothing but boors.

subject: English
topic: Words starting with B and C
text:
• Bovine: Relating to or affecting cattle, looking or acting like a cow. Synonyms: Cow-like, Cattle-like. Antonym: - . Example: She stared at us with a stupid bovine expression.
  • Brag: To speak proudly of what you have done or what you own. Synonyms: Swagger, Boast. Antonym: Be modest. Example: He was bragging about his success.
  • Brash: Showing too much confidence and too little respect. Synonyms: Arrogant, Brazen. Antonym: Diffident, Meek. Example: A brash man has less friends.
  • Bumble: To speak or move in a confused way. Synonyms: Lurch, Stumble. Antonym: Efficient, Expert. Example: Bumbling persons create a doubt to security.
  • Bungle: To do something badly or unsuccessfully. Synonyms: Mishandle, Mismanage. Antonym: Succeed. Example: He has bungled the whole work.
  • Buoyant: Happy and confident. Synonyms: Happy, Joyous. Antonym: Unhappy, Sad. Example: He was very buoyant about the visit to Agra.
  • Burgeon: To grow or develop quickly. Synonyms: Expand, Swell. Antonym: Shrink, Contract. Example: Terrorism is burgeoning across the border.
  • Burly: A large and strong person. Synonyms: Tawny, Gigantic. Antonym: Lean, Thin. Example: There must be a burly man for the role of a demon.
  • Bustling: If a place is bustling, it is full of busy activity. Synonyms: Dashing, Scurrying. Antonym: Quiet, Inactive, Dormant. Example: The house, usually bustling with activity, was strangely silent.
  • Cabal: A group of people who secretly work together. Synonyms: Clique, Faction. Antonym: Individual. Example: He was assassinated by a cabal of aides.
  • Cache: A hidden store of provision, weapons, treasure; to hide weapons or other things. Synonyms: Hoard, Store. Antonym: Discard, Remove. Example: People must create a cache of medicines for emergency.
  • Cajole: To persuade someone to do something by coaxing or flattery. Synonyms: Persuade, Coax. Antonym: Dissuade, Discourage. Example: He knows how to cajole people into doing what he wants.
  • Calamity: An event that brings terrible loss, lasting distress or severe affliction. Synonyms: Tragedy, Catastrophe. Antonym: Blessing, Godsend. Example: The great calamity was brought to rest.
  • Callous: Showing or having an insensitive and cruel disregard for others. Synonyms: Insensitive; Unsympathetic. Antonym: Sensitive, Sympathetic. Example: People often think that doctors are callous.
  • Calumny: A false accusation. Synonyms: Defamation, Slander. Antonym: Eulogy, Praise. Example: He is a victim of calumny.
  • Camouflage: To disguise. Synonyms: Hide, Conceal. Antonym: Reveal, Show. Example: The camouflaged players arrived at the airport.
  • Canard: A false, report or story. Synonyms: Tale, Story. Antonym: Truth. Example: The newspaper was sued for publishing a canard about a celebrity.
  • Canny: Very clever and able to make intelligent decisions. Synonyms: Clever, Shrewd. Antonym: Uncanny, Daft. Example: Rohan is a canny card player.
  • Cantankerous: Bad tempered, argumentative and uncooperative. Synonyms: Bad tempered, Uncooperative. Antonym: Affable, Good-natured. Example: Children are by nature cantankerous.
  • Capacious: Having a lot of space. Synonyms: Spacious, Open. Antonym: Small, Cramped. Example: A bunglow is a capacious house to live-in.
  • Cardinal: Of the greatest importance, fundamental. Synonyms: Significant, Fundamental. Antonym: Unimportant. Example: Cardinal facts of the case are hidden.
  • Careen: To go forward quickly while moving from side to side. Synonyms: Lurch, Rock. Antonym: Crawl, Creep. Example: I saw the duck careening through the ponds.
  • Castigate: To criticise severely. Synonyms: Rebuke, Chide, Scold. Antonym: Admire, Praise. Example: Odd behaviour of a person is a matter of castigation.
  • Catalyst: Stimulus; a person who causes change by his presence. Synonyms: Impetus, Incentive. Antonym: Inhibitor, Preventer. Example: Birbal was a catalyst in the court of Akbar.
  • Catapult: To suddenly put someone into an important position; to propel. Synonyms: Excel, Marshal. Antonym: To recede, Decline. Example: Someone cannot be catapulted to the chief straight way.
  • Charismatic: Possessing spiritual grace; inspiring. Synonyms: Charming, Fascinating. Antonym: Offensive, Frightening. Example: Modi is a charismatic leader.

subject: English
text:
• Chaste: Morally pure or decent. Synonyms: Decent, Pure. Antonyms: Impure, Indecent. Example: The chaste conduct of the austere person commands respect.
  • Cherubic: Good natured. Synonyms: Innocent, Angelic. Antonyms: Demonic, Devilish. Example: His behaviour reveals his approach to be cherubic.
  • Chide: To express mild disapproval of someone, to scold someone gently. Synonyms: Rebuke, Scold. Antonyms: Admire, Praise. Example: Mother chided the son for his rude behaviour with the guests.
  • Chronic: Happening or existing frequently or most of the time. Synonyms: Persistent, Long standing. Antonyms: Temporary, Mild. Example: She suffers from chronic pain in her knees.
  • Churlish: Rude, unfriendly and unpleasant. Synonyms: Arrogant, ill-mannered. Antonyms: Gracious, Polite. Example: Churlish behaviour is his trademark.
  • Clout: Power and influence. Synonyms: Sway, Power. Antonym: Powerless. Example: Hitler was a man of great clout.
  • Coalesce: To grow together or unite into one; to fuse. Synonyms: Fuse, Join. Antonyms: Split, Breakup. Example: The ice-masses coalesced into a glacier over time.
  • Cogent: Very clear and easy for the mind to accept and believe. Synonyms: Convincing, Compelling. Antonyms: Vague, Unconvincing. Example: His ideas were cogent and sound.
  • Conciliate: To end a disagreement or someone's anger by acting in a friendly way or to slightly change your opinion. Synonyms: Appease, Placate. Antonym: Provoke. Example: The nagging child was conciliated by the toys.
  • Concomitant: Naturally accompanying or associated with something. Synonyms: Linked, Associated. Antonyms: Disassociated, Unlinked. Example: Loss of memory is a concomitant of old age.
  • Concussion: Temporary unconsciousness or confusion caused by a blow on the head. Synonym: Violent shaking. Antonym: Consciousness. Example: The accident caused the man a severe concussion.
  • Condone: To accept behaviour that is morally wrong. Synonyms: Accept, Allow. Antonyms: Condemn, Punish. Example: Parents always condone the fault of children.
  • Contentious: Causing or likely to cause disagreement. Synonyms: Controversial, Argumentative. Antonyms: Agreeable. Example: The contentious issue may obstruct the development.
  • Contort: To twist or bend out of normal shape. Synonyms: Distort, Twist. Antonyms: Straighten, Smooth. Example: He contorted the instrument by rough handling.
  • Contrive: To invent or make something in a clever or unusual way. Synonyms: Create, Manufacture. Antonyms: Destroy, Ruin. Example: The Defence Ministry contrived a plan to tackle cross border terrorism.
  • Conundrum: A confusing and difficult question or problem. Synonyms: Dilemma, Quandary. Antonym: Easy-way. Example: Competitive exams make you face conundrums.
  • Convene: To call together for a meeting or activity. Synonyms: Summon, Call. Antonyms: Disperse, Leave. Example: We convened at the hotel for a seminar.
  • Convivial: (Of an event or atmosphere) Friendly, lively and enjoyable. Synonyms: Jovial, Pleasant. Antonyms: Sad, Unhappy. Example: The President of the club arranged a convivial cocktail party.
  • Copious: Ample, producing much. Synonyms: Plentiful, Abudant. Antonyms: Scarce, Meager. Example: The storm produced a copious amount of rain.
  • Dabble: Take part in an activity in a casual way. Synonyms: Tinker, Dally, Trifle. Antonym: Take seriously. Example: Rita dabbled in many things before she got married.
  • Dainty: Small and graceful. Synonyms: Elegant, Petite. Antonyms: Crude, Ugly. Example: The house looks dainty and beautiful.
  • Dank: Unpleasantly moist and cold. Synonyms: Wet, Damp. Antonyms: Arid, Dry. Example: He shivered as he entered the dank room.
  • Deadlock: A situation involving opposing parties, in which no progress can be made; stalemate. Synonyms: Gridlock, Dilemma. Antonyms: Solution, Agreement. Example: The mediator will help the opposing parties end the deadlock so the contract can be signed.
  • Debacle: A complete failure; a crushing defeat. Synonyms: Fiasco, Failure. Antonyms: Success, Accomplishment. Example: He faced a debacle in yesterday's game.
  • Debase: To adulterate, to make poor in quality or of less value. Synonyms: Degrade, Devalue. Antonyms: Upgrade, Enhance. Example: Debased commodities are sold in the market.

subject: English
text:
• Debauch: To destroy or damage something so that it is no longer considered good or moral.
    Synonyms: Abase, Corrupt
    Antonyms: Ennoble, Uplift
    Example: Western culture has debauched the moral fabric of our society.
  • Debilitate: To make someone very weak and infirm
    Synonyms: Cripple, Disable
    Antonyms: Strengthen, Enable
    Example: The virus debilitates the body's immune system.
  • Decadence: Having low moral standards and behaviour
    Synonyms: Corruption, Debauchery
    Antonyms: Ascent, Decency
    Example: Decadent people are not valued.
  • Decimate: To kill a large number of (something) or to reduce very heavily
    Synonyms: Annihilate, Exterminate
    Antonyms: Bear, Build, Create
    Example: Population of endangered animals have been decimated.
  • Decrepit: Worn out or ruined because of age or neglect
    Synonyms: Dilapidated, Battered
    Antonyms: Firm, Healthy
    Example: The building was a decrepit sample of bricks now.
  • Defalcate: To steal or misuse funds entrusted to one
    Synonyms: Embezzle, Loot, Filch
    Antonyms: Appropriate, Receive
    Example: Public funds are defalcated by leaders.
  • Demure: (of a woman or her behaviour) Modest; shy; reserved
    Synonyms: Meek, Bashful
    Antonyms: Brazen, Shameless
    Example: Her demure nature gets everybody's attention.
  • Deplore: To feel or express strong condemnation of something
    Synonyms: Abhor, Denounce
    Antonyms: Praise, Commend
    Example: Public deplored the casual steps taken by the administration for the safety of women.
  • Depravity: The state of being morally bad, or an action that is morally bad.
    Synonyms: Perversion, Criminality
    Antonyms: Goodness, Uprightness
    Example: People were shocked by the depravity of her actions.
  • Deprecate: To criticise or express disapproval of something
    Synonyms: Belittle, Detract
    Antonyms: Approve, Commend
    Example: Everybody deprecated the death of the charitable man.
  • Deride: To laugh at someone or something in a way that shows you think they are stupid or are of no value.
    Synonyms: Ridicule, Mock, Disdain
    Antonyms: Admire, Approve
    Example: He was derided at for his strange ways.
  • Desperado: A desperate or reckless person, especially a criminal
    Synonyms: Bandit, Villain
    Antonym: Civilised
    Example: Law must punish the desperado.
  • Despot: A ruler who has total power and often uses it in cruel and unfair ways.
    Synonyms: Tyrant, Oppressor
    Antonym: Democrat
    Example: Hitler was one of the biggest despots.
  • Desultory: Lacking a plan, purpose or enthusiasm
    Synonyms: Aimless, Chaotic
    Antonyms: Organised, Systematic
    Example: He wandered around, cleaning up in a desultory way.
  • Detract: Diminish the worth or value of something
    Synonyms: Belittle, Decrease
    Antonyms: Commend, Compliment
    Example: Numerous errors in the book detracted the reader's attention.
  • Devious: Showing a skilful use of underhand tactics to achieve goals
    Synonyms: Unfair, Fraudulent
    Antonyms: Honest, Fair
    Example: The minister was a devious politician.
  • Devolve: 1. Transfer of power to a lower level 2. Pass into a worse state; degenerate
    Synonyms: Delegate, Pass on
    Antonyms: Centralize, Improve
    Example: In a democratic system, power is devolved to the local level.
  • Diabolic: Extremely evil
    Synonyms: Cruel, Atrocious
    Antonyms: Kind, Moral
    Example: The police quickly mobilised to track down the diabolical serial killer.
  • Diffident: Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence
    Synonyms: Bashful, Meek
    Antonyms: Bold, Confident
    Example: He is too diffident to work in a company.
  • Disapprobation: Strong disapproval, typically on moral grounds
    Synonyms: Deprecation, Disapproval
    Antonyms: Approval, Approbation
    Example: Sherry was used to constant disapprobation of critics.
  • Disconcert: to make someone upset; unsettle
    Synonyms: Perplex, Baffle, Bewilder
    Antonyms: Assist, Calm
    Example: The whole experience had disconcerted him.

mcq.question: What is an antonym for the word 'Diffident'?

subject: English
text:
• Earmark: Designate funds or resources for a particular purpose, procure
    Synonyms: Attribute, Designate
    Antonym: Disallocate
    Example: The government earmarked a huge package for agriculture
  • Ebullient: Very happy and enthusiastic; exuberant
    Synonyms: Cheerful, Exuberant
    Antonyms: Unhappy, Depressed
    Example: The man seems to be ebullient on his success.
  • Edifice: A large impressive building; a system that has been established for a long time
    Synonyms: Monument, Building
    Example: The glass edifice is an architectural wonder.

subject: English
text:
• Effeminate: Womanish; Feminine, Unmanly. Synonyms: Effete, Unmanly. Antonyms: Masculine, Manly. Example: He had a high and somewhat effeminate voice.
  • Effete: Weak and Powerless. Synonyms: Unmanly, Effeminate. Antonyms: Manly, Powerful. Example: His effete body looks pale.
  • Effusive: Expressing gratitude, approval or pleasure in a way that shows very strong feeling. Synonyms: Gushing, Unrestrained. Antonyms: Restrained, Reserved. Example: The coach was effusive in praising Tendulkar.
  • Emaciated: Very thin and weak, usually because of illness or extreme hunger. Synonyms: Thin, Skeletal. Antonyms: Chubby, Fat. Example: Chronic diseases make one emaciated.
  • Embodiment: someone or something that represents a quality or an idea exactly. Synonyms: Personification, Incarnation. Antonym: Exclusion. Example: Mother Teresa was often regarded as the embodiment of selfless devotion to others.
  • Enervate: to make someone feel weak and without energy. Synonyms: Debilitate, Devitalise. Antonyms: Strengthen, Energise. Example: We were enervated by the lengthy discussion.
  • Enjoin: To instruct or urge someone to do something or behave in a particular way. Synonyms: Urge, Command, Insist. Antonyms: Obey, follow. Example: The boss enjoined the workers to do the best.
  • Ensconce: To make yourself very comfortable or safe in a place or position. Synonyms: Settle, Install. Antonyms: Unsettle, Exhibit. Example: He ensconced in his new abode there.
  • Entree: Admittance; the right to enter something. Synonyms: Entry, Ingress. Antonyms: Exit, Refusal. Example: Entree to the country club is through sponsorship.
  • Entropy: Lack of order or predictability, gradual decline into disorder. Synonyms: Break up, Collapse. Antonyms: Improvement, Order. Example: The mishandling of the situation led to entropy.
  • Ephemeral: Existing only for a short time. Synonyms: Fleeting, Transient. Antonyms: Enduring, Lasting. Example: Fame in the show business is ephemeral.
  • Epoch: A long period of time, especially one in which there are new advances and great changes. Synonyms: Era, Span, Age. Example: The development of the steam engine marked an important epoch in the history of industry.
  • Equitable: Treating everyone fairly and in the same way. Synonyms: Unbiased, Reasonable. Antonyms: Partial, Biased. Example: He is fighting for a more equitable distribution of funds.
  • Excruciating: Intensely painful. Synonyms: Acute, Agonising. Antonyms: Painless, Calm, Easy. Example: The Uttrakhand disaster was an excruciating experience for the victims.
  • Expatiate: Speak or write in detail. Synonyms: Expound, Lecture. Antonyms: Compress, Abridge. Example: It is useless to expatiate upon the beauty of nature to one who is blind.
  • Facade: The principal front of a building that faces on to a street or open space. Synonyms: Front, Elevation, Frontage. Antonyms: Rear, Back. Example: The gallery's 18th century facade attracted the visitors.
  • Facetious: Treating serious issues deliberately with inappropriate humour. Synonyms: Flippant, Frivolous. Antonyms: Serious, Formal. Example: The facetious boy was chided.
  • Facile: 1. Ignoring the true complexities of an issue; superficial. 2. A success which is easily achieved. Synonyms: Superficial, Hasty. Antonyms: Thorough, Profound. Example: This problem needs more than just a facile solution.
  • Factitious: Artificial, not natural. Synonyms: Fake, Bogus. Antonyms: Natural, Real. Example: His explanations were all factitious.
  • Fallacious: Based on a mistaken belief; misleading. Synonyms: Erroneous, False. Antonyms: Genuine, True. Example: Someone is spreading fallacious information.
  • Fastidious: Very attentive to and concerned about accuracy and details; very concerned about matters of cleanliness. Synonyms: Painstaking, Meticulous. Antonyms: Careless, Sloppy. Example: His culinary skills are fastidious.
  • Fatuous: Stupid, not correct or not carefully thought about. Synonyms: Silly, Foolish. Antonyms: Sensible, Intelligent. Example: All his reasons appeared fatuous to me.
  • Feckless: Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible. Synonyms: Useless, Worthless. Antonyms: Responsible, Competent. Example: Country does not need feckless people.
  • Fecund: Very fertile. Synonyms: Fertile, Fruitful. Antonyms: Unproductive, Infertile. Example: The soil of the plains is fecund.
  • Feisty: Having or showing exuberance, strong determination and lack of fear. Synonyms: Courageous, Gutsy. Antonyms: Cowardly, Dull. Example: Mountaineering needs feisty people.

subject: English
text:
• Felicity: 1. Intense happiness. 2. The ability to find appropriate expressions for one's thoughts.
    • Synonyms: Bliss, Delight, Eloquence
    • Antonyms: Sorrow, Unhappiness
    • Example: Felicity is a bliss to be enjoyed.
  • Fester: (of a problem or negative feeling) become worse or more intense, especially through long term neglect or indifference.
    • Synonyms: Smoulder, Aggravate
    • Antonyms: Flourish, Grow
    • Example: It is better to express your anger than let it fester inside you.
  • Fetid: Smelling extremely bad, Foul.
    • Synonyms: Smelly, Putrid
    • Antonyms: Aromatic, Perfumed
    • Example: The carcass of the dog has made the surroundings fetid.
  • Fidelity: Honest or lasting support, Loyalty, Faithfulness.
    • Synonyms: Loyalty, Constancy
    • Antonyms: Dishonesty, Infidelity
    • Example: Friendship survives on fidelity.
  • Fiend: 1. Cruel, inhuman. 2. An enthusiastic or devotee of a particular thing.
    • Synonyms: Barbarian, Ogre
    • Antonyms: Angel, God
    • Example: His hands were trembling as if he was some sort of fiend.
  • Flack: Strong criticism or opposition.
    • Synonyms: Criticism, Censure
    • Antonyms: Appraisal, Praise
    • Example: Dowry should be a matter of flack.
  • Flagrant: Too bad to be ignored.
    • Synonyms: Heinous, Shameless
    • Antonyms: Magnificent, Wonderful
    • Example: The killing of innocent villagers is an example of flagrant ways of Maoists.
  • Foment: To cause trouble to develop.
    • Synonyms: Incite, Instigate
    • Antonyms: Deter, Discourage
    • Example: He was accused of fomenting violence.
  • Fortitude: Courage in pain or adversity.
    • Synonyms: Courage, Bravery
    • Antonyms: Cowardice, Fear
    • Example: Fortitude makes you a winner.
  • Frenzied: Madly excited or uncontrolled.
    • Synonyms: Wild, Frantic
    • Antonyms: Controlled, Calm
    • Example: The office was a scene of frenzied activity this morning.

mcq.question: What is the antonym of the word 'FETID'?
mcq.explanation: 'Fetid' means smelling extremely bad or foul. Its antonym is 'Aromatic' or 'Perfumed'.

subject: English
text:
• Gainsay: To deny or contradict a fact or statement.
    • Synonyms: Dispute, Oppose
    • Antonyms: Accept, Confirm
    • Example: There is no gainsaying the fact that they have built a great building.
  • Gall: Bold and impudent behaviour.
    • Synonyms: Impudence, Insolence
    • Antonyms: Cordiality, Politeness
    • Example: After borrowing my car, he had the gall to complain about its seats.
  • Gallant: 1. Brave; heroic. 2. (Of a man) polite and kind towards woman.
    • Synonyms: Valiant, Unafraid
    • Antonyms: Timid, Rude
    • Example: Although she lost, she made a gallant effort.
  • Garble: To make words or messages unclear and difficult to understand.
    • Synonyms: Muddle, Jumble
    • Antonyms: Obvious, Clear
    • Example: The terrified child gave a garbled account of the incident to the police.
  • Garish: Too bright or colourful.
    • Synonyms: Gaudy; Bright
    • Antonyms: Dull, Unflashy
    • Example: The decoration looked garish.
  • Gauche: Awkward and uncomfortable with other people, specially because young and lacking in experience.
    • Synonyms: Awkward, Gawky
    • Antonyms: Elegant, Sophisticated
    • Example: She had grown from a gauche teenager to a self assured young woman.
  • Genial: Friendly and cheerful.
    • Synonyms: Affable, Cordial
    • Antonyms: Hostile, Unfriendly
    • Example: His genial outpour surprised me.
  • Ghastly: Unpleasant and shocking.
    • Synonyms: Terrible, Horrible
    • Antonyms: Pleasant, Charming
    • Example: The scene of the crime looks ghastly.
  • Giddy: Having a sensation of whirling and a tendency to fall or stagger.
    • Synonyms: Dizzy, Light-headed
    • Antonyms: Steady, Sensible
    • Example: He was walking giddily.
  • Gingerly: In a careful or cautious manner.
    • Synonyms: Warily, Cautiously
    • Antonyms: Carelessly, Rashly
    • Example: He did the work gingerly.
  • Gratify: To please someone or to satisfy a wish or need.
    • Synonyms: Please, Gladden
    • Antonyms: Dissatisfy, Displease
    • Example: I am gratified by his words.
  • Grimace: To make an expression of pain, strong dislike, etc in which the face twists in an ugly way.
    • Synonyms: Scowl, Frown
    • Antonyms: Smile
    • Example: After falling down, he started to stand up grimacing with pain.
  • Grisly: Causing horror or disgust.
    • Synonyms: Gruesome, Ghastly
    • Antonyms: Pleasant, Attractive
    • Example: The grisly figure made the child cry.
  • Grubby: Covered with dirt.
    • Synonyms: Filthy, Mucky, Grimy
    • Antonyms: Clean, Tidy
    • Example: One must clean off grubby hands before eating.
  • Gruff: (person's voice) Low and unfriendly.
    • Synonyms: Rough, Hoarse
    • Antonyms: Soft, Mellow
    • Example: He speaks in a gruff way, but is really kind.
