subject: English
text:
Vocabulary List H-I

  • Habituated: Used to something, especially something unpleasant. Synonyms: Accustom, Adapt. Antonyms: Avoid, Shun. Example: Bears can become habituated to people easily.
  • Haggard: Looking exhausted or unwell, especially from fatigue, worry or suffering. Synonyms: Drained, Tired. Antonyms: Fresh, Healthy. Example: The athletes looked haggard after the race.
  • Haggle: Dispute or bargain persistently. Synonyms: Barter, Negotiate. Antonyms: Concur, Comply. Example: Customers often haggle with the seller.
  • Hallowed: Very respected and praised because of great importance or great age. Synonyms: Holy, Sacred. Antonyms: Cursed, Unholy. Example: The site of the ancient temple is a hallowed ground.
  • Hapless: Having no luck; very unfortunate. Synonyms: Unlucky, Ill-fated. Antonyms: Fortunate, Lucky. Example: She plays the hapless heroine who is unlucky in love.
  • Harrowing: Extremely upsetting because connected with suffering. Synonyms: Tortuous, Painful. Antonyms: Calming, Comforting. Example: The harrowing news reached the village.
  • Headstrong: Very determined to do what one wants without listening to others. Synonyms: Wilful, Strong-willed. Antonyms: Undetermined, Tractable. Example: Being headstrong by nature, he did not listen to his wife's advice.
  • Heady: Having a strong exhilirating effect. Synonyms: Exciting, Thrilling. Antonyms: Boring, Dull. Example: The party seems heady today.
  • Hector: Talk to someone in a bullying way. Synonyms: Intimidate, Badger. Antonyms: Please, Assist. Example: The senior guy was hectoring the junior.
  • Heedless: Not giving attention to a risk or possible difficulty. Synonyms: Inattentive, Oblivious. Antonyms: Needful, Attentive. Example: He was driving heedlessly.
  • Heinous: Outrageously evil; horrifying. Synonyms: Wicked, Atrocious. Antonyms: Admirable, Delightful. Example: The man is facing charges over his heinous act.
  • Herald: To be a sign of something that is going to come or happen soon. Synonyms: Indicator, Sign. Antonyms: Aforeseen. Example: The early flowers are heralds of spring.
  • Horrendous: Shocking; horrible. Synonyms: Dreadful, Alarming. Antonyms: Pleasing, Wonderful. Example: Conditions in the refugee camps were horrendous.
  • Humane: Having or showing compassion. Synonyms: Compassionate, Kind. Antonyms: Unkind, Inhumane. Example: It is not humane to treat animals cruelly.
  • Hypothetical: Based on a situation that is not real, but that might happen. Synonyms: Imaginary, Theoretical. Antonyms: Real, Actual. Example: She described a hypothetical case to clarify her point.
  • Idolatry: Very great admiration or respect for someone, often too great. Synonyms: Reverence, Adoration. Antonyms: Vilification, Condemnation. Example: Newton was revered to the point of idolatry.
  • Impertinent: Rude and not showing respect towards someone older or in a higher position than you. Synonyms: Disrespectful, Rude. Antonyms: Polite, Mannered. Example: Its impertinent to ask strangers about their private lives.
  • Implausible: Not believable or realistic. Synonyms: Unbelievable, Doubtful. Antonyms: Reasonable, Convincing. Example: She's been making implausible claims.
  • Impolitic: Unwise words or actions that are likely to cause offence or problems. Synonyms: Unwise, Imprudent. Antonyms: Wise, Prudent. Example: I thought it impolitic to ask any question about her ex.
  • Improvident: Not giving thought to the future. Synonyms: Heedless, Inconsiderate. Antonyms: Provident, Farsighted. Example: He is improvident about his career.
  • Inalienable: Not subject to being taken away or given by the possessor. Synonyms: Absolute, Inviolable. Antonyms: Changeable, Alienable. Example: The group of women wanted equal inalienable rights as men.
  • Incorrigible: Beyond correction or change. Synonyms: Hardened, Hopeless. Antonyms: Correctable, Changeable. Example: She is an incorrigible chatterbox.
  • Incredulous: Not able or willing to believe something. Synonyms: Mistrustful, Doubtful. Antonyms: Believing, Credulous. Example: Everyone laughed the incredulous stories of the old man.
  • Indigent: Very poor. Synonyms: Penniless, Destitute. Antonyms: Rich, Affluent. Example: The heavy losses he incurred in business rendered him indigent.

subject: English
text:
• Infallible: Incapable of making mistakes or being wrong. Synonyms: Unerring, Flawless. Antonyms: Fallible, Erring. Example: I never claimed to be infallible.
  • Inimical: Harmful or limiting. Synonyms: Injurious, Harmful. Antonyms: Helpful, Advantageous. Example: A person with inimical behaviour is dangerous.
  • Iniquitous: Very unfair or evil. Synonyms: Wicked, Sinful. Antonyms: Good, Virtuous. Example: This decision seems iniquitous.
  • Innate: (of a quality) which you are born with or which is present naturally. Synonyms: Inborn, Ingrained. Antonyms: Acquired, Extrinsic. Example: He is a person with innate wisdom.
  • Insipid: Lacking flavour; weak or tasteless. Synonyms: Bland, Tasteless. Antonyms: Tasty, Delicious. Example: The dinner was insipid.
  • Jabber: Talk in a rapid, excited and often incomprehensible way. Synonyms: Prattle, Babble. Antonyms: Be silent, Speak clearly. Example: The train was full of people jabbering into their mobile phones.
  • Jaded: Not having interest or losing interest as you have experienced something too many times. Synonyms: Bored, Tired. Antonyms: Fresh, Activated. Example: Flying is exciting the first time you do it, but you soon become jaded.
  • Jaunty: Lively in manner or appearance. Synonyms: Merry, Cheerful. Antonyms: Unhappy, Depressed. Example: Success makes a person jaunty.
  • Jinx: Bad luck or a person or thing that brings bad luck. Synonyms: Misfortune, Curse. Antonyms: Good luck, Boon. Example: His luck has been so bad he feels jinxed.
  • Jocular: Funny or intended to make someone laugh. Synonyms: Funny, Humorous. Antonyms: Serious, Depressed. Example: Someone made a jocular remark to entertain the gathering.
  • Kaput: Broken; not working properly. Synonyms: Faulty, Broken. Antonym: Operational. Example: My fridge has gone kaput.
  • Ken: A person's range of knowledge or understanding. Synonyms: Knowledge, Awareness. Antonym: Ignorance. Example: Politics are beyond my ken.
  • Kernel: The central or most important part of something. Synonyms: Essence, Core. Antonyms: Exterior, Periphery. Example: We are to write the kernel of the story.
  • Kindle: Arouse or inspire (an emotion or feeling). Synonyms: Arouse, Rouse, Wake. Antonyms: Douse, Put out. Example: The trip kindled an interest in travel.
  • Knave: A dishonest man. Synonyms: Fraud, Cheat. Antonym: Honest. Example: A knave cheated me on the bus.
  • Labadisical: Lacking enthusiasm and determination. Synonyms: Lazy, Unenthusiastic. Antonyms: Enthusiastic, Excited. Example: Efforts from the man seem lackadaisical.
  • Laggard: A person who makes slow progress and lags behind others. Synonyms: Loiterer, Lingerer. Antonym: Leader. Example: A laggard can't win the race of life.
  • Lambaste: To criticise severely. Synonyms: Chastise, Castigate. Antonyms: Praise, Compliment. Example: His work was lambasted by everyone.
  • Languid: Showing or having very little strength, energy or activity. Synonyms: Enervated, Unenergetic. Antonyms: Energetic, Active. Example: He looked languid after a sleepless night.
  • Lassitude: A state of physical or mental weariness. Synonyms: Fatigue, Lethargy. Antonyms: Freshness, Vigour, Energy. Example: Symptoms of the disease include paleness and lassitude.
  • Leery: Cautious or wary due to realistic suspicions. Synonym: Careful. Antonym: Careless. Example: They were leery of their neighbours.
  • Leviathan: Extremely large and powerful. Synonyms: Titan, Huge. Antonyms: Powerless, Tiny. Example: Shakespeare is the leviathan of English literature.
  • Limber: (of a person or body part) Able to bend and move easily and smoothly. Synonyms: Flexible, Nimble. Antonyms: Rigid, Stiff. Example: His whole body is a limber of muscles.
  • Limpid: Clearly expressed and easily understood. Synonyms: Lucid, Clear. Antonyms: Unclear, Unintelligible. Example: The situation is a limpid one to get through.

subject: English
content:
### Livid
- **Definition:** Extremely angry.
- **Synonyms:** Infuriated, Irate.
- **Antonyms:** Calm, Peaceful.
- **Example Sentence:** *The boss was livid when yet another deadline was missed.*

subject: English
content:
### Macabre
- **Definition:** Horrible, because concerned with death.
- **Synonyms:** Shocking, Gruesome.
- **Antonyms:** Pleasant, Pleasing.
- **Example Sentence:** *Even the police were horrified at the macabre nature of the killings.*

subject: English
content:
### Magnanimous
- **Definition:** Generous or forgiving.
- **Synonyms:** Benevolent, Charitable.
- **Antonyms:** Selfish, Mean‑spirited.
- **Example Sentence:** *The king was magnanimous towards his subjects.*

subject: English
content:
### Magnate
- **Definition:** Successful businessman; tycoon.
- **Synonyms:** Tycoon, Mogul.
- **Antonyms:** Pawn, Nobody.
- **Example Sentence:** *Ratan Tata is a business magnate.*

subject: English
content:
### Maladroit
- **Definition:** Awkward in movement or unskilled in behaviour or action.
- **Synonyms:** Bumbling, Awkward.
- **Antonyms:** Adroit, Skilful.
- **Example Sentence:** *She can be a little maladroit in social situations.*

subject: English
content:
### Malodorous
- **Definition:** Stinking; foul‑smelling.
- **Synonyms:** Noxious, Fetid.
- **Antonyms:** Aromatic, Fragrant.
- **Example Sentence:** *The malodorous drain is a problem for the locality.*

subject: English
content:
### Maverick
- **Definition:** An unorthodox or independent‑minded person.
- **Synonyms:** Non‑conformist, Dissenter.
- **Antonyms:** Orthodox, Conformist.
- **Example Sentence:** *He was considered as something of a maverick in the publishing world.*

subject: English
content:
### Mellifluous
- **Definition:** Pleasingly smooth and musical to hear.
- **Synonyms:** Harmonious, Mellow.
- **Antonyms:** Noisy, Cacophonous.
- **Example Sentence:** *She has a rich and mellifluous voice.*

subject: English
content:
### Mendacious
- **Definition:** Not truthful; lying.
- **Synonyms:** Deceitful, Dishonest.
- **Antonyms:** Truthful, Honest.
- **Example Sentence:** *All his statements are mendacious.*

subject: English
content:
### Miffed
- **Definition:** Annoyed at someone’s behaviour towards you.
- **Synonyms:** Irritated, Angry.
- **Antonyms:** Pleased.
- **Example Sentence:** *The miffed employees called up a strike.*

subject: English
content:
### Minatory
- **Definition:** Expressing or conveying a threat.
- **Synonyms:** Aggressive, Threatening.
- **Antonyms:** Unthreatening.
- **Example Sentence:** *The minatory situation is under control.*

subject: English
content:
### Minuscule
- **Definition:** Extremely small.
- **Synonyms:** Tiny, Minute.
- **Antonyms:** Huge, Vast.
- **Example Sentence:** *The minuscule insects are hidden there in the bush.*

subject: General English
content:
### Obliterate
- **Definition**: 1. To destroy completely. 2. To remove a thought, feeling or memory from someone’s mind.
- **Synonyms**: Demolish, Annihilate
- **Antonyms**: Create, Establish
- **Example**: *An explosion obliterated the new building.*

subject: General English
content:
### Obnoxious
- **Definition**: Very unpleasant or rude.
- **Synonyms**: Repulsive, Offensive, Disgusting
- **Antonyms**: Agreeable, Decent
- **Example**: *When she’s in a bad mood she is obnoxious to everyone.*

subject: General English
content:
### Obstinate
- **Definition**: Unreasonably determined; stubborn.
- **Synonyms**: Adamant, Inflexible
- **Antonyms**: Flexible, Amenable
- **Example**: *He can be very obstinate at times.*

subject: General English
content:
### Obstreperous
- **Definition**: Difficult to deal with and noisy.
- **Synonyms**: Unruly, Boisterous
- **Antonyms**: Pacified, Tractable
- **Example**: *The executive refused to help the obstreperous clientele.*

subject: General English
content:
### Obverse
- **Definition**: Opposite or counterpart of a fact or truth.
- **Synonyms**: Complement, Counterpart
- **Antonyms**: Reverse, Rear
- **Example**: *The two brothers are of obverse nature.*

subject: General English
content:
### Obviate
- **Definition**: Remove (a need or difficulty); avoid or prevent something undesirable.
- **Synonyms**: Remove, Prevent
- **Antonyms**: Support, Allow

subject: General English
content:
### Occult
- **Definition**: Relating to magical powers and activities.
- **Synonyms**: Psychic, Magical
- **Antonyms**: Natural, Obvious
- **Example**: *Some books in the library were on occult subjects.*

subject: General English
content:
### Offbeat
- **Definition**: Unusual and strange; therefore surprising or noticeable.
- **Synonyms**: Bizarre, Unconventional
- **Antonyms**: Ordinary, Conventional
- **Example**: *She decided to choose an offbeat career in fine arts and was successful.*

subject: General English
content:

- **Definition**: Difficult to do or needing a lot of effort.
- **Synonyms**: Arduous, Demanding
- **Antonyms**: Effortless, Easy
- **Example**: *She found the duties of motherhood onerous.*

subject: General English
content:
### Overweening
- **Definition**: Too proud or confident in yourself.
- **Synonyms**: Brash, Haughty
- **Antonyms**: Modest, Unassuming

subject: General English
content:

subject: English
topic: Synonyms and Antonyms - Words Starting with 'P'
text:
• Plenary:

    Meaning: 1. Complete; full. 2. (of a meeting) To be attended by all participants, who otherwise meet in smaller groups.

    Synonyms: Absolute, Complete

    Antonyms: Incomplete, Limited

    Example: A plenary session of the UN Security Council was held this month.

  • Predicament:

    Meaning: A difficult, unpleasant or embarrassing situation.

    Synonyms: Crisis, Deadlock

    Antonyms: Advantage, Solution

    Example: I have taken a loan to get out of my financial predicament.

  • Prevaricate:

    Meaning: To avoid telling the truth or saying exactly what you think about something.

    Synonyms: Distort, Dodge

    Antonyms: Confront, Face

    Example: The convict prevaricated before the court.

  • Proclivity:

    Meaning: A strong natural liking for something or tendency to do something that is usually bad.

    Synonyms: Predilection, Predisposition

    Antonyms: Antipathy, Disinclination

    Example: Gambling is his main proclivity.

  • Profligate:

    Meaning: Wasteful with money and resources.

    Synonyms: Extravagant, Wasteful

    Antonyms: Thrifty, Frugal

    Example: She is well-known for her profligate spending habits.

subject: English
topic: Synonyms and Antonyms - Words Starting with 'Q'
text:
• Quagmire:

    Meaning: 1. An area of soft wet ground which one sinks into if one tries and walks on it. 2. An awkward, complex or hazardous situation.

    Synonyms: Dilemma, Entanglement

    Antonyms: Solution, Agreement

    Example: The quagmire he is in seems unavoidable.

  • Quail:

    Meaning: Feel or show fear or apprehension.

    Synonyms: Blanch, Cringe

    Antonyms: Calm, Steady

    Example: Students were quailing before the principal.

  • Quaint:

    Meaning: Attractive because of being unusual and especially old-fashioned.

    Synonym: Bizarre

    Antonym: Common

    Example: The writer talked about the quaint customs of the natives.

  • Quandary:

    Meaning: A state of not being able to decide what to do about a situation in which you are involved.

    Synonyms: Impasse, Difficulty

    Antonyms: Solution, Certainty

    Example: The unexpected results of the test have created a quandary for the researchers.

  • Querulous:

    Meaning: Complaining in an annoyed way.

    Synonyms: Petulant, Bemoaning

    Antonyms: Cheerful, Easy-going

    Example: He is becoming a querulous person day by day.

  • Quibble:

    Meaning: To argue or complain about small, unimportant things.

    Synonyms: Protest, Argument

    Antonyms: Approval, Agreement

    Example: There is no point quibbling over a couple of dollars.

  • Quip:

    Meaning: A humorous and clever remark.

    Synonyms: Gag, Gibe

    Antonyms: Seriousness, Praise

    Example: They traded quips over a beer.

  • Quisling:

    Meaning: A person who helps an enemy who has taken over his country.

    Synonyms: Collaborator, Betrayer

    Antonyms: Supporter, Loyalist

    Example: The ruler warned all the quislings.

  • Quixotic:

    Meaning: Having ideas or intentions that are impressive but not practical.

    Synonyms: Impractical, Idealistic

    Antonyms: Practical, Pragmatic

    Example: They had quixotic dreams about future.

subject: English
topic: Synonyms and Antonyms - Words Starting with 'R'
text:
• Rabid:

    Meaning: Having a very extreme opinion about or interest in something.

    Synonyms: Crazed, Fanatical

    Antonyms: Moderate, Liberal

    Example: Amit is a rabid cricket fan.

  • Rankle:

    Meaning: To make someone annoyed or angry for a long time.

    Synonyms: Anger, Embitter

    Antonyms: Calm, Comfort

    Example: It still rankles me that she got promoted and I didn’t.

  • Raspy:

    Meaning: Unpleasantly rough.

    Synonyms: Gruff, Hoarse

    Antonyms: Soothing, Soft

    Example: Her voice was raspy due to yelling so much.

  • Ratify:

    Meaning: To make a treaty, agreement etc official by signing it or voting for it.

    Synonyms: Sanction, Approve

    Antonyms: Disapprove, Deny

    Example: Project was ratified by the officials.

  • Ravishing:

    Meaning: Very beautiful.

    Synonyms: Gorgeous, Stunning

    Antonyms: Ugly, Hideous

    Example: She looked ravishing in her wedding dress.

  • Recondite:

    Meaning: (of a subject or knowledge) Not known by many people and difficult to understand.

    Synonyms: Obscure, Esoteric

    Antonyms: Obvious, Simple

    Example: Geochemistry is a recondite subject.

  • Recoup:

    Meaning: To get back money that one has spent or lost.

    Synonyms: Retrieve, Regain

    Antonyms: Forefeit, Lose

    Example: The gambler recouped his losses in the next game.

  • Rectitude:

    Meaning: The quality of being honest and morally correct.

    Synonyms: Righteousness, Goodness

    Antonyms: Infamy, Dishonesty

    Example: Gandhiji was a man of unquestioned moral rectitude.

  • Redolent:

    Meaning: Strongly reminiscent or suggestive of; fragrant; odorous; suggestive of an odour.

    Synonyms: Evocative, Suggestive

    Antonyms: Bland, Unsavoury

    Example: Rashi's house seemed to be redolent with the aroma of flowers.

  • Reek:

    Meaning: (v/n) To smell strongly and unpleasantly; stink.

    Synonyms: Stink, Smell

    Antonyms: Sweetness, Fragrance

    Example: Her breath reeked of garlic.

subject: English
text:
• Renunciation: The formal rejection of something, typically a belief, claim or course of action. Synonyms: Repudiation, Abandonment. Antonyms: Agreement, Allowance. Example: The company renunciated the agreement made by them.
  • Repartee: Conversation or speech characterised by quick, witty comments or replies. Synonyms: Banter, Pleasantry. Antonyms: Seriousness, Question. Example: The two comedians engaged in witty repartee.
  • Replete: Filled or well supplied with something. Synonyms: Filled, Loaded. Antonyms: Lacking, Empty. Example: The book is replete with photographs.
  • Reprieve: To cancel or postpone a punishment. Synonyms: Abatement, Absolution. Antonyms: Charge, Punish. Example: He was sentenced to death but was granted a last minute reprieve.
  • Reproach: To criticise someone, especially for not being successful or not doing what is expected. Synonyms: Disgrace, Rebuke. Antonyms: Approval, Commendation. Example: His mother reproached him for not eating his dinner.
  • Repugnant: Causing a strong feeling of dislike or disgust. Synonyms: Repulsive, Abhorrent. Antonyms: Pleasant, Delightful. Example: The idea of cheating in an exam is morally repugnant to me.
  • Scintillate: Emit flashes of light, sparkle. Synonyms: Shine, Gleam. Antonyms: Dull. Example: Her scintillating performance on stage won her accolades.
  • Scoff: To laugh and speak about a person or idea in a way that shows you think they are silly or stupid. Synonyms: Belittle, Deride. Antonyms: Approve, Compliment. Example: The critics scoffed at his paintings.
  • Sententious: Trying to appear wise, clever and important in a way that is annoying. Synonyms: Moralistic, Self-righteous. Antonym: Unimportant. Example: Due to his sententious and pompous way of speaking, he respected by none.
  • Servitude: The state of being under the control of someone else and of having no freedom; slavery. Synonyms: Bondage, Enslavement. Antonyms: Freedom, Mastery. Example: In the past, the majority of women were confined to a lifetime of servitude and poverty.
  • Sever: To put an end to (a connection or relationship); break off. Synonyms: Detach, Disconnect. Antonyms: Unite, Connect. Example: I severed myself from my double-faced friends.
  • Sham: Someone or something that is not what it pretends to be; pretence. Synonyms: Fake, Pretend. Antonyms: Real, Genuine. Example: They claimed that the election had been fair, but really it was a sham.
  • Skullduggery: Secret and dishonest behaviour. Synonyms: Trickery, Fraudulence. Antonym: Honesty. Example: Skullduggery is never appreciated.
  • Sleaze: Activities especially business or political, of a low moral standard. Synonyms: Corrupt, Immoral. Antonyms: Moral, Principled. Example: Molestation is an obvious sleaze.
  • Slipshod: Characterised by a lack of care, thought or organisation; shabby. Synonyms: Careless, Disorganised. Antonyms: Careful, Meticulous. Example: She complained that the carpenter's work had been slipshod.
  • Slovenly: 1. Untidy and dirty. 2. (of a person or action) careless; excessively casual. Synonyms: Messy, Scruffy. Antonyms: Tidy, Neat. Example: Change your slovenly habits right now.
  • Stalwart: 1. Loyal, reliable and hardworking. Synonyms: Staunch, Dependable. Antonyms: Non-reliable, Undependable. Example: I have a bunch of stalwart friends.
  • Stodgy: Dull and uninspired; lacking originality or excitement. Synonyms: Boring, Dull. Antonyms: Interesting, Lively. Example: The company did not succeed in shedding its stodgy image.
  • Stouthearted: Brave and determined. Synonyms: Fearless, Courageous. Antonyms: Timid, Cowardly. Example: The stouthearted soldiers won the battle.
  • Stupor: A state of near-unconsciousness or insensibility. Synonyms: Coma, Trance. Antonyms: Consciousness, Wakefulness. Example: He was lying under a table in a drunken stupor.
  • Taint: To damage something, especially by adding something harmful or undesirable to it. Synonyms: Contaminate, Pollute. Antonyms: Clean, Improve. Example: A leaky pipe can taint the entire water supply.
  • Tangible: Real or not imaginary; able to be shown, touched or experienced. Synonyms: Palpable, Touchable. Antonyms: Intangible, Abstract. Example: There is no tangible evidence to support her claim.
  • Thrifty: Using money and other resources carefully and not wastefully. Synonyms: Frugal, Prudent. Antonyms: Extravagant, Generous. Example: He is being thrifty in deciding his budget.

subject: English
text:
• Throttle: To attack or kill someone by choking or strangling; strangle. Synonyms: Gag, Smother. Antonyms: Release, Let go. Example: A leader was throttled by the Maoists.
  • Tirade: A long, angry speech of criticism or accusation. Synonyms: Diatribe, Invective. Antonyms: Compliment, Praise. Example: The coach directed a tirade at the team after the loss.
  • Titanic: Extremely powerful, strong, important or large. Synonyms: Colossal, Gigantic. Antonyms: Small, Puny. Example: A titanic wave let the Titanic sink in.
  • Titter: To give a short, half-suppressed laugh; giggle. Synonyms: Giggle, Snigger. Antonym: Cry. Example: He was tittering on his joke.
  • Toothsome: (Especially of food) attractive or pleasant. Synonyms: Tasty, Delicious. Antonyms: Unpleasant, Unsavoury. Example: Pizza is a toothsome food for this generation.
  • Torpid: Having or showing very little energy or movement; not active. Synonyms: Lethargic, Inactive. Antonyms: Energetic, Active. Example: The torpid boy is becoming obese day-by-day.
  • Tout: 1. To publicise; praise excessively. 2. To sell tickets unofficially, usually at a much higher rate than the official price. Synonyms: Laud, Praise. Antonyms: Criticise, Blame. Example: A local car dealership was touting its wares on the radio.
  • Ubiquitous: Existing everywhere; omnipresent. Synonyms: Universal, Pervasive. Antonyms: Rare, Scarce. Example: Reliance Jio's advertisements are ubiquitous.
  • Umbrage: A feeling of being offended by what someone had said or done. Synonyms: Annoyance, Chagrin. Antonyms: Calmness, Comfort. Example: Will she take umbrage if she isn't invited to the party?
  • Unabashed: Without any worry about possible criticism or embarrassment. Synonyms: Brazen, Unashamed. Antonyms: Ashamed, Sheepish. Example: He is an unabashed capitalist.
  • Unassuaged: Not soothed or relieved. Synonyms: Annoyed, Complaining. Antonyms: Contented, Pleased. Example: The customer is unassuaged with the services.
  • Unbridled: Not controlled or limited. Synonyms: Unrestricted, Unrestrained. Antonyms: Controlled, Restrained. Example: The unbridled riot caused a lot of damage.
  • Undiscerning: Lacking judgement, insight or taste. Synonyms: Obtuse, Indiscriminate. Antonyms: Insightful, Perceptive. Example: The situation showed undiscerning character of the lady.
  • Unequivocal: Leaving no doubt; unambiguous. Synonyms: Unambiguous, Absolute. Antonyms: Ambiguous, Doubtful. Example: The church is unequivocal in its condemnation of the violence.
  • Unexpurgated: (of a text) Complete and containing all the original material; uncensored. Synonyms: Exhaustive, Entire. Antonyms: Censored, Abridged. Example: Unexpurgated material has been sent for proof-reading now.
  • Vanity: 1. Excessive pride in or admiration of one's own appearance or achievements. 2. The quality of being worthless or futile. Synonyms: Egotism, Conceit. Antonyms: Modesty, Humility. Example: Vanity of a person thwarts his path of progress.
  • Vanquish: To defeat thoroughly. Synonyms: Conquer, Trounce. Antonyms: Surrender, Yield. Example: The school team was vanquished in the match.
  • Vaunt: Boast about or praise something, especially excessively. Synonyms: Boast, Brag. Antonyms: Deprecate, Condemn. Example: Even the noblest of fellows have been known to vaunt a bit.
  • Vehement: Expressing strong feelings; forceful, passionate or intense. Synonyms: Forceful, Passionate. Antonyms: Mild, Apathetic. Example: The proposal has faced vehement opposition from many people.
  • Venal: Willing to do dishonest things in return for money. Synonyms: Corrupt, Crooked. Antonyms: Honest, Ethical. Example: The country wants to get rid of venal leaders.
  • Venerable: Valued and respected because of old age, long use etc. Synonyms: Revered, Esteemed. Antonyms: Dishonourable, Disreputable. Example: The Hindu is a venerable newspaper.
  • Venerate: To honour or greatly respect a person or thing. Synonyms: Respect, Exalt. Antonyms: Denounce, Condemn. Example: The Ganges is a venerated river in India.
  • Verity: An important principle or fact that is always true. Synonyms: Accuracy, Veracity. Antonyms: Falseness, Falsehood. Example: Revolution of Earth on its axis is a verity.

subject: English
text:
Generally, 8-12 questions are asked on synonyms in the CDS exam. The questions can be in a direct format or sentence format. A candidate is expected to have a good vocabulary to solve these questions correctly.

Synonyms are the words which have a similar meaning to that of a given word.

e.g. The synonyms of the word reside is 'dwell'.

Questions on synonyms can be asked directly or in a sentence format in the CDS exam.

1. Direct Format

In this format a word is given and out of the given four options, a word is to be selected which is the nearest in meaning to the given word.

  • Example: Which of the given words is closest in meaning to the word provided?
    REMOTE
    • (a) Automatic
    • (b) Distant
    • (c) Mean
    • (d) Savage
    Explanation: (b) Remote means located far away and 'Distant' also means 'far away in space or time'. While, Automatic means done or occurring spontaneously; Mean means intend to convey or refer to and Savage means cruel and vicious. So, the right synonym for 'Remote' is 'Distant'. Hence, option (b) is the correct choice.

2. Sentence Format

In this format one word of a sentence is underlined or capitalized and out of the given four options, a word is to be selected which is similar in meaning to the underlined or capitalized word.

  • Example: Which of the given words has the same meaning to the word written in capital letters?
    Getting a WEAK mobile signal in remote areas is quite common.
    • (a) Fluctuating
    • (b) Falling
    • (c) Low
    • (d) Distant
    Explanation: (c) In this sentence 'Weak' means 'Low' mobile signal. While, Fluctuating (rise and fall); Falling (drop down) and Distant (far away) have different meanings. Hence, option (c) is the correct choice.

subject: English
text:
Generally, 8-10 questions are asked on antonyms in the CDS exam. The questions can be asked in a direct format or in a sentence format. The candidate is expected to have a good vocabulary to solve these questions.

An Antonym is a word that is directly opposite in meaning to a given word. e.g. The word 'Fresh' has its antonym as 'Stale'.

1. Direct Format

In this format a word is given and out of the given four options, a word is to be selected which is opposite in meaning to the given word.

2. Sentence Format

In this format one word of a sentence is highlighted and out of the given four options, a word is to be selected which is opposite in meaning to that of the highlighted word.

subject: English
text:
Idioms and Phrases form an essential part of any language. They add power, meaning and crispness to our everyday expressions, conversations and writings. There is a huge number of idioms, phrases and proverbs in English and we should not hesitate to use them to enhance the beauty of the language. Idioms and phrases do have an ornamental value but more than that, they are tools which can be used to get the desired impact.

Idioms are usually comprised of very few words but encompassed in them is a deep meaning. So, when one is at a dearth for words, Idioms can easily come to the rescue. We can put forth our thoughts more effectively and in an impressive manner using them.

The only disadvantage in using them is that in our eagerness and enthusiasm to impress others, we normally do not spend any time in understanding the meaning of the idiom. It is very crucial to do this because using an idiom inappropriately can entirely change the meaning of the sentence or twist the truth.

Idioms add value and power to our expressions, only if we use them accurately and efficiently.

subject: English
text:
Some Important Idioms and Phrases

  • A blessing in disguise: Something good that isn't recognised at first.
  • A chip on your shoulder: To seem angry all the time because you think you have been treated unfairly or feel you are not as good as other people.
  • A dime a dozen: Anything that is common and easy to get.
  • A doubting Thomas: A skeptic who needs physical or personal evidence in order to believe something.
  • A drop in the bucket: A very small part of something big or whole.
  • A fool and his money are easily parted: It's easy for a foolish person to lose his/her money.
  • A house divided against itself cannot stand: If the members of a group fight each other, the group will disintegrate.
  • A leopard can't change his spots: A person's character especially if it is bad, will not change, even if they pretend it has.
  • A penny saved is a penny earned: By not spending money, you are saving money (little by little).
  • A picture paints a thousand words: A visual presentation is far more descriptive than words.
  • A piece of cake: A task that can be accomplished very easily.
  • A slap on the wrist: A very mild punishment.
  • A taste of your own medicine: When you are mistreated the same way you mistreat others.
  • A toss-up: A situation where two or more possibilities are equally likely.
  • Actions speak louder than words: It's better to actually do something than just talk about it.
  • Add fuel to the fire: Something done to make a bad situation even worse than it is.
  • Against the clock: Against time; in a great hurry to get something done before a particular time.
  • All bark and no bite: When someone is threatening and/or is aggressive but not willing to engage in a fight.
  • All Greek to me: Something that is meaningless and incomprehensible to someone.
  • All in the same boat: When everyone is facing the same challenges.
  • An arm and a leg: Very expensive, costing a large amount of money.
  • Have an axe to grind: To have a strong personal opinion about something that you want people to accept and that is the reason you do something.
  • Apple of my eye: Someone who is cherished above all others.
  • Be as high as a kite: To feel very happy and excited.
  • At the drop of a hat: Willing to do something immediately.
  • Back to square one: Having to start all over again.
  • Back to the drawing board: Back to the beginning or planning phase after an approach has proved unsuccessful.
  • Barking up the wrong tree: To be wrong about the reason for something or the way to achieve something.
  • Beat a dead horse: To waste effort on something when there is no chance of succeeding.
  • Beating around the bush: Avoiding the main topic, not speaking directly about the issue.
  • Bend over backwards: To go out of one's way to do something for someone.
  • Between a rock and a hard place: Stuck between two very bad options.
  • Bite off more than you can chew: To decide or agree to do more than one can finally accomplish.
  • Bite your tongue: To stop yourself from saying something that you would really like to say.
  • Blood is thicker than water: Said to emphasize that you believe that family connections are always more important than other types of relationship.
  • Once in a blue moon: To do something rarely.
  • Break a leg: A superstitious way to say 'good luck' without saying 'good luck', but rather the opposite.
  • Buy a lemon: To purchase a vehicle that constantly gives problems or stops running after you drive it away.
  • Can't cut the mustard: Unable to deal with problems or difficulties.
  • Cast iron stomach: Someone who has no problems, complications or ill effects with eating anything or drinking anything.
  • Charley horse: A cramp in your arm or leg.
  • Chew someone out: Verbally scold someone.
  • Chow down: To eat something usually quickly, saying something rude or unpleasant.
  • Close but no cigar: To be very near and almost accomplish a goal, but fall short.
  • Cock and bull story: An unbelievable tale.
  • Come hell or high water: To decide to do something no matter what happens.

text:
Idioms and Phrases with Meanings:

  • Crack someone up: To make someone laugh.
  • Cross your fingers: To hope that something happens the way you want it to.
  • Cry over spilt milk: To regret in vain about what cannot be undone or rectified.
  • Cry wolf: Intentionally raise a false alarm.
  • Cup of joe: A cup of coffee.
  • Curiosity kills the cat: Being inquisitive can lead you into a dangerous situation.
  • Cut to the chase: Leave out all the unnecessary details and get to the main point.
  • Dark horse: Someone who unexpectedly wins a competition.
  • A dead ringer for someone/ something: Someone or something that looks exactly like someone or something else.
  • Devil’s advocate: Someone who argues against a cause or position either for the sake of argument or to help determine its validity.
  • Dog days of summer: The hottest days of the summer season.
  • Don’t count your chickens before they hatch: Don't make plans based on future events that might not happen.
  • Don’t look a gift horse in the mouth: When someone gives you a gift, accept it graciously.
  • Don’t put all your eggs in one basket: To not put all your resources in one area.
  • Down to the wire: Until the last possible moment.
  • Drastic times call for drastic measures: When you are extremely desperate you need to take extremely desperate actions.
  • Drive someone up the wall: To irritate and/or annoy someone very much.
  • Dropping like flies: A large number of people either falling ill or dying.
  • Dry run: Rehearsal; a dummy run or show.
  • Elvis has left the building: The show has come to an end; it’s all over.
  • Ethnic cleansing: Killing of a certain ethnic or religious group on a massive scale.
  • Every cloud has a silver lining: There is something good even in an unpleasant situation.
  • Everything but the kitchen sink: Almost everything imaginable.
  • Feeding frenzy: A situation in which people try to get as much as possible of something, for example information about an event, especially in an unpleasant way.
  • Field day: A time of great pleasure, activity or opportunity.
  • Finding your feet: To become familiar with and confident in a new situation.
  • Fixed in your ways: Not willing or wanting to change from your normal way of doing something.
  • Flash in the pan: Something that happened only once or for a short time and was not repeated.
  • Flesh and blood: The quality of being alive.
  • Foam at the mouth: To be extremely angry.
  • From rags to riches: To go from being very poor to being very wealthy.
  • Get down to brass tacks: To start talking about the most important or basic facts of a situation.
  • Get over it: To move beyond something that is bothering you.
  • Get up on the wrong side of the bed: To begin the day feeling unhappy and uncomfortable.
  • Get your walking papers: To get fired from a job.
  • Give him the slip: To get away from or escape someone.
  • Go down like a lead balloon: To be received badly by an audience.
  • Go for broke: To gamble everything you have.
  • Go out on a limb: Put yourself in a tough position in order to support someone/something.
  • Go the extra mile: Going above and beyond whatever is required for the task at hand.
  • Good Samaritan: Someone who helps others when they are in need, with no discussion for compensation and no thought of a reward.
  • Great minds think alike: Intelligent people think like each other.
  • Green room: The waiting room, especially for those who are about to go on a TV or radio show.
  • Gut feeling: Sense something about a person or situation, without knowing why, but you’re sure what you sense is right.
  • Haste makes waste: Quickly doing things results in a poor ending.
  • Have clean hands: Be guiltness.
  • He lost his head: To be angry and overcome by emotions.
  • Head over heels: To be very excited or joyful, especially when in love.
  • To be going to hell in a hand basket: To be rapidly deteriorating – on course for disaster.
  • Hit the books: To study especially for a test or an exam.
  • Hit the hay: Go to bed or go to sleep.

subject: English
text:
Generally, 10 to 15 questions based on sentence completion are asked in CDS exam. The question can be based on a sentence or paragraph format. The candidate has to choose to fill the blank from the given options.

Sentence completion comprises of filling up of the gaps given in a particular sentence individually or in a passage. The sentence has a blank and is followed by four options. A candidate has to pick the correct option to fill the blank in order to make the sentence meaningful and grammatically correct.

A candidate should read the given sentence first and try to deduce the meaning of the statement. After that, the inferred meaning should be matched with the given options. The closest inferential word is to be selected as the choice.

Language Skills Required for Sentence Completion

Sentence completion becomes a great ease when a student is well-versed in these areas of languages:

  • Using correct adjective forms
  • Words followed by prepositions
  • Idioms, phrases and phrasal verbs
  • Noun and its forms
  • Using the correct verb form

Apart from all these, a good command over vocabulary also helps a candidate in solving questions on Sentence Completion correctly.

content:
### Key Vocabulary & Contextual Clues

**1. Wildlife Behavior (Wild Dogs vs. Jackals)**
*   **Wild Dogs (Dholes):** Typically do not leave any kill behind; they finish the prey up to the bone. This behavior is a key identifier in forensic wildlife analysis.
*   **Jackals:** Often active in areas like Sariska and may leave partial kills or scavenge. Distinguishing between jackal and wild dog activity is crucial for conservation strategies.

**2. Forensic/Examination Terms**
*   **Carcass:** The correct term for a dead animal body, especially when referring to large animals in a wildlife context. 'Body' is too generic; 'corpse' is typically reserved for humans.
*   **Predator:** The animal that hunts and kills prey. In the context of finding a dead Chital (Spotted Deer), the goal is to identify the predator (wild dog vs. jackal).
*   **Clues/Information:** An examination of the kill site provides vital clues about the predator's identity and behavior.

**3. Seasonal Changes (Spring to Summer)**
*   **Buds:** In spring, buds *appear* or *emerge* in trees.
*   **World's Appearance:** The world *wears* or *don* a green dress (metaphorical usage for vegetation).
*   **Transition:** Spring passes *into* summer.
*   **Impermanence:** Summer will not *last* forever. The power of humans cannot keep it.
*   **Agricultural Cycle:** Corn becomes ripe, and leaves turn (color change) as seasons shift.

In some questions, first and the last sentences of a paragraph are given and the candidate is needed to place the middle sentences in a proper sequence. subject: English
content:
### Sentence Rearrangement Strategy

1. **Identify the Start (S1) and End (S6):**
   - S1 usually introduces the topic or the first event.
   - S6 often provides a conclusion, a result, or a final statement.

2. **Group Related Sentences:**
   - Look for pronouns (he, she, it, they) that refer to nouns in previous sentences.
   - Look for temporal markers (first, then, later, finally).
   - Look for logical connectors (however, therefore, thus, on the other hand).

3. **Specific Patterns Observed:**
   - **Narrative Sequence:** Event -> Problem -> Action -> Resolution -> Result.
   - **Expository Sequence:** Definition -> Components -> Details of Components -> Function/Result.
   - **Argumentative Sequence:** Thesis -> Example 1 -> Example 2 -> Counter-point/Refinement -> Conclusion.

subject: General English
content:
### Strategy for Ordering Sentences

1. **Identify the Start (S1) and End (S6):**
   - **S1** usually introduces the topic, a general statement, or a specific event.
   - **S6** often provides a conclusion, a result, or a final observation.

2. **Look for Logical Connectors:**
   - **Time Markers:** Words like "Before", "Since that time", "Now-a-days", "At last", "When midnight came" help establish chronological order.
   - **Causal/Resultant Markers:** "Thus", "Therefore", "Consequently" indicate a conclusion based on previous statements.
   - **Contrast/Transition:** "Although", "But", "However" link contrasting ideas.

3. **Pronoun Reference:**
   - Ensure that pronouns (he, she, it, they, this, that) refer back to a noun mentioned in the preceding sentence.

4. **Thematic Continuity:**
   - Group sentences that discuss the same specific aspect of the main topic before moving to the next aspect.

### Key Examples from Practice

**Example 1: Historical/Geographical Context**
- **Logic:** Start with the past state (Before 16th century), move to the change (Since that time), then the current state (Now-a-days), and finally the specific historical parallel or conclusion.
- **Sequence:** R (Before 16th century...) -> Q (Since that time...) -> P (Now-a-days...) -> S (Augustus... - *Note: In this specific question, the logic might vary based on the exact text, but typically historical progression is key.*).

**Example 2: Scientific Process (Photosynthesis)**
- **Logic:**
  1. Need for carbon (S1).
  2. Source of carbon (R: from CO2 in air).
  3. Process of breaking down CO2 (S: break up, absorb carbon, discharge oxygen).
  4. Energy requirement for the process (P: requires energy from Sun).
  5. Other needs (Q: nutrients from soil/water).
  6. Conclusion (S6: Through photosynthesis... receive requirements).
- **Correct Sequence:** R -> S -> P -> Q (or similar depending on exact phrasing, but R must follow S1 as it explains the source).

**Example 3: Narrative/Story**
- **Logic:** Chronological order of events.
  1. Search all day (S1).
  2. Feeling weary but not discouraged (P).
  3. Midnight arrives, can't walk further (R).
  4. Find a place to rest (S).
  5. Creep in and lie down (Q).
  6. Wake up (S6).
- **Sequence:** P -> R -> S -> Q.

subject: English
topic: Identifying the Correct Order of Sentences
content:
### Sentence Rearrangement Strategy

1. **Identify the Start (S1) and End (S6):**
   - The first sentence (S1) introduces the topic.
   - The last sentence (S6) often provides a conclusion, summary, or final definition.

2. **Analyze Linking Words and Pronouns:**
   - Look for pronouns (it, they, this, that) which refer back to nouns in previous sentences.
   - Identify transition words (however, therefore, moreover, whereas) that indicate logical flow.

3. **Group Related Ideas:**
   - Sentences discussing the same specific aspect of the topic should be kept together.
   - Example: If one sentence mentions 'two different things', the following sentences should likely describe those two things individually.

4. **Check for Chronological or Logical Progression:**
   - Ensure the sequence moves from general to specific, or cause to effect, or step-by-step process.

### Example Analysis from Page Content:

**Question 50 Analysis (Soda Water):**
- **S1:** Introduces the observation of soda water on a table.
- **Q:** "You will see that it is separating into two different things, a liquid and a gas." (This logically follows S1 as the immediate observation).
- **P:** "The liquid is plain water..." (Describes the first of the 'two things' mentioned in Q).
- **S:** "The other is a heavy, sour and invisible gas..." (Describes the second of the 'two things' mentioned in Q. 'The other' links back to the liquid in P).
- **R:** "The gas is so heavy..." (Further elaborates on the gas described in S).
- **S6:** "'Carbonic acid' is the old name for it..." (Provides the scientific name/conclusion for the gas).
- **Correct Sequence:** Q -> P -> S -> R -> S6. Note: The options provided in the text are (a) QRSP, (b) PRQS, (c) QPSR, (d) RSPQ. Based on standard logic, QPSR is the most coherent flow among the choices if R is considered part of the gas description before the final naming, or if the options imply a specific subset. *Note: In the provided text, option (c) QPSR is a strong candidate for the sequence of the middle sentences.*

subject: General English
content:
### How to order sentences in a paragraph

1. **Identify the role of each sentence**
   - **S (Statement/Scenario)** – introduces the situation or background.
   - **P (Premise/Problem)** – states a problem, a fact, or a premise that follows from the scenario.
   - **Q (Question/Query)** – raises a question or presents a contrast to the premise.
   - **R (Result/Resolution)** – gives the outcome, solution, or conclusion.

2. **Typical logical progression**
   - **S → P → Q → R** – most natural flow: set the scene, present a problem, ask a question, then answer it.
   - **Chronological order** – arrange sentences according to time sequence (earliest → latest).
   - **Cause‑effect order** – cause sentences first, followed by effect sentences.
   - **Problem‑solution order** – problem statement first, then the solution.

3. **Cohesive devices**
   - Use linking words such as *therefore, however, at the same time, consequently, when* to signal the relationship between sentences.
   - Ensure pronoun references are clear (e.g., *its mother*, *the lamb*).

4. **Common pitfalls**
   - Mixing up the order of cause and effect.
   - Placing a conclusion before the supporting statements.
   - Ignoring temporal cues like *when, after, before*.

5. **Practice strategy**
   - Read all sentences first.
   - Mark each sentence with its functional label (S, P, Q, R).
   - Sketch a simple flow‑chart showing the logical connections.
   - Test each answer option against the flow‑chart; the correct option will preserve the logical sequence without contradictions.

---

### Sample Formula for Quick Decision‑Making
```
If (Temporal cue) → place earlier
If (Cause → Effect) → cause first, effect later
If (Problem → Solution) → problem first, solution later
```
---

### Example of a Correct Sequence
Given:
- S: "When a lamb is born, its mother may die."
- P: "If a means of overcoming this natural tendency is found, the lives of millions of lambs can be saved."
- Q: "However a sheep which has lost its own lamb will not feed or look after a motherless lamb."
- R: "At the same time, some newborn lambs are too weak to live."

Logical order: **S → R → Q → P** (or any variation that respects cause‑effect and temporal flow). The answer option that matches this order is the correct one.

Around 15 to 20 questions based on comprehension are asked in CDS exam. The questions are based on the given passages.

Tips for Attempting Comprehension:

  • Skim once as rapidly as possible to determine the main idea before you look at the questions. Do not worry about words you do not know at this juncture.
  • Underline the Words that you do not understand to facilitate a complete understanding of the passage. This will help you to locate the words later.
  • Look Through the Questions Carefully You are advised to maintain the order in which the questions appear in the test paper. Read intensively the portion relevant to the answer.
  • Concentrate on the vocabulary items and re-read the portions of the passage containing the words you do not understand to find out their meanings.

Usually, options are quite tricky or some options are closely related. Therefore, analyse the questions and answer options carefully before answering. Answer strictly on the basis of the passage and avoid selecting general answers.

subject: Science
text:
Early earthquake measurement instruments utilized the principle of inertia. A simple device consisted of rods standing on end like ninepins; if the earthquake was gentle, only unstable rods fell, while severe quakes caused all to fall. The direction of the fall recorded the direction of the earthquake.

The ideal instrument design involves a pen recording movements on paper. Since the pen moves but the paper remains stationary, the challenge is to keep the pen steady while the paper moves, or vice versa, mimicking the observation that a person standing in a bus or train tends to fall when the vehicle moves suddenly because their feet move while their head stays still.

details.summary: Explanation of early seismometer design principles based on inertia and observation of motion.

subject: Science
text: Pressure Welding: The simplest method of welding two pieces of metal together. The ends of metal are heated to a white heat—for iron, the welding temperature should be about 1300°C—at this temperature the metal becomes plastic. The ends are then pressed or hammered together and the joint is smoothed off. Care must be taken to ensure that the surfaces are thoroughly cleaned first, for dirt will weaken the weld. Moreover, the heating of iron or steel to a high temperature causes oxidation, and a film of oxide is formed on the heated surfaces.

details.summary: Explanation of the pressure welding process, including temperature requirements for iron and the necessity of surface cleaning to prevent oxidation and weak joints.

chapter: Measurement, Motion, Work, Energy and Power
text:
Physical Quantities: All the quantities which can be measured directly or indirectly in terms of which law of physics are described and whose measurement is necessary, are called physical quantities. e.g. velocity, time, mass, etc.

Unit: The standard amount of a physical quantity chosen to measure the physical quantity of same kind is called a physical unit.

Fundamental and Derived Units: The unit of a defined set of physical quantities called fundamental quantities are known as fundamental units and the units for all other physical quantities, except fundamental quantities are known as derived units.

SI System: It is based on the following seven basic units and two supplementary units.
formulas: Unit of speed = Unit of distance / Unit of time = m / s = ms^-1

subject: Physics
text:
Scalar Quantities: Physical quantities which have magnitude only and no direction. Examples: mass, speed, volume, work, time, power, energy, etc.

Vector Quantities: Physical quantities which have magnitude and direction both and which obey triangle law. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, torque, etc.

details.summary: Definitions and examples of scalar and vector quantities.

subject: Physics
text:
Motion: A body is said to be in motion when its position changes continuously with respect to a stationary body taken as a reference point.

Distance: The actual length of the path travelled by a body between the initial position and final position. It is always positive, a scalar quantity, and its unit is metre.

Displacement: The change in position of the particle in a particular direction. It may be positive, negative or zero. It is a vector quantity, its unit is metre, and the magnitude of displacement may or may not be equal to the path length travelled (Displacement <= Distance).
image_descriptions: Figure (a) shows a curved path from A to B through points C, D, and E, where distance is AC + CD + DE + EB and displacement is AB. Figure (b) shows a triangular path from A to C through B, where distance is AB + BC and displacement is AC.

details.summary: Definitions of motion, distance, and displacement with their properties.

subject: Physics
text:
Speed: The path length or the distance covered by an object divided by the time taken. Its unit is m/s or km/h.

  • Uniform speed: Covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.
  • Variable speed: Covers equal distances in unequal intervals of time or unequal distances in equal intervals of time.
  • Average Speed: Ratio of total distance travelled to total time taken.
  • Instantaneous speed: Speed at a particular moment or instant of time.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for speed, uniform speed, variable speed, and average speed.

subject: Physics
text:
Velocity: The rate of change in position or displacement of a body with time. It is a vector quantity.

  • Uniform velocity: Equal displacements in equal intervals of time.
  • Variable velocity: Speed or direction changes with time.
  • Average Velocity: Net displacement divided by time taken.
  • Relative Velocity: Speed (or velocity) of one body with respect to another.
formulas: Velocity = Displacement in particular direction / Time taken

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for velocity, uniform/variable velocity, average velocity, and relative velocity.

subject: Physics
text:
Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity with respect to time.

  • SI unit: m/s^2
  • CGS unit: cm/s^2
  • It is a vector quantity.
  • Uniform acceleration: An object's velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.
  • Variable acceleration: An object's velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal intervals of time.
  • Positive acceleration: Velocity increases without change in direction.
  • Negative acceleration (deceleration or retardation): Velocity decreases without change in direction.
  • Acceleration is zero if the object is at rest or moving with uniform velocity.

details.summary: Definition and types of acceleration.

subject: Physics
text:
1. Position-Time Graphs:

  • (i) Increasing distance with time (positive acceleration): Curve bending upwards.
  • (ii) Decreasing distance with time (negative acceleration): Curve bending downwards.
  • (iii) Equal distance in equal time (uniform velocity): Straight line with positive slope.
  • (iv) Position does not change (at rest): Horizontal straight line.

2. Velocity-Time Graphs:

  • (i) Zero acceleration: Horizontal straight line.
  • (ii) Uniform positive acceleration (starting from origin): Straight line with positive slope.
  • (iii) Negative and constant acceleration: Straight line with negative slope.
  • (iv) Increasing acceleration: Curve bending towards velocity axis.
  • (v) Decreasing acceleration: Curve bending towards time axis.
