subject: Physics
text:
Amplitude (A): Maximum displacement of a vibrating particle of medium from its mean position is called amplitude.

Wavelength (λ): Wavelength is the distance between any two nearest particle of the medium, vibrating in the same phase.

Frequency (f): Frequency of vibration of a particle is defined as the number of vibrations completed by particle in one second.

Velocity of wave (v): Frequency (f) × Wavelength (λ)

details.summary: Definitions of fundamental wave parameters including amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and wave velocity.

subject: Physics
text:
According to their frequency range, longitudinal mechanical waves are divided into the following categories:

  • Audible or sound waves: Longitudinal mechanical waves in the range 20 Hz to 20000 Hz. Human ears are sensitive to these.
  • Infrasonic waves: Longitudinal mechanical waves having frequencies less than 20 Hz. Produced by earthquakes, volcanic eruption, ocean waves, and elephants and whales.
  • Ultrasonic waves: Longitudinal mechanical waves having frequencies greater than 20000 Hz.

Applications of Ultrasonic waves: Sending signals, measuring depth of sea, cleaning clothes and machinery parts of clocks, removing lamp soot from chimney of factories, and ultrasonography. Echocardiography is the use of ultrasonic waves to investigate the action of the heart.

details.summary: Classification of longitudinal mechanical waves based on frequency ranges: Audible, Infrasonic, and Ultrasonic.

subject: Physics
text:
Sound wave is the form of energy which make us hear and having frequency and high wavelength. These can not travel in vacuum. It is of two types i.e. longitudinal wave and mechanical wave.

  • Reflection of sound: The rebouncing back of sound when it strikes a hard surface. Utilised in megaphone, bullhorn, stethoscope and sound board.
  • Echo: The repetition of sound caused by the reflection of sound waves. Curtains, carpets and sofa-sets reduce echoes.
  • Reverberation: The persistence of sound in a big hall due to repeated reflections from walls, ceiling and floor.

Key Facts: To hear echo, the minimum distance between the observer and reflection should be 17m. Persistance of ear is 1/10 s. At the moon, the echo is not heared due to absence of atmosphere.

SONAR: Stands for sound navigation and ranging. Used to measure the depth of a sea and to locate the submarines and shipwrecks. Produces pulses of ultrasonic sound waves of frequency about 50000 Hz.

details.summary: Overview of sound wave properties, reflection phenomena (echo, reverberation), and the SONAR system.

subject: Physics
text:
The distance travelled by sound wave in one second is known as speed of sound.

Formulae:

  • Speed of sound (v) = Frequency × Wavelength
  • For a medium: v = sqrt(E/d), where E is modulus of elasticity and d is density.
  • For gases: v = sqrt(γp/d), where p is pressure and γ is ratio of specific heats.

Key Observations:

  • Speed of sound is maximum in solids and minimum in gases.
  • Speed of sound in air is 332 m/s, 1483 m/s in water and 5130 m/s in iron.
  • When sound enters from one medium to another, speed and wavelength change but frequency remains unchanged.
  • Speed of sound remains unchanged by the increase or decrease of pressure.
  • Speed of sound increases with the increase of temperature (in air by 0.61 m/s per 1°C).
  • Speed of sound is more in humid air than in dry air.
  • Speed of sound in air is very slower as compared to the speed of light in air.

Note: The astronauts who land on moon, talk to one another through wireless sets using radio waves.

details.summary: Mathematical and physical factors affecting the speed of sound in different media.

subject: Physics
text: Intensity: Intensity of sound at any point in space is defined as amount of energy passing normally per unit area held around that point per unit time. SI unit of intensity is W/m².

details.summary: Definition and SI unit of sound intensity.

subject: Physics
text:
Intensity of sound at a point is inversely proportional to the square of the distance of point from the source and directly proportional to the square of amplitude of vibration, square of frequency and density of the medium.

The loudness depends on intensity as well as on sensitivity of ear. It is measured in decibel (dB).

Sound level formula: β = 10 log10(I/I₀), where I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² at 1 kHz.

Pitch: Characteristic of sound distinguishing sharp sound from grave sound. Depends on frequency. Female voice has higher pitch than male voice; mosquito whisper has higher pitch than roaring lion.

Quality (or Timbre): Characteristic enabling distinction between sounds of same intensity and pitch.

Shock Waves: Produced by bodies moving at supersonic speed. They carry huge energy and can cause damage. Measured in Mach number = Velocity of source / Velocity of sound.

  • Mach number > 1: Supersonic
  • Mach number > 5: Hypersonic
  • Mach number < 1: Subsonic

Resonance: Occurs when external force frequency equals natural frequency of the body, leading to large amplitude oscillations. Example: Soldiers on a bridge walking in step can cause collapse.

Definitions:

  • Interference: Superposition of two waves of same frequency/wavelength/velocity results in energy redistribution.
  • Beat: Regular variation in intensity of sound due to superposition of two waves of slightly different frequencies.
  • Progressive Waves: Disturbance travels in medium, handed over from one particle to next.
  • Stationary Waves: Combination of two waves moving in opposite directions with same amplitude and frequency.

Doppler's Effect: Apparent frequency change due to relative motion between source and observer. Uses: Police speed checks, airport aircraft guidance, heart/blood flow monitoring, and determining velocity of stars/galaxies.
formulas: Mach number = Velocity of source / Velocity of sound
tables:
| Areas | Day time (dB) | Night time (dB) |
|---|---|---|
| Industrial area | 75 | 70 |
| Commercial area | 65 | 55 |
| Residential area | 55 | 45 |
| Silence | 50 | 40 |

details.summary: Comprehensive overview of sound physics including intensity, loudness, pitch, quality, shock waves, resonance, wave definitions, and Doppler's effect.

subject: Physics
text:
Light is the radiation which makes our eyes able to see the object. Its speed is 3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum.

  • Light is the form of energy. It is a transverse wave and it takes 8 min 19 s to reach on the earth from the sun.
  • The light reflected from the moon takes 1.28 s to reach the earth.
  • It represents the phenomenon of reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction, scattering and polarisation.

details.summary: Introduction to light, its speed, nature, and travel time from celestial bodies.

subject: Physics
text:
Reflection is the phenomenon of change in the path of light without any change in its medium. In reflection, the frequency, speed and wavelength do not change, but a phase change may occur depending on the nature of reflecting surface.

Laws of Reflection:

  • The angle of reflection (∠r) is always equal to the angle of incidence (∠i) i.e. ∠i = ∠r.
  • The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a light ray hitting a mirror surface at point P, with an incident ray coming from A, a reflected ray going to B, and a normal line N perpendicular to the mirror surface at P. Angles i and r are marked between the normal and the rays.

details.summary: Definition and laws governing the reflection of light.

subject: Physics
text:
A mirror is a polished surface (one side) like glass, which reflects almost all the light that is incident on it. There are two types of mirror.

Plane Mirror: If the reflecting surface of a mirror is plane, then the mirror is called a plane mirror.

  • Size of image is always equal to the size of object.
  • The minimum size of the mirror required to see the full image of an observer is half the height of the observer.
  • If the plane mirror is rotated in the plane of incidence by an angle θ, then the reflected ray rotates by an angle 2θ.
  • If the object is displaced by a distance x towards or away from the mirror, then its image will be displaced by a distance x towards or away from the mirror.
  • Focal length of plane mirror is infinity i.e. power of the plane mirror is zero.
  • Linear magnification produced by plane mirror is 1.
  • When two plane mirrors are kept facing each other at an angle θ and an object is placed between them, then:

(i) Number of images, n = (360° / θ) - 1. If (360° / θ) is even or object lies symmetrically.

(ii) Number of images, n = (360° / θ). If (360° / θ) is odd or the object lies symmetrically.

Uses of the Plane Mirror:

  • (i) Plane mirrors are used as looking glass.
  • (ii) Plane mirrors are used in constructing periscope which is used in submarines.
  • (iii) Plane mirrors are used to make kaleidoscope.

details.summary: Properties, mathematical rules for multiple images, and uses of plane mirrors.

subject: Physics
text:
Spherical mirrors can be regarded as a part of a hollow reflecting spheres of glass. These are of two types: (i) Concave mirror, (ii) Convex mirror.

Concave mirror: The spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is inwardly leaned, called concave mirror. It is also called converging mirror.

Convex mirror: The spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is outwardly leaned, called convex mirror. It is also called diverging mirror.

Real Image:

  • Real images can be formed on a screen by the actual intersection of reflected (or refracted) light rays.
  • The image formed on a cinema screen is a real image.
  • A concave mirror forms real image, when an object is placed beyond its focus.
image_descriptions: Diagram of a concave mirror showing the principal axis, pole (P), focus (F), and centre of curvature (C). The reflecting surface is curved inward.
Diagram of a convex mirror showing the principal axis, pole (P), focus (F), and centre of curvature (C). The reflecting surface is curved outward.

details.summary: Definitions of spherical mirrors (concave and convex) and real images.

subject: Physics
text:
Virtual Image:

  • Virtual images cannot be formed on the screen by the apparent intersection of reflected (or refracted) light rays.
  • The image of our face when we look into a plane mirror is a virtual image. A concave mirror forms a virtual image, when an object is placed between focus and pole of the mirror.
tables:
| Position of object | Position of image | Size of image | Nature of image |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F | Highly diminished | Real and inverted |
| Between infinity and C | Between F and C | Diminished | -do- |
| At C | At C | Same size | -do- |
| Between F and C | Between infinity and C | Enlarged | -do- |
| At F | At infinity | Highly enlarged | -do- |
| Between F and P | Behind the pole | Enlarged | Virtual and erect |

| Position of object | Position of image | Size of image | Nature of image |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F | Highly diminished | Erect and virtual |
| Between infinity and pole | Between F and P | Diminished in size | Erect and virtual |

details.summary: Definition and properties of virtual images, including tables summarizing image formation positions for concave mirrors.

subject: Physics
text:
Image Formation by Concave Mirror:

The following are the positions and nature of the images formed in a concave mirror for different positions of the object:

  • (i) When the object is at infinity: Image is formed at F.
  • (ii) When the rays are parallel to the principal axis: The image is formed at F.
  • (iii) When the object is between infinity and C: The image formed is real, inverted and smaller in size and is formed between F and C.
  • (iv) When the object is at C: The image formed is inverted, real, equal in size and is formed at C itself.
  • (v) When the object is between F and C: The image is formed beyond C and is inverted, real and larger than the object.
  • (vi) When the object is at focus: The image is formed at infinity. The image is real, inverted and infinitely large in size.
  • (vii) When the object is between F and P: The images formed behind the pole. The image is virtual, erect and large.
image_descriptions: (i) Ray diagram showing parallel rays from infinity converging at F on a concave mirror.
(ii) Ray diagram showing parallel rays hitting the concave mirror and reflecting through F.
(iii) Ray diagram showing object AB between infinity and C, forming inverted image A'B' between F and C.
(iv) Ray diagram showing object AB at C, forming inverted image A'B' at C.
(v) Ray diagram showing object AB between F and C, forming inverted image A'B' beyond C.
(vi) Ray diagram showing object AB at F, with reflected rays parallel to the principal axis.
(vii) Ray diagram showing object AB between F and P, forming a virtual, erect, enlarged image A'B' behind the mirror.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of image formation by concave mirrors based on object position.

subject: Physics
text:
Image Formation by Convex Mirror:

  • When the object is at infinity: The image is formed at focus.
  • When the object is between infinity and pole: The image is formed between pole and focus.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing light rays from an object at infinity hitting a convex mirror and converging to a focus point F behind the mirror.
Diagram showing an object placed between infinity and the pole of a convex mirror, with the resulting virtual image formed between the pole and focus.

details.summary: Covers image formation characteristics for convex mirrors.

subject: Physics
text:
Mirror Formula:

  • If v is the image distance, u is the object distance and f is the focal length of a mirror, then 1/v + 1/u = 1/f = 2/R
  • The linear magnification (m) produced by a mirror is equal to the ratio of the image distance to the object distance with negative sign, m = -v/u = f/(f-u) = (f-v)/f
  • If the magnification has positive sign, then the image is virtual and erect.
  • If the magnification has negative sign, then the image is real and inverted.

details.summary: Mathematical relations for spherical mirrors.

subject: Physics
text:
Concave Mirrors:

  • Used as reflectors in automobiles (car, buses, etc.), head light, search light, hand torches and table lamps.
  • Used as shaving mirrors.
  • Used by doctors for focussing intense light to examine inside of eye, ears, etc.
  • Large concave mirrors are used in the application of solar energy, to focus the sun's rays for heating solar furnaces etc.

Convex Mirrors:

  • Used as rear-view mirrors in automobiles as they give large view of the traffic.
  • Used as shop security mirrors.
  • Used wherever we want to see erect images.

Note: We cannot use a concave mirror as a rear-view mirror in motor vehicles.

details.summary: Practical applications of concave and convex mirrors.

subject: Physics
text:
When a ray of light passes from one medium to other, it bends from its path. This phenomenon of bending of light is called as refraction of light.

  • When light passes from rarer medium to a denser medium, it bends towards the normal at the point of incidence.
  • When light passes from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal.
  • When a ray of light enters from one medium to other medium its frequency and phase do not change but wavelength and velocity change.

Laws of Refraction:

  • The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
  • The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant for a given medium. sin i / sin r = μ [Snell's law]

where, μ is refractive index of the second medium with respect to first. μ = μ2 / μ1 = c/v2 / c/v1 = v1 / v2 or 1μ2 = v1 / v2

details.summary: Definition, laws, and mathematical formulation of light refraction.

subject: Physics
text:
Some Illustrations of Refraction:

  • Twinkling of stars.
  • Oval shape of sun in the morning and evening.
  • Bending of a linear object when it is partially dipped in a liquid inclined to the surface of the liquid.
  • A fish in a pond when viewed from air appears to be at a smaller depth than actual depth.
  • A coin at the base of a vessel filled with water appears raised.

Total Internal Reflection:

In case of propagation of light from denser to rarer medium through a plane boundary. Critical angle is the angle of incidence for which angle of refraction is 90°. If light is propagating from denser medium towards the rarer medium and angle of incidence is more than critical angle, then the light incident on the boundary is reflected back in the denser medium, obeying the law of reflection. This phenomenon is called total internal reflection.

details.summary: Real-world examples of refraction and the concept of total internal reflection.

subject: Physics
text:
Conditions of Total Internal Reflection:

  • Light must be propagating from denser to rarer medium.
  • Angle of incidence must exceeds the critical angle.

Sparkling of diamond, mirage and looming, shinning of air bubble in water and optical fibre are the examples of total internal reflection.

Note: Optical fibre is used for the transmitting and receiving the electrical signals after converting it into the light signal.

details.summary: Conditions and examples of Total Internal Reflection.

subject: Physics
text:
A lens is a piece of transparent glass bounded by two spherical surfaces.

There are two types of lenses:

  • Convex lens (converging lens): A lens which is thicker at the centre and thinner at its ends.
  • Concave lens (diverging lens): A lens which is thinner at the centre and thicker at its ends.

Key Definitions:

  • The centre point of a lens is known as its optical centre.
  • The line joining the centres of the surfaces of the lens is called the principal axis of the lens.
  • The distance of the first focus from the optical centre of the lens is called the first focal length.
  • The distance of the second focus from the optical centre of the lens is called the second focal length.
tables:
| Position of object | Position of image | Size of image | Nature of image |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F2 | Highly diminished | Real and inverted |
| Beyond 2F1 | Between F2 and 2F2 | Diminished | -do- |
| At 2F1 | At 2F2 | Same size | -do- |
| Between 2F1 and F1 | Beyond 2F2 | Enlarged | -do- |
| At F1 | At infinity | Highly enlarged | -do- |
| Between F1 and lens | Behind the object, on the same side of the object | Enlarged | Virtual and erect |
image_descriptions: Diagram (a) shows a Convex lens with principal axis, optical centre, first focus F1, and second focus F2. Diagram (b) shows a Concave lens with similar markings.

details.summary: Definitions and classification of spherical lenses.

subject: Physics
topic: Image Formation by a Convex Lens
text:
Image Formation by a Convex Lens:

  • (i) Object at infinity: The image formed is at second focus, real, inverted and highly diminished.
  • (ii) Object beyond 2F1: The image formed is between F2 and 2F2 on the right side of the lens, real, inverted and diminished.
  • (iii) Object at 2F1: The image formed is at 2F2, real, inverted and of same size as that of the object.
  • (iv) Object between F1 and 2F1: The image formed is beyond 2F2, real, inverted and magnified.
tables:
| Position of object | Position of image | Size of image | Nature of image |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F2 | Diminished | Erect and virtual |
| Between infinity and lens | Between F2 and lens | Diminished | Erect and virtual |
image_descriptions: Ray diagrams showing image formation by a convex lens for objects at infinity, beyond 2F1, at 2F1, and between F1 and 2F1, illustrating the path of light rays through the lens to form images A'B'.

details.summary: Rules and ray diagrams for image formation by convex lenses.

subject: Physics
text:
(v) Object at F1: The image formed is real, inverted, and highly enlarged at infinity.

(vi) Object between F1 and O: The image formed is behind the object, virtual, erect and enlarged.
image_descriptions: Ray diagram showing object at F1 of a convex lens with rays emerging parallel to the principal axis.
Ray diagram showing object between F1 and O of a convex lens with virtual image formed behind the object.

details.summary: Image formation characteristics for convex lens when object is at F1 or between F1 and O.

subject: Physics
text:
(i) Object at infinity: The image formed is at F2, erect, virtual and diminished.

(ii) Object anywhere between infinity and lens: The image formed is between F2 and lens, erect, virtual and diminished.
image_descriptions: Ray diagram showing parallel rays from infinity incident on a concave lens forming an image at F2.
Ray diagram showing object between infinity and concave lens forming a diminished virtual image between F2 and the lens.

details.summary: Image formation characteristics for concave lens.

subject: Physics
text:
If v is the image distance, u is the object distance and f is the focal length of a lens, then the lens formula applies. Magnification m is defined as the ratio of image size to object size.

  • If magnification m is positive, the image is virtual and erect.
  • If magnification m is negative, the image is real and inverted.
  • If m is the total magnification of two lenses in contact having magnification m1 and m2, then m = m1 x m2.
  • Power (P) of a lens is the reciprocal of focal length (f). SI unit is dioptre (D).
  • For combined lenses: P = P1 + P2 or 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
  • If two lenses of equal focal length but opposite nature are in contact, the combination behaves as a plane glass plate (f = infinity).

Note: When a lens is dipped in a liquid of higher refractive index, the focal length increases and convex lens behaves as concave lens and vice-versa. An air bubble in water appears as convex but behaves as concave lens.
formulas: m = v/u = I/O = Size of image / Size of object

details.summary: Mathematical relationships for lenses, power, and magnification.

subject: Physics
topic: Dispersion of Light and Primary Colours
text:
Dispersion of Light: Sir Isaac Newton observed that a narrow beam of light incident on a prism splits into a band of seven colours (VIBGYOR). Violet deviates the most, Red the least. Rainbows are formed due to dispersion, refraction, and total internal reflection in droplets.

Primary Colours: Red, Green, and Blue.
tables:
| Mixing | Result |
|---|---|
| Red + Green + Blue | White |
| Red + Blue | Magenta |
| Blue + Green | Peacock blue (Cyan) |
| Red + Green | Yellow |

details.summary: Explanation of light dispersion, VIBGYOR, and additive colour mixing.

subject: Physics
text:
• Magenta, Cyan and Yellow, etc., are called secondary colours.
  • A rose appears red, when day light falls on it because it absorbs all the constituent colour of white light except red which it reflects to us.
  • If all the colours of white light are reflected back from the object, then it appears white.
  • If all the colours of white light are absorbed by the object, then it appears black.
  • The natural colours of transparent objects are due to their selective transmission of light.

details.summary: Basic properties of color perception and reflection.

subject: Physics
text:
• Scattering of Light: When sunlight passes through the earth’s atmosphere, much of the light is absorbed by the fine dust particles and air molecules in the atmosphere which give out the absorbed light in some other direction. This is scattering of light.
  • The scattering of light by particle in its path is called Tyndall effect.
  • The blue coloured light present in white sunlight is scattered much more easily by air molecules causes the blue colour of the sky.
  • The sun and the surrounding sky appear red at sunrise and at sunset because at that time most of blue colour present in sunlight has been scattered out and away from our line of sight, leaving behind mainly red colour in the direct sunlight beam that reaches our eyes.
  • Dangers signals are of red colour because red colour of light scatter least and therefore signals can be seen from far.
  • If the earth had no atmosphere, there would have been no scattering of sunlight at all. In that case, no light from the sky would have entered our eyes and the sky would have looked dark and black to us.

details.summary: Explanation of Tyndall effect and atmospheric scattering phenomena.

subject: Physics
text:
• Interference of Light: When two waves of exactly same frequency travels in a medium, in the same direction simultaneously, then due to their superposition at same points, intensity of light is maximum while at some other points intensity is minimum. This phenomenon is called interference of light.
  • Thin layer of oil on water surface and soap bubbles show various colours in white light due to interference of waves reflected from the two surfaces of the film.
  • Polarisation is the only phenomenon which proves that light is a transverse wave.
  • Diffraction of Light: If an opaque obstacle is kept between a source of light and a screen, a sufficiently distinct shadow is obtained on the screen. This shows that light which travels the obstacle is small. There is a departure from straight line propagation and so the light bends round the corners of obstacle and enters in the geometrical shadow. This bending of the light is called diffraction.

details.summary: Wave nature of light including interference, polarization, and diffraction.

subject: Physics
text:
• Human Eye: An optical instrument which forms real image of the objects.
  • The ability of an eye to focus the distant objects as well as the nearby objects on the retina by changing the focal length of its lens is called accommodation.
  • Least distance of distinct vision is 25 cm.
  • Far point of normal eye is at infinity.
  • Defects of Human Eye:
  • Myopia: A person suffering from myopia can see the near objects clearly while far objects are not clear; concave lens is used to remove it. Myopia is caused (i) due to high converging power of eye lens or (ii) due to eye ball being too long.
  • Hypermetropia: A person suffering from hypermetropia can see the distant objects clearly but not the near objects. Caused (i) due to low converging power of eye lens or (ii) due to eye ball being too short.
  • Presbyopia: In the old age, the power of accomodation of the eye is so much lost that a person can neither see the near objects distinctly nor the distant objects. To correct this defect bifocal lens is used.
  • Astigmatism: In this defect, a person cannot distantly see the horizontal and vertical lines, simultaneously at a normal distance. To correct this defect, cylindrical lens is used.
  • Cataract: In this defect, an opaque, white membrane is developed on cornea due to which a person loses power of vision partially or completely. This defect can be removed by removing this membrane through surgery.
  • Note: Colour blindness is a genetic disorder which occurs by inheritance. John Dalton was colour blind.

details.summary: Anatomy of the eye and common vision defects with their corrections.

subject: Physics
text:
• Microscope: An instrument used to see objects that are too small for the naked eye.
  • A simple microscope consists of a convex lens of small focal length.
  • It is used to see the details of very small objects.
  • For compound microscope m = m_o * m_e, where m_o is magnification of objective lens and m_e is magnification of eye-piece.

details.summary: Magnification principles for simple and compound microscopes.

subject: Physics
text:
Telescope is an optical instrument used for observing distinct images of heavenly bodies like stars, planets, etc., when the final image is formed at infinity.

  • Types:
    • Astronomical telescope (invented by Kepler in 1611)
    • Galilean telescope (invented by Galileo in 1609)
  • Construction:
    • Astronomical: Objective lens is a convex lens of large focal length; eye-piece is a convex lens of short focal length.
    • Galilean: Objective lens is a convex lens of large focal length; eye-piece is a concave lens of short focal length.
  • Note: Periscope consists of two plane mirrors inclined at an angle of 45°. The principle of working of periscope is based upon reflection and refraction.

details.summary: Overview of telescope types, construction, and periscope principles.

subject: Physics
text:
Charge is the basic property associated with matter due to which it produces and experiences electrical and magnetic effects. The SI unit of electric charge is Coulomb.

  • Particles: Positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons.
  • Charge values: Proton = +1.6 x 10^-19 C; Electron = -1.6 x 10^-19 C.
  • Interaction: Similar charges repel, opposite charges attract.

details.summary: Definition and properties of electric charge.

subject: Physics
text:
When two or more charged bodies come in contact, the total charge is conserved.

  • Conductors: Allow passage of electrical charges, very low resistance (e.g., copper, aluminium, gold, silver). Human body and earth are conductors; silver is the best.
  • Distribution: Charges are always distributed on the surface of a conductor.
  • Resistors: Offer high resistance (e.g., eureka, nichrome).
  • Insulators: Infinite resistance, do not allow passage of current (e.g., rubber, glass, ebonite).
  • Note: Presence of free electrons makes a substance a conductor.

details.summary: Conservation of charge and classification of materials based on electrical conductivity.

subject: Physics
text: The force of attraction or repulsion between two point charges is proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the two charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

details.summary: Mathematical expression of Coulomb's Law.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Field: The region around an electric charge in which its effect can be experienced.

Electric Potential: Work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point. SI unit is volt (V).

  • Potential difference (V_A - V_B): Work done in bringing a unit charge from point B to point A. It is a scalar quantity.
  • Properties: Potential inside a spherical surface is same at each point and equal to the surface potential. Potential on earth is zero.
  • Measurement: Voltmeter connected in parallel measures potential difference.

details.summary: Definitions and properties of electric field and electric potential.

subject: Physics
text:
The rate of flow of electric charges through any cross-section of conductor is called electric current. The direction of positive charges is the same as the direction of conventional current.

  • SI Unit: Ampere.
  • Measurement: Ammeter, connected in series with the conductor.
formulas: Current = Charge / Time => I = Q / t

details.summary: Definition, unit, and measurement of electric current.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two types of electric current: (i) Alternating current (AC) and (ii) Direct current (DC).

  • Alternating current is used in houses and factories and its frequency is 50 Hz.
  • Ordinary DC ammeter and DC voltmeter cannot measure alternating current/voltages. They record zero reading, when used in AC circuits, because average value of alternating current/voltage over a full cycle is zero.

Galvanometer

It is a device used to detect and measure electric current in a circuit. It can measure current up to 10^-6 A. A galvanometer can be converted into a voltmeter by connecting a very high resistance in its series.

Note: Conventionally the direction of electric current is opposite to that of electrons. Since, electrons flow from negative terminal of a cell to its positive terminal, electric current flows from positive terminal to negative terminal.

details.summary: Overview of AC/DC current, galvanometer function, and conventional current direction.

subject: Physics
text:
A capacitor or condenser is a device over which a large amount of charge can be stored.

  • Its unit is coulomb/volt or farad.
  • A capacitor is used in several electrical devices having an electric motor and in several electronic circuits.

details.summary: Definition and usage of a capacitor.

subject: Physics
text:
OHM'S LAW

If the physical circumstances of the conductor (length, temperature, etc) remains constant then the current flowing through the conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends.

Resistance

The resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area. If l and A are respectively length and cross-sectional area of a conductor and R is its resistance, then R is proportional to l/A => R = rho * (l/A). Unit of resistance is ohm (Ω).

  • Where, rho is a constant of material of conductor is called specific resistance or resistivity. Its SI unit is ohm-metre.
  • On increasing the temperature of the metal, its resistance increases.
  • Those materials whose electrical conductivity lies in between that of insulators and conductors are called semiconductors. On increasing the temperature of semiconductor, its resistance decreases.

details.summary: Explanation of Ohm's Law, factors affecting resistance, and properties of semiconductors.

subject: Physics
text:
• The reciprocal of resistance of a conductor is called the electrical conductance of the conductor.
  • Unit of conductance is mho or siemen.
  • The specific resistance of the material depends only on the material of conductor and its temperature.
  • Resistivity increases with temperature.
  • Resistivity of a conductor change with impurity.
  • Resistivity of an alloy is greater than the resistivity of its constituents and remains unchanged with temperature.
  • If a wire is stretched or doubled on itself, its resistance will change, but its specific resistance will remains unaffected.
  • The reciprocal of resistivity of a conductor is called its conductivity. Its SI unit is mho m^-1 or siemen/metre (Sm^-1).

details.summary: Properties of conductance, resistivity, and conductivity.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two combinations given below:

(i) Series combination: R = R1 + R2 + R3 and here current flows through each conductor is same. The total resistance in the series combination is more than the greatest resistance in the circuit.

(ii) Parallel combination: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 and here potential across each conductor is same. The total resistance in parallel combination is less than the least resistance of the circuit.

Circuit diagram showing three resistors R1, R2, R3 in parallel connected to a voltage source E.

subject: Physics
text: Electrical power is the electrical work done per unit time. Its SI unit is watt (W).

details.summary: Definition and formulas for electric power.

subject: Physics
topic: Units and Heating Effect of Electric Current
text:
• 1 kilowatt hour = 3600000 J = 3.6 x 10^6 J
  • 1 Horse power (HP) = 746 W
  • 1 Horse power (HP) = 550 foot-pound/second
  • Unit = (volt x ampere x hour) / 1000
  • Unit = (watt x hour) / 1000

Heating Effect of Electric Current

Heat is produced when electric current is passed through a conductor. This effect is called the heating effect of electric current.

Note: The filament of an electric bulb gets very hot and therefore easily oxidised. Thus, bulbs are sealed with inactive nitrogen and argon gases to prevent oxidation of the filament and increase its life. In electric bulb, tungsten is used for the construction of filament because it has high melting point.

Important Points Based on Heating Effect

  • In home appliances like electric iron, electric heater and heating rod, the heating element used is of a nichrome (an alloy of Ni and Cr) wire. Nichrome has high melting point and high resistivity. To avoid the risk of electric shock, the metal body of electrical appliances is earthed.
  • An electric fuse is generally prepared from tin-lead alloy (63% tin + 37% lead). It should have high resistance and low melting point. It is connected in the series.
  • Tubelight contains a long tube of glass which is linked internally with a fluorescent substance. It is filled with an inert gas like argon along with some mercury.

details.summary: Covers electrical units, heating effect principles, and practical applications like bulbs, fuses, and heating elements.

subject: Physics
text:
Magnetic Effect of Current

When electricity passes through insulated copper wire, it develops a magnetic field around it. Larger the amount of electricity, stronger the magnetic field. And when we place compass needle in the radius of the magnetic field it diverts from its North-South position.

Magnets

Magnet is a piece of iron or other materials that can attract iron containing objects and the property of attracting the magnetic substance by a magnet is called magnetism.

  • The magnets which do not lose their magnetism with normal treatment are called permanent magnets.
  • The materials which retain their magnetism for a long time are called hard magnetic materials.
  • In bar, rod and horse-shoe magnets, North or South poles are either indicated by the letter N or S.
  • When poles of two magnets are brought close together, they exert force on each other. This force is called intersection between the poles.
  • If we cut a magnet in two parts, then each separate part will behave as a magnet.
  • Permanent magnets are usually made of alloys such as carbon steel, chromium steel, cobalt steel, tungsten steel and alnico (alloy of aluminium, nickel, cobalt and iron).
  • Such permanent magnets are used in microphones, loudspeakers, electric clocks, ammeters, voltmeters, speedometer and many other devices.
  • Note: The Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) technique which is used to scan inner human body parts in hospitals also uses magnets for its working.

Magnetic Field

The space in the surrounding of a magnet or a current carrying conductor in which its magnetic effect can be experience is called magnetic field.

  • Magnetic lines of force are imaginary lines in the magnetic field, which shows the direction of magnetic field continuously.
  • The magnetic field lines originate from the North pole of a magnet and end at its South pole.
  • The magnetic field lines do not intersect one another.

details.summary: Definitions and properties of magnets, magnetic fields, and permanent magnets.

subject: Physics
text:
Magnetic Materials

According to behaviour of magnetic substances, they are classified into three classes:

  • Diamagnetic substances: Substances when placed in an external magnetic field, acquire a very low magnetism in direction opposite to the field. e.g. copper, silver, bismuth, zinc, diamond, salt, water, mercury, etc. The permeability of diamagnetic substance is less than one.
  • Paramagnetic substances: Substances when placed in an external field, acquire a feeble magnetism in the direction of field. e.g. aluminium, sodium, potassium, oxygen, etc. The permeability of paramagnetic substance is slightly greater than one.
  • Ferromagnetic substances: Substances when placed in a magnetic field, acquire a strong magnetism in the direction of field. These substances when brought near the end of a strong magnet get radially attracted towards it. e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt, magnetite, etc. The permeability of ferromagnetic substance is much greater than one.

Electromagnet

An electromagnet is a solenoid coil that attains magnetism due to flow of current. It works on the principle of magnetic effect of current. It is used in electric bells, electric motors, telephone, diaphragms, loudspeakers etc.
tables:
| Magnetic Substance | Behavior in Magnetic Field | Examples | Permeability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Diamagnetic | Low magnetism in opposite direction | Copper, silver, bismuth, zinc, diamond, salt, water, mercury | < 1 |
| Paramagnetic | Feeble magnetism in direction of field | Aluminium, sodium, potassium, oxygen | > 1 (slightly) |
| Ferromagnetic | Strong magnetism in direction of field | Iron, nickel, cobalt, magnetite | >> 1 |

details.summary: Classification of magnetic materials based on permeability and behavior, and definition of electromagnets.

subject: Physics
text:
Magnetic Flux: The magnetic flux linked with a surface is equal to the total number of magnetic lines of force passing through that surface normally. Its unit is weber.

Electromagnetic Induction: When a change occurs in the magnetic flux linked with the coil, an emf is induced in the coil. The phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction.

  • The phenomenon of production of induced emf in a circuit due to change in magnetic flux in its neighbouring circuit is called mutual induction.
  • When the electric current flowing through a circuit changes, the magnetic flux linked with circuit also change. As a result an induced emf is set up in the circuit. This phenomenon is called self-induction.
  • Microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy and works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.

details.summary: Definitions and principles of magnetic flux, electromagnetic induction, mutual induction, and self-induction.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Generator: It is a device which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. An electric generator is based on the principle of electromagnetic induction. It is used to produce electric current by varying magnetic field through a coil.

  • A generator can produced both alternating current and direct current.
  • AC generator consists of slip rings, armature, magnet and brushes while DC generator consists of magnet commutator, armature and brushes.
  • Note: Electric motor is a rotating device which converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

Transformer: Transformer is a device which converts low voltage AC into high voltage AC and high voltage AC into low voltage AC. It is based on mutual induction.

  • Core of a transformer is made up of soft iron.
  • Step-up transformer converts a low voltage of high current into a high voltage of low current.
  • Step-down transformer converts a high voltage of low current into a low voltage of high current.
  • The main energy losses in a transformer are given below: (a) Iron loss (b) Flux loss (c) Hysteresis loss (d) Humming loss
  • Transformer is used in voltage regulators, refrigerators, computer, air conditioner.
  • Step-down transformer is used for welding purpose.
  • Audio transformer allowed telephone circuits to carry on a two-way conversation over a single pair of wires.
  • Radio frequency transformers are used in radio communication.
  • Note: A mobile phone charger is one of the best example of step down transformer as it extracts the power from the home supply (AC 220V) and convert it to DC of required voltage.

details.summary: Working principles and applications of electric generators and transformers.

subject: Physics
text:
Cathode Rays: If the gas pressure in a discharge tube is 10^-2 to 10^-3 mm of Hg and a potential difference of 10^4 V is applied between the electrode, then a beam of electrons emerges from the cathode which is called cathode rays.

  • Cathode rays are invisible and travel in a straight line.
  • These rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • These rays can ionise gases.
  • They can produce chemical change and thus affect a photographic plate.
  • When they strike a target of heavy metal such as tungsten, they produce X-rays.

X-Rays: When cathode rays strike on a heavy metal of high melting points, then a very small fraction of its energy converts into a new type of waves, called X-rays.

  • X-rays are electromagnetic waves and these produce photoelectric effect.
  • X-rays were discovered by scientist Roentgen.
  • These produce illumination on falling the fluorescent substances and travel in a straight line with the speed of light.
  • X-rays penetrate through different depth into different substances.
  • Soft X-rays have greater wavelength and lower frequency and hard X-rays have lower wavelength and higher frequency.
  • X-rays ionise gases through which they pass.
  • X-rays are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • They show all the important properties of light rays like, reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation, etc.
  • X-rays are used in surgery, radiotherapy, engineering department and searching.
  • Note: Barium and Iodine are some chemicals used as contrast mediums for X-ray based imaging method. i.e. they absorbs X-ray to highlight the targeted body part.

details.summary: Properties and applications of cathode rays and X-rays.

subject: Physics
text:
These rays are positively charged particles and are called positive rays or canal rays. These rays were discovered by Goldstein.

  • These rays can affect the photographic plates.
  • These rays are capable of producing physical and chemical changes.
  • These rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • These rays can produce fluorescence and phosphorescence.

details.summary: Overview of discovery and properties of positive/canal rays.

subject: Physics
text:
Fluorescence: Some substances absorb the light of higher frequency or shorter wavelength and emits a light having lower frequency or higher wavelength in the presence of light source. This phenomenon of emission of light is called fluorescence. Such substances are called fluorescence substances.

  • Fluoresphor, petrol, uranium oxide and barium platino cyanide are examples of fluorescence substances.
  • Barium platino cyanide is used in search of X-rays.

Phosphorescence: Some substances after being kept in sunlight for sometime emit light even after the light source is removed. This phenomenon is called phosphorescence. Zinc sulphide, calcium sulphide and barium sulphide are examples of phosphorescence.

details.summary: Definitions and examples of fluorescence and phosphorescence.

subject: Physics
text:
Compact fluorescent lamp converts electrical energy into radiant energy.

  • It has two components:
    • A glass tube filled with argon and mercury vapour and coated with layer of fluorescent materials.
    • An electronic ballast circuit.
  • The ballast circuit (small circuit board with rectifiers, a filter capacitor and usually two switching transistors) takes a 220V input from external power source and sends a current into the fluorescent tube as output.
  • When power supply is given to the CFL, filament attached with the cathode heats up and emits electrons in the tube. This ionises the argon and mercury vapour particles, causing it, ultraviolet light emission.

details.summary: Working principle and components of a CFL.

subject: Physics
text:
When the ultraviolet rays (or the visible light of low wavelength or any other kind of electromagnetic radiation) are made incident on a metal, the electrons are emitted from it. This phenomenon is called the photoelectric emission or photoelectric effect.

Photoelectric cell is based on photoelectric effect. It is a device by which light energy is converted into the electrical energy.

Applications of photoelectric effect:

  • In reproduction of sound in cinema, television and photo telegraphy.
  • In automatic switches for street lights.
  • In photoelectric sorters.
  • To control the temperature in furnace and in chemical process.
  • In industries for locating minor flows or holes in metallic sheets.

details.summary: Definition and applications of the photoelectric effect.

subject: Physics
text:
Semiconductor: Materials whose electrical conductivity at room temperature lies in between that of insulator and conductor. A semiconductor in an extremely pure form is known as intrinsic semiconductor.

  • If a measured and small amount of chemical impurity is added to intrinsic semiconductor, it is called extrinsic semiconductor or doped semiconductor.
  • External semiconductors are of two types: (i) n-type semiconductor (ii) p-type semiconductor.
  • An extrinsic semiconductor in which electrons are majority charge carrier is called n-type semiconductor.
  • An extrinsic semiconductor in which holes are the majority charge carrier is called p-type semiconductor.

Special Purpose Diodes:

  • p-n junction diode: An arrangement consisting a p-type semiconductor brought into a close contact with n-type semiconductor.
  • Rectifier: A device which converts alternating current (AC) or voltage into direct current (DC).
  • LED: Specially designed diode made up of GaAsP, used in electronic gadgets as indicator light. It converts electrical energy into optical energy.
  • Zener diode: A highly doped p-n junction diode which is not damaged by high reverse current. It can be used as voltage regulator.
  • Photo diode: A special p-n junction diode fabricated with a transparent window to allow light to fall on the diode. It is used in reverse biasing.
  • Note: Diode valve acts as a rectifier and triode valve can be used as amplifier oscillator and detector.

details.summary: Types of semiconductors and various special purpose diodes.

subject: Physics
text:
Solar cell is a p-n junction device which converts solar energy into electrical energy. It consists of a silicon or gallium arsenide p-n junction.

Uses of Solar Cell:

  • Solar cells are used as solar cooker.
  • Solar cells are used in wrist watches, calculators and light meters.
  • Solar cells are also used in artificial satellite to provide power inside the satellite.
  • Solar cells are used for charging storage batteries.

details.summary: Definition and applications of solar cells.

subject: Physics
text:
An IC can be defined generally as an arrangement of multifunction semiconductor devices. It consists of a single crystal chip of silicon, nearly 1.5 mm^2 in cross-section.

TV remote control is an electronic device containing an IC and few other components. If a key on a remote control is pressed, it emits infrared signals which are received by the electronic circuit of the TV receiver, etc.

details.summary: Definition and example of Integrated Circuits.

subject: Physics
text:
The word LASER is the short form of Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. It is an optical device, which produces an intensive beam highly coherent, monochromatic light.

Applications of laser rays:

  • Laser rays are used in treatment of detached retina, treatment of skin cancer and surgery of brain.
  • Laser beams are used in signals and radio communications.
  • The property of high intensity is used to cut hard metals.
  • The weather informations are collected with the help of radar, an instrument based on the properties of laser.
  • The laser rays are parallel and do not spread. This property of laser rays is used in the measurement of long distance.

details.summary: Definition and applications of LASER.

subject: Physics
text:
The term communication refers to the transmitting receiving and processing of information by electronic means. A basic communication system consists of an information source, a transmitter, a link and a receiver.

  • Electromagnetic waves which are used in radio, television and other communication system are radiowaves and micro waves.
  • Ground wave propagation: The radio wave travel through atmosphere following the surface of the earth from transmitting antenna to receiving antenna. Useful for low range frequencies upto 1500 kHz.
  • Space wave propagation: Utilises electromagnetic waves of very high frequency band (30 MHz to 300 MHz), ultra high frequency band (300 MHz to 3000 MHz) and microwaves (100 GHz to 300 GHz).
  • Sky wave propagation: The radio waves from the transmitting antenna reach the receiving antenna after entering in ionosphere. The sky wave frequency lies between 2 MHz to 30 MHz.
  • Communication satellite: A space craft provided with microwave receiver and transmitter. Placed in orbit around the earth. Frequencies lie in UHF/microwave regions.
  • Remote sensing: Technique to obtain information about an object by observing it from a distance without contact.
  • Cables: Parallel wire lines (not for microwaves), Twisted pair wires (telephone), Coaxial cables (long distance high frequency, e.g., TV channel).
  • Note: Maser means 'Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation'.

details.summary: Overview of communication systems, wave propagation types, and satellite communication.

subject: Physics
text:
It is a better communication system for large number of channels and higher bandwidth transmission. Now-a-days optical fibres of very small diameters (~ 10^-5 m) are used.

Advantages:

  • In optical fibres energy losses are less.
  • Secret information like banking, defence, etc., is more secure because optical signal is confined to the inside of fibre and cannot be tampered easily.
  • It can be used at high frequencies (~ 10^14 Hz).

Phenomenon of total internal reflection is the principle behind optical fibres.

details.summary: Principles and advantages of optical communication.

subject: Physics
text:
Rotational Motion and Gravitation

  • Torque is a vector quantity.
  • The rate of change of angular acceleration is equal to the torque.
  • The turning effect of a body is known as torque.
  • Torque is equal to the product of moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
formulas: Torque = Moment of Inertia * Angular Acceleration

details.summary: Basic definitions and properties related to torque and rotational motion.

subject: Physics
content:
### Surface Tension
- **Definition**: Surface tension (γ) is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid by unit area, or equivalently the force acting along a line of unit length on the surface of a liquid.  
  \[ \gamma =  rac{F}{L} \]  
- **Units**: N m⁻¹ (or J m⁻²).
- **Molecular Origin**: Molecules at the surface experience a net inward cohesive force because they are not surrounded by similar molecules on all sides. This creates a contractile ‘film’ that minimizes surface area.
- **Temperature Effect**: As temperature rises, kinetic energy of molecules increases, weakening cohesive forces. Consequently, surface tension **decreases** with temperature.
- **Related Forces**:
  - **Cohesive force** – attraction between like molecules (e.g., water‑water).
  - **Adhesive force** – attraction between unlike molecules (e.g., water‑glass).
- **Angle of Contact (θ)**: The angle formed between the liquid surface and a solid at the point of contact.
  - Acute θ (< 90°) → strong adhesion (wetting).
  - Obtuse θ (> 90°) → weak adhesion (non‑wetting).
  - Water on clean glass: acute angle; mercury on glass: obtuse angle.
- **Applications**:
  - **Raincoat coating** – hydrophobic coating gives a high contact angle; water beads up and does not spread, making the fabric waterproof.
  - **Droplet shape** – small droplets become spherical because surface tension minimizes surface area.
  - **Camphor dancing & needle floating** – both phenomena are sustained by surface tension forces acting at the liquid‑air interface.

---
### Capillary Action
- **Definition**: The rise (or fall) of a liquid in a narrow tube due to the combined effect of surface tension and adhesive forces between the liquid and tube material.
- **Capillary Rise Formula**:
  \[ h =  rac{2\gamma \cos	heta}{ho g r}

subject: Physics
text:
Oscillations and Waves

  • Simple harmonic motion involves a restoring force directly proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position.
  • Pendulum clocks are affected by gravity and altitude.
  • The time period of a simple pendulum is related to its length.
  • Wave types include transverse and longitudinal waves.

details.summary: Basic concepts of simple harmonic motion, pendulum mechanics, and wave classification.

subject: Physics
content:
### Cathode Rays
- **Definition**: A stream of electrons emitted from the cathode in a discharge tube.
- **Nature**: Charged particles (negative charge).
- **Deflection**: Can be deflected by both electric and magnetic fields; the direction of deflection is opposite to that of positively charged particles.
- **Speed**: Travel at speeds **much less than the speed of light** (typically a few % of *c* depending on the accelerating voltage).
- **Key Properties**:
  - Produce fluorescence on certain phosphorescent screens.
  - Responsible for the operation of CRT displays and electron microscopes.
- **Historical Note**: Discovered by J.J. Thomson (1897) leading to the identification of the electron.

subject: Physics
content:
### X‑rays
- **Discovery**: Discovered by **Wilhelm Röntgen** in 1895.
- **Nature**: A form of electromagnetic radiation; therefore they travel at the speed of light (*c*) in vacuum.
- **Interaction with Matter**:
  - Can **pass through thin aluminium** and many other low‑Z materials.
  - Not deflected by electric or magnetic fields because they are uncharged photons.
- **Classification**:
  - **Soft X‑rays**: Lower frequency, lower energy, lower penetrating power.
  - **Hard X‑rays**: Higher frequency, higher energy, greater penetrating power.
- **Velocity**: All X‑rays, like all EM waves, have the same velocity in vacuum as ultraviolet, visible, and radio waves.
- **Attenuation**: The distance an X‑ray travels before being significantly absorbed is **minimum in dense, high‑Z materials** (e.g., iron) and maximum in gases like air.
- **Applications**: Medical imaging, crystallography, security scanning, industrial non‑destructive testing.

subject: Physics
text:
Lens Formula and Properties:

  • For a concave lens, power is calculated as P = 1/f(m) = 100/f(cm).
  • Myopia is a defect of the human eye where one cannot see far-off objects clearly. It is remedied using a concave lens.
  • The focal length of a concave lens is negative.
  • For a plane mirror, the distance between a person and their image is twice the distance of the person from the mirror.

Ray diagram showing light rays passing through a concave lens, resulting in a virtual diminished image at focus.

subject: Physics
text:
Electrical Resistance and Heating:

  • The effective resistance of resistors in parallel is given by 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.
  • Power of an electric bulb is P = V^2/R.
  • Heat produced by a conductor is H = i^2Rt.
  • For a given current, the heat produced in a thinner wire (higher resistance) is greater than in a thicker wire.

subject: Physics
text:
Sound and Oscillations:

  • The relationship between velocity, frequency, and wavelength is v = f * lambda.
  • Sound level in decibels is calculated as beta = 10 log10(I/I0).
  • The time period of a simple pendulum T = 2 * pi * sqrt(l/g) is independent of mass.
  • Distance to a reflecting surface (like a wall) can be calculated using d = 1/2 * speed * time.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Matter: Anything that has mass, occupies space and can be felt by our one or more sense organs is called matter. Matter is found in five physical states: solid, liquid, gas, plasma, and Bose-Einstein condensate. Out of which, three states, i.e., solid, liquid and gas are more common.

  • Solid: They have a fixed shape, volume and high density. The particles in solids are (closely) packed and held in rigid positions. They can be true or crystalline (i.e., having ordered arrangement of constituent particles to a larger distance) like metals or amorphous or pseudo solids (i.e., having short range arrangement of constituents particles) like non-metals, glass, most of the polymers, etc.
  • Liquid: They have a fixed volume but no fixed shape and have moderate to high densities. The particles in liquids are loosely packed and free to move. Their thermal conductivity decreases with rise in temperature with the exception of water.
  • Gas: They have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume and have very low density. The particles in gas are widely spaced apart and uniformly distributed in the container.

Two More States of Matter:

  • Plasma: The state consists of super energetic and super excited particles which are in the form of ionised gases. Due to the presence of plasma, the sun and stars glow.
  • Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC): They are formed by cooling a gas of extremely low density to super low temperatures.

details.summary: Introduction to the definition of matter and the characteristics of its five physical states: solid, liquid, gas, plasma, and Bose-Einstein condensate.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Properties of Matter:

  • Density: Measure of relative heaviness of objects having constant volume. Defined as mass per unit volume. At 4°C, density of water is maximum while its specific volume is minimum. Gases possess very low density.
  • Compression: Gases are more compressible due to large intermolecular spaces; solids are least compressible. Liquids lie in between.
  • Thermal Expansion: Minimum in solids, maximum in gases due to intermolecular force of attraction.

details.summary: Covers density, compression, and thermal expansion properties of matter.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Change of States of Matter:

  • Boiling Point: Conversion of liquid into vapours by heating. Increases with impurity. Decreases at high altitude due to low atmospheric pressure.
  • Melting Point: Conversion of solid into liquid by heating.
  • Sublimation: Solid to gas directly (e.g., naphthalene, camphor).
  • Freezing: Liquid to solid.
  • Evaporation: Liquid to vapour at any temperature; causes cooling.
  • Latent Heat: Heat supplied to a body at melting/boiling point to change state without changing temperature.
formulas: Latent heat (L) = Quantity of heat (Q) / Mass (m)

details.summary: Explains phase transitions including boiling, melting, sublimation, freezing, evaporation, and latent heat.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Classification of Matter:

  • Elements: Simplest form of matter. Term used by Robert Boyle in 1661. 118 elements known (98 natural, rest artificial).
  • Compounds: Two or more elements in a fixed ratio. Cannot be separated by physical methods. Homogeneous (e.g., water, ammonia, sugar).
  • Mixtures: Two or more substances in any ratio. No definite formula.
    • Homogeneous Mixtures: Uniformly distributed (e.g., salt solution).
    • Heterogeneous Mixtures: Non-uniform, may exhibit Tyndall effect (e.g., colloidal solutions).

details.summary: Classification of matter into elements, compounds, and mixtures.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Physical and Chemical Changes:

  • Physical Changes: Only physical properties (colour, hardness, density) change; chemical composition remains the same. Examples: Crystallisation, boiling, dissolution of salt/sugar, vaporisation, melting of ice.

details.summary: Distinction between physical and chemical changes.

subject: Chemistry
chapter: Laws of Chemical Combination and Atomic Structure
text:
In chemical changes, the chemical composition as well as chemical properties of the matter changes and a new substance is formed. Burning of any substance, photosynthesis, ripening of fruits, etc., are examples of chemical change. Physical changes are reversible (i.e. can be reversed to obtain the original substance) while chemical changes are irreversible.

Laws of Chemical Combination

Combination of elements/atoms to form compounds is governed by following basic laws:

  • Law of Conservation of Mass: This law was put forth by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789. It states that, matter can neither be created nor destroyed but can be converted from one form to another. In a chemical reaction, total mass of reactants is equal to total mass of products. In terms of energy, it is called law of conservation of energy.
  • Law of Definite Proportions: A pure compound always contains same elements combined in same proportions by mass, whatever be its source. This is called law of definite proportions by weight and is given by Joseph Proust, e.g. water obtained from any source like tap water, well water, etc., always contain hydrogen and oxygen in 1:8 by mass.
  • Law of Multiple Proportions: This law was proposed by John Dalton in 1803. It states that when the fixed mass of an element combines with different masses of another element, then the masses of other elements (in two or more compounds) are in the ratio of small whole numbers. e.g. H2O (2g H : 16g O), H2O2 (2g H : 32g O) or 1g H : 32g O. Thus, ratio of O combining with same mass of H = 1:2.
  • Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes: The volume of reactants and products in large number of chemical reactions are related to each other by small integers, provided the volumes are measured at same temperature and pressure. These statements are considered as the law of definite proportions by volume given by Gay-Lussac.

details.summary: Overview of fundamental laws governing chemical combinations including Conservation of Mass, Definite Proportions, Multiple Proportions, and Gaseous Volumes.

subject: Chemistry
chapter: Laws of Chemical Combination and Atomic Structure
text:
MOLECULES

The term molecule was given by Avogadro. It is the smallest particle of a compound which can exist in free state. All the properties of a compound depend on its constituent molecules. Molecules of a compound contain two or more different types of atoms in a fixed ratio. e.g. ammonia (NH3), water (H2O), etc.

  • Molecular mass: is the mass of a molecule. It is an additive property and is calculated by adding the atomic masses of total atoms present in a molecule. e.g. NH3 = 14 + (1)x3 = 17.
  • Equivalent weight: is obtained by dividing molecular or atomic mass by valency.

Mole Concept

The number of molecules present in 12 g of C-12 atom is called one mole. 1 mol = 6.022 x 10^23 = Avogadro's number.

  • Number of moles = Mass (in g) / Atomic or molecular mass (g mol^-1)
  • 1 mol of atom = 6.022 x 10^23 atoms
  • 1 mol of molecules = 6.022 x 10^23 molecules
  • Atomic mass: is the relative mass as compared with an atom of C-12 and is expressed in amu. (1 amu = 1.6 x 10^-24 g).
formulas: Equivalent weight = (Molecular mass or atomic mass) / Valency
Number of moles = Mass (in g) / Atomic or molecular mass (g mol^-1)

details.summary: Definitions and calculations related to molecules, molecular mass, equivalent weight, and the mole concept.

subject: Chemistry
chapter: Laws of Chemical Combination and Atomic Structure
topic: Atomic Structure and Dalton's Atomic Theory
text:
ATOMIC STRUCTURE

Atoms are the basis of chemistry, even they are the basis for everything in the universe. Maharishi Kanad was one of the first person to propose that matter is made up of every small particles called parmanu. John Dalton called the particles by the name of atom.

DALTON'S ATOMIC THEORY

In 1808, John Dalton gave a theory, called atomic theory of matter which is based upon laws of chemical combination. According to this theory:

  • Atom is the smallest indivisible particle of an element, i.e. it can neither be created nor be destroyed.
  • Atoms of different elements differ in mass, size and chemical properties.
  • Atoms of same or different elements combine together to form compound or molecule. The 'number' and 'kinds' of atoms in a given molecule is fixed.
  • Atoms of the same elements can combine in more than one ratio to form different compounds.

details.summary: Historical context of atomic theory, mentioning Maharishi Kanad and John Dalton, and the postulates of Dalton's Atomic Theory.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Properties of Atom and Subatomic Particles
text:
Atom: The smallest particle of the element that can exist independently and retain all its capable of independent chemical reactions. Atoms are made up of subatomic particles like electrons, protons, neutrons, meson, positron, etc.

Molecule: The smallest particle of an element or a compound existence under ordinary conditions.

Properties of Atom:

  • Atomic Number (Z): Number of protons inside the nucleus of its atom. (In case of neutral atom, Z = number of protons = number of electrons).
  • Mass Number (A): Total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) present in one atom of an element. (A = number of protons + number of neutrons = atomic number + number of neutrons = number of electrons + number of neutrons).

Properties of Subatomic Particles:

  • Electron (-1e0): Negatively charged particle. Discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897. Charge = -1.6 x 10-19C, Mass = 9.1 x 10-31g. Magnitude of negative charge determined by Millikan in his oil drop experiment.
  • Proton (1H1): Positively charged particle. Discovered by E. Goldstein. Charge = 1.6 x 10-19C, Mass = 1.6 x 10-27kg.
  • Neutron (0n1): Neutral particle. Discovered by Chadwick. Mass = 1.6 x 10-27kg.

Note: Hydrogen and protium is the only atom that does not possess neutrons.
formulas: Z = number of protons = number of electrons
A = number of protons + number of neutrons
A = atomic number + number of neutrons
A = number of electrons + number of neutrons

subject: Chemistry
topic: Discovery of Subatomic Particles and Nucleus
text:
Discovery of Subatomic Particles:

  • Cathode Rays: Travel in straight lines, cast shadows of metallic objects. In electrical/magnetic fields, behavior is similar to negatively charged electrons. First precise measurement of charge on electron made by Robert A. Millikan in 1909.
  • Anode Rays: Discovered by Engen Goldstein in 1886. Also called canal rays. Travel in straight lines, produce mechanical effects, and are positively charged (made of protons).

Nucleus: Atom consists of a heavy and positively charged part at its centre, called the nucleus (dia = 10-4m). Discovered by Rutherford by alpha-particle scattering experiment. Negatively charged electrons revolve around the nucleus in well-defined orbits.

details.summary: Historical discovery of cathode and anode rays and the structure of the atomic nucleus.

subject: Chemistry
text: Planck's Quantum Theory (Particle Nature of Electromagnetic Radiation): The radiant energy which is emitted or absorbed discontinuously in the form of small discrete packets of energy known as quantum and in case of light, the quantum of energy is called photon.

details.summary: Introduction to Planck's Quantum Theory and the concept of photons.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Different Atomic Species:

  • Isotopes: Atoms of the same element having the same atomic number (Z) but different mass number (A). Examples: 1H1, 1H2, 1H3; 6C12, 6C13, 6C14; 8O16, 8O17, 8O18; 10Ne20, 10Ne21, 10Ne22.
  • Isobars: Atoms of different elements having the same mass number (A) but different atomic number (Z). Examples: 1H3 and 2He3; 18Ar40, 19K40, 20Ca40; 52Te130, 56Ba130, 54Xe130.
  • Isoelectronic Species: Species having the same number of electrons but different nuclear charge. They have the same bond order. Example: Mg2+ and Na+ (both have 10 electrons).
  • Isotones: Atoms having the same number of neutrons. Example: 6C14, 7N15.

Bohr-Bury Scheme: Shows electron distribution in shells. A shell has a maximum of 2n2 electrons (n = shell number). K shell (n=1) = 2, L shell (n=2) = 8. Outermost shell cannot have more than 8 electrons.

Quantum Numbers: Four types: 1) Principal (n=1, 2, 3...), 2) Azimuthal (l=0 to n-1), 3) Magnetic (m = -1 to +1 including 0), 4) Spin (s = +1/2, -1/2).

details.summary: Covers atomic species definitions, Bohr-Bury electron distribution rules, and quantum numbers.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Radioactivity: Discovered by Henri Becquerel (1896). Term given by Marie Curie. It is the spontaneous emission of invisible radiations by disintegration of heavy elements.

Types of Radiations:

  • Alpha (α) particles: 2He4, +2 charge, mass 4 units. High ionising power. Deflected towards negative plate.
  • Beta (β) particles: Electrons, -1 charge, zero mass. Deflected towards positive plate.
image_descriptions: Nuclear decay equations showing alpha decay (loss of 2 protons and 4 mass units) and beta decay (increase of 1 atomic number).

details.summary: Introduction to radioactivity, historical discovery, and properties of alpha and beta particles.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Gamma (γ) rays: They have no charge and no mass. They are not deflected from their path in the electric or magnetic field. These are electromagnetic radiations and have very high penetrating power. Emission of γ-rays is the secondary effect of radioactive charge.

  • Note 1: Stable nuclei are those for which number of neutrons and protons are equal.
  • Note 2: The time taken by half of the atoms of a radioactive element to disintegrate is called its half-life. Its unit is time^-1.
  • Note 3: X-rays were discovered by Roentgen in 1896. These are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength and are used to detect cracks in fractured bones.
  • Note 4: If the energies of α, β and γ-particles is same, then penetrating power α < β < γ.

details.summary: Properties of Gamma rays and general notes on radioactivity.

subject: Chemistry
text:
This law was put forward by Soddy, Fajan and Russel on the basis of following fact:

  • (i) When a radioactive element emits an α-particle, the atomic number of the resulting nuclide decreases by 4 units e.g., 238/92 U -> 234/90 Th + 4/2 He
  • (ii) When a radioactive element emits a β-particle, the atomic number of the resulting nuclide increases by one unit but the atomic mass remains unchanged e.g., 238/92 U -> 238/93 Np + 0/-1 e

subject: Chemistry
text:
The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller of nearly comparable masses and release of about 200MeV of energy is called nuclear fission. Nuclear fission was discovered by 'Hahn' and 'Strassmann' in 1939.

  • Atom bomb is the result of uncontrolled nuclear fission.
  • The device in which controlled nuclear fission (chain reactions) is carried out is called nuclear reactor. The fission is controlled by absorbing neutrons by using cadmium or boron rods.
  • Heavy water (D2O, molecular weight 20) and graphite are used as moderator for slowing down the fast moving neutrons. U235 is used as a nuclear fuel.

details.summary: Definition and mechanism of nuclear fission, including components of a nuclear reactor.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The union of (two or more) lighter nuclei to form a heavier nucleus is called the nuclear fusion. It is also accompanied by release of energy because the total mass of products is lesser than the total mass of reactants.

  • Nuclear fusion occurs only at extremely high temperature (> 10^6 K), so it is also called thermonuclear reactions.
  • Hydrogen bomb (mixture of deuterium oxide and tritium dioxide) is the result of nuclear fusion.
  • Source of solar (sun) and stellar energy is nuclear fusion.
  • The source of emission of large amount of energy during nuclear fission or fusion processes is conversion of mass into energy. It is given by the relation, E = mc^2 and calculated in MeV.

details.summary: Definition and characteristics of nuclear fusion and its relation to mass-energy equivalence.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The forces of attraction like interatomic, intermolecular or interionic forces which holds two or more constituents (atoms, molecules or ions) together are called chemical bonding and the process of their combination is called chemical bonding.

In general, it is believed that atoms combine in order to complete their octet, i.e. 8 electrons in their outermost shell (with the exception of hydrogen and helium in case of which outermost shell can have a maximum of two electrons).

details.summary: Definition of chemical bonding and the octet rule.

subject: Chemistry
text:
An ion is an electrically charged species. A positively charged ion is called cation, e.g. Na+, H+, Mg2+ while a negatively charged ion is called anion, e.g. Cl-, F-, I-.

  • A cation contains less electrons than a normal atom while an anion contains more electrons than a normal atom.
  • When an atom loses one electron, it carries one positive charge, i.e. converted into cation, and if it gains one electron, it carries one negative charge, i.e. converted into anion.
  • There is no change in atomic number or number of protons when an atom forms ion.

details.summary: Definition and properties of cations and anions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
An electron of an atom, located in the outermost shell (valence shell) of the atom, that can be transferred to or shared with another atom is called valence electrons.

  • Elements having same number of valence electrons have similar chemical properties.
  • Elements having 1, 2 or 3 valence electrons in their atoms are metals and form cation while those having 4, 5, 6 or 7 are non-metals and form anion.
  • Elements with 8 valence electrons (except H and He which have 2 valence electrons) are inert, i.e. unreactive and exist as neutral atom.
  • If number of valence electrons = 1, 2 or 3, Valency = Number of valence electrons.
  • If number of valence electrons >= 4, Valency = 8 - number of valence electrons.

details.summary: Definition of valence electrons and rules for determining valency.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom (usually metal) to another (usually non-metal) is called electrovalent bond and the compound is called electrovalent or ionic compound. In other words, it is an intercoulombic forces of attraction between two oppositely charged species. The number of electrons transferred shows the electrovalency of the atom.

The properties of electrovalent compounds are as follow:

  • They are usually crystalline solids, i.e. have definite shape and are hard and brittle.
  • They have high melting and boiling points.
  • They conduct electricity when dissolved in water or in molten state due to the presence of free or mobile ions.
  • These are soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents like alcohol, benzene, etc.
  • If the electronegativity difference of two atoms is 1.7, the bond between them is 50% ionic.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The bond formed by the sharing of electrons between two atoms of same or different elements is called covalent bond and the compound is called covalent compound. When a non-metal combines with another non-metal, a covalent bond is formed. Covalent bond may be single, double or triple depending upon the number of sharing pairs of electrons. The number of electrons shared shows the covalency of the element.

The properties of covalent compounds are as follow:

  • Normal covalent compounds are gases or liquid under ordinary conditions of temperature and pressure.
  • These do not conduct electricity (due to the absence of free ions) and are insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents.
  • Graphite although is covalent but conducts electricity because of the presence of free electrons (electrical conduction).
  • These show stereoisomerism because covalent bond is directional in nature.

details.summary: Definition and properties of covalent bonds.

subject: Chemistry
text:
This type of bond is formed by one sided sharing of one pair of electrons between two atoms. The atom having complete octet which provides the electron pair for sharing is known as donor atom. The other atom which accepts the electron pair is called the acceptor atom.

e.g. NH3 -> BF3, NH4+
