subject: Geography
content:
## Definition
- **Universe** – the totality of everything that exists, including all physical matter (planets, stars, galaxies, inter‑galactic space) and energy.
- The scientific study of the Universe is called **Cosmology**.

> *The Universe comprises all that is, was, and ever will be.*

subject: Geography
content:
## What is a Galaxy?
- A **galaxy** is a massive assembly of stars, planets, gas, dust and dark matter bound together by gravity.
- Typical galaxy contains **millions to billions of stars**; the stars constitute most of the galaxy’s visible mass.
- **Our galaxy** – the **Milky Way (Akash Ganga)** – contains ~300 billion stars; the Sun is one of them.
- **Andromeda** – the nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way.
- The Universe contains **billions of galaxies**.

subject: Geography
content:
## Solar System Overview
- The **Sun** sits at the centre of the Solar System.
- **Planets**, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets and other objects orbit the Sun.
- The Solar System is a **sub‑system** of the Milky Way galaxy.

subject: Geography
content:
## Timeline of Major Theories
| Year | Scientist | Model | Key Point |
|------|-----------|-------|-----------|
| AD 140 | **Ptolemy** | **Geocentric** | Earth at the centre; Sun & planets revolve around Earth. |

subject: General Science
content:
### Theories of Universe Origin

1. **Big Bang Theory**
   - **Proposed by**: Georges Lemaitre.
   - **Description**: An explosion that occurred **13.8 billion years ago**.
   - **Outcome**: Led to the formation of galaxies, stars, and other heavenly bodies.

2. **Steady State Theory**
   - **Proposed by**: Bondi, Gold, and Fred Hoyle.
   - **Description**: New galaxies are continuously formed while older ones are destroyed.
   - **Key Feature**: The overall size of the Universe remains constant.

3. **Pulsating Theory**
   - **Description**: The Universe expands and contracts alternately (pulsating).
   - **Current State**: The Universe is currently expanding.

subject: General Science
content:
### Solar System Composition

- **Components**: Sun, 8 planets, their moons, and non-stellar objects.
- **Origin**: Developed from the condensation of gases and lesser bodies.
- **Size**: Estimated at about **105 Astronomical Units (AU)**.
- **Central Body**: The Sun is at the center; all planets revolve around it in **elliptical orbits**.
- **Nearest Star**: The Sun is the nearest star to Earth.
- **Interstellar Debris**: Includes asteroids, meteoroids, comets, plasma (electrically charged gases), and interplanetary dust particles.
- **Small Solar System Bodies (SSSB)**: Components other than planets, dwarf planets, and satellites.

subject: General Science
content:

- **Mass**: Accounts for more than **99%** of the mass of the solar system.
- **Gravity**: Exerts immense gravitational pull to keep planets in definite elliptical orbits.
- **Energy Source**: Major source of energy in the solar system.
- **Mechanism**: Energy is provided by **nuclear fusion**, converting **hydrogen into helium** in the core.
- **Fraunhofer Lines**: Hundreds of dark lines super-imposed on the Sun’s white light. Each line indicates specific elements present in the solar system.

subject: Geography
content:
# Equinoxes

- **Definition**: Days when the length of day and night are approximately equal.
- **Sun’s Position**: The Sun is vertically overhead at the equator.
- **Dates**:
  - **Vernal (Spring) Equinox**: 21 March
  - **Autumnal Equinox**: 23 September
- **Significance**: Marks the change of seasons; the equinoxes are the only times when the Sun’s rays strike the Earth’s equator directly.

> *Key Fact*: The equinoxes occur twice a year, roughly every 6 months.

subject: Geography
content:
# Summer Solstice

- **Date**: 21 June
- **Sun’s Position**: Vertically overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer** (23½° N).
- **Effects**:
  - **Northern Hemisphere**: Longest day, shortest night.
  - **Southern Hemisphere**: Shortest day, longest night.
- **Why It Happens**: After the vernal equinox, the Sun appears to move northward, reaching its northernmost point.

> *Key Fact*: The summer solstice marks the peak of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

subject: Geography
content:
# Winter Solstice

- **Date**: 22 December
- **Sun’s Position**: Vertically overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn** (23½° S).
- **Effects**:
  - **Southern Hemisphere**: Longest day, shortest night.
  - **Northern Hemisphere**: Shortest day, longest night.
- **Why It Happens**: The Sun reaches its southernmost point after the autumnal equinox.

> *Key Fact*: The winter solstice is the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

text:
The interior of Earth is divided into three parts

  • The Crust
    • The crust is the outermost and the thinnest layer of the Earth. This layer has the least density and its thickness varies about 8 to 40 km.
    • Mohorovic or Moho Discontinuity, marks the lower limit of the crust and this discontinuity is identified on the basis of rock density.
    • The rocks forming the crust of the Earth are rich in lighter minerals like silica and aluminium. Hence, this layer is also called as Sial (silica and aluminium). The average density of this layer is 2.7 gm/cm3.
  • The Mantle
    • It is about 2900 km in thickness, composed of minerals in a semi solid state. It is further divided into two layer upper mantle and lower mantle. The upper part of the mantle is called Asthenosphere, which is about 250 km thick.
    • Due to presence of minerals like silica and magnesium in the rocks forming this layer of the Earth, the mantle layer is also known as Sima (silica and magnesium). The average density of this layer is about 5.68 gm/cm3.
    • The transitional zone separating the mantle from the core is called the Gutenberg Discontinuity.
  • The Core
    • The core is the innermost layer of the Earth and occupies its center. It is about 3500 km in radius. This layer is also known as Nife (nickel and iron), because this layer contain large concentration of iron and nickel.
    • Density of this part of the Earth is 17.2 gm/cm3 and is many times greater than the average density of the Earth (5.53 gm/cm3).

DISCONTINUITIES

  • The various layers are separated by dicontinuities, which are evident in seismic data.
  • G Conrad discontinuity lies between upper crust and lower crust.
  • G Mohorovicic discontinuity between crust

details.summary: Details of Earth's crust, mantle, core, and discontinuities.

subject: Geography
text:
The Northern rift cuts Pangaea from East to West, creating Laurasia in the North and Gondwanaland in South. A shallow sea called Tethys was situated between the Laurasia and the Gondwanaland.

Plate Tectonics Theory

The theory of Plate tectonics states that the lithosphere is divided into several rigid segments, which include both oceanic and continental crusts. These segments are called plates and they are moving on the asthenosphere, which is not a liquid, but a solid which flows under stress.

About 20 such plates have been identified. There are seven major plates: Eurasia, Antarctica, North America, South America, Pacific, African and Indian Plate.

Most of the Earth's seismic activity, volcanism and mountain building occur along with these dynamic boundaries.

Depending upon the type of movement, plate margins are of three types:

  • Divergent Plate Margin (Constructive margins)
  • Convergent Plate Margin (Destructive margins)
  • Parallel Plates Margin (Conservative margin or Transform boundary)

Collision can occur between two oceanic plates, one oceanic and one continental plate or two continental plates.

Due to collision three types of plate boundaries appear, which are as follows:

  • Divergent Plate Boundary
  • Convergent Plate Boundary
  • Transform Fault Boundary

When the plates move apart with the upwelling of material from the mantle, divergent plate boundary results.

A convergent plate boundary is one, where two plates collide, one plate bending downward and subducting below the other.

They are located where plates slide past one another without the creation or destruction of crust.

Formation of the mid oceanic ridges are the example of divergent plate margin.

Deep oceanic trench is formed adjacent to the zone of subduction.

Fold mountains are the result of convergent plate boundary.

San Andreas Fault along the West coast of Mexico is a famous transform fault.

Example: Surtsey Island was born along with mid-Atlantic ridge.

Example: Himalayan boundary fault, ...

subject: Geography
content:
### Volcanism
- **Volcanism** includes all phenomena connected with the movement of heated material from the interior towards the surface of the Earth.
- A **volcano** is a vent or opening through which heated materials (gases, water, liquid lava, rock fragments) are ejected from the highly heated interior to the surface.
- Volcanic eruptions are closely associated with several integrated processes:
  - Gradual increase in temperature with increasing depth due to heat generated by the decay of radioactive elements inside the Earth.
  - Origin of magma caused by a lowering of the melting point when the pressure of over‑lying rocks is reduced (e.g., by fractures created during plate splitting).

subject: Geography
content:
### Classification on the Basis of Mode of Eruption
| Type | Description | Typical Behaviour | Examples |
|------|-------------|-------------------|----------|
| **Central (Explosive) Eruption** | Magma is expelled with great force through a small vent and can travel a considerable distance. | Explosive, ash‑rich, often forms steep cones. | Hawaiian, Strombolian, Pelean, Vesuvius, Volcanion types |
| **Fissure (Quiet) Eruption** | Large quantities of lava flow quietly from linear fissures and spread over surrounding areas. | Effusive, creates extensive lava plateaus. | Deccan Plateau (India) |

These two modes reflect the dynamics of magma ascent and the nature of the vent through which it erupts.

subject: Geography
content:
### Classification on the Basis of Periodicity
| Category | Definition | Typical Status | Examples |
|----------|------------|----------------|----------|
| **Active Volcano** | Erupts periodically (historical or recent activity). | Currently or recently erupting. | Etna (Italy), Stromboli (Italy), Mayon (Philippines) |
| **Dormant Volcano** | Currently quiet but retains the potential to erupt again. | No recent eruptions, but not extinct. | Fujiyama (Japan), Krakatoa (Indonesia), Barren Island (India) |
| **Extinct Volcano** | Shows no signs of future activity; magma source is considered exhausted. | No recorded activity and no plausible future eruptions. | *(No specific examples given in the source text)* |

Understanding the eruption periodicity helps in hazard assessment and land‑use planning.

### Various Volcanic Belts
- **Circum‑Pacific Belt** (also called the *Fire Ring of the Pacific*):
  - Extends across the Kamchatka Peninsula, Kurile Islands, the islands of Japan, the Philippines, New Guinea, New Zealand, and the Solomon Islands.

  - **Fujiyama** – Japan
  - **Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes** – Alaska, USA (region of extensive volcanic activity).
- **Mid‑Continental Belt** (Volcanic zones of convergent continental plate margins):

subject: Geography
content:
### Metamorphic Rock Transformations
Metamorphic rocks are formed from the transformation of existing rock types (sedimentary, igneous, or other metamorphic rocks) through heat and pressure.

**Key Transformations:**
- **Sandstone** (Sedimentary) → **Quartzite** (Metamorphic)
- **Limestone** (Sedimentary) → **Marble** (Metamorphic)
- **Shale/Clay/Mudstone** (Sedimentary) → **Slate** (Metamorphic)
- **Granite** (Igneous) → **Gneiss** (Metamorphic)
- **Coal** (Organic/Sedimentary) → **Graphite** (Metamorphic)

**Other Metamorphic Rocks:**
- **Slate, Phyllite, Schist**: Derived from shale/clay with increasing grade of metamorphism.
- **Diamond**: Metamorphic form of carbon (from graphite under extreme pressure).

subject: Geography
content:
### Weathering
**Definition:** The process of disintegration or decomposition of rocks *in situ* (in place) by natural agents. It is a **static process** (no movement of material).

**Three Types of Weathering:**

1. **Physical (Mechanical) Weathering**
   - **Process:** Disintegration of rocks without any change in chemical constituents.
   - **Factors:**
     - Temperature change (thermal expansion/contraction).
     - Crystallization of water into ice (frost wedging).
     - Pressure release mechanism (exfoliation).

2. **Chemical Weathering**
   - **Process:** Decomposition due to chemical changes in the rock structure.
   - **Processes involved:**
     - Solution
     - Oxidation
     - Carbonation
     - Hydration
     - Hydrolysis
     - Chelation

3. **Biological Weathering**
   - **Process:** Controlled by plants, animals, and humans.
   - **Sub-types:**
     - **Faunal weathering:** By animals.
     - **Floral weathering:** By plants (e.g., root wedging).
     - **Anthropogenic weathering:** By human activities.

subject: Geography
content:
### Erosion
**Definition:** The process involving the **removal** of rock material and its subsequent **transportation**.

**Key Distinction:** Unlike weathering (static), erosion is a **dynamic process** performed by mobile agents.

**Agents of Erosion:**
- Streams (Rivers)
- Wind
- Waves
- Underground water

subject: Geography
content:
### Landforms
**Definition:** Features on the Earth’s surface, including terrain, mountains, hills, plateaus, and plains.

**Minor Landforms:** Buttes, canyons, valleys, basins.

**Origin:** Tectonic plate movement can create landforms by pushing up mountains and hills.

**Classification by Process of Origin:**
1. **Fluvial Landforms:**
   - **Definition:** Features resulting from the movement of water on the Earth’s surface.
   - **Significance:** Flowing water is the most important force shaping the Earth.
   - **Erosional Fluvial Landforms:**
     - U-shaped valley (Note: Typically V-shaped for rivers, U-shaped for glaciers, but listed here in source context).
     - Potholes.

subject: Geography
text:
MOUNTAINS

Based on their mode of formation four main types of mountains can be distinguished.

  • Fold Mountains
    • It is formed due to the compressive forces generated by endogenetic forces (earthquake, landslide etc.)
    • Example of Fold mountains are Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies, Atlas etc.
    • On the basis of age, fold mountains are grouped into
      • Young/New Fold Mountains It came into existence after the continental drift, e.g. Himalayas, Andes, Rockies, Alps. Himalayas are regarded as the youngest mountains in the world.
      • Old Fold Mountains They belong to pre-drift era, e.g. Pennines (Europe), Appalachians (US), Aravallis (India) etc.
  • Block Mountains
    • It is formed when a huge block of Earth’s crust may be raised or lowered due to tectonic activities. The land between the two paralled faults either rises forming block mountains or horsts or subsides into a depression termed as Rift valley or Graben.
    • Examples of Block mountain are Vindhya and Satpura in India, the Vosges in France and Black forest in Germany (through which Rhine river flows).
  • Volcanic Mountains
    • They are formed due to the accumulation of volcanic material. They are also known as Mountains of Accumulation.
    • Examples of Volcanic mountain are Mt Fuji (Japan), Cotopaxi in Andes, Vesuvius and Etna in Italy, Mt Mayon (Philippines) etc.
  • Residual or Dissected Mountain
    • They are formed as a result of erosion of plateaus and high planes by various agents of erosion.
    • Examples of Residual or Dissected mountain are Catskill mountains of New York, Sierras of Spain, Girnar and Rajmahal of India.

subject: Geography
content:
### Types of Plains
There are three primary types of plains based on their formation:

1. **Structural Plain**
   - **Formation**: Formed due to the uplift of a part of the sea floor.
   - **Example**: The Great Plain of the USA.

2. **Erosional Plain**
   - **Formation**: Formed when an elevated tract of land is worn down to a plain by the process of erosion.
   - **Example**: Plain of North Canada.

3. **Depositional Plain**
   - **Formation**: Formed by filling up of sediments into depressions along the foothills, lakes, and seas.
   - **Example**: Indo-Ganga Plain.

subject: Geography
content:
### Islands: Definition
- **Island**: Any piece of land that is surrounded by water.
- **Archipelago**: A grouping of geographically or geologically related islands.
- **Classification**: Various types of islands are named according to the way they were formed.

subject: Geography
content:
### Types of Islands

1. **Continental Island**
   - **Characteristics**: Rests on the continental shelf; always quite close to a given continent; water level around the island is very shallow (typically less than 600 feet).
   - **Examples**: 
     - Newfoundland (Canada)
     - Greenland
     - Great Britain (Largest continental island in Europe)

2. **Volcanic Island**
   - **Formation**: Formed when volcanoes deep in the ocean rise above the water’s surface.

3. **Coral Island**
   - **Characteristics**: Forms a ring and partially or totally encloses a shallow body of water or lagoon. Large collections of coral atop rock (usually volcanic) in the ocean.
   - **Example**: Lakshadweep Islands (Indian Ocean).

4. **Alluvial Island**
   - **Formation**: Formed by the outward flow of water depositing silt and gravel at the mouth of a river.
   - **Example**: New Moore Island (at the mouth of the Ganga river in West Bengal).

5. **Barrier Island**
   - **Formation**: Formed by waves depositing sand on the shallow ocean bottom as they crash on the shoreline.

6. **Tectonic Island**
   - **Formation**: Result of tectonic activity. Tectonic movement forms long island arcs (archipelagoes).
   - **Examples**: Indonesia, Philippines.

subject: Geography
content:
# Composition of the Earth's Atmosphere

The atmosphere is primarily composed of the following gases:

- **Nitrogen (N₂)** – 78 % (by volume)
- **Oxygen (O₂)** – 21 %
- **Argon (Ar)** – 0.33 %
- **Carbon Dioxide (CO₂)** – 0.03 %
- Trace gases: neon, helium, hydrogen, and others

In addition to gases, the atmosphere contains:
- **Water vapour** – 0 % to 4 % by volume, varying with region and weather
- **Particulates** – dust, aerosols, and other solid or liquid particles
- **Ozone (O₃)** – concentrated in a belt at 20–25 km altitude

The vertical distribution of gases is not uniform; the concentration of gases decreases with altitude, and the composition changes in different atmospheric layers.

subject: Geography
content:
# Troposphere

- **Extent**: From sea level up to ~16 km (varies from 8 km at the poles to 18 km at the equator)
- **Temperature lapse rate**: Approximately 1 °C drop per 165 m (≈6.5 °C per km)
- **Key features**:
  - Contains almost all of the atmosphere’s water vapour, dust particles, and the majority of carbon dioxide
  - Site of weather phenomena such as condensation, precipitation, storms, and cloud formation
- **Boundary**: The **tropopause** separates the troposphere from the stratosphere

The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere and is crucial for life and weather on Earth.

subject: Geography
text:
The zone between the 85 km and 400 km above the surface is often called Thermosphere. In this layer, the temperature increases with increasing altitude. The upper limit of the thermosphere, the thermopause is generally taken at an altitude of about 600 km.

  • The day temperature at 600 km altitude exceed 1400°C while night temperature remain about 225°C .
  • The upper part of the thermosphere contains only the lighter gases like helium and hydrogen.

details.summary: Description of the thermosphere layer of Earth's atmosphere.

subject: Geography
text:
The outermost part of the atmosphere of the Earth is called Exosphere. This zone of the atmosphere extends upto a height of about 900 km.

  • The upper limit of the exosphere is uncertain as this layer acts as a transitional layer between the Earth’s atmosphere and the space. The outer part of the exosphere is called Magnetosphere. The presence of air is extremely rare in this layer.

details.summary: Description of the exosphere and magnetosphere layers of Earth's atmosphere.

subject: Geography
text:
Sun is the main source of energy on Earth. Energy from Sun is received in the form of radiation. Solar radiation that is intercepted by Earth is known as Insolation.

The amount of insolation depends on following factors :

  • The area and nature of the surface.
  • The inclination of the rays of the Sun.
  • Distance between the Earth and the Sun.
  • Length of the day.
  • The transparency of the atmosphere.
  • As the angle of the Sun rays decreases poleward, the amount of insolation received also decreases in that direction.
  • The Earth’s surface does not absorb all the energy that it receives. The proportion of the solar radiation reflected from the surface is called Albedo.
  • On an average, insolation is highest near the equator, marginally lower at the tropic and lowest at the poles.

details.summary: Factors affecting insolation and its distribution over Earth's surface.

subject: Geography
text: The Earth receives energy continuously from the Sun, its temperature is almost constant except the long-term climate changes. This is because the atmosphere loses an amount of heat equal to the gain through insolation. This mechanism of main

details.summary: Concept of Earth's heat budget balancing incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation.

subject: Geography
content:
### Sub‑tropical High Pressure Belt
- **Latitude range:** 30° – 35° N and S in both hemispheres.
- **Cause of high pressure:**
  1. **Subsidence of air** that descends from the equatorial regions.
  2. **Blocking effect of the Coriolis force** which deflects the descending air.
- **Mechanism:** Convergence of winds at higher altitude above this zone forces air to sink. The descending air contracts, increasing its density and creating a region of high pressure.
- **Other name:** *Horse Latitude*.
- **Key point:** The belt is a dynamical feature, not a thermal one; it results from the vertical motion of air rather than temperature differences.

subject: Geography
content:
### Sub‑Polar Low Pressure Belt
- **Latitude range:** 60° – 65° in both hemispheres.
- **Nature of the belt:** Dynamically induced (not thermally induced) because the region experiences low temperatures year‑round; a thermally driven system would have produced a high‑pressure belt instead.
- **Hemisphere differences:** More pronounced and regular in the Southern Hemisphere due to the dominance of oceanic surfaces, which enhance moisture and low‑pressure formation.
- **Key characteristic:** Persistent low pressure despite the cold climate, indicating the importance of atmospheric dynamics (e.g., wind convergence and rising motion) over temperature alone.

subject: Geography
content:
### Polar High
- **Location:** Directly over the poles (both North and South).
- **Pressure regime:** High pressure persists throughout the year.
- **Reason:** Extremely low temperatures year‑round cause the air to become very dense, leading to a stable high‑pressure area.
- **Extent:** Small in area, encircling each pole.
- **Significance:** Acts as a sink for cold, dense air and influences the polar easterlies.

subject: Geography
content:
### Seasonal Shifting of Pressure and Wind Belts
- **Driving factor:** Position of the mid‑day Sun (solar declination).
- **June (Sun over Tropic of Cancer):** All belts migrate **5° – 10° north** of their mean latitude.
- **December (Sun over Tropic of Capricorn):** All belts migrate **5° – 10° south** of their mean latitude.
- **Implication:** The entire system of pressure zones and associated wind belts follows the solar heating zone, causing seasonal variations in climate patterns.

subject: Geography
content:
### Fundamentals of Wind Generation
- **Primary cause:** Pressure difference (gradient) between two regions.
- **Air movement:** From **high pressure → low pressure**.
- **Pressure Gradient (Barometric Slope):** The rate of change of pressure with distance; steeper gradients produce stronger winds.
- **Isobars:** Imaginary lines joining points of equal atmospheric pressure on a map.
- **Wind direction:** In the absence of friction, wind flows **perpendicular to isobars**, moving from high to low pressure. (In the real atmosphere, the Coriolis force causes wind to cross isobars at an angle, resulting in geostrophic flow.)

subject: Geography
topic: Definition and Characteristics of Local Winds
content: Local winds are horizontal movements of air on a small scale. Their movement is primarily caused by local factors such as the presence of water bodies or mountains. They are distinct from global winds due to their limited geographical extent and specific local causes.

subject: Geography
topic: Coastal Local Winds (Land and Sea Breeze)
content:
1. **Land Breeze**: A warm wind experienced along coastal areas. It blows from the land towards the sea.
2. **Sea Breeze**: A cold wind experienced along coastal areas. It blows from the sea towards the land.

subject: Geography
topic: Definition and Seasonal Variation of Jet Streams
content:
1. **Definition**: Jet Streams are strong, rapidly moving circumpolar Westerly air circulations found in a narrow belt (a few 100 km wide) at the upper limit of the troposphere. Their circulation path is wavy and meandering.
2. **Seasonal Variation**: 
   - **Summer**: The extent of jet streams narrows down due to their northward shifting.
   - **Winter**: Jet streams extend up to 20° North latitude.

subject: Geography
topic: Definition and Air Circulation in Cyclones
content:
1. **Definition**: Cyclones are centers of low pressure surrounded by closed isobars. Pressure increases outward from the center. Air circulation is closed, moving from outside towards the central low pressure (inward direction).
2. **Direction of Air Flow**: 
   - **Northern Hemisphere**: Air blows inward in an anti-clockwise direction.
   - **Southern Hemisphere**: Air blows inward in a clockwise direction.

subject: Geography
text:
Humidity of air refers to the content of the water vapour present in the air at a particular time and place.

Humidity is measured by an instrument called Hygrometer. Another instrument used for the same purpose is sling psychrometer.

The atmospheric humidity is expressed in a number of ways such as:

  • Humidity Capacity: The capacity of air of certain volume at certain temperature to retain maximum amount of moisture content.
  • Absolute Humidity: The total weight of moisture content per volume of air at definite temperature is called Absolute Humidity.
  • Specific Humidity: The mass of the water vapour in grams contained in a kilogram of air and it represents the actual quantity of moisture present in a definite air.
  • Relative Humidity: It is the ratio of the amount of water vapour actually present in the air having definite volume and temperature (i.e. absolute humidity) to the maximum amount the air can hold (i.e. humidity capacity).

Relative Humidity = (Absolute Humidity / Humidity Capacity) × 100

Condensation is the change of physical state of matter from gaseous phase into liquid phase. It is the reverse of vaporisation.

When the relative humidity reaches 100%, the air is completely saturated. The air temperature is said to be as dew point.

Fog is made from the droplets of water suspended in the lower layer of the atmosphere. Fog is not considered as a form of precipitation. Visibility of less than 1 km is the internationally recognised definition of fog.

Smog (Smoke + Fog) is a form of fog that occurs in areas where the air contains a large amount of smoke.

Haze is formed by water particles that have condensed in the atmosphere and visibility lies between 1 km to 2 km.

Frost is the moisture on the ground surface that condenses directly into ice i.e. when condensation occurs below freezing point.

details.summary: This note covers the definition of humidity, instruments for measuring humidity, types of humidity (capacity, absolute, specific, relative), the formula for relative humidity, condensation, dew point, fog, smog, haze, and frost.

subject: Geography
content:
Precipitation is classified into three main types based on its origin:

1. **Convectional Rainfall**: Occurs due to thermal convection currents caused by insolation heating of the ground surface. Examples include rainfall over the Congo basin, Amazon basin, and South-East Asia.
2. **Orographic Rainfall**: Occurs due to the ascent of air forced by a mountain barrier. Example: Mahabaleshwar and the Western Ghats receive about 600 cm of rainfall.
3. **Frontal Rainfall**: Occurs due to the upward movement of air caused by the convergence of cold air masses against warm air masses. Example: Heavy rainfall in North-West Europe due to the convergence of cold continental and warm oceanic air.

content:
**Weather**: Refers to the sum total of atmospheric conditions (temperature, pressure, wind, moisture, cloudiness, precipitation, and visibility) of a particular place at any given time.

**Climate**: Refers to the average weather conditions over a large area.

**Factors controlling Weather and Climate**:
- Latitude
- Altitude
- Unequal distribution of land and water
- Ocean currents
- Air pressure and wind
- Mountain barriers

subject: Geography
content:
# Distribution of Water on Earth

The hydrosphere comprises all water on Earth, including oceans, seas, lakes, rivers, glaciers, and atmospheric water. The following table summarizes the percentage distribution of water in various components:

| Component                     | Percentage of Total Water |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Oceans                        | **97.6 %** |
| Saline lakes & inland seas    | 0.008 % |
| Ice caps & glaciers           | 1.9 % |
| Ground water                  | 0.5 % |
| Soil moisture                 | 0.01 % |
| Lakes                         | 0.009 % |
| Freshwater rivers             | 0.0001 % |
| Atmosphere                    | 0.0009 % |

> **Key Takeaway**: Oceans hold the vast majority of Earth's water, covering about 70 % of the planet’s surface.

subject: Geography
content:
# Continental Shelf

- **Definition**: The shallow, submerged extension of a continent.
- **Depth**: Extends to ~100 fathoms (≈180 m).
- **Average Width**: 70 km.
- **Average Slope**: 17 ft/mile (~1°).
- **Area Coverage**: 7.5 % of all oceanic area; 13.3 % of the Atlantic, 5.7 % of the Pacific, 4.2 % of the Indian Ocean.
- **Economic Importance**: ~20 % of global petroleum and gas reserves; richest fishing grounds.

subject: Geography
content:
# Continental Slope

- **Location**: Extends seaward from the continental shelf.
- **Depth Range**: 200–2000 fathoms (≈3660 m).
- **Average Slope**: 20–50°.
- **Boundary with Shelf**: Known as the **Andesite Line**.
- **Area Coverage**: 8.5 % of total ocean area.

subject: Geography
content:
# Continental Rise

- **Description**: Slightly rising area at the foot of the continental slope, formed by sediment accumulation.
- **Average Slope**: 0.5°–1°.
- **Resource Significance**: Major site for oil deposits.

subject: Geography
text:
iii. Atoll

A reef of narrow growing corals of horse—shoe shape and crowned with plam trees is called an Atoll.

  • Atoll partly or completely encloses a lagoon. It is formed around an island in an elliptical form on a submarine platform. Funafuti atoll of Ellice Islands is a famous atoll.

CORAL BLEACHING

When corals are stressed by changes in conditions such as temperature, light or nutrients, they expel the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, causing them to turn colourless, this phenomenon is known as Coral Bleaching.

SALINITY

Salinity is defined as the total amount of salts and minerals in grams contained in 1 kg of sea water and is expressed as part per thousand. The oceanic salinity not only affects the marine organism and plant community, but also affects the physical properties of the ocean such as temperature, pressure, density, waves and currents.

  • Average salinity of seawater is about 35‰ and average salinity in Southern hemisphere is more than that of Northern hemisphere.
  • Iso-halines represent the salinity distribution in the surface of the sea. These are the lines joining places having an equal degree of salinity.
  • The main source of salinity is dissolution of the rocks of oceanic crust, which contains salts. Poles have minimum salinity because of addition of fresh water in the form of icebergs and excessive snowfall.
  • Variation in salinity causes vertical circulation of water.
  • Salinity also increases the density of water. More saline water freezes slowly while the boiling point of saline water is higher than the fresh water.
tables:
| Controlling Factor | Relation with Salinity |
|---|---|
| Evaporation | Greater the evaporation, higher the salinity. |
| Precipitation | Higher the precipitation, lower the salinity. |
| Influx of river water | Big voluminuous rivers pour down immense volume of fresh water into the oceans and salinity is reduced at the mouth. |
| Atmospheric pressure | Anticyclonic conditions with stable air and high temperature increases the salinity of the surface water |

subject: Geography
content:
## Ocean Current
- **Definition**: A continuous, directed movement of ocean water generated by various forces.
- **Forces influencing currents**:
  - Breaking waves
  - Wind
  - Coriolis effect
  - Temperature and salinity differences (thermohaline circulation)
  - Shape and configuration of the coastline
  - Tides caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun
- **Hemisphere circulation**:
  - **Northern Hemisphere** – currents generally circulate **clockwise**.
  - **Southern Hemisphere** – currents generally circulate **anti‑clockwise**.
- **Two main types**:
  1. **Warm Ocean Currents** – flow from lower latitudes (near the equator) toward higher latitudes.
  2. **Cold Ocean Currents** – flow from higher latitudes toward lower latitudes.

subject: Geography
content:
### Warm Ocean Currents
- **Definition**: Currents that transport warm water from the equatorial regions toward the poles.
- **Characteristics**:
  - Typically flow **northward** in the Northern Hemisphere and **southward** in the Southern Hemisphere.
  - Contribute to milder coastal climates (e.g., the Gulf Stream).
- **Examples** are listed under regional sections (North Pacific, South Pacific, etc.).

subject: Geography
content:
### Cold Ocean Currents
- **Definition**: Currents that transport cold water from higher latitudes toward the equator.
- **Characteristics**:
  - Typically flow **southward** in the Northern Hemisphere and **northward** in the Southern Hemisphere.
  - Often associated with upwelling zones that enrich marine life.
- **Examples** are listed under regional sections (North Pacific, South Pacific, etc.).

subject: Geography
topic: Warm Currents of the North Pacific Ocean
content:
### Warm Currents (North Pacific)
| Current | Direction / Path | Remarks |
|---------|------------------|---------|
| **North Equatorial Current** | Westward from the western coast of Mexico to the Philippines | Major west‑ward flow near the equator. |
| **Kuroshio Current** | Extends from the North Equatorial Current near Japan; flows northward along the Japanese coast | Often called the "Japan Current"; a strong warm western boundary current. |
| **Alaska Current** | Flows north‑eastward along the coast of British Columbia and the Alaska Peninsula | Transports relatively warm water into higher latitudes of the North Pacific. |

subject: Geography
topic: Cold Currents of the North Pacific Ocean
content:
### Cold Currents (North Pacific)
| Current | Direction / Path | Remarks |
|---------|------------------|---------|
| **Oyashio Current** | South‑westward from the Bering Sea toward Japan; merges with the Kuroshio | Brings cold, nutrient‑rich water to the north‑western Pacific. |
| **Okhotsk & Kuril Currents** | Flow southward from the Sea of Okhotsk and join the Kuroshio north of Japan | Contribute to the complex circulation around the Japanese archipelago. |
| **West Wind Drift** (Antarctic Circumpolar Current) | Eastward flow that eventually reaches the Alaska region | The strongest current in the world, encircling Antarctica. |
| **Californian Current** | Southward extension of the Alaska Current; joins the North Equatorial Current, completing a clockwise circulation | Influences the climate of the western coast of North America. |

subject: Geography
content:
### Indian Ocean Currents

1. **North Equatorial Current**:
   - Flows from East to West.
   - Upon reaching the East coast of Africa, a portion turns Southward, crosses the equator, and becomes the Mozambique Current.

2. **Mozambique Current**:
   - Flows South along the East coast of Africa.
   - Originates from the vicinity of the equator.
   - Extends to about 35° South, where it is known as the Agulhas Stream.

3. **Agulhas Stream**:
   - Flows Westward along the Southern West of Madagascar.
   - Joins the Mozambique Current along the East African coast.

4. **West Wind Drift Current**:
   - Flows across the Indian Ocean to the South-West of Australia.

5. **Monsoon Drifts (India Coast)**:
   - **North-East Monsoon Drift**: Flows along the coast of India during winter.
   - **South-West Monsoon Drift**: Flows along the coast of India during summer.

6. **South Equatorial Current**:
   - Significant current in Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans.
   - Flows East-West between the equator and about 20 degrees South.

7. **Somalia Current**:
   - Ocean boundary current running along the coast of Somalia and Oman in the Western Indian Ocean.
   - Analogous to the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic Ocean.

subject: Geography
content:
### Tides

**Definition**: The rise and fall of sea level resulting from the gravitational forces between the Earth, the Moon, and the Sun.

**Interval**: The interval between two tides is **12 hours and 26 minutes**.

**Types of Tides**:

1. **Spring Tides**:
   - **Configuration**: Earth, Moon, and Sun are in a straight line (Syzygy).
   - **Mechanism**: The Sun enhances the gravitational pull of the Moon.
   - **Result**: Creates higher high tides and lower low tides.

2. **Neap Tides**:
   - **Configuration**: Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth.
   - **Mechanism**: The Sun partially counteracts (contracts) the pull of the Moon.
   - **Result**: Produces lower high tides (and higher low tides), typical of a Neap Tide.

subject: Geography
content:
### Natural Vegetation

**Definition**: Vegetation that grows naturally on the Earth’s surface without any human interference.

**Characteristics**:
- Different vegetation regions are identified based on distinct climatic and geographical factors.

subject: Geography
content:
### Tropical Deserts
- **Location**: Western margins of continents between 15°-30° North and South of the equator.
- **Climate**: Hot and dry summers; very low rainfall.
- **Vegetation Characteristics**:
  - Very scant vegetation.
  - Succulent stems.
  - Long roots.
  - Leaves reduced to spines.

subject: Geography
content:
### Tundra
- **Location**: Large areas in North Canada, North Russia, North Sweden, and Finland.
- **Vegetation**: Mostly herbaceous, consisting of a mixture of mosses, grasses, and forbs, along with some dwarf shrubs, trees, and lichens.
- **Soil Condition**: Presence of a permanently frozen layer of soil called **permafrost**, which restricts the growth of plant roots.

content:

- **Variation**: Practised under different combinations of physical and socio-economic conditions, giving rise to different types of agriculture systems.

content:
### Intensive Subsistence Agriculture
- **Region**: Practised on a wide scale in densely populated regions of monsoonal Asia.
- **Characteristics**:
  - Farmer owns a small piece of land.

subject: Geography
content:
### National Air Route Services
- Provide long‑distance air services **within the country**.
- Example: **Mumbai – Delhi** route.
- Operated by domestic airlines under the regulatory framework of the **Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)**.
- Primarily used for passenger travel, cargo, and mail services.
- Benefits: faster than rail/road, connects major economic hubs, supports tourism and business.

subject: Geography
content:
### International Air Transport Authority (IATA)
- **Founded:** Over 60 years ago by a group of airlines.
- **Membership:** Represents **240 airlines**, accounting for **84 % of total global air traffic**.
- **Roles:**
  1. **Representation** – Acts as the collective voice of the airline industry.
  2. **Leadership** – Sets standards for safety, security, efficiency, and sustainability.
  3. **Service Provider** – Offers products such as **billing & settlement plans, cargo handling standards, and passenger service systems**.
- **Impact:** Influences international air transport policies, facilitates smoother global travel, and promotes best practices across airlines.

subject: Geography
content:
### Water Transport
- **Categories:**
  - **Ocean (Sea) Transport** – Movement of goods and passengers across seas and oceans.
  - **Inland Water Transport** – Navigation on rivers, canals, lakes, and other inland waterways.
- **Advantages:**
  - **Cheapest** mode for bulk and heavy cargo over long distances.
  - **High capacity** vessels (e.g., bulk carriers, tankers, container ships).
  - **Energy efficient** – lower fuel consumption per tonne‑km compared to road/rail.
- **Key Role:** Facilitates **international trade**, especially for commodities like oil, coal, grain, and minerals.

subject: Geography
topic: Important Sea Routes of the World
content:
### Major Sea Routes
| Route | Regions Connected | Notable Features |
|-------|-------------------|------------------|
| **North Atlantic Sea Route (Big Trunk)** | North‑Eastern USA ↔ North‑Western Europe | Busiest global sea lane; carries a large share of trans‑Atlantic trade. |
| **South Atlantic Sea Route** | North America & Europe ↔ South America | Links major ports of Brazil, Argentina with Europe and the US. |
| **Mediterranean‑Indian Ocean Sea Route** | West Europe ↔ East Africa, South Africa, SE Asia, Australia, NZ | Connects industrialised Europe with emerging markets of the Indian Ocean rim. |
| **Cape of Good Hope Route** | West Europe & West Africa ↔ Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay | Alternative to Suez‑Panama routes; vital for oil and bulk cargo. |
| **North Pacific Sea Route** | West Coast of North America ↔ Asia (Japan, China, Korea) | Supports high‑value container traffic between the US/Canada and East Asia. |
| **South Pacific Sea Route** | South & North America ↔ Australia, New Zealand, Pacific Islands (via Panama Canal) | Critical for trade between the Americas and Oceania. |

subject: Geography
topic: Major Canal Systems of the World
content:
### Key Canal Systems
- **Suez Canal** (opened 1869)

**Definition of Mixed Farming:**
Mixed farming is an agricultural system where farmers cultivate crops and rear animals simultaneously. The chief characteristic is the integration of crop cultivation and livestock rearing, allowing for mutual benefits such as manure for crops and fodder for animals.

**Key Distinctions:**
- **Mixed Farming:** Crops + Livestock.
- **Mixed Cropping:** Two or more crops grown in the same field (often in rows or mixed).
- **Shifting Cultivation (Jhum):** Slash-and-burn agriculture. Typically, cash crops are *not* grown in traditional jhuming; it is primarily for subsistence food crops.

**Definition of Infant Mortality Rate (IMR):**
IMR is defined as the ratio of the number of deaths of children under **1 year** of age to the number of live births in a given year.

**Formula:**
$$ IMR = \frac{\text{Number of infant deaths (under 1 year)}}{\text{Number of live births}} \times 1000 $$

**Common Misconceptions:**
- It is not based on children under 3 or 6 months.
- The denominator is live births, not the total population of children under 5.

3. **High Latitudes:** Arctic and sub-Arctic regions.

- Eastern Asia (e.g., China, India, Japan) due to favorable climate, fertile land, and historical agricultural development.
- North-Eastern America (e.g., USA, Canada) has moderate to high density in urban corridors, but vast low-density areas. However, in the context of global comparisons, Equatorial forests and Deserts are the primary examples of *very* low density.

content:
### Evidence for Permanency of Ocean Basins

The hypothesis that ocean basins and continents are permanent (or have distinct, stable boundaries) is supported by:
1. **Sediment Distribution**: Absence of normal sedimentary rocks on oceanic islands (which are often volcanic) compared to continental margins.
2. **Ocean Basin Cross-Section**: The distinct structure comprising broad abyssal plains flanked by rim-like continental shelves.
3. **Sediment Types**: Shallow-water sands and muds are limited to the continental shelf and slope, while pelagic oozes are limited to the abyssal plain. This distinct separation supports the idea of stable, distinct oceanic and continental environments.

In the Northern Hemisphere, they blow from the Northeast (NE Trade Winds), and in the Southern Hemisphere, from the Southeast (SE Trade Winds). They are **beneficial for agriculture** as they can melt snow and raise temperatures, but they are **dry** and do **not** bring lots of rain. In fact, they can cause drought conditions.

content: The riverbank is weakest where the river turns (meanders) because the water **flows faster on the outer bank** due to centrifugal force. This higher velocity causes greater **erosion** on the outer bank, while deposition occurs on the inner bank. The water does not 'bounce off' or get 'concentrated' in a way that makes the inner bank denser; rather, the dynamic pressure and velocity on the outer bank cause undercutting and erosion.

- **Common Misconception**: Some think the line is based on the Earth's tilt; it is not.
- **Key Fact**: The line passes mainly through the Pacific Ocean, avoiding heavily populated areas.

  - **Gravitational Force:** Variations in gravity help determine density distribution.
  - **Earth Magnetism:** Helps understand the composition of the core (liquid outer core, solid inner core).
- **Note:** In many standard geography contexts, **Volcanoes** are considered the primary *direct* source, while earthquake waves are the primary *indirect* source. However, some curricula classify seismic data as a direct probe of the interior structure. If it allows multiple, it depends on the specific syllabus definition. However, looking at the options provided in the source text (a) 1 and 2, (b) Only 2, (c) 3 and 4, (d) All of these. Standard answer for 'Direct source' is typically **Volcanoes** (and drilling). Seismic waves are indirect. **Atacama Desert Characteristics:**
- The Atacama Desert in South America is considered the driest non-polar desert in the world.
- **Cause of Aridity:** Its extreme aridity is primarily due to its geographical location between two major mountain chains (the Andes to the east and the coastal range to the west).
- **Moisture Barrier:** These mountain ranges are of sufficient height to act as barriers, preventing moisture advection (transport of water vapor) from both the Pacific Ocean (west) and the Atlantic Ocean (east) from reaching the desert interior.

**Definition of Seismic Gaps:**
- Seismic gaps are sections of plate boundaries that have **not** ruptured in the recent past.
- They are identified as areas where stress is accumulating because they have not experienced significant earthquake activity compared to adjacent segments that have ruptured repeatedly.
- They are not defined by the frequency of tsunamis or the absence of volcanic activity, but specifically by the lack of recent seismic rupture.

**Impact of Cold Labrador Current:**
- The Cold Labrador Current flows southward along the coast of Canada and the USA.
- It plays a crucial role in the formation of the **North-West Atlantic fishing grounds** (specifically the Grand Banks of Newfoundland) by mixing with the warm Gulf Stream, causing upwelling of nutrients.
- **Hypothetical Scenario:** In the absence of the Cold Labrador Current, the North-West Atlantic fishing grounds would not exist in their current form due to the lack of nutrient-rich mixing.
- Note: The North-East Atlantic fishing grounds are primarily influenced by the North Atlantic Drift and the Canary Current, not the Labrador Current.

4. **Agulhas Current:** Flows along the coast of **Mozambique and Madagascar** (Africa). It is a warm current.

topic: Upper, Middle and Lower Ganga Plains
content:
# Ganga Plain

- **Upper Ganga Plain**: Located in the Himalayan foothills, characterized by steep slopes and high rainfall.
- **Middle Ganga Plain**: Extends from the foothills to the plains of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh; features fertile alluvium and a network of rivers.
- **Lower Ganga Plain**: Covers parts of Bihar and all of West Bengal. It is formed by sediment deposited by the Tista, Jaldhaka, and Torsa rivers.
- The Lower Ganga Plain contains the largest delta in the world, covering about two‑thirds of the plain.
- The delta is largely covered by the Sunderbans tidal forests, which are dense mangrove ecosystems.
- The plain is marked by a drawn and barren landscape, with old alluvium between the Kosi‑Mahananda corridor (west) and the Sankosh river (east).

subject: Geography
content:
# Brahmaputra Plain

- The western boundary of the Brahmaputra Plain is formed by the Indo‑Bangladesh border and the boundary of the Lower Ganga Plain.
- The Brahmaputra River enters the plain near Sadiya, flows eastward, and turns southward near Dhubri before entering Bangladesh.
- The plain contains large marshy tracts and numerous ox‑bow lakes.
- Southern tributaries of the Brahmaputra have meandering courses, creating fertile floodplains.
- The region is rich in biodiversity, with many wetlands and wetlands ecosystems.

subject: Geography
content:
# Peninsular Plateau

- The plateau is a tableland composed mainly of **Archean gneisses and schists**.
- It was formed by the breaking and drifting of the Gondwana landmass, making it part of the oldest continental crust.
- The plateau is surrounded on three sides by water, giving it a peninsular character.
- The Narmada River, which flows into a rift valley, divides the plateau into the Central Highlands (north) and the Deccan Plateau (south).

content:
### Climate Zones of India

**1. Northern Zone (Sub-tropical)**
- Characterized by distinct cold winter seasons and hot summer seasons.
- The mid-day Sun is **never** vertically overhead during any part of the year.

**2. Southern Zone (Tropical)**
- Warmer than the Northern zone.
- Does **not** have a clear-cut winter season.
- The mid-day Sun is almost vertically overhead at least **twice every year**.

### Factors Influencing India's Climate
1. **Location and Latitude**: The Tropic of Cancer divides India into tropical (South) and sub-tropical (North) climatic regions.
2. **Indian Ocean**: Significantly influences the climate of the peninsular region.
3. **Himalayan Range**:
   - Acts as a barrier against bitterly cold and dry winds from Central Asia.
   - Acts as a barrier in bringing monsoonal rainfall (trapping moisture).
4. **Thermal Factors**:
   - **Summer**: Heating of the interior part attracts monsoon winds, causing rainfall.
   - **Winter**: Western disturbances cause snowfall in the mountains and rainfall in the plains.

- **Formation conditions:** Formed under well‑drained conditions; high texture; contain low soluble salts.

subject: Geography
content:
### Laterite Soil
- **Occurrence:** Peculiar to India and other tropical countries with high temperature and heavy rainfall alternating with dry periods.
- **Process of formation:** During rainfall, silica is leached downwards; iron and aluminium oxides accumulate in the top layers.
- **Acidity:** More acidic in hilly areas than in low‑lying areas.
- **Fertility:** Less fertile; poor in humus, nitrogen, phosphate and calcium.
- **Distribution in India:**
  - Odisha
  - West Bengal
  - Parts of Andhra Pradesh
  - Tamil Nadu
  - Kerala

  - Maharashtra

content:
### Desert Soil
- **Location in India:** North‑Western part – major parts of Rajasthan, southern Haryana and Punjab, and northern Gujarat.
- **Parent material:** Mostly derived from alluvium.
- **Physical characteristics:**
  - Colour: Pale brown → brown → yellow‑brown.
  - Texture: Fine sandy to loamy fine sand; structureless.
  - Clay content: Low.
  - Presence of alkaline earth carbonates.
- **Improvement measures:** Water‑holding capacity and productivity can be increased by adding organic matter and clay.

content:

- **Formation cause:** Accumulation of soluble salts, primarily chlorides (text truncated; other common salts include sulfates and carbonates).
- **Typical features:** High electrical conductivity, poor structure, and reduced plant growth due to osmotic stress.
- **Management hint:** Leaching with good quality water and proper drainage are essential to reclaim saline soils.

India’s mineral belt is divided into five major belts:

- **North‑Eastern Peninsular Belt** – Chota Nagpur plateau, Odisha plateau, West Bengal; richest in coal and iron.
- **Central Belt** – Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra; deposits of manganese, bauxite, limestone, marble, coal, gems, mica, iron.
- **Southern Belt** – Karnataka plateau extending to Tamil Nadu upland; rich in ferrous minerals and bauxite, lacking coal.
- **South‑Western Belt** – Southern Karnataka, Kerala, Goa; deposits of iron‑ore, garnet, China clay, monazite sand.
- **North‑Western Belt** – along the Aravalis in Rajasthan and adjoining Gujarat; rich in non‑ferrous minerals (copper, lead, zinc), uranium, mica, precious stones.

subject: General Studies
content: A **disaster** is a result of natural or man‑made causes that leads to a sudden disruption of normal life, causing severe damage to life and property to an extent that the available social and economic protection mechanisms are inadequate to cope.

subject: General Studies
content:
**Disaster Management** is the managerial function which deals with creating the framework within which communities can reduce vulnerability to hazards and cope with disasters. It involves four phases:
1. **Mitigation** – measures to reduce the impact of a disaster.
2. **Preparedness** – planning, training, and capacity building before a disaster occurs.
3. **Response** – immediate actions taken during and after a disaster to save lives and protect property.
4. **Recovery** – restoring normalcy and rebuilding after the disaster.

subject: General Studies
content:
Disasters can be broadly classified into:
- **Natural Disasters** – caused by natural processes (e.g., floods, earthquakes, cyclones).
- **Man‑made Disasters** – caused by human activities (e.g., industrial accidents, nuclear incidents).

subject: General Studies
content:
Based on the nature of the hazard, disasters are grouped into five generic categories:
1. **Water and Climate** – floods, droughts, cyclones, storms.
2. **Geological** – earthquakes, landslides, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis.
3. **Biological** – epidemics, pandemics, pest infestations.
4. **Accidental and Chemical** – industrial spills, chemical leaks.
5. **Industrial and Nuclear** – nuclear accidents, radiological releases.

subject: General Studies

- Floods

### Tsunami: Definition and Causes

*   **Etymology**: The word 'Tsunami' is Japanese, meaning 'Harbor waves'.
*   **Definition**: Tsunamis, also known as seismic sea waves, are high vertical waves caused by the abrupt movement of the sea-floor due to earthquakes or volcanic eruptions, resulting in the sudden displacement of ocean water.
*   **Causes**: Various phenomena have the potential to generate a tsunami, including:
    *   Earthquakes
    *   Volcanic eruptions
    *   Underwater explosions (including underwater nuclear detonations)
    *   Landslides
    *   Glacier calvings
    *   Meteorite impacts
    *   Other disturbances above or below water

### Landslides: Definition

*   **Definition**: Landslides include all varieties of mass movements of hill slopes. They are defined as the downward and outward movement of slope-forming materials (rocks, soils, artificial fills, or combinations) along a surface of separation.
*   **Modes of Movement**: Falling, sliding, and flowing.
*   **Speed**: Can occur either slowly or quickly.

    3.  Western Ghats
    4.  Nilgiris

    6.  Vindhyas
*   **Coverage**: These regions cover approximately **15% of India's landmass**.
*   **Regional Characteristics**:
    *   **Himalayas**: Account for landslides of every fame, name, and description (big/small, quick/creeping, ancient/new).
    *   **North-Eastern Region**: Badly affected by landslide problems of a bewildering variety.
    *   **Specific Threat**: A different variety of landslides characterized by a **lateritic cap** poses a constant threat (specifically in regions like the Western Ghats/Nilgiris, though the text cuts off, the lateritic cap is a key identifier for these specific landslides).

- **Himalayas**: Tertiary **Fold Mountains**.

- *Incorrect Match in Question*: The question asks for the incorrectly matched pair. In standard geography, Western Ghats are often associated with volcanic activity or specific folding, but **Aravalli** is definitely Pre-Cambrian. **Himalayas** are Tertiary Fold. **Deccan** is Volcanic. The 'incorrect' match in the source question context is likely **(c) Western Ghat: Palaeozoic fold Mountains** if the exam considers them differently, or potentially **(b)** if Deccan is considered purely volcanic plateau. However, based on standard NDA/CDS keys for this specific question, **(c)** is often the intended 'incorrect' or tricky one, but let's look at the options. Actually, **Western Ghats** are not typically called 'Palaeozoic fold mountains' in the same way Aravallis are 'Pre-Cambrian'. They are often considered a faulted block or folded. Let's stick to the facts: Aravalli = Pre-Cambrian. Himalayas = Tertiary Fold. Deccan = Volcanic. Western Ghats = Folded (but age varies). The question asks for the *incorrectly* matched. Usually, **Western Ghats** are not classified simply as 'Palaeozoic fold' in basic texts compared to the others. *Self-Correction*: In many competitive exams, the answer key for this specific question identifies **(c)** as the incorrect match because Western Ghats are often associated with volcanic activity or are considered a different structural type, or the age classification is disputed. However, **Aravalli** is the definitive Pre-Cambrian relict. **Himalayas** are Tertiary. **Deccan** is Volcanic. Therefore, **(c)** is the outlier.

subject: Geography
content:
- **Altitude of Coniferous Forests**: The belt of coniferous forests in the Sikkim and Assam Himalayas is found at a **higher altitude** compared to the Kashmir Himalayas.
- **Reasons**:
    1. Sikkim and Assam Himalayas are at **lower latitudes** (closer to the equator), meaning temperatures are generally higher at the same altitude compared to Kashmir.
    2. They have **higher temperatures at lower heights**, pushing the cold-adapted coniferous zone to higher elevations.
    3. They get **lesser snowfall at lower heights** compared to the western Himalayas (Kashmir), which also influences the vegetation zone distribution.
    - *Correct Combination*: 1, 2, and 3.

Water scarcity is the most critical constraint for increasing agricultural output.

subject: Geography
content:
The Trans-Himalayas (also known as Tibet Himalaya) are located north of the Great Himalayan range. Key facts:
1. They are geographically distinct from the main Himalayan range but are often grouped under the broader Himalayan system in some contexts, though technically they are not part of the core Himalayas.
2. They act as a watershed, separating the Indus river system (flowing north) from the Ganga-Brahmaputra system (flowing south).
3. Major ranges include Karakoram, Ladakh, and Zanskar.

subject: Geography
content:
The Himalayas are divided into four sections from west to east:
1. Punjab Himalayas (Kashmir to Sutlej)
2. Kumaon Himalayas (Sutlej to Kali)
3. Nepal Himalayas (Kali to Teesta)
4. Assam Himalayas (Teesta to Brahmaputra)

**Nanda Devi** is the highest peak in the **Kumaon Himalayas**.

subject: Geography
content: Most major mountain ranges in India span multiple states. However, the **Ajanta** hills (part of the Satpura range in Maharashtra) are often cited in competitive exams as being confined to a single state (Maharashtra) compared to ranges like Aravalli (Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana, Delhi), Satpura (MP, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh), and Sahyadri (Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka).

subject: Geography
content: Coffee is primarily grown in the Western Ghats (Sahyadris) and Eastern Ghats. **Chikmagalur** in Karnataka is one of the most famous districts for coffee cultivation in India. Other major coffee-growing regions include Coorg (Karnataka), Wayanad (Kerala), and parts of Tamil Nadu.

subject: Geography
content:
Key agricultural facts:
1. **Pulses**: Approximately 90% of the area under pulses in India is rainfed. The share of pulses in the gross cropped area has not doubled in the last two decades.
2. **Rice**: India accounts for a significant portion of global rice production, but the specific claim of 15% of total area is often debated; however, rice occupies a large share of India's gross cropped area (historically around 30-35%, but the option stating 34% is often considered incorrect in favor of the rainfed pulse fact in this specific question context). The most consistently correct statement in this set is that ~90% of pulse area is rainfed.

subject: Geography
content:
**Humus** is the organic component of soil, formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter. Key characteristics:
1. It is **not** a mineral; it is organic.
2. It helps retain moisture in the soil.
3. It aids plants in absorbing nutrients from the soil.
4. The presence of humus gives soil a dark color.

subject: History

subject: Geography

subject: Geography
content: Soil erosion can be prevented by **afforestation** (planting trees). Removing vegetation and overgrazing accelerate erosion. Increasing bird population is not a primary method for preventing soil erosion.

subject: Geography

The Ganga plains also have significant resources, but the North-Eastern region is typically cited as having the highest potential in specific contexts of precipitation and river flow per unit area.

subject: Geography
content: The main aim of the watershed management strategy in India is **soil conservation**. While it involves hillslope management and silviculture, the primary objective is to prevent soil erosion and conserve soil fertility.

subject: Geography
topic: Sun's Position and Tropic of Cancer
content: Cities located exactly on the **Tropic of Cancer** (23.5° N) experience the mid-day Sun exactly overhead only once a year (during the summer solstice). In India, **Nagpur** and **Kolkata** are located very close to or on the Tropic of Cancer. Delhi and Chennai are not on the Tropic of Cancer. Srinagar and Darjeeling are in the Himalayas. Hyderabad and Kohima are not on the Tropic of Cancer.

subject: Geography
content:
Key tribal groups and their predominant locations:

- **Dimasa**: Predominantly in **Assam**.
- **Konyak**: Predominantly in **Nagaland**.

subject: Geography
content: The **Krishna River** originates in the Western Ghats in **Maharashtra** (near Mahabaleshwar), flows through **Karnataka** and **Andhra Pradesh**, and meets the **Bay of Bengal** in Andhra Pradesh. The Godavari originates in Maharashtra but flows into the Bay of Bengal via Andhra Pradesh, but the Krishna is specifically known for its course through Karnataka and AP before reaching the coast. The Kaveri originates in Karnataka. The Mahanadi originates in Chhattisgarh.

subject: Geography
content: The **Karewas** of Kashmir are **Aeolian and glacial** deposits. They are flat, elevated tablelands formed by wind-blown silt (aeolian) and glacial activity. They are famous for saffron cultivation.

subject: Geography
topic: Winter High Pressure over North-Western India
content:
A feeble high‑pressure system over the north‑western part of India during mid‑winter results in:
- Outward flow of high and dry winds from the high‑pressure centre.
- A noticeable drop in temperature over the Northern Plains.
- No occurrence of scorching **loo** winds (which are characteristic of summer) nor torrential thunderstorms, as high pressure suppresses convection and precipitation.

subject: Geography
content:
**Laterite Soils:**
- **Color:** Generally red in color due to high iron oxide content.
- **Nutrient Content:** Poor in nitrogen and potash. They are rich in iron and aluminum but leached of nutrients due to heavy rainfall.
- **Distribution:** Found in areas with high rainfall and high temperature, such as the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, and parts of Northeast India. They are **not** well developed in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh (which are arid/semi-arid or alluvial).
- **Agriculture:** Suitable for cashew nuts, tea, coffee, and tapioca (cassava). Rice and wheat are not typically grown in pure laterite soils without significant amendment.

subject: Geography
content:
## Environment
- **Literal meaning**: The surrounding and everything that affects an organism during its lifetime.
- **Comprehensive definition**: *Environment is the sum of the components of water, air and land; inter‑relationships among them and also with human beings, other living organisms and property.*
- It includes **all physical and biological surroundings** and their interactions.

subject: Geography
content:
### Abiotic Components
- Non‑living elements such as **land, water, air** and other physical factors.

### Biotic Components
- All **living forms**: plants, animals, decomposers, and other organisms.

subject: Geography
content:
1. **Natural Environment** – Consists of all abiotic (non‑living) and biotic (living) components that exist naturally on Earth.
2. **Man‑Made (Artificial) Environment** – Places created by human activities through planned manipulation, e.g., crop fields, urban centres, industrial set‑ups.
3. **Social Environment** – Encompasses cultural norms, values, and the network of political, economic, and religious institutions that influence how environmental resources are utilised.

subject: Geography
content:
## Ecology
- A scientific discipline that studies **organisms in relation to their environment**.
- Developed in response to growing awareness of the inter‑relationships among plants, animals, and their physical habitats.

subject: Geography
content:
### Definition
- The term **ecosystem** was first introduced by **A.G. Tansley (1935)**.
- Defined as *a particular category of physical system, consisting of organisms and inorganic components in a relatively stable equilibrium, open and of various sizes and kinds.*

### Key Characteristics
- **Biotic and abiotic components are inseparably inter‑related** and interact continuously.
- Ecosystems are **open systems** (exchange of energy and matter with surroundings).
- They exist in **relatively stable equilibrium** but are dynamic.
- Can vary widely in **size** – from a puddle to a forest, to the entire biosphere.

subject: Ecosystem
content:
# Food Chain

- **Definition**: A sequence of organisms where each organism feeds on the next, transferring energy from one to another.
- **Energy Source**: Typically originates from the Sun via photosynthesis.
- **Typical Flow**: *Grass → Insect → Frogs → Snake → Hawk*.
- **General Rule**: All food chains start with photosynthesis and end with decay, except in deep‑sea hydrothermal ecosystems.
- **Key Points**:
  - Represents a linear pathway of energy transfer.
  - Highlights the role of producers, consumers, and decomposers.

> **Note**: Food chains are simplified representations; real ecosystems involve complex interactions.

subject: Ecosystem
content:
# Food Web

- **Definition**: A network of interconnected food chains showing feeding relationships among species.
- **Purpose**: Illustrates how energy and nutrients flow through an ecological community.
- **Graphical Representation**: Depicts who eats whom, often using arrows to indicate direction of energy flow.
- **Key Insight**: Unlike a single food chain, a food web captures the complexity of multiple trophic interactions.

subject: Ecosystem
content:
# Trophic Levels

- **Primary Producers**: Green plants (first trophic level).
- **Herbivores**: Consume producers (second trophic level).
- **Primary Carnivores**: Consume herbivores (third trophic level).
- **Secondary/tertiary Carnivores**: Consume other carnivores (fourth trophic level and beyond).
- **Omnivores**: Can occupy multiple trophic levels.

> **Tip**: The number of trophic levels in a food web can vary, but most ecosystems have at least three.

subject: Ecosystem
content:
# Ecological Pyramids

- **Definition**: Graphical representations that show the number of organisms, energy, or biomass at each trophic level.
- **Named After**: Charles Elton (Eltonian pyramids).
- **Common Types**:
  - **Pyramid of Numbers**: Shows the number of individuals.
  - **Pyramid of Biomass**: Shows the total mass of living matter.
  - **Pyramid of Energy**: Shows the energy available at each level.
- **Interpretation**: A typical pyramid narrows as you move up trophic levels, indicating loss of energy/biomass.

subject: General Studies
content:
- **Definition**: The role and position a species has in its environment.
- **Scope**: Includes all interactions of the species with both biotic and abiotic factors of its environment.

subject: General Studies
content:
- **Definition**: A natural process by which different groups or communities colonize the same area over a period of time in a definite sequence.
- **Alternative Definition**: A series of stages, one after the other, by which a group of organisms living in a community reaches its final stable state or climax.

subject: General Studies
content:
- **Definition**: Introduction of contaminants or impurities into the natural environment.
- **Pollutants**: May be natural or foreign substances.
- **Impact**: Causes adverse changes in nature and affects life on Earth in the long term.

subject: General Studies
content: - **Definition**: The effect of undesirable changes in our surroundings that have harmful effects on plants, animals, and human beings.

subject: General Studies
content:
- **Definition**: Air pollutants emitted directly from a source.
- **Examples**:
  - Sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$)
  - Nitrogen oxides ($NO_x$)
  - Carbon monoxide ($CO$)
  - CFCs (Chlorofluorocarbons)
  - Carbon dioxide ($CO_2$)
  - Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM)

subject: General Studies
content:
- **Definition**: Pollutants not directly emitted, but formed when primary pollutants react in the atmosphere.
- **Examples**:
  - Particulate matter formed from gaseous primary pollutants.
  - Compounds in photochemical smog (e.g., Nitrogen dioxide).
  - Ground-level ozone ($O_3$): Formed from NO and Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs).
  - Peroxyacetyl Nitrate (PAN): Formed from $NO_2$ and VOCs.

subject: General Studies
content:
- **Definition**: Presence of contaminants released by human activities into the Earth's atmosphere having the potential to cause harm to property or the lives of plants, animals, or humans.
- **Causes/Sources**: Various types of pollutants, including emissions from petroleum refineries.

subject: Geography
content:
### Effects of Water Pollution
- **Human Health:** Polluted water is unsafe for drinking, recreation, agriculture, and industrial use. It poses a direct hazard to human health.
- **Aquatic Life:** Contamination destroys aquatic organisms and reduces their reproductive ability, leading to loss of biodiversity in water bodies.
- **Aesthetic Degradation:** Lakes and rivers lose their visual appeal, affecting tourism and local economies.
- **Economic Impact:** Reduced water quality hampers agricultural productivity, industrial processes, and fisheries.
- **Overall Impact:** The cumulative effect is a serious threat to ecosystems and human societies.

subject: Geography
content:
### Thermal Pollution
- **Definition:** Degradation of water quality caused by any process that changes the ambient temperature of water bodies.
- **Common Sources:** 
  - Use of water as a coolant in power plants and industrial manufacturing.
  - Discharge of heated storm‑water runoff.
- **Mechanism of Harm:** 
  - Hot water released into natural water bodies raises the temperature.
  - Elevated temperature reduces dissolved oxygen levels, stressing aquatic organisms.
  - Alters ecosystem composition, favoring heat‑tolerant species and disrupting food chains.
- **Broader Impact:** Considered a contributor to global warming because it releases excess heat into the environment.
- **Mitigation Measures:** Cooling towers, closed‑loop cooling systems, and proper thermal discharge regulations.

subject: Geography
content:
### Marine Pollution
- **Definition:** Introduction of chemicals, particles, or other harmful substances into the ocean, adversely affecting marine ecosystems.
- **Pathway into Food Chain:** Pollutants are taken up by plankton and benthos, moving up the trophic levels and potentially reaching humans.
- **International Framework:** The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) emphasizes protection and preservation of the marine environment.
- **Major Sources (as identified by UNCLOS):**
  1. **Land‑based and coastal activities** – runoff, sewage, industrial waste.
  2. **Continental shelf drilling** – oil and gas extraction.
  3. **Potential seabed mining** – disturbance of sediments.
  4. **Ocean dumping** – deliberate disposal of waste.
  5. **Vessel source pollution** – oil spills, ballast water discharge.
  6. **Atmospheric deposition** – pollutants carried by wind and rain.
- **Consequences:** Loss of marine biodiversity, degradation of fisheries, health risks to coastal populations, and economic losses in tourism and shipping.

subject: Biology
content:
### Genetic Diversity
- **Definition:** Variation found in the genes within a species. Each individual possesses a unique genetic composition.
- **Importance:**
  - Provides the raw material for evolution and adaptation.
  - Increases resilience of populations to environmental changes, diseases, and pests.
  - Enhances overall ecosystem stability.
- **Examples:** Different blood types in humans, varied coat colors in animals, resistance genes in crops.
- **Conservation Note:** Maintaining genetic diversity is crucial for the long‑term survival of species and for sustainable agriculture and forestry.

subject: General Science
content:
Conservation of biodiversity is crucial for:
1. Preventing the loss of genetic diversity of a species.
2. Saving species from becoming extinct.
3. Protecting ecosystems from damage and degradation.

subject: General Science
content:
Conservation efforts are grouped into two main categories:

1. **In situ (on-site) conservation**: Protection of plants and animals within their natural habitats or in protected areas. Protected areas are land or sea dedicated to protecting and maintaining biodiversity.
2. **Ex-situ (off-site) conservation**: Conservation of plants and animals outside their natural habitat. Methods include:
   - Botanical gardens
   - Gene banks of seeds
   - Tissue culture
   - Cryopreservation

subject: General Science
content: The Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF) is a global programme that provides funding and technical assistance to non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and private sector partners. Its primary focus is on protecting critical ecosystems, specifically targeting **biodiversity hot-spots**.

subject: General Science
content:
The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) is an international legally binding treaty. It has three main goals:
1. Conservation of biodiversity.
2. Sustainable use of its components.
3. Fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources.

subject: General Science
content: Adopted on **29th January, 2000**, by the Conference of the Parties (CoP) to the CBD. It is a supplementary agreement to the CBD. The protocol aims to protect biological diversity from the potential risks posed by **Living Modified Organisms (LMOs)** resulting from modern biotechnology.

subject: General Science
content: The Nagoya Protocol on Access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their utilisation is an international agreement supplementary to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
