subject: Mathematics
text:
Properties of Determinants:

  • (i) If each entry in any row or column of a determinant is 0, then the value of the determinant is zero.
  • (ii) If rows be changed into columns and columns into rows, then the value of the determinant remains unchanged.
  • (iii) If any two adjacent rows (columns) of a determinant are interchanged, then the determinant remains its absolute value but changed in sign.
  • (iv) If a determinant have any two rows or columns identical, then its value is zero.
  • (v) If all the constituents (elements) of one row or of one column, multiplied by the same quantity, then the value of new determinant is k times the value of original determinant.
  • (vi) If each constituent of any row or of any column be the sum of the two quantities, then the determinant can be expressed as the sum of the two determinants of the same order.
  • (vii) If each element of a row or column of a determinant is multiplied by a constant k and then added to the corresponding elements of some other row or column, then value of determinant remains same.
  • (viii) Number of elements in nth order determinant = n^2
  • (ix) If A and B are two determinants of order n, then |AB| = |A||B|
  • (x) det(kA) = k^n det(A), if A is of order n x n.
  • (xi) If AB = AC, then B = C is true only, when |A| != 0.
image_descriptions: Mathematical representation of determinant properties (i) through (vii) showing matrix transformations.

details.summary: Comprehensive list of 11 fundamental properties of determinants used in matrix algebra.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Minors and Cofactors:

Minor of an Element of a Determinant: If we delete the row and column passing through the element a_ij, the determinant, thus obtained is called the minor of a_ij and is usually denoted by M_ij.

Cofactor of an Element of a Determinant: The cofactor of an element a_ij is (-1)^(i+j) M_ij and it is denoted by C_ij. Thus, C_ij = M_ij when i+j is even, and -M_ij when i+j is odd.

topic: Relation between a determinant and its cofactor determinant
content:
### Cofactor Determinant Relation

- Let \(\Delta\) be the determinant of an \(n	imes n\) matrix \(A\).
- Let \(\Delta_c\) denote the determinant of the **cofactor matrix** of \(A\).
- **Result:**
  1. If \(\Delta 
eq 0\), then
     $$ rac{\Delta}{\Delta_c}=(-1)^{n}$$
  2. If \(\Delta = 0\), then \(\Delta_c = 0\).
- **Zero‑sum property:** The sum of the products of the elements of any row (or column) with the cofactors of the elements of any *other* row (or column) is zero, i.e.
  $$\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}C_{kj}=0 \quad (i
eq k)$$
  where \(C_{kj}\) is the cofactor of element \(a_{kj}\).

---

### Example
For the matrix
$$A= egin{bmatrix} a & b \ b & a \end{bmatrix}$$
its determinant is \(\Delta = a^{2}-b^{2}\).
The cofactor matrix is
$$C =  egin{bmatrix} a & -b \ -b & a \end{bmatrix}$$
and \(\Delta_c = \det(C)= a^{2}-b^{2}=\Delta\).  Hence \( rac{\Delta}{\Delta_c}=1 = (-1)^{2}\).

### Adjoint (Adjugate) Matrix

- For a square matrix \(A = [a_{ij}]\) of order \(n\), let \(C = [C_{ij}]\) be its **cofactor matrix**, where \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\) and \(M_{ij}\) is the minor of \(a_{ij}\).
- The **adjoint** (also called **adjugate**) of \(A\) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix:
  $$\operatorname{adj}(A)=C^{T}$$
- **Computation example**
  $$A =  egin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 4 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
  The cofactors are:
  \[ egin{aligned}
  C_{11}= -3,\; &C_{12}= 6,\; &C_{13}= -3,\
  C_{21}= 5,\; &C_{22}= -10,\; &C_{23}= 5,\
  C_{31}= 2,\; &C_{32}= -4,\; &C_{33}= 2.
  \end{aligned}\]
  Hence
  $$C =  egin{bmatrix} -3 & 6 & -3 \ 5 & -10 & 5 \ 2 & -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix},\qquad
  \operatorname{adj}

If A and B are invertible matrices of the same order, then:

  • (i) (A^-1)^-1 = A
  • (ii) (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1
  • (iii) (A^k)^-1 = (A^-1)^k, k ∈ N
  • (iv) adj(A^-1) = (adj A)^-1
  • (v) |A^-1| = 1/|A| = |A|^-1

Note: If A is an invertible matrix, then:

  • If A is symmetric matrix, then A^-1 is also symmetric matrix.
  • If A is skew-symmetric matrix, then A^-1 is also skew symmetric matrix.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Solution of System of Linear Equations
text:
Consider the system of linear equations:

a11x1 + a12x2 + a13x3 = b1

a21x1 + a22x2 + a23x3 = b2

a31x1 + a32x2 + a33x3 = b3

We can write these equations in matrix form as AX = B. Where A is the coefficient matrix, X is the variable matrix, and B is the constant matrix. Then, X = A^-1 B. This method is known as the matrix method.

Criterion of Consistency:

  • (i) If |A| ≠ 0 (non-singular), the system is consistent and has a unique solution X = A^-1 B.
  • (ii) If |A| = 0 (singular) and [adj(A)]B = 0, the system is consistent and has infinitely many solutions.
  • (iii) If |A| = 0 and [adj(A)]B ≠ 0, the system is inconsistent and has no solution.

Homogeneous Equations (AX = 0):

  • (i) If |A| ≠ 0, only trivial solution X = 0.
  • (ii) If |A| = 0, non-trivial solution exists (infinitely many).

details.summary: Methods for solving linear equations using matrices and criteria for consistency.

text:
For a system of equations in two variables:

a1x + b1y = c1

a2x + b2y = c2

Then, Δ = |a1 b1; a2 b2|, Δ1 = |c1 b1; c2 b2|, and Δ2 = |a1 c1; a2 c2|. The solution is x = Δ1/Δ, y = Δ2/Δ, provided Δ ≠ 0.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Cramer's Rule and System of Equations
text:
Cramer's Rule for three variables:

For a system of equations:

  • a1x + b1y + c1z = d1
  • a2x + b2y + c2z = d2
  • a3x + b3y + c3z = d3

The solution is given by x = Δ1/Δ, y = Δ2/Δ, and z = Δ3/Δ.

Consistency Conditions:

  • If Δ ≠ 0, the system is consistent and has a unique solution.
  • If Δ = 0 and at least one of Δ1, Δ2, Δ3 is non-zero, the system is inconsistent.
  • If Δ = 0 and Δ1 = Δ2 = Δ3 = 0, the system is consistent and dependent with infinitely many solutions.

Δ = |a1 b1 c1; a2 b2 c2; a3 b3 c3|
Δ1 = |d1 b1 c1; d2 b2 c2; d3 b3 c3|
Δ2 = |a1 d1 c1; a2 d2 c2; a3 d3 c3|
Δ3 = |a1 b1 d1; a2 b2 d2; a3 b3 d3|

Applications of Determinant in Geometry

  • Area of triangle: If (x1, y1), (x2, y2) and (x3, y3) are the vertices of a triangle, then Area of triangle = 1/2 |[x1, y1, 1; x2, y2, 1; x3, y3, 1]| = 1/2 |x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|
  • Condition of collinearity of three points: Let three points be A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2) and C(x3, y3), then these points will be collinear, if Area of ΔABC = 0
  • Equation of straight line passing through two points: Let two points be A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2) and P(x, y) be a point on the line joining points A and B, then the equation of line is given by |[x, y, 1; x1, y1, 1; x2, y2, 1]| = 0

chapter: Measurement of Angles and Trigonometric Ratios
text:
Angle: Let a revolving line starting from OA revolves about its end point 'O' on a plane in clockwise or anti-clockwise direction and occupy the position 'OB'. It is said to trace out ∠AOB. Here, OB is called the terminal side and OA is called initial side. The fixed point 'O' is called the vertex.

Measurement of Angles: The amount of rotation from the initial side to the terminal side is called the measure of the angle.

Note: If the rotation is in anti-clockwise sense, the angle measured is positive and if the rotation is in clockwise sense, the angle measured is negative.

Systems of Measurement of Angles: There are three major types of systems of measurement of angles which are as follows:

  • Sexagesimal system (Degree measure): In this system a right angle is divided into 90 equal parts, called degrees. Each degree is divided into 60 equal parts, called minutes and each minute is further divided into 60 equal parts, called seconds.
  • Centesimal system: In this system a right angle is divided into 100 equal parts, called grades. Each grade is subdivided into 100 centesimal minutes and each minute is further divided into 100 centesimal seconds.
image_descriptions: A geometric diagram showing an angle formed by two rays OA and OB originating from a vertex O. OA is labeled as the 'Initial side', OB is labeled as the 'Terminal side', and the arc between them is labeled as theta (θ).

details.summary: Introduction to the definition of an angle, its components (initial side, terminal side, vertex), sign convention for rotation, and the first two systems of measurement (Sexagesimal and Centesimal).

subject: Mathematics
text:
Circular system: In this system the unit of measurement is radian.

  • One radian, written as 1c, is the measure of an angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc of length equal to the radius of the circle.
  • The number of radians in an angle subtended by an arc of a circle at the centre is equal to arc/radius.

Relation between Degrees, Grades and Radians:

Degree/90 = Grade/100 = 2 Radian/pi

  • To convert radians into degrees multiply by (180/pi).
  • To convert degrees into radians multiply by (pi/180).

details.summary: Covers circular system of angle measurement and conversion formulas between degrees, grades, and radians.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The ratios between different sides of a right angled triangle with respect to its acute angles are called trigonometric ratios.

Let PMR be a right angled triangle at M.

  • sin theta = Perpendicular/Hypotenuse = q/r
  • cos theta = Base/Hypotenuse = p/r
  • tan theta = Perpendicular/Base = q/p
  • cosec theta = Hypotenuse/Perpendicular = r/q
  • sec theta = Hypotenuse/Base = r/p
  • cot theta = Base/Perpendicular = p/q

Relation between Trigonometric Ratios:

  • sin theta = 1/cosec theta or cosec theta = 1/sin theta
  • cos theta = 1/sec theta or sec theta = 1/cos theta
  • cot theta = 1/tan theta or tan theta = 1/cot theta
  • tan theta = sin theta/cos theta
  • cot theta = cos theta/sin theta

Fundamental Trigonometric Identities:

  • sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1
  • 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta
  • 1 + cot^2 theta = cosec^2 theta
image_descriptions: A right-angled triangle PMR with the right angle at M. The side opposite to angle theta is q (Perpendicular), the side adjacent to angle theta is p (Base), and the hypotenuse is r.

Solutions or Roots of a Trigonometric Equation:

A value of the unknown angle which satisfies the given equation is called a solution or root of the equation.

  • Principal solution: The least value of unknown angle which satisfies the given equation.
  • General solution: The solution consisting of all possible solutions of a trigonometric equation.

Note: A function f(x) is said to be a periodic function, if a least positive real number T is such that f(x + T) = f(x), then T is known as period of function f(x).

Maximum and Minimum Values of (a sin θ ± b cos θ):

The maximum and minimum values are respectively, sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and -sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

Trigonometric Equation:

An equation involving one or more trigonometric ratios of unknown angles is called a trigonometric equation. e.g., 2cos θ + 3cos 2θ = 0, cos^2 θ + sin θ = 1/3 etc.

text:
Inverse Function: If f: X → Y is a function which is both one-one and onto, then its inverse function f-1: Y → X is defined as y = f(x) ⇔ f-1(y) = x, ∀ x ∈ X, ∀ y ∈ Y.

Inverse Trigonometric Functions: Trigonometric functions are not one-one and onto on their natural domains and ranges, so in order to make them one-one and onto, we restrict their domain and codomain. And thus we obtain inverses of trigonometric functions. Inverse of f is denoted by f-1. Let y = f(x) = sin x be a function. Then, its inverse is x = sin-1 y.
formulas: y = f(x) = sin x => x = sin^-1 y
image_descriptions: A simple flow diagram showing the transformation: sin x --(Inverse)--> sin^-1 x.

text:
Properties of Inverse Trigonometric Functions:

  • (i) (a) sin-1(sin θ) = θ and sin(sin-1 x) = x, -π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, -1 ≤ x ≤ 1
  • (b) cos-1(cos θ) = θ and cos(cos-1 x) = x, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, -1 ≤ x ≤ 1
  • (c) tan-1(tan θ) = θ and tan(tan-1 x) = x, -π/2 < θ < π/2, x ∈ R
  • (d) cot-1(cot θ) = θ and cot(cot-1 x) = x, 0 < θ < π, x ∈ R
  • (e) sec-1(sec θ) = θ and sec(sec-1 x) = x
  • (f) cosec-1(cosec θ) = θ and cosec(cosec-1 x) = x
  • (ii) (a) sin-1 x = cosec-1(1/x) or cosec-1 x = sin-1(1/x)
  • (b) cos-1 x = sec-1(1/x) or sec-1 x = cos-1(1/x)
  • (c) tan-1 x = cot-1(1/x) or cot-1 x = tan-1(1/x), if x > 0
  • (d) tan-1 x = cot-1(1/x) - π or cot-1 x = tan-1(1/x) - π, if x < 0
  • (iii) (a) sin-1(-x) = -sin-1(x)
  • (b) cos-1(-x) = π - cos-1(x)
  • (c) tan-1(-x) = -tan-1(x)
  • (d) cot-1(-x) = π - cot-1(x)
  • (e) sec-1(-x) = π - sec-1(x)
  • (f) cosec-1(-x) = -cosec-1(x)
  • (iv) (a) 2sin-1 x = sin-1 2x√(1-x2) = cos-1(1-2x2)
  • (b) 2cos-1 x = cos-1(2x2-1) = sin-1(2x√(1-x2))
  • (c) 2tan-1 x = tan-1(2x/(1-x2)) = sin-1(2x/(1+x2)) = cos-1((1-x2)/(1+x2))
  • (d) 3sin-1 x = sin-1(3x - 4x3)
  • (e) 3cos-1 x = cos-1(4x3 - 3x)
  • (f) 3tan-1 x = tan-1((3x - x3)/(1 - 3x2))
  • (v) (a) sin-1 x + cos-1 x = π/2, (-1 ≤ x ≤ 1)
  • (b) tan-1 x + cot-1 x = π/2, x ∈ R
  • (c) sec-1 x + cosec-1 x = π/2, x ≤ -1 or x ≥ 1
  • (vi) (a) tan-1 x + tan-1 y = tan-1((x+y)/(1-xy)), if xy < 1
  • (b) tan-1 x + tan-1 y = π + tan-1((x+y)/(1-xy)), if xy > 1
  • (c) tan-1 x - tan-1 y = tan-1((x-y)/(1+xy)), if x > 0, y > 0
  • (vii) (a) sin-1 x ± sin-1 y = sin-1{x√(1-y2) ± y√(1-x2)}
  • (b) cos-1 x ± cos-1 y = cos-1{xy ∓ √(1-x2)√(1-y2)}
  • (viii) (a) sin-1 x = cos-1(√(1-x2)) = tan-1(x/√(1-x2)) = cot-1(√(1-x2)/x) = sec-1(1/√(1-x2)) = cosec-1(1/x)

details.summary: Comprehensive list of properties and identities for inverse trigonometric functions.

Height and distance is one of the most important applications of trigonometry which helps us to find the height of any object and distance of objects between points which are not directly measurable.

Line of Sight

When the eye of a person at a point O looks at an object P, then the line OP is called the line of sight.

Angle of Elevation

Let P be an object and OX be a horizontal line, an observer at O to perceive the object P has to elevate his eye from direction OX to the direction OP. As such, we define angle XOP as the angle at elevation of P at O.

mcq.question: The angle of elevation of a ladder leaning against a wall is 60° and the foot of the ladder is 4.6 m away from the wall. The length of the ladder is
mcq.explanation: Let AB be the wall and BC be the ladder. Then, angle ACB = 60° and AC = 4.6 m. In triangle ACB, cos 60° = AC/BC => 1/2 = 4.6/BC => BC = (4.6 * 2) m = 9.2 m.

Let P be an object and OX be a horizontal line, an observer at O to perceive the object P has to depress his eye from the direction OX to direction OP. As such, we define ∠XOP as the angle of depression of P at O.

text:
A triangle has six components: three sides and three angles. The angles of a triangle ABC are denoted by A, B, and C, and the sides opposite to these angles are denoted by a, b, and c respectively (a = BC, b = CA, c = AB).

  • Semi-perimeter (s): s = (a + b + c) / 2
  • Area: Denoted by Δ
  • Sum of angles: A + B + C = 180°

Sine Rule: In any triangle ABC, sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c. The sines of the angles are proportional to the lengths of the opposite sides.

Let a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C = K. Then, a = K sin A, b = K sin B, c = K sin C, or sin A = a/K, sin B = b/K, sin C = c/K.
formulas: sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c
a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C = K
a = K sin A, b = K sin B, c = K sin C

Circumradius of triangle is given by:
formulas: R = a / (2 sin A) = b / (2 sin B) = c / (2 sin C) = abc / (4 * delta)

subject: Mathematics
text:
The circle which can be inscribed within the triangle so as to touch each of its sides is called its inscribed circle or incircle and its centre is called incentre and its radius is called inradius (r).

In any triangle ABC:

  • r = delta / s
  • r = (s - a) tan(A/2) = (s - b) tan(B/2) = (s - c) tan(C/2)
  • r = 4R sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2)
  • r = (a sin(B/2) sin(C/2)) / cos(A/2) = (b sin(A/2) sin(C/2)) / cos(B/2) = (c sin(B/2) sin(A/2)) / cos(C/2)

subject: Mathematics
text:
The circle which touches the sides BC and two sides AB and AC produced of a triangle ABC, is called the escribed circle opposite to the angle A. Its radius is denoted by r1. Similarly, r2 and r3 denote the radii of the escribed circles opposite to the angles B and C, respectively. The centres of the escribed circles are called excentres.

In any triangle ABC:

  • r1 = delta / (s - a) = s tan(A/2) = 4R sin(A/2) cos(B/2) cos(C/2)
  • r2 = delta / (s - b) = s tan(B/2) = 4R sin(B/2) cos(C/2) cos(A/2)
  • r3 = delta / (s - c) = s tan(C/2) = 4R sin(C/2) cos(A/2) cos(B/2)
  • r1 + r2 + r3 = 4R + r
  • r1*r2 + r2*r3 + r3*r1 = s^2 = (r1*r2*r3) / r
  • r1 = (a cos(B/2) cos(C/2)) / cos(A/2)
  • r2 = (b cos(C/2) cos(A/2)) / cos(B/2)
  • r3 = (c cos(A/2) cos(B/2)) / cos(C/2)
  • 1/r1 + 1/r2 + 1/r3 = 1/r = s / delta
  • r1*r2*r3 = r^2 * (cot(A/2) cot(B/2) cot(C/2))^2

A system in which points are defined as the ordered pair (x, y) is called the coordinate system. Here, x and y are called abscissa and ordinate, respectively.

Cartesian Coordinates

In coordinate system, there are two mutually perpendicular straight lines XOX' and YOY', called X and Y-axes, respectively. These axes divide the coordinate plane into four parts called quadrants. OX and OX' are called positive and negative directions, respectively of X-axis and similarly OY and OY' are called positive and negative directions, respectively of Y-axis.

text:
The distance between any two points in the plane is the length of the line segment joining them.

Let P(x1, y1) and Q(x2, y2) be any two points in the XY-plane, then:

  • |PQ| = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)
  • or |PQ| = sqrt((Difference of abscissas)^2 + (Difference of ordinates)^2)

Note: Distance between the origin O(0, 0) and the point P(x, y) is OP = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).

details.summary: Definition and formula for calculating the distance between two points in a 2D plane, including the specific case of distance from the origin.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Collinear Points: Three points in alpha-y plane will be collinear, if sum of distances between two pairs of points is equal to third pair of points.

Three Points In A Plane: Any three non-collinear points always form a triangle. Given three points would form:

  • Isosceles triangle: If lengths of any two sides are equal.
  • Equilateral triangle: If lengths of all three sides are equal.
  • Right angled triangle: If sum of squares of lengths of two sides is equal to length of third side.

Four points in a plane: Any four non-collinear points form a quadrilateral. Given four points would form:

  • Square: If all four sides are equal and diagonals are also equal.
  • Rhombus: If all four sides are equal.
  • Rectangle: If opposite sides are equal and diagonals are equal.
  • Parallelogram: If opposite sides are equal.

Important Notes:

  • In a parallelogram, diagonals cut each other at mid-point.
  • In a rhombus, diagonals bisect each other at right angles.

details.summary: Covers geometric properties of points in a plane and section formulae for internal and external division.

Let A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2) and C(x3, y3) be the vertices of a triangle ABC, then:

Area of triangle ABC = 1/2 |x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|

Note: The three points A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2) and C(x3, y3) are collinear, if the area of triangle ABC is zero.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Incentre, Circumcentre, Orthocentre, and Excentre of a Triangle
text:
Incentre of a Triangle

If (x, y) is the incentre of the triangle ABC, where A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2), C(x3, y3) are coordinates and a, b, c are the sides of the triangle, then incentre = ((ax1 + bx2 + cx3)/(a + b + c), (ay1 + by2 + cy3)/(a + b + c))

Circumcentre of a Triangle

If P(x, y) is the circumcentre of triangle ABC, then PA = PB = PC. Note: The circumcentre of a right angled triangle is the mid-point of its hypotenuse.

Orthocentre of a Triangle

The coordinates of the orthocentre are given by ((x1 tan A + x2 tan B + x3 tan C)/(tan A + tan B + tan C), (y1 tan A + y2 tan B + y3 tan C)/(tan A + tan B + tan C))

Some Important Points

  • (i) Orthocentre of the right angled triangle ABC, right angled at A, is A.
  • (ii) Orthocentre of a triangle will lie inside, if triangle is acute and in case of obtuse triangle, orthocentre will lie outside.
  • (iii) In a triangle ABC, the circumcentre S, centroid G and orthocentre O are collinear and SG : GO = 1 : 2.
  • (iv) In equilateral triangle, orthocentre, centroid, circumcentre and incentre coincide.

Excentre of a Triangle

There are three excentres in a triangle. The coordinates of I1 are given by ((-ax1 + bx2 + cx3)/(-a + b + c), (-ay1 + by2 + cy3)/(-a + b + c))
formulas: Incentre = ((ax1 + bx2 + cx3)/(a + b + c), (ay1 + by2 + cy3)/(a + b + c))

subject: Mathematics
text: The curve described by a point which moves under given condition or conditions is called its locus. The equation of the locus of a point is the relation which is satisfied by the coordinates of every point on the locus of the point.

details.summary: Definition of the locus of a point.

mcq.question: The sum of the squares of the distances of a moving point from two fixed points (p, 0) and (-p, 0) is equal to a constant quantity 2λ^2, find the equation of the locus.
mcq.explanation: Let P(h, k) be any position of the moving point and A(p, 0), B(-p, 0) be the given points. Then, PA^2 + PB^2 = 2λ^2. Substituting coordinates: (h - p)^2 + (k - 0)^2 + (h + p)^2 + (k - 0)^2 = 2λ^2. Simplifying gives 2h^2 + 2k^2 + 2p^2 = 2λ^2, which leads to h^2 + k^2 = λ^2 - p^2. Hence, the locus is x^2 + y^2 = λ^2 - p^2.

subject: Mathematics
text: A straight line is the locus of all those points which are collinear with two given points. The equation of a straight line l is a linear relationship in x and y, i.e. it is a first degree polynomial equation in x and y. An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0, where a, b and c are constants, represents a straight line in general form.

details.summary: Definition and general form of a straight line.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Slope or Gradient of a Line
text:
The trigonometrical tangent of the angle α (α ≠ π/2) which a given line makes with the positive direction of X-axis, is called the slope or gradient of the line. It is generally denoted by m, i.e. m = tan α.

Slopes in Different Conditions

  • Slope of X-axis or a line parallel to X-axis is m = tan 0° = 0
  • Slope of Y-axis or a line parallel to Y-axis is m = tan(π/2) = ∞
  • The slope of the line joining the points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is obtained as m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) = Difference of ordinates / Difference of abscissas

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for calculating the slope of a line.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let θ be the angle between two lines of slopes m1 and m2, then tan θ = ± (m2 - m1) / (1 + m1m2).

  • Above lines are parallel, if m1 = m2
  • Above lines are perpendicular, if m1m2 = -1

Some Facts about General Equation of Line ax + by + c = 0

  • The slope of the line ax + by + c = 0 is m = -a/b = -(Coefficient of x) / (Coefficient of y)
  • Let two straight lines be given by a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0. Then, the lines are:
    • (a) coincident or identical, if a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2
    • (b) parallel, if their slopes are equal, i.e. m1 = m2 or -a1/b1 = -a2/b2 or a1/b1 = a2/b2
    • (c) perpendicular, if the product of their slopes is -1, i.e. m1m2 = -1 or (-a1/b1)(-a2/b2) = -1 or a1a2 + b1b2 = 0
    • (d) intersecting, if a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2
  • The equation of a line which is:
    • (a) parallel to ax + by + c = 0 can be written as ax + by + k = 0 [∵ m1 = m2]
    • (b) perpendicular to ax + by + c = 0 can be written as bx - ay + k = 0 [∵ m1m2 = -1]
    where, k is an arbitrary constant to be determined using given condition.

details.summary: Formulas for angle between lines, conditions for parallel/perpendicular lines, and properties of the general equation of a line.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Equations of Line in Different Forms
text:
1. Slope-intercept form: y = mx + c, is called the slope form or slope intercept form or the tangent form of the equation of the line, the constant c is called the intercept made by the line on the Y-axis. To find the slope and the intercept on the Y-axis of a line given in the form ax + by + c = 0, we write it in the form y = (-a/b)x - (c/b). Therefore, the slope of the line is m = -a/b and the intercept of the line on the Y-axis is -c/b.

2. Slope-point form: The equation of a line passing through the point (x1, y1) and having the slope 'm' is y - y1 = m(x - x1).

3. Two points form: The equation of a line passing through the points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is (y - y1) = [(y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)] * (x - x1).

4. Intercept form: If a line cuts the intercepts a and b on the axes, then the equation of line is x/a + y/b = 1.

5. Normal or perpendicular form: If p is the normal from the origin to the line AB and if the normal makes an angle alpha with X-axis, then the equation of the line in the form, x cos alpha + y sin alpha = p is called the normal form of the line. Note: In the normal form of a straight line the sum of the squares of the coefficient of x and y is equal to one.
formulas: x cos alpha + y sin alpha = p

Diagram showing normal form: A line AB with a perpendicular line segment 'p' from the origin to the line, where the segment 'p' makes an angle alpha with the X-axis.

text: Let L1 = a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and L2 = a2x + b2y + c2 = 0 be two given lines. Then, the equation, L1 + lambda*L2 = 0 i.e., a1x + b1y + c1 + lambda(a2x + b2y + c2) = 0 represents the equation of a line, passing through the point of intersection of the given lines, where lambda belongs to R.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Perpendicular Distance of a Point from a Line
text:
The perpendicular distance d from a point P(x1, y1) to the line ax + by + c = 0 is given by the formula:

d = |(ax1 + by1 + c) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2)|

The perpendicular distance from the origin (0,0) to the line ax + by + c = 0 is:

d = |c / sqrt(a^2 + b^2)|

details.summary: Formulae for calculating the perpendicular distance from a point to a line and from the origin to a line.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The distance between two parallel lines ax + by + c1 = 0 and ax + by + c2 = 0 is given by:

d = |(c1 - c2) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2)|

details.summary: Formula for the distance between two parallel lines.

subject: Mathematics
text:
To find whether three lines are concurrent, find the point of intersection of any two lines. If this point lies on the third line, the lines are concurrent.

The condition that the three lines a1x + b1y + c1 = 0, a2x + b2y + c2 = 0, and a3x + b3y + c3 = 0 are concurrent is given by the determinant:

| a1 b1 c1 |
| a2 b2 c2 | = 0
| a3 b3 c3 |

Note: Three or more straight lines are said to be concurrent if they meet at a point.

details.summary: Condition for concurrency of three straight lines using determinants.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Image of a Point about a Straight Line or Mirror
text:
Let AB be a line and P(x1, y1) be a point. The image Q(h, k) of point P about the line ax + by + c = 0 is given by:

(h - x1) / a = (k - y1) / b = -2(ax1 + by1 + c) / (a^2 + b^2)

subject: Mathematics
topic: Foot of Perpendicular and Angle Bisectors
text:
Foot of the perpendicular: The foot of the perpendicular (h, k) from (x1, y1) to the line ax + by + c = 0 is given by (h - x1)/a = (k - y1)/b = -(ax1 + by1 + c)/(a^2 + b^2).

Equations of the Bisectors of Angles between Two Lines: Let AB and CD be two given lines represented by a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0. The equation of the bisector of the angle between them is (a1x + b1y + c1) / sqrt(a1^2 + b1^2) = ± (a2x + b2y + c2) / sqrt(a2^2 + b2^2).

A line which is equally inclined to given two lines is parallel to the angle bisectors of the given lines.
tables:
| Conditions | Acute angle bisector | Obtuse angle bisector |
|---|---|---|
| a1a2 + b1b2 > 0 | - | + |
| a1a2 + b1b2 < 0 | + | - |

subject: Mathematics
text:
Properties of rectangles and triangles in coordinate geometry:

  • Rectangle: For a rectangle with sides x=a, x=a', y=b, y=b', the vertices are A(a, b'), B(a, b), C(a', b), and D(a', b'). Diagonals bisect each other at ((a+a')/2, (b+b')/2).
  • Area of Triangle: Calculated using the determinant method: Area = 1/2 * |x1(y2-y3) + x2(y3-y1) + x3(y1-y2)|.
  • Angle Bisector: The bisector of an angle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the other two sides.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Perpendicular distance from point (sqrt(a^2 - b^2), 0) is d1:

d1 = |(b cos alpha * sqrt(a^2 - b^2) + 0 - ab) / sqrt(b^2 cos^2 alpha + a^2 sin^2 alpha)|

Similarly, perpendicular distance from point (-sqrt(a^2 - b^2), 0) is d2:

d2 = |(-b cos alpha * sqrt(a^2 - b^2) + 0 - ab) / sqrt(b^2 cos^2 alpha + a^2 sin^2 alpha)|

Product d1 * d2:

d1 * d2 = |(b^2 cos^2 alpha(a^2 - b^2) - a^2 b^2) / (b^2 cos^2 alpha + a^2 sin^2 alpha)| = |-b^2| = b^2
formulas: d1 = |(b cos alpha * sqrt(a^2 - b^2) - ab) / sqrt(b^2 cos^2 alpha + a^2 sin^2 alpha)|
d2 = |(-b cos alpha * sqrt(a^2 - b^2) - ab) / sqrt(b^2 cos^2 alpha + a^2 sin^2 alpha)|

subject: Mathematics
text:
A circle is defined as the locus of a point which moves in a plane such that its distance from a fixed point in that plane is always constant. The fixed point is called the centre and the constant distance is called the radius of the circle.

Equation of a Circle in Standard Form: Let C(h, k) be the centre of the circle and the radius of the circle be r, then the equation of the circle in standard form is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2.

Note: The above equation is known as the central form of the equation of a circle.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a circle with centre C(h, k) and a point P(x, y) on the circumference, with a line segment of length r connecting them.

details.summary: Definition of a circle and its standard equation based on centre (h, k) and radius r.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Circle touching the X-axis: Let the circle touch the X-axis and have its centre C(h, k). Then, the equation of the circle is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = k^2 or x^2 + y^2 - 2hx - 2ky + h^2 = 0.

2. Circle touching the Y-axis: Let the circle touch the Y-axis and have its centre C(h, k). Then, the equation of the circle is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = h^2 or x^2 + y^2 - 2hx - 2ky + k^2 = 0.

3. Circle touching both the axes: Let the circle touch both the axes. Then, the equation of the circle is (x - r)^2 + (y - r)^2 = r^2 or x^2 + y^2 - 2rx - 2ry + r^2 = 0.
image_descriptions: Diagram 1: Circle touching the X-axis at a point, with centre C(h, k) and radius r=k.
Diagram 2: Circle touching the Y-axis at a point, with centre C(h, k) and radius r=h.
Diagram 3: Circle in the first quadrant touching both X and Y axes, with centre C(h, k) and radius r=h=k.

details.summary: Equations for circles touching the X-axis, Y-axis, or both axes.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Circle centre at origin: If the centre of the circle is at origin and radius is 'r', then the equation of the circle is (x-0)^2 + (y-0)^2 = k^2 => x^2 + y^2 = k^2.

General Equation of a Circle: The general second degree equation in x and y is ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, represents a circle whose centre is (-g, -f) and radius = sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c), when a = b and h = 0.

Intercepts on the Axes: The lengths of intercepts made by the circle x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 with X-axis = 2*sqrt(g^2 - c) and Y-axis = 2*sqrt(f^2 - c). Note: Intercepts are always positive.

Concentric Circle: Two circles having the same centre C(h, k) but different radii r1 and r2 are called concentric circles. Equation of concentric circle with x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 is x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c1 = 0.

Equation of Circle if Coordinates of End Points of Diameter are Known: If (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) are the end points of the diameter of a circle, then equation of circle is (x - x1)(x - x2) + (y - y1)(y - y2) = 0.

Nature of Circle:

  • If g^2 + f^2 - c > 0, then the radius of the circle is real and circle is also real.
  • If g^2 + f^2 - c = 0, then radius of circle is zero and circle is known as a point circle.
  • If g^2 + f^2 - c < 0, then radius is imaginary but the centre is real and such circle is called imaginary circle, not possible to draw such a circle.

Position of a Point with Respect to the Circle: Let S = x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 be the equation of a circle, then a point P(x1, y1) in the XY-plane lies:

  • (i) on the circle, if S1 = 0
  • (ii) outside the circle, if S1 > 0
  • (iii) inside the circle, if S1 < 0
where S1 = x1^2 + y1^2 + 2gx1 + 2fy1 + c.

Equation of Tangent:

  • 1. Equation of tangent at the point P(x1, y1) to a circle x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 is xx1 + yy1 + g(x + x1) + f(y + y1) + c = 0
  • 2. Equation of tangent to circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 at (x1, y1) is given by xx1 + yy1 = a^2.
formulas: xx1 + yy1 + g(x + x1) + f(y + y1) + c = 0
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a circle centered at origin (0,0) with radius k on a Cartesian plane.
Diagram showing a circle intersecting both X and Y axes, labeling intercepts A1A2 and B1B2.
Diagram showing a circle with diameter endpoints (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) and center C.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Length of Tangent:

  • The length of tangent from an external point (x1, y1) to the circle x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, is sqrt(x1^2 + y1^2 + 2gx1 + 2fy1 + c).
  • The length of the tangent from an external point (x1, y1) to the circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 is sqrt(x1^2 + y1^2 - a^2).

details.summary: Formulas for calculating the length of a tangent to a circle from an external point.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Contact of Two Circles:

Given two circles with equations (x - h1)^2 + (y - k1)^2 = a1^2 and (x - h2)^2 + (y - k2)^2 = a2^2, with centres C1(h1, k1) and C2(h2, k2) and radii a1 and a2, the following cases of intersection may arise:

  • (i) C1C2 > a1 + a2: two circles do not touch each other. Number of common tangents = 4
  • (ii) C1C2 = a1 + a2: two circles touch each other externally. Number of common tangents = 3
  • (iii) C1C2 < a1 + a2: two circles intersect each other. Number of common tangents = 2
  • (iv) C1C2 = |a1 - a2|: two circles touch each other internally. Number of common tangents = 1

details.summary: Conditions for intersection of two circles and the number of common tangents.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Common Chord of Two Circles:

Let the two circles be S1 = x^2 + y^2 + 2g1x + 2f1y + c1 = 0 and S2 = x^2 + y^2 + 2g2x + 2f2y + c2 = 0. The equation of the common chord is S1 - S2 = 0, or 2(g1 - g2)x + 2(f1 - f2)y + 2(c1 - c2) = 0.

details.summary: Formula for the equation of the common chord of two circles.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Angle of Intersection of Two Circles
text:
Angle of Intersection of Two Circles:

The angle of intersection θ of the two circles with centres at C1 and C2 and the respective radii r1 and r2 is given by cos θ = (r1^2 + r2^2 - (C1C2)^2) / (2r1r2) = (r1^2 + r2^2 - d^2) / (2r1r2), where C1C2 = d. Two circles intersect orthogonally if the angle of intersection is 90 degrees.

details.summary: Formula for the angle of intersection between two circles and the condition for orthogonality.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The condition for two circles to be orthogonal is derived from the triangle formed by their centers and intersection point, leading to the condition (C1C2)^2 = r1^2 + r2^2.

Equation of a Circle in Parametric Form: Let P(x, y) be any point on the circle with centre at C(h, k) and radius r, then x = h + r cos α and y = k + r sin α. Here, α is called the parameter.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing two intersecting circles with centers C1 and C2, radii r1 and r2, and an angle θ at the intersection point.

details.summary: Covers the condition for orthogonal circles and the parametric representation of a circle.

subject: Mathematics
text:
37. Equations of circles are x^2 + y^2 + 2ax + c = 0 and x^2 + y^2 + 2by + c = 0. Centres are (-a, 0) and (0, -b). Distance between two centres = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

38. Two circles touch each other if distance between centres = sum of radii. This leads to the condition c = sqrt((a^2 - c)(b^2 - c)).

39. For a line y = mx + c touching circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2, the condition is r = c / sqrt(1 + m^2).

40. Equation of circle with centre (h, k) and radius a is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = a^2.

41. For a circle with radius b and centre (0, b) touching line y = x - sqrt(2), the perpendicular distance from centre to line equals radius.

42. Distance between centres of two circles (x - 1)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = r^2 and x^2 + y^2 - 8x + 2y + 8 = 0 is calculated using the distance formula.

43. Condition for two circles to intersect at two distinct points is: distance between centres < sum of radii.

44-45. Derivations for circle passing through (0, 0), (a, b), and (-b, -a).
image_descriptions: A geometric diagram showing a circle with centre (0, b) and a tangent line represented by the equation y = x - sqrt(2), with the point of tangency labeled A.

details.summary: This page covers advanced properties of circles, including tangency conditions, distance between centres, and equations of circles passing through specific coordinate points.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A conic section or conic is the locus of a point which moves in such a way that its distance from a fixed point always bears a constant ratio to its perpendicular distance from a fixed line, all being in the same plane. Shape of the conic section obtained depends on the position of cutting plane. This section deals with parabola, hyperbola and ellipse etc.

Various Terms Related to Conic Section

  • Focus: The fixed points is called the focus of the conic section.
  • Directrix: The fixed straight line is called the directrix of the conic section.
  • Eccentricity: The constant ratio of distance of point lying on conic, from focus to its perpendicular distance from directrix is called the eccentricity of the conic section and is denoted by e.
    • (i) For an ellipse, e < 1
    • (ii) For a parabola, e = 1
    • (iii) For a hyperbola, e > 1
    • (iv) For a circle, e = 0
    • (v) Pair of straight lines, e = infinity
  • Axis: The straight line passing through the focus and perpendicular to the directrix, is called the axis of the conic section.
  • Vertex: The point of intersection of the conic section and its axis, is called vertex of the conic section.
  • Centre: The point which bisects every possible chord of the conic passing through it, is called the centre of conic.
  • Latusrectum: The latusrectum of a conic is the chord passing through the focus and perpendicular to the axis.
  • Focal chord: Any chord passing through the focus of a conic is called the focal chord of the conic.
  • Double ordinate: Any chord perpendicular to the axis of a conic is called the double ordinate of that conic.
  • Focal distance or focal length: The distance between the focus and a point lying on the conic, is known as focal distance or focal length of the given point.

details.summary: Introduction to conic sections, defining key geometric terms (focus, directrix, eccentricity, axis, vertex, centre, latusrectum, focal chord, double ordinate, focal distance) and the general second-degree equation.

subject: Mathematics
topic: General Equation of Conics of Second Degree
text: General equation of conics of second degree viz. ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 where, discriminant Delta = abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2

details.summary: General second-degree equation for conic sections and its discriminant formula.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The general equation of a non-degenerate conic section is classified based on specific conditions:

  • If Δ ≠ 0, h = 0, a = b, e = 0, it is a Circle.
  • If Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 = 0, e = 1, it is a Parabola.
  • If Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 > 0, e < 1, it is an Ellipse.
  • If Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 < 0, e > 1, it is a Hyperbola.
  • If Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 < 0, a + b = 0, e = 1/sqrt(2), it is a Rectangular hyperbola.
tables:
| S.No. | Condition | Nature of conic |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Δ ≠ 0, h = 0, a = b, e = 0 | A circle |
| 2 | Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 = 0, e = 1 | A parabola |
| 3 | Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 > 0, e < 1 | An ellipse |
| 4 | Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 < 0, e > 1 | A hyperbola |
| 5 | Δ ≠ 0, ab - h^2 < 0, a + b = 0, e = 1/sqrt(2) | A rectangular hyperbola |

details.summary: Classification of conic sections based on discriminant and eccentricity.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A parabola is the locus of a point which is equidistant from a fixed point called focus and from a fixed straight line called directrix.

Since point P(x, y) lies on the parabola, PS/PM = e = 1 (where e = 1). This leads to the derivation: PS^2 = PM^2 => (x - a)^2 + (y - 0)^2 = (x + a)^2 => y^2 = 4ax (standard form).

Note: The distance between vertex of parabola and focus is equal to perpendicular distance of vertex from directrix. Vertex is the mid-point of line joining focus and point of intersection of directrix and axis.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a parabola opening to the right with vertex at origin (0,0), focus at S(a,0), directrix at x = -a, and latus rectum passing through focus.

details.summary: Definition and derivation of the standard parabola equation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Other standard forms include:

  • y^2 = -4ax: Focus lies on the negative side of X-axis.
  • x^2 = 4ay: Focus lies on the positive side of Y-axis.
  • x^2 = -4ay: Focus lies on the negative side of Y-axis.
tables:
| Feature | y^2 = 4ax | y^2 = -4ax | x^2 = 4ay | x^2 = -4ay |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eccentricity | e = 1 | e = 1 | e = 1 | e = 1 |
| Coordinates of vertex | (0, 0) | (0, 0) | (0, 0) | (0, 0) |
| Coordinates of focus | (a, 0) | (-a, 0) | (0, a) | (0, -a) |
| Equation of directrix | x = -a | x = a | y = -a | y = a |
| Equation of the axis | y = 0 | y = 0 | x = 0 | x = 0 |
| Length of the latusrectum | 4a | 4a | 4a | 4a |
| Focal distance of a point P(x, y) | x + a | a - x | y + a | a - y |
| Extremities of latusrectum | (a, 2a) | (-a, 2a) | (2a, a) | (2a, -a) |
| Parametric coordinates | (at^2, 2at) | (-at^2, 2at) | (2at, at^2) | (2at, -at^2) |
| Parametric equation | x = at^2, y = 2at | x = -at^2, y = 2at | x = 2at, y = at^2 | x = 2at, y = -at^2 |
image_descriptions: Three diagrams showing parabolas: y^2 = -4ax opening left, x^2 = 4ay opening up, and x^2 = -4ay opening down.

details.summary: Comparison table and visual representation of four standard forms of parabolas.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If the vertex of the parabola is at the point A(h, k) and its latusrectum is of length 4a, then its equation is:

  • (y - k)^2 = 4a(x - h), if its axis is parallel to OX, i.e. parabola opens rightward.
  • (y - k)^2 = -4a(x - h), if its axis is parallel to OX, i.e. parabola opens leftward.
  • (x - h)^2 = 4a(y - k), if its axis is parallel to OY, i.e. parabola opens upward.
  • (x - h)^2 = -4a(y - k), if its axis is parallel to OY, i.e. parabola opens downward.
image_descriptions: A Cartesian coordinate system showing a parabola with vertex at (3, 4). The original axes are X and Y, and new axes are X' and Y' shifted to the vertex. The focus is marked at (13/4, 4).

subject: Mathematics
topic: Position of a Point with Respect to a Parabola
text:
Let S = y^2 - 4ax = 0 be the equation of a parabola, then a point P(x1, y1) in the XY-plane lies:

  • on the parabola, if S1 = 0
  • outside the parabola, if S1 > 0
  • inside the parabola, if S1 < 0

where, S1 = y1^2 - 4ax1

subject: Mathematics
text:
Equation of Chord: The equation of chord joining the points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) on the parabola y^2 = 4ax is y(y1 + y2) = 4ax + y1y2.

Condition for the Chord to be a Focal Chord: The chord joining the points (at1^2, 2at1) and (at2^2, 2at2) passes through focus provided t1t2 = -1.

Tangents and Normals to the Parabola:

  • Equation of tangent to the parabola y^2 = 4ax:
    • (i) at (x1, y1) is yy1 = 2a(x + x1)
    • (ii) at (at^2, 2at) is ty = x + at^2
    • (iii) If m is the slope of tangent to the parabola y^2 = 4ax, then its equation is y = mx + a/m. Point of contact is (a/m^2, 2a/m).
  • Equation of normal to the parabola y^2 = 4ax:
    • (i) at (x1, y1) is y - y1 = -y1/2a * (x - x1)
    • (ii) at (at^2, 2at) is y + tx = 2at + at^3
    • (iii) If m is the slope of normal to the parabola y^2 = 4ax, then its equation is given as y = mx - 2am - am^3.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Definition: An ellipse is the locus of that point which moves in a plane such that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point (focus) to a fixed straight line (directrix) is constant and less than unity. This constant ratio is called eccentricity and denoted by e. Or, the locus of a point whose sum of distance from two fixed points remains constant is called an ellipse.

Standard Form: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1, where b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2), b < a. AA' = 2a and BB' = 2b are called major and minor axes, respectively.

Another Form of Ellipse: x^2/b^2 + y^2/a^2 = 1 [where, b > a]. Here, AA' = 2a and BB' = 2b are minor and major axes, respectively.
image_descriptions: Diagram of a horizontal ellipse centered at origin O(0,0) with foci S(ae, 0) and S'(-ae, 0), vertices A(a,0) and A'(-a,0), and minor axis endpoints B(0,b) and B'(0,-b). Directrices are lines x = a/e and x = -a/e.

Diagram of a vertical ellipse centered at origin O(0,0) with foci S(0, be) and S'(0, -be), vertices A(a,0) and A'(-a,0), and major axis endpoints B(0,b) and B'(0,-b). Directrices are lines y = b/e and y = -b/e.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Some Important Results Related to Ellipse

The table below summarizes key properties for ellipses with centers at (0,0).

Note: If the centre of ellipse is at (h, k) and its axis are parallel to the coordinate axes, then the equation of ellipse is given as (x-h)^2/a^2 + (y-k)^2/b^2 = 1

Position of a Point with Respect to an Ellipse

If S = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 - 1 = 0, is the equation of an ellipse, then a point P(x1, y1) in the XY-plane lies:

  • (i) on the ellipse, if S1 = 0
  • (ii) outside the ellipse, if S1 > 0
  • (iii) inside the ellipse, if S1 < 0 where, S1 = x1^2/a^2 + y1^2/b^2 - 1

Equation of Ellipse in Parametric Form

Parametric equation of ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 is x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ and parametric coordinates of point lying on it is given by (a cos θ, b sin θ). The angle θ is called the eccentric angle of the point (a cos θ, b sin θ) on the ellipse.

Equation of Chord

The equation of the chord of the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1, whose mid-point be (x1, y1) is T = S1, where T = xx1/a^2 + yy1/b^2 - 1, S1 = x1^2/a^2 + y1^2/b^2 - 1.

The equation of the chord joining the points P(a cos θ1, b sin θ1) and Q(a cos θ2, b sin θ2) is (x/a) cos((θ1+θ2)/2) + (y/b) sin((θ1+θ2)/2) = cos((θ1-θ2)/2).

Tangents and Normals to the Ellipse

Equation of tangent to the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1:

  • (i) at the point (x1, y1) is xx1/a^2 + yy1/b^2 = 1.
  • (ii) having slope m is y = mx ± sqrt(a^2 m^2 + b^2) and coordinates of point of contacts are (± a^2 m / sqrt(a^2 m^2 + b^2), ± b^2 / sqrt(a^2 m^2 + b^2)).

Equation of normal to the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1:

  • (i) at the point (x1, y1) is a^2 x / x1 - b^2 y / y1 = a^2 - b^2.
  • (ii) having slope m is y = mx ± m(a^2 - b^2) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 m^2).
formulas: x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ

mcq.question: The equation of the ellipse, whose centre is at origin (0, 0), foci (±1, 0) and eccentricity 1/2, is
mcq.explanation: Here, foci = (±1, 0) and eccentricity, e = 1/2. ae = 1 and e = 1/2 => a = 2. b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2) => b^2 = 4(1 - 1/4) = 4(3/4) = 3. So, the equation of required ellipse is x^2/4 + y^2/3 = 1.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A hyperbola is the locus of that point which moves in a plane such that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point (focus) to a fixed straight line (directrix) is constant and greater than unity. This constant ratio is called eccentricity and denoted by e.

Alternatively, the locus of points whose difference of distance from two fixed points remains constant.

The standard equation is derived from PS/PM = e, leading to x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1, where b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1).
image_descriptions: A coordinate plane showing a hyperbola opening left and right. The center is at O(0,0). Foci are at S(ae, 0) and S'(-ae, 0). Vertices are at A(a, 0) and A'(-a, 0). Directrices are vertical lines at x = a/e and x = -a/e.

details.summary: Definition of hyperbola and derivation of its standard equation.

mcq.question: Find the equation of the hyperbola, the length of whose latusrectum is 8 and eccentricity is 3/sqrt(5).
mcq.explanation: Given length of latusrectum = 2b^2/a = 8 => b^2 = 4a. Also b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1). Substituting e = 3/sqrt(5), we get b^2 = a^2(9/5 - 1) = a^2(4/5). Equating 4a = 4a^2/5 => a = 5. Then b^2 = 4(5) = 20. Equation is x^2/25 - y^2/20 = 1.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Conjugate Hyperbola: The hyperbola whose transverse and conjugate axes are respectively the conjugate and transverse axes of the given hyperbola. The equation of the conjugate hyperbola of x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 is x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = -1 (or y^2/b^2 - x^2/a^2 = 1).

Rectangular Hyperbola: A particular kind of hyperbola which has its transverse and conjugate axis of equal length. It is also known as equilateral hyperbola. The eccentricity of rectangular hyperbola is sqrt(2).

subject: Mathematics
text:
Equation of Hyperbola with centre (h,k): If the centre of the hyperbola is at point (h,k) and its axes are parallel to the coordinate axes, then the equation is given as (x-h)^2/a^2 - (y-k)^2/b^2 = 1.

Equation of Hyperbola in Parametric Form: The parametric equation of the hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 is x = a sec θ, y = b tan θ. The parametric coordinates of a point lying on it are (a sec θ, b tan θ).

Position of a Point with Respect to a Hyperbola: Let S = x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 - 1 = 0. Then, the point P(x1, y1) lies:

  • On the hyperbola, if S1 = 0
  • Outside the hyperbola, if S1 > 0
  • Inside the hyperbola, if S1 < 0
where S1 = x1^2/a^2 - y1^2/b^2 - 1.

Intersection of a Line and a Hyperbola: The straight line y = mx + c will cut the hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 in two points which may be real, coincident or imaginary, as c^2 > = < a^2m^2 - b^2.

Auxiliary Circle of Hyperbola: If x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 is the hyperbola, then the equation of the auxiliary circle is x^2 + y^2 = a^2.

Equation of Chord: The equation of chord joining the points P(a sec θ1, b tan θ1) and Q(a sec θ2, b tan θ2) is (x/a) cos((θ1-θ2)/2) - (y/b) sin((θ1+θ2)/2) = cos((θ1+θ2)/2).

Tangents and Normals to the hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1:

  • Tangent:
    • At point (x1, y1): (x*x1)/a^2 - (y*y1)/b^2 = 1
    • Having slope m: y = mx ± sqrt(a^2m^2 - b^2)
  • Normal:
    • At point (x1, y1): (a^2*x)/x1 + (b^2*y)/y1 = a^2 + b^2
    • Having slope m: y = mx ± (m(a^2 + b^2)) / sqrt(a^2 - b^2m^2)
formulas: x = a sec θ, y = b tan θ
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a hyperbola centered at (0,0) with vertices at A(a,0) and A'(-a,0). An auxiliary circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 is drawn centered at the origin. A point P(x,y) is on the hyperbola, and a point Q is on the auxiliary circle such that the angle between the x-axis and the line segment OQ is θ.

subject: Mathematics
text:
In 3-D, there are three mutually perpendicular straight lines XOX', YOY' and ZOZ' called axes.

Coordinates of a Point in a Space: Three mutually perpendicular lines in space divide the space into 8 octants. Let the lines be XOX', YOY' and ZOZ' intersecting at O. XOY is called the XY-plane, YOZ is called the YZ-plane, ZOX is called the ZX-plane and all three planes taken together are called the coordinate planes. If P(x, y, z) is a point in space, then:

  • |x| = distance from YZ-plane
  • |y| = distance from ZX-plane
  • |z| = distance from XY-plane

Distance Formula:

  • (i) The distance between two points P(x1, y1, z1) and Q(x2, y2, z2) is given by PQ = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2)
  • (ii) Three points P(x1, y1, z1), Q(x2, y2, z2) and R(x3, y3, z3) are collinear, if PR = PQ + QR

Note: Let O be the origin and P(x, y, z) be any point, then OP = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2).

text:
Section Formula:

  • If a point R divides PQ internally in the ratio m:n, the coordinates of R are ((mx2 + nx1)/(m+n), (my2 + ny1)/(m+n), (mz2 + nz1)/(m+n)).
  • If a point R divides PQ externally in the ratio m:n (m != n), the coordinates of R are ((mx2 - nx1)/(m-n), (my2 - ny1)/(m-n), (mz2 - nz1)/(m-n)).

Mid-point and Centroid:

  • Mid-point of PQ = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2, (z1 + z2)/2).
  • Centroid G of a triangle with vertices A(x1, y1, z1), B(x2, y2, z2), and C(x3, y3, z3) is ((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3, (z1+z2+z3)/3).

subject: Mathematics
text:
Direction Cosines: If a line makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with positive X, Y, Z axes, then cos(alpha), cos(beta), cos(gamma) are direction cosines (l, m, n).

Direction Ratios: Three numbers a, b, c proportional to direction cosines l, m, n such that l/a = m/b = n/c.

Important Results:

  • l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1 or cos^2(alpha) + cos^2(beta) + cos^2(gamma) = 1.
  • DC's of X-axis: (1, 0, 0); Y-axis: (0, 1, 0); Z-axis: (0, 0, 1).
  • l = a/sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2), m = b/sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2), n = c/sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2).
  • Direction ratios of line joining A(x1, y1, z1) and B(x2, y2, z2) are (x2-x1, y2-y1, z2-z1).
formulas: l = cos(alpha), m = cos(beta), n = cos(gamma)

text: Area of a triangle with vertices A(x1, y1, z1), B(x2, y2, z2), and C(x3, y3, z3) is given by sqrt(Delta_x^2 + Delta_y^2 + Delta_z^2), where Delta_x, Delta_y, Delta_z are determinants involving coordinates.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Equation of a Line: If a, b, c are the direction ratios of a line passing through the point (x1, y1, z1), then the equation of line is (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c. In terms of direction cosines l, m, n, it is (x - x1)/l = (y - y1)/m = (z - z1)/n.

  • General coordinates: (x - x1)/l = (y - y1)/m = (z - z1)/n = r, giving coordinates (x1 + lr, y1 + mr, z1 + nr).
  • Equation through two points (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2): (x - x1)/(x2 - x1) = (y - y1)/(y2 - y1) = (z - z1)/(z2 - z1).
  • Parallel to line with direction ratios a, b, c: (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c.

details.summary: Covers the vector and cartesian equations of a straight line in 3D space.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Angle between two lines: If lines have direction cosines l1, m1, n1 and l2, m2, n2, the angle θ is given by cos θ = l1l2 + m1m2 + n1n2.

Perpendicular condition: l1l2 + m1m2 + n1n2 = 0.

Parallel condition: l1/l2 = m1/m2 = n1/n2.

For direction ratios a1, b1, c1 and a2, b2, c2: cos θ = |(a1a2 + b1b2 + c1c2) / (sqrt(a12 + b12 + c12) * sqrt(a22 + b22 + c22))|.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A plane is a surface such that any two points lying on it when joined by a line lies completely on it.

Equations of Plane in Different Form

  • General equation: ax + by + cz + d = 0, where a, b, c are constants and a^2 + b^2 + c^2 != 0.
  • Passing through (x1, y1, z1): a(x - x1) + b(y - y1) + c(z - z1) = 0
  • Normal form: lx + my + nz = p, where l, m, n are direction cosines and p is the perpendicular distance from origin.
  • Intercept form: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1, where a, b, c are intercepts on axes.
  • Coordinate planes: XY-plane is z = 0, YZ-plane is x = 0, XZ-plane is y = 0.
  • Parallel planes: Parallel to YZ-plane at distance a is x = a; parallel to ZX-plane at distance b is y = b; parallel to XY-plane at distance c is z = c.
  • Passing through three points: Determinant of [[x-x1, y-y1, z-z1], [x-x2, y-y2, z-z2], [x-x3, y-y3, z-z3]] = 0.

Angle between Two Planes

For planes a1x + b1y + c1z + d = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2z + d = 0:

  • Angle formula: cos(theta) = |(a1a2 + b1b2 + c1c2) / (sqrt(a1^2 + b1^2 + c1^2) * sqrt(a2^2 + b2^2 + c2^2))|
  • Perpendicular condition: a1a2 + b1b2 + c1c2 = 0
  • Parallel condition: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2

Distances

  • Distance from point (x1, y1, z1) to plane: P = |(ax1 + by1 + cz1 + d) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)|
  • Distance between two parallel planes: |(d1 - d2) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)|

Intersection of Two Planes

For planes P1 = 0 and P2 = 0, the equation of plane passing through intersection is P1 + lambda*P2 = 0.
formulas: P = |(ax1 + by1 + cz1 + d) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)|
(a1x + b1y + c1z + d1) + lambda(a2x + b2y + c2z + d2) = 0

subject: Mathematics
topic: Angle between a Line and a Plane
text:
Let the equations of a line and a plane be (x - x1)/l = (y - y1)/m = (z - z1)/n and ax + by + cz + d = 0 respectively, then the angle θ between them is given by:

sin θ = |al + bm + cn| / [sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) * sqrt(l^2 + m^2 + n^2)]

  • If a line is parallel to the plane, then θ = 0 ⇒ al + bm + cn = 0
  • If line is perpendicular to the plane, then a/l = b/m = c/n
formulas: sin θ = |al + bm + cn| / [sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) * sqrt(l^2 + m^2 + n^2)]

text: The two lines (x - x1)/l1 = (y - y1)/m1 = (z - z1)/n1 and (x - x2)/l2 = (y - y2)/m2 = (z - z2)/n2 are coplanar if the determinant of the matrix formed by (x2-x1, y2-y1, z2-z1), (l1, m1, n1), and (l2, m2, n2) is equal to 0.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A sphere is the locus of a point which moves in space in such a way that its distance from a fixed point always remains constant.

  • General equation: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 2ux + 2vy + 2wz + d = 0. Centre = (-u, -v, -w), Radius = sqrt(u^2 + v^2 + w^2 - d)
  • Equation with centre (a, b, c) and radius r: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 + (z - c)^2 = r^2
  • Diameter form: (x - x1)(x - x2) + (y - y1)(y - y2) + (z - z1)(z - z2) = 0
  • Orthogonal intersection: Condition for two spheres is 2u1u2 + 2v1v2 + 2w1w2 = d1 + d2

subject: Mathematics
topic: Intercept Form of a Plane and Centroid of Intercept Triangle
text:
When a plane intersects the coordinate axes at points A(a, 0, 0), B(0, b, 0), and C(0, 0, c), the equation of the plane in intercept form is given by:

x/a + y/b + z/c = 1

If the centroid of the triangle ABC is given by (alpha, beta, gamma), the coordinates of the centroid are:

  • alpha = a / 3 ⇒ a = 3 × alpha
  • beta = b / 3 ⇒ b = 3 × beta
  • gamma = c / 3 ⇒ c = 3 × gamma

Hence, the equation of the plane becomes:

x / (3 × alpha) + y / (3 × beta) + z / (3 × gamma) = 1

|---|---|---|
| X-axis | (a, 0, 0) | x_c = a/3 |
| Y-axis | (0, b, 0) | y_c = b/3 |
| Z-axis | (0, 0, c) | z_c = c/3 |

mcq.question: If a plane intersects the coordinate axes at A, B, and C such that the centroid of triangle ABC is (1, 2, 3), what is the equation of the plane?
mcq.explanation: Intercepts are a = 3(1) = 3, b = 3(2) = 6, c = 3(3) = 9. Equation is x/3 + y/6 + z/9 = 1 => 6x + 3y + 2z = 18.

subject: Mathematics
topic: General Equation of Sphere and Tangency with a Plane
text:
The general second-degree equation representing a sphere is:

x2 + y2 + z2 + 2ux + 2vy + 2wz + d = 0

  • Centre: (-u, -v, -w)
  • Radius: r = √(u2 + v2 + w2 - d)

For a plane Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 to touch a sphere with centre (x0, y0, z0) and radius r:

r = |Ax0 + By0 + Cz0 + D| / √(A2 + B2 + C2)
formulas: Radius r = sqrt(u^2 + v^2 + w^2 - d)
Perpendicular distance p = |Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D| / sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + C^2)

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Sphere Centre | (-u, -v, -w) |
| Sphere Radius | sqrt(u^2 + v^2 + w^2 - d) |

### Definition of Limit

Let \(y = f(x)\) be a function of \(x\). If at \(x = a\) the expression \(f(x)\) takes an indeterminate form, we examine the values of the function for \(x\) **very close** to \(a\).

- If these values approach a **single, definite number** as \(x 	o a\), that number is called the **limit of \(f(x)\) at \(x = a\)**.
- Notation: \[\lim_{x 	o a} f(x) = L\]
- The limit \(L\) exists only when the approach from **both sides** yields the same value.

---

**Key Points**
- The limit describes the behaviour of the function **near** the point, not necessarily at the point.
- An *indeterminate form* (e.g., \( rac{0}{0}\), \( rac{\infty}{\infty}\)) requires further analysis (algebraic simplification, L'Hôpital's rule, etc.).

subject: Mathematics
content:
### Right‑Hand Limit (RHL)

When \(x\) approaches \(a\) **from the right** (i.e., from values larger than \(a\)), the limit is called the **right‑hand limit**.

- Notation: \[\lim_{x 	o a^{+}} f(x)\]  or  \[\lim_{x 	o a^{+}} f(x) = L\]
- Practical substitution: set \(x = a + h\) with \(h 	o 0^{+}\).
  
  Then
  \[\lim_{h 	o 0^{+}} f(a + h) = L\]
- Compute the expression by simplifying after the substitution.

**Example** (illustrative):
```text
If f(x) =  rac{x-2}{|x-2|},
RHL at x = 2:
  set x = 2 + h, h>0
  f(2+h) =  rac{h}{h} = 1
  \lim_{h	o0^{+}} 1 = 1
```
---

**When to use**: Piece‑wise defined functions, absolute‑value (modulus) functions, or any function that behaves differently on either side of a point.

subject: Mathematics
content:
### Left‑Hand Limit (LHL)

When \(x\) approaches \(a\) **from the left** (i.e., from values smaller than \(a\)), the limit is called the **left‑hand limit**.

- Notation: \[\lim_{x 	o a^{-}} f(x)\]  or  \[\lim_{x 	o a^{-}} f(x) = L\]
- Practical substitution: set \(x = a - h\) with \(h 	o 0^{+}\) (or equivalently \(x = a + h\) with \(h 	o 0^{-}\)).
  
  Then
  \[\lim_{h 	o 0^{+}} f(a - h) = L\]
- Simplify the expression after substitution to evaluate the limit.

**Example** (illustrative):
```text
If f(x) =  rac{x-2}{|x-2|},
LHL at x = 2:
  set x = 2 - h, h>0
  f(2-h) =  rac{-h}{h} = -1
  \lim_{h	o0^{+}} -1 = -1
```
---

**When to use**: Same scenarios as RHL – especially useful for functions defined by different rules on either side of a point.

2. **Limit of a constant multiple**
   $$\lim_{x	o a} c\,f(x) = c\,\lim_{x	o a} f(x)$$
   where \(c\) is a constant.

3. **Limit of a quotient**
   $$\lim_{x	o a}  rac{f(x)}{g(x)} =  rac{\lim_{x	o a} f(x)}{\lim_{x	o a} g(x)}$$

eq 0\).

   $$\lim_{x	o a}  igl[f(x)+g(x) igr] = \lim_{x	o a} f(x) + \lim_{x	o a} g(x)$$

   $$\lim_{x	o a} \log igl(f(x) igr) = \log igl(\lim_{x	o a} f(x) igr)$$

   $$\lim_{x	o a}  rac{e^{f(x)}-1}{x-a}=\lim_{x	o a} f'(a)\quad	ext{(when the derivative exists)}$$

   If \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o a} g(x)=L\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(L\), then
   $$\lim_{x	o a} f igl(g(x) igr)=f(L).$$

9. **Continuity and limit interchange**
   If \(f\) is continuous at \(\phi\) and \(\phi\) is the limit of a function as \(x	o a\), then

1. **Logarithmic over power**
   $$\lim_{x	o 0^+} rac{\log x}{x^a}=0 \quad (a>0)$$

   $$\lim_{x	o \infty} rac{e^x}{x^a}=\infty \quad (a>0)$$

   $$\lim_{x	o \infty} rac{x^n}{e^{ax}}=0 \quad (a>0,\; n\in\mathbb{N})$$

   $$\lim_{x	o \infty} rac{a^x}{x^n}=\infty \quad (a>1,\; n\in\mathbb{N})$$

5. **Logarithm of a power**
   $$\lim_{x	o 0^+}\log_{m} x = -\infty \quad (m>0,\; m

   $$\lim_{x	o \infty}\log_{a} x = \infty \quad (a>1)$$

   $$\lim_{x	o \infty} rac{\log x}{x}=0$$

### Exponential Series

The Maclaurin (Taylor) series expansion of the exponential function \(e^x\) is:

1. **Standard form**
```math
e^x = 1 +  rac{x}{1!} +  rac{x^2}{2!} +  rac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}  rac{x^n}{n!}
```

2. **Alternating form** (useful for \(e^{-x}\))
```math
e^{-x} = 1 -  rac{x}{1!} +  rac{x^2}{2!} -  rac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}  rac{(-1)^n x^n}{n!}
```

These series converge for all real (and complex) \(x\).

### Definition of a Limit
A limit of a function \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches a point \(c\) is the value that \(f(x)\) gets arbitrarily close to when \(x\) gets arbitrarily close to \(c\) (from either side, unless a one‑sided limit is specified).

```
lim_{x	o c} f(x) = L
```
If such an \(L\) exists and is finite, we say the limit **exists**. If the function grows without bound, we write \(\lim_{x	o c} f(x)=\pm\infty\). If the left‑hand and right‑hand limits are different, the (two‑sided) limit **does not exist**.

### Common Limit Forms
- \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o 0} rac{x^2}{x}=0\) – the limit exists because the expression simplifies to \(x\).
- \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o 0} rac{x}{x^2}=\lim_{x	o 0} rac{1}{x}\) – does **not** exist as a finite number; it diverges to \(\pm\infty\).
- \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o 0} rac{|x|}{x}\) – does **not** exist because the right‑hand limit is \(1\) and the left‑hand limit is \(-1\).

### Continuity
A function \(f\) is continuous at a point \(c\) if:
1. \(f(c)\) is defined,

content:
### Differentiability of $|x|$
- The function $f(x) = |x|$ is **not differentiable** at $x = 0$.
- **Reason**: The left-hand derivative (LHD) at $x=0$ is $-1$ and the right-hand derivative (RHD) at $x=0$ is $1$. Since LHD $
eq$ RHD, the derivative does not exist at $x=0$.
- For $x > 0$, $ rac{d}{dx}|x| = 1$.
- For $x < 0$, $ rac{d}{dx}|x| = -1$.

### Differentiability of $|x-a|$
- The function $|x-a|$ is not differentiable at $x=a$.
- Example: $|x-3|$ is not differentiable at $x=3$.

### Continuity vs Differentiability
- If a function is differentiable at a point, it must be continuous at that point.
- The converse is not true: A function can be continuous at a point but not differentiable (e.g., $|x|$ at $x=0$).

### Fundamental Limit

The most important limit in elementary calculus is:

\[
\lim_{x	o0} rac{\sin x}{x}=1
\]

**Proof (using the squeeze theorem)**
1. For \(0<x< rac{\pi}{2}\) we have the geometric inequality
   \[\cos x <  rac{\sin x}{x} < 1.\]
2. As \(x	o0\), \(\cos x	o1\). Hence by the squeeze theorem the limit equals 1.

This limit is used repeatedly to evaluate limits of the form
\[\lim_{h	o0} rac{\sin(ah)}{bh}= rac{a}{b}.\]

---

### Related Limits
- \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o0} rac{1-\cos x}{x}=0\)
- \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o0} rac{	an x}{x}=1\)

These follow directly from the fundamental limit above.

### Standard Trigonometric Limits

1. **Limit of \( rac{\sin x}{x}\) as \(x	o 0\)**
   \[\lim_{x	o0} rac{\sin x}{x}=1\]
   This result is fundamental and is often proved using the squeeze theorem or the unit‑circle geometry.

2. **Limit of \( rac{1-\cos x}{x^2}\) as \(x	o 0\)**
   \[\lim_{x	o0} rac{1-\cos x}{x^2}= rac12\]
   It follows from the series expansion \(\cos x=1- rac{x^2}{2}+\dots\).

3. **Limit of \( rac{	an x}{x}\) as \(x	o 0\)**
   \[\lim_{x	o0} rac{	an x}{x}=1\]
   Since \(	an x =  rac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) and both \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) have known limits at 0.

4. **Limit of \( rac{\cos x-1}{x}\) as \(x	o 0\)**
   \[\lim_{x	o0} rac{\cos x-1}{x}=0\]
   Directly from the series expansion of \(\cos x\).

These limits are repeatedly used in solving more complex limit problems involving products, quotients, and compositions of trigonometric functions.

### One‑Sided Limits

- **Left‑hand limit (LHL)** of \(f(x)\) as \(x	o a\) is denoted \(\displaystyle\lim_{x	o a^-}f(x)\).
- **Right‑hand limit (RHL)** of \(f(x)\) as \(x	o a\) is denoted \(\displaystyle\lim_{x	o a^+}f(x)\).
- The (two‑sided) limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{x	o a}f(x)\) exists **iff** LHL = RHL = finite number.

### Example of Non‑Existence
Consider \(f(x)= rac{1}{x}\). As \(x	o0^-\), \(f(x)	o-\infty\) (LHL). As \(x	o0^+\), \(f(x)	o+\infty\) (RHL). Since LHL \(
eq\) RHL, the limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{x	o0} rac{1}{x}\) does **not** exist.

### Modulus (Absolute Value) Function

The function \(f(x)=|x|\) is defined as:
\[
 f(x)= egin{cases}
   x, & x\ge 0 \
  -x, & x<0
 \end{cases}
\]

- **Continuity**: Both pieces \(x\) and \(-x\) are continuous everywhere. At \(x=0\) the left‑hand limit \(\lim_{x	o0^-}f(x)=0\) and the right‑hand limit \(\lim_{x	o0^+}f(x)=0\) coincide with \(f(0)=0\). Hence \(|x|\) is continuous for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).

- **Differentiability**: \(|x|\) is **not** differentiable at \(x=0\) because the left‑hand derivative \(-1\) and right‑hand derivative \(+1\) are different.

content:
### L’Hospital’s Rule

- **Statement**: If \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o c} rac{f(x)}{g(x)}\) yields an indeterminate form \( rac{0}{0}\) or \( rac{\pm\infty}{\pm\infty}\), and the derivatives \(f'(x)\) and \(g'(x)\) exist in a neighbourhood of \(c\) (except possibly at \(c\)), then
  
  \[\displaystyle \lim_{x	o c} rac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x	o c} rac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}\]
  
  provided the limit on the right‑hand side exists (or is \(\pm\infty\)).
- **Typical usage**:
  1. Identify the indeterminate form.
  2. Differentiate numerator and denominator separately.
  3. Re‑evaluate the limit.
- **Example from the text**: For the limit
  \[\lim_{h	o 0} rac{e^{h}-1}{h}\]
  the direct substitution gives \( rac{0}{0}\). Applying L’Hospital’s rule:
  \[\lim_{h	o 0} rac{ rac{d}{dh}(e^{h}-1)}{ rac{d}{dh}h}=\lim_{h	o 0} rac{e^{h}}{1}=e^{0}=1\]
  Hence the limit equals 1.
- **Important points**:
  * The rule can be applied repeatedly if the resulting limit is still indeterminate.
  * It does **not** apply to other indeterminate forms such as \(0\cdot\infty,\;\infty-\infty,\;1^{\infty},\;0^{0},\;\infty^{0}\) unless they are first transformed into a \( rac{0}{0}\) or \( rac{\pm\infty}{\pm\infty}\) form.

3. \(\displaystyle \lim_{x	o c^+} f(x)\) (right‑hand limit) exists.
4. Both one‑sided limits are equal and equal to the function value:
   \[\lim_{x	o c^-} f(x)=\lim_{x	o c^+} f(x)=f(c)\]

content: The greatest integer function, denoted as $f(x) = [x]$, is continuous at all real numbers except at integer values. content: If a function $g(x)$ is continuous at a point $x=c$ and a function $h(x)$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then the composite function $h(g(x))$ is continuous at $x=c$. Consequently, the composite function $f(x) = h(g(x)) = \sin|x|$ is continuous for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

### Definition
Differentiation is the method used to compute the **rate of change** of a dependent variable \(y\) with respect to an independent variable \(x\). This rate of change is called the **derivative** of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).

### First Principle (Limit Definition)
For a function \(f(x)\), the differential coefficient (derivative) is defined as:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=f'(x)=\lim_{\delta x \to 0}\frac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}
$$

### Derivative at a Point \(x = a\)
$$
\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=a}=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}
$$

or equivalently

$$
\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=a}=\lim_{\delta x\to 0}\frac{f(a+\delta x)-f(a)}{\delta x}
$$

content:
### (i) Constant Rule
$$\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[C\bigr]=0 \quad\text{(where }C\text{ is a constant)}$$

### (ii) Constant Multiple Rule
$$\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[k\,f(x)\bigr]=k\,\frac{df}{dx}\quad\text{(where }k\text{ is a constant)}$$

### (iii) Sum/Difference Rule
$$\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[f(x)\pm g(x)\bigr]=\frac{df}{dx}\pm\frac{dg}{dx}$$

### (iv) Product Rule (Two Functions)
$$\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[f(x)\,g(x)\bigr]=f'(x)\,g(x)+f(x)\,g'(x)$$

### (v) Quotient Rule
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{f'(x)\,g(x)-f(x)\,g'(x)}{\bigl[g(x)\bigr]^2}$$

### (vi) Generalised Product Rule
For the product of *n* differentiable functions \(u_1(x)u_2(x)\dots u_n(x)\):
$$\frac{d}{dx}\Bigl[\prod_{i=1}^{n} u_i(x)\Bigr]=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left( u'_j(x)\prod_{\substack{i=1\ i\neq j}}^{n} u_i(x)\right)$$

### Important Substitutions for Inverse Trigonometric Functions

When an expression of the form \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\), \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\), \(\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\) etc. appears, the following substitutions reduce the integral or derivative to a simple trigonometric form:

| S.No. | Function involving \(x\) | Substitution |
|-------|--------------------------|--------------|
| 1 | \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\) | \(x = a\sin	heta\)  or \(x = a\cos	heta\) |
| 2 | \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\) | \(x = a	an	heta\)  or \(x = a\cot	heta\) |
| 3 | \(\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\) | \(x = a\sec	heta\)  or \(x = a\csc	heta\) |
| 4 | \( rac{a\pm x}{a\mp x}\) | \(x = a\cos 2	heta\) |
| 5 | \( rac{a\pm x}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\) | \(x = a\cos	heta\) (gives \(a\cos	heta\) after simplification) |
| 6 | \( rac{x}{\sqrt{x^2\pm a^2}}\) | \(x = a	an	heta\)  (or \(x = a\cot	heta\)) |
| 7 | \( rac{a\sin\alpha}{b\cos\alpha}\) | \(	an\alpha =  rac{b}{a}\) |

These substitutions are extremely useful for simplifying derivatives and integrals that contain square‑root expressions or rational functions of trigonometric forms.

### Differentiation of an Infinite Series

If a function \(y\) is expressed as an infinite series, e.g.

\[
y = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \sin^{k} x = \sin x + \sin^{2}x + \sin^{3}x + \dots\]

the derivative can be obtained term‑by‑term because **deleting (or adding) a finite number of terms does not affect the convergence of the series**. Hence,

\[
 rac{dy}{dx}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k\,\sin^{k-1}x\,\cos x = \cos x\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (k+1)\sin^{k}x.
\]

In many exam problems the series is a geometric series, allowing a closed‑form expression for \(y\) first, then differentiating the closed form. For the example above:

\[
y =  rac{\sin x}{1-\sin x}\quad (|\sin x|<1)
\]

Differentiating gives

\[
 rac{dy}{dx}= rac{\cos x}{(1-\sin x)^{2}} =  rac{\cos x}{1-\sin x}\; -\; \cos x.
\]

The answer can be written in the compact form

\[
 rac{dy}{dx}= rac{\cos x}{1-\sin x} - \cos x =  rac{\cos x}{1-\sin x} - \cos x.
\]

### Derivative of a Function with Respect to Another Function

If \(u(x)\) and \(v(x)\) are differentiable functions of \(x\), the derivative of \(u\) with respect to \(v\) is defined as

\[
 rac{du}{dv}= rac{\dfrac{du}{dx}}{\dfrac{dv}{dx}}= rac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}
\]

This formula is useful when the independent variable is not \(x\) but another function of \(x\). The steps are:
1. Compute \(\dfrac{du}{dx}\).
2. Compute \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\).
3. Form the ratio \(\dfrac{du/dx}{dv/dx}\).

**Example** (from the source material):
Find \(\dfrac{d}{dx} ig[\sin^{-1}\! ig( rac{t+1}{t} ig) ig]\) where \(t=	an	heta\) and \(x\) is the underlying variable.
The solution proceeds by letting
- \(u(t)=\sin^{-1}\! ig( rac{t+1}{t} ig)\)
- \(v(t)=\cos^{-1}\! ig( rac{t+1}{t} ig)\)
and then using \( rac{du}{dv}= rac{du/dt}{dv/dt}=1\).
Thus the derivative equals **1**.

### Logarithmic Differentiation

Logarithmic differentiation is a technique used when a function is:
- A product or quotient of many factors, **or**
- An exponent that itself contains a function.

**Procedure**
1. Take natural logarithm on both sides: \(y = f(x) \Rightarrow \ln y = \ln f(x)\).
2. Use logarithm properties to simplify the right‑hand side.
3. Differentiate implicitly with respect to \(x\).
4. Solve for \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).

**Important Logarithm Identities**
- \(\log_{b}(mn)=\log_{b}m+\log_{b}n\)
- \(\log_{b}\left( rac{m}{n}ight)=\log_{b}m-\log_{b}n\)
- \(\log_{b}\left(m^{n}ight)=n\log_{b}m\)

**Example** (from the source material):
If
\[
y = e^{x + x^{2} + \dots + x^{K}}\]
then
\[
 rac{dy}{dx}= rac{y}{y-1}\]
The steps are:
- Write \(\ln y = x + x^{2}+\dots + x^{K}\).
- Differentiate: \( rac{1}{y} rac{dy}{dx}=1+2x+\dots+Kx^{K-1}\).
- Recognise that the right‑hand side equals \( rac{y-1}{y}\) after algebraic manipulation, giving \( rac{dy}{dx}= rac{y}{y-1}\).

### Key Formulas for Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric Functions

1. **Derivative of $	an^{-1} x$**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(	an^{-1} x) =  rac{1}{1+x^2} $$

2. **Derivative of $\sin^{-1} x$**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(\sin^{-1} x) =  rac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} $$

3. **Derivative of $\cos^{-1} x$**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(\cos^{-1} x) = - rac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} $$

4. **Derivative of $\sec^{-1} x$**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(\sec^{-1} x) =  rac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}} $$

5. **Derivative of $\cot^{-1} x$**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(\cot^{-1} x) = - rac{1}{1+x^2} $$

### Chain Rule Application
For composite functions $y = f(g(x))$, the derivative is:
$$  rac{dy}{dx} = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x) $$

### Logarithmic Differentiation
For functions involving products, quotients, or powers of variable bases:
1. Take natural logarithm on both sides: $\ln y = \ln(f(x))$.
2. Differentiate implicitly: $ rac{1}{y}  rac{dy}{dx} =  rac{d}{dx}[\ln(f(x))]$.
3. Solve for $ rac{dy}{dx}$: $ rac{dy}{dx} = y \cdot  rac{d}{dx}[\ln(f(x))]$.

### Parametric Differentiation
If $x = f(t)$ and $y = g(t)$, then:
$$  rac{dy}{dx} =  rac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} $$

### Specific Identities Used in Problems
- $	an^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x =  rac{\pi}{2}$
- $\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x =  rac{\pi}{2}$
- $\sec^{-1} x + \csc^{-1} x =  rac{\pi}{2}$ (for $x > 1$)

### Derivatives of Logarithmic Functions

1. **Natural Logarithm**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(\ln x) =  rac{1}{x} $$

2. **Logarithm with Base $a$**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(\log_a x) =  rac{1}{x \ln a} $$

3. **Chain Rule for Logarithms**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(\log_a (g(x))) =  rac{g'(x)}{g(x) \ln a} $$

### Derivatives of Exponential Functions

1. **Natural Exponential**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(e^x) = e^x $$

2. **Exponential with Base $a$**:
   $$  rac{d}{dx}(a^x) = a^x \ln a $$

### Common Mistakes to Avoid
- Confusing $ rac{d}{dx}(\log_a x)$ with $ rac{1}{x}$. Remember the factor $ rac{1}{\ln a}$.
- Forgetting the chain rule when the argument of the log or exponential is a function of $x$.

### Key Concepts for Differentiation

1. **Derivative of Composite Functions (Chain Rule):**
   If $y = f(g(x))$, then $ rac{dy}{dx} = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$.
   - Example: $ rac{d}{dx}(\sin^2 x) = 2\sin x \cos x = \sin 2x$.
   - Example: $ rac{d}{dx}(\cos^2 x) = -2\cos x \sin x = -\sin 2x$.

2. **Differentiation with respect to a function:**
   To find $ rac{du}{dv}$, use the formula $ rac{du}{dv} =  rac{du/dx}{dv/dx}$.
   - Example: $ rac{d(\sin^2 x)}{d(\cos^2 x)} =  rac{\sin 2x}{-\sin 2x} = -1$.

3. **Implicit Differentiation:**
   For equations involving $x$ and $y$ (e.g., $x + y^2 = 2$), differentiate both sides with respect to $x$.
   - $ rac{d}{dx}(x) +  rac{d}{dx}(y^2) =  rac{d}{dx}(2)$
   - $1 + 2y  rac{dy}{dx} = 0 \implies  rac{dy}{dx} = - rac{1}{2y}$.

4. **Logarithmic Differentiation:**
   For functions like $y = x^{\log x}$ or derivatives of $\log x$ with respect to $\log x$.
   - Note: $ rac{d(\log x)}{d(\log x)} = 1$.

5. **Parametric Differentiation:**
   If $x = f(t)$ and $y = g(t)$, then:
   - $ rac{dy}{dx} =  rac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$
   - $ rac{d^2y}{dx^2} =  rac{d}{dt}\left( rac{dy}{dx}ight) \cdot  rac{dt}{dx}$.

6. **Inverse Function Derivative:**
   If $\phi$ is the inverse of $f$, then $\phi'(x) =  rac{1}{f'(\phi(x))}$.

7. **Higher Order Derivatives:**
   - $ rac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is the derivative of $ rac{dy}{dx}$.
   - For $y = e^{ax}$, $ rac{d^2y}{dx^2} = a^2 e^{ax}$.
   - For $y = e^x \sin x$, use product rule repeatedly.

8. **Polynomial Derivatives:**
   If $y = P(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$, then $ rac{d^n y}{dx^n}$ is a constant, and $ rac{d^{n+1} y}{dx^{n+1}} = 0$.

3. Rearranging gives $ rac{d^2y}{dx^2} =  rac{2}{3}$ or $3 rac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2$. Note: The specific question in the source text involves a slightly different form, but the principle remains: differentiate to remove constants $B$ and $C$.

### Rate of Change of Quantities

**Definition:**
The rate of change of any variable (say $x$) with respect to some other variable is the derivative of the first variable with respect to the other variable.

**Kinematics Application:**
If $x$ and $v$ denote the displacement and velocity of a particle at any instant $t$:
1. **Velocity ($v$):** The rate of change of displacement ($x$) with respect to time ($t$).
   $$ v = \frac{dx}{dt} $$
2. **Acceleration ($a$):** The rate of change of velocity ($v$) with respect to time ($t$), which is also the second derivative of displacement with respect to time.
   $$ a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} $$

**Key Applications of Differentiation:**
- Rate of change of quantities
- Maxima and minima
- Increasing and decreasing functions
- Slope of tangent to a curve
