subject: Physics
text:
Scalar Quantities: Physical quantities which have only magnitude but no direction are called scalar quantities. e.g., mass, speed, volume, work, time, power, energy, etc.

Vector Quantities: Physical quantities which have both magnitude and direction and obey all the laws of vector algebra are called vector quantities. e.g., displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, torque, etc.

Representation of a Vector: Any vector r can be written as r = xi + yj + zk where i, j and k are unit vectors along the perpendicular axes OX, OY and OZ, respectively. The magnitude of vector r is given by |r| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2).

Product of Vector Quantities:

  • Scalar product or Dot product: The scalar product or dot product of two vectors A and B is defined as the product of the magnitude of two vectors A and B and the cosine of the angle between them. A . B = AB cos(theta)
  • Cross product or Vector product: The cross product or vector product of two vectors A and B is defined as the product of the magnitude of two vectors A and B and sine of the angle between them. A x B = AB sin(theta)n (where n is a unit vector perpendicular to A and B).

details.summary: Definitions and mathematical representation of scalar and vector quantities, including dot and cross product definitions.

subject: Physics
text:
Velocity: The time rate of change of displacement an object in a particular direction is called the velocity of the object.

Velocity = Displacement / Time taken

Types of velocity:

  • Uniform Velocity: If an object undergoes equal displacements in equal intervals of time.
  • Non-uniform Velocity: If an object undergoes unequal displacements in equal intervals of time.
  • Average Velocity: The ratio of the total displacement to the total time taken. Average velocity = Total displacement / Total time taken
  • Instantaneous Velocity: Velocity at a given instant of time. v = lim(Δt→0) Δr/Δt = dr/dt

Acceleration: The time rate of change of velocity of an object.

Acceleration (a) = Change in velocity / Time taken. It is a vector quantity.

Types of acceleration:

  • Uniform Acceleration: If velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.
  • Non-uniform Acceleration: If velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal intervals of time.
  • Average Acceleration: a = (a1t1 + a2t2) / (t1 + t2)
  • Instantaneous Acceleration: a = lim(Δt→0) Δv/Δt = dv/dt

Important Notes:

  • If velocity decreases with time, acceleration is negative (retardation/deceleration).
  • Velocity and acceleration need not be zero simultaneously.
formulas: Average velocity = Total displacement / Total time taken
Instantaneous velocity, v = lim(Δt→0) Δr/Δt = dr/dt
Acceleration (a) = Change in velocity / Time taken
Instantaneous acceleration, a = lim(Δt→0) Δv/Δt = dv/dt

subject: Physics
text:
One-Dimensional Motion: Motion along a straight line path. Also known as rectilinear or linear motion.

Equations for One-dimensional Motion:

  • v = u + at
  • s = ut + 1/2 at^2
  • v^2 = u^2 + 2as

Important Conditions:

  • Starts from rest: u = 0
  • Comes to rest: v = 0
  • Uniform velocity: a = 0

Graphs (Displacement-Time):

  • Case I (At rest): Graph is a straight line parallel to time axis.
  • Case II (Zero acceleration): Graph is a straight line with positive slope.
  • Case III (Uniform positive acceleration): Graph is a curve with positive slope.
image_descriptions: Case I: Displacement-Time graph showing a horizontal line parallel to the t-axis at position A.
Case II: Displacement-Time graph showing a straight line with a positive slope starting from point A on the s-axis.
Case III: Displacement-Time graph showing a curve with an increasing slope starting from point X on the s-axis.

subject: Physics
topic: Motion Graphs and Equations of Motion
text:
Case IV: Negative Acceleration (s-t graph): The graph is a curve with negative slope. The body is initially at some distance from the origin. In equal intervals of time, the body covers lesser and lesser distances, meaning speed is decreasing. The slope of the displacement-time graph gives average velocity.

Velocity-Time Graphs:

  • Case I (Constant velocity, zero acceleration): Graph is a straight line parallel to the time axis. Slope is zero.
  • Case II (Positive constant acceleration, initial velocity u ≠ 0): Graph is a straight line. Velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time.
  • Case III (Constant positive acceleration, zero initial velocity u = 0): Graph is a straight line passing through the origin.
  • Case IV (Increasing acceleration, zero initial velocity): Graph is a curve, indicating unequal changes in velocity over equal time intervals.

Acceleration-Time Graphs:

  • Case I (Constant decreasing acceleration): Graph is a straight line with negative slope, making an angle θ > 90° with the time axis.
  • Case II (Constant increasing acceleration): Graph is a straight line OA, making an angle θ < 90° with the time axis.

Equations of Motion Under Gravity: Replace s with h (height) and a with g (acceleration due to gravity).

  • Upward Motion: (i) v = u - gt, (ii) h = ut - 1/2gt^2, (iii) v^2 = u^2 - 2gh
  • Downward Motion (u=0): (i) v = u + gt, (ii) h = ut + 1/2gt^2, (iii) v^2 = u^2 + 2gh
image_descriptions: Displacement-time graph showing a curve with negative slope starting away from the origin.
Velocity-time graph (Case I): Horizontal line parallel to time axis (a=0).
Velocity-time graph (Case II): Straight line starting at u > 0.
Velocity-time graph (Case III): Straight line starting from origin (u=0).
Velocity-time graph (Case IV): Upward curving line starting from origin.
Acceleration-time graph (Case I): Downward sloping line making angle > 90 degrees.
Acceleration-time graph (Case II): Upward sloping line OA making angle < 90 degrees.

details.summary: Covers displacement-time, velocity-time, and acceleration-time graphs for various motion scenarios, and defines equations of motion for objects under gravity.

subject: Physics
text:
Two-dimensional Motion: If only one out of three coordinates specifying the position of the object changes with respect to time, then the motion is called two-dimensional motion. Examples include motion of a car on a circular turn and motion of a billiards ball.

Equations for Two-dimensional Motion: To deal with motion on a plane (xy), we break the motion along x and y-directions and apply equations of motion of one-dimension separately for x and y-axes.

Projectile Motion: When an object is thrown from horizontal making an angle (θ) except 90°, its motion under gravity is a curved parabolic path, called trajectory and its motion is called projectile motion. The horizontal component of velocity (u cos θ) is responsible for horizontal motion and vertical component (u sin θ) is responsible for vertical motion. Examples: motion of a bullet shot from a gun, motion of a rocket after burn-out, motion of a bomb dropped from an aeroplane.

  • Time of flight (T): Time taken by the projectile to cover the journey from point of projection (O) to end point (A).
  • Maximum Height (H): Maximum height attained by the projectile during the journey from O to A.
  • Range (R): Distance between starting point (O) and final point (A).
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a projectile trajectory on a Cartesian plane (x, y). The projectile starts at origin O, reaches a maximum height h, and lands at point A on the x-axis. The initial velocity u is shown at angle θ, with components u cos θ and u sin θ.

details.summary: Covers the fundamentals of 2D motion, specifically projectile motion, including definitions of trajectory, time of flight, maximum height, and range.

subject: Physics
text:
Circular Motion: When an object moves in a circular path with a constant speed, the motion is called uniform circular motion.

Terms Related to Uniform Circular Motion:

  • Angular Displacement (θ): The angle turned by an object moving in a circular path from some reference line. θ = length of arc / radius = Δs / r.
  • Angular Velocity (ω): Time rate of change of angular displacement. ω = Δθ / time. For time period T, ω = 2π / T = 2πf.
  • Relation between Linear and Angular velocity: v = ω × r.
  • Angular Acceleration (α): Time rate of change of angular velocity. Unit is rad/s^2. α = dω / dt = d^2θ / dt^2.
  • Centripetal Acceleration: Acceleration acting on an object undergoing uniform circular motion, acting along the radius towards the centre. a = v^2 / r = ω^2 r.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a circle with radius r, an arc length Δs, and an angle θ representing angular displacement.

details.summary: Defines uniform circular motion and key kinematic variables including angular displacement, velocity, acceleration, and centripetal acceleration.

subject: Physics
text:
Centripetal Force: The force required to move an object along the radius and towards the centre.

Linear Momentum: The product of mass and velocity of an object. It is represented by p. Its unit is kg-m/s and it is a vector quantity.
image_descriptions: None

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for centripetal force and linear momentum.

subject: Physics
topic: Force and Law of Parallelogram of Forces
text:
Force: Any action which causes pull or push on an object. Two types:

  • Balanced Forces: Resultant of all forces is zero.
  • Unbalanced Forces: Resultant of all forces is not zero.

Law of Parallelogram of Forces: If two forces act on a point simultaneously, their magnitude and direction are represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two forces.
image_descriptions: A vector diagram showing two forces P and Q originating from point O, forming a parallelogram with diagonal R representing the resultant force.

details.summary: Classification of forces and the mathematical representation of the parallelogram law of forces.

subject: Physics
text:
Inertia: The property of an object to resist any change in its state of motion or rest. Three types:

  • Inertia of Rest: Resists change in state of rest.
  • Inertia of Motion: Resists change in state of motion.
  • Inertia of Direction: Resists change in direction of motion.

details.summary: Definition and classification of inertia.

subject: Physics
text:
Newton's First Law: Any object remains in the state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force. Also known as Law of Inertia. Applications: Passengers falling backward in a bus when it starts suddenly; dust particles separating from a carpet when beaten.

Newton's Second Law: The rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied external force. Applications: A fielder moving hands backward while catching a ball; high jumpers landing on cushions or sand.
formulas: F = K * (p2 - p1) / t = K * (m(v-u)) / t = Kma

details.summary: Explanation of Newton's first and second laws of motion with real-world applications.

subject: Physics
topic: Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum
text:
When no external force acts on a system of several interacting particles, the total linear momentum of the system is conserved. The total linear momentum is the vector sum of the linear momentum of all the particles of the system.

Consider an isolated system (the system on which no external force acts) of n particles. Suppose the n particles have masses m1, m2, m3, ..., mn and are moving with velocities v1, v2, v3...vn, respectively.

Then total linear momentum of the system is p = m1v1 + m2v2 + m3v3 +...+ mnvn = p1 + p2 + p3 +...+ pn

If F is the external force acting on the system, then according to Newton's second law, F = dp/dt. For an isolated system, F = 0 or dp/dt = 0. As the derivative of a constant is zero, so p = constant, or p1 + p2 + p3 +...+ pn = constant. Thus in the absence of any external force, the total linear momentum of the system is constant. This is the law of conservation of linear momentum.

details.summary: Explanation of the Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum for an isolated system of particles.

subject: Physics
topic: Newton's Third Law of Motion and Applications
text:
Newton's Third Law of Motion: Whenever one object exerts a force on another object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first object.

Applications of Newton's Third Law of Motion:

  • Walking of a person: A person is able to walk because of the Newton's third law of motion. During walking, a person pushes the ground in backward direction and in the reaction the ground also pushes the person with equal magnitude of force but in opposite direction. This enables him to move in forward direction against the push.
  • Recoil of gun: When bullet is fired from a gun, the bullet also pushes the gun in opposite direction with equal magnitude of force. This results gunman feeling a backward push, i.e., recoil force from the butt of gun.
  • Propulsion of a boat in forward direction: Sailor pushes water with oar in backward direction resulting water pushes the oar in forward direction. Consequently, the boat is pushed in forward direction. Force applied by oar and water are of equal magnitude but in opposite directions.
  • Rocket propulsion: The propulsion of rocket is based on the principle of action and reaction. The rapid burning of fuel produces hot gases which rush out from the nozzle at the rear end at a very high speed. The equal and opposite reaction force moves the rocket upward at a great speed.

details.summary: Definition and real-world applications of Newton's Third Law of Motion.

subject: Physics
text:
IMPULSE: A large force which acts on an object for a very short interval of time and produces a large change in its momentum is called and impulsive force. The impulse of a force acting on an object equal to the product of the large force and small time interval for which its acts on the object. Impulse (I) = Force * Time. Its unit is newton-second.

FRICTION: Friction is a force which opposes the relative motion between the two objects when one object actually moves or tries to move over the surface of another object.

Types of Friction: There are three types of friction:

  1. Static Friction: It is an opposing force which comes into play when one object tends to move over the surface of another object.
  2. Limiting Friction: The maximum static frictional force which comes into play when one object just begins to slide over the surface of another object.
  3. Kinetic Friction: The opposing force that comes into play when one object actually moves over the surface of another object.

Kinetic friction is of two types:

  • Sliding Friction: It comes into play when one object slides over the surface of another object.
  • Rolling Friction: It comes into play when one object rolls over the surface of another object.

details.summary: Definitions of Impulse and various types of Friction.

subject: Physics
content:
In a velocity-time (v-t) graph, the slope of the line represents acceleration.
- **Positive Slope**: Indicates acceleration (speeding up).
- **Negative Slope**: Indicates retardation or deceleration (slowing down).
- **Zero Slope (Horizontal Line)**: Indicates constant velocity (zero acceleration).

**Key Concept**: Retardation is represented by the segment of the graph where the velocity decreases over time, resulting in a negative slope.

subject: Physics
topic: Velocity with respect to a moving frame
content:
**Relative Velocity**: The velocity of an object as observed from a specific frame of reference.

- If an observer is sitting inside a moving vehicle (e.g., a train moving at 60 km/h), their velocity **with respect to the train** is **zero**.
- Formula: $v_{A/B} = v_A - v_B$. If $A$ is the man and $B$ is the train, and they move together, $v_{man} = v_{train}$, so $v_{man/train} = 0$.

subject: Physics
content:
When two forces act perpendicular to each other (e.g., along X and Y axes):
1. **Resultant Force ($F_{net}$)**: Calculated using the Pythagorean theorem.
   $$F_{net} = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$$
2. **Resultant Acceleration ($a_{net}$)**: Using Newton's Second Law ($F = ma$).
   $$a_{net} =  rac{F_{net}}{m} =  rac{\sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}}{m}$$

**Example**: For $F_x = 3\,	ext{N}$, $F_y = 4\,	ext{N}$, and $m = 1\,	ext{kg}$:
$$F_{net} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\,	ext{N}$$
$$a_{net} =  rac{5\,	ext{N}}{1\,	ext{kg}} = 5\,	ext{m/s}^2$$

subject: Physics
content:
The SI unit of force is the **Newton (N)**.

**Definition**: One Newton is the force required to accelerate a mass of 1 kilogram at a rate of 1 meter per second squared.

**Formula**: 
$$1\,	ext{N} = 1\,	ext{kg} \cdot 	ext{m/s}^2$$

This is derived from Newton's Second Law: $F = ma$.

subject: Physics
content:
**Key Kinematic Statements**:
1. **Slowing Down**: If velocity and acceleration have **opposite signs**, the object is slowing down (retarding).
2. **Zero Velocity vs. Zero Acceleration**: 
   - If velocity is zero at an **instant**, acceleration **need not** be zero (e.g., a ball at the highest point of its throw has $v=0$ but $a=g$).
   - If velocity is zero for a **time interval**, acceleration **must** be zero (the object is at rest).
3. **Direction of Motion**: If position and velocity have opposite signs, the object is moving towards the origin.

subject: Physics
topic: Velocity, Speed, and Acceleration in Circular Motion
content:
For an object moving uniformly in a horizontal circle:
1. **Speed**: Constant (magnitude of velocity).
2. **Velocity**: **Not constant** because the direction changes continuously.
3. **Acceleration**: 
   - The **magnitude** of centripetal acceleration ($a_c = v^2/r$) is constant.
   - The **direction** of acceleration changes continuously (always pointing towards the center).
   - Therefore, the acceleration vector is **not constant**.

**True Statements**:
- The ball moves with constant speed.
- The magnitude of the acceleration of the ball is constant.

subject: Physics
text:
Calculations for average velocity and force vectors:

  • Average Velocity: For a journey with segments, v_av = Total Distance / Total Time. Example: v_av = (20 * 30) / (20 + 30) = 12 m/s.
  • Force Vector Magnitude: Given F = 6i - 8j + 10k, |F| = sqrt(6^2 + (-8)^2 + 10^2) = sqrt(36 + 64 + 100) = 10*sqrt(2) N.
  • Newton's Second Law: F = ma.
  • Resultant Force: If two forces are applied, F = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2).
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a projectile motion scenario where a bullet is fired from point A, passes through point B at 400m height, and hits the ground at point C. Initial velocity u = 80 m/s.

details.summary: Contains solutions to physics problems involving kinematics, force vectors, and Newton's laws.

subject: Physics
text:
Work: When a force acts on an object and the object actually moves in the direction of force, then the work is said to be done by the force.

Work done by a Constant Force: Work done by a constant force is equal to the product of the force and displacement of the object in the direction of force.

Work done = Force × Displacement of the object in the direction of force

Work is a scalar quantity. Its SI unit is joule and CGS unit is erg.

1 joule = 10^7 erg
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a block on a horizontal surface being pulled by a force F at an angle theta to the horizontal, resulting in a displacement s.

details.summary: Definition and calculation of work done by a constant force, including units and scalar nature.

subject: Physics
text:
Types of Work: Work can be of three types:

  • Positive Work: If a force acting on an object has a component in the direction of displacement, then the work done by the force is positive.
  • Negative Work: If a force acting on an object has a component in the opposite direction of displacement, then the work done by the force is negative.
  • Zero Work: Work done by a force is zero, if the object gets displaced along a direction perpendicular to the direction of the applied force.

details.summary: Classification of work into positive, negative, and zero based on the direction of force relative to displacement.

subject: Physics
text:
Conservative Force: A force is conservative, if the work done by the force in displacing an object from one point to another point is independent of the path followed by the object and depends only on the end points.

e.g. Gravitational force, electrostatic force and elastic force of a spring are all conservative forces.

details.summary: Definition of conservative forces with examples.

subject: Physics
text:
Non-conservative Force: If the amount of work done in moving an object against a force from one point to another point depends on the path along which the body moves, then such a force is called a non-conservative force. The work done in moving an object against a non-conservative force along a closed path is not zero. e.g., Forces of friction and viscosity are non-conservative forces.

Energy: The energy of an object is defined as its capacity of doing work. Energy is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is joule. There are several types of energies such as kinetic energy, potential energy, heat energy, sound energy, etc. Kinetic energy and potential energy are combinedly known as mechanical energy.

details.summary: Definitions of non-conservative forces and general energy concepts.

subject: Physics
text:
Kinetic Energy: The energy possessed by an object by virtue of its motion is called kinetic energy.

Relation between Kinetic Energy and Linear Momentum: From the relation KE = p^2 / 2m, it is clear that an object cannot have kinetic energy without having momentum and vice-versa.

Work-Energy Theorem: This theorem states that work done by a force acting on an object is equal to the change in the kinetic energy of the object. Work done = Change in kinetic energy; W = Kf - Ki

details.summary: Covers kinetic energy definition, relation to momentum, and the work-energy theorem.

subject: Physics
text:
Potential Energy: The energy possessed by an object by virtue of its position or configuration is called potential energy. There are three types of potential energy:

  • Gravitational Potential Energy: Energy associated with the state of separation of two objects. For two objects of masses m1 and m2 separated by distance r, U = -Gm1m2/r. If an object of mass m is at height h relative to Earth's surface, U = mgh / (1 + h/R). If h << R, U = mgh.
  • Elastic Potential Energy: Energy associated with the state of compression or extension of an elastic (spring like) object. U = (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)Fx = F^2 / 2k.
  • Electrostatic Potential Energy: Energy due to the interaction between two electric charges. U = (1 / 4πε0) * (q1q2 / r).

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of Gravitational, Elastic, and Electrostatic potential energy.

subject: Physics
text:
Law of Conservation of Energy: Energy can only be transformed from one form to another, it can neither be created nor be destroyed. The total energy before and after transformation, always remains constant.

Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: This law states that, if only the conservative forces are doing work on an object, then the total mechanical energy (KE + PE) of the object remains constant. KE + PE = constant.

details.summary: Principles of conservation of energy and mechanical energy.

subject: Physics
text:
Power is defined as the rate of doing work or the rate at which energy is transferred or used or transformed.

If work W is done in time t, then power, P = work / time.

Since work = F.s, then P = (F.s) / t = F.v = Fv cos θ.

The SI unit of power is watt (in honour of James Watt), having the symbol W.

Larger units of energy transfer include:

  • 1 kW = 1000 W = 1000 Js^-1
  • 1 MW = 10^6 W
  • 1 HP (horse power) = 746 W

details.summary: Definition and mathematical derivation of Power, including SI units and conversion factors.

subject: Physics
text:
The commercial unit of electric energy is kilowatt-hour (kWh).

It is the amount of electric energy consumed by an appliance of power 100 W in one hour.

Calculation: 1 kWh = 1 kW × 1h = 1000 W × 3600 s = 1000 Js^-1 × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10^6 J.

details.summary: Definition and conversion of the commercial unit of energy (kWh) into Joules.

subject: Physics
text:
A collision occurs between two objects if they physically collide or if the path of one object is affected by the force exerted by the other.

Types of Collision:

  1. Elastic collision: No loss of kinetic energy. Characteristics: (i) Kinetic energy is conserved, (ii) Momentum is conserved, (iii) Total energy is conserved, (iv) Forces involved are conservative.
  2. Inelastic collision: Loss of kinetic energy occurs. Characteristics: (i) Kinetic energy is NOT conserved, (ii) Momentum is conserved, (iii) Total energy is conserved, (iv) Some or all forces are non-conservative.

Law of Conservation of Momentum in Collision:

For particles of masses m1 and m2 with velocities u1 and u2 before collision and v1 and v2 after collision: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2.

If an object of mass m strikes a wall with velocity v and bounces back with the same velocity, the change in momentum is 2mv.

details.summary: Definitions of elastic and inelastic collisions and the law of conservation of momentum.

subject: Physics
text:
For two objects A and B of masses m1 and m2 moving in the same straight line, if u1 > u2, they collide head-on. After collision, they separate if v2 > v1.

Conservation of momentum: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2

Conservation of kinetic energy: 1/2 m1u1^2 + 1/2 m2u2^2 = 1/2 m1v1^2 + 1/2 m2v2^2

Solving these yields final velocities:

  • v1 = ((m1 - m2) / (m1 + m2))u1 + ((2m2) / (m1 + m2))u2
  • v2 = ((m2 - m1) / (m1 + m2))u2 + ((2m1) / (m1 + m2))u1
image_descriptions: Diagram showing three stages of a one-dimensional elastic collision: 'Before collision' (two spheres approaching), 'During collision' (two spheres in contact), and 'After collision' (two spheres separating).

details.summary: Mathematical derivation of final velocities for two objects in a one-dimensional elastic collision.

subject: Physics
text:
Consider an object of mass m1 moving with velocity u1 collides head-on with another object of mass m2 at rest. After the collision, the two objects move together with a common velocity v.

As the linear momentum is conserved, so m1u1 + m2 × 0 = (m1 + m2)v ... (i)

or v = [m1 / (m1 + m2)]u1

The loss in kinetic energy on collision is ΔK = Ki - Kf = (1/2)m1u12 - (1/2)(m1 + m2)v2 ... (ii)

After putting the value of v in Eq. (ii), we get ΔK = [1/2 * (m1m2 / (m1 + m2))]u12
image_descriptions: Diagram showing two circles representing masses m1 and m2. Before collision, m1 moves with velocity u1 towards m2 at rest. After collision, they are joined together moving with velocity v.

details.summary: Derivation of common velocity and kinetic energy loss for a perfectly inelastic collision in one dimension.

subject: Physics
text:
Suppose a particle of mass m1 moving along X-axis with velocity u1 collides with another particle of mass m2 at rest. After the collision, the two particles move with velocities v1 and v2, making angles θ1 and θ2 with X-axis.

After the collision, the rectangular components of the momentum of m1 are: (i) m1v1 cosθ1 along +ve X-axis, (ii) m1v1 sinθ1 along +ve Y-axis.

After the collision, the rectangular components of the momentum of m2 are: (i) m2v2 cosθ2 along +ve X-axis, (ii) m2v2 sinθ2 along +ve Y-axis.

Applying conservation of momentum along X-axis: m1u1 = m1v1 cosθ1 + m2v2 cosθ2 ... (i)

The initial momentum of m1 or m2 along Y-axis is zero. Applying conservation of momentum along Y-axis: 0 = m1v1 sinθ1 - m2v2 sinθ2 ... (ii)

As KE is conserved in elastic collision: (1/2)m1u12 = (1/2)m1v12 + (1/2)m2v22 ... (iii)
image_descriptions: Vector diagram showing m1 moving along X-axis colliding with m2 at rest. After collision, m1 moves at angle θ1 with velocity v1, and m2 moves at angle θ2 with velocity v2. Components v1cosθ1, v1sinθ1, v2cosθ2, and v2sinθ2 are shown.

details.summary: Analysis of elastic collision in two dimensions using conservation of momentum in X and Y axes and conservation of kinetic energy.

subject: Physics
text:
The ratio of relative velocity of particles after and before collision is known as coefficient of restitution.

e = (Relative velocity of separation (after collision)) / (Relative velocity of approach (before collision))

e = (v2 - v1) / (u1 - u2)

For a perfectly elastic collision, e = 1.

For an inelastic collision, e = 0.

details.summary: Definition and values of the coefficient of restitution for different types of collisions.

subject: Physics
chapter: Centre of Mass and Rotational Motion
topic: Rigid Body and Centre of Mass
text:
Rigid Body: A rigid body is defined as that body which does not undergo any change in shape or volume when external forces are applied on it. When a force is applied on a rigid body, then the distance between any two particles of the body will remain unchanged, however larger the forces may be.

Centre of Mass (CM): The centre of mass of a body is a point, where the whole mass of the body is supposed to be concentrated.

  • Centre of mass of two particles system consisting of two particles of masses m1 and m2 and respective position vectors r1 and r2 is given by rCM = (m1r1 + m2r2) / (m1 + m2).
  • If m1 = m2 = m, then rCM = (r1 + r2) / 2. Thus, the centre of mass of two equal masses lies exactly at the centre of the line joining the two masses.
  • For a system consisting of N-particles, let the mass of the ith particle be mi and its coordinates with reference to the chosen axes be xi, yi and zi. Then, xCM = (1/M) * sum(mi*xi), yCM = (1/M) * sum(mi*yi) and zCM = (1/M) * sum(mi*zi).
  • For continuous bodies, x = (1/M) * integral(xdm), y = (1/M) * integral(ydm) and z = (1/M) * integral(zdm).
  • The centre of mass of sphere, cylinder and ring is at its geometric centre.
  • The centre of mass may lie outside the body when there is no material as in case of ring, hollow sphere, hollow cylinder, etc.

details.summary: Introduction to rigid bodies and the definition and calculation of the Centre of Mass for discrete and continuous systems.

subject: Physics
chapter: Centre of Mass and Rotational Motion
topic: Location of Centre of Mass for Different Bodies
text:
Location of Centre of Mass for Different Bodies:

  • For uniform rod, xCM = L/2, yCM = 0 and zCM = 0.
  • Centre of mass of a uniform rectangular square or circular plate lies at its centre.
  • For uniform semicircular ring, yCM = 2R/pi, xCM = 0 and zCM = 0.
  • For uniform semicircular disc, yCM = 4R/3pi, xCM = 0 and zCM = 0.

details.summary: Specific coordinates for the centre of mass of common geometric shapes.

subject: Physics
topic: Centre of Mass and Motion Types
text:
Centre of Mass Facts:

  • For hemispherical shell, y_CM = R/2, x_CM = 0 and z_CM = 0
  • For solid hemisphere, y_CM = 3R/8 and x_CM = 0 and z_CM = 0
  • If a body falling under gravity explodes into pieces, then the centre of mass of the system remains along the same vertical line.
  • Centre of mass and centre of gravity of a regular body coincide.

Motion of Rigid Body:

  • Translational Motion: Motion by which a body shifts from one point in space to another point. Example: motion of bullet fired from a gun.
  • Rotational Motion: A body is said to possess rotational motion, if all its particles move along circles in parallel lines. The centres of these circle lie on a fixed line perpendicular to the parallel lines and this fixed line is called the axis of rotation.

subject: Physics
topic: Moment of Inertia and Radius of Gyration
text:
Moment of Inertia: Moment of inertia of a body with respect to an axis of rotation is the product of the mass (m) and the square of perpendicular distance from axis of rotation (r). Moment of inertia, I = mr^2. The moment of inertia of the rigid body, I = Σmr^2. Its SI unit is kgm^2. Moment of inertia is the property of a body due to which it opposes any change its state of rest or uniform motion.

Factors affecting Moment of Inertia:

  • Mass of the body.
  • Size and shape of the body.
  • Distribution of mass about the axis of rotation.
  • Position and orientation of the axis of rotation w.r.t. the body.

Radius of Gyration: The radius of gyration of a body about its axis of rotation may be defined as the distance from the axis of rotation at which, if the whole mass of the body were concentrated, its moment of inertia about the given axis would be same as with the actual distribution of mass.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two theorems in moment of inertia, i.e. theorem of parallel axes and theorem of perpendicular axes.

1. Theorem of Parallel Axes

Moment of inertia of a body about a given axis I is equal to the sum of moment of inertia of the body about an axis parallel to given axis and passing through centre of mass of the body Ig and Ma2, where M is the mass of the body and a is the perpendicular distance between the two axes.

Formula: I = Ig + Ma2

Example: Moment of inertia of a disc about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to the plane is (1/2)MR2, so moment of inertia of the disc about an axis through its tangent and perpendicular to the plane will be I = Ig + Ma2 = (1/2)MR2 + MR2 = (3/2)MR2.

2. Theorem of Perpendicular Axes

According to this theorem, the sum of moment of inertia of a plane lamina about two mutually perpendicular axes lying in its plane is equal to its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane of lamina and passing through the point of intersection of first two axes.

Formula: Iz = Ix + Iy

Example: Moment of inertia of a disc about an axis through its centre of mass and perpendicular to its plane is (1/2)MR2, if the disc is in xy-plane, then by theorem of perpendicular axes, Iz = Ix + Iy. Since the disc is a symmetrical body, Ix = Iy = ID, therefore Iz = (MR2/2) => (1/2)MR2 = 2ID.

subject: Physics
text:
The turning effect of a force about the axis of rotation is known as torque. It is measured as the product of the magnitude of the force and the perpendicular distance of the line of action of the force from the axis of rotation.

When a force F acts at point, whose position vector is r, then torque due to force is given by τ = r × F.

The torque is also known as moment of force. It is a vector quantity. The SI unit of torque is N-m.

details.summary: Definition and mathematical representation of Torque (moment of force).

subject: Physics
text:
The angular momentum of a particle is defined as the cross product of position with respect to origin and linear momentum of the particle.

Relation between Torque and Angular Momentum:

  • Torque: τ = r × F
  • Angular Momentum: L = r × p
  • On differentiating both sides w.r.t. time t, we get: dL/dt = d/dt(r × p) = dr/dt × p + r × dp/dt
  • Since dr/dt × p = v × p = v × mv = 0 and dp/dt = F, we get dL/dt = 0 + τ.
  • Therefore, τ = dL/dt.

Thus, the torque acting on a particle is equal to its rate of change of angular momentum.

Conservation of Angular Momentum:

The law of conservation of angular momentum states that if there is no external torque acting on the body, then the total angular momentum will remain unchanged.

  • If τ = dL/dt = 0, then L_initial = L_final.
  • In other form: L = Iω = constant.
formulas: L = r × p = rp sin θ

details.summary: Covers definition of angular momentum, its relationship with torque, and the principle of conservation of angular momentum.

subject: Physics
topic: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Rolling Motion
text:
Rotational Kinetic Energy: The energy possessed by the rotation of a body is known as rotational kinetic energy (K_R).

Rolling Motion: In this type of rotational motion, the axis of rotation is in motion. Plane motion can be considered as a combination of translational motion of the centre of mass and rotational motion of the body about an axis passing through the centre of mass.

Net Kinetic Energy: K_N = K_T + K_R = 1/2 mv^2 + 1/2 Iω^2 = 1/2 mv^2(1 + K^2/R^2)
tables:
| Motion / Physical Quantity | Velocity | Acceleration | Time of Descend |

| Sliding motion | v_s = sqrt(2gh) | a_s = g sin θ | T_s = (1 / sin θ) * sqrt(2h / g) |
| Falling motion | v_f = sqrt(2gh) | a_f = g | T_f = sqrt(2h / g) |

details.summary: Explains rotational kinetic energy and the dynamics of rolling motion on an inclined plane, including comparisons with sliding and falling motion.

subject: Physics
text:
Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force which is known as force of gravitation. Gravitation is the force of attraction between any two objects in the universe.

Universal Law of Gravitation (Newton's Law): The universal law of gravitation was given by Issac Newton. According to this law, the attractive force between any two objects in the universe is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of distance between them.

Consider two bodies A and B having masses M and m, whose centres are at a distance r from each other.

  • Gravitational force, F ∝ (Mm)/r^2
  • F = G(Mm)/r^2

where, G = 6.67 × 10^-11 N-m^2/kg^2 and is called as universal gravitational constant.

details.summary: Introduction to Gravitation and Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation.

subject: Physics
text:
Whenever an object falls towards the earth an acceleration is involved. This acceleration is due to the earth's gravitational pull and hence is called acceleration due to gravity or acceleration due to the gravitational force of the earth.

Acceleration due to gravity, g = (GM_e)/(R_e^2)

where, M_e = mass of the earth, R_e = radius of the earth. The value of the g on the surface of the earth is equal to 9.8 m/s^2.

Variation in the Value of g:

  1. The value of g is minimum at equator and maximum at poles (it happens due to shape of the earth).
  2. The observed value of g at the latitude λ is g' = g - R_eω^2 cos^2 λ

At equator, λ = 0°, cos λ = cos 0° = 1, g' = g_e = g - R_eω^2

At pole, λ = 90°, cos λ = 0, g' = g_p

details.summary: Definition of acceleration due to gravity and its variation based on latitude and earth's shape.

subject: Physics
text:
Gravitational Field: The space surrounding the material body in which its gravitational force of attraction can be experienced.

Intensity of Gravitational Field: The force acting on the unit mass at that point. Intensity is given by GM/r^2. Its SI unit is N/kg.

Gravitational Potential: Work done in carrying a unit mass from infinity to that point. Potential due to mass m at distance r is V = -GM/r.

details.summary: Covers variations of g with height and depth, definitions of gravitational field, intensity, and potential.

subject: Physics
topic: Gravitational Intensity and Potential for Solid Sphere and Shell
text:
Solid Sphere:

  • Outside: E = -GM/r^2, V = -GM/r
  • Surface: E = -GM/R^2, V = -GM/R
  • Inside: E = -GM/R^3 * r, V = -GM/2R^3 * (3R^2 - r^2)

Spherical Shell:

  • Outside: E = -GM/r^2, V = -GM/r
  • Surface: E = -GM/R^2, V = -GM/R
  • Inside: E = 0, V = -GM/R

details.summary: Mathematical expressions for gravitational intensity and potential for solid spheres and spherical shells at different positions.

subject: Physics
topic: Gravitational Potential Energy and Kepler's Laws
text:
Gravitational Potential Energy: Work done in assembling the system of masses from infinity. U = -GMm/r. On earth's surface, U = -GMm/R.

Kepler's Laws:

  • 1st Law: Planets revolve in elliptical orbits with the sun at one of the two foci.
  • 2nd Law: The position vector sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time (dA/dt = constant).
  • 3rd Law: T^2 ∝ a^3 or T^2 = Ka^3, where a is the semi-major axis and T is the time period.
image_descriptions: Diagram of the Sun-Planet system showing an elliptical orbit, the Sun at one focus, the major and minor axes, and the planet's position.

details.summary: Covers gravitational potential energy and the three laws of planetary motion formulated by Kepler.

subject: Physics
text:
A satellite is a body which is revolving continuously in an orbit around a comparatively much larger body.

Satellite are of two types:

  • Natural Satellite: A satellite created by nature is called a natural satellite. e.g. Moon
  • Artificial Satellite: A man made satellite is called an artificial satellite. e.g. SPUTNIK-I

Orbital Velocity of a Satellite: Orbital velocity of a satellite is the velocity required to put the satellite into its orbit around the earth.

Where, M = mass of the earth, R = radius of the earth, h = height of the satellite above the earth's surface, and R + h = orbital radius of the satellite.

If g is the acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface, then g = GM/R^2 or gR^2 = GM.

When the satellite revolves close to the surface of the earth, i.e. h = 0, the orbital velocity becomes v_o = sqrt(gR). Given g = 9.8 m/s^2 and R = 6.4 x 10^6 m, v_o = 7.92 km/s ≈ 8 km/s.

details.summary: Definitions of natural and artificial satellites and derivation of orbital velocity.

subject: Physics
text:
It is the time taken by a satellite to complete one revolution around the earth.

T = circumference of the orbit / orbital velocity = 2π(R + h) / v_o

When the satellite revolves close to the surface of the earth, i.e. h = 0, the time period is T = 2π * sqrt(R/g) = 2π * sqrt(3π / Gρ). Putting g = 9.8 m/s^2 and R = 6.4 x 10^6 m, T = 5078 s = 84.6 min.

details.summary: Derivation of the time period of a satellite and calculation for near-earth orbit.

subject: Physics
text:
Total Energy of a Satellite: The potential energy of a satellite is U = -GMm/r. The kinetic energy is K = GMm/2r. The total energy E = K + U = -GMm/2r.

Binding Energy of a Satellite: The energy required to remove the satellite from its orbit around the earth to infinity is called binding energy. The total energy is -GMm/2r. In order to escape to infinity, it must be supplied an extra energy equal to +GMm/2r. Hence, binding energy of a satellite = GMm/2r.

details.summary: Energy relations for a satellite in orbit and definition of binding energy.

subject: Physics
content:
### Escape Velocity
- **Definition**: The minimum velocity with which a body must be projected vertically upwards in order that it may just escape from the gravitational field of the earth.
- **Formula**: $v_e = \sqrt{2gR}$
- **Value on Earth**: The value of escape velocity on the earth’s surface is **11.6 km/s**.
- **Relation to Orbital Velocity**: The relation between the orbital velocity of a satellite ($v_o$) and escape velocity ($v_e$) is given by:
  $$v_e = \sqrt{2} v_o$$

subject: Physics
content:
### Mass and Weight
- **Mass**: 
  - Measure of inertia of a body.
  - Greater the mass, greater the inertia.
  - Always constant for a body regardless of location.
- **Weight**:
  - Product of mass and gravitational acceleration at a specific place.
  - Formula: $w = mg$
  - Can vary slightly from place to place on Earth.
- **Variation on Earth**:
  - **Maximum Weight**: At the poles.
  - **Minimum Weight**: At the equator.

subject: Physics
content:
### Weight of a Body in Elevator or Lift
When a person is inside an accelerating lift, the apparent weight changes based on the motion:
1. **Weight Increased**: When the lift is ascending with upward acceleration OR descending with downward deceleration.
2. **Weight Decreased**: When the lift is descending with downward acceleration OR ascending with upward deceleration.
3. **Weightlessness**: When the lift is moving downward with an acceleration equal to gravitational acceleration ($a = g$).

subject: Physics
content:
### Weight of a Body at the Moon
- The mass and radius of the Moon are less than those of the Earth.
- Consequently, the force of gravity on the Moon is less than on Earth.
- **Gravitational Acceleration on Moon**: $g_{moon} = \frac{g_{earth}}{6}$

subject: Physics
text:
Matter: Any substance which has mass and occupies space is called matter.

There are three states of matter:

  • (i) Solid: Substances in which intermolecular forces are so strong that the molecules or ions remains almost fixed at their equilibrium positions.
  • (ii) Liquid: Substances in which intermolecular forces are lesser compared to solid and their shape can be changed.
  • (iii) Gases: In gases intermolecular forces are very small and their shape and volume can be easily changed.

details.summary: Definition and classification of matter based on intermolecular forces.

subject: Physics
text:
Elasticity: Elasticity is the property of body by virtue of which a body regains or tends to regain its original configuration (shape as well as size), after the removal of applied forces and body itself is called elastic body.

Some Terms Related to Elasticity:

  • (i) Deforming Force: If a force applied on a body produces a change in the normal positions of the molecules of the body which results in a change in the configuration of the body either in length, volume or shape, then the force applied is called deforming force.
  • (ii) Perfect Elastic Body: If a body completely regains its original configuration on removal of external deforming forces, it is called a perfectly elastic body.
  • (iii) Plastic Body: If a body has no tendency to regain its original configuration and tends to maintain its deformed state even after the removal of the deforming force, then the body is called a plastic (or non-elastic) body.
  • (iv) Elastic Limit: The maximum deforming force upto which a body retains its property of elasticity is called elastic limit of the material of body.

details.summary: Definitions of elasticity, deforming force, elastic bodies, plastic bodies, and elastic limit.

subject: Physics
text:
Stress: The internal restoring force acting per unit area of a deformed body is called stress.

The SI unit of stress is Nm^-2 or pascal (Pa).

There are two types of stress:

  • (i) Normal stress: The normal stress is defined as the deforming force acting per unit area normal to the surface of the body.
  • (ii) Tangential stress: The tangential stress is defined as the deforming force acting per unit area tangential to the surface of the body.

details.summary: Definition, formula, units, and types of stress.

subject: Physics
text:
Strain is the ratio of change in configuration produced in a body to the original configuration of the body. Being the ratio of two similar quantities, strain is a unitless and dimensionless quantity. Strain is of three types:

  • Longitudinal Strain: Change in length per unit original length.
  • Volume Strain: Change in volume per unit original volume.
  • Shearing Strain: When there is change in shape of a body without change in its volume, then the strain produced is called shearing strain and it is defined as the angle through which a plane perpendicular to the fixed surface of the cubical body gets turned under the effect of tangential force.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a cubical body fixed at the bottom surface, with a tangential force applied at the top, causing a shear angle theta.

subject: Physics
text:
When a deforming force is applied at the free end of a suspended wire of length l and radius R, then its length increases by dl but its radius decrease by dR. The ratio between the lateral strain and the longitudinal strain is known as Poisson's ratio (σ).

  • Theoretical value of σ lies between -1 and +1/2.
  • Practical value of σ lies between 0 and +1/2.

subject: Physics
text:
Hooke's Law: Within the elastic limit, the stress developed in a body is directly proportional to the strain produced in the body (Stress = E × Strain). There are three types of modulus of elasticity:

  • Young's modulus of elasticity (Y): Ratio of normal stress to longitudinal strain.
  • Bulk modulus of elasticity (K): Ratio of normal stress to volumetric strain.
  • Modulus of rigidity or shear modulus of elasticity (η): Ratio of tangential stress to shearing strain.
formulas: η = (tangential stress) / (shearing strain) = (F/A) / θ = FL / Ax

subject: Physics
text:
Hydrostatics is a branch of physics that deals with the characteristics of fluids at rest. Thrust is the force or push acting on an object perpendicular to its surface. Pressure (p) is defined as Thrust / Area. The SI unit of pressure is N/m^2, also called pascal (Pa). It is a scalar quantity.

Atmospheric Pressure: The pressure on the surface of the earth due to the atmosphere. SI unit is Nm^-2 or pascal, CGS unit is dyne/cm^2.

subject: Physics
text:
Barometer: A device used to measure atmospheric pressure. It consists of a glass tube open at one end, filled with mercury. Measured pressure is given by p = ρgh, where ρ is the density of mercury and h is the height of the mercury column. Atmospheric pressure for a 76 cm mercury column is 1.01 x 10^5 Pa.

Density: Defined as mass per unit volume. Density (d) = Mass (m) / Volume (V). The SI unit is kgm^-3.

Change in Density of a Liquid:

  • If equal volumes of two liquids of densities d1 and d2 are mixed, the density of the mixture is d = (d1 + d2) / 2.
  • If two liquids of masses m1 and m2, and densities d1 and d2 are mixed, the density of the mixture is d = (m1 + m2) / (m1/d1 + m2/d2).
  • Liquids are incompressible; their density is the same throughout.

Relative Density (Specific Gravity): The ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water at 4°C. It has no unit. Density of water at 4°C is 1.0 x 10^3 kgm^-3.

Pressure of Liquid: The normal force exerted by a liquid per unit area. p = hρg, where h is height, ρ is density, and g is acceleration due to gravity. For a point at depth h below the surface of a liquid of density ρ, p = p_o + hρg. The excess pressure ρgh is called gauge pressure.
formulas: Relative density = Density of substance / Density of water at 4°C

details.summary: Covers fundamental fluid properties including barometer mechanics, density calculations for mixtures, relative density, and hydrostatic pressure formulas.

subject: Physics
topic: Laws of Liquid Pressure, Pascal's Law, Buoyancy, and Archimedes' Principle
text:
Laws of Liquid Pressure:

  • Pressure inside a liquid is same at every point on the same horizontal plane.
  • Pressure exerted by liquid is normal to any surface in contact.
  • Pressure at any point is independent of the shape of the liquid surface or area.
  • Centre of pressure is the point where the resultant liquid pressure acts.

Pascal's Law: If pressure is applied to an enclosed liquid, it is transmitted into the entire liquid without being diminished in magnitude.

Buoyant Force or Buoyancy: An upward force acting on a body immersed in a liquid, equal to the weight of the liquid displaced.

Archimedes' Principle: When a body is immersed in liquid at rest, it appears lighter. Apparent weight = Actual weight - Upthrust = mg(1 - ρ/d), where d is density of body and ρ is density of liquid.

Laws of Floatation: Two forces act: (i) Weight (w) downwards, (ii) Upthrust (F) upwards.

  • w > F: Body sinks.
  • w = F: Body floats with whole volume inside.
  • w < F: Body floats with some part outside.

details.summary: Covers the laws governing liquid pressure, Pascal's principle, buoyancy, Archimedes' principle, and the conditions for floatation.

subject: Physics
text:
Flow of fluids mainly are of three types:

  • Streamlined flow: Flow of a fluid is said to be streamlined, if each element of the fluid passing through a particular point travels along the same path, with exactly the same velocity as that of the preceding element.
  • Laminar flow: A special case of streamline flow is known as laminar flow, in which a fluid has a steady flow in the form of parallel layers and these do not mix with one another.
  • Turbulent flow: A turbulent flow is the one in which the motion of the fluid particles is disordered or irregular. In such a flow, most of the energy used up in maintaining the flow, is spent in causing eddies in the fluid and only a small part of the energy is used for the actual forward flow.

details.summary: Classification of fluid flow into Streamlined, Laminar, and Turbulent.

subject: Physics
text:
Critical Velocity: For a fluid, the critical velocity is that limiting velocity of the fluid flow upto which the flow is streamlined and beyond which the flow becomes turbulent. Value of critical velocity for the flow of liquid of density ρ and coefficient of viscosity η flowing through a horizontal tube of radius r is given by:

Reynolds' Number (NR): It is a unitless and dimensionless number. A smaller value of Reynolds' number (generally NR ≤ 1000) indicates a streamline flow but a higher value (NR ≥ 1500) indicates that the flow is turbulent and between 1000 to 1500, the flow is unstable.

details.summary: Definitions and mathematical relations for critical velocity and Reynolds' number.

subject: Physics
text: Let us consider the streamline flow of an ideal, non-viscous fluid through a tube of variable cross-section. At the two sections, the cross-sectional areas be A1 and A2 respectively and the fluid velocities are v1 and v2, then according to the equation of continuity A1v1ρ1 = A2v2ρ2 where, ρ1 and ρ2 are the respective densities of the fluid. Equation of continuity is based on the conservation of mass. If the fluid which is flowing, is incompressible, then ρ1 = ρ2. So, equation of continuity is simplified as A1v1 = A2v2 or Av = constant. This is known as equation of continuity.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a tube with variable cross-section, where area A1 narrows to A2, with fluid entering at velocity v1 and exiting at velocity v2.

details.summary: Explanation of the equation of continuity based on the principle of conservation of mass.

subject: Physics
text:
Flowing liquid has three types of energy:

  • Pressure energy: If there is a pressure p on the surface area A of liquid and liquid covers a distance l due to this, then pressure energy = pAl. Pressure energy per unit volume = p.
  • Kinetic energy: If mass m and volume V of a liquid is flowing with velocity v, then kinetic energy per unit volume = 1/2 dv2, where d = density of liquid.
  • Potential energy: If mass m of liquid is at a height h above the earth's surface, then potential energy is mgh. For unit volume of liquid m = d, therefore potential energy per unit volume = dgh.
formulas: Pressure energy per unit volume = p
Kinetic energy per unit volume = 1/2 dv^2
Potential energy per unit volume = dgh

details.summary: Breakdown of pressure, kinetic, and potential energy in a flowing liquid.

subject: Physics
text:
Bernoulli's Theorem: According to this theorem, "if a liquid is in streamline motion, then at each point of its path, its total energy of unit volume, i.e. sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy is constant."

Torricelli's Theorem: It states that the velocity of efflux i.e. the velocity with which the liquid flows out of an orifice (i.e. a narrow hole) in a vessel containing liquid is equal to that which a freely falling body would acquire in falling through a vertical distance equal to the depth of orifice below the free surface of liquid in vessel. Quantitatively, velocity of efflux, v = sqrt(2gh), where h is the depth of orifice below the free surface of liquid in vessel.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for Bernoulli's and Torricelli's theorems.

subject: Physics
text:
Viscosity: The property of liquids due to which they oppose the relative motion between their different layers is called viscosity. If viscous force F is acting between two layers of liquid of area A and having a velocity gradient dv/dx between them, then F = -ηA(dv/dx), where η = coefficient of viscosity, A = area of cross-section. Here, negative sign shows viscous force is acting in opposite direction to the flow of a liquid.

Stokes' Law: When a spherical body is dropped in a liquid, then the liquid applies a retarding force, F = 6πηrv, where v = velocity of the body, r = radius of the body and η = coefficient of viscosity of liquid.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for viscosity and Stokes' Law.

subject: Physics
text: If a small spherical body is dropped in a fluid, then initially it is accelerated under the action of gravity. However, with an increase in speed, the viscous force increases and soon it balances the weight of the body. Now, the body moves with a constant velocity is called the terminal velocity.

details.summary: Definition and formula for terminal velocity of a spherical body in a fluid.

subject: Physics
text:
Poiseuille's studied the rate of flow of a liquid through a horizontal capillary tube and concluded that the volume (V) of a liquid flowing out per second through a capillary tube varies:

  • (i) directly as the pressure difference (p) across the two ends of the tube, i.e. V ∝ p.
  • (ii) directly as the fourth power of radius (r) of the tube, i.e. V ∝ r^4.
  • (iii) inversely as the length (l) of the tube, i.e. V ∝ 1/l.
  • (iv) inversely as the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid, i.e. V ∝ 1/eta.

On combining these factors, we get V ∝ (p * r^4) / (eta * l) or V = (pi * p * r^4) / (8 * eta * l). This formula is true only for the steady flow of liquid through a horizontal capillary tube.

details.summary: Factors affecting the rate of flow of liquid through a capillary tube.

subject: Physics
text:
The forces between the molecules of the substances are called intermolecular forces. There are two types:

  • Cohesive force: The intermolecular force of attraction acting between the molecules of same substance.
  • Adhesive force: The intermolecular force of attraction acting between the molecules of different substances.

Important Notes:

  • Both cohesive and adhesive forces are attractive having range of 10^-9 m to 1 Å.
  • The liquid for which cohesive force is larger than adhesive force, does not wet the walls of vessel, e.g. mercury does not wet the glass vessel.
  • The liquid for which adhesive force is larger than cohesive force, wets the walls of vessel, e.g. water wets the glass vessel.

details.summary: Distinction between cohesive and adhesive forces and their effect on wetting.

subject: Physics
text:
It is property by virtue of which the free surface of liquid at rest behaves like stretched membrane tending to contract, so as to possess minimum surface area.

  • Surface tension is the force acting normally on unit length of imaginary line drawn on the surface of liquid. Its unit is Nm^-1.
  • Surface tension of a liquid is independent of area of the surface.
  • A steel needle may be made to float on the surface of liquid due to surface tension.

Applications:

  • Spherical shape of drops and bubbles is due to surface tension as they tend to have minimum surface area.
  • Excess pressure for liquid drop (Δp)_d = 2S / r
  • Excess pressure for bubble (Δp)_b = 4S / r

details.summary: Definition, properties, and applications of surface tension.

subject: Physics
text:
The potential energy of the molecules in the surface of liquid is called the surface energy.

Surface energy = T * ΔA, where T = surface tension of liquid and ΔA = increase in surface area.

Concept Related to Factorization to Recombination of Liquid Drop:

  • When a big drop of water factorized in n small drops, then energy is absorbed. Energy = 4πR^2T(n^(1/3) - 1)
  • When n small drops make a big drop, then energy is released. Energy = 4πR^2T(n^(1/3) - 1)

details.summary: Surface energy definition and energy changes during drop factorization/recombination.

subject: Physics
text:
The angle between the tangent to the liquid surface and the tangent to the solid surface at the point of contact is known as angle of contact.

Important Points Relates to Angle of Contact:

  • The angle of contact is always measured through the liquid.
  • If angle of contact θ = 90°, then:
    • liquid will wet the walls of the vessel.
    • the level of liquid will be horizontal in the capillary tube.
  • If θ < 90°, then:
    • liquid will wet the walls of the vessel.
    • liquid will rise in the capillary tube.
    • level of liquid in capillary tube will be concave.
  • If θ > 90°, then:
    • liquid will not wet the walls of the vessel.
    • liquid will fall in capillary tube.
    • level of liquid in capillary will be convex.
  • Angle of contact increases on increasing the temperature.
  • Addition of detergent to a liquid decreases angle of contact, hence the surface tension also decreases.

details.summary: Definition and properties of the angle of contact in fluids.

subject: Physics
text:
A tube with a fine and uniform bore throughout its length is called a capillary tube. The phenomenon of rise or fall of liquid in a capillary tube is called capillarity.

If a liquid rises or falls a height h in a capillary tube and angle of contact is θ, then h = (2T cos θ) / (rdg), where r = radius of capillary tube, d = density of liquid and T = surface tension of liquid.

Rate of flow of liquid in a capillary is Q = (πpr^4) / (8n&l)

details.summary: Definition of capillary tube, capillarity, and associated mathematical formulas for height and flow rate.

subject: Physics
chapter: Heat and Kinetic Theory of Gases
text:
Temperature is the measure of degree of hotness or coldness of a body. The temperature of a body can be defined as the state/condition which would determine the direction of flow of heat when this body is placed in contact with another body.

Temperature Scales: To measure temperature, two fixed points are taken; one of them is freezing point of water, known as icepoint and other point is boiling point of water, known as steam point.

  • (i) Celsius Scale (°C): In this scale, the melting point of ice is taken as 0°C and the boiling point of water as 100°C and the space between these two points is divided into 100 equal parts. This scale was designed by Anders Celsius in 1710.
  • (ii) Fahrenheit Scale (°F): In this scale, the melting point of ice is taken as 32°F and the boiling point of water as 212°F and the space between these two points is divided into 180 equal parts. This scale was designed by Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1717.
  • (iii) Kelvin Scale (K): In this scale, the ice point and the steam point (boiling point) are taken as 273 K and 373 K, respectively and the space between these two points is divided into 100 equal parts. It was designed by Kelvin.
  • (iv) Reaumur Scale (R): In this scale, ice point and boiling point are taken as 0°R and 80°R respectively. 1°R is equal to the 80th part of difference between two points. This scale was designed by RA Reaumur in 1730.
  • (v) Rankine Scale (Ra): In this scale, ice point and steam point are taken as 460° Ra and 672° Ra, respectively. 1°Ra is equal to the 212th part of difference between two points.

details.summary: Introduction to temperature definitions and various temperature scales including Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin, Reaumur, and Rankine.

subject: Physics
text:
Some Important Temperature on Various Scales:

  • Freezing of water: 0°C, 32°F, 273 K
  • Normal temperature of the room: 27°C, 80.6°F, 300 K
  • Normal temperature of the human: 37°C, 98.6°F, 310 K
  • Boiling point of the water: 100°C, 212°F, 373 K

Thermometer: The device which measures the temperature of the body is called a thermometer.

Types of Thermometers:

  • Constant-Volume Gas Thermometer: If p0, p100, ptr and pt are the pressures of gas at temperatures 0°C, 100°C, triple point of water and unknown temperature (t°C) respectively, then t = ((p - p0) / (p100 - p0)) * 100 °C or T = 273.16 * (p / ptr) K
  • Platinum Resistance Thermometer: If R0, R100, Rtr and Rt are the resistances of a platinum wire at temperatures 0°C, 100°C, triple point of water and unknown temperature (t°C) respectively, then t = ((Rt - R0) / (R100 - R0)) * 100 °C or T = (Rt / Rtr) * 273.16 K
  • Mercury Thermometer: In this thermometer, the length of a mercury column from some fixed point is taken as thermometric property. Thus, t = ((lt - l0) / (l100 - l0)) * 100 °C or T = (lt / ltr) * 273.16 K
