subject: Physics
text:
Thermal Expansion: Change in temperature of a body causes change in its dimensions. Thus, increase in the dimensions (i.e., length, breadth and thickness) of a body due to increase in its temperature is called thermal expansion.

Thermal Expansion of Solids: All solids expand on heating. It is of three types:

  • Linear Expansion: Expansion along a line. Coefficient of Linear Expansion (α) = ΔL / (L * Δt). Unit is per °C.
  • Superficial Expansion: Expansion in two dimensions (area). Coefficient of Superficial Expansion (β) = ΔA / (A * Δt). Unit is per °C.
  • Volume Expansion or Cubical Expansion: Expansion in three dimensions (volume). Coefficient of Volume Expansion (γ) = ΔV / (V * Δt). Unit is per °C.

Relation between α, β and γ: β = 2α, γ = 3α, also α:β:γ = 1:2:3

Thermal Expansion of Liquids: Liquids have only cubical expansion. Two types:

  • Apparent Expansion: Expansion of liquid neglecting expansion of vessel. Apparent expansion coefficient (γa) = ΔVa / (V * Δt).

details.summary: Definitions and mathematical coefficients for linear, superficial, and volume expansion of solids, the relationship between these coefficients, and the concept of apparent expansion in liquids.

subject: Physics
text:
Real Expansion: It is the actual increase in volume of liquid.

Relation between γa and γr: γr = γa + γg, where γr = real expansion of liquid, γa = apparent expansion of liquid, γg = volume expansion coefficient of material vessel.

Anomalous/Exceptional Behaviour of Water: As the temperature of water increases from 0 to 4°C, the density of water increases and as temperature increases beyond 4°C, the density decreases.

Thermal Expansion of Gases: Two coefficients: (i) Volume Coefficient (γv) - change in volume per unit volume per unit degree celsius at constant pressure. (ii) Pressure Coefficient (γp) - change in pressure per unit degree celsius at constant volume.

Heat: Form of energy that flows from one body to another because of temperature difference. SI unit is Joule (J), CGS unit is calorie (cal). 1 Calorie = 4.18 J.

Specific Heat: Amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1°C. Unit: cal/g°C or joule/g°C.

Molar Specific Heat: Amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 mole of a gas by 1°C. Two types: (i) Molar specific heat at constant volume (Cv), (ii) Molar specific heat at constant pressure (Cp). Mayer's formula: Cp - Cv = R.

Latent Heat: Amount of heat required to change the state of unit mass of a substance at constant temperature. Two types: (i) Latent heat of Fusion. Latent heat of fusion of ice is 80 cal/gm.
image_descriptions: Graph showing the anomalous behaviour of water: Density on Y-axis vs Temperature on X-axis, showing a peak at 4°C.

details.summary: Covers real expansion, anomalous behaviour of water, thermal expansion of gases, specific heat, molar specific heat, and latent heat.

subject: Physics
topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
text:
(ii) Latent heat of vaporisation: The amount of heat required to change the state of unit mass of a substance from liquid to vapour at its boiling point is called latent heat of vaporisation. In case of water the latent heat of vaporisation is 536 cal/gm.

Note: Latent heat of vaporisation is more than the latent heat of fusion. This is because when a substance gets converted from liquid to vapour, there is a large increase in volume. Hence, more amount of heat is required. But when a solid gets converted to a liquid, then the increase in volume is negligible. Hence, very less amount of heat is required.

Terms Related to Change of State

There are some important terms related to change of state are given below:

  • (i) Melting and Melting Point: The process of change of state from solid to liquid is called melting. The temperature at which solid starts to liquify is known as the melting point of that solid. The melting point of a substance at atmospheric pressure is called normal melting point.
  • (ii) Fusion and Freezing Point: The process of change of state from liquid to solid is called fusion. The temperature at which liquid starts to freeze is known as the freezing point of the liquid.
  • (iii) Vaporisation and Boiling Point: The process of change of state from liquid to vapour (or gas) is called vaporisation. During the change of state (completely), the temperature remains constant which implies both liquid and vapour are at the thermal equilibrium. The temperature at which the liquid starts to evaporate is called the boiling point of the liquid.
  • (iv) Sublimation: The process of change of state directly from solid to vapour (or gas) is known as sublimation. There is no matter of liquid state of substance. The reverse process of sublimation is not possible e.g., camphor, nephthalene balls etc.

details.summary: Definitions and concepts regarding latent heat of vaporisation, melting, fusion, boiling, and sublimation.

subject: Physics
text:
Heat Capacity or Thermal Capacity

The heat capacity of a body is defined as the amount of heat required to raise its temperature through one degree.

Heat capacity = Mass x Specific heat

S = mc

The SI unit of heat capacity is JK^-1

Water Equivalent

The water equivalent of a body is defined as the mass of water which requires the same amount of heat as is required by the given body for the same rise of temperature.

Water equivalent = Mass x Specific heat

w = mc

The SI unit of water equivalent is kg.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for Heat Capacity and Water Equivalent.

subject: Physics
text:
Principle of Calorimetry

The branch of physics that deals with the measurement of heat is called calorimetry. The principle of calorimetry states that the heat gained by the cold body must be equal to the heat lost by hot body, provided there is no exchange of heat with the surroundings.

Heat gained = Heat lost

This principle is a consequence of the law of conservation of energy.

details.summary: Definition and principle of calorimetry based on the law of conservation of energy.

subject: Physics
text:
KINETIC THEORY OF GASES

All matter is made up of molecules. The molecules of a gas are in state of rapid and continuous motion. Their velocity depends on temperature. Using this molecular motion, various properties of a gas like temperature, pressure, energy etc can be explained. Hence, this theory is called kinetic theory of gases.

Kinetic theory of gases was developed by Claussius and Maxwell.

Assumptions of Kinetic Theory of Gases

The entire structure of the kinetic theory of gases is based on the following assumptions:

  • All gases consist of molecules. The molecules are rigid, elastic spheres identical in all respects for a given gas and different for different gases.
  • The size of the gas molecules is very small as compared to the distance between them.
  • The molecules of a gas are in a state of continuous random motion, moving in all directions with all possible velocities.
  • During the random motion, the molecules collide with one another and with the walls of the vessel.
  • The collisions are perfectly elastic and there are no forces of attraction or repulsion between the molecules.
  • Between two collisions a molecule moves in a straight path with a uniform velocity.
  • The collisions are almost instantaneous i.e., the time of collision of two molecules is negligible as compared to time interval between two successive collisions.
  • Inspite of the molecular collisions, the density remains uniform throughout the gas.

details.summary: Introduction to Kinetic Theory of Gases, its developers, and its fundamental assumptions.

subject: Physics
text:
Mass (m), volume (V), pressure (p) and temperature (T) are measurable properties of a gas. Gas laws inter-relate these properties.

  • Boyle's Law: At constant temperature, the volume of a given mass of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.
  • Charles' Law: At constant pressure, the volume of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.
  • Pressure Law or Gay Lussac's Law: At constant volume, pressure of the gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.
  • Absolute zero: The temperature at which all molecular motion ceases.

details.summary: Overview of Boyle's, Charles', and Gay Lussac's laws relating pressure, volume, and temperature.

subject: Physics
text:
An ideal or perfect gas is that gas which strictly obeys the gas laws. Characteristics include:

  • The size of the molecule of an ideal gas is zero (point mass with no dimensions).
  • There is no force of attraction or repulsion amongst the molecules of an ideal gas.

details.summary: Definition and characteristics of an ideal gas.

subject: Physics
text: Real gases obey the Vander Waal's equation at high pressure and low temperature.

details.summary: Equations for real gases using constants a and b.

subject: Physics
text: Critical temperature (Tc): Maximum temperature below which a gas can be liquefied by pressure alone. Critical pressure (Pc): Minimum pressure necessary to liquefy a gas at critical temperature. Critical volume (Vc): Volume of 1 mole of gas at critical pressure and temperature.

details.summary: Definitions of critical state parameters.

subject: Physics
text: Gaseous pressure is caused by the collision of gas molecules with the walls of the vessel.

details.summary: Kinetic theory derivation of gaseous pressure.

subject: Physics
text:
Thermodynamics is the branch of physics which deals with the study of heat and temperature and the relation of heat energy with different types of energy.

Thermodynamic System: An aggregate of an extremely large number of atoms or molecules which are confined with certain boundaries. It may be characterised by certain thermodynamic variables e.g. pressure, volume, temperature, mass, density etc.

Internal Energy: The net energy (i.e. the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies) contained by the molecules of the substance. It is represented by U.

details.summary: Definition of thermodynamics, thermodynamic systems, and internal energy.

subject: Physics
text:
Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: Formulated by RH Fowler in 1931. It states that if two systems A and B are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

First Law of Thermodynamics: The amount of heat given to a system is used up in two ways: first to increase the internal energy and second to do external work.

  • It is a form of the law of conservation of energy.
  • Work done by the system depends on the path followed by it.
formulas: W = integral(from V1 to V2) p dV

details.summary: Covers Zeroth Law and First Law of Thermodynamics including mathematical expressions.

subject: Physics
text:
If the thermodynamic variables of a system undergo a change with time, then the thermodynamical process is said to be occurred.

  • Cyclic process: When the system returns to its initial state after doing work, then the process is called cyclic process. For cyclic process, ΔU = 0. From 1st law, ΔQ = ΔW.
  • Isobaric process: If during a process in the system, pressure remains constant, then the process is called isobaric process, so heat supplied is used up partially in changing the volume and partially in changing the temperature. W = pΔV = p(V2 - V1).
  • Isochoric process: If during a process in a system, volume remains constant, then the process is called isochoric process. For this process, ΔW = 0. ΔQ = ΔU. Heat supplied is used to increase in internal energy.
  • Isothermal process: If a physical process in a system takes place in such a way, that during the whole process temperature remains constant, then the process is called isothermal process. For isothermal process, Boyle's law is followed, i.e., pV = constant [from the equation, pV = μRT]. Since, temperature remains constant, so there is no change in internal energy, i.e., ΔU = 0. ΔQ = ΔW = pΔV. Work done in isothermal process: The work done in isothermal process from volume V1 to V2 is W = 2.3026 μRT log10(V2/V1). The workdone in isothermal process from pressure p1 to p2 is W = 2.3026 μRT log10(p1/p2).
  • Adiabatic process: If physical process in a system takes place in such a way that there is no exchange of heat between system and the atmosphere, then process is called adiabatic process. For adiabatic process, Poisson's law is followed, i.e., pV^γ = constant or TV^(γ-1) = constant or T^γ / p^(γ-1) = constant. For adiabatic process, ΔQ = 0. From 1st law of thermodynamics, ΔU = -ΔW. During adiabatic process, specific heat is zero. Work done in adiabatic process: W = (p1V1 - p2V2)/(γ - 1) = μR(T1 - T2)/(γ - 1), where R = principal gas constant and μ = number of moles. During an adiabatic process, system performs the work on the basis of internal energy. For the adiabatic process more pressure difference is required to produce equal change in volume.
image_descriptions: Graph showing Slope of Adiabatic and Isothermal Curves for expansion: A p-V diagram where the Isothermal process curve is above the Adiabatic process curve, both sloping downwards from point P to Q and R respectively.

Graph showing Slope of Adiabatic and Isothermal Curves for compression: A p-V diagram where the Adiabatic process curve is above the Isothermal process curve, both sloping upwards from point R and Q to P.

details.summary: Overview of various thermodynamic processes including cyclic, isobaric, isochoric, isothermal, and adiabatic processes, along with their governing laws and work done formulas.

subject: Physics
text:
Entropy

It is molecular disorder of system and it is thermodynamic function depending only on temperature of system. ΔS = heat absorbed / absolute temperature => ΔS = ΔQ/T. Entropy is the thermodynamic function which remains unchanged in an adiabatic process.

Second Law of Thermodynamics

It is impossible for a self acting device, unaided by an external agency which acts in a cycle to absorb heat from the source and convert whole amount of it into work.

Heat Engine

Heat engine is a device which converts heat into mechanical work. A heat engine essentially consists of three parts: (i) source of heat at higher temperature (ii) working substance (steam in steam engine, fuel vapours and air in diesel engine) (iii) sink of heat at lower temperature.

details.summary: Definitions of entropy, the second law of thermodynamics, and the basic components of a heat engine.

subject: Physics
text:
Thermal Efficiency of Heat Engine (η): It is defined as the ratio of net work done per cycle by the engine to the total amount of heat absorbed per cycle by the working substance from the source.

Efficiency of heat engine is given by: η = (1 - T2/T1) x 100%, where T1 = temperature of source, T2 = temperature of sink.
formulas: η = (Net work done per cycle) / (Total amount of heat absorbed per cycle)

details.summary: Definition and formula for thermal efficiency of a heat engine.

subject: Physics
text:
Carnot Cycle: Carnot cycle is the ideal cycle of operation of a heat engine, devised by Nicholas Leonard Sadi Carnot. This consists of the following four stages:

  • (i) Isothermal expansion (heat absorbed)
  • (ii) Adiabatic expansion (work done is positive, W_expansion)
  • (iii) Isothermal compression (heat released)
  • (iv) Adiabatic compression (work done is negative, W_compression)

Efficiency of Carnot engine: η = (1 - T2/T1) x 100% = (W/Q1) x 100% = ((Q1 - Q2)/Q1) x 100%. For Carnot cycle, Q1/Q2 = T1/T2.

Carnot Theorem: No heat engine operating between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine.
image_descriptions: A P-V diagram showing the Carnot cycle with four points. The path from 1 to 2 is Isothermal expansion (Heat absorbed), 2 to 3 is Adiabatic expansion (Positive work done), 3 to 4 is Isothermal compression (Heat released), and 4 to 1 is Adiabatic compression (Negative work done).

details.summary: Explanation of the Carnot cycle stages, efficiency formulas, and Carnot's theorem.

subject: Physics
text:
Refrigerator: It is a device which takes heat from a cold body, work is done on it and the heat is rejected to the source.

Coefficient of performance, β = Q2/W = Q2/(Q1 - Q2), where Q1 = heat absorbed and Q2 = heat rejected.

For Carnot refrigerator, β = T2/(T1 - T2) = (1 - η)/η

details.summary: Definition and coefficient of performance formulas for a refrigerator.

subject: Physics
text:
Transmission of Heat: Heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature. There are three processes by which transmission of heat takes place:

  • (i) Conduction: Process of transmission of heat in which heat goes from one particle to another particle of substance, but no particle leaves its position. In solids, transmission of heat takes place by conduction. All metals are good conductors of heat. Good absorbers are always also good radiators. Cooking utensils are provided with wooden or ebonite handles. Silver is the best conductor of heat.
  • (ii) Convection: Process of transmission of heat in which particles of substance go to another place after taking heat from the source and other particles come to their place. Land and see breezes are due to convection. The chimney used in a kitchen or in a factory is based on the convection. In rooms, ventilators are provided to escape the hot air by convection.
  • (iii) Radiation: Process of transmission of heat in which there is no need of medium for transfer of heat. It is the quickest way of transmission of heat. Heat from the sun comes to the earth by radiation.

Important Definitions:

  • Stable State: The state of material in which material cannot absorb or emit the heat.
  • Isothermal Surface: The conductor which have some temperature at all the points.
  • Temperature Gradient: The rate of change in temperature with the distance. Unit: °C/meter. Formula: Temperature gradient = (Q1 - Q2)/r

details.summary: Explanation of heat transmission methods (Conduction, Convection, Radiation) and related definitions.

subject: Physics
text:
Thermal Conductivity: The ability of a material to conduct heat through it. It is defined as the time rate of heat flow in a material for a given temperature difference.

For a metal rod of length l and area of cross-section A with ends at temperatures T1 and T2, the rate of heat flow (H) is:

  • H = KA(T1 - T2) / L
  • H = Q / t
  • Q = KA(ΔT / L) * t

K is the coefficient of thermal conductivity. SI unit: Js^-1m^-1K^-1 or Wm^-1K^-1.
tables:
| Types of combination | Series combination | Parallel Combination |
|---|---|---|
| Rate of Heat transfer | H = K1A(θ1 - θ2) / l1 = K2A(θ - θ2) / l2 | K = (K1A1 + K2A2) * Δθ / l |
| Contact surface temperature | Q = K1θ1l2 + K2θ2l1 / (k1l2 + k2l1) | — |
| Equivalent heat conductivity | K = (l1 + l2) / (l1/k1 + l2/k2) | K = (K1A1 + K2A2) / (A1 + A2) |
| Equivalent heat resistance | R = R1 + R2 | 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 |
image_descriptions: Table summarizing formulae for combination of metal rods in series and parallel configurations.

details.summary: Covers thermal conductivity, heat flow rate, thermal resistance, and combination of metal rods.

subject: Physics
text:
Definitions Related to Radiation:

  • Emissive Power (e): Amount of heat radiated by unit area of surface in one second. Unit: J/m^2s.
  • Emissivity (ε): Ratio of emissive power of a body to total emissive power of a perfectly black body at that temperature (ε = e/E).
  • Absorptive Power (a): Ratio of energy absorbed to energy incident.
  • Spectral Emissive Power (eλ): Amount of heat radiated by unit area in one second in unit spectral region at wavelength λ.
  • Spectral Absorptive Power: Ratio of radiations absorbed to total radiations incident at wavelength λ.
  • Perfectly Black Body: Absorbs all incident radiation; neither reflects nor transmits.
  • Kirchhoff’s Law: At any temperature and wavelength, the ratio of emissive power to absorptive power is constant for all substances and equal to that of a perfectly black body (eλ / aλ = Eλ).

details.summary: Definitions of radiation parameters and Kirchhoff's Law.

subject: Physics
text:
Stefan's Law: According to this law, the amount of heat radiated by unit area of surface in one second, is directly proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature of the body.

E ∝ T^4 or E = σT^4

where, σ is Stefan's constant. The unit of σ is Jm^-2s^-1K^-4 or Wm^-2K^-4 and its value is 5.67 × 10^-8 Wm^-2K^-4.

details.summary: Definition and formula for Stefan's Law regarding heat radiation.

subject: Physics
text:
Newton's Law of Cooling: According to this law, the rate of cooling of a body is directly proportional to the temperature difference of body and its surroundings.

Example: Hot water takes much less time in cooling from 100°C to 95°C than from 20°C to 15°C. If hot water and fresh tap-water are kept in a refrigerator, the rate of cooling of hot water will be faster than the tap-water.

details.summary: Definition and practical examples of Newton's Law of Cooling.

subject: Physics
text:
Wien's Displacement Law: According to this law, at a particular temperature of perfectly black body, the product of maximum wavelength (λm) and absolute temperature T is constant.

i.e., λmT = constant or λmT = b

where, the value of b is 29 × 10^-3 mK.

This is used to compute the temperature of the Sun or of the Stars.

details.summary: Definition and application of Wien's Displacement Law.

subject: Physics
text:
Optics is the branch of physics which deals with the study of behaviour, effect and properties of light.

LIGHT: Light is a form of energy which produces visual sensation in our eyes. Light is an electromagnetic wave which is transverse in nature. The speed of light in vacuum is 3 x 10^8 m/s.

Note: Ray of light - A straight line path along which the transfer of light energy takes place is called a ray of light.

Reflection of Light: The phenomenon of bouncing back of light rays in the same medium on striking a smooth surface is called reflection of light. There are two types of reflection:

  • (i) Regular reflection: If the reflecting surface is perfectly smooth surface, then the reflection is called regular reflection.
  • (ii) Irregular reflection: If the reflecting surface is rough, then the reflection is called irregular reflection.

Laws of Reflection: There are two laws of reflection:

  • (i) Angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.
  • (ii) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane.

Mirror: Mirror is a polished surface of glass from which all the light is reflected. If the reflecting surface is plane, then mirror is called plane mirror and if reflecting surface is spherical, then it is called spherical mirror.

Image: If light rays coming from a point on object meets at another point after reflection or appear to come from other point, then this second point is called the image of first point. There are two types of image:

  • (i) Real image: If the light rays coming from a point, meets at another point actually after reflection, then the image formed is called real image.
  • (ii) Virtual image: If the light rays coming from a point, does not meet actually after reflection or appear to come from another point, then the image formed is called virtual image.
formulas: Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection (i = r)
Speed of light in vacuum = 3 x 10^8 m/s

A normal line (N) is drawn perpendicular to the surface. subject: Physics
text:
In the plane mirror, the size of image is always equal to the size of the object and it is of virtual nature. The image in a plane mirror appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

Important points related to simple mirror:

  • If the object is displaced by a distance a towards or away from the mirror, then its image will be displaced by a distance a towards or away from the mirror.
  • The minimum size of the mirror required to see the full image of an observer is half the height of the observer.
  • If the plane mirror is rotated in the plane of incidence by an angle θ, then the reflected ray rotates by an angle 2θ.
  • Focal length of plane mirror is infinity, i.e. power is zero. Linear magnification produced by plane mirror is 1.
  • When two plane mirrors are kept facing each other at an angle θ and an object is placed between them, then number of images, n = (360°/θ) - 1, if (360°/θ) is even or the object lies symmetrically. Number of images, n = (360°/θ), if (360°/θ) is odd or the object lies asymmetrically.
  • When two plane mirrors are parallel to each other, then the number of images are infinity.

Note: The plane mirror is utilised in the form of kaleidoscope, periscope and looking glass, etc.

details.summary: Properties and mathematical relations for plane mirror reflection and multiple images.

subject: Physics
text:
If the reflecting surface of the mirror is curved inwards or outwards, then the mirror is called a spherical mirror. Spherical mirrors are of two types:

  • Concave mirror: The spherical mirror with inward curved reflecting surface is called concave mirror. A beam of light generally diverges after reflection from its surface, hence it is also called convergent mirror. e.g. The inner curved surface of a shining spoon can be considered as a concave mirror.
  • Convex mirror: The spherical mirror with outward curved reflecting surface is called convex mirror. A beam of light generally diverges after reflection from its surface, hence it is also called divergent mirror. e.g. The outer curved surface of a shining spoon can be considered as a convex mirror.

Some Definitions Related to Spherical Mirrors:

  • Centre of curvature: Centre of curvature of a spherical mirror is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is apart.
  • Radius of curvature: Radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is the radius of sphere of which the mirror is apart.
  • Pole: The pole of the spherical mirror is mid-point of its reflecting surface.
  • Principal axis: The principal axis of a spherical mirror is the line joining the pole and centre of curvature.
  • Aperture of mirror: The part of the reflecting surface of a mirror which can be exposed to the incident light is called its aperture.
  • Principal focus or focus: It is a point on the principal axis of the mirror at which the light rays coming parallel to principal axis, after reflection actually meet or appear to be coming from.
  • Focal length: The distance between pole and focus of a spherical mirror is called its focal length.

Relation between Focal Length and Radius of Curvature of Spherical Mirror: f = R/2

Diagram of a convex mirror showing principal axis, centre of curvature (C), focus (F), pole (P), aperture (M1-M2), and radius of curvature (R).

subject: Physics
topic: Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors
text:
While dealing with the reflection of light by spherical mirrors, we shall follow a set of sign convention called the new cartesian sign convention based on cartesian coordinates. In this convention, the pole (P) of the mirror is taken as the origin. The principal axis of the mirror is taken as X-axis of the coordinate system.

  • The object is always placed to the left of the mirror.
  • All distances parallel to principal axis (X-axis) are measured from the pole of the mirror.
  • Distances to the left of pole (-ve X-axis) are negative. Distances to the right of pole (+ve X-axis) are positive.
  • Distances measured perpendicularly above the principal axis (along + Y-axis) are taken as positive.
  • Distances measured perpendicularly below the principal axis (along - Y-axis) are taken as negative.

subject: Physics
topic: Image Formation by a Convex Mirror
text:
For studying the image formed by a convex mirror, there are two positions of the object which are considered: at infinity and at a finite distance from the mirror.

Identification of Mirrors

  • Plane mirror: Image is of same size as that of object for different positions.
  • Convex mirror: Image is diminished for all positions of object.
  • Concave mirror: Image formed behind the mirror is longer than the object.

Uses of Mirrors

  • Plane mirror: As looking glass.
  • Concave mirror: As shaving mirrors, used by doctors, shades of table lamp, for search lights.
  • Convex mirror: As back view mirrors in vehicles, in street lamps, etc.
  • Cylindrical mirror: Reflecting surface from the part of a cylinder.
tables:
| Position of object | Ray diagram | Position of image | Nature and size of image |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | Parallel rays incident on convex mirror reflecting away from focus | At the focus, behind the mirror | Virtual, erect and extremely diminished |
| Between infinity and the pole of the mirror | Rays incident on convex mirror forming image between P and F | Between the focus and the pole, behind the mirror | Virtual, erect and diminished |

subject: Physics
topic: Mirror Formula and Refraction of Light
text:
Mirror Formula

In spherical mirror, the distance of the object from its pole is called the object distance (u). The distance of the image from pole is called the image distance (v). The relation between quantities (u, v and f) is the mirror formula.

Linear Magnification

The ratio of height of image to the height of object is called linear magnification (m). Linear magnification produced by plane mirror is 1.

Refraction of Light

Change in path of a light ray as it passes from one medium to another. When light travels from a rarer medium to a denser one, it bends towards the normal (i > r) and when travels from a denser medium to a rarer one, it bends away from the normal (i < r).

Note: A medium in which the speed of light is more is known as optically rarer medium and the medium in which speed of light is lesser is known as optically denser medium. When a ray of light suffers refraction, its velocity and wavelength changes but frequency remain same.
formulas: m = height of image (I) / height of object (O)
image_descriptions: Diagram showing refraction of light: (1) Ray moving from rarer to denser medium bending towards the normal (i > r). (2) Ray moving from denser to rarer medium bending away from the normal (i < r).

details.summary: Covers the mirror equation, magnification definitions, and the fundamental principles of light refraction.

subject: Physics
content:
### Laws of Refraction
1. **First Law**: The incident ray, the normal to the surface of separation at the point of incidence, and the refracted ray all lie in the same plane.
2. **Second Law (Snell's Law)**: For a light ray of the same color passing between two media, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence ($i$) to the sine of the angle of refraction ($r$) is constant.
   $$  rac{\sin i}{\sin r} =  rac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} = 	ext{constant} $$
   Where $ rac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}$ is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first medium.

subject: Physics
content:
### Refractive Index ($\mu$)
- **Definition**: The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum ($c$) to the speed of light in the medium ($v$).
  $$ \mu =  rac{c}{v} =  rac{\lambda_{air}}{\lambda_{medium}} $$
- **Speed of Light in Vacuum**: $c = 3 	imes 10^8 \, 	ext{m/s}$.
- **Dependencies**: The value of refractive index depends on:
  1. Nature of the two mediums.
  2. Color (wavelength) of the light ray.
  3. Temperature of the two mediums.
- **Temperature Effect**: On increasing the temperature of a medium, its refractive index **decreases**.
- **Properties**:
  - It is an optical property of the medium.
  - Refractive indices of all mediums are measured with respect to air.
  - **Diamond** has the maximum refractive index among common materials.
- **Absolute Refractive Index**: If light travels from vacuum to a medium, the refractive index is called the absolute refractive index.
- **Relative Refractive Index**: $\mu_{12} =  rac{v_1}{v_2} =  rac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$.
- **Note**: For a glass/water pair, $\mu_{wg} =  rac{\mu_g}{\mu_w}$.

subject: Physics
topic: Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab
content:
### Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab
- **Behavior**: When a light ray enters a glass slab, the emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray but is shifted sideward.
- **Process**: Refraction occurs twice:
  1. When the ray enters the glass slab from air.
  2. When the ray exits the glass slab to air.
- **Lateral Shift ($d$)**: The perpendicular distance between the incident ray and the emergent ray.
  $$ d = t  rac{\sin(i - r)}{\cos r} $$
  *(Note: The provided text formula appears garbled as `t [1 - cos i / sin i]` or similar, but standard physics defines lateral shift as $d = t  rac{\sin(i-r)}{\cos r}$. Based strictly on the text's variable definitions:)*
  - $i$ = angle of incidence
  - $r$ = angle of refraction
  - $e$ = angle of emergence
  - $t$ = thickness of the slab

subject: Physics
text:
Refraction at spherical surface are of two types:

  • (i) Convex
  • (ii) Concave

For both surfaces refraction formula is given by: (mu_2 / v) - (mu_1 / u) = (mu_2 - mu_1) / R

Where 1mu2 is refractive index of second medium with respect to first. If mu1 and mu2 are refractive indices of first and second medium with respect to air, then: (mu_2 / v) - (mu_1 / u) = (mu_2 - mu_1) / R

subject: Physics
text:
A lens is a uniform refracting medium bounded by two spherical surfaces or one spherical and one plane surfaces. Lens are mainly of two types:

  • (i) Convex or Convergent Lens: The transparent medium bound by two bulging surfaces is called convex lens. Convex lens are of three types: (a) Double convex lens, (b) Plano-convex lens, (c) Concavo-convex lens. If the plane surface of a plano-convex lens is polished, then it behaves like a concave mirror of focal length half of the initial value.
  • (ii) Concave or Divergent Lens: The transparent medium bounded by two hollow surfaces is called concave lens. Types: (a) Double concave lens, (b) Plano-concave lens, (c) Convexo-concave lens.

Diagrams showing three types of concave lenses: Double concave, Plano-concave, and Convexo-concave.

subject: Physics
text:
• (i) Optical centre: The centre point of a lens is known as its optical centre. It is represented by O. The optical centre is a point within or outside the lens, directed to which incident rays refract without any deviation in the path.
  • (ii) Principal focus: Lens has two principal foci. (a) First principal focus: It is a point on the principal axis of lens, the rays starting from or directed to which become parallel to principal axis after refraction. (b) Second principal focus: It is the point on the principal axis at which the rays coming parallel to the principal axis, converge on the other side of lens (convex) or appear to meet on the same side of lens (concave), after refraction from the lens. Both the foci of convex lens are real while that of concave lens are virtual.
  • (iii) Centres of curvature: The centres of the two imaginary spheres of which the lens is a part are called centres of curvature of the lens. A lens has two centres of curvature with respect to its two curved surfaces.
  • (iv) Radii of curvature: The radii of the two imaginary spheres of which the lens is a part are called radii of curvature of the lens. It is represented by C. A lens has two radii of curvature. These may or may not be equal.

subject: Physics
text:
(i) Lens formula: The formula connecting the object and image distance, for both convex and concave lens.

(ii) Power of lens: The ability of lens to converge or diverge the light ray. Its unit is diopter (D). Power of a plane mirror is zero.

(iii) Newton's formula for lenses: Relates focal length to distances from foci.

(iv) Areal magnification: Relates area of image to area of object.
formulas: ms = area of image / area of object = Ai/Ao = m^2 = (f / (f+u))^2

subject: Physics
text:
Linear magnification (m): Ratio of size of image to size of object.

Lens immersed in a liquid: If a_mu_g is refractive index of lens and a_mu_l is refractive index of liquid, the total focal length changes.

Cutting of a lens: Symmetrical convex lens of focal length f cut along optical axis results in two plano-convex lenses of focal length 2f.
formulas: m = size of image(I) / size of object(O) = distance of image / distance of object = v/u

subject: Physics
text:
Symmetrical Convex Lens: If a symmetrical convex lens of focal length f is cut into two parts along the principal axis, the focal length of each part remains f. If these two parts are joined with curved ends on one side, the focal length of the combination is f/2. If joined in opposite sense, the focal length becomes infinite (net power = 0).

Combination of Thin Lenses:

  • If two or more lenses are placed in contact, the equivalent focal length is 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2 + ... = sum(1/fi).
  • Power of combination: P = P1 + P2 + ... = sum(Pi).
  • If two lenses of focal lengths f1 and f2 are separated by a distance x, the equivalent focal length is 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2 - x/(f1*f2).
  • Power of combination: P = P1 + P2 - x*P1*P2.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a convex lens cut into two halves and rearranged in four different configurations (a, b, c, d) to demonstrate changes in focal length.

subject: Physics
text:
Prism: A uniform transparent refracting medium bounded by two plane surfaces inclined at an angle.

Angle of Deviation: The angle subtended between the directions of incident ray (i) and emergent ray (e) is called the angle of deviation (delta).

Dispersion of Light: When white light is incident on a glass prism, it splits into its seven colour components in the sequence of VIBGYOR. The refractive index of glass is maximum for violet colour and minimum for red colour; therefore, violet deviates maximum and red deviates least.

Rainbow: Formed due to dispersion of sunlight by water droplets followed by total internal reflection. Types: primary and secondary rainbow.

Angular Dispersion: theta = delta_V - delta_R = (mu_V - mu_R)A

Dispersive Power (omega): omega = (delta_V - delta_R) / delta = (mu_V - mu_R) / (mu - 1). It is a unitless and dimensionless term. Dispersive power of flint glass is more than that of crown glass.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing white light entering a triangular prism and dispersing into seven colours (VIBGYOR).
Diagram showing a light ray passing through a prism with incident ray, emergent ray, angle of prism, and angle of deviation marked.

subject: Physics
text:
To produce dispersion without mean deviation, we use a combination of two prisms of different materials such that:

  • Net dispersion caused: = (μV - μR)A + (μ'V - μ'R)A' = (μ - 1)A(ω - ω') = δ(ω - ω')
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a combination of two prisms (Flint and Crown) illustrating dispersion without deviation. Light rays enter and exit with specific angles A and A'.

details.summary: Explanation of Direct Vision Prism setup to achieve dispersion without mean deviation.

subject: Physics
text:
To produce deviation without dispersion, we use a combination of two prisms of different materials such that:

  • Resultant deviation produced: δ[1 - (ω/ω')]
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a combination of two prisms (Flint and Crown) illustrating deviation without dispersion.

subject: Physics
text:
When light passes through a medium in which particles are suspended whose sizes are of the order of wavelength of light, then light on striking these particles, deviated in different directions. This phenomenon is called scattering of light. Therefore, red colour of light is scattered least (wavelength is highest) and violet colour of light is scattered most (wavelength is least).

  • Danger signals: are of red colours because red colour of light scatters least and therefore these signals can be seen from far away.
  • Sky appears blue: because in sunlight, the blue colour of light is scattered maximum and this scattered blue light enters our eyes and therefore sky appears blue.
  • Clouds appear white: because clouds consists of large size of droplets of water and dust particles which scatter all colours of light equally. The mixture of all seven colours of sunlight is white.
  • Sky appears black to astronauts: from space because there is no atmosphere in space and therefore no scattering of light takes place.

details.summary: Principles of light scattering and its applications in natural phenomena.

subject: Physics
text:
Human eye is one of the most valuable and sensitive sense organs in the human body. It consists of a lens made up of living tissues.

Main parts of the human eye:

  • Cornea: Transparent spherical membrane covering the front of the eye. Light enters the eye through this membrane.
  • Crystalline lens: A convex lens made of a transparent, soft and flexible material like a jelly made of proteins.
  • Iris: A dark muscular diaphragm between the cornea and the lens. It controls the size of the pupil.
  • Pupil: A small hole between the iris through which light enters the eye.
  • Ciliary muscles: They hold the lens in position and help in modifying the curvature of the lens.
  • Retina: The light sensitive surface of eye on which the image is formed. It contains light sensitive cells rods and cones.
  • Optic nerve: It transmits visual information from the retina to the brain.
  • Sclera: An opaque, fibrous, protective, outer layer of an eye containing collagen and elastic fibre. It is also known as white of the eye.
  • Blind spot: It is the point at which the optic nerve leaves the eye. It contains no rods and cones, so an image formed at this point is not sent to the brain.
image_descriptions: Anatomical diagram of the human eye labeling: Crystalline lens, Aqueous humour, Pupil, Iris, Cornea, Ciliary muscles, Sclera, Retina, Blind spot, Optic nerve, and Vitreous humour.

details.summary: Anatomy and function of the human eye components.

subject: Physics
topic: Human Eye and Defects of Vision
text:
Aqueous humour: Behind the cornea, we have a space filled with a transparent liquid called the aqueous humour.

Vitreous humour: The space between eye lens and retina is filled with another liquid called vitreous humour.

Accommodation of eye: It is the ability of eye lens, to change its focal length to form sharp images of objects at different positions from the eye on the retina of the eye.

Range of vision: It is the distance between near point and the far point of an eye. For normal eye, the range of vision is 25 cm to infinity.

Near point: It is the nearest position of an object from human eye, so that its sharp images is formed on the retina.

Defects of Vision:

  • Myopia or short sightedness: It is a defect of eye due to which a person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see far away objects clearly. In this defect, the far point of eye shifts from infinity to a nearer distance. The defect can be removed by using a concave lens of appropriate power.
  • Hypermetropia or long sightedness: It is a defect of eye due to which a person can see far away objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects clearly.
  • Presbyopia: It is found in old age people. In this defect, one cannot read comfortably and clearly. This defect can be corrected by using bifocal lenses. In this defect, the near point of eye shifts away from the eye. The defect can be removed by using a convex lens of appropriate power.
  • Astigmatism: In this defect, a person cannot focus on horizontal and vertical lines at the same distance at the same time. This defect can be removed by using suitable cylindrical lenses.
  • Colour Blindness: In this defect, a person is unable to distinguish among few colours. The reason of this defect is the absence of cone cells sensitive for few colours. This defect cannot be removed.
  • Cataract: In this defect, an opaque, white membrane is developed on cornea due to which a person loses power of vision partially or completely. This defect can be removed by removing this membrane through surgery.

details.summary: Overview of human eye anatomy, accommodation, and common vision defects including myopia, hypermetropia, presbyopia, astigmatism, colour blindness, and cataract.

subject: Physics
text:
Optical Instruments: Optical instrument is a device which is made from proper combination of mirrors, prisms and lenses. The principle of working of optical instruments depends on laws of reflection and refraction of light.

Microscope: It is an optical instrument which forms a magnified image of a small nearby object and thus increases the visual angle subtended by the image at the eye, so that the object is seen to be bigger and distinct.

Simple Microscope: A simple microscope is a convex lens of short focal length which is fixed in a frame provided with handle.

Compound Microscope: It consists of two converging lenses arranged coaxially. The one facing the object is called objective and the one close to eye is called eye piece. The objective has a smaller aperture and smaller focal length than those of the eyepiece.
formulas: M = 1 + D/f (Simple Microscope, least distance of distinct vision)
M_infinity = -(v_o / u_o) * (D / f_e) (Compound Microscope, relaxed eye)
M_D = -(v_o / u_o) * (1 + D / f_e) (Compound Microscope, least distance of distinct vision)
image_descriptions: Ray diagram of a simple microscope showing a convex lens forming a magnified virtual image of an object.
Ray diagram of a compound microscope showing two converging lenses (objective and eyepiece) forming a final magnified image.

details.summary: Definitions and magnification formulas for simple and compound microscopes.

subject: Physics
text:
Telescope is an optical instrument which increases the visual angle at the eye by forming the image of a distant object at the least distance of distinct vision, so that the object is seen distinct and bigger.

Astronomical Telescope: It consists of two converging lenses placed coaxially. The one facing the distant object is called the objective and has a large aperture and large focal length. The other is called the eyepiece, as the eye is placed closed to it. The eyepiece tube can slide within the objective tube, so that the separation between the objective and the eye-piece may be varied.

Magnification of astronomical telescope:

  • (i) For relaxed eye, M = -fo/fe. In this position, length of telescope, L = fo + fe.
  • (ii) When final image is formed at least distance of distinct vision, M = -(fo/fe)(1 + fe/D). Length of telescope, L = fo + fe.

Note: A refracting telescope consists of two convex lenses of unequal focal length.
image_descriptions: Ray diagram of an astronomical telescope showing two convex lenses, objective and eyepiece, with light rays from a distant object forming an image.

details.summary: Overview of astronomical telescope construction, magnification formulas for relaxed eye and least distance of distinct vision, and note on lens composition.

subject: Physics
content:
# Convex Lens Image Formation

- **Lens formula**: \( rac{1}{f} =  rac{1}{v} +  rac{1}{u}\)
  - *f* = focal length (positive for convex lens)
  - *u* = object distance (negative if measured from lens to object)
  - *v* = image distance (positive if real, negative if virtual)

- **Magnification**: \(m =  rac{v}{u} = - rac{h_i}{h_o}\)
  - *m* > 1 → magnified
  - *m* < 1 → reduced
  - Sign of *m* indicates image orientation (negative → inverted, positive → erect)

- **Case**: Object at 10 cm, focal length 15 cm (u < f)
  - Image is **virtual** (v negative)
  - Magnification > 1 → **magnified**
  - Image is erect (positive *m*)

- **Key takeaway**: For a convex lens, if the object is inside the focal length, the image is virtual, erect, and magnified.

subject: Physics
text:
Key Concepts:

  • Relative Velocity of Image: For an object moving with velocity v towards a mirror, the image approaches with velocity 2v.
  • Number of Images: For two mirrors at angle θ, number of images n = (360/θ) - 1 (if n is even).
  • Lens/Mirror Power: P = 1/f(in meters).
  • Lens Combination: 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2 (for thin lenses in contact).
  • Refraction: Snell's Law: n1 sin i = n2 sin r.
  • Velocity in Medium: v = c/μ. Velocity decreases as light moves from rarer to denser medium.
  • Magnification: m = -v/u (for mirrors), m = v/u (for lenses).
  • Rainbow Formation: Involves refraction, dispersion, and total internal reflection.
formulas: n1 sin i = n2 sin r
image_descriptions: Diagram showing light ray refraction between two media with incident angle i and refracted angle r.
Diagram showing a light ray entering a triangular prism (A, B, C) and undergoing dispersion into constituent colors (V to R).

subject: Physics
text:
Periodic Motion: A motion which repeats itself over and again after a regular interval is called a periodic motion.

  • The revolution of earth around the Sun is a periodic motion.
  • The motion of hands of a clock is a periodic motion.

Periodic Function: A function which repeats its value after a fix interval of time is called a periodic function.

y(t) = y(t + T), where T is the period of the function.

Trignometric function sinθ and cosθ are simplest periodic functions having period of 2π.

details.summary: Definitions and examples of periodic motion and periodic functions.

subject: Physics
text:
Oscillatory Motion: A periodic to and fro motion of a body about a fixed point, is called an oscillatory or vibratory motion.

  • The motion of the pendulum of a wall clock.
  • The motion of a loaded spring.
  • The motion of a bar magnet suspended in the earth's magnetic field.
  • Simple pendulum, spring pendulum, etc.

Note: Every oscillatory motion is periodic but every periodic motion is not an oscillatory motion.

Types of Oscillatory Motion:

  • (i) Harmonic Oscillation: When a body repeats its motion about a fixed point after a regular time interval is known as the harmonic oscillation. e.g., sine or cosine function is called harmonic function.
  • (ii) Non-harmonic Oscillation: A non-harmonic oscillation is the combination of two or more than two harmonic oscillations.

details.summary: Definitions of oscillatory motion and its types (harmonic and non-harmonic).

subject: Physics
text:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM): Simple harmonic motion is a simplest form of vibratory or oscillatory motion in which a particle moves to and fro repeatedly about a mean position.

Some Important Terms Related to SHM:

  • (i) Restoring Force: The force acting on the particle (executing SHM) which tends to bring it towards its mean position is called restoring force. Restoring force is always directed towards mean position or acts in the direction opposite to that of displacement. Restoring force, F = -kx, where k is a constant and x is displacement about mean position.
  • (ii) Amplitude: The maximum displacement of the particle from mean position, is called the amplitude of the oscillation. It is denoted by a.

details.summary: Definition of SHM and key terms like Restoring Force and Amplitude.

subject: Physics
text:
Phase: The physical quantity which expresses the position and direction of the motion of an oscillating particle is called phase. It is denoted by φ.

Time Period: The time after which the particle keeps on repeating its motion is called time period. It is denoted by T.

Frequency: The number of oscillations made by the particle is called frequency. Its unit is per second or Hertz.

Angular Frequency: The rate of change of a phase angle of particle (executing SHM) with respect to time is called angular frequency. Its unit is radian/second.

details.summary: Definitions of Phase, Time Period, Frequency, and Angular Frequency in SHM.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two types of SHM:

  • Linear SHM: When a particle moves to and fro about a fixed point along a straight line, then its motion is called linear simple harmonic motion. e.g., Motion of a mass connected to a spring.
  • Angular SHM: Instead of straight line motion, if particle or centre of mass of body is oscillating on a small arc of circular motion, then its motion is called angular simple harmonic motion. e.g., Motion of a bob of simple pendulum.

details.summary: Classification of SHM into Linear and Angular types.

subject: Physics
text:
Simple harmonic motion can be defined as the straight line motion of the foot of perpendicular drawn from the particle on the diameter of the circle.

Displacement: The displacement of a particle executing SHM at any instant is given by:

  • y = a sin ωt = a sin(2π/T)t = a sin 2πnt ...(i)
  • y = a cos ωt = a cos(2π/T)t = a cos 2πnt ...(ii)
  • y = a sin(ωt ± φ) ...(iii)

Velocity: The velocity of the particle executing SHM at any instant, is defined as the time rate of change of its displacement at that instant. v = ω√(a² - y²)

  • When the particle is at mean position (y=0), velocity is maximum: v_max = ωa
  • When the particle is at extreme position (y=±a), velocity is zero: v = 0

Acceleration: The acceleration of the particle executing SHM at any instant, is defined as the rate of change of its velocity at that instant. A = -ω²y

  • When the particle is at mean position (y=0), acceleration is zero: a_mean position = 0
  • When the particle is at extreme position (x=a), acceleration is maximum: a_extreme position = -ω²a
image_descriptions: A circle diagram showing a particle P moving in a circle, with a perpendicular dropped to the diameter (y-axis) forming a point M, illustrating the projection of circular motion as SHM.

details.summary: Kinematic equations for displacement, velocity, and acceleration in SHM.

subject: Physics
text:
A particle executing SHM possesses two types of energy:

Potential Energy: When a body is displaced from its equilibrium position by doing work upon it, acquires potential energy. U = (1/2)mω²y²

  • Potential energy is maximum at extreme position (y=±a): U_max = (1/2)mω²a²
  • Potential energy is minimum (zero) at mean position (y=0): U_min = 0

Kinetic Energy: When a body is released, it begins to move back with a velocity, thus acquiring kinetic energy.

details.summary: Energy distribution in SHM, specifically Potential Energy.

subject: Physics
topic: Energy in SHM and Comparison of Linear vs Angular SHM
text:
Kinetic Energy (K) = 1/2 mω²(a² - y²)

K.E is maximum at mean position i.e y = 0. Therefore, K_max = 1/2 mω²a².

Kinetic energy is minimum (zero) at extreme position i.e., y = ± a, K = 0.

Total Energy: Total energy can be obtained by adding potential and kinetic energies. Therefore, E = K + U = 1/2 mω²(a² - y²) + 1/2 mω²y² = 1/2 mω²a².
tables:
| S. No. | Linear Simple Harmonic Motion | Angular Simple Harmonic Motion |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Restoring force, f ∝ -x => f = -kx (where, k = restoring force constant) | Restoring torque τ ∝ -θ => τ = -Cθ (where, C = restoring torque) |
| 2 | Acceleration, a = -(k/m)x => d²x/dt² + (k/m)x = 0 (Differential equation of linear SHM) | Acceleration, α = -(C/I)θ => d²θ/dt² + (C/I)θ = 0 (Differential equation of angular SHM) |
| 3 | Displacement y = a sin ωt | Angular displacement θ = θ_0 sin ωt |
| 4 | Acceleration, A = -ω²y. So, ω = sqrt(k/m) = 2π/T = 2πn (where, T = time period and n = frequency) | Acceleration α = -ω²θ. So, w = sqrt(C/I) = 2π/T = 2πn (where, T = time period and n = frequency) |
| 5 | Time period T = 2π sqrt(m/k), n = (1/2π) sqrt(k/m) | Time period T = 2π sqrt(I/C), n = (1/2π) sqrt(C/I) |

details.summary: Comparison of linear and angular simple harmonic motion parameters including force, acceleration, displacement, and time period.

subject: Physics
topic: Simple Pendulum and Pendulum in a Lift
text:
Simple Pendulum: If a heavy point mass is suspended by a weightless, inextensible and perfectly flexible string from a rigid support, then this arrangement is called a simple pendulum. The time period is given by T = 2π sqrt(l/g), where l = effective length and g = acceleration due to gravity.

Oscillation of a Simple Pendulum in a Lift:

  • (i) Lift at rest or moving upward with constant velocity: T = 2π sqrt(l/g), n = (1/2π) sqrt(g/l)
  • (ii) Lift moving upward with constant acceleration a: T = 2π sqrt(l/(g+a)), n = (1/2π) sqrt((g+a)/l). Time period decreases and frequency increases.
  • (iii) Lift moving downward with constant acceleration a: T = 2π sqrt(l/(g-a)), n = (1/2π) sqrt((g-a)/l). Time period increases and frequency decreases.
  • (iv) Lift moving downward with acceleration a = g: T = 2π sqrt(l/(g-g)) = ∞, n = 0. No oscillation.

details.summary: Definition of a simple pendulum and the effect of lift acceleration on its time period and frequency.

subject: Physics
text:
There are five types of simple pendulum:

  • Second's Pendulum: A simple pendulum having time period of 2 s. The effective length is approximately 1 m on the earth.
  • Conical Pendulum: If a simple pendulum is fixed at one end and the bob is rotating in a horizontal circle.
  • Compound Pendulum: Any rigid body mounted so that it is capable of swinging in a vertical plane about some axis passing through it.
  • Physical Pendulum: When a rigid body of any shape is capable of oscillating about an axis.
  • Spring Pendulum: A point mass suspended from a massless (or light) spring.

details.summary: Classification of pendulums into Second's, Conical, Compound, Physical, and Spring pendulums.

subject: Physics
text:
A spring pendulum consists of a point mass m suspended from a massless spring or placed on a smooth horizontal plane. A restoring force F = -kl acts on it, where k is the force constant. The time period T and frequency n are given by:

  • T = 2π * sqrt(m/k)
  • n = (1/2π) * sqrt(k/m)

If the spring has a mass m_s, the time period is T = 2π * sqrt((m + m_s/3)/k). For two masses m_1 and m_2 connected by a spring, T = 2π * sqrt(μ/k), where μ = (m_1 * m_2) / (m_1 + m_2) is the reduced mass.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing a mass m attached to a vertical spring hanging from a fixed support.

details.summary: Covers basic spring-mass oscillation dynamics, including effects of spring mass and two-body systems.

subject: Physics
text:
1. Series Combination: Two springs with constants k_1 and k_2 joined in series. Equivalent constant k_s is given by 1/k_s = 1/k_1 + 1/k_2, so k_s = (k_1 * k_2) / (k_1 + k_2). The time period is T = 2π * sqrt(m/k_s) = 2π * sqrt(m(k_1 + k_2) / (k_1 * k_2)).

2. Parallel Combination: Two springs with constants k_1 and k_2 joined in parallel. Equivalent constant k_p = k_1 + k_2. The time period is T = 2π * sqrt(m/k_p) = 2π * sqrt(m / (k_1 + k_2)).
image_descriptions: Diagrams showing series combination (a: horizontal, b: vertical) and parallel combination (a: vertical, b: horizontal) of two springs with constants k_1 and k_2 attached to mass m.

details.summary: Explains series and parallel spring combinations and their effect on equivalent spring constants and oscillation periods.

subject: Physics
text:
A wave is a vibratory disturbance in a medium carrying energy without movement of the medium. Types:

  • Mechanical Waves: Propagated only in a material medium.
  • Electromagnetic Waves: Require no medium for propagation.
  • Matter Waves: Associated with moving particles like electrons and protons.

Types of Mechanical Waves:

  • Longitudinal Waves: Particles vibrate in the same direction as wave propagation (e.g., sound waves, waves in a slinky). Regions of closer coils are compressions, and farther apart coils are rarefactions.
image_descriptions: Diagram of a slinky showing longitudinal wave propagation with labeled Compressions (C) and Rarefactions (R).

details.summary: Defines waves, classifies them into mechanical, electromagnetic, and matter waves, and details longitudinal waves.

subject: Physics
text: When a longitudinal wave passes through air, the density of air changes continuously and the pressure and energy are being transferred.
image_descriptions: Representation of Longitudinal Wave showing alternating regions of Compression (Greater density) and Rarefaction (Less density).

details.summary: Longitudinal wave propagation involves continuous changes in density and pressure.

subject: Physics
text:
A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation of wave, is called transverse wave. Transverse waves can be produced only in solids and liquids.

  • Light is a transverse wave but it is not a mechanical wave.
  • The waves produced by moving one end of long spring or rope up and down rapidly and whose other end is fixed, are transverse waves.
  • The water waves (or ripples) formed on the surface of water in a pond (when a stone is dropped in the pond of water), are transverse waves.

A transverse wave travels horizontally in a medium and the particles of the medium vibrate up and down in the vertical direction. In transverse waves, crest and trough are formed. A crest is that part of the transverse wave which is above the line of zero disturbance of the medium. A trough is that part of the transverse wave which is below the line of zero disturbance.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing direction of vibrations of particles perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
A Transverse Wave by a Displacement-Distance Graph showing crests (A, C) and troughs (B, D) relative to the line of zero disturbance.

details.summary: Definition and characteristics of transverse waves, including examples like light, rope waves, and water ripples.

subject: Physics
text:
When a large number of particles vibrates simultaneously in a medium, then disturbance propagates in the medium. The motion of disturbance is called wave motion. Energy of momentum is transferred to the neighbouring particles of the medium as wave proceeds.

  • Amplitude: It is the maximum displacement suffered by the particles of the medium about their mean positions. It is denoted by A.
  • Time Period: The time period of a wave is the time in which a particle of medium completes one vibration to and fro about its mean position. It is denoted by T.
  • Frequency: The frequency of a wave is the number of waves produced per unit time in the given medium. It is equal to the reciprocal of the time period T of the particle and is denoted by n. S.I unit of n is S^-1 or hertz (Hz).
  • Angular Frequency: The rate of change of phase with time is called angular frequency of the wave. It is denoted by ω. SI unit of ω is rad S^-1.
  • Wavelength: The distance between two nearest particles of the medium which are vibrating in the same phase. It is denoted by λ.
  • Wave Number: The number of waves present in a unit distance of the medium is called wave number. It is equal to the reciprocal of wavelength λ. SI unit of wave number is m^-1.
  • Angular wave number of propagation constant: The quantity 2π/λ is called angular wave number or propagation constant of a wave. It represents phase change per unit path difference. It is denoted by K. The SI unit of K is radian per metre or rad m^-1.
  • Wave velocity or phase velocity: The distance covered by a wave per unit time in its directions of propagation is called its wave velocity or phase velocity. It is denoted by v.

details.summary: Key definitions and mathematical relationships for wave motion parameters.

subject: Physics
text:
Relation between Wave Velocity, Frequency and Wavelength: Wave velocity = Distance / Time. i.e., Wave velocity = Frequency × Wavelength.

Sound: Sound is a form of energy, which produces the sensation of hearing. These are longitudinal mechanical waves. Sound waves have low frequency and high wavelength. Sound waves cannot travel in vacuum.

Reflection of Sound: The rebouncing back of sound, when it strikes a hard surface is called reflection of sound. The repetition of sound due to reflection of sound wave is called an echo.

Categories of Waves based on frequency:

  • Audible or Sound Waves: Longitudinal mechanical waves in the frequency range 20 Hz to 20000 Hz.
  • Infrasonic Waves: Frequencies less than 20 Hz. Produced by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, ocean waves, elephants and whales.
  • Ultrasonic Waves: Frequencies greater than 20000 Hz. Human ear cannot detect these, but creatures like dog, cat, bat, mosquito etc., can. Note: Bat not only detects but also produces ultrasonic waves.

details.summary: Covers basic wave equations, definition of sound, reflection, echo, and classification of sound waves by frequency range.

subject: Physics
text:
Intensity or Loudness: Intensity of sound at any point in space is defined as the amount of energy passing normally per unit area held around that point per unit time. Its SI unit is watt/metre. Loudness depends on intensity of sound. Unit of loudness is bel and 1/10th of bel is decibel (dB).

Quality or Timbre of Sound: Characteristic which enables us to distinguish between sound produced by two sources having the same intensity and pitch. It depends on harmonics and their relative order and intensity.

Pitch or Frequency: Characteristic which distinguishes between a shrillness or graveness of sound. Depends upon frequency. A still and sharp sound has higher pitch and grave and dull sound has lower pitch.
