| Source of Sound | Noise level (dB) |
|---|---|
| Whisper | 20 |
| Ordinary conversation | 65 |
| Traffic on a busy road | 70 |
| Amplified rock music | 120 |
| Jet aeroplane, 30 m away | 140 |

details.summary: Explains intensity, loudness, quality/timbre, and pitch, including a table of noise levels for various sources.

subject: Physics
topic: SONAR, Shock Waves, and Speed of Sound
text:
SONAR: Acronym for Sound Navigation And Ranging. A device that uses ultrasonic waves to measure distances, directions and speed of objects under water. Applications: Target location for torpedoes, Resources location for mines, Submarine navigation, In aircraft, Remotely operated vehicles, Detecting the vehicle location.

Shock Waves: A body moving with supersonic speed in air leaves behind a conical region of disturbance. These waves carry huge energy and may even damage a building. Earthquakes have shock waves.

Speed of Sound: Depends upon elasticity and density of medium. Speed of sound in air is 332 m/s, in water is 1483 m/s and in iron is 5130 m/s. Resonance column method and Kundt’s tube method are used for determination of speed of sound. Note: Liquids and solids generally have higher speeds of sound than in gases.

Effect of Temperature: The speed of sound in a gas is directly proportional to the square root of absolute temperature of the gas, i.e., v ∝ √T. So, velocity of sound in air increases due to rise in temperature.

details.summary: Covers SONAR technology, shock waves, speed of sound in different media, and the effect of temperature on sound velocity.

subject: Physics
text:
Effect of Pressure: If temperature remains constant, then there is no effect of change in pressure on the velocity of sound.

Effect of Humidity: In humid air, velocity of sound increases as compared to the dry air.

Effect of Frequency: There is no effect of frequency on the velocity of sound.

Effect of Wind: If wind is blowing, then the speed of sound changes. The speed of sound is increased, if wind is blowing in the direction of propagation of sound wave.

details.summary: Factors affecting the velocity of sound including pressure, humidity, frequency, and wind.

subject: Physics
text:
When a sound wave moves from one mechanical medium to another mechanical medium, then the waves are refracted or transmitted. This phenomenon is called refraction of sound.

The refracted waves deviated from the original path of the incident waves. The main reason for occurrence of refraction in sound is different speeds of sound, in different media at different temperatures.

details.summary: Definition and cause of refraction of sound waves.

subject: Physics
topic: Speed of Longitudinal Waves in Gases
text:
Newton Formula: Newton gave a relation to calculate the velocity of sound in a gas. According to Newton, the velocity of sound v = sqrt(B/d), where B is volume coefficient of elasticity (also called bulk modulus of elasticity) of the gas and d is density.

Newton assumed that the changes in pressure and volume of a gas when sound waves are propagated through it, are isothermal. Hence, in the above formula, B is isothermal bulk modulus of the gas whose value is equal to the initial pressure (p) of the gas. Therefore, according to Newton, the speed of sound in a gas v = sqrt(p/d).

Laplace's Correction: Laplace pointed out that Newton's assumption was wrong. According to Laplace, the changes in pressure and volume of a gas when a gas propagates through the air, are not isothermal but should be adiabatic. Because when sound waves are propagated through air, these are accompanied by the change of temperature of gas. Hence, changes are adiabatic and not isothermal.

Hence, in Newton's formula, B should represent the adiabatic bulk modulus of the gas whose value is equal to gamma * p i.e., B = gamma * p, where gamma = Cp/Cv = ratio of two principal specific heat of gas. Thus, Laplace's formula for the speed of sound in a gas is v = sqrt(gamma * p / d).

details.summary: Derivation of the speed of sound in gases using Newton's formula and Laplace's correction.

subject: Physics
text:
ECHO: When a person shouts in a big empty hall, we first hear his original sound, after that we hear the reflected sound of that shout. This reflected sound is known as echo. An echo is nothing but just the reflected sound. So, the repetition of sound caused by reflection of sound waves is called an echo.

SUPERPOSITION OF WAVES: When a number of waves meet simultaneously at a point in a medium, this is called superposition of waves.

Principle of Superposition of Waves: The principle of superposition of waves states that when a number of waves travel through a medium simultaneously, the resultant displacement of any particle of the medium at any given time is equal to the algebraic sum of the displacement due to the individual waves. If y1, y2, y3, ... yn are the displacements due to waves acting separately, then according to the principle of superposition the resultant displacement, when all the waves act together is given by the algebraic sum y = y1 + y2 + y3 + .... + yn.

details.summary: Definitions of echo and the principle of superposition of waves.

subject: Physics
text:
When two identical waves of same amplitude and frequency travelling in opposite directions with the same speed along the same path superpose each other, the resultant wave does not travel in either direction and is called stationary or standing wave.

On the path of stationary wave, there are some points where the amplitude is zero. These points are known as nodes.

On the other hand, there are some points where the amplitude is maximum. These points are known as antinodes.

There are two types of stationary waves:

  • Longitudinal Stationary Waves: Longitudinal stationary waves are formed as a result of superimposition of two identical longitudinal waves travelling in opposite directions. e.g., Stationary waves produced in organ pipes and in air column of resonance tube apparatus are longitudinal stationary waves.
  • Transverse Stationary Waves: Transverse stationary waves are formed as a result of superimposition of two identical transverse waves travelling in opposite directions. e.g., Stationary waves produced on the vibrating string of a Sonometer are transverse stationary waves.

details.summary: Definition, characteristics (nodes/antinodes), and types of standing or stationary waves.

subject: Physics
text:
When a wave is set up on a string of length L fixed at two ends, this wave gets reflected from the two fixed ends of the string continuously and as a result of superimposition of these waves, transverse standing waves are formed on the string.

Consider a string of length L and mass m per unit length stretched with tension T.

  • Fundamental frequency or frequency in first normal mode of vibration: The fundamental note or first harmonic is produced.
  • Frequency in second normal mode of vibration: The frequency of vibrating string becomes twice the fundamental frequency. The note or sound so produced, is called second harmonic or first overtone.
  • Frequency in third normal mode of vibration: The frequency of vibration of string becomes three times the fundamental frequency. The note or sound so produced, is called third harmonic or second overtone.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing first normal mode of vibration in a string with length L = lambda1 / 2, showing one antinode (A) and two nodes (N) at the ends.
Diagram showing second normal mode of vibration in a string with length L = lambda2 / 2, showing two antinodes (A) and three nodes (N).
Diagram showing third normal mode of vibration in a string with length L = 3 * lambda3 / 2, showing three antinodes (A) and four nodes (N).

details.summary: Explanation of standing waves in a string fixed at both ends, including fundamental frequency and harmonics.

subject: Physics
topic: Standing Waves in Closed Organ Pipe
text:
Organ pipes are musical instruments which are used for producing musical sound by blowing air into the pipe. A closed organ pipe is closed at one end and open at the other.

  • Fundamental frequency or frequency in first normal mode of vibration: This is the lowest frequency of vibration and is called the fundamental frequency. The note or sound so produced, is called fundamental note or first harmonic.
  • Frequency in second normal mode of vibration: The frequency of vibration in 2nd normal mode is thrice the fundamental frequency. The note or sound so produced, is called third harmonic or first overtone.
  • Frequency in third normal mode of vibration: The frequency of vibration in 3rd normal mode is five times the fundamental frequency. The note or sound so produced, is called fifth harmonic or second overtone.

The ratio of frequencies is n1 : n2 : n3 : ... = 1 : 3 : 5 : ...
image_descriptions: Diagram of first normal mode in closed organ pipe: length L = lambda1 / 4, node at closed end, antinode at open end.
Diagram of second normal mode in closed organ pipe: length L = 3 * lambda2 / 4, nodes and antinodes marked.
Diagram of third normal mode in closed organ pipe: length L = 5 * lambda3 / 4, nodes and antinodes marked.

details.summary: Explanation of standing waves in a closed organ pipe, including the relationship between harmonics.

subject: Physics
text:
An open organ pipe is a cylindrical tube of which both ends are open. A source of sound near one of the ends sends the wave in the pipe. The wave is reflected by the other open end and travels towards the source. It suffers second reflection at the open end near the source and then interferes with the new wave sent by the source.

  • Fundamental frequency or frequency in first normal mode of vibration: This is the lowest frequency of vibration and is called fundamental frequency. The note or sound so produced is called fundamental note or first harmonic.
  • Frequency in second normal mode of vibration: Frequency in second normal mode is twice the fundamental frequency. The note so produced is called second harmonic or first overtone.
  • Frequency in third normal mode of vibration: Frequency in third normal mode is thrice the fundamental frequency. The note so produced is called third harmonic or second overtone.

Therefore, even and odd harmonics are produced by an open organ pipe. The ratio is n1 : n2 : n3 : ....... = 1 : 2 : 3 : ...
image_descriptions: Diagram showing fundamental mode of vibration in an open organ pipe with length L, wavelength lambda1/2, and nodes/antinodes.
Diagram showing second normal mode of vibration in an open organ pipe with length L, wavelength lambda2, and nodes/antinodes.
Diagram showing third normal mode of vibration in an open organ pipe with length L, wavelength 3lambda3/2, and nodes/antinodes.

subject: Physics
text: When two sound waves of equal amplitudes and nearly equal frequencies are produced simultaneously, then the intensity of resultant sound wave increases and decreases with time. This change in the intensity of sound is called phenomenon of beats. Resultant frequency is equal to the difference in frequencies of two sound sources.

subject: Physics
text:
When there is a relative motion between source and observer of the sound, a variation in the frequency (pitch) of sound is observed by the observer. This phenomenon is called Doppler's effect. Here, change in frequency is called Doppler's shift. The variation in frequency (pitch) of sound depends on the three different relative motions between source and observer.

Special Cases

  • Case 1: If only source S is in motion towards the observer, then vo = 0 and vs is +ve. n = n0 [v / (v - vs)]
  • Case 2: If source S is in motion away from the observer, then vs is -ve. n = n0 [v / (v + vs)]
  • Case 3: If only observer O is in the motion towards the source, then vs = 0 and vo is -ve. n = n0 [(v - (-vo)) / v] = n0 [(v + vo) / v]
  • Case 4: If observer O is the motion away from the source, then vo is +ve. n = n0 [(v - vo) / v]
  • Case 5: If both source S and observer O are in motion and approaching each other, then vs is +ve, but vo is -ve. n = n0 [(v + vo) / (v - vs)]
  • Case 6: If both source S and observer O are in motion such that they are receding from each other, then vs is -ve but vo is +ve. n = n0 [(v - vo) / (v + vs)]

Conditions of Doppler Effect

There will be no change in observed frequency due to Doppler's effect when:

  • (i) The source S and observer O are at rest or moving in such a way that distance between them remains constant.
  • (ii) Source and observer are moving in mutually perpendicular directions.
  • (iii) The velocity of source S and of observer O is equal to or greater than the velocity of sound in the given medium.

subject: Physics
text: The branch of physics, which deals with the study of charges at rest (i.e. static charges), the forces between the static charges, fields and potentials due to these charges is called electrostatics.

details.summary: Definition of electrostatics as the study of charges at rest.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric charge is the property associated with matter due to which it produces and experiences electrical and magnetic effects. It is a scalar quantity. Its SI unit is coulomb (C). The proton possesses positive charge (+e) and electron possesses an equal negative charge (-e), where, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 coulomb (C).

Properties of Electric Charge

  • Two like charges repel each other, while two unlike charges attract each other.
  • Electrification by friction can be explained on the basis of transfer of electron (i.e. negative charged particles of an atom) from one object to other, when these are rubbed to each other. Charges are invariant and always distributed on the surface of the conductor.
  • A charged body attracts lighter neutral body.
  • During any process, the net electric charge of an isolated system remains constant.
  • Charge is conserved i.e., it can neither be created nor be destroyed.

details.summary: Definition and properties of electric charge.

subject: Physics
text:
The force of interaction (attraction or repulsion) between two stationary point charges in vacuum is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of distance between them. Mathematically, electrostatic force between two stationary charges is given by:

F = k * |q1 * q2| / r^2

where, k is a proportionality constant. In SI unit, k is given by:

k = 1 / (4 * pi * epsilon_0) = 9 x 10^9 Nm^2C^-2

where, epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2N^-1m^-2 and is called the permittivity of free space.

i.e. F = 9 x 10^9 * |q1 * q2| / r^2

The coulomb force acts along the straight line connecting the points of location of the charges. It is central and spherically symmetric.

If q1 = q2 = 1 C and r = 1 m, Then, F = 9 x 10^9 * (1 * 1) / 1^2 = 9 x 10^9 N

subject: Physics
text: According to the superposition principle, forces on any charge due to number of other charges is the vector sum of all the forces on that charge due to other charges, taken one at a time. The individual forces are unaffected due to the presence of other charges. Consider a system of n point charges q1, q2, q3...qn be distributed in space in a discrete manner. The charges are interacting with each other. Let the charges q2, q3...qn exert forces F12, F13...F1n, respectively on charge q1. Then, according to the principle of superposition, the total force on charge q1 is given by F1 = F12 + F13 +...+ F1n ... (i). If the distance between the charges q1 and q2 is denoted as r12 and r12-hat is unit vector from charge q2 to q1, then F12 = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (q1*q2 / r12^2) * r12-hat. Similarly, the force on charge q1 due to other charges is given by F13 = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (q1*q3 / r13^2) * r13-hat, F1n = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (q1*qn / rn1^2) * rn1-hat. Substituting these values in Eq.(i), we get F1 = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (q1*q2/r12^2 * r12-hat + q1*q3/r13^2 * r13-hat +...+ q1*qn/rn1^2 * rn1-hat) = (q1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * sum(qi / ri1^2 * ri1-hat) from i=2 to n. The interaction must be on the charge which is to be studied due to other charges.
formulas: F1 = (q1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * sum(qi / ri1^2 * ri1-hat) from i=2 to n
image_descriptions: A vector diagram showing a central charge q1 being acted upon by forces F12, F13, ..., F1n from surrounding charges q2, q3, ..., qn, with corresponding position vectors r12, r13, ..., r1n.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Field: Electric field due to a given charge is the space around the charge in which electrostatic force of attraction or repulsion due to the charge can be experienced by any other charge.

Electric Field Intensity: The electric field intensity at any point is the strength of electric field at that point. It is defined as the force experienced by unit positive charge placed at that point. If F is the force acting on a small test charge +q0 at any point r, then electric field intensity at that point is given by E(r) = F(r) / q0. The SI unit of electric field intensity is newton per coulomb (N/C).

Electric Field Lines: An electric field line in general is a curve drawn in such a way that the tangent to it at each point is in the direction of the electric field at that point. A field line is a space curve, i.e. a curve in three-dimensions.

Properties of Electric Field Lines:

  • (i) Electric field lines start from positive charges and end at negative charges. In the case of a single charge, they may start or end at infinity.
  • (ii) Tangent to any point on electric field lines shows the direction of electric field at that point.
  • (iii) Two field lines can never intersect each other because, if they intersect, then two tangents drawn at that point will represent two-directions of field at that point, which is not possible.
  • (iv) In a charge free region, electric field lines can be taken to be continuous curves without any breaks.
  • (v) Electric field lines do not form closed loops (because of conservative nature of electric field).
  • (vi) Electric field lines are perpendicular to the surface of a charged conductor.
  • (vii) Electric field lines contract lengthwise to represent attraction between two unlike charges.
  • (viii) Electric field lines exert sideways pressure to represent repulsion between two like charges.
  • (ix) The number delta(N) of lines per unit cross-sectional area perpendicular to the field lines (i.e. density of lines of force) is directly proportional to the magnitude of the intensity of electric field in that region. delta(N) / delta(A) proportional to E.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Potential: Defined as the amount of work done in bringing a unit positive charge, without any acceleration, from infinity to that point, along any arbitrary path. If W work is to be done to bring a test charge q0 from infinity to a point, then the potential of that point is V = W / q0. The SI unit of potential is volt, where 1V = 1J / 1C.

Potential Difference: Potential difference between two points in an electric field is equal to the work done per unit charge in carrying a positive test charge from one point to the other point. Potential difference between two points A and B is given as, ΔV = VB - VA = W / q0. The SI unit is volt or joule/coulomb. It is a physical quantity that decides the direction of flow of charge between two points in the electric field. Positive charge always tends to move from higher potential towards lower potential.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for Electric Potential and Potential Difference.

subject: Physics
text:
The surface drawn in an electric field, at which each point has same potential, is called equipotential surface.

  • Equipotential surfaces are always normal to lines of force.
  • The work done in moving a charge on equipotential surface is zero because potential difference is zero.
  • Two equipotential surfaces never intersect each other.

Electric field (E) and electric potential (V) are related as dV = -E · dr, where dr is small displacement. If θ is the angle between dr and E, then dV = -Edr cosθ.

details.summary: Properties and mathematical relations of Equipotential Surfaces.

subject: Physics
topic: Electric Potential Energy and Energy Density
text:
Electric Potential Energy: A potential energy that results from conservative coulomb forces and is associated with the configuration of particular set of point charge within a defined system. Electric potential energy (U) = (q1 q2) / (4πε0 r). Unit is Joule.

Energy Density: The amount of energy stored in a given system or region of space per unit volume or mass. Termed specific energy Ve = (1/2) ε0 E^2.

details.summary: Definitions of Electric Potential Energy and Energy Density.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Dipole: Consists of a pair of equal and opposite point charges separated by some small distance.

Dipole Moment of an Electric Dipole: The strength of an electric dipole is measured by a vector quantity known as electric dipole moment (p) which is the product of the charge (q) and separation between the charges (2l).
image_descriptions: Diagram showing an electric dipole with two charges +q and -q separated by a distance 2l, labeled A and B.

details.summary: Definition and dipole moment of an electric dipole.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Dipole: Defined by the product of charge and distance, p = q x 2l. It is a vector quantity directed from negative to positive charge. The SI unit is coulomb-metre (C-m). An ideal dipole is the smallest dipole having almost no size.

Electric Field Intensity due to an Electric Dipole: The space around the dipole where electric effects are experienced. Calculated using the superposition principle.

(i) At a Point on the Axial Line: The electric field intensity is given by E_p = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (2px / (x^2 - l^2)^2). For a short dipole where 2l << x, this simplifies to E_p = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (2p / x^3).

(ii) At a Point on the Equatorial Line: The resultant electric field intensity is E_theta = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (|p| / (x^2 + l^2)^(3/2)). For a short dipole where 2l << x, this simplifies to E_theta = (1 / 4*pi*epsilon_0) * (|p| / x^3).
image_descriptions: Diagram showing an electric dipole on an axial line with charges -q and +q separated by 2l, with point P at distance x from the center O.
Diagram showing an electric dipole on an equatorial line with point Q at distance x from center O, forming a triangle with charges -q and +q.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Flux: Defined as the total number of electric field lines crossing through an area. SI unit is Nm^2C^-1. Flux through a small area element delta_S is delta_Phi_E = E * delta_S * cos(theta).

Special Cases:

  • 0 < theta < 90 degrees: Flux is positive.
  • theta = 90 degrees: Flux is zero.
  • 90 < theta < 180 degrees: Flux is negative.

Gauss's Theorem: The electric flux over any closed surface is 1/epsilon_0 times the total charge enclosed by that surface. Phi_E = Sigma_q / epsilon_0. If total enclosed charge is zero, total electric flux is zero.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing electric field lines E passing through a surface S with an area vector dS at an angle theta.

subject: Physics
text:
Conductors: Materials through which electric charge can flow easily. Silver is the best conductor of electric charge.

Insulators: Materials like glass, rubber, wood, etc., through which electric charge cannot flow. These are also called dielectrics when an electric field is applied, as induced charges appear on the surface without conducting.

Dielectrics: In a dielectric, an external field induces a net dipole moment. Induced charges produce a field (E_in) opposing the external field (E_0), resulting in a reduced field inside the dielectric: E = |E_0| - |E_in|.

Dielectric Constant (K): The ratio of the strength of the external field to the reduced value of the electric field. Also known as relative permittivity or specific inductive capacity (denoted by K or epsilon_r). Note: The value of K is always greater than 1.

Polarisation (P): The induced dipole moment developed per unit volume in a dielectric slab. If p is the induced dipole moment and N is the number of atoms per unit volume, then P = Np.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a rectangular dielectric slab placed in an external electric field E_0. The slab shows internal induced charges with an opposing internal electric field E_in pointing in the opposite direction to E_0. A vector sigma_p is shown at the bottom.

details.summary: Overview of electrical properties of materials including conductors, insulators, dielectrics, dielectric constant, and polarisation.

subject: Physics
text:
Electrical Capacitance: The amount of charge needed to raise the potential of a conductor by unity. It is a scalar quantity. The SI unit is farad (1F = 1C/1V).

Capacitance of an isolated spherical conductor: C = 4 * pi * epsilon_0 * R = R / (9 * 10^9).

Capacitor: A device that stores electrostatic energy. Net charge on a capacitor is zero, but charge on either plate is finite.

Capacitance of Capacitor: Ratio of charge (q) and applied potential (V), i.e., C = q/V.

Spherical Capacitor Capacitance: Formulas provided for cases where external or internal spheres are connected to earth, in air or medium.
formulas: C = 4 * pi * epsilon_0 * (ab / (b - a)) [In air, external sphere earthed]
C = 4 * pi * epsilon_0 * K * ab / (b - a) [In medium, external sphere earthed]
C = 4 * pi * epsilon_0 * (b^2 / (b - a)) [In air, internal sphere earthed]
C = 4 * pi * epsilon_0 * K * ab / (b - a) [In medium, internal sphere earthed]

details.summary: Definitions and mathematical formulas for electrical capacitance, capacitors, and spherical capacitor configurations.

subject: Physics
topic: Factors Affecting Capacitance of a Capacitor
text:
The capacitance of a capacitor is affected by the following factors:

  • Area (A): Capacitance is directly proportional to area (C ∝ A).
  • Distance (d): Capacitance is inversely proportional to the distance between the plates (C ∝ 1/d).
  • Dielectric Medium (K): Capacitance is directly proportional to the dielectric constant of the medium (C ∝ K).

details.summary: Factors influencing the capacitance of a capacitor include plate area, distance between plates, and the dielectric medium.

subject: Physics
text:
There are two common methods of grouping capacitors:

1. Series Grouping

In a series arrangement, the charge on each plate of each capacitor has the same magnitude, equal to the charge supplied by the battery. The potential difference is distributed inversely in the ratio of capacitors.

  • V = V1 + V2 + V3 + ...
  • V1 : V2 : V3 ... = 1/C1 : 1/C2 : 1/C3 ...

The equivalent capacitance Cs is given by:

1/Cs = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3 + ... = sum(1/Ci)

2. Parallel Grouping

In a parallel arrangement, the potential across each capacitor is exactly the same. The charge is distributed in the ratio of capacitance:

  • Q = Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + ...
  • Q1 : Q2 : Q3 ... = C1 : C2 : C3 ...

The equivalent capacitance Cp is given by:

Cp = C1 + C2 + C3 + ... = sum(Ci)
image_descriptions: Circuit diagram showing three capacitors C1, C2, and C3 connected in series with a battery V.
Circuit diagram showing three capacitors C1, C2, and C3 connected in parallel with a battery V.

details.summary: Explanation of series and parallel grouping of capacitors and their equivalent capacitance formulas.

subject: Physics
text:
The energy of a charged capacitor is measured by the total work done in charging the capacitor to a given potential. For an additional small charge (dq) transferred from one plate to another, the work done is dW = V'dq = (q'/C)dq.

The total work done in transferring charge Q is:

W = integral(q'/C dq) from 0 to Q = Q^2 / 2C

This work is stored as electrostatic potential energy U:

U = Q^2 / 2C = (CV)^2 / 2C = 1/2 CV^2

The energy stored per unit volume is called energy density:

Energy density = 1/2 * epsilon_0 * E^2

Total energy stored in any combination is the sum of energies stored in individual capacitors: U = U1 + U2 + U3 + ...

details.summary: Derivation and formulas for electrostatic potential energy stored in a capacitor and energy density.

subject: Physics
text:
Rate of flow of charge is called the electric current (i).

Current is a scalar quantity. Unit of electric current is ampere. The direction of flow of current is opposite to the direction of flow of electrons.

According to its magnitude and direction, electric current is of two types:

  • Direct Current (DC): An electric current whose magnitude and direction do not change with time. e.g., a cell, battery or DC dynamo are the sources of direct current.
  • Alternating Current (AC): An electric current whose magnitude changes continuously and direction changes periodically. e.g., AC dynamo is the source of alternating current.

details.summary: Definition and types of electric current.

subject: Physics
text:
The current flowing normally through the unit of cross-section is called current density. If current i is distributed uniformly over area A, then current density J = i / A.

The direction of current density is in the direction of motion of positive charge.

details.summary: Definition and direction of current density.

subject: Physics
text:
When an electric field is applied across the conductor, then the electric field gives a constant velocity to the free electrons along the length of the wire, this velocity is called drift velocity (v_d). It is of the order of 10^-4 m/s.

Current flowing in a wire is i = neAv_d, where n = number of free electrons in unit volume of wire and A = area of cross-section of the wire.

details.summary: Definition and formula for drift velocity.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Potential: The electric potential at a point in an electric field is defined as the amount of work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point.

Potential Difference: The potential difference between two points in an electric field is defined as the amount of work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point the other point.

Note: Variable DC potential is represented by the symbol: (Diagram shows a line with an arrow crossing it diagonally).

details.summary: Definitions of electric potential and potential difference.

subject: Physics
text: If there is no change in the physical state of a conductor, then the ratio of potential difference across its ends and the current flowing through it is constant.

details.summary: Statement and formula for Ohm's Law.

subject: Physics
text:
Constant R is called electric resistance of the circuit. Unit of electric resistance R is ohm (Ω). Inverse of electric resistance is called the electric conductance. Its unit is ohm-1 or mho.

Ohmic Conductor: The conductor which obey the Ohm's law is known as ohmic conductor. e.g. Metallic wire.

Non-ohmic Conductor: The conductor which not obey the Ohm's law is known as non-ohmic conductor. e.g. Diode valve, triode valve.

Electrical Resistance

Electrical resistance is defined as the ratio in the potential difference (V) across the ends of the conductor to the current (i) flowing through it, i.e. R = V/i. The SI unit of electrical resistance is Ω (ohm) and its dimension is [ML2T-3A-2].

Effect of Temperature on the Resistance

  • On increasing the temperature of the metal, its resistance increases.
  • On increasing the temperature of semiconductor its resistance decreases.
  • On increasing the temperature of alloy, their resistance increase but it is small compared to the pure metals.
  • On increasing the temperature of electrolytes, their resistance decreases.

details.summary: Definitions of resistance, conductance, ohmic/non-ohmic conductors, and temperature effects on resistance.

subject: Physics
text:
Specific Resistance

Ratio of electric field and the current density at a point in the conductor is called the current density at a point in the conductor is called the specific resistance or resistivity. It is a constant for the material. ρ = E/J or ρ = RA/l. Its unit is ohm-metre.

Some factors affecting specific resistance are given below:

  • Resistivity increases with increases of temperature.
  • Resistivity increases on mixing of impurity and increase of mechanical stress.
  • The resistance of super conductor is zero.

Conductivity

Inverse of specific resistance is called conductivity (σ). Unit of conductivity is mho/metre.

Conductance

Inverse of resistance is called conductance. Unit of conductance is ohm-1 or siemen or mho.

details.summary: Definitions of specific resistance (resistivity), conductivity, and conductance.

subject: Physics
text:
Different electrical conducting materials of specific uses

  • The filament of bulb is made of tungsten. The resistivity and melting point of tungsten both are high.
  • In heating equipments (heater, gyser and electric press), the coils are made of nichrome because the resistivity and melting of nichrome is very high.
  • In resistance box, the standard resistances are made of manganin or constantan. Their resistivity do not depend upon temperature, therefore the value of standard resistance does not vary.
  • Fuse wire is made of mixed conductor (63% tin and 37% lead). The value of melting point is low but resistivity is very high. The fuse wire is placed in the series to protect the main line.

details.summary: Practical applications of various conducting materials.

subject: Physics
text:
Combination of Resistance

(i) Series combination: In this combination, resistances are joined end to end. In series combination, equivalent resistance is equal to sum of individual resistance. R = R1 + R2 + R3. In series combination, current through each resistance is same. i = i1 = i2 = i3. In series combination potential difference across each resistance is different. V = V1 + V2 + V3. Such that V1 : V2 : V3 = R1 : R2 : R3.

(ii) Parallel combination: In this combination, first ends of all the resistances is connected to one point and second ends of all the resistances is connected to other point. In parallel combination, equivalent resistance is given by 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing three resistors R1, R2, R3 connected in series with a voltage source V.
Diagram showing three resistors R1, R2, R3 connected in parallel between two points A and B with a voltage source V.

details.summary: Formulas and properties for series and parallel resistor combinations.

subject: Physics
text:
Electric Cell: A device which maintains a continuous flow of charge (or electric current) in a circuit by a chemical reaction. It contains two rods of different metals called electrodes.

Types of Electric Cell:

  • Electrochemical cell: Chemical energy is converted into electric energy.
    • Primary cell: Used only for discharge. Current leaves the cell at the positive terminal, goes through the external circuit, and enters at the negative terminal. Examples: Daniell cell, Leclanche cell.
    • Secondary cell: Current passes in both directions. During discharge, current leaves at the positive terminal and enters at the negative terminal. Most commonly used is a lead accumulator.
  • Photo cell: Radiant energy is converted into electric energy.
  • Thermocouple cell: Thermal energy is converted into electric energy.

Electromotive Force (emf):

The energy given by the cell in the flow of unit charge in the whole circuit. Alternatively, the potential difference across the terminals of the cell when no current is being taken from the cell. Unit is volt. It is a constant for the cell.

Internal Resistance of a Cell (r):

The resistance offered by the electrolyte of the cell. If current i is taken, potential difference is V, then r = (E - V) / i or r = R(E/V - 1), where R is external resistance.

Factors affecting internal resistance:

  • Increases if distance between plates increases.
  • Decreases if area of electrodes increases.
  • Decreases if concentration of electrolyte increases.

Terminal Voltage:

Voltage across the terminals of a cell. It is not constant and depends on the current drawn (larger current = smaller terminal voltage). Relation: E = V + ir.
image_descriptions: Circuit diagram showing n cells in series, each with emf E and internal resistance r, connected to an external resistor R.

details.summary: Overview of electric cells, including types (primary, secondary, photo, thermocouple), definitions of emf and internal resistance, and factors affecting internal resistance.

subject: Physics
text:
Combination of Cells:

  • In series: Negative end of each cell is connected to the positive end of the next. For n cells with emf E and internal resistance r: Total emf = nE, Total internal resistance = nr. Current i = nE / (nr + R).
    • If nr < R: Current is n times the current from one cell.
    • If nr >> R: No benefit in joining cells in series.
  • In parallel: Positive terminals connected to one point, negative to another. For n cells: Total emf = E, Total internal resistance = r/n.
image_descriptions: Circuit diagram showing n cells in series.

details.summary: Mathematical analysis of cells connected in series and parallel configurations.

subject: Physics
text:
Combination of cells in parallel: Current taken from the combination is given by i = (nE) / (r + nR).

  • If (r/n) >> R, i.e., total internal resistance of cells is greater than external resistance, then current taken from the combination is n times that from one cell.
  • If (r/n) << R, i.e., total internal resistance of cells is less than external resistance, then current taken from the combination is equal to that from one cell. So, there is no benefit of connecting cells of low internal resistance in parallel.

Mixed grouping: In this combination, a certain number of cells are connected in various series and all such series are then connected in parallel. Number of cells = mn, emf of combination = nE, total internal resistance = (nr)/m. Current taken in external resistance, i = (mnE) / (nr + mR). For maximum current in the circuit, mR = nr.

If two cells oppose each other, then current taken from them is I = (E1 - E2) / (r1 + r2 + R). Similarly, if cells support each other, then I = (E1 + E2) / (r1 + r2 + R).

Charging current of a cell: i = (emf of charger - emf of cell) / (total resistance of the circuit). In a battery of N cells each of emf E, if n cells are wrongly connected, then net emf, E' = NE - 2nE.
formulas: i = (emf of charger - emf of cell) / (total resistance of the circuit)
image_descriptions: Circuit diagram showing multiple cells connected in parallel, each with emf E and internal resistance r, connected to an external resistor R.
Circuit diagram showing a mixed grouping of cells arranged in n columns and m rows, connected to an external resistor R.

subject: Physics
topic: Rheostat, Kirchhoff's Laws, and Wheatstone's Bridge
text:
Rheostat: It is a variable resistor which is used to control current in the circuit. The construction is very similar to the construction of a potentiometer.

Kirchhoff's Laws:

  • Junction law: The algebraic sum of the current flowing into any junction is zero. Thus, ΣI_junction = 0.
  • Loop law: The algebraic sum of the potential difference in any closed loop is equal to zero. Thus, Σ_closed_loop ΔV = 0 => ΣE + RI = 0, ΔE = - ΣRI.

Wheat Stone's Bridge: It is an arrangement of four resistances making a closed circuit. The resistance of a given conductor can be determined with its help. When there is no deflection in the galvanometer, then P/Q = R/S. In this case, V_B = V_D and the bridge will be balanced.
image_descriptions: Symbol of a rheostat.
Circuit diagram of a Wheatstone bridge with four resistors P, Q, R, S arranged in a diamond shape with a galvanometer in the center.

subject: Physics
text:
Different Measuring Devices:

  • Ammeter: A device used to measure electric current in a circuit. It is always connected in series with the current source and has very low resistance.
  • Voltmeter: A device used to measure the potential difference across the ends of a conductor. It is always connected in parallel and has very high resistance.
  • Galvanometer: A device used to detect the presence of the electric current in a circuit.

subject: Physics
text:
To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, a low resistance wire called a shunt is connected in parallel with the galvanometer.

  • Resistance of shunt, S = (i_g * G) / (i - i_g)
  • where, G = resistance of galvanometer, i = range of ammeter, and i_g = safe current for galvanometer coil.

To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, a high resistance (R) is connected in series with the galvanometer.

  • R = (V / i_g) - G
  • where, V = range of voltmeter.

details.summary: Methods for converting a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter.

subject: Physics
text:
Whenever electric current passes through a conductor, it becomes hot. This indicates electric energy is converted into heat energy, known as Joule heating effect.

  • H = (W / 4.2) = (VIt / 4.2) = (V^2t / 4.2R) = (I^2Rt / 4.2)

Electrical Power: The rate at which work is done by the source of emf in maintaining current in a circuit. P = VI = V^2/R = I^2R. SI unit is watt.

Electrical Energy: Total work done by the source of emf. SI unit is joule.

Kilowatt-hour (kWh): Known as Board of Trade Unit (BTO). 1 kWh = 1000 * 3600 = 3.6 * 10^6 Joule.
formulas: W = (V(in volt) * I(in amp) * t(in hour)) / 1000

details.summary: Principles of Joule heating, electrical power, and energy consumption.

subject: Physics
text:
The production of electricity with the help of heat is called thermoelectricity.

  • Seebeck Effect: Current flows in a couple of wires due to temperature difference at junctions without an external battery.
  • Peltier Effect: Absorption or evolution of heat at a junction of two dissimilar metals when current is passed. Peltier coefficient, pi = T * (dE/dtheta).
  • Thomson Effect: Absorption or evolution of heat along the length of a wire when current is passed through it while kept at different temperatures. Thomson coefficient, sigma = -T * (dS/dtheta).

details.summary: Definitions of Seebeck, Peltier, and Thomson effects.

subject: Physics
text:
Electrolysis: The process where electric current passes through an electrolyte and decomposes it into constituents.

Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis:

  • (i) First law: Amount of substance deposited (m) is directly proportional to charge (q). m = zq or m = zit, where z = electrochemical equivalent.
  • (ii) Second law: If same current is passed through different electrolytes for same time, ratio of masses liberated is equal to ratio of their chemical equivalents. m1/m2 = E1/E2 or z1/z2 = E1/E2.

Faraday Constant (F): Quantity of charge required to liberate one gram equivalent of a substance. F = E/A = 96500 coulomb or F = Ne, where N = Avogadro's number and e = electronic charge.

details.summary: Chemical effects of current, Faraday's laws of electrolysis, and Faraday constant.

subject: Physics
chapter: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current and Magnetism
text:
Electromagnetics: The branch of physics in which we study the effect of magnetic field produced due to current or moving charge, is known as magnetic effects of electric current.

Magnetic Field: It is a region or space around a magnet or current carrying conductor or a moving charge in which its magnetic effect can be felt. Its SI unit is tesla (T).

details.summary: Introduction to electromagnetics and definition of magnetic field.

subject: Physics
chapter: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current and Magnetism
text:
Biot-Savart Law: According to this law, the magnetic field dB at the point P due to the small current element of length dl is given by:

dB = (μ₀ / 4π) * (i dl sinθ / r²)

In vector form: dB = (μ₀ / 4π) * (i dl x r) / r³

Where μ₀ is a constant called permeability of free space, and μ₀ = 4π x 10⁻⁷ Wb/A-m.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a curved current-carrying wire element 'i dl', a point 'P' at a distance 'r' from the element, with an angle 'θ' between the element and the position vector.

details.summary: Mathematical formulation of Biot-Savart Law.

subject: Physics
chapter: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current and Magnetism
topic: Rules to Find the Direction of Magnetic Field
text:
Rules to Find the Direction of Magnetic Field:

  • Right hand palm rule: If we spread our right hand in such a way that thumb is towards the direction of current and fingers are towards that point, where we have to find the direction of field, then the direction of field will be perpendicular to the palm.
  • Maxwell's right handed screw rule: If a right handed cork screw is rotated, so that its tip moves in the direction of flow of current through the conductor, then the rotation of the head of the screw gives the direction of magnetic lines of force.

details.summary: Rules for determining the direction of magnetic fields.

subject: Physics
text: The table below summarizes the mathematical forms of magnetic fields for various current-carrying geometrical shapes based on Biot-Savart's Law.
tables:
| S.No | Current Carrying Geometrical Shape | Diagram | Mathematical form |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Finite length current carrying conductor | Triangle with angles theta1, theta2 at point P | B = (mu_0 * I) / (4 * pi * d) * (sin(theta_1) + sin(theta_2)) |
| 2 | Infinite length current carrying conductor | Straight line with distance d to point P | theta_1 + theta_2 = pi/2, B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * d) |
| 3 | At the terminal of infinite length current carrying conductor | Straight line with distance d to point P | theta_1 = 0, theta_2 = pi/2, B = (mu_0 * I) / (4 * pi * d) |
| 4 | If P point lie outside area of wire | Triangle with angles alpha1, alpha2 | B_p = (mu_0 * I) / (4 * pi * d) * (cos(alpha_1) - cos(alpha_2)) |
| 5 | On the axis of current carrying coil | Coil of radius R at distance x | B = (mu_0 * N * I * R^2) / (2 * (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)) |
| 6 | On the center of current carrying loop coil | Circular loop of radius R | x = 0, B = (mu_0 * N * I) / (2 * R) |
| 7 | On the center of current carrying loop | Circular loop of radius R | N = 1, B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * R) |
| 8 | On the center of segment of current carrying circle | Circular arc of angle theta | B = (mu_0 * I) / (4 * pi * R) * theta |
| 9 | On the axis of current carrying solenoid | Solenoid of length L, radius R | B = (mu_0 * n * I) / 2 * (cos(theta_1) - cos(theta_2)) |
| 10 | On the center of long solenoid | Solenoid | theta_1 = 180, theta_2 = 0, B_e = mu_0 * N * I |
| 11 | On the terminal of solenoid | Solenoid | theta_1 = 90, theta_2 = 0, B_e = (mu_0 * N * I) / 2 |
image_descriptions: Diagrams for each of the 11 geometrical shapes showing current direction, distance d, radius R, and angles theta/alpha relative to point P.

subject: Physics
text:
Ampere's Circuital Law states that the line integral of magnetic field around any closed path in vacuum is equal to mu_0 times the total current enclosed by the loop.

Formula: integral(B dot dl) = mu_0 * I_net

Simplified form: B * l = mu_0 * I_net

Conditions:

  • At every point of the closed circuit, B is parallel to dl.
  • The magnetic field at every point of the closed circuit remains uniform.

subject: Physics
text:
1. Magnetic field due to straight wire of infinite length: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * r)

2. Magnetic field due to conducting rod of radius R at a point at distance r:

  • If r < R: B = (mu_0 * I * r) / (2 * pi * R^2) (B proportional to r)
  • If r = R: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * R)
  • If r > R: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * r) (B proportional to 1/r)

3. Magnetic field due to hollow cylindrical pipe of radius R:

  • If r < R: B = 0
  • If r >= R: B = (mu_0 * I) / (2 * pi * r)
image_descriptions: Graph showing B vs r for a conducting rod. The graph increases linearly from origin to R (B proportional to r) and then decreases as 1/r for r > R.

subject: Physics
topic: Force on Current Carrying Conductors and Moving Charges
text:
Force between two Parallel Current Carrying Conductor: Two linear parallel conductor carrying currents in the same direction attract each other while in opposite direction they repel each other. Therefore, force between two current carrying parallel conductor per unit length is F = (μ₀ / 4π) * (2I₁I₂ / r²)

Magnetic Field of a Moving Point Charge: The magnetic field due to a charge q, moving with speed v at a point P at distance r from the charge is given by B = (μ₀ / 4π) * (q / r²) * (v x r)

Force on a Moving Charge in Magnetic Field: Force on a moving charge in the magnetic field is given by Fₘ = qvB sinθ = q(v x B). It is also called Lorentz force.

  • Electromagnetic and gravitational forces act on neutral and large bodies.
  • If the moving charge is moving perpendicular to the magnetic field, then its kinetic energy remains constant.
  • The force acting in the presence of electric and magnetic field simultaneously: F = q(E + v x B)

Rules to Find the Direction of Force:

  • Right hand palm rule: If a linear conductor is grasped in the palm of the right hand with thumb pointing along the direction of the current, then the finger tips will point in the direction of lines of force.
  • Fleming’s left hand rule: If we spread the forefinger, central finger and thumb of our left hand in such a way that these three are perpendicular to each other, then first forefinger is in the direction of magnetic field, second central finger is in the direction of current and thumb will represent the direction of force.

Motion of Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field: When a charged particle enters in a magnetic field perpendicularly, then it moves on a circular path. Radius of circular path, r = mv / Bq = sqrt(2mEₖ) / qB. Time period of particle, T = 2πm / Bq. Frequency of particle, n = Bq / 2πm.

  • If a charged particle is moving in the direction of magnetic field, then it experiences no force.
  • The velocity of proton moving in a magnetic field changes continuously.

Force on a Current Carrying Conductor in Magnetic Field: When a current carrying conductor is placed in magnetic field, then it experiences a force on it, this force is given by Fₘ = Bil sinθ = il x B. When θ = 90° or sinθ = 1, then F = ilB (Maximum). When θ = 0 or sinθ = 0, then F = ilB x 0 = 0.

Application of Current Carrying Conductor:

  • (i) Magnetic force acting on a current carrying conductor is not central force because F = BIdl sinθ expression does not depends upon r.
  • (ii) The force dF is always perpendicular to B and idL.

MAGNET: A naturally occurring black coloured substance called lodestone can attract pieces of iron kept nearby. In early days, the Greeks observed this property of loadstone an oxide called magnetite (Fe₃O₄). This type of substance is called magnet. Magnet is of two types: (i) Natural Magnet, (ii) Artificial Magnets.
formulas: Fₘ = qvB sinθ = q(v x B)
Fₘ = Bil sinθ = il x B
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, with vectors indicating the direction of the magnetic field (B), the current (i), and the resulting force (F) acting on the conductor.

details.summary: Covers magnetic forces on moving charges and current-carrying conductors, including Lorentz force, Fleming's rules, motion of charged particles in magnetic fields, and basic definitions of magnets.

subject: Physics
text:
Important Facts Related to Magnet:

  • Artificial magnets have short life and natural magnets have long life.
  • Magnetism of earth has infinite time.
  • Unstable magnet is an induced magnet.
  • Magnets are used in electric bells, fans, washing machines, etc.

Pole Strength: The ability of a magnetic pole to attract magnetic material is known as pole strength. It is denoted by m. The pole strength of North and South pole is represented by +m and -m.

Magnetic Axis: The line joining north pole and the south pole of a magnet is called the magnetic axis.

Effective Length of Magnet: The distance between the north pole and the south pole of the magnet is called the effective length of the magnet.

Magnetic Dipole: Two equal and opposite poles separated by a distance 2l are said to constitute a dipole.

Magnetic Moment: The magnetic moment of a bar magnet is given by the product of its length and pole strength. It is represented by M.

Magnetic Field: The area surrounding the magnet in which, another magnet experiences a force on it is called magnetic field.

Magnetic Field Lines: The imaginary lines which represents the direction of magnetic field. Properties:

  • Magnetic lines of force always form closed curves.
  • They leave the north pole and enter the south pole externally.
  • They move from the south pole to the north pole within the magnet.
  • They tend to contract laterally.
  • The magnetic field lines never intersect each other.
formulas: Pole strength (m) = Magnetic force / Magnetic induction = F/m
τ = mBl sin θ + mBl sin θ = 2mBl sin θ = MB sin θ
image_descriptions: Diagram of a Magnetic Dipole showing a bar magnet with poles -m and +m separated by distance 2l.
Diagram of Torque on Bar Magnet in Magnetic Field showing a bar magnet NS at angle θ within a uniform magnetic field B, with forces mB acting at the poles.

details.summary: Covers fundamental properties of magnets, definitions of pole strength, magnetic dipole, magnetic moment, magnetic field lines, and mathematical relations for magnetization, permeability, susceptibility, and torque.

subject: Physics
text:
Some Properties of Magnet:

  • Intensity of magnetisation: Defined as magnetic moment per unit volume (I = M/V).
  • Magnetic permeability: Measure of degree to which magnetic field can penetrate or permeate a medium (μ = B/H).
  • Magnetic susceptibility: Intensity of magnetisation per unit magnetising field (φ = I/H).
  • Relation between magnetic susceptibility and permeability: Relative magnetic permeability μ_r = 1 + φ, where μ_r = μ/μ_0.

details.summary: Definitions and mathematical relations for intensity of magnetisation, magnetic permeability, and magnetic susceptibility.

subject: Physics
topic: Work Done in Rotating a Dipole in a Magnetic Field
text:
The total work done in deflecting the dipole through an angle θ from 0° is:

  • W = MB(1 - cosθ)
  • If θ = 0°, then W = MB[1 - 1] = 0
  • If θ = 90°, then W = MB
  • If θ = 180°, then W = 2MB

where, M is magnetic dipole moment.

details.summary: Work done in rotating a magnetic dipole in a magnetic field.

subject: Physics
topic: Field due to Small Bar Magnet (Magnetic Dipole)
text:
(i) In end on position (on axial point): B = (μ0 / 4π) * (2M / r3), where r is distance of the required point from the centre of dipole.

(ii) In broad side on position (on perpendicular bisector): B = (μ0 / 4π) * (M / r3)

(iii) At any general point (r, θ) relative to centre of dipole: B = (μ0 / 4π) * (M / r3) * sqrt(1 + 3cos2θ)

details.summary: Magnetic field formulas for a small bar magnet at different positions.

subject: Physics
text: The earth is a natural source of magnetic field. It behaves as a magnet which causes a freely suspended magnet to point always in a north-south direction. The south pole of a earth's magnet is towards the earth's north pole (geographical north), while the north pole of earth's magnet is towards the earth's south pole (geographical south). The positions of the earth's magnetic poles are not well defined on the globe, they are spread over an area.

details.summary: Overview of Earth's magnetic field properties.

subject: Physics
text:
To have a complete knowledge of the earth's magnetism at a place, the following three elements must be known:

  • (i) Angle of declination: The angle between the magnetic meridian and geographical meridian at a place.
  • (ii) Angle of dip or inclination: The angle which the axis of needle makes with the horizontal.
  • (iii) Horizontal component of the earth's field: The direction of the earth's field at the magnetic poles is normal to the earth's surface and at magnetic equator it is parallel to the earth's surface.

The resultant earth's field can be resolved into two components:

  • BH = Be cosθ
  • BV = Be sinθ
  • BV / BH = tanθ
  • Be = sqrt(BH2 + BV2)
image_descriptions: A diagram showing the Geographic North, Magnetic North, Geographic Meridian, and Magnetic Meridian. It illustrates the horizontal component (H) and vertical component (B) of the Earth's magnetic field, with angle of dip (theta) between the resultant field and the horizontal component.

details.summary: Explanation of magnetic elements: declination, dip, and horizontal component.

subject: Physics
text:
Important Points:

  • At any place, angle of dip is θ and magnetic meridian is α, then tanθ = 2tanα
  • Intensity of Earth magnetic field: I = I0 * sqrt(1 + 3sin2α), where I0 = M / R2 (R = radius of Earth)
  • At magnetic equator line λ = 0 and at poles λ = 90°, then Ipole = 2Iequator

details.summary: Key formulas and relationships for Earth's magnetic field intensity.

subject: Physics
text:
On the basis of magnetic properties, materials are classified into three categories:

  • Diamagnetic substance: These substances when placed in an external magnetic field, acquire feeble magnetism opposite to the direction of the magnetic field. Examples: Bi, Zn, Au, NaCl, H2O, etc.
  • Paramagnetic substance: These substances when placed in an external magnetic field, acquire feeble magnetism in the direction of the magnetic field. Examples: Al, Na, Pt, Mn, CuCl2, O2, etc.
  • Ferromagnetic substance: These substances when placed in an external magnetic field are strongly magnetised in the direction of the field. Examples: Fe, Ni, Co, Fe2O3, etc.

details.summary: Classification of magnetic materials based on their response to external magnetic fields.

subject: Physics
text:
Curie's Law: According to Curie's Law, the magnetic susceptibility of paramagnetic substance is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature.

Curie Temperature: Above a certain temperature, the substance loses its ferromagnetic character and begins to behave as a paramagnetic substance. This particular temperature is called the Curie temperature of the substance.

details.summary: Relationship between magnetic susceptibility and temperature for paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials.

subject: Physics
text:
Magnetic flux is defined as the total number of magnetic lines of force passing normally through any surface. If surface of area A is placed perpendicular to uniform magnetic field B, then magnetic flux φ = BA. Its unit is Wb (weber) or kg-m²/s²A.

If a plane is parallel to the magnetic field, then no flux link will pass through it and magnetic flux link with coil will be zero. If the coil is rotated through 90° in the magnetic field, then magnetic flux linked with the coil is zero.

details.summary: Definition and properties of magnetic flux.

subject: Physics
text:
Electromagnetic Induction: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit changes, an induced emf is produced in the circuit. This emf lasts only, so long as the change in flux lasts. This phenomena is called electromagnetic induction.

Faraday's Laws:

  • First Law: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a coil changes, an induced emf is induced in the circuit.
  • Second Law: Induced emf is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux.

Induced Current and Induced Charge: If a circuit has a resistance (R):

  • Induced current, i = (1/R) * (dφ/dt)
  • Induced charge, q = (1/R) * Δφ

details.summary: Principles of electromagnetic induction, Faraday's laws, and calculations for induced current and charge.

subject: Physics
topic: Lenz's Law and Induced EMF in Conducting Rod
text:
Lenz's Law: The direction of the induced emf is such as to oppose the change that causes it. It is one form of law of conservation of energy.

Induced emf in a Conducting Rod:

  • Moving perpendicularly in magnetic field: e = Bvl
  • If velocity makes angle θ: e = Bvl sinθ
  • Rotating about an end in uniform magnetic field: e = (Bωl²)/2

details.summary: Lenz's law and formulas for induced EMF in moving or rotating conductors.

subject: Physics
text:
Electromagnetic induction is of two types:

  • (i) Self-induction: When the current flowing through a coil changes, then induced current produces in the same coil, it is called self-induction.
  • (ii) Mutual induction: When two coils are placed near each other, then if there is a change in current in one coil, then emf is induced in the another coil, this phenomena is called mutual induction.
tables:
| S.No | Combination of inductor | Combination diagram | Equivalent Inductance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Series Combination | L1, L2, L3 in series | L = L1 + L2 + L3 |
| 2 | Parallel Combination | L1, L2, L3 in parallel | 1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2 + 1/L3 |
image_descriptions: Symbol for self-inductance showing a coiled wire.
Diagram for series combination of inductors showing three inductors L1, L2, L3 connected in a line.
Diagram for parallel combination of inductors showing three inductors L1, L2, L3 connected in parallel branches.

details.summary: Covers definitions and formulas for self-induction and mutual induction, including coefficients for solenoids and plane coils.

subject: Physics
topic: Coefficient of Coupling of the Two Circuits
text: The coefficient of coupling K is a number, depending on the geometry of the coils and their relative closeness having value between 0 and 1.

details.summary: Derivation of mutual inductance in terms of self-inductance and the coupling coefficient K.

subject: Physics
text:
Magnetic Resonance Image: It is produced due to the presence of hydrogen atoms in tissues. The nucleus of the hydrogen atoms produce magnetic resonance. This resonance is absorbed by special coil and send it to computer. This technique is used to analyse the various activities of brain.

Transformer: It is a static electrical device used to step-up a low voltage to a high voltage or to step down a high voltage into a low voltage and is used on AC circuits. Transformer works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.

Step-up Transformer: A step-up transformer steps the primary voltage up to a higher value. If the numbers of turns of secondary coil is more than the number of turns of primary coil, then it is called step-up transformers.

details.summary: Brief overview of MRI technology and the definition/function of transformers.

subject: Physics
text:
A step-down transformer steps the primary voltage down a lower value. If the number of turns of the secondary coil is less than that of the primary coil, it is called a step down transformer.

For transformer: I_s / I_p = V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s = k

  • I_p and I_s = current in primary and secondary coil.
  • V_p and V_s = potential in primary and secondary coil.
  • N_p and N_s = Number of turns in primary and secondary.
formulas: I_s / I_p = V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s = k

details.summary: Definition and transformer ratio formula for a step-down transformer.

subject: Physics
text:
Alternating Current: The current whose magnitude and direction changes with time and after a fixed period of time, it repeats the same magnitude and direction, called alternating current. Equation of alternating current is I = I_0 sin ωt

Alternating Voltage: The voltage whose magnitude and direction changes with time and after a fixed period of time, it repeats the same magnitude and direction, called alternating voltage. Equation of alternating voltage is V = V_0 sin ωt

  • I_0 = peak value of AC
  • ω = angular frequency of AC

details.summary: Definitions and mathematical equations for alternating current and voltage.

subject: Physics
topic: Mean and RMS Value of AC
text:
Mean Value of AC: Mean value for half-cycle of AC is given by I_m = 2 I_0 / π or I_m = 0.637 I_0. For complete cycle, mean value of AC is zero.

Root Mean Square Value of AC: For a complete cycle of AC, the root mean square value of current is called root mean square value. I_rms = I_0 / √2 = 0.707 I_0

In India distribution of electricity for domestic purpose is done in the form of 220V and at 50 Hz.

details.summary: Formulas for mean and RMS values of AC, and standard domestic electricity parameters in India.

subject: Physics
topic: Power in Alternating Circuit and Choke Coil
text:
Power in Alternating Circuit:

  • (i) If a circuit have only resistor then average power: P_av = V_rms × I_rms
  • (ii) If a circuit have resistor and inductor, then: P_av = V_rms × I_rms cos φ, where cos φ = R / √(R^2 + ω^2 L^2)
  • (iii) If a circuit have only inductor or capacitor, then P_av = 0.

Choke Coil: Choke coil is a device used to control the AC circuit. In choke coil power loss is negligible.

details.summary: Power dissipation formulas in different AC circuits and definition of a choke coil.

subject: Physics
text:
The entire positive charge and nearly the entire mass of an atom is concentrated in a very small space called the nucleus of an atom. The radius of nucleus is of the order of nearly 10^-15 m to 10^-14 m. The nucleus consists of protons and neutrons. They are called nucleons.

  • Number of protons = Atomic number (Z)
  • Number of neutrons = Mass number (A) - Atomic number (Z)

Thus, the nucleus of an atom is represented as ZXA

details.summary: Introduction to nuclear structure, defining nucleons, atomic number, and mass number.

subject: Physics
text:
Basic particle of nucleus is Neutron. It is discovered by James Chadwick.

Reaction: 0n1 -> 1H1 + -1β0 + ν (Proton, Electron, Anti-neutrino)

Properties of Neutron:

  • Mass of neutron is 1.6750 x 10^-27 kg.
  • Spin angular momentum of neutron is 1/2 * (h/2π).
  • Magnetic torque of neutron is 9.57 x 10^-27 Joule/Tesla.
  • Half life of neutron is 12 min.

details.summary: Properties and discovery of the neutron.

subject: Physics
text:
Properties of nucleus are given below:

  • Size of the nucleus is of the order of fermi. (1 fermi = 10^15 m)
  • The radius of the nucleus is given by R = R_0 A^1/3 where, R_0 = 1.3 fermi and A is the mass number.
  • The size of the atom is of the order of 10^-19 m.
  • The volume of nucleus is V = 4/3 π R^3 = 4/3 π (R_0 A^1/3)^3
  • Density = Mass of nucleus / Volume of the nucleus = (A * m_p) / (4/3 π (R_0 A^1/3)^3) = m_p / (4/3 π R_0^3) where, m_p = 1.6 x 10^-27 kg = mass of proton and R_0 = 1.3 fermi.
  • Density of nuclear matter is of the order of 10^17 kg/m^3
  • Density of nuclear matter is independent of the mass number.

details.summary: Mathematical properties of the nucleus including radius, volume, and density.

subject: Physics
text:
Atomic mass unit or amu is the unit in which atomic masses are expressed. 1 amu is defined as 1/16th the mass of an atom of 8O16 which is the most abundant isotope of oxygen.

1 amu = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg

details.summary: Definition of Atomic Mass Unit (amu).

subject: Physics
text:
Atomic species are of three types:

  • Isotopes: The atoms of same element which have same atomic number but different mass number are called isotopes. e.g., 17Cl35, 17Cl37, 1H1, 1H2, 1H3. The chemical properties of isotopes are same. Isotope used for treatment of blood cancer is Ag191.
  • Isobars: The atoms of different elements which has same mass number but different atomic number are called isobars. e.g., 18Ar40, 20Ca40.
  • Isotones or Isoneutronic: The atoms of different elements of which the nuclei have the same number of neutrons but different number of protons are called the isotones. e.g., (11Na23 and 12Mg24) and (19K39 and 20Ar40) are the isotones.

Mirror Nuclei: The nuclei, having the same mass number A but with the proton and neutron number interchanged, are called mirror nuclei.

details.summary: Classification of atomic species into isotopes, isobars, and isotones, plus definition of mirror nuclei.

subject: Physics
text:
Nuclear force are the strong forces of attraction which hold together the nucleons in the tiny nucleus of an atom, inspite of strong electrostatic force of repulsion between proton. The nuclear forces arise due to exchange of sub-nuclear particles, hence very complex in nature.

Some properties of nuclear force are given below:

  • Nuclear force is short range force. It cannot work beyond 10^-15 meter.
  • It is the strongest force in nature.
  • It gives the stability to Nuclei.
  • This force does not depend on charge.
  • It is not a central force.

details.summary: Properties and definition of nuclear forces.

subject: Physics
topic: Einstein Mass-Energy Equivalence and Pair Production
text:
Einstein Mass-Energy Equivalence Principle: Einstein made the suggestion that energy mass are equivalent. He predicted that if the energy of a body changes by an amount E, then it's mass changes by an amount given by the equation: E = mc^2 (where c is the speed of light).

Pair Production: When an energetic gamma-ray photon falls on a heavy substance, it is absorbed by some nucleus of the substance and an electron and a positron are produced. This phenomenon is called 'pair production' and may be represented by the equation: hv -> +1B^0 + -1B^0

Pair Annihilation: The converse phenomenon of pair production is called pair annihilation. When an electron and a positron come very close to each other, they annihilate each other by combining together and two gamma-photons are produced. This phenomenon can be represented by the following equation: +1B^0 + -1B^0 -> hv + hv

details.summary: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence, pair production, and pair annihilation.

subject: Physics
topic: Mass Defect and Nuclear Binding Energy
text:
Mass Defect: It is found that mass of the nucleus is less than the total mass of protons and neutrons, this mass difference is called mass defect. If mass defect is delta m, then: delta m = Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n - M. Where Z = atomic number, m_p = mass of proton, m_n = mass of neutron, and M = mass of nucleus.

Nuclear Binding Energy: The minimum energy required to separate the nucleons up to an infinite distance from the nucleus, is called nuclear binding energy. It is expressed as: delta E = delta m * c^2 = delta m * 931.5 MeV. Nuclear binding per nucleon = Nuclear binding energy (delta E) / Total number of nucleons (A). Packing fraction was introduced by Aston and is expressed by packing fraction, f = (delta m / A) * 10^4.
formulas: delta E = delta m * c^2 = delta m * 931.5 MeV
Nuclear binding per nucleon = delta E / A

details.summary: Definitions and mathematical expressions for mass defect, binding energy, and packing fraction.

subject: Physics
text:
Nuclear Fission: The process of splitting of a heavy nucleus into two nuclei of nearly comparable masses with the liberation of energy is called nuclear fission. When U^235 is bombarded with fast moving neutrons, it splits: 92U^235 + 0n^1 -> 56Ba^141 + 36Kr^92 + 30n^1 + Energy. The reason for liberation of energy is that total mass of resultant nuclei is less than the mass of initial nucleus, this mass defect changes into energy. Nuclear fission was discovered by Otto han and Strassman.

  • Thermal neutrons have energy approx 0.25 eV.
  • The number of neutrons is produced is proportional to r^3 (r = size of fissionable material).

details.summary: Explanation of nuclear fission, the reaction equation, and key properties of thermal neutrons and fissionable material.

subject: Physics
text:
If the particle starting the nuclear fission reaction is produced as a product and further takes part in the nuclear fission reaction, then a chain of fission reaction started, which is called nuclear chain reaction.

Nuclear chain reactions are of two types:

  • Controlled Chain Reaction: A fission chain reaction which proceeds slowly and in balanced manner without any explosion and in which the energy released can be controlled.
  • Uncontrolled Chain Reaction: A nuclear chain reaction in which fission neutrons keep on increasing until the whole of the fissile substance is consumed. Atom bomb works on the principle of uncontrolled chain reaction.

Critical Size: The minimum size of piece of a radioactive element to continue the chain reaction is called critical size. The critical mass of uranium is 10 kg.

details.summary: Explanation of nuclear chain reactions, types (controlled vs uncontrolled), and the definition of critical size.

subject: Physics
text:
It is a device that can initiate a self-sustaining controlled chain reaction of a fissionable material. They are used at nuclear power plants for generating electricity and in propulsion of ships. It is based upon controlled nuclear chain reaction.

  • Nuclear Fuel: Fissionable material are used link U^235, U^233, PU^239 etc.
  • Moderator: Used to slow down the fast moving neutrons produced during the fission. e.g. Heavy water graphite, deuterium, etc.
  • Control Rods: They have the ability to capture the slow neutrons.
  • Coolant: Used to remove the heat produced. e.g. Liquid sodium.

subject: Physics
text:
When two light nuclei combine together to form a single nucleus, then this phenomena is called nuclear fusion.

  • Fusion is possible only when there is an abundance of lighter element.
  • Fusion takes place at high temperature 10^7 or 10^8 C.
  • Fusion reaction is also called thermonuclear reaction and energy released is called thermonuclear energy.
  • The fusion of nuclei is an uncontrolled process. Till now there is no method available for controlling the release of fusion energy. Therefore, fusion cannot be used for the service of mankind.

details.summary: Definition and characteristics of nuclear fusion.

subject: Physics
text:
Solar Energy: The secret of sun energy is nuclear fusion. In sun due to very high temperature, fusion of hydrogen nuclei takes place to form helium nuclei.

Hydrogen Bomb: It is based on the concept of nuclear fusion. The process is initiated by nuclear fission of uranium, which there after used for fusion of light elements like hydrogen. When hydrogen bomb explodes, it generates the huge amount of energy and produces very high temperature.

details.summary: Application of nuclear fusion in the Sun and Hydrogen bombs.

subject: Physics
text:
The spontaneous emission of some types of invisible rays from some substances is called radioactivity and these substances are called radioactive substances. The emitted rays are called radioactive rays.

For radioactive elements ratio of number of neutrons to number of protons is greater than 1.

1. Alpha-rays: Rays of relatively low penetrating power emitted by radium and other radioactive substances are known as alpha-rays. Alpha-rays consists of alpha-particles 2He^4. Alpha-particles have two unit positive charge and has a mass of four times that of a proton.

Some properties of alpha-rays:

  • Alpha-particles are deflected in electric and magnetic fields.
  • Velocity of alpha-particles is of the order 1/10th to that of light.
  • Alpha-particles ionise the gases through which they pass.
  • Alpha-particles have very less penetrating power. These are stopped by aluminium foil of thickness of a 0.1 mm.
  • Alpha-particles produce fluorescence in substances like zinc sulphide.
  • Alpha-particles get scattered while passing through metal foils.
  • On being stopped alpha-particles produce heating effect.
  • Alpha-particles can produce artificial radioactivity in certain elements.
  • The energies of alpha-particles emitted from a radioactive substance is not the same.

2. Beta-rays: A form of ionising radiation, emitted by radioactive substances, which consists of negatively charged electrons. Beta-rays are very fast moving electrons. Beta-particles carry 1 unit negative charge.

  • Beta-particles are deflected in electric and magnetic fields.

details.summary: Definition of radioactivity and properties of alpha and beta rays.

subject: Physics
text:
• Beta-particles have velocity approximately equal to the speed of light.
  • Beta-particles can ionise the gas through which they pass but their ionising power is 1/100th that of alpha-particles.
  • Penetrating power of beta-particles is 100 times to that of alpha-particles.
  • Beta-particles produce fluorescence in substance like zinc sulphide.
  • Beta-particles can affect a photographic plate.
  • Beta-particles can produce artificial radioactivity.
  • Gamma-rays: Penetrating electromagnetic radiation arising from the radioactive decay of atomic nuclei. They have no charge and no mass.
  • Gamma-rays have no metallic properties; they are electromagnetic rays.
  • Gamma-rays are not deflected in electric and magnetic fields.
  • Ionising power of gamma-rays is very less than alpha and beta-rays.
  • Velocity of gamma-rays is equal to that of light.
  • Gamma-rays have very high penetrating power; they pass through 30 cm thick iron sheet.
  • They can affect the photographic plate.
  • They knock out the electrons from the surface on which they fall.
  • Gamma-rays can produce fluorescence in substance.
  • They produce heating effect on the surface exposed to them.
  • Wavelength of gamma-rays is of the order of 10^-12 m.

details.summary: Properties of beta-particles and gamma-rays.

subject: Physics
text:
Half-Life (T_1/2): The time interval in which mass of a radioactive substance or the number of atoms reduced to half its initial value.

  • Half-life is constant for a radioactive element.
  • Half-life cannot be changed by physical or chemical changes.
  • C^14 is used to predict the age of archaeological findings.
  • Mean Life (tau): The sum of life times of all atoms divided by the number of atoms present initially.
  • Mean life is greater than half-life.
  • The percentage of atoms left one mean life time is equal to 37%.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for half-life and mean life of radioactive substances.

subject: Physics
text:
Activity (A): Rate of decay per second or the number of nuclei N disintegrating per second.

Soddy-Fazan's Displacement Rule:

  • Alpha-decay: Atomic number decreases by 2, mass number decreases by 4.
  • Beta-decay: Atomic number increases by 1, mass number remains same.
  • Gamma-decay: Mass number and atomic number remain unchanged.
