| Periodic property | In a period from left to right | In a group from top to bottom |
|---|---|---|
| Ionisation energy | Increase | Decrease |
| Electron affinity | Increase | Decrease |
| Electronegativity | Increase | Decrease |
| Non-metallic character | Increase | Decrease |
| Oxidising character | Increase | Decrease |
| Acidic nature of oxides | Increase | Decrease |
| Atomic size | Decrease | Increase |
| Electropositivity | Decrease | Increase |
| Metallic character | Decrease | Increase |
| Basic nature of oxides | Decrease | Increase |

details.summary: Electronegativity definition and a comprehensive table of periodic trends.

subject: Chemistry
text:
IA Group Elements (Alkali Metals)

Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. The general electronic configuration is ns1.

  • Elements of IA group are called alkali metals because their oxides and hydroxides on dissolving in water gives alkaline solution.
  • All alkali metals are soluble in liquid ammonia to give blue coloured solution (due to solvated or ammoniated electron) which conducts electricity. This solution acts as powerful reducing agent.
  • Hydration energy decreases from Li to Cs because extent of hydration varies inversely with size.
  • Alkali metals and their compounds impart characteristic colour to the flames.
  • These metals have very low melting and boiling points which decreases on moving down the group. It is due to the presence of weak intermetallic bonds, which also become more weaker as the size increases.
  • Li-red, Na-yellow, K-pale violet, Rb-violet and Cs-reddish violet.
  • Li and Na burns in air to form peroxides (Li2O and Na2O while K, Rb and Cs forms superoxides (KO2, RbO2, Cso2).
  • Reactivity of alkali metals Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs
  • Melting point of halides: (a) For same halide NaCl > LiCl > KCl > RbCl > CsCl (max m.pt to min m.pt); (b) For same alkali metal NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI (max m.pt to min m.pt)
  • Basic character and solubility of hydroxides: LiOH < NaOH < KOH < RbOH < CsOH
  • Solubility and stability of carbonates: Li2CO3 < Na2CO3 < K2CO3 < Rb2CO3 < Cs2CO3

USES OF ALKALI METALS

  • Lithium is used in aircraft manufacture and in certain batteries. Lithium carbonate is used in treatment of bipolar disorder.
  • Sodium and potassium play a role in transmission of nerve signals. Calcium and magnesium are also essential for transmission of impulses along nerve fibres.
  • In bones and teeth, Ca is present as apatite and fluorapatite. Ca2+ ions play a role in blood clotting and in contraction of muscles.
  • Caesium is used in caesium atomic clocks.

details.summary: Detailed properties, trends, and uses of Alkali Metals (Group IA).

subject: Chemistry
text:
IIA Group Elements (Alkaline Earth Metals) (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra)

  • General electronic configuration is ns2.
  • They impart characteristic colour to flame (except Be and Mg due to small size and high IP).
  • Beryllium compound with N, Cl, S are covalent in nature while those of other alkaline elements are ionic.
  • Reactivity of alkaline earth metals: Be < Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba
  • Basic character and solubility of hydroxides: Be(OH)2 < Mg(OH)2 < Ca(OH)2 < Sr(OH)2 < Ba(OH)2 (Solubility increases from Mg(OH)2 to Ba(OH)2 due to decrease in lattice energy).
  • The solubility and stability of carbonates: Their carbonates are quite insoluble. MgCO3 > CaCO3 > SrCO3 > BaCO3 (Slightly soluble to Insoluble). BeCO3 < MgCO3 < CaCO3 < SrCO3 < BaCO3 (Min. stable to Max. stable).
  • Solubility of sulphates: BeSO4 > MgSO4 > CaSO4 > SrSO4 > BaSO4 (Fairly soluble to Insoluble).
image_descriptions: Flame test colours: Ca (Brick red), Sr (Crimson), Ba (Apple green), Ra (Caramine).

details.summary: Properties of Alkaline Earth Metals including reactivity, solubility trends of hydroxides, carbonates, and sulphates.

subject: Chemistry
text:
IIIA Group Elements (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl)

  • General electronic configuration is ns2np1.
  • These generally show +3 oxidation state. Some elements also exhibit +1 oxidation state due to inert pair effect.
  • Ba, Al show +3 oxidation state, while Ga, In, Tl show +1 and +3 states. Compound of boron due to incomplete octet act as Lewis acids.
  • All compounds of boron are used in manufacture of glass to reduce thermal expansion of glass.
  • Boron absorbs neutrons, therefore, they are used in nuclear reactor.
  • Aluminium form amphoteric oxide.
  • Basic nature of oxides and hydroxides follows the order: B < Al < Ga < In < Tl
  • Among hydroxide of elements of IIIA group, the order of acidity is: B(OH)3 < Al(OH)3 < Ga(OH)3 < In(OH)3 < Tl(OH)3
  • Strength of Lewis acids of boron follows the order: BI3 > BBr3 > BCl3 > BF3
  • Al and Ga have similar atomic radii due to poor shielding effect of d-electrons of Ga atom.
  • Aluminium is powerful reducing agent, hence it is used in thermite process.
  • Thallium is stored in air tight containers under kerosene, glycerine or vaseline.
  • In general alums are potash alums. Alums containing aluminium are known by the name of monovalent metal atom whereas alums which do not contain aluminium are known by the name of trivalent metal atom.

details.summary: Properties of Group IIIA elements including oxidation states, Lewis acidity, and specific uses of Boron and Aluminium.

subject: Chemistry
text:
IVA Group Elements (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb)

  • General electronic configuration is ns2np2.
  • Common oxidation states are +2 and +4. Ge, Sn and Pb are more stable in +2 oxidation state due to inert pair.
  • Generally elements with +2 oxidation state form ionic compounds and +4 oxidation state form covalent compounds.
  • Carbon lacks d-orbitals therefore, it cannot expand its valence shell so maximum covalency in its compound is not more than four. On the other hand, Si and elements of this group have vacant d-orbitals so it can extend its covalency from 4 to 6.
  • Carbon due to catenation power (chain forming property) forms millions of compounds.
  • Various compounds of carbon are used as fuel, e.g. coal gas, producer gas (CO + N2), semiwater gas (CO + N2 + H2) etc. (semi water gas is a mixture of water gas and producer gas).
  • Stability of their hydrides follows the order: CH4 > SiH4 > GeH4 > SnH4 > PbH4
  • Si forms most complicated compounds, e.g. zeolite, mica, talc, asbestos etc.
  • CO2 molecule is linear whereas SiO2 is three dimensional giant molecule like diamond.
  • The thermal stability of halides of IVA group is in the order: CCl4 > SiCl4 > GeCl4 > SnCl4 > PbCl4
  • Stability and volatility of tetrahalide is: CF4 > CCl4 > CBr4 > CI4
  • Order of hardness is B4C > SiC > Diamond > Glass.

details.summary: Properties of Group IVA elements including oxidation states, catenation, stability of hydrides/halides, and structural differences between CO2 and SiO2.

subject: Chemistry
text:
VA Group Elements (N, P, As, Sb, Bi)

  • General electronic configuration is ns2np3.
  • Due to half-filled orbitals these are quite inert and have abnormally higher IP and lower value of EA.
  • They exhibit variable oxidation states as: N = -3, -2, -1, +1, +2, +3, +4, +5; P, As, Sb = -3, +3, +5; Bi = +3, +5
  • These form trihydrides which act as Lewis base.
  • N shows anomalous behaviour than rest of the elements due to their small size, high electronegativity, high ionisation energy, non-availability of d-orbitals and ease of formation of multiple bonds.

details.summary: Properties of Group VA elements including oxidation states, Lewis base behavior of trihydrides, and anomalous behavior of Nitrogen.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• N2 can show maximum four covalency in their compounds, e.g. NH4+.
  • Various oxides of nitrogen:
    • N2O: laughing gas, neutral, diamagnetic, linear.
    • NO: neutral, paramagnetic, exists as a dimer in solid state.
    • N2O3: acidic, diamagnetic.
    • NO2: acidic, paramagnetic, V-shape.
    • N2O5: most acidic (solid).
  • Basic nature of hydrides: SbH3 < AsH3 < PH3 < NH3.
  • Bond angle of hydrides decreases as: NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3.
  • Order of boiling point of hydrides: SbH3 > NH3 > AsH3 > PH3 (due to H-Bond).
  • Red phosphorus is less reactive than white phosphorus and used in match industry.
  • VIA Group Elements (O, S, Se, Te, Po):
    • General electronic configuration: ns2np4. Known as chalcogens or ore forming elements.
    • Oxidation states: +2, +4, +6.
    • O2 molecule is paramagnetic due to two unpaired electrons.
    • Oxygen oxidation states: -2, -1 (peroxides), 0 (O2), +2 (OF2), +1 (O2F2).
    • Ozone is an allotrope of oxygen and acts as a good bleaching agent.
    • Order of acidic nature and reducing power of hydrides: H2O < H2S < H2Se < H2Te.
    • Bond angle order: H2O (104.5°) > H2S (92.2°) > H2Se (91.0°) > H2Te (90°).
    • Decreasing order of volatile nature of hydrides: H2O > H2Te > H2Se > H2S.
    • H2S is more volatile than H2O due to hydrogen bonding in H2O.

details.summary: Covers nitrogen oxides, properties of group 15 hydrides, and properties of group 16 (chalcogens) elements including trends in acidity, volatility, and bond angles.

subject: Chemistry
topic: VII A, Zero Group, and Transition Elements
text:
• VII A Group Elements (F, Cl, Br, I, At):
    • General electronic configuration: ns2np5. Known as halogens.
    • F shows -1 oxidation state; others show -1, +1, +3, +5, +7.
    • Reactivity: F > Cl > Br > I.
    • Electron affinity: Cl > Br > F > I.
    • Oxidising character: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
    • Hydroacid strength: HF < HBr < HCl < HI.
    • Stability of halides: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
    • Bond dissociation energy: I2 < Br2 < F2 < Cl2.
  • Zero Group Elements (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn):
    • Configuration: ns2np6.
    • First noble gas compound XePtF6 obtained by N. Bartlett in 1962.
    • Colourless, tasteless, odourless gases.
    • Monoatomic, atomic size increases down the group, zero electron affinities.
  • Transition Elements (VIII Group Elements):
    • d-block elements.
    • Small atomic size, high ionisation potential.
    • Show variable oxidation states, form metallic bonds, coloured and paramagnetic.
    • Mn shows maximum oxidation state of +7 in KMnO4.
    • Insoluble silver halides are soluble in sodium thiosulphate (used as fixer): AgBr + 2Na2S2O3 → Na3[Ag(S2O3)2] + NaBr.
    • Most abundant transition element is Fe.

| Uses of Noble Gases | |
|---|---|
| He | Gas cooled atomic reactors (cooling medium) |
| He + H_2 | Filling balloons and airships (light, non-combustible) |
| He + O_2 | Respiration of sea divers |
| Ne | Neon discharge lamps and signs |
| Ar + N_2 | Electric bulb |
| Radon | Treatment of cancer |

details.summary: Covers halogen trends, noble gas properties and uses, and general characteristics of transition elements including specific chemical reactions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Important Periodic Trends:

  • Valency: Elements in the same group generally exhibit common valency. For example, the carbon family (carbon, silicon, germanium, tin, and lead) typically shows a valency of four. However, some elements in this group can also exhibit a valency of two.
  • Ionisation Potential: The first ionisation potential order for Na, Mg, Al, Si is Na < Mg < Al < Si.
  • Anomalous behaviour of Nitrogen: Attributed to its small size, high electronegativity, and the non-availability of d-orbitals in its valence shell.
  • Ionic Radii: Zirconium and hafnium have almost identical ionic radii due to lanthanide contraction.
  • Ionisation Energy: The second ionisation energy is always greater than the first. Within a group, there is a gradual increase in ionisation energy as nuclear charge increases. Noble gases possess high ionisation energies.

details.summary: Notes on periodic trends including valency, ionisation potential, anomalous behaviour of nitrogen, and ionic radii.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Chemical Bond: The attractive force which holds various constituents (atoms, ions, etc) together in different chemical species is called a chemical bond. During the formation of a chemical bond, energy is released.

Valency: The capacity of an element to form chemical bonds is known as its valency. The valency of an element is the combining capacity of an element.

  • The valency of an element decides the number of other atoms which can combine with one atom of that element.
  • Valency of metal = Number of valence electrons in its atom (e.g., sodium (Na) = 2, 8, 1; Valency of sodium = 1).
  • Valency of non-metal = 8 - Number of valence electrons in its atom (e.g., chlorine Cl17 = 2, 8, 7; Valency of Cl = 8 - 7 = 1).

Important elements and their valencies:

  • (i) H, Cl, Br, I, Cu (ous) etc. are monovalent as their valency is 1.
  • (ii) O, S, Mg, Ca Zn, Fe (ous), Cu (ic), Pb, Co, Ni etc. are divalent as their valency is 2.
  • (iii) N, P, Al, Cr, B etc are trivalent as their valency is 3.
  • (iv) C, Si etc are tetravalent as their valency is 4.
  • Some elements e.g., Cu, Fe exhibit more than one valencies (variable valency). Cu and Hg exhibit + 1 and + 2 valencies and Fe exhibits + 2 and + 3 valencies.
formulas: Valency of metal = Number of valence electrons
Valency of non-metal = 8 - Number of valence electrons
image_descriptions: Diagram showing the combination of Carbon (valency 4) and Hydrogen (valency 1) to form Methane (CH4), illustrating the cross-linking of valencies.

details.summary: Introduction to chemical bonding, definition of valency, calculation methods for metals and non-metals, and classification of elements by valency.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Electronic Theory of Chemical Bonding (Octet Rule)
text:
Electronic Theory of Chemical Bonding (Octet Rule): Kossel and Lewis in 1916 developed a theory of chemical combination between atoms known as electronic theory of chemical bonding which was based on inertness of noble gases.

According to this theory, "atoms can combine either by transfer of valence electrons from one atom to another (gaining or losing) or by sharing of valence electrons in order to have an octet or stable configuration just like noble gases in their valence shells". This is known as octet rule.

Types of Chemical Bond:

  1. Electrovalent or ionic bond
  2. Covalent bond
  3. Coordinate bond

details.summary: Explanation of the Octet Rule proposed by Kossel and Lewis (1916) and the classification of chemical bonds.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Electrovalent or Ionic Bond: These types of bonds are formed by the transference of one or more electrons from one atom to another atom.

  • Electrovalent bond is formed between most electropositive elements i.e. metals (like, Na, K, Ca, Ba, Mg, etc) and most electronegative elements i.e. non-metals (like, O, F, N, S, Cl, Br etc.).
  • The number of electrons lost or taken up by the element is called electrovalency of the element which is equal to charge of cation or anion respectively and these types of compounds are called electrovalent compounds.
  • Electropositive elements form cations by losing electrons and electronegative elements form anions by gaining electrons.
  • If the difference in electronegativity of the atoms is around 1.9 and more, then bond is generally ionic.

Characteristics of Ionic Compounds:

  • (i) Ionic compounds are crystalline in nature. Their constituent units are ions. These ions are arranged together in a regular way in an ionic lattice, e.g., in NaCl lattice each sodium ion is bonded with six Cl- ions and each Cl- ion is surrounded by six Na+ ions.
  • (ii) Ionic compounds are hard and brittle in nature due to the strong force of attraction between oppositely charged ions. These solids have low volatility, high stability and high density.
  • (iii) These have high melting and boiling points due to the presence of powerful electrostatic force between the ions.
  • (iv) These are good conductors of heat and electricity in molten state or aqueous medium due to the mobility of ions.
  • (v) These are soluble in polar solvents like water but insoluble in non-polar solvents like CCl4, C6H6 etc.
  • (vi) Ionic compounds form ions in solution, hence exhibit ionic reactions which are quite fast and instantaneous.
  • (vii) The bond in ionic compound is non-rigid and non-directional, so these do not show isomerism.
image_descriptions: Electron dot structure showing the transfer of an electron from a Sodium atom (Na) to a Chlorine atom (Cl) to form Na+ and Cl- ions.

details.summary: Definition and characteristics of ionic bonds and compounds.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Variable Electrovalency: The elements which change their valency and have more than one electrovalency are said to possess variable electrovalency. This is due to following two reasons:

  • (i) Inert pair effect: It is observed that in the case of heavy elements like Pb, Bi, etc ns^2 electrons have extra stability and hence do not take part in bond formation. This effect is called inert pair effect. This effect increases with increasing the atomic number in a group. e.g. Ge and Pb belongs to the 14th group of Periodic Table, but Ge stable in Ge^4+ state and Pb stable in Pb^2+ state. Thus, Pb^2+ salts are stable than Pb^4+ salts.
  • (ii) Unstable configuration of the core: In d-block elements, core possess unstable arrangement of electrons. Hence, they show variable valency, e.g. Fe^2+ (3s^2, 3p^6, 3d^6) lose an electron to change into Fe^3+ which cannot lose further electrons.

details.summary: Explanation of why certain elements exhibit variable valency.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Covalent Bonds: These types of bonds are formed by the mutual sharing of equal number of electrons by the atoms in the molecules. Thus, the bond formed by the sharing of electrons is called covalent bond and compounds possesing covalent bond are called covalent compounds.

Formation of H2 molecule H + H -> H:H or (H - H)

  • Single, double and triple bonds are formed by the sharing of one, two and three electron pairs respectively.

Covalent bonds are of two types:

  • (i) Non-polar Covalent Bonds: These types of covalent bonds are formed between two identical atoms or atoms having the same electronegativity. The atoms which share electrons have approximately equal electronegativity, the electron pair is equally shared between them, such a bond is called polar covalent bond e.g. Cl2, O2 etc.
  • (ii) Polar Covalent Bonds: These types of covalent bonds are formed between different elements or elements having different electronegativity. In this bond the electron pair is attracted towards more electronegative atom, therefore one atom have partial negative charge and other atom have partial positive charge, e.g. HBr, HCl etc.

Characteristics of Covalent Compounds:

  • (i) In general covalent compounds are gases or liquids. Some of the compounds are soft solids.
  • (ii) These compounds are slightly soluble in water but highly soluble in organic solvents such as alcohols, ethers etc.
  • (iii) Those covalent molecules which form hydrogen bonds with water molecules becomes fairly soluble in water. e.g. lower alcohols, lower carboxylic acids etc.
  • (iv) They are bad conductors of electricity because they do not contain ion, but, when a covalent molecule reacts with water, it dissolves and produces ions, and hence, begins to conduct electricity.
  • (v) They have relatively low melting and boiling points [except diamond, silica, carborundum (SiC)] due to weak covalent bonds.

details.summary: Definition, types, and characteristics of covalent bonds and compounds.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The property which measures the extent of polarity in the bond is called dipole moment.

Formula: Dipole moment = Magnitude of charges (e) x distance (d)

  • Dipole moments of diatomic molecules is zero because they are non-polar, e.g. H2, Cl2, F2, O2, N2 etc.
  • Dipole moments of HF, HCl, HBr and HI are very large due to their high electronegativity differences.
  • Molecules like CO2, CS2 and BeF2 are linear and possess polar covalent bonds. The bond moments of two bonds being equal but opposite in direction cancel each other so their dipole moment is zero.
  • The dipole moment of CH4, CCl4, BF3 are zero due to their symmetrical structure.
formulas: Dipole moment = Magnitude of charges (e) * distance (d)

details.summary: Definition and characteristics of dipole moment in various molecules.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom is called coordinate covalent bond.

Such type of bond is formed between atoms one of which is deficient in atleast two electrons, while the other atom has already acquired stable noble gas configuration.

The atom which donates the electrons is called the donor while the other which only accepts the electrons pair is known as acceptor. This bond is usually represented by an arrow (->) pointing from donor to the acceptor atom.

e.g., a hydrogen ion can combine with water molecules by coordinate covalent bond to form hydronium ion (H3O+).
image_descriptions: Chemical structure showing the formation of a hydronium ion (H3O+) via a coordinate covalent bond from a water molecule and a hydrogen ion.

details.summary: Explanation of coordinate covalent bonds, donor-acceptor relationship, and hydronium ion formation.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The main characteristics are as following:

  • These exist as solids, liquids, and gases under normal conditions.
  • These are sparingly soluble in polar solvent like water but readily soluble in non-polar solvents.
  • These are bad conductor of heat and electricity.
  • The melting and boiling points are higher than purely covalent compounds.
  • Coordinate bond is rigid and directional. Thus, these compounds show isomerism.
  • Compounds which have coordinate covalent bond possess high values of dielectric constant.

Note: According to octet rule, an atom has a tendency to occupy 8 electrons (2 in H like He) in its valence shell, which is stable arrangement, but a number of molecules are known which violates octet rule.

e.g. (i) BeF2, BF3 (incomplete octet) (ii) NO, NO2 (odd number electrons) (iii) PCl5, SF6 (expanded octet)

details.summary: Key properties of coordinate covalent compounds and exceptions to the octet rule.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The attractive interaction of a hydrogen atom with an electronegative atom such as nitrogen (N), oxygen (O) or fluorine (F) that comes from another molecule or chemical group, is called hydrogen bond.

It is stronger than van der Waals' interaction and has energy 5 to 30 kJ/mol. It occurs in both inorganic molecules such as water and organic molecules such as DNA.

Hydrogen bonds can be of the following two types:

  • (i) Intermolecular H-bonding: It occurs between different molecules of a substance and results in increasing solubility in water and high boiling point. e.g. HF, H2O, C2H5OH etc. H-F.....H-F.....H-F
  • (ii) Intramolecular H-bonding: It is found within different parts of a single molecule and results in decreasing solubility in water and low boiling point e.g. o-nitrophenol.
image_descriptions: Structural diagram of o-nitrophenol showing intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the oxygen of the nitro group and the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group.

details.summary: Definition, types (intermolecular and intramolecular), and properties of hydrogen bonding.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Metals possess metallic bond.
  • Soft metals like Na, K possess weak metallic bond and hence can be cut with a knife.
  • The atoms of transition metals are held together by strong metallic bonds because of large number of unpaired electrons in their atoms. Therefore, all transition metals are much harder and less volatile.

details.summary: Brief overview of metallic bonding and its effect on the physical properties of metals.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Acids are substances which have a sour taste and turn blue litmus red.

  • Arrhenius concept: Acids are substances which give H+ ions in their aqueous solutions. e.g., HCl -> H+ + Cl-
  • Bronsted-Lowry concept: Acids are proton donors. e.g., CH3COOH -> CH3COO- + H+; HCl -> Cl- + H+. A conjugate base is obtained when an acid gives up a proton (H+). The acid and base which differ by a proton form a conjugate acid-base pair. Generally, a strong acid has a weak conjugate base and a weak acid has a strong conjugate base.
  • Lewis concept: Acids are electron pair acceptors, i.e., these are generally positively charged or electron-deficient species. e.g., BF3, AlCl3, Na+, K+, PF3, SF4 etc.

details.summary: Definitions and concepts of acids according to Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, and Lewis theories.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Classification of Acids:

  • Class I (On the basis of degree of dissociation):
    • Strong acids: Dissociate completely even in concentrated solution, e.g., HCl, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4 etc. (HCl + H2O -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq))
    • Weak acids: Dissociate partially when dissolved in water, e.g., acetic acid (CH3COOH), formic acid (HCOOH) etc. (CH3COOH + H2O <=> CH3COO-(aq) + H+(aq))
  • Class II (On the basis of presence of oxygen or hydrogen):
    • Hydracids: Do not contain oxygen. Besides hydrogen, they contain other non-metallic elements like hydrochloric acid (HCl), hydrofluoric acid (HF) etc.
    • Oxyacids: Contain both oxygen and hydrogen and also another non-metallic element, e.g., sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3) etc.

Basicity of Acid: The number of displacing protons present in an acid is known as basicity of the acid. Monobasic acid has only one hydrogen ion and can combine with one hydroxyl (OH) group to give one kind of salt, e.g., HCl, HNO3, CH3COOH etc.

details.summary: Classification of acids based on dissociation and composition, and definition of basicity.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Boric acid is a weak monobasic acid. It is not able to release H+ ions on its own. It receives OH- ions from water molecule to complete its octet and in turn release H+ ions.
  • Dibasic acid has two hydrogen ions and hence can combine with two hydroxyl groups to give two kinds of salts, e.g. H2SO4, H2SO3, (COOH)2 etc.
  • Tribasic acid has three hydrogen ions and can combine with three hydroxyl groups to give three kinds of salts, e.g. H3PO4 etc.

Factors Affecting Acidic Strength of Acids

  • Acidic strength of acids increase with increase in the size of atom. e.g. HF < HCl < HI
  • Acidic strength of acids increase with increase in electronegativity of elements. e.g. H—CH3 < H—NH2 < H—OH < H—F
  • Among oxyacids of some element, acidic strength increase with increase in the oxidation state of that element. e.g. HClO1 < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4

Properties of Acids

Acids possess the following general properties:

  • Acids when react with reactive metals like Zn, Fe, Na liberates hydrogen. Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2
  • Acids when react with carbonates and bicarbonates produces CO2 gas which turns lime water milky. CaCO3 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + H2O + CO2
  • Acid react with base to give salt and water. It is known as neutralisation reaction. HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)
  • Acids also react with metallic oxides to form salt and water. Na2O + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O
  • Aqueous solution of acids conduct electricity.
  • A concentrated solution of 3 part conc. HCl and 1 part conc. HNO3 is called aqua-regia. All metals dissolve in it.

| Vinegar | Acetic acid |
| Orange/Lemon | Citric acid |

details.summary: Overview of acid classification (monobasic, dibasic, tribasic), factors affecting acidic strength, chemical properties of acids, and the composition of aqua-regia.

subject: Chemistry
text:
BASES

These are the substances, which have bitter taste and turn red litmus blue.

  • According to Arrhenius, these give hydroxyl ion (OH-) in aqueous solutions. e.g. NaOH(aq) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq). Similarly, KOH(aq) -> K+(aq) + OH-(aq).
  • According to Bronsted-Lowry concept, these are proton acceptors. e.g. NH3 + H+ -> NH4+. Similarly, H2O + H+ -> H3O+.
  • According to Lewis concept, bases are electron pair donors. e.g. NH3, ROH, R2O, pyridine etc.
  • Note: Conjugate acid of a weak base is strong or vice-versa. Base + H+ -> Conjugate acid

details.summary: Definitions of bases according to Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, and Lewis concepts.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Nitric acid is used in manufacture of artificial silk, dyes, drugs, perfumes, explosives (TNT), fertilisers and in purification of silver and gold.
  • Sulphuric acid (king of chemicals) is used in manufacture of hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, fertilisers, explosives, paints and pigments, coaltar, dyes, lead storage batteries and as an oxidising and dehydrating agent.
  • Hydrofluoric acid is used in etching of glass and in pickling of alloy steel.
  • Hydrochloric acid is the main constituent of gastric acid and is used in manufacture of chlorine, chlorides and in textile, dyeing and tanning industry.
  • Boric acid is used as an antiseptic, for eye wash.
  • Acetic acid is used in food processing, in the manufacture of acetone and as a solvent.

details.summary: Industrial and practical applications of common acids.

subject: Chemistry
text:
On the basis of degree of dissociation, bases are of two types:

  • Strong base: Dissociates completely even in concentrated solutions, e.g., KOH, NaOH etc.
  • Weak base: Partially dissociates in water, e.g., Mg(OH)2, NH4OH, NaHCO3, Ca(OH)2 etc.

details.summary: Classification of bases based on dissociation.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Bases possess the following general properties:

  • (i) Bases react with metals to form salt with the evolution of hydrogen gas. 2NaOH + Zn -> Na2ZnO2 + H2 (Sodium zincate). This reaction is not given by all bases.
  • (ii) The reaction of bases with acids is known as neutralisation reaction, which leads to the formation of corresponding salt and water.
  • (iii) Bases react with non-metallic oxides to form salt and water. 2NaOH + SO3 -> Na2SO4 + H2O. Non-metallic oxides are acidic.
  • (iv) Bases on dissolving in water give hydroxide ions (OH- ions). e.g., NaOH(s) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq).

All bases do not dissolve in water. The bases which dissolve in water are called alkali e.g., NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2, NH4OH. Hence, all alkalis are bases but all bases are not alkalis.

details.summary: Chemical properties of bases and definition of alkali.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The number of hydroxyl ions present in a base is known as acidity of the base.

  • Monoacidic bases: Produces one hydroxide ion in aqueous solutions, e.g., KOH, NH4OH, NaOH.
  • Diacidic bases: Produces two hydroxide ions in aqueous solutions, e.g., Ca(OH)2, Fe(OH)2, Zn(OH)2.
  • Triacidic bases: Produces three hydroxide ions in aqueous solutions, e.g., Fe(OH)3, Al(OH)3.

details.summary: Classification of bases based on acidity.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Sodium hydroxide: Used in manufacture of soap, purification of bauxite and manufacture of rayon.
  • Potassium hydroxide: Used in the manufacture of soft soap. A suspension of magnesium hydroxide in water is used in medicines as an antacid (milk of magnesia).
  • Calcium hydroxide: Used in preparation of sodalime (mixture of calcium hydroxide and caustic soda), for white washing buildings and softening of hard water.

details.summary: Industrial and medicinal uses of common bases.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The acidic or basic strength of a solution is expressed on a scale known as pH scale. The idea of pH scale and the scale was given by Sorensen.

pH of a solution is defined as the negative logarithm of the concentration in moles per litre of H+ ions which it contains.

pH is a measure of acidity. As the pH increases, the acidic nature decreases. For pure water or neutral solutions, pH = 7, for bases pH > 7 and for acids pH < 7.

  • pH of the solution of strong or weak neutral salt in water is always neutral.
  • pH of the solution of acidic salt in water is always acidic (i.e., <7).
  • pH of the solution of basic salt in water is always basic (i.e., >7).
  • On dilution, pH of an acidic solution increases but pH of a basic solution decreases.

details.summary: Definition and properties of the pH scale.

subject: Chemistry
text:
An indicator is a substance which gives different colours in an acid and a base. Thus, it is possible to check whether a given substance is acid or base or neutral with the help of indicator.

  • Litmus, red cabbage leaves, turmeric (haldi) coloured petals of some flowers such as hydrangea, petunia and geranium etc. are natural acid-base indicators.
  • Methyl orange, phenolphthalein etc. are synthetic indicators.
  • Universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. It shows different colours at different concentrations of hydrogen ions. We can estimate the strength of acids and bases by using universal indicators.

details.summary: Definition and types of indicators.

subject: Chemistry
text:
• Alizarin: Yellow at pH 5.5 and red at pH 6.8.
  • Cochineal: Yellow in acidic solution, and deep violet in alkaline solution.
  • Curcumin: Yellow at pH 7.4 and red at pH 8.6.
  • Turmeric: Turmeric solution stays yellow in the presence of acids and changes to purple brown in the presence of bases. Dry turmeric paper is bright yellow and changes to red in the presence of bases.
  • Phenolphthalein: Purple in very basic solutions and colourless in acidic solutions.
  • Red cabbage: Red cabbage juice indicator is red in acid solution, purple in neutral solutions and greenish yellow in basic solutions. Cabbage paper turns green in the presence of bases and pink to red in the presence of acids.

details.summary: List of chemical indicators and their color changes based on pH levels.

subject: Chemistry
text:
A buffer solution maintains its pH or reserve acidic or basic nature even upon addition of a small amount of acid or a base. These solutions have a definite pH value.

Applications: Used in industries for alcoholic fermentation (pH 5 to 6.5), tanning of leather, electroplating, sugar and paper industries. In biological systems, a buffer system of carbonic acid and sodium bicarbonate is found in our blood, maintaining the pH at about 7.4.

Types of Buffers:

  • Acidic Buffer: Mixtures of weak acids and its conjugate bases (e.g., CH3COOH + CH3COONa).
  • Basic Buffer: Mixtures of weak bases and its conjugate acids (e.g., NH4Cl + NH4OH).

details.summary: Definition, applications, and types of buffer solutions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
When acid and base react together, they form salt and water. This reaction is known as neutralisation reaction.

Example: HNO3 + KOH -> KNO3 + H2O

When acid and base both are strong, 13.7 kcal energy is released. If either the acid or the base is weak, energy released is less than 13.7 kcal because some energy is utilised to ionise the weak acid or weak base. This energy is called enthalpy of neutralisation.

Types of Salts:

  • Simple salts: Obtained by complete neutralisation (e.g., NaCl, KCl, BaCl2, CaCl2).
  • Acidic salts: Salts having replaceable H-atom formed due to incomplete neutralisation (e.g., NaHSO4, NaH2PO4).
  • Basic salts: Salts having replaceable OH group formed due to incomplete neutralisation (e.g., Ca(OH)NO3).
  • Double salts: Two or more normal salts in a molecule in crystalline state (e.g., Mohr's salt: FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, Potash alum: K2SO4.Al2(SO4)3.24H2O, Carnallite: KCl.MgCl2.6H2O).
  • Mixed salts: More than one type of cations or anions present (e.g., NaKSO4, Ca(OCl)Cl).
  • Complex salts: Retain identity even when dissolved in water (e.g., K4[Fe(CN)6]).

details.summary: Definition of neutralisation, enthalpy of neutralisation, and classification of salts.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Hydrolysis is the reverse process of neutralisation. When a salt of strong base and weak acid or weak base and strong acid is dissolved in water, it reacts to give back the original acid and base.

Key Principles:

  • Only salt of weak acid + strong base, or weak base + strong acid undergo hydrolysis.
  • Cation or anion of a salt reacting with water to produce acidic or alkaline solution is hydrolysis.

Equations:

  • CA + H2O -> C+ + A- (Hydrolysis)
  • C+ + 2H2O <-> COH + H3O+ (Cationic hydrolysis)
  • A- + H2O <-> HA + OH- (Anionic hydrolysis)

Aqueous solution characteristics:

  • Strong acid + strong base: Neutral (e.g., NaCl, KCl, Na2SO4).
  • Strong acid + weak base: Acidic (e.g., FeCl3, NH4Cl, (NH4)2SO4).
  • Weak acid + strong base: Basic (e.g., CH3COONa, Na2CO3).

details.summary: Explanation of salt hydrolysis and the nature of aqueous solutions based on parent acid/base strength.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The process of addition of oxygen or any other electronegative element or removal of hydrogen or any other electropositive element (or radical) by a substance, is known as oxidation.

  • e.g. C + O2 → CO2 (oxidation of carbon)
  • SnCl2 + Cl2 → SnCl4 (oxidation of SnCl2)
  • H2S + Cl2 → 2HCl + S (oxidation of H2S)
  • 2KI + H2O → 2KOH + I2 (oxidation of KI)

The loss of one or more electrons by an atom, ion or molecule, is known as oxidation.

  • e.g. Na → Na+ + e-
  • Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e-
  • 2I- → I2 + 2e-

Increase in valency or oxidation number of an element is oxidation.

  • e.g. FeCl2 → FeCl3 (valency of Fe changes from +2 to +3)
  • Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu (oxidation number of Zn changes from zero to +2)
image_descriptions: Chemical reaction diagram showing Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu with an arrow indicating oxidation of Zn from 0 to +2.

details.summary: Definition and examples of oxidation based on oxygen addition, electron loss, and increase in oxidation number.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The substance which undergoes reduction in a chemical reaction is known as oxidising agent or oxidant. Thus, oxidant is an electron acceptor.

Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu (CuSO4(Cu2+) is an oxidising agent as it undergoes reduction).

  • F2 is the strongest oxidising agent.
  • Some oxides like MgO, CuO, CO2 and CrO3 are oxidants.
  • Some molecules are made up of electronegative elements, e.g. O2, O3, Cl2, Br2, I2, H2O2 etc., acts as oxidants.
  • The compounds in which elements are present in its highest oxidation number are oxidising agent, e.g. HNO3, KMnO4, K2Cr2O7, Na2Cr2O7, H2SO4, FeCl3, CuCl2 etc.
  • All the positively charged species behaves as oxidising agents.
  • Oxidising agents are Lewis acids.
image_descriptions: Chemical reaction diagram showing Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu with an arrow indicating reduction of Cu from +2 to 0.

details.summary: Definition, properties, and examples of oxidising agents (oxidants).

subject: Chemistry
text:
Reduction: The process of addition of hydrogen or any other electropositive element (or radical) or removal of oxygen or any other electronegative element (or radical) by a substance.

  • H2S + Cl2 → 2HCl + S (reduction of Cl2)
  • 2FeCl3 + Fe → 3FeCl2 (reduction of FeCl3)
  • CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O (reduction of CuO)
  • FeCl3 + H2S → FeCl2 + S (reduction of FeCl3)

The process of gain of one or more electrons by an atom, ion or molecule is known as reduction, e.g., Hg2+ + e- → Hg+; I2 + 2e- → 2I-; Cl + e- → Cl-.

Decrease in valency or oxidation number of an element is reduction, e.g., Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu.

Reducing Agents: The substance which undergoes oxidation in a chemical reaction is known as reducing agent or reductant. Thus, reactant is an electron loser. e.g., Zn is reducing agent.

  • All metals like Zn, Na, Fe, Al, Mg, K and few non-metals C, S etc., are reductants.
  • Hydracids of electronegative elements e.g. HCl, HBr, HI, H2S etc., are reductants.
  • Compounds containing element in its lower oxidation state are also reductant, e.g. Cu2Cl2, Hg2Cl2, SnCl2, FeCl2, CO, Cu2O, Na2S2O3, KI etc.
  • All negatively charged species behave like reducing agents.
  • Reducing agents are Lewis bases.

Note: White phosphorus has the property of only slow oxidation in air.
image_descriptions: Reaction diagram showing Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu with an arrow indicating reduction for Cu.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Redox Reactions: The reactions involving oxidation and as well as reduction as its two half reactions are called redox reactions. In these reactions, one substance is oxidised and other substance is reduced.

Disproportionation Reaction: The reaction in which same element is oxidised as well as reduced.

  • Oxidation and reduction take place together in equivalent amounts.
  • All metal displacement reactions are redox reactions.
  • The formation of ionic solid from its elements is always a redox reaction.
  • Compounds like H2O, O3, HNO3, H2SO3, NaNO2, SO2, NO2S2O3 act as oxidising as well as reducing agents.
  • Reducing agents are oxidised and oxidising agents are reduced in a chemical reaction.
image_descriptions: Reaction diagram for 2Cu2O + Cu2S -> 6Cu + SO2 showing oxidation and reduction paths.
Reaction diagram for Cl2 + NaOH -> NaCl + NaClO3 + H2O showing disproportionation.
Reaction diagram for Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu showing oxidation and reduction.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Oxidation Number: The real or imaginary charge which an atom appears to have in its combined state. Oxidation number of an element in a compound is determined as the number of electrons that have passed from one atom of a given element to other atom (positive oxidation) or to one atom of a given element from other atom (negative oxidation).

General Rules for Calculation of Oxidation Number:

  • The oxidation number of hydrogen is +1 in all its compounds but in metallic hydride the oxidation state of hydrogen is -1 (NaH, CaH2).
  • The common oxidation state of oxygen is -2.
  • Oxidation number of oxygen in peroxides like H2O2, Na2O2 is -1, in superoxides like KO2, RbO2 it is -1/2 and compounds in which O-atom bonded to fluorine like OF2, O is in +2 while in O2F2 is in +1 state.
  • The common oxidation state of halogen (Cl, F, etc.) is -1.
  • The common oxidation state of alkali metal (e.g. Li, Na, K etc.) is +1.
  • The oxidation number of alkaline earth metals (e.g. Be, Mg, Ca, Ba, etc.) is +2.
  • Oxidation number of elements in its elementary state is taken to be zero. e.g. N2, Cl2, O2 H2, Br2 etc., has oxidation number zero.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Rules for Calculating Oxidation Numbers and Examples
text:
• Oxidation number of an ion is same as its charge, e.g. oxidation number of Na+, Ba2+, Al3+, Cl- is +1, +2, +3, -1, respectively.
  • Oxidation number of metal in metal carbonyl is zero e.g., Fe is in 0 oxidation state in Fe(CO)5.
  • In C3O2 [carbon suboxide] oxidation number of carbon is 4/3, Br3O8 [tribromooctaoxide], Br is in 16/3 oxidation state and Na2S4O6 [sodium tetrathionate], S is in 2.5 oxidation state.
  • The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the atoms in the formula of compound is always zero.

Some Examples:

(i) Oxidation number (ON) of S in H2SO4:
Let oxidation number of S be x.
Now, oxidation number of hydrogen is +1, oxygen is -2.
∴ 2 × 1 + x + (-2) × 4 = 0
⇒ 2 + x - 8 = 0
⇒ x = +6

(ii) Oxidation number of Mn in KMnO4 (potassium permanganate):
Let oxidation number of Mn be x.
Now, oxidation number of K is +1 and O is -2.
∴ +1 + x + (-2) × 4 = 0
⇒ x + 1 - 8 = 0; x = +7

(iii) Oxidation number of Fe in [Fe(H2O)5NO]SO4:
Let oxidation number of Fe be x.
Oxidation number of H2O = 0, NO = +1, SO4 = -2.
[Fe(H2O)5NO]SO4 = x + 0 × 5 + (+1) - 2 = 0
⇒ x + 1 - 2 = 0 ⇒ x = +1

details.summary: Covers essential rules for determining oxidation states, fractional oxidation numbers in specific compounds (C3O2, Br3O8, Na2S4O6), and step-by-step calculations for H2SO4, KMnO4, and [Fe(H2O)5NO]SO4.

mcq.question: What is the oxidation state of iron (Fe) in the brown ring complex [Fe(H2O)5NO]SO4?
mcq.explanation: In the brown ring complex [Fe(H2O)5NO]SO4, NO is in the nitrosonium ion form (NO+ with +1 charge), H2O is neutral (0), and sulfate carries a -2 charge. Thus, x + 0*5 + 1 - 2 = 0, giving x = +1.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Fundamentals of Electrochemistry, Electrolytes, and Electrochemical Cells
text:
ELECTROCHEMISTRY
The branch of chemistry dealing with the interconversion of chemical energies and electrical energies during spontaneous redox reactions.

Electrolytes:
The substances, which allow the electricity to pass through them in their molten state or aqueous solution are called electrolytes. e.g. common salt (NaCl), sulphuric acid (H2SO4) etc.

Non-Electrolytes:
The substances which do not allow the electricity to pass through them in their molten state or aqueous solution are called non-electrolytes. e.g. sugar, wax, naphthalene etc.

Electrochemical Cell:
A device in which spontaneous redox reaction is carried out to produce an electric current is called electrochemical cell.

  • An electrochemical cell comprises of two metallic electrodes namely anode [-ve electrode] and cathode [+ve electrode] dipped in electrolytic solution.
  • There are two types of electrochemical cell: galvanic cell and electrolytic cell. In galvanic cell, the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction is converted into electrical energy while in electrolytic cells, electrical energy is used to carry out a non-spontaneous reaction.

details.summary: Defines electrochemistry, distinguishes electrolytes from non-electrolytes, and explains the components and primary types of electrochemical cells (galvanic vs electrolytic).

mcq.question: Which of the following substances acts as a non-electrolyte in aqueous solution?
mcq.explanation: Naphthalene, sugar, and wax do not dissociate into ions in molten state or solution and are classified as non-electrolytes.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Electrodes, Electrode Potential, Batteries, and Fuel Cells
text:
Electrode:
It is a metal conducting plate (anode or cathode) that emits or collects electrons in a cell. Electrode made up of an element with lower reduction potential acts as anode. Oxidation takes place at anode. While reduction takes place at cathode.

Electrode Potential:
The potential of an electrode with respect to its solution is called the electrode potential. It is a measure of its tendency to lose or gain electrons, when it comes in contact with a solution of its own ions. The tendency of an electrode to gain electrons or to get reduced is called its reduction potential while the tendency of an electrode to lose electrons or to get oxidised is called its oxidation potential. It depends upon the following:

  • (i) Concentration of solution
  • (ii) Nature of electrolyte
  • (iii) Nature of metal
  • (iv) Conditions of temperature and pressure

BATTERY:
The arrangement of one or more cells in a series connection is called battery. It is basically a galvanic cell. There are two types of battery:

  • (i) Primary battery: (non-rechargeable) can be used only once. e.g. dry cell (Lechlanche cell), mercury cell.
  • (ii) Secondary battery: (rechargeable) can be reused again and again. This battery can act both as galvanic and electrolytic cell. e.g. lead storage battery, nickel-cadmium battery.

Fuel Cell:
The type of galvanic cell in which the energy released by the combustion of fuels (hydrogen, methane, methanol) is directly converted into electrical energy is called fuel cell. e.g. fuel cell using H2 and O2 to form water in order to produce electricity. Efficiency of these cells is 70%. This cell was used first-time in Apollo Space Programme.

details.summary: Comprehensive coverage of electrode function, electrode potential factors, classifications of batteries (primary vs secondary), and operational characteristics of fuel cells including historical space program usage.

mcq.question: Which of the following cells was used for the first time to provide electrical power in the Apollo Space Programme?
mcq.explanation: A hydrogen-oxygen (H2-O2) fuel cell was used for the first time in the Apollo Space Programme with an efficiency of around 70%.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The process of decomposition of an electrolyte on passing an electric current through its aqueous solution or in the fused state is called electrolysis. Cations move towards cathode, gain electrons and become neutral atoms. Similarly anions move towards anode, lose electrons and become neutral atoms. In electrorefining of metals, impure metals act as anode and a strip of pure metal acts as cathode.

Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis

Faraday gave following two laws to explain a relation of amount of substance produced with current or its equivalent weight.

First Law of Electrolysis: It states that “the quantity (mass) of any substance deposited or liberated at any electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through electrolyte.”

Second Law of Electrolysis: It states, “when same quantity of electricity is passed through solutions of different electrolytes connected in series, the weight of substance produced at the electrodes is directly proportional to their equivalent weight.”
formulas: Weight of Cu deposited (w1) / Weight of Ag deposited (w2) = Equivalent weight of Cu (E1) / Equivalent weight of Ag (E2)

details.summary: Covers the definition of electrolysis and Faraday's two laws of electrolysis.

subject: Chemistry
text:
The arrangement of elements in order of increasing their standard reduction potential values is known as electrochemical series or activity series.

K < Ca < Na < Mg < Al < Zn < Cr < Fe < Ni < Sn < H2 < Cu < Hg < Ag < Pd < Pt < Au [as reactivity follows the reverse order].

  • Thus, gold is least reactive while potassium is most reactive element.
  • Substances which have lower reduction potentials are stronger reducing agents.
  • Only those metals can liberate hydrogen from the acid which have negative values of reduction potentials or which are placed before H-atom.
  • The more reactive metals of the activity series displaces the less reactive metals from their salt solutions.
image_descriptions: Chemical reaction equation: Cu + FeSO4 -> No reaction
Chemical reaction equation: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (Blue coloured solution becomes Colourless)

details.summary: Explanation of the electrochemical series, reactivity trends, and displacement reactions.

subject: Chemistry
text:
It is a process of oxidative deterioration of a metal as a result of its reaction with air and moisture present in the environment.

  • Corrosion of iron is called rusting. Rust is hydrated iron (III) oxide.
  • Similarly, in presence of moist air, copper acquires a green coating of basic copper carbonate, [Cu(OH)2 · CuCO3] silver acquires a black coating of silver sulphide [Ag2S] and aluminium acquires a dull coating of aluminium oxide (a protective layer).
  • A sliced apple turns brown if left open for sometime due to the oxidation of iron present in it as a nutrient.
  • The rusting of iron can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising (coating of iron with zinc) and chrome plating.
  • Anodisation (an electrolytic process) is the process of forming a thick oxide layer on the surface of the metal. This oxide layer is protective and prevents the metal from further oxidation.
  • Formation of a layer of Al2O3 on aluminium surface protects the metal from further corrosion.

details.summary: Definition of corrosion, specific examples like rusting, and methods of prevention.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Non-metals have properties opposite of metals. They are found on the right side of the periodic table. In the modern periodic table, there are 22 non-metals (11 gas, 10 solid, 1 liquid).

Hydrogen: The first element in the periodic table and the lightest element known. It exists as a diatomic molecule H2 (dihydrogen). Discovered by Henry Cavendish, named by Lavoisier. Prepared by treating iron with dilute H2SO4. Atomic number is 1, electronic configuration is 1s1. It resembles both alkali metals and halogens (can donate electron to form H+ or accept one to form H-). It is the most abundant element in the universe. Jupiter and Saturn consist mainly of hydrogen. It constitutes about 0.9% by weight of earth crust.

details.summary: Overview of non-metals and fundamental properties of Hydrogen.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Methods for preparation of hydrogen gas:

  • Laboratory preparation: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 (upward displacement of water).
  • Electrolysis of water: Dihydrogen of high purity is prepared by electrolysis of water in the presence of acid or base. (2H2O(l) -> 2H2(g) + O2(g)).
  • Action of acids on metal: Metals placed above hydrogen in the electrochemical series or having positive value of standard oxidation.

details.summary: Chemical methods for preparing hydrogen gas.

subject: Chemistry
content:
Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series liberate hydrogen gas when they react with dilute acids.

**Examples:**
1. Zinc with Dilute Sulfuric Acid:
   $$Zn_{(s)} + H_2SO_{4(dil.)} ightarrow ZnSO_{4(aq)} + H_{2(g)} \uparrow$$
   *Note:* A small amount of $SO_2$ is also produced because $H_2$ reduces $H_2SO_4$ to $SO_2$.

2. Iron with Hydrochloric Acid:
   $$Fe_{(s)} + 2HCl_{(aq)} ightarrow FeCl_{2(aq)} + H_{2(g)} \uparrow$$

**Reactivity Series of Metals (Decreasing Order):**
$K > Ca > Na > Mg > Al > Mn > Zn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au$

*Key Point:* Only metals positioned above Hydrogen (H) in this series can displace hydrogen from acids.

subject: Chemistry
content:
Certain amphoteric metals like Zinc (Zn), Magnesium (Mg), and Tin (Sn) liberate hydrogen gas upon reaction with alkalies (bases).

**Examples:**
1. Aluminum with Sodium Hydroxide:
   $$2Al + 2NaOH + 2H_2O ightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + 3H_{2(g)}$$

2. Tin with Sodium Hydroxide:
   $$Sn + 2NaOH + H_2O ightarrow Na_2SnO_3 + 2H_{2(g)}$$

3. Zinc with Sodium Hydroxide:
   $$Zn + 2NaOH ightarrow Na_2ZnO_2 + H_{2(g)}$$

subject: Chemistry
content:
The reactivity of metals with water depends on their position in the reactivity series.

1. **Very Active Metals (Na, K, Ca):** React with water at room temperature.
   - Sodium: $2Na + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{Cold} 2NaOH + H_{2(g)} \uparrow$
   - *Storage Note:* Sodium is kept under kerosene oil to prevent reaction with moisture in the air.

2. **Less Reactive Metals (Zn, Mg, Al):** React with water only upon heating.
   - Magnesium: $Mg + H_2O \xrightarrow{Heat} MgO + H_{2(g)} \uparrow$
   - Aluminum: $2Al + 6H_2O ightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3H_{2(g)} \uparrow$

subject: Chemistry
content:
The Bosch process is a method for manufacturing dihydrogen by passing steam over red-hot coke.

**Conditions:**
- Temperature: 1270 K (400-600°C for coke ignition context, but reaction occurs at high temp).
- Reactants: Coke (C) and Superheated Steam ($H_2O$).

**Reaction:**
$$C_{(s)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow{Red\ Hot\ Coke} CO_{(g)} + H_{2(g)}$$

**Product:** The mixture of CO and $H_2$ is known as **Water Gas** or **Syn Gas**.

**Purification of $CO_2$:**
If $CO_2$ is present, it is removed by:
1. Dissolving in water under pressure (25-30 atm).
2. Scrubbing the mixture with sodium arsenite.

subject: Chemistry
content:
Lane’s process involves passing alternate currents of steam and water gas over red-hot iron. It consists of two stages:

**Stage 1: Oxidation Stage**
Superheated steam is passed over iron filings heated to 1025–1075 K.
$$3Fe + 4H_2O \xrightarrow{1025-1075\ K} Fe_3O_4 + 4H_2 + 161\ kJ$$
*Product:* Magnetic oxide of iron ($Fe_3O_4$) and Hydrogen gas.

**Stage 2: Reduction Stage**
Once the iron is oxidized, steam is stopped, and water gas (CO + $H_2$) is passed to reduce $Fe_3O_4$ back to iron.
$$Fe_3O_4 + 4CO ightarrow 3Fe + 4CO_2$$
$$Fe_3O_4 + 4H_2 ightarrow 3Fe + 4H_2O$$
This cycle allows for the continuous production of hydrogen.

subject: Chemistry
content:
Key physical properties of Hydrogen gas:
1. **Appearance:** Colorless, tasteless, and odourless gas.
2. **Solubility:** Slightly soluble in water.
3. **Molecular Nature:** The molecules are non-polar, which contributes to its low solubility in polar solvents like water.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Some uses of dihydrogen are given below:

  • It is used in the manufacture of synthetic petrol.
  • It is used as a rocket fuel in the form of liquid hydrogen which does not cause any pollution and produces greater energy per unit mass of fuel.
  • It is used in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
  • It is used as a reducing agent in the laboratory and industry.
  • It is used in the preparation of compounds like ammonia (Haber's process), water gas, and fertiliser such as urea, ammonium sulphate etc.
  • It is used in the preparation of many organic compounds such as methanol.

details.summary: Overview of industrial and practical applications of dihydrogen.

subject: Chemistry
text:
A molecule of dihydrogen contains two atoms, the nuclei of both the atom in each molecule are spining.

  • Molecules of hydrogen in which spins of both the nuclei are in same directions are called ortho hydrogen.
  • Molecules in which both the nuclei spin in the opposite directions are called para hydrogen. The compound usually consist of discrete covalent molecules. Only weak van der Waals' forces holding the molecule together.
  • para hydrogen has lower energy and at 0°K the gas contains 100 % para hydrogen.
  • At room temperature, the ratio of ortho to para hydrogen is 3 : 1.
  • Ortho and para hydrogen, both have similar chemical properties but their properties like boiling points, heating conductivity and specific heat etc. are different.

details.summary: Distinction between ortho and para forms of hydrogen based on nuclear spin.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Compounds of hydrogen in which hydrogen is suppose to be present as H- are called hydrides. Oxidation state of H in these compounds is -1. These are the binary compounds of hydrogen with other elements.

Types of Hydrides

Hydrides are the following types:

  • (i) Ionic or Saline Hydrides: These are formed by reaction of alkali metal, alkaline earth metals (except Be and Mg) and some lanthanides with hydrogen. These hydrides are crystalline, non-volatile and conducting in fused state. Their aqueous solution is alkaline in nature. Their reaction with water is explosive. NaH + H2O -> NaOH + H2
  • (ii) Covalent or Molecular Hydrides: These are formed by reaction of p-block elements (except noble gases) and by Be and Mg with hydrogen. Molecular hydrides are of three types:
    • (a) Electron-deficient hydrides: These are formed by group-13 (IIIA) elements e.g. B2H6 etc.
    • (b) Electron-precise hydrides: These are formed by group-14 (IV A) elements e.g. CH4 etc.
    • (c) Electron rich hydrides: These are formed by group 15, 16 and 17 elements e.g. NH3, H2O, HF etc.
  • (iii) Metallic or Interstitial (Non-stoichiometric) Hydrides: These are formed by reaction of transition metals and inner-transition metals with hydrogen. These are non-stoichiometric compounds and show conductivity. d-block elements of group 7, 8 and 9 do not form hydride, therefore this region in the periodic table is called hydride gap.
  • (iv) Polymeric Hydrides and Complex Hydrides: These are formed by reaction of elements having electronegativity in the range 1.4 to 2.0 like Al, Si etc with hydrogen.

details.summary: Classification of hydrides based on bonding and stoichiometry.

subject: Chemistry
text:
A major part of all living organisms is made up of water (H2O). Human body has 65% (about) and some plants have as much as 95% water. 97% part of the entire water is assumed to be confined in oceans while rest is present in pure form. Rain water is the purest form of water.

Properties of Water

  • Water is the neutral oxide of hydrogen.
  • It is colourless liquid under ordinary conditions.
  • It is polar compound (dipole moment = 1.85 D) and possesses a high dielectric constant (approx 81). Which makes it a universal solvent.
  • It has abnormally high melting point and boiling point due to the association of H2O molecules through hydrogen bonding.
  • Melting point of ice is lowered with increase in pressure.
  • In solid state (ice) water molecules are joined together in three dimension network. It is responsible for low density of water. As the temperature of ice is increased above 0°C, some H-bond are broken, this results in decrease in volume and increase in density. Density of water is maximum at 4°C.

details.summary: Physical and chemical properties of water.

subject: Chemistry
text:
General Properties:

  • Density of ice is less than water hence it floats on water.
  • pH of water is 7.
  • Covalent molecules which are capable of forming hydrogen bonds with water molecules get dissolved e.g. lower alcohols, lower carboxylic acid, sugars are soluble in water due to hydrogen bond formation.
  • Covalent molecules which cannot form hydrogen bonds with water are not soluble in it, e.g. CHCl3, CCl4, benzene, alkanes etc.

Water is a universal solvent:

The various properties of water which make it a universal solvent are:

  • (i) The polar nature of water molecule.
  • (ii) The ability of water molecule to make hydrogen bonds with molecules of many compounds.
  • (iii) High dielectric constant of water molecule.
  • (iv) The ability of water molecule undergo chemical reaction with many element and compounds.

details.summary: Overview of water's chemical properties, solubility, and role as a universal solvent.

subject: Chemistry
text:
Hard Water: Presence of calcium and magnesium salts (mainly) and iron salt in the form of hydrogen carbonate, chloride and sulphate in water makes water hard. Hard water does not give lather with soap. Hard water forms scum/precipitate with soap. It is, therefore, unsuitable for laundry. It is harmful for boilers as well because of deposition of salts in the form of scale.

Soft Water: Rain water is almost pure. The water free from soluble salts of calcium and magnesium, is called soft water. It gives lather with soap.

Temporary Hardness: Temporary hardness is due to the presence of magnesium and calcium hydrogen carbonates in water. It can be removed by:

  • (i) Boiling: During boiling, the soluble magnesium hydrogen carbonate is converted into insoluble magnesium hydroxide and calcium hydrogen carbonate is converted into insoluble calcium carbonate. These insoluble precipitates can be removed by filtration.
  • (ii) Clark's Method: In this method, calculated amount of lime is added to hard water. It precipitates out calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide which can be filtered off.

Permanent Hardness: It is due to the presence of soluble salts of magnesium and calcium in the form of chlorides and sulphates in water. Permanent hardness can be removed by the following methods:

  • (i) Treatment with Washing Soda (Na2CO3 or Sodium Carbonates): Washing soda reacts with soluble calcium and magnesium chlorides and sulphates in hard water to form insoluble carbonates.
  • (ii) Calgon's Method: Sodium hexametaphosphate (Na6P6O18), commercially called 'calgon', when added to hard water, complex anions are formed. The complex anion keeps the Mg2+ and Ca2+ ions in solution.
  • (iii) Ion Exchange Method: This method is also called zeolite/permutit process. Hydrated sodium aluminium silicate is called zeolite. When zeolite is added to hard water, exchange reactions take place which results in softening of water. Na2Al2Si2O8 .xH2O, (also known as zeolites) which have property of exchanging cations such as Ca2+, Mg2+ with sodium salt ions.
  • (iv) Synthetic Resins Method: Now-a-days hard water is softened by using synthetic cation exchangers. This method is more efficient than zeolite process.

details.summary: Detailed explanation of hard vs soft water, causes of temporary and permanent hardness, and methods for removal.

subject: Chemistry
topic: Structure of Water Molecule and Heavy Water
text:
Structure of Water Molecule:

  • The molecule of water consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to oxygen atom by covalent bonds.
  • The density of ice is less than water.
  • In water molecule, the central oxygen atom is sp3 hybridised and contain two lone pairs.
  • The geometry of water is distorted and H—O—H bond angle is 104.5°.

Heavy Water:

  • Chemically heavy water is deuterium oxide (D2O). It was discovered by Urey in 1932. It is colourless, odourless and tasteless liquid.
  • It is used in nuclear reactor as moderator because it slow down the fast moving neutrons.

| Freezing point | 0°C | 3.8°C |
| Boiling point | 100°C | 101.42°C |
| Temperature of maximum density | 4°C | 11.6°C |
| Dielectric constant | 81 | 80 |
| Solubility of substances | High | Low |
| Density | 1.0000 g cm^-3 | 1.1059 g cm^-3 |
