subject: Biology
text:
• Sternum is absent in fishes.
  • Tibia fibula is the longest bone of frog.
  • Funny bone (ulna) is a bone found in bend of the elbow.
  • Spondylitis is the inflammation of vertebrae.
  • Arteries of ancient mummies remain intact due to well-preserved fibroblast fibres.
  • Synovitis is an inflammation leading to swelling at joint.
  • Chondrology is the study of cartilages.
  • Fibro cartilage is the strongest cartilage.
  • Skeleton have 12 pairs of ribs in human.
  • True ribs are first seven pairs of ribs, while 8th, 9th and 10th pairs are false ribs and last two pairs (11th and 12th) are known as floating ribs.
  • Cartilage of ear lobes have less blood supply. Tendons and ligaments are dense connective tissues. They are made up of collagen and elastic yellow fibre, respectively.
  • Tendon connects skeletal muscles to bones.
  • Ligament attaches one bone to another bone, it is highly flexible and contains very little matrix.
  • Bone marrow is absent in birds, but in human, it is the site of production of blood cells in some bones.
image_descriptions: A detailed anatomical diagram of the human skeleton labeling the following parts: Skull, Cranium, Eye orbit, Nasal bone, Maxilla, Mandible, Cervical vertebrae, Clavicle, Pectoral girdle, Humerus, Sternum, Vertebral column, Pelvic girdle, Sacrum, Coccyx, Radius, Ulna, Carpals, Metacarpals, Phalanges, Femur, Patella, Fibula, Tibia, Metatarsals, Tarsals.

details.summary: Overview of skeletal system facts and anatomical structure.

subject: Biology
text:
Muscles contribute most of the total weight of the body (about 40%).

  • Muscles are helpful in locomotion and movement.
  • The study of muscles is called Myology.
  • Muscles have glycogen (polysaccharide), which are used to obtain energy.
  • Muscle tissues are of three types, i.e. striated, non-striated and cardiac.
  • Muscles have proteins, which are myoglobin, actin, myosin, etc.
  • Muscles of face contract slowly, but can remain contracted for a longer time.
  • Lactic acid is a chemical, which is responsible for fatigue after muscular activity in human beings.
  • Lactic acid accumulates in muscles due to anaerobic respiration.
  • Myograph instrument is used to record single muscle twitch.
  • Cori's cycle is relationship between muscles glycogen and liver glycogen through lactic acid.
  • Motor unit acts as an independent unit of muscle.
  • Ca+2 and Mg+2 are required for muscle contraction.
  • Myostasis is inflammation of a muscle.

details.summary: Overview of muscular system functions, composition, and physiology.

subject: Biology
text:
A joint is the meeting place of two bones. Arthrology is the study of joints.

(i) Immovable Joints (Fibrous or Synarthrose Joints)

  • In these, the adjoining bones are joined by strong bundles of collagen fibres, so that the bones cannot move freely.
  • The bones of the skull articulate with one another in a type of immovable joint called suture, e.g. (a) Articulation of teeth with mandible and maxillae. Here, peg-shaped roots fit into cone-shaped sockets in the jawbones. (b) Articulation between the first pair of ribs and the breast bone.

details.summary: Definition and classification of immovable joints.

subject: Biology
text:
Slightly Movable (Cartilaginous Joints): In these joints, there is a pad of fibro-cartilage between two adjoining bones, which allows for very slight movements. These are also called symphysis, e.g. joints between pubic bones of pelvic girdles and the joints between the vertebrae (intervertebral disc).

Freely Movable (Synovial Joints): In these joints, the movement is possible in one or other directions. These are of following types:

  • (a) Ball and socket between humerus and glenoid cavity of pectoral girdle, femur and pelvic girdle.
  • (b) Hinge joint between knee, ankle, elbow, phalanges of digits.
  • (c) Pivot joint between atlas and axis of mammals.
  • (d) Saddle joint between metacarpal and carpal of thumb.
  • (e) Gliding joint between radio-ulna and carpals.
  • (f) Ellipsoidal joint between skull and first vertebra.

RESPIRATORY SYSTEM: Structurally and functionally the conducting part of human respiratory system is highly complicated. The respiratory system is derived from embryonic endoderm. The respiratory system includes respiratory organs and conducting organs. The main respiratory organs of humans are lungs. The lungs and related structures together constitute the respiratory system of humans.

Respiratory Organs:

  • Lungs acts as the major respiratory organs.
  • Each lung is covered by double membrane called pleurae.
  • In human, the right lung has three lobes and left lung has two lobes.
  • The alveoli are the ultimate structural and physiological units of lung.
  • Alveoli provide great surface area (like villi of intestine in mammals) for gaseous exchange by diffusion.
  • Gaseous exchange occurs across the respiratory membrane of the alveoli.
  • Residual air of lungs can be traced in alveoli.
  • The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscular structure separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities.
  • The diaphragm is characteristic of mammals.

Conducting Organs: Conducting organs conduct air to lungs. These are as follows:

  • (i) Nostrils: Holes of the nose are called nostrils, these are paired openings that open up into the nasal chambers. There are two nasal chambers separated by the nasal septum. Each nasal chamber consists of three regions, i.e. vestibular, respiratory and olfactory regions. It consists of many goblet cells.
  • (ii) Pharynx: It provides passage to both air and food.
  • (iii) Larynx: It is the uppermost portion of trachea made up of cartilages in humans. It is also called voice box. Human larynx consists of glottis, cartilages, hyoid bone, thyrohyoid membrane, vocal cords, laryngeal ligaments and muscles. Glottis is an opening in the floor of pharynx leading to larynx. There are nine pieces of cartilages (3 are single and 3 are paired). There is a little difference in the size of the larynx in man and woman. It grows larger and becomes prominent in man, therefore it is called adam's apple in man.
  • (iv) Trachea: The trachea or windpipe is a continuation of the larynx. Trachea is supported by incomplete (C-shaped) rings of hyaline cartilages.
  • (v) Bronchus: These are one pair of small, thin-walled tubular structures formed by the division of trachea at the level of 5th thoracic vertebra.
  • (vi) Bronchiole: The tertiary bronchi is subdivided into smaller branches called bronchioles. Bronchioles can enter into group of alveoli by means of their edges. Each group consists of air sacs.

Respiration: It is the process by which gases are exchanged between the blood and the air. It is a physical process. It is simply the intake of oxygen and giving out of carbon dioxide. It includes inspiration and expiration.

Inspiration:

  • It is a process, by which fresh air enters in the lungs.
  • In this, diaphragm becomes flat and gets lowered by the contraction of its muscle fibres and increases the volume of thoracic cavity.
  • The external intercostal muscles contract and pull the ribs and sternum upwards and outwards direction and thus, the volume of thoracic cavity is increased.
image_descriptions: Diagram of the human respiratory system showing nasal cavity, nostril, glottis, larynx, trachea, right lung, left lung, left bronchus, and a detailed inset showing blood flow, smooth muscle, pulmonary arteriole, pulmonary venule, bronchiole, alveolar sac, and alveoli.

details.summary: Overview of joint types and the human respiratory system, including respiratory organs, conducting organs, and the process of respiration/inspiration.

subject: Biology
text:
Expiration is a process by which CO2 is expelled out from the lungs.

  • Muscle fibres of the diaphragm relax make it convex, decreasing the volume of the thoracic cavity.
  • External intercostal muscles relax and pull the ribs downwards and inwards direction, thus decreasing the size of the thoracic cavity.
  • 12-15 times in a minute.
  • Newborns breath 40 times per minute.
  • Respiration rate is minimum while sleeping.
  • The air passage in humans occurs in following manner: Nasal chamber -> Pharynx -> Voice box -> Trachea -> Bronchus -> Bronchiole -> Air sac -> Cells -> Blood.
tables:
| Measurement | Adult Male Average Value | Adult Female Average Value | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tidal Volume (TV) | 500 mL | 500 mL | Amount of air inhaled or exhaled with each breath under resting conditions. |
| Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) | 1200 mL | 700 mL | Amount of air that can be forcefully exhaled after a normal tidal volume exhalation. |
| Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) | 3100 mL | 1900 mL | Amount of air that can be forcefully inhaled after a normal tidal volume inhalation. |
| Residual Volume (RV) | 1200 mL | 1100 mL | Amount of air remaining in the lungs after a forced exhalation. |
| Inspiratory Capacity (IC) | 3600 mL | 2400 mL | Maximum amount of air that can be inspired after a normal expiration, IC = TV + IRV |
| Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) | 2400 mL | 1800 mL | Volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal tidal volume expiration, FRC = ERV + RV |
| Total Lung Capacity (TLC) | 6000 mL | 4200 mL | Maximum amount of air contained in lungs after a maximum inspiratory effort, TLC = TV + IRV + ERV + RV |
| Vital Capacity (VC) | 4800 mL | 3100 mL | Maximum amount of air that can be expired after a maximum inspiratory effort, VC = TV + IRV + ERV (should be 80% TLC) |

details.summary: Overview of the expiration process and respiratory volumes/capacities.

subject: Biology
text:
Digestion is the process in which complex, non-diffusible food gets converted into simple diffusible food particles with the help of digestive enzymes. It consists of the Alimentary Canal which starts from mouth to anus.

(i) Mouth or Buccal Cavity:

  • Palate forms the roof of mouth and separates mouth from nasal chamber.
  • Tongue is muscular and bears taste buds. Anterior part is sensitive to sweet taste.
  • Saliva contains salivary amylase (ptyalin) and lysozyme (kills bacteria).
  • Teeth are of four types: incisors, canines, premolars, and molars.
  • An adult has 16 teeth on each jaw.
  • Dental formula in human is 2123/2123.
  • Teeth are made of bone-like material called dentine and covered by enamel (hardest part of our body).
  • Last molars are called wisdom teeth.
  • Canines are absent in rabbit and squirrel.
  • Milk teeth start erupting after 6 months of birth. Dental formula of milk teeth is 2102/2102.
image_descriptions: Diagram of the human digestive system showing the oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, ascending/transverse/descending colon, caecum, vermiform appendix, rectum, and anus.

details.summary: Structure and components of the human digestive system, focusing on the buccal cavity and teeth.

subject: Biology
topic: Pharynx, Oesophagus, Stomach, Small Intestine, Large Intestine
text:
• Pharynx: Small sized (12-14 cm), conical part where food and air passages cross. Divided into nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.
  • Oesophagus: Long (22-25 cm) narrow, muscular tube with longitudinal folds (oesophageal rugae). Conducts food to stomach via peristalsis.
  • Stomach: Temporary reservoir that churns food into chyme. Secretes gastric juice (HCl and pepsin). Digestion of protein occurs here. Ruminant stomachs have four chambers: rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum.
  • Small Intestine: Longest part (approx 6m). Divided into duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Contains villi and microvilli to increase surface area. Site of complete digestion of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates.
  • Large Intestine: Consists of caecum, colon, and rectum. Caecum is a vestigial organ in humans (appendix). Site of water reabsorption.

details.summary: Overview of the human alimentary canal components and their specific functions in digestion.

subject: Biology
text:
• Salivary Glands: Produce saliva containing salivary amylase (ptyalin) to convert starch into maltose. Types: Parotid (below ear), Submaxillary (beneath jaw), Sublingual (floor of buccal cavity), Zygomatic (beneath eyes).
  • Gastric Glands: Located in stomach mucosa. Types: Cardiac (alkaline mucus), Pyloric (alkaline mucus), Fundic (contains Peptic/zymogen cells for pepsinogen, Oxyntic cells for HCl, Goblet cells for mucus, Argentaffin cells for gastrin).
  • Liver: Largest gland. Consists of right, left, quadrate, and caudate lobes. Stores bile in gall bladder. Bile contains bile salts and pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin). Contains Kupffer's cells (phagocytic). Functions: blood clotting, glycogen formation, blood sugar regulation, synthesis of Vitamin-A, fat breakdown, and deamination of amino acids.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of digestive glands including salivary, gastric, and liver functions.

subject: Biology
text:
Pancreas

  • It functions both as an exocrine and endocrine gland.
  • It secretes amylase, trypsin and chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, lipase and nucleases in the digestive system.
  • It secretes pancreatic juice, which is helpful in digestion of both starch and proteins.

details.summary: Functions and secretions of the pancreas.

subject: Biology
text:
Circulatory System

  • Circulatory system was discovered by William Harvey (1628).
  • Circulatory system can be either of open type or closed type.
  • In open circulatory system, blood does not flow in vessels.
  • The circulatory system consists of heart and blood vessels.

Heart

The heart is a hollow, fibromuscular organ of somewhat conical or pyramidal form with upper broad part, the base and the lower narrow apex, which is slightly directed to the left.

Structure of Heart

  • Human heart is situated in the pericardial cavity.
  • The heart wall is made of three layers, i.e. pericardium, myocardium and endothelium.
  • Pericardial fluid is the fluid present between layers of heart wall. It allows frictionless movements of heart and protects it from mechanical shocks.
  • In males, weight of heart is about 280-340 g. While in females it is 230-280 g.
  • Weight of heart of a newborn baby is 20 g.
  • Human heart is consist of two atrium and two ventricles.

(i) Right Auricle or Atrium

  • It receives deoxygenated blood from superior vena cava and inferior vena cava.
  • Right auricle opens in right ventricle through a wide circular right auriculoventricular aperture guarded by tricuspid valve.
  • Tricuspid valve regulates unidirectional flow of blood from right auricle to right ventricle.

(ii) Right Ventricle

  • It gives off a large blood vessel called pulmonary artery leading to the lungs, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Semilunar valve stops blood to return back to ventricle.

(iii) Left Auricle or Atrium

  • It receives oxygenated blood from lungs through pulmonary veins.
  • They have no valve.
  • Left auricle opens in left ventricle by an aperture called left auriculoventricular aperture.
  • This aperture is guarded by bicuspid valve (mitral valve).
  • Bicuspid valve prevents backflow of blood from left auricle to left ventricle.

(iv) Left Ventricle

  • It gives off a large blood vessels called the aorta.
  • Aorta carries oxygenated blood to various body parts.
  • The thickest part of the human heart is the wall of the left ventricle.
image_descriptions: A flow chart illustrating double circulation. Lungs connect to the left auricle via pulmonary veins. Left auricle connects to left ventricle. Left ventricle connects to Aorta, which supplies all body organs except lungs. Body organs return deoxygenated blood via veins to the right auricle. Right auricle connects to right ventricle. Right ventricle connects to pulmonary artery, which returns to lungs.

details.summary: Detailed anatomy and function of the human heart and circulatory system.

subject: Biology
text:
Circulation of Blood

Blood circulation in humans is an example of double circulation. It includes pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation.

  • (i) Pulmonary Circulation: In this type of circulation, the deoxygenated blood is pushed by the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation through pulmonary artery. The oxygenated blood is brought back to left atrium of pulmonary vein.
  • (ii) Systemic Circulation: In this type of circulation, the oxygenated blood brought to left atrium goes to left ventricle and then passed on to different body parts through aorta.

Cardiac Cycle

  • The study of structure and functioning of heart is called as cardiology.
  • Heart constantly contracts or relaxes, due to which transportation of blood occurs in the whole body.
  • Cardiac cycle is the event, during which one heartbeat or one cycle of systole and diastole of cardiac muscle occurs.
  • Cardiac cycle consists of systole and diastole of atria and ventricles.
  • The cardiac impulse starts from SA node, than via a conducting system, this impulse is conducted to all parts of heart.
  • SA node is called as the pacemaker of heart.
  • Rate of heartbeat in humans is 72-75 per minute.
  • One cardiac cycle takes 0.8 seconds.

details.summary: Explanation of double circulation and the cardiac cycle.

subject: Biology
text:
Heart Sounds: The beating of heart produces sounds, heard by stethoscope.

  • First sound (lubb): A long and louder sound created by the closure of atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) at the beginning of ventricular systole.
  • Second sound (dupp): A short and sharper sound created by the closure of semilunar valves towards the end of ventricular systole (beginning of ventricular diastole).

Cardiac Output: It is the amount of blood pumped by the heart per minute.
formulas: Cardiac output = Normal heart rate of an adult per min * Amount of blood pumped by heart per min = 72 * 70 = 5040 mL per min (5 L/min)

details.summary: Definitions of heart sounds and calculation of cardiac output.

subject: Biology
text: In circulatory system, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood is transported to different body parts through different vessels namely arteries, veins and capillaries.
tables:
| Arteries | Veins |
|---|---|
| Arteries distribute blood from the heart to the different parts of the body. | Veins collect blood from different parts of the body and pour it into the heart. |
| Tunica media is thick, having more muscle fibres. | Tunica media is thin, having fewer muscle fibres. |
| Tunica interna has strong elastic membrane and more elongated endothelial cells. | Tunica interna has simple, elastic membrane and elongated endothelial cells. |
| The walls of the arteries are thick and muscular and hence, are non-collapsable. | The walls of the veins are thin and collapsable. |
| Arteries have no valves. | Veins have valves, which prevent backward flow of blood. |

details.summary: Comparison between arteries and veins.

subject: Biology
text:
The process of elimination of metabolic wastes from the body is called excretion. Removal of excess of water from the body or keep water content constant is called osmoregulation.

Depending on the type of waste, nitrogen elimination is of three types:

  • Ammonotelism: Elimination of nitrogen mainly in the form of ammonia, e.g., aquatic invertebrates, bony fishes and amphibians.
  • Ureotelism: Elimination of nitrogen mainly as urea. Ammonia combines with CO2 in liver to form urea, e.g., mammals, man, frogs, toads.
  • Uricotelism: Elimination of nitrogen mainly as uric acid, e.g., birds, reptiles, many insects. Uric acid is commercially extracted from bird dropping.

details.summary: Overview of excretion, osmoregulation, and types of nitrogenous waste elimination.

subject: Biology
text:
• Flame cells are the organs of excretion in tapeworm.
  • Sponges remove their wastes through their water canal system.
  • In Hydra, cells release waste into coelenteron.
  • In annelids, excretion takes place by nephridia.
  • In insects, excretion takes place by Malpighian tubules.
  • In some arthropods (prawns), green glands also help in excretion.
  • Waste material in Amoeba is taken out by plasmalemma.
  • Spiders have coxal glands.

details.summary: List of excretory organs in various invertebrate species.

subject: Biology
text:
Excretory system of human consists of following organs:

1. Kidney:

  • Kidney is a paired bean-shaped organ, that is present in abdomen just below the diaphragm.
  • The left kidney is placed a little higher than the right kidney (reverse in rabbit).
  • Concavity of kidney called hilus is always inwardly directed.
  • They form urine and drain it ultimately into pelvis of the kidney from where the ureter arises.
  • Water reabsorption in kidney is controlled by a hormone called ADH.
  • In anuria, kidneys become unable to form urine.

Nephron:

  • It is the functional unit of kidney.
  • In one kidney around 1 million nephrons are found.
  • It has two parts:

(i) Bowman's Capsule:

  • (a) It has a network of blood capillaries called glomerulus, which together form Malpighian body.
  • (b) Blood enters glomerular capillaries through afferent arteriole and leaves through efferent arteriole.

(ii) Renal Tubule: It consists of three parts:

  • (a) Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT).
  • (b) Loop of Henle with thin descending and thick ascending limb.
  • (c) Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT), which opens into collecting duct.

Other excretory functions:

  • Skin excretes mainly water and NaCl in sweat. Evaporation of sweat requires latent heat from the body due to which body feels cool. This is known as perspiration.
  • Lungs excrete CO2 and some water vapour. Liver excretes bile pigments and cholesterol in the bile.

details.summary: Detailed anatomy of the human kidney, nephron structure, and accessory excretory organs.

subject: Biology
text:
2. Ureters: This muscular tube emerges out from the hilum of kidneys. Urine enters the ureter from the renal pelvis.

3. Urinary bladder: Sac-like structure, which stores urine temporarily. It is absent in birds.

4. Urethra:

  • Membranous tube, which conducts urine to the exterior. Urethral sphincters keep the urethra closed except during voiding of urine.
  • The act of voiding urine is called micturition.
  • An adult man secretes 1-1.8 L of urine in 24 hours.
  • The yellow colour of urine is due to the presence of the pigment urochrome. pH of urine should be 5.8.
  • When water intake is high, the urine is hypotonic.
  • When there is less body water, the urine is hypertonic.
image_descriptions: Diagram showing the human urinary system including kidneys, renal pelvis, aorta, post-cava, ureter, bladder, and urethra. A cross-section of the kidney is also shown, labeling the capsule, cortex, medulla, papilla, renal artery, renal vein, and pelvis.

details.summary: Overview of the human excretory system components including ureters, bladder, and urethra, along with characteristics of urine.

subject: Biology
text:
Reproductive System: A process by which living organisms produce young ones of their own types is called reproduction. It includes asexual and sexual reproduction.

  • Asexual reproduction occurs without the formation and union of sex cells, e.g. budding (Hydra), binary fission (Amoeba) and multiple fission (malaria parasite).
  • Sexual reproduction includes fusion of male and female gametes.

Male Reproductive System:

Testes:

  • A pair of glandular, oval-shaped organs present in scrotum.
  • Temperature of scrotum is 2°C below the body temperature.
  • Endocrine tissues of testes produce testosterone.
  • Seminiferous tubules are the structural and functional unit of testes.
  • In seminiferous tubules, spermatogenic cells are present, which produce sperm cells. Sertoli cells provide nutrition to sperm cells. Leydig’s cells in testes secrete testosterone.

Vas Deferens:

  • Vas deferens is a term used for ducts extending from the epididymis to the ejaculatory ducts.
  • These store spermatozoa temporarily and transport them during ejaculation.
  • Removal of vas deferens is called vasectomy.

Urethra: It is a thick-walled muscular duct and it is a common passage for both urine and semen. It is also called urinogenital duct. It traverses and opens at the tip of the penis.

Penis: It is erectile copulatory organ. It helps in deposition of sperms into female genital tract.

Accessory Sex Glands:

  • (i) Seminal Vesicle: Situated behind the urinary bladder. About 70% of the semen in seminal fluid is produced by seminal vesicles. Seminal fluid contains fructose, (energy source for sperm) citrate, inositol, prostaglandins and several proteins. The product of the testes (spermatozoa) and prostate gland along with the fluid from the seminal vesicle are collectively known as semen. Seminal fluid has a pH of about 7.4.
  • (ii) Prostate Gland: Situated around the first part of the urethra. Secretes a thin, milky fluid that contains calcium, citrate ion, phosphate ion, a clotting enzyme and a profibrinolysin called as semen. Enlargement of prostate results in prostatitis, in which urination is difficult or impossible.
  • (iii) Cowper’s Gland: Also known as bulbourethral glands. The secretion of Cowper’s glands acts as lubricant for the glans penis. It also neutralises any urine in urethra.

Path of Sperms in Mammals: Seminiferous tubules -> Rete testis -> Vas efferentia -> Epididymis -> Vas deferens -> Urethra -> Vagina
image_descriptions: Diagram of the male reproductive system showing the seminal vesicle, bladder, prostate gland, penis, urethra, vas deferens, testis, and scrotum.

details.summary: Detailed anatomy and physiology of the male reproductive system, including accessory glands and the path of sperm.

subject: Biology
text:
Female Reproductive System

Parts of female reproductive system are as follows:

  • Ovaries: Primary sex organs present in upper pelvic cavity on both lateral sides of uterus. Produces ova and sex hormones progesterone and oesterogen.
  • Fallopian Tube (Oviducts): Extends from ovary to the uterus. Conducts egg and provides site for fertilisation. Tubectomy is the removal of Fallopian tube.
  • Uterus: Situated above and behind the urinary bladder, attached to the body wall by ligaments. Wall is composed of smooth muscle fibres called myometrium. Lumen is lined by a mucous membrane called endometrium. Receives ova or egg; foetus gets attached by placenta.
  • Vagina: Opens to the exterior between the urethra and the anus. Receives semen from penis during mating. Serves as birth canal at the time of baby birth.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing the female reproductive system, labeling the Fallopian tube, Ovary, Endometrium, Uterus, Cervix, and Vagina.

details.summary: Overview of the anatomy and function of the female reproductive system.

subject: Biology
text:
Gametogenesis

  • Process of formation of gametes in gonads. Includes spermatogenesis and oogenesis.
  • Spermatogenesis is the formation of sperms. Oogenesis is the formation of eggs (ovum).
  • Controlled by gonadotropic hormones (FSH, LH, ICSH, etc.) secreted by pituitary gland.

Menstrual Cycle

Cyclic changes in the uterus, extending approximately a month period (mesum). Has three phases:

  • (i) Proliferative Phase: FSH stimulates follicle to secrete oestrogen. Duration of 10-12 days. Also called follicular phase.
  • (ii) Secretory Phase: Corpus luteum secretes progesterone. Duration of 12-14 days. Discharge of ovum from Graafian follicle is known as ovulation, taking place at 14th day.
  • (iii) Menstrual Phase: If ovum is not fertilised, corpus luteum degenerates causing fall in progesterone level. Breakdown of endometrium leads to discharge of blood. Controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone. Suspended during pregnancy and lactation.

Menopause

  • Ovulation and menstrual cycle are stopped permanently.
  • Occurs around 45-50 years of age.
  • Women lose the ability to reproduce.

Important Facts

  • Sex of a newborn baby is determined by the chromosome inherited from father's sperm (XY) while mother has only XX-chromosomes.
  • Amniocentesis: Technique to detect chromosomal abnormalities in the developing foetus by analysing cells in the amniotic fluid.
  • Population explosion: Enormous increase in population in a short span of time.
  • Test tube baby: A baby born from the ovum fertilised in vitro and then implanted in the woman's uterus.

details.summary: Detailed explanation of gametogenesis, the menstrual cycle phases, menopause, and related reproductive health concepts.

subject: Biology
text:
Accessory Sex Glands

  • (i) Bartholin's Gland (Vestibular Gland): Occurs in female mammals and helps in vestibular lubrication. Corresponds to bulbourethral gland (Cowper's gland) of the male.
  • (ii) Mammary Glands: Modified sweat glands. Production of milk is stimulated by the hormone prolactin (secreted by anterior pituitary), while ejection of milk into ducts is stimulated by the hormone oxytocin (secreted by posterior pituitary).

details.summary: Description of female accessory sex glands and their hormonal regulation.

subject: Biology
text:
The neural system is a control system, which coordinates with the endocrine system to coordinate various body parts, thus maintaining physiology. It gives the ability to think and understand. The nervous system receives and conducts stimuli to show a specific response against that stimuli, mainly with the help of neurons.

  • Neurons are structural and functional units of the nervous system.
  • Functional classification of neurons:
    • Sensory (receptor/afferent): Connect sense organs with CNS.
    • Motor (effector/efferent): Connects CNS to effectors like muscles and glands.
    • Interneurons/connector/relaying/adjuster: Occurs between sensory and motor neurons for distant transmission of impulses.
  • Classification by number of nerve processes:
    • Unipolar: Only axon with no dendron (e.g., early embryo).
    • Bipolar: 1 dendrite and 1 axon (e.g., olfactory epithelium and retina).
    • Multipolar: 1 axon and multiple dendrites (e.g., brain and spinal cord).
    • Pseudounipolar: Appear as unipolar (e.g., dorsal root ganglion of spinal cord).
  • Synapse: A gap between two neurons. It helps in the transmission of nerve impulses from one neuron to another. The membranes of pre and postsynaptic neurons are separated by a synaptic cleft.
  • The human nervous system is divided into three parts: central nervous system, peripheral nervous system, and autonomic nervous system.
image_descriptions: A hierarchical flowchart showing the structure of the Brain. The Brain is divided into three main parts: Forebrain, Midbrain, and Hindbrain. The Forebrain branches into Cerebrum and Diencephalon (which further branches into Thalamus and Hypothalamus). The Midbrain includes Corpora quadrigemina and Cerebral peduncle. The Hindbrain includes Cerebellum and Medulla oblongata.

details.summary: Overview of the nervous system, classification of neurons by function and structure, definition of synapse, and hierarchical structure of the human brain.

subject: Biology
text:
CNS is the part of the nervous system that controls the whole body. It consists of the brain and spinal cord.

Brain

It is the anterior portion of the CNS, lodged in the cranial cavity (cranium of the skull). It weighs from 1220 to 1400 grams and consists of three membranes (meninges):

  • Piamater membrane: Innermost, thin, very delicate, vascular, and inverts the brain closely.
  • Arachnoid membrane: Outer to piamater, thin, spider webby structure.
  • Duramater membrane: Outermost, tough fibrous membrane, adhering closely to the inside of the skull.

details.summary: Details on the Central Nervous System, specifically the brain's location, weight, and the three protective meninges layers.

subject: Biology
topic: Parts of the Brain (Forebrain, Midbrain, Hindbrain)
text:
(a) Forebrain

  • It is the largest part of brain.
  • It occupies 2/3 portion of brain.
  • It is the main thinking part of brain.
  • It consists of two parts, i.e. cerebrum and diencephalon.
  • Cerebrum is the most developed part in human. It is divided into right and left cerebral hemispheres connected by corpus callosum.
  • Cerebrum consists of many fold having small grooves (sulci), large grooves (fissures) and bulges between two (gyri).
  • Diencephalon is consists of three parts, i.e. thalamus, hypothalamus and epithalamus.
  • Thalamus controls emotions and memory.
  • Hypothalamus control visceral activities. It helps to maintain homeostasis, control thirst, hunger, temperature, respiration, heartbeat.

(b) Midbrain

  • It is made of two parts, i.e. cerebral peduncle and corpora quadrigema (corpora quadrigemina). It lies between the hindbrain and forebrain.
  • It consists of group of fibres that arouses the forebrain when something unusual happens.
  • Midbrain is responsible for vision and hearing.

(c) Hindbrain

  • It consists of the medulla, cerebellum and pons.
  • The medulla is the swelling at the tip of the brain that serves as the passage way for nerves extending to and from the brain.
  • The pons is the swelling between the medulla and midbrain. The pons acts as a bridge between various portions of the brain.
  • Hind brain is responsible for muscular activities, breathing, coughing, etc.
image_descriptions: A sagittal section anatomical line diagram of the Human Brain enclosed within the Cranium (skull). Key labeled regions include: Forebrain (comprising the deeply folded Cerebrum and the centrally located Hypothalamus and Pituitary gland), Midbrain positioned centrally, Hindbrain (consisting of the Pons, Medulla, and Cerebellum located postero-inferiorly), and the continuation into the Spinal cord extending downward.

details.summary: Covers the anatomical divisions of the human brain: Forebrain (cerebrum, diencephalon), Midbrain (cerebral peduncles, corpora quadrigemina), and Hindbrain (medulla, cerebellum, pons), along with their key structural and physiological functions.

mcq.question: Which part of the human brain is primarily responsible for maintaining homeostasis, controlling thirst, hunger, and body temperature?
mcq.explanation: Hypothalamus controls visceral activities and helps maintain homeostasis, regulating thirst, hunger, body temperature, respiration, and heartbeat.

subject: Biology
text:
(ii) Spinal Cord

  • It extends from the base of the brain and is continuous to the second lumbar vertebra. In adults, the spinal cord ranges from 42 to 45 cm in length.
  • It mainly lies in the neural canal of the vertebral column.
  • It is basically the posterior part of CNS, which runs mid-dorsally within the vertebral column. The three meninges, i.e. duramater, arachnoid, and piamater, which covers the brain, also continue over the spinal cord.
  • The two indentations, i.e. posterior median sulcus and the anterior median fissure (tissues), separate the spinal cord into left and right halves.
  • The inner area is the grey matter, while outside to it are white columns called the white matter.

Functions of Spinal Cord:

  • (i) The stimuli pass from and to the brain through the spinal cord.
  • (ii) It also acts as the centre of spinal reflex action.

details.summary: Detailed structural features of the spinal cord (dimensions: 42-45 cm, extension to L2 vertebra, three meningeal coverings, inner grey and outer white matter distribution) and its dual functional role in signal transmission and reflex control.

mcq.question: In the human spinal cord, the spatial organization of matter is arranged such that:
options: Grey matter lies on the outside and white matter on the inside
Grey matter lies on the inside and white matter on the outside
Only grey matter is present throughout
Only white matter is present throughout
mcq.explanation: In the spinal cord, the inner core is composed of grey matter, while the outer surrounding columns are made of white matter.

subject: Biology
topic: Peripheral Nervous System, Autonomic Nervous System, and Reflex Action
text:
2. Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

  • The nerves that originate from central nervous system connect either with receptor or effector organs from peripheral neural system.
  • Nerves which arise from the brain are called cranial nerves, while the nerves originating from the spinal cord are termed as spinal nerves.
  • It relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles. In the human body, there are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

3. Autonomic Nervous System (ANS)

  • It transmits impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles of the body. This system was discovered by Langly in 1921.
  • It is further divided into two types:
    • (i) Sympathetic Nervous System: Accelerates heartbeat, enlarges pupils, supplies blood to muscles, contracts nerves of urinary bladder, lowers intestinal digestion activities, helps in blood clotting, increases secretion of sweat glands, makes breathing easier, promotes liver to release sugar, and decreases bile production.
    • (ii) Parasympathetic Nervous System: Works just analogous (antagonistic) to the sympathetic nervous system, i.e. slows down heartbeat, dilates arteries and lowers blood pressure, speeds up peristalsis, stimulates salivary gland secretion, contracts gall bladder, promotes pancreas for secretion, decreases secretion of sweat glands, etc.

Reflex Action

  • A reflex action is an automatic response to a stimulus.
  • The pathway taken by nerve impulses in a reflex action is called the reflex arc.
  • Reflex actions are under the control of the spinal cord (CNS).
  • Reflex actions were discovered by Marshall Hall.

details.summary: Describes the PNS (12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves), ANS (sympathetic vs. parasympathetic antagonistic functions, discovered by Langley in 1921), and the physiology and discovery of reflex action by Marshall Hall.

mcq.question: How many pairs of cranial and spinal nerves are present in the human peripheral nervous system?
options: 10 pairs of cranial nerves and 30 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
31 pairs of cranial nerves and 12 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 33 pairs of spinal nerves
mcq.explanation: In the human body, there are 12 pairs of cranial nerves originating from the brain and 31 pairs of spinal nerves originating from the spinal cord.

subject: Biology
text:
Reflex actions are rapid, involuntary responses to stimuli.

  • Examples: Moving foot away from sharp objects, pulling hand away from hot plates, knee-jerk, diaphragm movement during respiration, coughing, yawning.
  • Types:
    • (i) Uncondition reflex action: Rapid actions not controlled by the brain (e.g., tears, knee-jerk).
    • (ii) Conditioned reflex action: Actions learnt through continuous practice and experience (e.g., dancing, cycling, swimming). These are under cerebral control.

details.summary: Overview of reflex actions and their classification into unconditioned and conditioned types.

subject: Biology
text:
Eyes are sense organs for vision that convert light energy into nerve impulses.

  • Structure: Located in the bony cavity called the orbit. The eyeball is a hollow spherical organ with three layers: sclera, choroid, and retina.
  • Sclera: Outer layer of white fibrous tissue. Cornea is covered by a transparent membrane called conjunctiva.
  • Choroid: Middle layer containing blood vessels; forms the ciliary body which holds the lens via ligaments.
  • Retina: Innermost light-sensitive layer containing rod cells (rhodopsin, sensitive to dim light/UV) and cone cells (iodopsin, sensitive to bright light/colour).
  • Fluids: Aqueous humour fills the space between lens and cornea; vitreous humour fills the space between lens and retina.
  • Vision Defects:
    • Colour blindness (Daltonism): Deficiency of cones.
    • Presbyopia: Age-related defect due to weakened ciliary muscles.
    • Myopia (short-sightedness): Image formed in front of retina; corrected by concave lens.
    • Hypermetropia (long-sightedness): Image formed behind retina; corrected by convex lens.
image_descriptions: Diagram of the internal structure of the eye showing the crystalline lens, ciliary muscles, sclera, choroid, retina, blind spot, optic nerve, vitreous chamber, aqueous humour, pupil, iris, and cornea.

details.summary: Detailed anatomy of the human eye, including layers, fluids, and common vision defects.

subject: Biology
text:
The human ear detects sound in the 60-80 decibel range and consists of three parts:

  • External Ear: Includes pinna and external auditory canal; collects and directs soundwaves.
  • Middle Ear: Contains three small bones (ossicles): malleus (hammer-shaped), incus (anvil-shaped), and stapes (stirrup-like).
  • Internal Ear: Consists of a bony labyrinth and membranous labyrinth. Includes the vestibule and a coiled tube called the cochlea filled with perilymph.
image_descriptions: Diagram of the human ear structure showing the pinna, temporal bone, malleus, incus, stapes, oval window, cochlear nerve, cochlea, eustachian tube, tympanic membrane, and external auditory canal.

details.summary: Anatomy of the human ear, detailing the external, middle, and internal structures.

subject: Biology
text:
The tongue is the organ for taste sensation.

  • Contains chemoreceptors known as taste buds.
  • Humans possess approximately 10,000 taste buds.
  • Sensitivity: The anterior part is most sensitive to sweet taste; back and sides are sensitive to salty and sour.
  • Chilli sensation: The taste of chillies is a sensation of burning, caused by pain receptors on the tongue.

details.summary: Function and sensory distribution of the human tongue.

subject: Biology
text:
Nose: Receptors for smell occur in a modified form of pseudostratified epithelium covering a part of the nasal mucosa, called olfactory epithelium. Olfactory receptors function as chemoreceptors, stimulated by specific chemical substances to produce impulses of smell.

Endocrine System: Works in coordination with the nervous system. It is a system of glands that pour secretions (hormones) directly into venous blood or lymph to control functioning, metabolism, growth, and stress conditions. Endocrinology is the branch of Biology dealing with the study of endocrine glands, hormones, and their effects. Thomas Addison (1793-1863) is the Father of Endocrinology.

details.summary: Introduction to the olfactory system and the definition/history of the endocrine system.

subject: Biology
text:
Hormones: Active messenger (organic) compounds secreted by endocrine cells, circulating in blood. The term was first used by Hippocrates. In 1903, Baylis and Starling extracted the first hormone from duodenal mucosa, named secretin. Hormones are not found in food; they are synthesised in the body by endocrine cells.

Types: (i) Protein hormones (e.g., parathyroid, pituitary, hypothalamus, pancreas), (ii) Steroid hormones (e.g., adrenal cortex, gonads), (iii) Amino acid derivatives (e.g., adrenal medulla, thyroid).

Hormones Vs Enzymes: Enzymes are biological catalysts. Both are synthesised in cells, required in small amounts, and involved in cellular metabolism. Dissimilarities: Hormones are synthesised only in endocrine cells; enzymes in all cells. Hormones do not function outside cells; enzymes can.

details.summary: Definition, history, types of hormones, and comparison with enzymes.

subject: Biology
text:
Pineal Gland: Known as the biological clock, located on the roof of the diencephalon in the brain. It starts degenerating in children at age 7. It secretes melatonin, serotonin, and adrenoglomerulotropin. Melatonin affects melanophores.

Pituitary Gland: Pea-shaped, located at the base of the brain. Known as the master endocrine gland/chief executive gland. Two parts: (i) Adenohypophysis (anterior/intermediate lobes), (ii) Neurohypophysis (posterior lobe).
tables:
| Part | Hormone | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Adenohypophysis (interior lobe) | Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) | Promotes release of glucocorticoid and androgens from adrenal cortex. |
| Adenohypophysis (interior lobe) | Follicle-stimulating hormone | Stimulates follicle maturation and production of estrogen. |
| Adenohypophysis (interior lobe) | Luteinising hormone | Triggers ovulation and production of estrogen and progesterone in female and secretion of androgens in males. |
| Adenohypophysis (interior lobe) | Growth hormone (somatotropic hormone) | Stimulates body growth, protein, fat and carbohydrate metabolism. |
| Adenohypophysis (interior lobe) | Prolactin | Over secretion-Gigantism (in childhood), Acromegaly (in Adults) and under secretion (cause dwarfism). Regulates growth of mammary glands and formation of milk in them. |
image_descriptions: Anatomical diagram showing the location of endocrine glands in the human body: Hypothalamus, Pineal gland, Pituitary gland, Thyroid and Parathyroid glands, Thymus gland, Pancreas, Adrenal gland, Ovaries (in female), and Testes (in male).

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of Pineal and Pituitary glands including functions and hormonal secretions.

subject: Biology
text:
The pituitary gland contains an intermediate lobe and a neurohypophysis (posterior lobe).

  • Intermediate lobe: Secretes Melanocyte stimulating hormone which acts on melanocytes and regulates pigmentation of the skin.
  • Neurohypophysis (posterior lobe): Secretes Oxytocin (initiates labour and milk ejection) and Vasopressin or Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) (stimulates water reabsorption by kidneys; deficiency causes diabetes insipidus).
tables:
| Part | Hormone | Function |
|---|---|---|
| - | Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) | Stimulate the synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones. |
| Intermediate lobe | Melanocyte stimulating hormone | Acts on melanocytes and regulates pigmentation of the skin. |
| - | Oxytocin | Initiates labour and milk ejection. |
| Neurohypophysis (posterior lobe) | Vasopressin or Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) | Stimulates water reabsorption by kidneys. Deficiency causes diabetes insipidus. |

details.summary: Overview of pituitary gland hormones and their functions.

subject: Biology
text: The hypothalamus secretes both releasing and inhibitory hormones controlling the secretion of some anterior pituitary hormones. Appetite, thirst and satiety-centres are located in hypothalamus.

details.summary: Functions of the hypothalamus in hormone regulation and physiological control.

subject: Biology
text:
• It is the largest endocrine gland located in the larynx region of neck. It is bilobed in mammals and birds.
  • It secretes thyroxine (T4), tri ido thyronine (T3) and calcitonin.
  • T3 and T4 increase metabolism, blood pressure and regulate tissue growth.
  • Calcitonin regulates calcium levels during childhood.
  • Thyroid disorders are more frequent in female than males.
  • Hyposecretion in children leads to cretinism and in adults myxoedema (sluggish appearance, feeble mindedness, low body temperature).
  • In insufficient quantity of iodine in diet (which is required for the synthesis of thyroxine) is the cause of simple goitre (swelling in the neck).
  • Table salt is often iodised for certain area to prevent goitre.
  • Excess of thyroxine (hyperthyroidism) leads to increased metabolic activity (highly nervous, overactive and irritated person). Sometimes it leads to exophthalmic goitre or Grave's disease (bulging eyeballs, irregular heartbeat and loss of weight).
  • The deficiency of calcitonin results in osteoporosis or loss of bone density.
  • Due to age factor or autoimmune disease in thyroid gland, secretion of thyroid reduces, which results in Hashimoto disease.

details.summary: Detailed overview of the thyroid gland, its hormones, and associated disorders.

subject: Biology
text:
• Parathyroid hormone maintains Ca2+ level in blood.
  • It lowers the serum phosphate.
  • It decreases the excretion of calcium.
  • On hyposecretion Ca2+ become less in blood plasma and so muscle contraction decreases and sometimes may stop and may result tetany (parathormone deficiency disease).
  • Hypersecretion leads to ostioporosis and weaken bones.

details.summary: Functions and clinical implications of parathyroid hormone.

subject: Biology
text:
• It is an endocrine gland nearest to the heart.
  • It is partially endocrine and partially lymphoid gland.
  • It produces thymine hormone.
  • It helps in the formation of antibodies in embryo and infants.
  • Absence of thymus in embryo brings about lack of lymphocytes, lymph nodes and antibodies.
  • T-cells or T-lymphocytes are produced in thymus.
  • It is responsible for immunity.

details.summary: Role of the thymus in immunity and lymphocyte production.

subject: Biology
text:
Adrenal (Supra Renal) or Emergency Gland is situated at the top of the kidney.

  • It is also known as 3F gland, i.e., Fear, Fight, Flight.
  • It is also called 4S gland, i.e., Source of energy, Sex hormone, Salt retaining, Sugar metabolism.
  • It has two parts: (i) Cortex (ii) Medulla.
tables:
| Gland | Hormone | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Adrenal cortex | Glucocorticoids (cortisol) | Long-term stress response. Increased blood glucose levels, blood volume maintenance, immune suppression. Oversecretion-Cushing's syndrome. |
| - | Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) | Long-term stress response; blood volume and pressure maintenance, sodium and water retention by kidneys. Excess secretion-Aldosteronism, less secretion-Addison's disease. |
| - | Sexocorticoids (androgen) | Acts as a precursor of both testosterone and estrogens (sex hormones). Excess section in female-Adrenal virilism. (male like character in females). |
| Adrenal medulla (emergency hormones) | Adrenaline (epinephrine), Nor-adrenaline (nor-epinephrine) | Short-term stress response; Increased blood sugar levels, vasoconstriction, increased heart rate and blood diversion. Short-term stress response; increased blood sugar levels, blood volume maintenance and immune suppression. |
image_descriptions: Diagram showing the Adrenal gland at the top of the kidney with labels for 3F (Fear, Fight, Flight) and 4S (Source of energy, Sex hormone, Salt retaining, Sugar metabolism).

details.summary: Structure and function of the adrenal gland, including cortex and medulla hormones.

subject: Biology
text:
• Exocrine as well as endocrine gland.
  • Endocrine part constitutes 2-3% and represented by 'islets of Langerhans'. The islets have five types of endocrine cells secreting different hormones are:
  • (i) α-cells → Glucagon (a hyperglycaemic hormone)
  • (ii) β-cells → Insulin (a hypoglycaemic hormone)
  • (iii) γ-cells → Gastrin
  • (iv) δ-cells → Somatostatin
  • (v) F-cells → Pancreatic polypeptide

details.summary: Endocrine functions of the pancreas and the types of cells in the islets of Langerhans.

subject: Biology
text:
• Insulin: An anabolic hormone that controls blood sugar levels. Hyposecretion leads to diabetes mellitus.
  • Glucagon: Increases blood sugar level.
  • Somatostatin: Controls the functioning of alpha and beta cells.
  • Kidney: Produces erythropoietin (regulates erythropoiesis/haemopoiesis in bone marrow), influences ultrafiltration in nephron, and produces renin (controls aldosterone secretion via renin-angiotensin pathway).
  • Liver: Largest gland in humans. Produces angiotensinogen (changes to angiotensin in presence of renin) and controls blood pressure.
  • Gonads: Reproductive organs (ova and sperm formation). Function as endocrine glands secreting sex hormones.
  • Testes: Produce male hormones (androgens). Testosterone (secreted by Leydig cells) is responsible for deep voice, enlargement of genital organs, and beard growth. Surgical removal is called castration or orchidectomy. At puberty, FSH and ICSH from the pituitary stimulate testosterone production.
  • Ovary: Produces female hormones (oestrogen). Oestrogen is responsible for thin voice and development of reproductive organs. It controls the menstrual cycle. Corpus luteum is a temporary endocrine gland that produces progesterone, maintains pregnancy, and helps in embryo implantation.

IMPORTANT POINTS:

  • Contraceptive pills contain oestrogens and progesterone.
  • Corpus luteum secretes relaxin hormone during parturition.
  • Placenta releases HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) during pregnancy; its presence in urine indicates pregnancy.

details.summary: Overview of endocrine functions of various organs including pancreas, kidney, liver, and gonads.

subject: Biology
text:
Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. It is the functional or metabolic efficiency of a living being. Some basic factors such as balanced diet, personal hygiene and regular exercise contributes to good health. Apart from these, awareness about diseases and immunisation, etc., also affects health.

Diseases is a condition of disturbed or damaged functioning of the body due to infection, defective diet, heredity and environment. The causes of disease in humans can be pathogens, genetical, etc.

Communicable Diseases are infectious, i.e. they spread from affected individual to normal individual. These are caused by pathogens such as bacteria, virus, Protozoa and fungi. These pathogens can spread the disease by means of air, water, vectors or sexual contact.
image_descriptions: A flowchart showing the classification of diseases: Disease branches into Communicable diseases, Non-communicable diseases (e.g. cancer), and Genetic disorders (e.g. Haemophillia). Communicable diseases further branch into Bacterial diseases, Viral diseases, Protozoan diseases, and Fungal diseases.

details.summary: Overview of health, definition of diseases, and classification of communicable diseases.

subject: Biology
text:
Bacterial Diseases are caused by bacteria. Some of them are as follows:

  • 1. Tuberculosis (TB)
    • It is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (gram positive).
    • It spreads through coughing, sneezing, talking and splitting droplets. Symptoms of this disease are fever, cough, sputum with blood, chest pain, loss of appetite, weight loss.
    • It can be prevented by immunisation that includes BCG (Bacillus Calmette Guerin) vaccine, isolation of patient, sanitation, etc.
    • Antibiotics such as rifampicin, isoniazid, etc.
  • 2. Diphtheria
    • It is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae (gram positive).
    • Infection occurs through droplets.
    • It is characterised by slight fever, oozing of semisolid material in throat (sore throat).
    • Immunisation is done with DPT vaccine.
  • 3. Pertussis/Whooping Cough
    • It is caused by Bacillus pertussis or Bordetella pertussis (gram negative).
    • Infection occurs through direct contact and droplets, characterised by inflamation of respiratory passage, cold, cough and mild fever in beginning leading to accumulation of mucus and inspiratory whoop.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of Tuberculosis, Diphtheria, and Pertussis including causative agents, transmission, symptoms, and prevention.

subject: Biology
text:
• Tetanus / Lock Jaw Disease (Dhanustamba): Caused by Clostridium tetani (rod-shaped, gram positive). Infection occurs through spores of bacteria entering into body via wounds, accidents and unsterilised surgical instruments as this bacterium secretes tetanospasmin toxin. Characterised by muscular rigidity (lock jaw) and painful muscular spasm. Injection of ATS (Anti Tetanus Serum) within 24 hours of injury leads to protection.
  • Cholera: Caused by Vibrio cholerae. Spreads through contaminated food and water or by direct contact. Characterised by effortless watery stool, vomiting, rapid dehydration, muscular cramps. Treated by use of ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) and sanitation. ORS contains (1L) 1.5 g glucose, 3.5 g NaCl, 2.9 g KCl and 12.9 g trisodium citrate.
  • Diarrhoea: Caused by Salmonella typhimurium (salmonellosis) and Shigella shigae (shigellosis). Spreads through contaminated meat and other proteinaceous food articles and transmitted through fingers, beds, clothes and utensils and most importantly by faeces. Symptoms include vomiting, nausea, headache, paratyphoid fever and frequent passage of stool with mucus, blood and abdominal cramps. Oral and intravenous rehydration is required for treatment.
  • Pneumonia: Caused by Diplococcus pneumoniae or Streptococcus pneumoniae (gram positive). Transmits through droplets (sputum). Symptoms are sudden chill, chest pain, cough with rusty mucoid sputum and rise in temperature. Treated by uses of drugs like erythromycin, tetracycline and penicillin.
  • Syphilis: Caused by Treponema pallidum (a spirochaete). Transmits through sexual contact and from mother to children. Common symptoms are painless ulcer on the genitals and swelling of local lymph glands, rashes, hair loss, swollen joints and flu-like illness. Disease is curable through appropriate antibiotics, e.g. penicillin and tetracycline.
  • Gonorrhoea: Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Diplococcus gonorrhoeae. Transmits through sexual contact, common toilets and under clothes. Bacterium lives in genital tubes, produces pus containing discharge, pain around genitalia and burning sensation during urination. Use of antibiotics, e.g. penicillin, ampicillin and maintain high moral characters. It is Venereal Disease (VD) or Sexually Transmitted Disease (STD).
  • Plague/Bubonic Plague (Black Death): This disease is caused by Yersinia pestis or Pasturella pestis. It spreads through rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis) to man. Symptoms are armpit and groin swell up into painful buboes, high-fever, chill, exhaustion and haemorrhages, which turns black. Treatment with antiplague vaccine, spraying of pesticides for killing of rats. Wayson stain test is performed for diagnosis.
  • Typhoid: Caused by Salmonella typhi. Spreads through food, milk and water contaminated with intestinal discharge either directly or through houseflies. High fever in steps, lesions and ulceration in the intestinal wall are common symptoms. Use of antibiotics (ampicillin and chloramphenicol), prolonged treatment is required. Widal test is performed for diagnosis.
  • Leprosy (Hansen’s Disease): Caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It does not spread by initial contact, but prolonged closer contact through skin lesions, nasal and throat discharges also spreads this disease. Sanitation and use of suitable drugs like dapsone, rifampicin, ofloxacin and chaulmoogra oil along with surgery may protect from the disease. Bacterium can enter into the body and damage nerves, skin, lymph nodes, eyes, nose, mouth, larynx, muscles, spleen, etc. Appearance of skin patches, numbness in some body parts, fever, finally ulcer, nodules, lesions, scaly scabs, deformities in finger, toes and wasting of body parts are symptoms.
  • Botulism: Caused by Clostridium botulinum. Symptoms are double vision, blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, difficulty in swallowing, dry mouth and muscle weakness. It spreads through contaminated food and water or food stuffs product. To remove the source of toxin producing bacteria, the administration of proper antibiotics are used.

details.summary: Overview of various bacterial diseases, their causative agents, transmission methods, symptoms, and treatments.

subject: Biology
text:
Measles (Khasra) is a contagious viral disease.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by Rubeola virus / Polynosa morbillorum.
  • Transmission: Transmitted by direct contact, fomites, or droplet methods.
  • Path of Entry: The virus enters through the respiratory tract and conjunctiva.
  • Symptoms: Characterised by itching, skin rash, and small raised red spots arranged in crescent-shaped groups starting from the back of the ears and reaching the forehead, face, and then spreading over the entire body.
  • Treatment and Prevention: Antibiotics and Vitamin-A are administered to prevent complications. Vaccination with the MMR (Mumps, Measles, Rubella) vaccine is given at the age of one year.

details.summary: Measles is caused by Rubeola virus/Polynosa morbillorum, entering via the respiratory tract and conjunctiva, characterized by crescent-shaped rashes starting behind the ears, and prevented using the MMR vaccine and Vitamin-A.

mcq.question: Which vaccine is administered at the age of one to prevent Measles?
mcq.explanation: MMR (Mumps, Measles, Rubella) vaccine is given at the age of one to provide immunity against Measles.

subject: Biology
text:
Mumps is an acute viral infection that primarily affects the salivary glands.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by Paramyxo virus or Mumps virus.
  • Transmission: Transmitted through direct contact and airborne droplets.
  • Symptoms: The patient experiences difficulty in swallowing and opening the mouth, high fever, chills, headache, general body aches, and loss of appetite.
  • Treatment and Prevention: Treated and prevented by vaccination with MMR (Mumps, Measles, Rubella).

details.summary: Mumps is caused by Paramyxovirus, transmitted via droplets/contact, causes difficulty in swallowing and opening the mouth, and is prevented by the MMR vaccine.

mcq.question: Mumps is caused by which of the following pathogens?
mcq.explanation: Mumps is caused by Paramyxo virus (or Mumps virus).

subject: Biology
text:
Smallpox (Chechuk) is a severe infectious viral disease.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by Variola virus.
  • Susceptibility: Common but less severe in children up to 10 years of age; severe, but rare, in adults.
  • Transmission: Spreads through oral and nasal secretions, vesicular discharges, pustules, and scabs.
  • Symptoms: Begins as reddish spots which progress into papules, then pustules, and finally form scabs. Spots appear first on the hairline, then on the face, followed by the rest of the body, with fewer spots appearing on the trunk. On falling off, these spots leave permanent marks (pockmarks).
  • History/Vaccine: The vaccine for smallpox was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796.

details.summary: Smallpox is caused by the Variola virus, spreads via secretions/pustules, leaves permanent marks on falling off, and had its vaccine discovered by Edward Jenner in 1796.

mcq.question: Who developed the vaccine for Smallpox in the year 1796?
mcq.explanation: Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796.

subject: Biology
text:
Chickenpox is a highly contagious viral illness.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by Varicella zoster.
  • Incubation Period: 14 to 16 days.
  • Seasonality: Occurs predominantly during winter and spring.
  • Symptoms: Characterised by prodromal rashes with crops of pinkish centripetal spots appearing first on the trunk, forehead, and face. Uneasiness, aches, and high fever accompany each new crop of lesions. Spots develop into fluid-filled vesicles and eventually scabs.
  • Key Feature: Scabs fall off without leaving any permanent mark.
  • Treatment: No specific antiviral drugs or vaccines are mentioned here; the application of boric acid and calamine lotion helps reduce itching.

details.summary: Chickenpox is caused by Varicella zoster with a 14-16 day incubation period, characterized by centripetal rashes on the trunk, face, and forehead that leave no permanent marks upon scab shedding.

mcq.question: Which of the following is the causative agent of Chickenpox?
mcq.explanation: Chickenpox is caused by the virus Varicella zoster.

subject: Biology
text:
Poliomyelitis (Infantile Paralysis) is a crippling viral disease.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by Polio virus or Entero virus.
  • Susceptibility: Highly infectious disease affecting infants and young children.
  • Transmission: Transmitted via faeces, urine, and nasal secretions contaminating food, water, and drinks directly or mechanically through flies; incubation period ranges from 5 to 17 days.
  • Pathology & Symptoms: Produces inflammation of the nervous system causing an inability to bend the head forward. Paralysis ensues following the weakness of specific skeletal muscles.
  • Prevention & Vaccination: Polio is a preventable disease. Salk's vaccine (injected) and later Sabin's oral vaccine (OPV) are administered at the ages of 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks, with a booster dose at 18–24 months.
  • Key Institution: The Hoffkine Institute in Mumbai is well known for the production of the polio vaccine.

details.summary: Polio is caused by Enterovirus/Poliovirus, transmitted through contaminated food/water (fecal-oral route), affects the nervous system causing skeletal paralysis, and is prevented by Salk and Sabin vaccines.

mcq.question: Which institute in Mumbai is known for the production of the polio vaccine according to Pathfinder?
mcq.explanation: The Hoffkine Institute of Mumbai is renowned for the production of the polio vaccine.

subject: Biology
text:
Influenza (Flu) is an acute respiratory infection.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by Haemophilus influenzae or Myxovirus influenzae.
  • Transmission: Spreads through inhalation of contaminated air into the respiratory tract.
  • Symptoms: Begins with fever, headache, sore throat, cold with sneezing, pain all over the body, and restlessness.
  • Management: No specific vaccine mentioned; controlled through general hygiene and sanitation measures.

details.summary: Influenza is caused by Myxovirus influenzae (or Haemophilus influenzae), transmitted via respiratory droplets/air, presenting with fever, sore throat, sneezing, and body ache.

mcq.question: Which virus is responsible for causing Influenza (Flu)?
mcq.explanation: Influenza is caused by Myxovirus influenzae (or Haemophilus influenzae).

subject: Biology
text:
Rabies (Hydrophobia) is a fatal neurotropic viral disease.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by Rhabdo virus.
  • Transmission: Transmitted to humans through the bite and saliva of rabid animals (mad dog or cat). Jackals, wolves, foxes, mongooses, and bats are also natural reservoirs.
  • Symptoms: Excessive salivation from the mouth, severe headache, high fever, depression, and inability to swallow even fluids due to a choked throat. Hydrophobia (fear of water) is the most characteristic symptom. The virus destroys the brain and spinal cord.
  • Post-Exposure Prophylaxis: The bitten individual must be administered vaccines immediately (earlier 14 inoculations were given; currently 6 doses are recommended).
  • Surveillance: The biting dog should be observed for 10 days for signs of rabies (running amuck, changes in vocalisation/bark, and excessive salivation).

details.summary: Rabies is a lethal viral encephalitis caused by Rhabdovirus, transmitted by the bite of rabid animals, featuring hydrophobia and throat choking, and treated with post-exposure vaccination.

mcq.question: What is the most characteristic symptom of Rabies?
mcq.explanation: Hydrophobia (fear of water) due to severe throat spasms and inability to swallow is the hallmark symptom of rabies.

subject: Biology
text:
Dengue Fever (Breakbone Fever) is an arboviral infection.

  • Causative Agent: Caused by the DEN-1–4 virus.
  • Vector: Transmitted by the bite of the female Tiger mosquito (Aedes aegypti).
  • Symptoms: Headache, fever, chills, severe pain in joints, and skin rashes. The disease manifests more severely in adults.
  • Clinical Marker: Blood platelet count drops critically below 70,000/mm³.
  • Management: Paracetamol administration accompanied by replenishment of blood platelets.

details.summary: Dengue fever is caused by the DEN-1-4 virus and transmitted by the female Aedes aegypti mosquito, leading to high fever, severe joint pain, and a dangerous drop in platelet count below 70,000/mm³.

mcq.question: Which mosquito acts as the vector for Dengue Fever?
mcq.explanation: Dengue virus (DEN-1-4) is transmitted by the female Tiger mosquito, Aedes aegypti.

subject: Biology
text:
Hepatitis is a viral disorder of the liver.

  • Common Name: Commonly known as jaundice.
  • Pathology: Jaundice results from the incomplete or defective metabolism of bilirubin, a bile pigment derived from broken-down/worn-out red blood cells (RBCs).
  • Transmission: The infection is primarily spread through the faecal-oral route and ingestion of contaminated/polluted water.

details.summary: Hepatitis (commonly known as jaundice) results from the incomplete metabolism of bilirubin pigment from worn-out RBCs and spreads via contaminated water and the faecal-oral route.

mcq.question: Jaundice is the clinical result of the incomplete metabolism of which pigment?
mcq.explanation: Jaundice is caused by the incomplete metabolism and accumulation of bilirubin pigment from worn-out red blood cells.

subject: Biology
text:
• 10. AIDS
    • Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is a disease of human immune system.
    • It is caused by Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
    • HIV is a lentivirus of the retrovirus family.
    • HIV can spread by: (i) Sexual contact (oral, vaginal, anal), (ii) Blood transfusions (accidental needle sticks/sharing), (iii) Mother to child (pregnancy/breast milk).
    • Symptoms: loss of weight, prolonged fever, chronic diarrhoea, red or brown blotches on skin of nose, mouth, throat, fatigue.
    • In children < 12 years, persistent cough is not a clinical symptom.
    • Confirmatory tests: ELISA, PCR, RIP/IFA.
    • Treatment: Anti-retroviral drugs (e.g., AZT/Azidothymidine, zidovudine, norvir).
    • AIDS day: 1st December.
  • 11. Yellow Fever
    • Caused by Flavi virus. Transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquito.
    • Symptoms: aching muscles (back/knees), dizziness, loss of appetite, nausea, shivers, vomiting, yellow tinge to skin/whites of eyes.
    • Treatment: No effective antiviral; maintain blood pressure and treat secondary infections. Not prevalent in India.
  • 12. Chikungunya
    • Caused by Alphavirus, spread by Aedes mosquito.
    • Symptoms: fever, joint pain, swelling, rashes.
    • Prevention: Check mosquito populations. Treatment: Paracetamol and anti-inflammatory drugs.
  • 13. Swine Flu
    • Caused by H1N1 virus. Also called hog flu or pig influenza.
    • Higher risk for pork consumers. Symptoms: fever, lethargy, sneezing, coughing, breathing difficulty, decreased appetite.
    • Treatment: Tamiflu and relenza vaccine. No effective cure/vaccine for swine flu.
  • Helminthic Diseases
    • 1. Ascariasis: Caused by Ascaris lumbricoides. Spreads through raw vegetables, dirty hands, contaminated soil. Symptoms: nausea, cough, abdominal pain, intestinal destruction. Prevention: sanitation, antihelminthic drugs.
    • 2. Taeniasis: Caused by Taenia solium. Spreads through improperly cooked food/raw vegetables. Symptoms: chronic indigestion, anorexia, epilepsy-like symptoms. Treatment: sanitation, cooked food, antihelminthic drugs.
    • 3. Filariasis: Caused by Wuchereria bancrofti. Transmitted by Culex sp. mosquito. Symptoms: swollen legs (resembling elephant), called elephantiasis. Prevention: destroy mosquitoes, use repellent creams/mats, antihelminthic drugs.

details.summary: Detailed notes on viral diseases (AIDS, Yellow Fever, Chikungunya, Swine Flu) and helminthic diseases (Ascariasis, Taeniasis, Filariasis) including causative agents, transmission, symptoms, and prevention.

subject: Biology
text:
These diseases are caused by protozoans. Some protozoan diseases are:

  • 1. Malaria:
    • It is caused by Plasmodium species. It affects several body parts like liver (initial multiplication), RBCs, spleen and brain. But it does not affect kidney. It shows multiplication in liver.
    • Plasmodium has two hosts: (i) Female Anopheles mosquito (definitive or primary host), (ii) Human beings (intermediate or secondary host).
    • Plasmodium vivax: (i) It causes benign tertian malaria. (ii) Most common in India.
    • Plasmodium falciparum: (i) It causes cerebral malaria. (ii) Common in certain parts of India.
    • Plasmodium ovale: (i) Rarest species, which infects man.
    • Plasmodium malariae: (i) Common in tropical Africa, Burma, Sri Lanka and parts of India. (ii) Use of mosquito nets, repellent creams and mats, use of chloroquine, primaquine tablets may prevent malaria. (iii) Most effective medicine for malaria is quinine (obtained from cinchona tree).
  • 2. Amoebiasis / Amoebic Dysentry:
    • It is caused by Entamoeba histolytica (an endoparasite).
    • Parasite lives in the large intestine of humans.
    • Infection occurs by ingesting cysts with food and water.
    • The symptoms are mild diarrhoea, presence of mucus and blood in stool and abdominal pain.
    • Proper sanitation and personal hygiene is useful for protection. Antiamoebic drugs are used for protection.
  • 3. Leishmaniasis:
    • It is commonly called as kala-azar.
    • It is caused by Leishmania donovani. It multiplies by multiple fission.
    • Spreads by sandfly (Phlebotomus) bite.
    • The symptoms often resemble malaria with irregular recurrent fever and leukopenia with enlargement of spleen and liver.
  • 4. African Sleeping Sickness (Trypanosomiasis):
    • It is caused by Trypanosoma gambiense.
    • The parasite is transmitted by blood sucking tse-tse fly (Glossina palpalis).
    • Parasite lives in blood plasma.
    • Fever with glandular swelling.
    • In acute condition, parasite enters into cerebrospinal fluid and damage the brain. It makes the patient lethargic and unconscious.
    • Prevention is done by eradicating from flies and shrubs.

details.summary: Overview of common protozoan diseases including Malaria, Amoebiasis, Leishmaniasis, and African Sleeping Sickness, detailing causative agents, transmission, and symptoms.

subject: Biology
text:
• Fungal Diseases:
    • Fungal diseases are also called mycoses. Mycoses are common in human as well as in animals.
    • Ringworm:
      • It is caused by Microsporum.
      • It spreads by unbathed cats, dogs or infected persons.
      • In this disease, sores are formed, which become reddish and contain blisters.
      • Treated by proper sanitation and hygiene.
      • Some other fungal diseases with their causative agents are aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus), meningitis (Cryptococcus neoformans), dermatitis of beard and hair (Trichophyton verrucosum) and athlete's foot (Tinea pedis).
  • NON-COMMUNICABLE DISEASES:
    • There are various kinds of non-communicable diseases, which affect the health of human beings.
    • 1. Diabetes:
      • Diabetes is a long-term condition caused by too much glucose (sugar) in the blood.
      • There are two main types of diabetes: (i) Type 1 diabetes occurs when the body does not produce enough insulin to function properly or the body's cells do not react to insulin. This is known as insulin resistance. (ii) Type 2 diabetes is far more common than type 1 diabetes, which occurs when the body does not produce any insulin at all. Type 2 diabetes usually affects people over the age of 40.
      • Symptoms are feeling very thirsty, urination frequently particularly at night, feeling very tired, weight loss and loss of muscle bulk.

details.summary: Overview of fungal diseases (mycoses) and non-communicable diseases, specifically focusing on Ringworm and Diabetes.

subject: Biology
text:
Cancer is the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in the body.

  • Cancer occurs when normal cells due to uncontrolled mitotic division are converted into tumour cells.
  • The resulting uncontrolled growth forms masses of cells called tumour.
  • Cancerous cells are also called malignant cells.
  • Symptoms of cancer depend on the type and location of the cancer.
  • These are induced by physical, chemical and biological factors or agents. The agents causing cancer are called carcinogens or cancer causing agents.
  • Tobacco smoke contains chemical carcinogens that cause lung cancer.
  • Viruses also cause cancer. These are called oncogenic viruses as they have genes called viral oncogenes.
  • Leukaemia or blood cancer can be detected based on biopsy and histopathological studies of the tissue and blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts.

Cancer therapies:

  1. Cryo surgery
  2. Proton therapy
  3. Radiation therapy
  4. Stem cell transplantation (also involved in spinal injury cure)
  5. Peripheral Blood Stem Cell Transplantation (PBSCT)

details.summary: Overview of cancer definition, causes, detection methods, and therapies.

subject: Biology
text:
A genetic disorder is an illness caused by one or more abnormalities in the genome. These may be of three types:

1. Autosomal Recessive Disorders

  • Albinism: Caused due to inability to produce melanin pigment. Characterised by absence of normal colouration of the skin.
  • Galactosaemia: Due to defect in galactose metabolism. May cause mental retardation.
  • Phenylketonuria: Due to the deficiency of an enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine into tyrosine. Symptoms are mental retardation, typical colour of skin and urine.
  • Alkaptonuria: Metabolic disorder, there is absence of homogentisic acid oxidase, which oxidises homogentisic acid. The urine of such patients darkens on exposure.
  • Sickle-cell Anaemia: Genetic disorder. RBCs of patient become elongated and curved to become sickle-shaped in O2 deficiency. In defective haemoglobin, the glutamin amio acid at 6th place of beta-chain of Hb is replaced by valine.

2. X-Linked Recessive Disorders

  • Haemophilia: Appeared in several interrelated Royal families of Europe, apparently arising from a mutation in one parent of Queen Victoria of England (1819-1901), hence is called 'Royal disease'. In this disorder, blood coagulation does not take place. It is due to deficiency of Factor VIII (antihaemophilic factor).
  • Colour Blindness: Also known as Daltonism. Affected person cannot distinguish between green and red colour. Colourblind persons cannot service in Railway department.

3. Y-Linked Recessive Disorders

  • Hypertrichosis: i.e. excessive hairs on ear pinna is a Y-linked recessive disorder.

details.summary: Classification and description of Autosomal, X-Linked, and Y-Linked recessive genetic disorders.

subject: Biology
text:
The principle of vaccination and immunisation is based upon the 'memory' of immune system.

  • In vaccination a preparation of inactivated or weakened pathogen (vaccine) are introduced into the body. The antibodies are produced against these antigen would neutralise the pathogenic agents during actual infection. The vaccine also generate memory B and T-cells that recognise the pathogens quickly on subsequent exposure and act against them with a massive production of antibodies.
  • Edward Jenner discovered the first vaccine.
  • Pasteur invented the vaccine for rabies.
  • Robert Koch discovered anthrax bacteria.
  • Penicillin was discovered by Sir Alexander Flemming from Penicillium fungus.
