details.summary: Comprehensive overview of the Later Vedic Age (1000 BC–600 BC), covering geographical expansion towards the Gangetic doab, administrative functionaries, emergence of the varna system and gotra, religious shifts to Prajapati/Rudra/Vishnu, and distinct pottery types (PGW and Red Ware).

mcq.question: Which official was designated as the tax collector during the Later Vedic period?
mcq.explanation: In the Later Vedic administrative organization, Bhagdugha functioned as the tax collector, while Sangrahita was the treasurer.

subject: History
text:
The word Veda is derived from Sanskrit word vid, meaning 'to know signifying knowledge par excellence'. The Vedic text are shruti i.e., directly revealed to authors by God.

  • Smritis are remembered and collected parts of literature of later period. They are also called samhitas in the sense that they represent oral tradition of the time.
  • Four Vedas and their samhitas, the Brahmanas, the Aranyakas and the Upanishads form a class of literature known as Shruti.

details.summary: Introduction to Vedic literature, defining Shruti and Smritis.

subject: History
text:
The Rig Veda

  • Divided into 10 books or mandalas. Mandalas II to VII are considered the oldest and known as Family Mandalas. Book I, VIII and X seem to be added later.
  • Dated 1500-1000 BC. Has 1028 hymns written by number of priestly families.
  • The 10th mandala contains the famous Purushasukta hymns that explains the origin of four varnas (Chatur-varna theory).
  • The hymns of Rig Veda were recited by Hotri.

The Yajur Veda

  • Ritualistic Veda. Divided into Shukla Yajur Veda (Poetry) and Krishna Yajur Veda (Prose and Poetry).
  • Written in prose, it deals with procedure for performance of sacrifices, and contains rituals as well as hymns.
  • The hymns of Yajur Veda were recited by Adhvaryu.

The Sama Veda

  • Word sama is derived from the root word saman that means 'melody/music'.
  • Has 1875 verses, but except 75, the rest of the hymns have been borrowed from the Rig Veda. It contains Dhrupada Raga.
  • The hymns of Sama Veda were recited by Udgatri.

The Atharva Veda

  • Chronologically the last of the four Vedas.
  • The Satapatha Brahmana used the term trayi i.e., the Rig Veda, Yajur Veda and Sama Veda.
  • Mentions beliefs and practices of non-Aryans, contains magical mantra etc.
  • The sabha and the samiti are described as sisters and the two daughters of Prajapati.
  • Also known as Brahma Veda.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of the four Vedas: Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva.

subject: History
topic: Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upavedas, Upanishads, and Vedangas
text:
The Brahmanas

  • Prose commentaries on various Vedic hymns explaining hidden meanings behind the hymns of Brahmans.
  • Shatapatha Brahmana is the largest Brahmana book.

The Aranyakas

  • Authors were sages dwelling in the forest. Aranyakas mean belonging to the forest, hence known as Forest Books.
  • They form the concluding part of Brahmanas.

The Upavedas

  • Subsidiary Vedas dealing with secular subjects:
    • Ayur Veda: Medicine
    • Dhanur Veda: Art of warfare
    • Gandharva Veda: Music
    • Shilpa Veda: Art and literature

The Upanishads

  • Indicates knowledge acquired by sitting close to the teacher.
  • Metaphysical topics: origin of universe, nature of God, origin and death of mankind.
  • Followers of Karma (Action), Atma (Soul) and God (Brahma).
  • Spiritual and philosophical in nature.
  • 108 in number (800-500 BC).
  • Satyamev Jayate is extracted from Mundaka Upanishad.

Vedangas (Limbs of Vedas)

  • Treaties on Science and Arts.
  • The six Vedangas are Shiksha (phonetics), Kalpa (rituals), Vyakarna (grammar), Chanda (metrics), Nirukta (etymology) and Jyotisha (astronomy).
  • Yaska's Nirukta (5th century BC) is the oldest linguistic text.

details.summary: Overview of secondary Vedic literature including Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upavedas, Upanishads, and Vedangas.

subject: History
text:
Six systems of Hindu philosophies, given by six philosophers of ancient India:

  • Nyaya (Analysis) – Gautam
  • Vaisheshika (Atomic characteristic) – Kanada
  • Sankhya (Enumeration) – Kapil
  • Yoga (Application) – Patanjali
  • Purva Mimamsa (Enquiry) – Jaimini
  • Uttar Mimamsa (Vedanta) – Vyasa

Smriti:

  • Dharma Shastra is the other name for smritis, which are law books written in sloka form.
  • Manusmriti is the oldest and most famous. Manu is supposed to be the first king and law maker.

Other Literature:

  • Apart from these, 18 Puranas in which Matsya, Vishnu, Varaha, Vamana etc are also main vedic literature.
  • Ramayana and Mahabharata are the epics of this age.

details.summary: Overview of six systems of Hindu philosophy, Smritis, and Vedic literature.

subject: History
text:
Buddhism: Founded by Gautam Buddha (Sakyamuni or Tathagat) known originally as Siddhartha. Buddhism stands on three pillars:

  • Buddha – The enlightened
  • Dhamma – The doctrine
  • Sangha – Order of Buddhist monks and nuns

Buddha's Life:

  • Born in 563 BC in a sal groove of Lumbini garden in Kapilavastu. Mother was Mahamaya (a Kosalan princess).
  • Father was Suddhodana (of Sakya tribe).
  • Name was Siddhartha and gotra was Gautama. Mother died after 7 days of his birth and he was brought up by Mahaprajapati Gautami.
  • Devadutta was his cousin. Buddha's wife was Yashodhara and his son was Rahul. Buddha chariot was Channa and favourite horse was Kanthak.
  • Moved by misery, he left home at age 29; incident known as Mahabhinishkramana - 'great going forth'.
  • First became a disciple of Alara Kalam (specialist of Samakhya philosophy).
  • Left Alara and joined Rudraka, then practised great penance.
  • Conception of religion was purely ethical.
  • Got enlightenment under the pipal tree known as Bodhi tree at Gaya in Bihar. According to Buddha, soul is a myth.
  • Gave first sermon at Sarnath (ancient name Rishipattan). First sermon became famous as Dharma Chakrapravartan (turning of wheel of law).
  • Spent last days near Vaishali. At Pava, a man named Chunda fed him pork, after eating it Buddha died of dysentery at age 80 in 483 BC.
  • Death was known Mahaparinirvana i.e., final blowing out. In the outskirts of Kushinagar is the capital of Mallas. Favourite disciple was Ananda.

Teachings of Buddha:

Four Noble Truths (Arya Satyas):

  • The world is full of sorrows Sabbam Dukkham.
  • The cause of sorrow is desire Dwadash Nidan/Pratitya Samutpada.
  • Cessation of sorrow (Dukkha Nirodha).
  • The path leading to the cessation of sorrow (Dukkha Nirodhagamini Pratipad) is the 8-fold path Ashtangika Marga.

The second truth is based on Buddha's doctrine of Paticheha samutpada or Pratitya samutpada i.e., law of dependent origination or causation.

Eight-fold Path (Ashtangika Marga):

  • i. Right understanding
  • ii. Right thought
  • iii. Right speech
  • iv. Right action
  • v. Right livelihood
  • vi. Right effort
  • vii. Right mindfulness
  • viii. Right concentration

Three Jewels (Triratnas):

  • i. Buddha (the enlightened)
  • ii. Dhamma (doctrine)
  • iii. Sangha (order)

Code of Conduct:

  • i. Do not convert the property of others
  • ii. Do not commit violence
  • iii. Do not use intoxicants
  • iv. Do not tell a lie
  • v. Do not indulge in corrupt practices

Belief in Nirvana: Also known as moksha or salvation, it refers to belief in the concept of ultimate bliss, whereby the person gets freedom from the cycle of birth and death.

Belief in Ahimsa: Law of Karma and Madhya Marga/Madhyama Pratipada (the middle path).

details.summary: Comprehensive biography of Gautam Buddha, his teachings, the Four Noble Truths, Eight-fold Path, and core Buddhist beliefs.

subject: History
text:
Buddhist Councils

  • First Council (483 BC): Held at Sattapanni (Saptaparni) cave near Rajagriha under the chairmanship of Maha Kassapa. Vinaya Pitaka and Sutta Pitaka were compiled by Upali and Ananda respectively. Ajatshatru was the king at that time.
  • Second Council (383 BC): Held at Vaishali during the reign of Kalashoka (Shishunaga dynasty). Chairman was Sabakami. The council led to division into Sthavirvadins and Mahasamghikas.
  • Third Council (250 BC): Held at Pataliputra during the reign of Ashoka (Mauryan ruler). Held under the presidentship of Mogaliputta Tissa to revise Buddhist texts.
  • Fourth Council (AD 72): Held during the reign of Kanishka (Kushana ruler) in Kashmir under the presidentship of Vasumitra and Ashwaghosha. Buddhism was divided into Hinayana and Mahayana.

details.summary: Chronological overview of the four major Buddhist councils.

subject: History
text:
Buddhist Sects

  • During Kaniska time, Buddhist religion clearly got divided between Hinayana and Mahayana buddhism.
  • Hinayana buddhism believes in original philosophy and ideologies of Mahatma Buddha, whereas believers of Mahayana buddhism apart from believing in Buddha also have faith in life and teachings of bodhisattva.
  • Bodhisattva help others in attainment of nirvana. Nagarjuna propounded the main tenets of Mahayana Buddhism.
  • Vajrayana is a form of tantric buddhism that tends to favour fierce deities and significantly expanded the bodhisattva pantheon. It employs mantras, mandalas and other rituals.

Buddhist Literature

In Buddha texts, the most famous is 'Tripitaka', as mentioned below:

  • Vinaya Pitaka: Contains the rules and regulations of monastic discipline for monks. An account of the life and teaching of the Buddha is also given.
  • Sutta Pitaka: Few discourses delivered by many Buddhist scholars like Sariputta, Ananda and others are given in it. It lays down the principles of Buddhism. It is a collection of Buddha's sermon and is divided into five groups.
  • Abhidhamma Pitaka: Having the philosophy of Buddha's teachings, it investigates mind and matter to help the understanding of things as they truly are.

details.summary: Overview of Buddhist sects and the composition of the Tripitaka.

subject: History
text:
Jainism

Jainism is one of the three major religions of early India. Its name derives from the word Jina, meaning 'Liberator or Victor'. There are 24 Tirthankaras. The first Tirthankara was Rishabhadev, 23rd was Parshvanath and 24th was Mahavira.

Mahavir

  • Vardhamana (Mahavira) was the 24th and last Tirthankara. Born in 540 BC at Kundagrama near Vaishali.
  • Father: Siddhartha (head of Kshatriya clan); Mother: Trishala (sister of Lichchhavi Princess Chief Chetaka, whose daughter was wedded to Bimbisara).
  • At age 30, became an ascetic. Attained Kevala Gnana (highest spiritual knowledge) and was called Mahavira and Jina.
  • Attained Kaivalya (perfect knowledge) under a sal tree near village Jimbhikagrama on the bank of river Rijupalika.
  • Preached for 30 years. Died at age 72 at Pavapuri in 486 BC.
  • Sects: After a famine in the Ganges valley during Chandragupta Maurya's reign, the religion divided into Svetambers (white-clad, stayed in North under Sthulabahu) and Digambaras (sky-clad/naked, migrated to South under Bhadrabahu).
  • Three Ratnas: Right faith (Samyak Vishwas), Right knowledge (Samyak Gyan), Right conduct (Samyak Karma).

Principles of Jainism

  • Rejected the authority of the Vedas and the Vedic rituals.
  • Did not believe in the existence of God.
  • Attainment of salvation (Moksha) by believing in penance and dying of starvation.
  • Laid great emphasis on equality or universal brotherhood.

details.summary: Core tenets, history of Mahavira, and the division of Jainism.

subject: History
text:
There are five main teachings of Jainism:

  • Non-injury (Ahimsa)
  • Non-lying (Satya)
  • Non-possession (Aparigraha)
  • Non-stealing (Asteya)
  • Observe continence (Brahmacharya)

The first four principles were given by Parsavanath and the fifth, Brahmacharya, was added by Mahavira.

Jain Councils

  • First Council: Held at Pataliputra (Bihar) by Sthulabhadra in the beginning of the 3rd century BC; resulted in the compilation of 12 Angas to replace 14 Purvas.
  • Second Council: Held at Vallabhi (Gujarat) in AD 512 under the leadership of Devardhi; resulted in the final compilation of 12 Angas and 12 Upangas.

Jain Literature

The sacred books are known as Siddhanta or Agama. The six sacred books include:

  1. Twelve Angas
  2. Twelve Upangas
  3. Ten Prikarnas
  4. Six Chheda Sutras
  5. Four Mulasutras
  6. Two Sutra Granthas

Written in Prakrit language or a form called Ardhamagadhi. Svetambaras believe in the first five literatures. Important writers include Bhadrabahu, Siddhasena, Divakara, Manibhadra, Siddha, Hemachandra, Nayachandra, and Mallinath.

details.summary: Overview of Jain teachings, councils, and literature.

subject: History
text: During the age of Buddha, there were 16 large states called Mahajanapadas mentioned in the Buddhist text Angkuttar Nikaya. These were either monarchical or republican in character.
tables:
| Mahajanapada | Capital | Mahajanapada | Capital |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kashi | Varanasi | Kuru | Hastinapur, Indraprastha and Isukara |
| Kosala | Shravasti | Panchala | Ahichatra and Kampilya |
| Anga | Champa | Matsya | Viratnagar |
| Magadh | Girivraj or Rajgriha | Surasena | Mathura |
| Vajji | Vaishali | Ashmaka | Pratisthana |
| Malla | Kushinagar and Pavapuri | Avanti | Mahismati |
| Chedi | Shuktamati | Gandhara | Taxila |
| Vatsa | Kausambi | Kamboja | Rajouri, Hazara district |

details.summary: List of the 16 Mahajanapadas and their capitals.

subject: History
text:
The Magadha Empire

The period from 6th to 4th century BC saw the struggle for supremacy among four Mahajanapadas: Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, and Avanti. The founder of Magadha was Jarasandha and Brihadratha, but growth started under the Haryankas.

Causes for the Rise of Magadha

  • Advantageous geographical location with Rajgriha and Pataliputra.
  • Abundance of natural resources (iron) for weapons.
  • Use of elephants in war.
  • Alluvial soil of the Gangetic valley and sufficient rainfall.

Haryanka Dynasty (542-414 BC)

Founded by Bimbisara.

  • Bimbisara (544-492 BC): Contemporary of Buddha. Conquered Anga. Strengthened position via matrimonial alliances (Kosala, Vaishali, Madra). Capital Rajgriha was surrounded by 5 hills, making it impregnable.
  • Ajatshatru (492-460 BC): Son of Bimbisara, seized the throne. Annexed Vaishali and Kosala using a war engine. Buddha died during his reign; he arranged the first Buddhist Council.

details.summary: Rise of the Magadha Empire and the Haryanka Dynasty.

subject: History
text:
Udayin (460-444 BC)

  • The immediate successor of Ajatasutru was Udayin.
  • He laid the foundation of the new capital at Pataliputra, situated at the confluence of the two rivers, the Ganga and the Son.
  • Udayin's successors were weak rulers and hence, Magadha was captured by Shishunaga.
  • The last ruler of Haryanka Dynasty was Nagdasak.

Shishunaga Dynasty (414-344 BC)

  • The founder of Shishunaga Dynasty was Shishunaga, he was an Amatya (Minister) of the Nagdasaka.
  • He was placed on the throne by people who revolted against the Nagdasaka.
  • He was succeeded by Kalashoka (Second Buddhist Council was held during his period). Dynasty lasted for two generations only.
  • Greatest achievement was the destruction of power of Avanti.
  • Last ruler of the Dynasty was Nandivardhan, his empire was inherited by his illegitimate son Mahapadma Nanda.

details.summary: Covers the transition from Haryanka to Shishunaga dynasty and key rulers.

subject: History
text:
Nanda Dynasty (344-323 BC)

  • It is considered as the first of the non-Kshatriya dynasties founded by Mahapadma Nanda. He added Kalinga to his empire. He claimed to be the Ekarat, the sole sovereign who destroyed all the other ruling princes.
  • According to the Buddhist tradition, Mahapadma Nanda ruled about 10 years. He was succeeded by his eight sons, who ruled successively.
  • The last Nanda ruler was Dhana Nanda. During his reign he kept the Magadhan empire intact and possessed a powerful army and enormous wealth.
  • During his reign, the Greek invader, the Alexander invaded India.
  • Nandas maintained 200000 infantry, 60000 cavalry and 6000 war elephants. This is supposed to have a check on Alexander's army from advancing towards Magadha.

Alexander's Invasion

  • Alexander (356-323 BC) was the son of Philip of Macedonia (Greece) who invaded India in 326 BC.
  • At that time, North-West India was split up into a number of small independent states like Taxila, Punjab (kingdom of Porus), Gandharas etc.
  • Porus fought the famous battle of Hydaspes (on bank of Jhelum) with Alexander.
  • When Alexander reached Beas, his soldiers refused to go further, so he was forced to retreat.
  • He erected 12 huge stone altars on the Northern bank of Beas to mark the farthest point of his advance.
  • He remained in India for 19 months and died in 323 BC at Babylon.
image_descriptions: Boxed section detailing Alexander's invasion of India, including his lineage, the state of North-West India, the Battle of Hydaspes, and his retreat.

details.summary: Details regarding the Nanda Dynasty's military strength and the timeline of Alexander the Great's invasion.

subject: History
text:
The Mauryan Empire

The most immediate and unexpected by product of Alexander's invasion of North-West was that it hastened the Mauryan conquest of the whole country.

Chandragupta Maurya (322-298 BC)

  • He was the founder father of the Mauryan empire. He overthrew the last Nanda ruler, Dhana Nanda with the help of Kautilya also known as Chanakya.
  • Chanakya has written Arthashastra. It is about statecraft, economic policy, military strategy and how administration of state should be carried.
  • In 305 BC, Chandragupta defeated Seleucus Nicator (the Greek ambassador) who surrendered a big territorial part to him including Kabul, Afghanistan, Baluchistan and Herat also received a Greek ambassador i.e., Megasthenes sent by Seleucus (wrote Indica having the description of Mauryan administration, society etc.)
  • Chandragupta adopted Jainism and went to Shravanabelagola with Bhadrabahu, where he died of starvation (Sallekhana) at Chandragiri hill.

Bindusara (298-273 BC)

  • The son and successor of Chandragupta Maurya. He was called Amitraghata (slayer of foes) by Greek writers.
  • He asked Antiochus-I of Syria to send some sweet wine, dried fig and a Sophist. Except Sophist, Antiochus-I sent other things.
  • He is said to have conquered "the land between the two seas" i.e., the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. At the time of his death, almost the entire sub-continent came under the Mauryan rule. Greek ambassador, Deimachus visited the court sent by Antiochus.

Ashoka (273-232 BC)

  • The son and successor of Bindusara. It is said that he became king by killing his 99 brothers.
  • During succession of thron, Radhagupta, a Minister of Bindusara, helped him.

details.summary: Overview of the early Mauryan rulers: Chandragupta, Bindusara, and Ashoka.

subject: History
text:
Under Ashoka, the empire reached its zenith. For the first time in history, the entire Indian sub-continent came under a single umbrella (except extreme Southern India).

  • He was famous as Devanpriya. The name Ashoka occurs only once in the inscription of Maski edict.
  • He fought the Kalinga War in 261 BC in the 8th year of his coronation, in which one lakh people died.
  • Ashoka sent peace missionaries inside India as well as abroad.

Ashoka's Edicts: Inscribed on pillars of stone or rocks. Decoded by British archaeologist and historian James Princep.
tables:
| Edict | Content |
|---|---|
| MRE I | Prohibits animal slaughter. |
| MRE II | Provides care for man and animal. Describes kingdom of South India. |
| MRE III | Generosity to Brahmans and spread the Dhamma policy of Ashoka. |
| MRE IV | Impact of Dhamma on society. Ideal is Dhammaghosa not the Bherighosa. |
| MRE V | Appointment of Dhamma Mahamatyas. |
| MRE VI | King's duty to be informed about condition of people. |
| MRE VII & XII | Request tolerance for all religions. |
| MRE VIII | Ashoka's Dhamma yatra to Bodhgaya and Bodhi tree. |
| MRE IX | Condemn popular ceremonies. |
| MRE X | Condemn desire of fame and glory. |
| MRE XI | Elaborates Dhamma. |
| MRE XII | Ashoka's victory over Kalinga. This is the largest edict. |
| MRE XIII | Describes engraving of inscription in different parts of country. |

details.summary: Overview of Ashoka's reign, Kalinga War, and the classification of his Major Rock Edicts.

subject: History
text:
Minor Rock Edicts: Spread in 13 places (Bairat, Brahmagiri, Gavimath, Gujarra, Jatinga-Rameshwar, Maski, Palkigunda, Maadagiri, Rupanath, Sasaram, Siddhapur, Suvarnagiri and Yerragudi).

  • Kandhar Inscriptions: Located at Kandhar.
  • Bhabru Inscriptions: Located at Bairat in Rajasthan; deals with Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism.

Major Pillar Edicts: Seven edicts found at Allahabad, Meerut, Sopara, Lauriya Areraj, Lauriya Nandangarh and Rampurva. Engraved on Monolithic pillars. Kausambi edicts are known as Queen's edict (donations by queen Karukaki).

Minor Pillar Edicts:

  • Rummindei Pillar Inscription: Mentions exemption of Lumbini from tax.
  • Nigalisagar Pillar Inscription: Located at Kapilvastu; informs about Ashoka increasing the size of stupa of Buddha Konakamana.
  • Scheism Edict: Located at Kausambi, Sanchi and Sarnath; appeals for unity in Buddhist order.
  • Barabara Cave Inscriptions: Located in Bihar; speaks about Ashoka's donation of cave to the Ajivikas.

subject: History
text:
Later Mauryas: Ashoka ruled for 27 years. The last Mauryan king was Brihadratha, murdered by his General Pushyamitra Shunga, ending the dynasty.

Mauryan Administration:

  • Welfare state with highly centralised government.
  • According to Megasthenes, army administration was carried by a board of 30 officers divided into six committees (5 members each).
  • Slavery was a recognised institution despite Megasthenes' claims to the contrary.
  • Tamralipti in the Gangetic delta was the most prosperous port.
  • Megasthenes' Indica mentions 7 castes in Mauryan society.

Art and Architecture: Classified by Ananda Coomaraswamy into:

  1. Popular/Folk Art: Sculpture of Yaksha and Yakshini (e.g., Yaksha of Parkham, Yakshini of Vidisha and Didarganj).
  2. Royal/Court Art: Royal Palace of Chandragupta Maurya at Kumhrar, Patna (referred to by Fa hien as creation of God), City of Patliputra, Ashokan Pillars, stupas and caves.

subject: History
topic: Mauryan Legacy and Post Mauryan Dynasties
text:
Mauryan Legacy:

  • Mauryans introduced stone masonry on a large scale.
  • Pillars: Masterpiece of Mauryan sculpture. Examples: Single lion capital at Rampurva and Lauriya at Nandangarh; Four lion capital at Sarnath and Sanchi; Carved elephant at Dhauli and Kalsi.
  • Stupas: Built to enshrine relics of Buddha. Examples: Sanchi and Bharhut.
  • Varanasi was the best producer of silk.

Post Mauryan Period:

  • Succeeded by ruling dynasties from Central Asia in North-West India and native rulers (Shungas, Kanvas, Satavahanas) in Eastern, Central, and Deccan regions.

details.summary: Overview of Mauryan architectural contributions and the transition to post-Mauryan regional dynasties.

subject: History
text:
The Shunga Dynasty:

  • Founded by Pushyamitra. Dominions extended to the Narmada river, including Pataliputra, Ayodhya, and Vidisha.
  • The fifth king, Bhagabhadra, received the Greek ambassador Heliodorus.
  • Revival of Bhagvatism. Agnimitra is the hero of Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram.
  • Patanjali's Mahabhashya was written during this period.
  • Pushyamitra defeated the Bactrian king, Demetrius.
  • Manusmriti (Hindu Law) was compiled during this period.

The Kanva Dynasty:

  • Founded by Vasudeva, who killed the last Shunga king, Devabhuti.
  • Swept away by Satavahanas of the Deccan.

details.summary: Details on the Shunga and Kanva dynasties, their rulers, and cultural contributions.

subject: History
text:
The Satavahanas:

  • Founder: Simuka. Successors of Mauryans in the Deccan and central India.
  • Important king: Gautamiputra Satakarni (AD 106-130). Capital at Paithan on the bank of river Godavari.
  • First evidence of land grants to Brahmins.
  • Built Nagarjunakonda Stupa and Amravati Stupa.
  • Issued lead coins (apart from copper and bronze). Acted as a bridge between North and South India.
  • Rulers called themselves Brahmins, performed Vedic rituals, but also promoted Buddhism by granting land to monks.
  • Religious constructions: Chaitya (Buddhist temple) and Vihara (monasteries). Famous Chaitya at Karle.
  • Administrative terms: Provinces called Ahara; officials called Amatyas and Mahamatyas.

details.summary: Key aspects of the Satavahana dynasty, including administration, religion, and architecture.

subject: History
topic: The Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, and Kushanas
text:
The Indo-Greeks:

  • Invaded around 200 BC. Also called Bactrian Greeks.
  • Most famous ruler: Menander (165-145 BC), also known as Milinda. Capital at Sankala (modern Sialkot).
  • Converted to Buddhism by Nagasena or Nagarjuna (described in Milindapanho).
  • First to issue gold coins in India. The term 'Horoscope' is derived from the Greek term for astrology.

The Shakas or Scythians:

  • Followed the Greeks. Had 5 branches in India and Afghanistan.
  • A king of Ujjain, Vikramaditya, defeated Shakas in 58 BC and started the Vikram era.
  • Most famous ruler: Rudradaman I (AD 130-150). Famous for repairs of Sudarshana lake; his inscription is the Junagarh inscription.

The Parthians/Pahalvas:

  • Invaded at the beginning of the Christian era.
  • Most famous king: Gondophernes (AD 19-45). St. Thomas is said to have come to India during his reign.

The Kushanas:

  • Empire included Central Asia, Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, and North India.
  • First to start the tradition of putting names and images of rulers on coins.
  • Issued gold coins with higher gold content.

details.summary: Overview of foreign dynasties in India: Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, and Kushanas.

subject: History
text:
Kanishka was the most famous king. He patronised the following persons:

  • Ashvaghosha (wrote 'Buddhacharita', which is the biography of Buddha and 'Sutralankar'), Nagarjuna (wrote 'Madhyamik Sutra').
  • Charakh (a physician, wrote 'Charakhsamhita').
  • Kanishka is known in history because of two reasons:
    • He started an era in AD 78, which is now known as Saka era and is used by the Government of India.
    • He extended his whole-hearted patronage to Buddhism (held a Buddhist Council in Kashmir).

Some of the successors of Kanishka bore typical Indian names as Vasudeva.

SANGAM AGE

  • The age of 3 Southern kingdoms Cheras, Pandyas and Cholas was known as Sangam Age.
  • The word 'Sangam' means 'assembly'. It was an assembly of Tamil poets and scholars.

The Three Sangam Kingdoms

  • The Pandyas: Their capital was Madurai. Important king was Nedunjeliyan. It was first mentioned by Megasthenes. According to him, their kingdom was famous for pearls and was ruled by a woman.
  • The Cholas: The kingdom was called Cholamandalam or Coromandal. The chief centre was Uraiyur, a place famous for cotton trade. Capital was Kaveripattanam/Puhar. A Chola king named Elara conquered Sri Lanka and ruled it over for 50 years. Karikala was their famous king.
  • The Cheras: Their capital was Vanji (also called Kerala country). Fought against the Cholas about AD 150. It owed its importance to trade with the Romans. The Romans set up two regiments there to protect their interests. The greatest king was Senguttuvan, the Red Chera.

Other Aspects of the Three Kingdoms

  • Silappadikaram by Ilango Adigal (story of a married couple) and Manimekalai by Sattanar are the famous epics of this time.
  • 'Pariyars'—agricultural labourers who used to work in animal skin.
  • Civil and military offices held by Vellalas (rich peasants).
  • The ruling class was called Arahar.
tables:
| Kingdom | Capital | Royal Emblem |
|---|---|---|
| Cholas | Uraiyur later Puhar | Tiger |
| Cheras | Vanji or Karur | Bow |
| Pandyas | Madurai | Carp (fish) |

details.summary: Overview of Kanishka's reign, the Sangam Age, and the three major Southern kingdoms (Pandyas, Cholas, Cheras).

subject: History
text:
THE GUPTA PERIOD

  • After the decline of Mauryas, Guptas came into existence.
  • Srigupta and Ghatotkacha were the early kings.

Chandragupta I (AD 319-335)

  • He was the first prominent ruler of Gupta dynasty and assumed the title of Maharajadhiraja. He started the Gupta Era in AD 320.
  • He made his empire strong by his own efforts and also by making marriage with Lichchhavi princess.
  • Lichchhavis were a very powerful family or ruling class of Mithila at that time.

Samudragupta (AD 335-375)

  • He was perhaps the greatest king of Gupta dynasty.
  • The most detailed and authentic record of his reign is preserved in the Allahabad pillar inscription known as Prayag Prasasti written by his court poet 'Harisena'.
  • He always believed in policy of war and conquest and has been termed as Napolean of India by 'VA Smith'.
  • He was a Vaishnavite and an accomplished veena player.

Chandragupta II (AD 380-413)

  • He was the first Gupta ruler to issue silver coin. He was also known as Vikramaditya.
  • He also strengthened his empire by making marriages with powerful dynastic princess. He himself married with Kuber Naga, the Naga princess. And his daughter Prabhavati was married with Vakataka prince Rudrasena II.
  • Mehrauli Iron pillar inscription claims his authority over North-Western India and a good portion of Bengal.
  • Fa-hien, a Chinese traveller also came during the reign of Chandragupta II (AD 399-414).
  • He was also a man of art and culture, his court at Ujjain was adorned by Navaratna (Nine gems) including Kalidasa, Amarsimha, Acharya Dinanga etc.

Kumaragupta I (AD 413-455)

  • Kumaragupta adopted the title of Mahendraditya.
  • He founded Nalanda University (a renowned university of ancient India).
  • Kalidasa (The Shakespeare of India) flourished in the reign of both Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta I.
  • Kumaragupta was the worshipper of Lord Kartikeya (son of Lord Shiva, his vehicle is peacock).

Skandagupta (AD 455-467)

  • He faced Hunas (a fierce nomads of Central Asia) effectively.

Fall of Gupta Empire

  • The weak successors of Skandagupta could not check the growing Huna power.
  • Feudatories rose in Bihar, Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Vallabhi etc.

Administration

  • Kings adopted titles like Parameshwara/Maharajadhiraja/Parama Bhattaraka.
  • They issued the largest number of gold coins in Ancient India, which were called Dinars.

details.summary: Detailed account of the Gupta Empire, its rulers, administration, and decline.

subject: History
topic: Social Life, Religion, Art and Craft, Literature
text:
Social Life

  • The castes were further divided into sub-castes.
  • The practice of untouchability intensed (especially hatred for Chandalas). Fa-hien mentions that the Chandalas lived outside the village and were distanced by the upper class.

Religion

  • The Bhagwad Gita was written during Guptas, Buddhism declined a large extent.
  • Vishnu temple at Deogarh (near Jhansi), a small temple near Sanchi and a brick temple at Bhitargaon (near Kanpur) belong to the Gupta architecture.

Art and Craft

  • Samudragupta is represented on his coins playing the flute.
  • 2 metre high bronze image of Buddha belonging to the Mathura school (The Gandhara Buddha represents mask like coldness, while the Buddha from the Mathura school imparts a feeling of warmth and vitality).
  • Images of Vishnu, Shiva and some other Hindu Gods were featured first time in this period.
  • Artisans were organised into their guilds.
  • Guilds of artisans were found at Bhila and Vaisali.
  • Mandsour and Varanasi were important silk producing centre.

Literature

  • Kalidasa, the great Sanskrit dramatist, belonged to this period. His books are The Abhigyanashakuntalam (considered as one of the best literary works in the world and one of the earliest Indian works to be translated into European language, the other work being the Bhagwad Gita), Ritusamhara, Meghadutam, Kumarsambhavam, Malvikagnimitram, Raghuvamsa, Vikramovarshiyam etc.
  • Ramayana and the Mahabharata were almost completed by the AD 4th century.

details.summary: Overview of social, religious, artistic, and literary developments during the Gupta and post-Gupta periods.

subject: History
text:
Science and Technology

  • Aryabhatt, the great Mathematician, wrote the Aryabhattiya and the Suryasiddhanta.
  • In the Aryabhattiya, he described the placing value of the first nine numbers and the use of zero. He also calculated the value of π and invented Algebra.
  • In the Suryasiddhanta, he proved that the Earth revolves around the Sun and rotates on its axis. In this way, he discovered the cause of the solar and lunar eclipses and the methods for calculating the timings of their occurrence.
  • He also said that the heavenly bodies, like the Moon, were spherical and they are shone by reflecting the light.
  • Varahamihira wrote the Panchasidhantika and the Brihatsamhita. He said that the Moon moves around the Earth and the Earth, together with the Moon, moves round the Sun.
  • Brahmagupta was a great Mathematician. He wrote the Brahma-sphuta Siddhanta in which he hinted at the Law of Gravitation.
  • Palakapya wrote the Hastyagarveda, a treatise on the disease of elephants. Court language was Sanskrit.
  • Dhanvantri was a physician famous for Ayurveda knowledge.

details.summary: Scientific and mathematical advancements during the Gupta period.

subject: History
topic: Post Guptas, Vardhan Dynasty, Deccan Rulers
text:
Post Guptas

With the decline of the imperial Guptas at the close of 5th century, the beginning of 6th century, Magadha and its capital Pataliputra, lost their importance. After the fall of the Guptas, five major centres of power emerged in North India.

The Age of Smaller Kingdoms

  • The disintegration of the Gupta empire gradually paved the way for the growth of many smaller kingdoms.
  • The Maukharis started gaining political power towards the end of 5th century and hold over modern UP and parts of Magadha.
  • From the middle of 6th century till about AD 675, the kings who ruled Magadha were known as later Guptas.

Vardhan Dynasty

  • Founder of Vardhan dynasty was Pushyabhuti Vardhana. He established his empire in Thaneshwar, Haryana.
  • Raja Vardhana, Aditya Vardhana and Prabhakar Vardhana were other kings of the dynasty. But Harshavardhana was most famous king of the dynasty.

Harshavardhana

  • Harshavardhana was born in 590 AD, he was younger son of Prabhakar Vardhana. He became the king in 606 till his death in 647 AD.
  • The history of the early years of his reign is taken from a study of his biography Harshacharita by Banabhatta, one of the court poets.
  • The famous center of learning Nalanda prospered during his reign. The Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang visited India during this period.

Deccan Rulers: The Vakatakas

  • In the beginning of the 7th century, the Chalukyas of Badami, the Vakatakas and the Ikshavakus emerged as the three major states in Deccan. While in South India after the fall of Satavahanas, the Pallavas established a powerful kingdom.
  • The kingdom was founded by Vindhyasakti, basically Brahmins.
  • Most important king was Pravarsena-I who performed Ashwamedha Yajnas.
  • Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavati to a Vakataka king Rudrasenar-II and with his support succeeded in conquering Gujarat.

details.summary: Political landscape of India following the decline of the Gupta Empire.

subject: History
text:
The Chalukyas grew powerful in Deccan in the middle of the AD 6th century. The dynasty had two branches: Vatapi (Badami) and Kalyani.

  • Pulakesin-I was the founder of the Chalukya dynasty.
  • Pulakesin-II (ruled AD 610-642) was the most important ruler; he sent an ambassador to the Persian king Khusro II.
  • His greatest achievement was inflicting a defeat on Harshavardhana.

details.summary: Overview of the Chalukyas of Badami, focusing on Pulakesin-I and Pulakesin-II.

subject: History
text:
Simha Vishnu was the founder of the Pallavas dynasty. They set up their capital at Kanchi (modern Kanchipuram).

  • Pallava temples were usually free-standing.
  • Example: Seven Ratha temple (seven pagoras) at Mahabalipuram.

details.summary: Overview of the Pallava dynasty and their architectural contributions.

subject: History
text:
The first and famous king of Gangas of Orissa (now, Odisha) was Ananta Varman (1076-1147), who established his power over the whole territory between the Ganga and the Godavari.

  • He built the famous temple of Lord Jagannath at Puri.
  • Kesari, who used to rule Odisha before Gangas, built the famous Lingaraja temple at Bhubhaneswar.

details.summary: Overview of the Ganga dynasty in Odisha and their temple architecture.

subject: History
text:
Founder of Cholas was Vijayalya. Their capital was Tanjore. Cholas were feudal of Pallavas.

  • Rajaraj I built the Vrihideshwar temple at Tanjore (also known as Rajrajeshwar temple).
  • His son Rajendra I annexed the whole of Sri Lanka. After defeating Pala king Mahipala, he took the title of Gangaikonda.
  • The empire was divided into 6 mandalas or provinces administered by Governors.
  • Mandala were further divided into Valanadus, Valanadus into Nadus and Nadus into Kottam and Kurrams.
  • The Gopuram style of art developed under Cholas.
  • Local self-government existed (concept of Panchayati Raj borrowed from it).

details.summary: Overview of the Chola dynasty, their administration, and architectural style.

subject: History
text:
Ruled between AD 10-14 centuries in areas of modern Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, parts of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.

  • Initially capital was at Belur, later moved to Halebidu.
  • Hoysala period saw growth of art, literature, religion and architecture.
  • Famous temples: Chennkeseva temple at Belur, Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu, and Kesava temple at Somnathpura.

details.summary: Overview of the Hoysala dynasty and their temple architecture.

subject: History
text:
The Rashtrakutas rose up against the Chalukyas under Dantidurga, who founded this dynasty in AD 753 and made Manyakheta his capital.

  • King Krishna-I is best remembered as the builder of the rock-cut Kailash temple at Ellora.
  • Amoghavarsha I (AD 814-880) is compared to Vikramaditya in giving patronage to men of letters. He wrote the first Kannada poetry Kaviraj Marg and Prashnottar Mallika.
  • King Krishna-III set up a pillar of victory and a temple at Rameshwaram.

details.summary: Overview of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, their rulers, and cultural contributions.

subject: History
topic: Bengal Rulers: The Palas and The Senas
text:
The Palas: In the middle of the AD 8th century, the Pala dynasty came into power. Its founder was Gopal (AD 750). He was a Buddhist. He was succeeded by Dharamapala (AD 770-810) who won Kannauj. He was succeeded by Devapala who won Odisha and Assam. Dharamapala founded the University of Vikramashila and revived Nalanda University.

The Senas: After the Palas, the Senas established an empire in Bengal. The earliest member was Samanta Sena. The greatest ruler was Vijayasena, a devotee of Shiva. The Muslim ruler Muhammad Bakhtyar Khilji attacked its capital Nadia and captured it.

details.summary: Overview of the Pala and Sena dynasties in Bengal.

subject: History
topic: Northern Indian Kingdoms and The Rajputs
text:
The powerful kingdom arose between AD 750-1000. The Rashtrakutas were ruling Northern Deccan, the Pratiharas in Avanti and parts of Southern Rajasthan, and the Palas in Bengal. All three were engaged in a continual tripartite struggle. The first invader was Mahmud of Ghazni.

The Rajputs: Came into prominence in 9th and 10th centuries. There is a body of opinions claiming that some of them were foreign immigrants assimilated into the Hindu fold over the centuries. Lastly there were the Agnikulas, the fire family.

details.summary: Overview of the tripartite struggle and the rise of the Rajputs.

subject: History
text:
The Pratiharas (or Gurjara Pratihara)

  • The foundation of one branch of Pratiharas was laid down by Harichandra, a Brahaman near modern Jodhpur in the middle of the AD 6th century.
  • Bhoj was the greatest ruler of this vast empire from Kannauj. He was also known as Adivaraha and Mihira.
  • Mahendrapala I is believed to have started his reign in about AD 893. His teacher was Rajashekhara a celebrated poet, dramatist and critic author.
  • Rajashekhara was court poet of the Gurjara Pratiharas. The work attributed to him include – Viddasalashanjika, Balabharata, Karpuramanjari, Balaramayana and Kavyamimamsa.

The Chandellas

  • The Chandellas became rulers in Southern Bundelkhand under Nannuka early in the 9th century.
  • They had their capital at Kharjuravahaka (modern Khajuraho).
  • They were a patron of learning, fine arts and built Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho in AD 1000.

The Chauhans

  • They ruled over Shakambri (modern Sambhar– Rajasthan). Founder of Chauhan kingdom was Semharaja.
  • Important king was Prithviraj Chauhan.
  • First Battle of Tarain, 1191 Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Mohammad Ghori.
  • Second Battle of Tarain, 1192 Mohammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan.
  • His court poet was Chandbardai who composed Prithviraj Raso.

The Gahadavals

  • They ruled over Kannauj. Jai Chand was the important ruler. He was defeated by Mohammad Ghori in 1194 in Battle of Chandawar.

The Chalukayas (Anhilwara)

  • The Chalukayas or Solankis were rulers of Gujarat and Kathiawar for about three and a half centuries.
  • Important ruler was Pulakesin II. Aihole inscription is associated with him, composed by his court poet Ravikirti.

The Paramaras

  • The main branch of the Paramaras comprised descendants of the Rashtrakutas who ruled Malwa.
  • The dynasty was founded by Upendra or Krishnaraja.
  • Bhoja (1010-1055) is the greatest king of the Paramara rulers, also called as Kaviraj. He wrote the Samarangana Sutradhar (a rare work on architecture) and the Ayurvedasaravasva (work on medicine).

Architecture, Arts and Paintings

Harappan Period

The excavations at Harappa and Mohenjodaro and several other sites of the Indus Valley Civilisation revealed the existence of a very modern urban civilisation with expert town planning and engineering skills.

Pallava Style

  • The earliest examples of temples in the Dravidian style belong to the Pallava period.
  • The temple architecture of the Pallavas is divided into two groups: rock-cut (AD 610-690) and structural (AD 690-900).
  • The greatest accomplishments of the Pallava architecture are the rock-cut temples at Mahabalipuram.

Chola Style

  • The Chola art is a continuation of that of Pallava times. The Cholas had built several hundreds of temples, the earlier examples of which were modest in size, while the later ones were huge and large with the Vimanas or Gopuras dominating the landscape.
  • The temple of Koranganatha at Srinivasanallur in the Trichinopoly district, built during the reign of Parantaka I (AD 907-949), is one of the earliest examples of the Chola architecture.

The Vijayanagara Architecture

  • The Vijayanagara rulers built strong fortresses, gorgeous palaces and beautiful temples.
  • The characteristic feature of this period is the development of the temple complex with concentric series of rectangular enclosure walls with the gopuras (towered gateways) in the middle of each side.

Schools of Art

During first and second century AD there was emergence of three schools of art in India that had developed their own particular styles and distinctions. These were the Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati schools.

Gandhara School of Art

  • The Gandhara region extending from Punjab to the borders of Afghanistan saw the emergence of a new school of Indian sculpture known as the Gandhara School.

details.summary: Overview of major medieval Indian dynasties (Pratiharas, Chandellas, Chauhans, Gahadavals, Chalukayas, Paramaras) and evolution of Indian architecture from Harappan to Vijayanagara periods.

subject: History
text:
Gandhara School of Art

Also known as the Graeco-Buddhist School of Art. Greek techniques were applied to Buddhist subjects. Features include images of Buddha and Bodhisattvas in black stone, depicted in standing or seated positions.

Mathura School of Art

  • Flourished around Mathura, transforming Buddhist symbols into human form.
  • Buddha's first image traced to Kanishka's reign (about AD 78).
  • Earliest sculptures based on the yaksha prototype.
  • Produced images of Jain Tirthankaras and Hindu deities.
  • Gupta period saw further improvisation with jewelled female figures (yakshinis, naginis, apsaras).

Amravati School of Art

Developed on the banks of the Krishna River in modern Andhra Pradesh. Site of the largest Buddhist stupa of South India. Known for figures of males and females with physical beauty and expression of human emotions in different moods and poses.

Paintings

The history of Indian paintings is as old as the history of the people of India, traceable to cave paintings.

Cave Paintings

  • Earliest evidence on cave walls and palaces; miniature paintings are small-sized, vibrant, sophisticated artworks.
  • Themes describe Hinduism and Buddhism.
  • Ranges from prehistoric Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh) to Ajanta (Maharashtra) and Bagh (Madhya Pradesh).
  • Ajanta depicts life/teachings of Buddha and Jataka; Ellora depicts Hindu deities.

Ajanta Paintings

  • Located in Maharashtra, 106 km from Aurangabad; 29 caves.
  • Period: 200 BC to AD 7th century (Sunga, Kushan, Gupta rulers).
  • Characteristics: Fresco wall paintings, limited colours, decorative designs (animals, flowers), expressive emotions via hand postures, Jataka stories.
  • Religious and secular in character.
  • 'Dying Princess' is a highly praised painting.

Ellora Paintings

  • Composition in rectangular panels with thick borders, confined within frames.

Bagh Paintings

  • Located on banks of river Bagh, Madhya Pradesh.
  • Similar to Ajanta in subject matter.
  • Best paintings found in Cave number 4 (now in museum for preservation).

Sittanavasal Paintings

  • Located in Sittanavasal village, Tamil Nadu.
  • Built by Mahendra Verman and son Narsimha Verman.
  • Connected to Jain themes; technique similar to Ajanta.
  • Contours are firmly drawn dark on a light red ground.

details.summary: Overview of major Indian art schools (Gandhara, Mathura, Amravati) and historical painting sites (Ajanta, Ellora, Bagh, Sittanavasal).

subject: History
text:
Mohammad-bin-Qasim

  • The Arabs, long carriers of Indian trade with Europe, were attracted by rich sea-ports of Sind.
  • Two expeditions sent by Al-Hajaj, the governor of Iraq, failed.
  • The third expedition under his nephew and son-in-law Mohammad-bin-Qasim acquired control over Sind after a tough fight in AD 712. Multan was conquered in AD 713.

Mahmud of Ghazni

  • Mahmud came to the throne of Ghazni in AD 997.
  • Started raids on India in AD 1001 by attacking and killing Jaipala, the King of Punjab in the First Battle of Waihind.
  • The sixth expedition (the Second Battle of Waihind) was against Anandapala (Hindushahi ruler of Punjab) in 1008.
  • The next expedition in 1009 was against Nagarkot in the Kangra hills.
  • Ghazni led 17 expeditions between 1001 and 1027, plundering Thaneshwar, Mathura, Kannauj and Somnath.
  • The temple of Somnath dedicated to Shiva was plundered in 1026 on the sea coast of Kathiawar (Gujarat).
  • Utbi was Mahmud’s court historian; his book is Kitab-ul-Yamni or Tarikh-I-Yamni.
  • Firdausi (Persian poet) wrote the Shahanama; Al Beruni wrote Tahqiq-i-hind.

Mohammad Ghori

  • Muizzuddin Mohammad-bin-Sam (Mohammad Ghori), the last Turkish conqueror of North India.
  • The King of Delhi Prithviraj Chauhan routed Ghori’s forces in AD 1191 at Tarain (First Battle of Tarain).
  • Prithviraj was defeated in the Second Battle of Tarain (AD 1192), and Delhi and Ajmer were captured by Mohammad Ghori, laying the foundation of Muslim Rule in India.

details.summary: Overview of early Arab and Turk invasions including Mohammad-bin-Qasim, Mahmud of Ghazni, and Mohammad Ghori.

subject: History
text:
The Delhi Sultanate

The assumption of sovereign powers by Qutub-ud-din Aibak in 1206 is regarded as the foundation of the Sultanate of Delhi and the first ruling dynasty father of the Sultanate. The Delhi Sultanate (AD 1206-1526) had five ruling dynasties.

1. The Slave or Ilbari Dynasty (AD 1206-1290)

Also known as the Mamluk Dynasty.

Qutub-ud-din Aibak (AD 1206-1210)

  • Founder of the Sultanate of Delhi; first Muslim King of India.
  • Began reign with the title Malik and Sipahsalar conferred by Mohammad Ghori.
  • Capitals: Lahore and later Delhi.
  • Died in 1210 while playing Chaugan (Polo) at Lahore.
  • Earned the sobriquet lakh-baksh (giver of lakhs) for his generosity.
  • Laid the foundation of Qutub Minar in Delhi after the Sufi Saint Khwaja Qutub-ud-din Bakhtiyar Kaki.
  • Constructed the first mosque in India: Quwat-ul-Islam (Delhi) and Adhai Din ka Jhopara (Ajmer).
  • Patronised Hasan Nizami and Fakhr-ud-din; their works are Taj ul Massir and Tarikhi Mubarik Shahi.

Shams-ud-din Iltutmish (AD 1210-1236)

  • Real founder of the Sultanate of Delhi; succeeded Aibak.
  • Consolidator of Turkish conquest in India; made Delhi the capital.
  • Suppressed revolts of ambitious nobles, fought sons of Aibak, and sent expeditions against Rajputs in Ranthambore, Jalor, and Mewar.

details.summary: Introduction to the Delhi Sultanate and the early rulers of the Slave Dynasty: Qutub-ud-din Aibak and Iltutmish.

subject: History
text:
Iltutmish (continued):

  • His governing class was entirely of foreign origin, consisting of Turkish slave officers and Tazik.
  • He organised the iqtas, the army, and the currency, the three most important organs of the imperial structure of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • He is called the father of Tomb building (built Sultan Garhi).
  • Chengiz Khan Mongol invaded during his period.

Razia (AD 1236-1240):

  • She was the first and the last Muslim woman ruler of medieval India.
  • The first rebellion was raised against her by Kabir Khan, the Governor of Lahore.
  • Altunia, the Governor of Bhatinda, was also a revolutionary. Razia moved towards Bhatinda but was defeated and taken as prisoner by Altunia, who married her.
  • Razia was defeated by Bahram Shah, a son of Iltutmish, while moving towards Delhi.
  • Razia succession continued with three rulers: i. Bahram Shah (AD 1240-1242), ii. Ala-ud-din Masud Shah (AD 1242-1246), iii. Nasir-ud-din Mahmud (AD 1246-1266).
  • Nasir-ud-din Mahmud was the grandson of Iltutmish.

Balban (AD 1266-1287):

  • Balban ascended the throne in 1266-67 with a host of problems.
  • He ordered the separation of the military department from the finance department (Diwan-i-wizarat) and placed the former under a minister for military affairs (Diwan-i-ariz).
  • He impressed upon the people that kingship was the vice regency of God on Earth (Niyabat-i-khudai) and the king was the shadow of God (Zil-i-ilahi).
  • Balban introduced Sijdah or Paibos and started Nauroz festival.
  • He took strong measures to safeguard the North-West frontier against Mongol invasions.

details.summary: Covers the later years of Iltutmish, the reign of Razia Sultan, the succession period, and the reforms of Balban.

subject: History
text:
2. The Khiljis (AD 1290-1320):

  • The coming of the Khiljis to power was known as Khilji Revolution, marking the end of monopolisation of power by the Turkish nobility.
  • The accession of Jalal-ud-din Firoz Khilji marked the end of an epoch.

Jalal-ud-din Firoz Khilji (AD 1290-1297):

  • He was 70 when he came to the throne.
  • He married his daughter to the Mongol leader Ulugh khan, a descendent of Chengiz Khan.
  • Important event: Invasion of Devagiri by Ala-ud-din (his nephew and son-in-law).

Ala-ud-din Khilji (AD 1296-1316):

  • First major conquest: Rich kingdom of Gujarat, ruled by Vaghela King Karna.
  • In 1299, his army under Ulugh Khan and Nusarat Khan invaded Anhilwad.
  • Acquired Kafur (Hazar Dinari), who became a great military general.
  • Architectural works: Hauz Khas, Mahal Hazar Satoon, Jamait Khana Mosque, Alai Darwaza, and capital at Siri.
  • Adopted title: Sikandar-i-Sani.
  • Last ruler: Qutub-ud-din Mubarak Khilji.

details.summary: Overview of the Khilji dynasty, focusing on the reigns of Jalal-ud-din and Ala-ud-din Khilji.

subject: History
text:
3. The Tughlaqs (AD 1320-1412):

  • A Muslim family of Turkish origin.

Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq (AD 1320-1325):

  • Real name: Ghazi Malik.
  • Founded the third dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Discarded Ala-ud-din's system of measurement of land for assessment of land revenue.
  • Constructed canals for irrigation and formulated a famine policy.
  • Built the fortified city of Tughlaqabad.
  • Conflict with Sufi Saint Nizam-ud-din Auliya.

details.summary: Introduction to the Tughlaq dynasty and the reign of Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq.

subject: History
text:
Mohammad-bin-Tughlaq (AD 1325-1351)

  • Real name: Jauna Khan. Succeeded Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq.
  • Shifted capital from Delhi to Devagiri (Daulatabad) in 1327; later re-transferred to Delhi.
  • Introduced token currency (1327-30) using bronze tankas in place of silver tankas.
  • Set up a new department for agriculture: Diwani-i-Amir-Kohi.
  • Ibn Batuta (famous traveller) visited Delhi in 1334, served as Qazi for 8 years, and wrote Rehla.
  • Vijaynagar Empire established in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka; Bahamani Kingdom established in 1346 by Hasan Gangir Behman Shah.

details.summary: Overview of Mohammad-bin-Tughlaq's reign, administrative reforms, and contemporary events.

subject: History
text:
Firoz Shah Tughlaq (AD 1351-1388)

  • Patron of arts and literature. Banned inhumane punishments (cutting hands, nose, etc.).
  • Khutba was read in his name for the first time.
  • Abolished taxes, substituted with four: Kharaj, Jaziya, Zakat, and Khams.
  • Made civil and military posts hereditary.
  • Founded cities: Hissar, Fatehabad, Jaunpur, Firozabad, and Firoz Shah Kotla.
  • Brought Ashokan pillars from Topara (Ambala) and Meerut to Firozabad.

details.summary: Administrative and architectural contributions of Firoz Shah Tughlaq.

subject: History
text:
The Sayyids (AD 1414-1451)

  • Founder: Khizr Khan, rewarded with governorship of Lahore and Multan for services to Timur.
  • Successors: Mubarak Shah (1421-33), Mohammad Shah (1434-43), and Ala-ud-din Alam Shah (1443-51).

details.summary: Brief overview of the Sayyid dynasty rulers.

subject: History
text:
The Lodhis (AD 1451-1526)

  • Bahlul Lodhi (1451-1489): Founder of the dynasty, Afghan Sardar.
  • Sikandar Lodhi (1489-1517): Original name Nizam Shah. Introduced 'Gaz-i-Sikandari' for measuring fields. Wrote Persian verses under the name 'Gul-rukhi'. Founded Agra. Imposed ban on non-Persian languages and women visiting saint graves. Built Moth Masjid.
  • Ibrahim Lodhi (1517-1526): Defeated and killed by Babur in the first battle of Panipat (1526). Administration divided into iqtas; Wazir (finance), Mushrif-i-mumalik (Accountant General), and Maustauji-i-mumalik (Auditor General).

details.summary: Chronology and administrative details of the Lodhi dynasty.

subject: History
text:
Malwa

  • Annexed by Alauddin Khalji in 1305.
  • Husan Shah built Jama Masjid, Hindol Mahal, and Jahaz Mahal at Mandu.
  • Mahmud Khalji defeated by Rana Kumbha; later annexed by Gujarat (1531) and Mughal state (1562).

details.summary: Historical progression of the Malwa kingdom.

subject: History
text:
Bengal

  • Bengal was made a part of the Delhi Sultanate by Ikhtiyar-ud-din Mohammad bin Bakhtiyar Khilji in 1204.
  • In AD 1342, Iliyas Khan founded the new Iliyas Shahi Dynasty.
  • Ghiyasuddin Azam established friendly relations with China and established trade and commerce.
  • The famous poet, Maladhar Basu, compiler of Sri-Krishna Vijay, was patronised by the Sultans and was given the title of 'Gunaraja Khan'.
  • Chaitanya and Shankaradeva belonged to this period. Sher Shah Suri occupied Bengal in AD 1538.

Gujarat

  • Disintegrated from Delhi in AD 1397, under Zaffar Khan who assumed the title of Sultan Muzaffar Shah.
  • Ahmed Shah I (his grandson), built a new city Ahmedabad and also built Jama Masjid and Tin Darwaza at Ahmedabad.
  • Mahmud Beghra, another prominent ruler, in whose reign Portuguese set-up a factory at Diu.
  • Sanskrit scholar, Udayraja, was his court poet. Akbar annexed Gujarat in AD 1573.

Jaunpur

  • Sharqi dynasty was founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq’s eunuch-Malik Sarwar.
  • Firoz Shah’s son Mohammad Shah gave the title of Malik-us-Sharq to him as a governor of Jaunpur. He claimed independence after Timur’s invasion.
  • Malik Mohd. Jaisi the author of 'Padmavat' lived in Jaunpur.
  • In 1484, Bahlol Lodhi, the ruler of Delhi, occupied Jaunpur and annexed the Sharqi dynasty.

Kashmir

  • Kashmir was previously ruled by Hindu rulers. The greatest Muslim ruler of Kashmir was Zain-ul-Abidin (1420-70). He was a secular ruler.
  • He started many constructive works: Introduced the art of shawl-making in Kashmir; Built Zaina lake and artificial island in the Wular lake.
  • Kashmiri people gave him the title of Badshah.

Mewar

  • It was an old principality of Gahlot dynasty then Sirohis came to rule.
  • The first great ruler of medieval Mewar was Rana Kumbha. He was proficient in the Vedas, Smritis, Mimansa, Upanishads and literature.
  • He wrote commentaries on Jayadeva’s 'Gitagovinda' and on 'Chandisatakam'.
  • He built Kirtistambha (Tower of Victory) at Chittor (Rajasthan).
  • Mandan was his court-poet, wrote many books on architecture the Prasad Mandan, The Rupa Mandan.

details.summary: Overview of regional kingdoms in medieval India including Bengal, Gujarat, Jaunpur, Kashmir, and Mewar.

subject: History
text:
The Vijayanagara Empire

Vijayanagara kingdom was founded by Harihar I and Bukka I who were feudatories of Kakatiyas and later became ministers in the court of Kampili. Harihara and Bukka were brought to the centre by Mohammad-bin-Tughlaq, converted to Islam and were sent to South again to control rebellion. Harihar and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336 on the advice of Vidyaranya, who converted them back to Hindu.

Sangama Dynasty (AD 1336-1485)

Harihara I (AD 1336-1356)

He made Anagundi his capital. He annexed the Hoyasala State in AD 1364.

Bukka I (AD 1356-79)

  • He made Gutti his capital. The war with Bahmanis started in AD 1367, during the reign of Bukka I.
  • The empire saw expansion under Bukka I. His son Kumara Kampan successfully led an expedition against Madurai and annexed it.
  • This is mentioned in Madura Vijayam written by Ganga Devi (Kampan’s wife).

Harihara II (AD 1379-1404)

Bukka I was succeeded by his son Harihara II, who embarked upon a policy of expansion towards the Eastern sea coast.

Deva Raya I (AD 1406-1422)

  • He assumed the title Maharajadhiraja. The reign of Deva Raya I began with a renewed fight for the Tungabhadra doab.
  • Deva Raya I undertook a number of schemes for the welfare of the people.
  • In AD 1410, he got constructed a dam across the Tungabhadra, with canals leading to the city. This greatly helped in agriculture. He was also a great patron of the scholars.
  • Niclo De Conti, an Italian (Venetian), visited the Vijayanagara Empire under Deva Raya I. Conti describes the city of Vijayanagara as having a circumference of 96 km and employing 90000 potential soldiers and also mentions the festivals like Deepawali, Navaratri etc.

details.summary: Detailed history of the Sangama Dynasty of the Vijayanagara Empire, covering rulers from Harihara I to Deva Raya I.

subject: History
text:
Few foreign travellers to India during medieval period:

  • Marco Polo: An Italian traveller from Venice who visited India in 1295 AD.
  • Niclo De conti: An Italian (Venetian) who visited the Vijayanagara Empire in 1419, is author of India Recognita.
  • Abdur Razzaq: An Uzbek Islamic scholar and ambassador of Shah Rukh, visited India from 1442-1445.
  • Edordo Barbosa: A Jasuit missionary and visited India in 1560.

details.summary: List of notable foreign travellers who visited India during the medieval period.

subject: History
text:
Deva Raya II was the greatest ruler of the Sangama Dynasty.

  • In order to strengthen his army, he inducted more Muslims in, and asked all his Hindu soldiers and officers to learn the art of archery from them.
  • Three hard battles were fought, but in the end, the two sides had to agree to the existing frontiers.
  • Deva Raya II was called Immadi Devaraya and also proudha Devaraya or the great Devaraya by his subjects.
  • Some quarter varahas (gold coins of Vijayanagara) of Deva Raya II describe him as Gajabetakara (the elephant hunter). Deva Raya II was a great patron of literature and himself an accomplished scholar in Sanskrit.
  • He is credited with the authorship of two Sanskrit works Mahanataka Sudhanidhi and a commentary on the Brahma Sutras of Badarayana.
  • The king had leaning for Vira Saivism, yet he showed tolerance in religious views. He appointed people belonging to different religions as his minister.
  • He got constructed a mosque in the Vijayanagara and ordered that a copy of Quran be placed before his throne.

details.summary: Overview of the reign, military reforms, and cultural contributions of Deva Raya II.

subject: History
text: Vijayanagara witnessed chaos and disorder after 1465 due to weak rulers. However, the situation was saved by the Governor of Chandragiri, Narasimha Saluva, who seized the throne in about 1485 in what is known in history as the First Usurpation. Narasimha was succeeded by Timma and Imadi Narasimha, who were minors at the time of their coronation. The real power was in the hands of Narsa Nayak, who was the Reagent.

details.summary: The rise of the Saluva Dynasty following the First Usurpation.

subject: History
text:
Following the death of Narsa Nayak in 1505, his son Vira Narasimha, succeeded as the reagent. He deposed the Imadi Narsimha and laid the foundation of the Tuluva Dynasty by what is known in history as the Second Usurpation. Babur talked about Krishna Deva Raya (1509-1529) as the greatest ruler of the Tuluva Dynasty.

Krishnadeva Raya

  • He maintained friendly relations with Albuquerqur, the Portuguese Governor, whose Ambassador Friar Luis was a resident in Vijayanagara. He gave Albuquerque permission to built a Fort of Bhatkal. He built the Vijaya Mahal (House of Victory) and expanded the Hazara Rama temple and the Vithal Swami temple.
  • He took the titles of Yavanaraja Sthapanacharya (restorer of the Yavana kingdom, i.e., Bahmani) and Abhinava-Bhoja.
  • Abolished marriage taxes also known as Andhra Pitamaha and Andhra Bhoja. He was a gifted scholar in both Telugu and Sanskrit of which only two works are extant.
  • The Telugu work on polity Amuktamalyada and the Sanskrit drama Jambavati Kalyanam. Krishna Deva Rai was also a great patron of art and literature.

details.summary: Establishment of the Tuluva Dynasty and the achievements of Krishnadeva Raya.

subject: History
text:
• The Bahamani kingdom of Deccan was founded by Hasan Gangu whose original name was Ismail Mukh. The capital was Gulbarga.
  • Mahmud Shah I (1358-75) son of Bahaman Shah established a council consisting of eight ministers and decentralised his provincial administration. He fought with Vijayanagar.
  • Firoz Shah (1397-1422) was the most remarkable figure in Bahamani kingdom. He was determined to make Deccan the cultural centre of India.
  • Firoz Shah was succeeded by his brother Ahmad Shah I (AD 1422-36). He shifted his capital from Gulbarga to Bidar, Ahmed Shah is known as Wali or saint due to his association with Gesu Daraz.
  • Humayun was succeeded by his son Nizam Shah (1461-63) and then by Mohammad Shah III (AD 1463-82). Mahmud Gawan was the Prime Minister of Mohammad Bahamani kingdom saw a resurgence under Mahmud Gawan's guidance. His military conquests included Konkan, Goa and Krishna-Godavari delta, Nikitin a Russian merchant, visited Bidar during his reign.
  • Adil Shahis of Bijapur (1490-1686) founded by Yusuf Adil Shah. It was annexed by Aurangazeb. Greatest ruler of the kingdom was Ibrahim Adil Shah. He Introduced 'Dakhini' in place of Persian language. Another ruler Mohammad Adil Shah built the Gol Gumbaz.
  • Imad Shahis of Berar (1490-1574) founded by Fateullah Khan II Mad-ul-Mulk with Daulatabad as capital. Later, it was conquered and annexed by one of the Nizam Shahi rulers of Ahmadnagar.

details.summary: History and key rulers of the Bahamani Kingdom and its successor states.

subject: History
text:
• Qutub Shahis of Golconda (1518-1687): Founded by Quli Qutub Shah. He built the Golkonda fort and made it his capital. Mohammad Quli Qutub Shah was the greatest of all; he founded the city of Hyderabad and built the Charminar. Masulipatnam was the most important port. The kingdom was annexed by Aurangzeb in 1687.
  • Barid Shahis of Bidar (1528-1619): Founded by Ali Barid. Annexed by Adil Shahis of Bijapur.

details.summary: Overview of Qutub Shahi and Barid Shahi dynasties.

subject: History
text:
The Sufis

  • During the 13th century, Sufism was divided into 14 silsilas.
  • Visiting place of pilgrimage is called ziyarat.

The Chistis

  • Founder: Khwaza Abu-e-Chisti; popularized in India by Moin-ud-din Chisti (tomb in Ajmer).
  • Main disciple: Khwaza Qutub-ud-din Bakhtiyar Kaki (Qutub Minar named after him).
  • Nizam-ud-din Auliya: Known as Mahboob-i-Ilahi (beloved of God) and Sultan-ul-Auliya (king of the saints). Tomb in Delhi.
  • Other famous Chistis: Sheikh Nasir-ud-din (Chirag-i-Delhi), Mohd Gesudraz, Sheikh Salim Chisti.

Qadiri

  • Founder: Sheikh Muhi-ud-din Qadir Zillani.
  • Popularized by Shah Nizamat Ullah. Dara Shikoh (son of Shah Jahan) was a disciple of Mullah Shah Badakshi.
  • Dara Shikoh wrote Safinat-ul-Auliya and Sakinat-ul-Auliya. He translated books as Sir-e-Akbar and Sir-e-Asrar.

Naqshabandi

  • Founder: Khwaza Baha-ud-din Naqshabandi.
  • Popularized by Khwaza Khwand Mahmud (centre in Kashmir).
  • Other Saints: Baqi-Billah, Shahwali ullah, Khwaza Mir Dard Naqshaband. Mir Dard wrote Dard-e-Dil, Sham-e-Mahfil, and Ilm-ul-Khitab.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of major Sufi orders in India.

subject: History
text:
Bhakti Movement

Devotional worship of God with the objective of attaining Moksha or Salvation. Divided into two branches: Nirguna and Saguna.

Nirguna Saints

  • Guru Nanak (1469-1539): Born at Talwandi. Propagated monotheism, Hindu-Muslim unity, and denounced idol worship. Disciple Mardana played Rabao. Started Sikh religion.
  • Dadu Dayal (1554-1603): Born in Ahmedabad to Muslim parents. Teachings in Bani. Disciples: Sundardasa, Rajjab, Bakham, Warid. Founded Brahma sect (Brahma Sampradaya). Also known as Mahabali.
  • Kabir (1440-1510): Opposed caste creed and idol worship. Works: Sabada Doha, Holi, Rekhtal. Verses included in Adi Granth.

Saguna Saints-Ram Bhakti

  • Tulsidas (1532-1623): Hindu poet-saint, contemporary to Akbar. Works: Ramcharitamanas, Kavitawali, Gitawali, Parvati, Janki Mangal, Vinaya Patrika.
  • Nabhaji: Wrote Bhaktmal (mentions 200 Bhaktas).
  • Ramananda (14th-15th Centuries): Founder of Ramanandi Sampradaya. Author of Ghyan Lila, Yog-chintamani, Ramarcana Paddhati.
  • Ravidas (15th-16th Centuries): North Indian mystic poet-saint. Founder of 21st century Ravidassia religion.

Saguna Saints-Krishna Bhakti

  • Surdas (1483-1563): Disciple of Vallabhacharya. Blind poet from Agra. Wrote Sursagar.

details.summary: Overview of Bhakti movement saints and their contributions.

subject: History
topic: Important Saints and The Sikh Gurus
text:
Mirabai (AD 1498-1546): Rathor princess of Maata and daughter-in-law of Rana Sanga of Mewar. Her husband Bhoja Raja wrote the verse Padavali. Follower of Krishna.

Lalleshwari (AD 1320-1392): Follower of Shaivite Sect and also known as Lal Ded, Lalla or Lal Diddi. Created a mystic poetry called vastu or vakhs. Her creation is among earliest important part of Kashmiri literature.

Appar Tirunavukkarasar Nayana (17th Century): A philosopher and social reformer. Shaivite Bhakti poet in Kannada. His literary world includes vachana sahitya.

Basavanna (12th Century): Also known as Appar and was a Saiva Tamil poet. He composed many hymns and few of these are in Tevaram.

Chaitanya (AD 1486-1533): Known as Gaudiya Mahaprabhu and he was devotee of Krishna. Founder of Gaurang or Bengal Vaishnavism. His teacher was Ishwapuri. Kirtan system given by Chaitanya.

Shankara Deva (AD 1449-1568): Assam Established EK Sharan Sampradaya or Mahapurushiya Sampradaya. Divided universe into two parts Aswatantra and Swatantra.

Namdev (AD 1270-1350): He was a poet-saint from Maharashtra, India who is significant to the Varkari sect of Hinduism. The literary work of Namdev were influenced by vaishnava philosophy. His work occurs in Guru Granth Sahib.

Tukaram (AD 1598-1650): He was a poet-saint of the Bhakti Movement in Maharashtra. Sant Tukaram composed Abhanga poetry. He was contemporary of Shivaji.

Shankaracharya (AD 788-822): He was born at Kalindi Kerala. Teachings concepts of Maya (illusion), Advaita and importance of Vedanta. He established four Mathas at Badrinath, Puri, Sringeri and Dwarka. Works commentaries on Upanishads, Bhagwad Gita and Brahmasutras of Badrayana. He is also known as Pseudo-Buddhist as many of his doctrines were similar to that of Budhist doctrines.

Ramanuja Acharya (AD 1017-1137): Tamil Vaishnavite saint. Philosophy of Visist-advait. Works Vedanta Samgraha, commentaries on Brahmasutras and Bhagwad Gita.

Madhavacharya (13th Century): Kannada Vaishnavite saint. Philosophy of Dvaita.

Nimbarka (13th-14th Centuries): Telugu Vaishnavite saint, contemporary of Ramayana. Concept of Dvaitadvaita.

Vallabhacharya (AD 1497-1531): He was a Telugu Vaishnavite saint. He was born at Varanasi in 1479 and went to Brindavan, where he resided permanently. He established the philosophy of Shuddhadvait. Vallabhacharya’s teachings are also known as Pushtimarga. He was the contemporary of Vijayanagara King Krishna Deva Raya.

Raghunandan: He belonged to Navadwipa (Nadia) in Bengal. He was considered to be the most influential writer in the Dharamashastras.
